RYAN HAMILTON (National—Hamilton East): This bill literally unlocks infrastructure growth, just like Te Awa Lakes north of Hamilton. We’ve got a $50 million Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act loan to unlock 2,500 houses. This is about fixing the basics and building the future, literally.
Dr TRACEY McLELLAN (Labour): Thank you, Mr Speaker, and aren’t we peppy this morning, on this real Friday—perpetual Tuesday?
Hon Todd McClay: You mean last Friday wasn’t real?
Dr TRACEY McLELLAN: Ha, ha! Labour supports the Infrastructure (Funding and Financing) Amendment Bill, as was very eloquently noted last night, when we started this debate, by my colleague Arena Williams. However, she did raise some concerns, and I want to go through those a little bit today as well.
: Infrastructure funding matters—we know that—but who ultimately pays matters just as much, and I want to highlight some of those concerns. Ultimately, we support better tools for unlocking housing and infrastructure. We know that New Zealand needs to unlock our infrastructure. We’ve got a huge deficit that we need to figure out better ways of grappling with. We know that too many developments have been delayed because things like the pipes, the roads, and other sorts of essential services don’t get funded upfront.
: Financing infrastructure is never cost-free. The key question in this particular bill is who carries that cost and where is it transparent, and whether, actually, households can genuinely afford it. I agree with my colleague Mike Davidson: sometimes, we do have to think about the nature of growth. This bill does create a model that makes funding easier, but it cannot be used as an excuse to simply shift costs on to families already dealing with rates increases, mortgages, and everyday expenses in the cost of living. Ultimately, we can’t solve one affordability problem by simply shifting and creating a problem somewhere else.
: The infrastructure levies, we acknowledge, can help new houses to get built, which is a good thing, but those levies remain attached to a property, sometimes for 20, 30, 40, 50 years. A developer or a current owner may support the levy because it makes a project easier to proceed with initially, but it’s often the future homeowners who are the ones who are going to make those payments. They almost certainly wouldn’t have been involved in the original decisions, so they might not fully understand the long-term costs when they purchase that property. Labour’s concern is that removing the affordability assessments, which has been done in some circumstances, could make a house appear more affordable upfront, which is alluring, but it does leave the new owner with a substantial ongoing charge.
: The other thing that we are concerned about is the expansion into transport, and that raises some unresolved questions. One of the most significant changes is allowing this type of financing model to be used more widely for transport projects, including projects that have traditionally been led by national transport agencies for national transport infrastructure, and therefore funded through those national mechanisms. Labour doesn’t want this bill to become, essentially, a backdoor to fund things that have traditionally been funded by central government—just shifting it on to local government and, therefore, local communities and ratepayers. This concern is even sharper when, obviously, the Government is also proposing a cap to rates. Some of that doesn’t quite add up, and I think that that does require a little bit more scrutiny. Obviously, the councils could be expected to collect new infrastructure levies via this model, whilst also having a restriction placed on them about how they could fund their own essential services. That contradiction, I think, remains unresolved via this process.
: I think the other important factor to take note of is that local communities and councils absolutely have to retain a meaningful voice in this process. The bill significantly narrows the circumstances in which a council can refuse to endorse a levy. In practice, this means that councils may be required to support a levy unless collecting it would put rate collection at risk. What does that necessarily even mean? The process around that remains a little bit opaque. Whilst we, again, support the streamlining of a process, we think that communities deserve some proper information and, actually, some genuine consultation so that they can have confidence that not only are their views being taken into account but the ultimate outcome is a good one.
: The select committee, we believe, has strengthened protections around some of the forced land sales, which was a really important topic. As has been noted last night and this morning, the bill as introduced gave special purpose vehicles (SPV) a very broad power where development failed. An SPV could have sought the sale of undeveloped land based largely on its own assessment—sometimes, possibly, without even the requisite necessary information to make that independent process very clear to the landowner, to challenge the debt, which is an important part of that process.
: My colleague Arena Williams talked a little bit last night about the situation that Māori land owners would find themselves in, and the fact that they absolutely deserve more than a tick-box consultation during this process. It’s a different set of circumstances with unique and sometimes complicated but bespoke considerations. Any piece of legislation that we enact needs to account for that properly so that we don’t create unintended or even intended negative consequences down the track.
: Going back to the SPV, the select committee has recommended that that vehicle must first obtain a court decision, a court judgment, before it can apply for a forced sale, and that seems absolutely sensible to us, and congratulations to those people on that select committee that made that happen. We welcome that amendment; it was important to go through that process. It restores, ultimately, judicial oversight and protects natural justice, which is always absolutely important, and it ensures that the amount claimed can be properly tested before someone risks losing their land. You can imagine all the various situations where that could occur. A forced land sale is always a stressful and unfortunate situation, and there absolutely has to be public confidence that that’s done properly.
: The affordability must be assessed cumulatively, not levied by levy, and that was another important consideration for the select committee. Households don’t experience rates, water charges, infrastructure levies in isolation; they experience it as one combined bill. They get their rates notice, they perhaps pay it annually, they pay it quarterly—whatever—but they get their rates notice, and not that many people go through it line by line and pontificate about the contribution that each thing makes to its overall rating. But that is how they experience the rating system.
: Labour therefore welcomes the select committee’s recommendation that the Minister must consider the cumulative impact of a new levy alongside existing rates, water services charges, and other levies. This responds, we think, directly to concerns raised about double-dipping. Even just saying the word out loud—no one likes the concept of double-dipping. We’ve had various examples of that over the years. It feels, hence, like the fact that someone’s doing something to you that you didn’t realise was happening, and there’s nothing worse than feeling like you’re getting a bit ripped off.
: In this particular example, where people may be charged several times for overlapping infrastructure costs—and you can imagine how potentially complicated some of that levying could end up being—it’s really important that that safeguard be there. Labour will obviously continue to argue for affordability protections and make sure that they are applied consistently, including for future homeowners, who are the ones who are ultimately going to bear these costs, but we support building houses. We think unlocking the potential to ensure that the pipes, the roads, and all those other services are financed out-front—because we acknowledge that that is often the sticking point for growth and development, and therefore we support this bill.
DAN BIDOIS (National—Northcote): This is such a good bill. I’m going to commend it to the House.
Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB (Labour—Christchurch Central): Thank you, Mr Speaker. This bill does build on an excellent initiative of the last Labour Government—
Hon Member: Is that Helen Clark’s?
Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB: —because we’ve always recognised the need for well-planned and well-funded development. This bill essentially improves in some respects the—
Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall: Oh, now they have opinions over there—saying they can’t give speeches!
Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB: Why are you heckling me? Ha, ha! It improves in some respects the infrastructure framework that we put in place. In fact, here in Wellington, if I recall correctly, the sludge plant is funded exactly by this framework.
: I think we do need to remember that, essentially, what this does is it allows a funding stream to repay what is usually commercial lending. By having a statutory framework, it gives some assurance to any lender that there will be a long-term source of income to finance interest costs and principal repayments, but it is still, essentially, borrowing for infrastructure. There is no magic way to come up with this cash—we’ve got to come up with it from somewhere. This is simply deferring and stretching out the repayments, usually across 30 or 50 years. It’s a little bit of the old magic cup—moving the costs around. Let’s be upfront about this, and it’s quite right that we need to be very careful about making sure that the overall costs imposed on homeowners in particular are affordable, because we’ve set up a new water system and we’ve seen water rates going up pretty significantly. Here in Wellington, we’ve had some accounting errors with the sludge levy where that’s caused some issues as well. : I do want also to just express a little bit of concern about the watering down of protections for Māori land. Obviously, development does benefit Māori land, but we need to be cautious that we don’t think that just because we’re building some infrastructure plant or roading which benefits Māori land, we’ve got an untrammelled right to levy that land. Consultation on those projects is very important. In fact, as I understand it, previously, Māori land owners, iwi, and hapū were required to consent, but now, once you’re across a certain threshold, it can be imposed on them. In terms of tino rangatiratanga, that’s a bit of a concern, because Māori land—how it’s rated and how it’s dealt with and how it’s held—has always kind of been the last bastion of autonomy for Māori. This is just encroaching on it a little bit. I’m concerned about these small encroachments. I’m sure there’ll be more to be said about that.
: The other thing, I guess, that I’d just like to say is the dangers around failed projects, because exactly what amounts to a failed project? A lot of these projects take a long time. They might not take off—look at Rolleston; didn’t take off overnight, but it took off eventually. We’ve got to be really cautious about leaping to a conclusion that there’s been a failure, when, in fact, all that’s needed is more time. I understand the select committee had a look at that—that’s good—but caution is required there. But, overall, it’s building on a good Labour initiative.
TOM RUTHERFORD (National—Bay of Plenty): It’s time to get this done. I commend it to the House.
TANGI UTIKERE (Labour—Palmerston North): Kia orana. Good morning, Mr Speaker. Look, it’s a pleasure to rise and speak in support of the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Amendment Bill. : There were 60 submissions. I think it was around about half a dozen who did front up and appear in front of the select committee. I do want to acknowledge the officials, particularly what was the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development and the Office of the Clerk, and obviously the Parliamentary Counsel Office as well.
: We support this bill because we do recognise the need for good tools in order to fund and deliver infrastructure. The funding is the important part, as is the delivery. As my colleague the Hon Dr Duncan Webb has already indicated this morning, this was a bill that was introduced under the previous Labour Government. Naturally, we have had a look at this and have continued to support it, based on what we see currently in front of us.
: New Zealand has, as we know, a bit of an infrastructure deficit in this country. : The question is not whether infrastructure should be built; it must be built in this country. We’ll go on to talk a little bit around what some of those particular parts of infrastructure will be in a moment, but whether the funding model is fair, whether it’s affordable, and whether it is transparent is what we have been looking at when we have considered this bill. Colleagues have already touched on that in earlier contributions as part of this bill, as well.

I do hope that the Government, in terms of thinking about the wider brief of infrastructure, do consider that as well.
: The important thing is when we, I guess, look at this particular bill, and some might see that as a form of streamlining a particular process—what is important is that that doesn’t soon become a euphemism for simply removing safeguards that need to be in place to make sure that there are checks and balances; that there isn’t a reduction in engagement with community as to how that might work, or, indeed, a weakening of accountability for when these decisions are made and when they’re taken; and that there is accountability as a key part of that. For Labour, we have been constructive in this space. We support the objective of enabling infrastructure—good infrastructure—infrastructure that connects communities but that also stacks up, and we will continue to scrutinise the detail. : One of the changes that the select committee did make—and it’s one that the Labour Party were very, very keen on—is this issue of cumulative affordability. It’s something that my colleague Dr Tracey McLellan has touched on, and that is looking at affordability through the lens of not just whether in isolation these costs and items can be afforded or not, but actually an acknowledgment of the fact that households get a number of calls on their household budget. The Minister, in considering any sort of levy proposal, whether to advance that or not—one of the changes that has been made is that the Minister needs to consider that proposal alongside the existing levies, the existing rates, the existing costs that are already in place; the existing water charges that Dr Webb has touched on.
: We’ve called for that change, and it’s good to see that that is a change that has been included in here. It means that the consideration as to whether a proposal should succeed or not, or even be put on the table, will have those cumulative considerations on households and their budgets made before those future decisions are actually taken. While a levy may, in a traditional sense, sit outside traditional rates, for families, that is still another bill that is coming through the door. That’s why there is a real need for there to be that active consideration.
: One of the aspects that the select committee did spend a little bit of time on is the requirement for consultation with those landowners who would be affected by a proposal, and also with iwi and hapū as well. I want to acknowledge the officials who, under the direction of the select committee, did spend quite a bit of time going through this. Permission was granted for them to go out and consult concurrently at the same time that the select committee was considering this bill, and on page 5 of the select committee’s report, this arose out of concern that engagement needed to occur with iwi Māori organisations and other individuals around levy areas or charges that may affect Māori land, for Māori land that is subject to the Treaty settlement process, and also acknowledging the fact that infrastructure decisions that may be taken may affect Māori land. It’s pleasing to see that a result of that is a change to the bill that will require there to be active consultation, and the requirement also indicates and shows the lengths that have been taken to ensure that that consultation has been disclosed with the affected parties, with iwi, with hapū as well, and that that’s part of the whole process.
: I want to just make some brief comments on transport because part of the focus of this bill is to allow for the funding, potentially, of transport infrastructure that leads to growth opportunities. In terms of transport infrastructure, we all know that this Government has a $56 billion suite of roads of national significance, and that number continues to grow. They accept that they need to reprioritise and reassess that, to rescope those projects, because right now they have a $30 billion fiscal hole in terms of that plan. One could say that that’s why they’re perhaps looking at any funding and financing opportunity around transport infrastructure to meet that .
: We need to be very clear that this is not to be seen as an opportunity to grab every single bit of coin and every dollar that is out in the community to fund transport projects that do not stack up. For the sort of shift in this space to allow transport agencies like Waka Kotahi, NZ Transport Agency, to trigger projects that may result in local levies, it is important that that transparency at the local level still exists. It is important that the accountability for the decisions that have been taken by those that make those decisions still exists, and it is important that the consultation and accountability exists there as well.
: Our concern is not with enabling infrastructure per se. Our concern, and my concern in the transport space, is with who pays for these projects. Who decides where these projects are going to go? Do they stack up through that independent lens, and are those costs affordable over time? What is very clear, under the current Government, is that their roads of national significance are not affordable, they are not funded, they are not going to be delivered anytime soon, and so they need to go through a process of reprioritisation, and we all wait as to when that is going to happen. We all think that there’s not going to be a Government policy statement on land transport before the election. That would be the first time in more than two decades that that has been the case. Hon MATT DOOCEY (Associate Minister of Health): on behalf of the Minister of Health: Thank you very much, Mr Speaker. I move, That the Pae Ora (Healthy Future) (3 Day Postnatal Stay) Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
: This bill is about guaranteeing women the choice of a minimum of three days of post-natal in-patient care after childbirth to ensure all mothers and babies get the support they need during this vitally important time. This Government believes that every child deserves the best-possible start in life. That start does not begin weeks or months after birth; it begins immediately, in those first precious days, when mothers are recovering from childbirth and families are learning to care for a newborn together. This bill responds directly to what women and families have told us about their post-natal experiences. They’ve told us that greater certainty and support in the early days following childbirth is needed. We know that quality early post-natal care can shape positive long-term outcomes well beyond the hospital stay.
: It is for these reasons that this Government is proud to back this bill with significant new funding delivered in Budget 2026. We are committed to ensuring that this legislation is matched with the investment needed to deliver it. This new funding of $34.4 million over four years increases maternity system capacity so mothers can confidently choose up to three days of in-patient post-natal stay knowing it will be supported by the beds and the workforce required to do this safely.
: First-time mothers will be the first to benefit. Starting immediately, up to 2,000 new mothers per year will be able to access a three-day post-natal stay within the first two years, utilising existing capacity. As access is expanded to all mothers after three years, we anticipate that up to 18,000 mothers per year will be able to access a 3-day post-natal stay.
: I want to acknowledge the original sponsor of this legislation. How good, Catherine Wedd. This bill began its life as a member’s bill grounded in a genuine concern for the post-natal experiences of women and families. This Government made the decision to adopt the bill because we agreed with the fundamental importance of guaranteeing three days of in-patient post-natal care for all women if they choose to access it.
: I also want to acknowledge and thank the Health Committee, specially chaired by the very hard-working Sam Uffindell, for its consideration of this bill and for the work it has done through the select committee process. I also want to thank the many individuals, the midwives, and other health professionals who took the time to make submissions and share their experiences. There was widespread support for the intent of the bill and for the principle that post-natal care should be a stronger and more consistent part of our maternity system. That feedback reflects just how significant the post-natal period is for families across this country.
: Taking this bill forward with the support of my colleague the Hon Casey Costello also delivers on a clear commitment in the National - New Zealand First coalition agreement to strengthen maternity services and post-natal support for women. Crucially, it’s a practical and compassionate step that puts women and their wellbeing at the centre of our health system.
: I intend to table an Amendment Paper as part of its adoption as a Government bill. The Amendment Paper will include transitional arrangements, requiring Health New Zealand to have a plan setting out how it will progressively build its capability and capacity across New Zealand to deliver this entitlement to all mothers. It also builds in more time to ensure that the system can safely deliver the entitlement to all women.
: This is about increasing maternity services to mothers and babies in a responsible, well-managed, and well-funded way. The Budget allocation of $34.4 million over four years will address the workforce and capacity constraints the system is currently facing. I look forward to consideration of this Amendment Paper when this bill is debated in the committee of the whole House.
: The bill established a clear entitlement that women can access three days of in-patient post-natal care if they choose, rather than leaving that decision uncertain or inconsistently applied. In doing so, it supports better outcomes for mothers and babies and reinforces that post-natal care is a valued and essential part of that maternity journey.
: It does not mandate that women stay in in-patient care for three days. Many women will continue to choose to return home earlier, supported by community-based services and their families, just as they do now. What this bill does is ensure that women who would benefit from staying longer have that option available to them without ambiguity or inconsistency.
: For some families, particularly first-time parents, the early post-natal period can feel overwhelming. There is a great deal to learn in a very short space of time. Having the option of additional support, monitoring, and reassurance within an in-patient setting can make a meaningful difference to confidence and wellbeing. Some women have told us they would have welcomed more time in in-patient care—more time to recover physically, more time to establish breastfeeding, more time to receive advice, and reassurance before returning home. Others have reported leaving hospital within 48 hours, even though they did not feel ready because they were unsure whether staying longer was an option. This uncertainty adds pressure at a time when families already have a great deal to manage. The bill removes the uncertainty and replaces it with clarity and confidence. This bill respects that different families will make different choices about what is right for them, and it ensures the system is better equipped to support those choices.
: This legislation is not the only change. The Government has a broader programme of work to strengthen the maternity system and ensure it can deliver high-quality post-natal care in a sustainable way. Health New Zealand is already taking action to build and support the maternity workforce needed to deliver the strengthened post-natal care set out in this bill. This includes targeted recruitment initiatives, including international recruitment where appropriate, as well as return-to-practice support to help experienced midwives and clinicians re-enter the workforce safely and confidently.
: I also understand that retention matters just as much as recruitment, particularly in districts facing ongoing workforce pressures. Supporting and retaining skilled staff is essential to maintaining safe services, continuity of care, and good outcomes for mothers and babies. That is why I’m focused on backing the maternity workforce and ensuring they’re supported to do their jobs well.
: The community sector will have an important part to play in the implementation of this bill. Primary maternity units run by both the public and community providers, including the private sector, will expand the range of in-patient post-natal care options available to mothers, including care that is closer to home. Mothers may remain in hospital, where hospital level care is required, or transfer to a primary maternity unit once that level of care is no longer needed, depending on their preferences and clinical need. Having a broader range of options, both public and private, reduces pressure on hospital facilities while continuing to deliver safe and appropriate post-natal care to woman and babies.
: Taken together, this work underpins the delivery of this bill and will support its long-term success. It reflects my commitment to ensuring women and their babies receive safe, timely, and appropriate care when they need it. I want to acknowledge the midwives and other health professionals who care for women and babies every day. Their experience and advice has been central to shaping the approach set out in this bill. They understand better than anyone the importance of post-natal support and the need for careful, well planned implementation. I thank them for their professionalism, dedication, and ongoing commitment to high-quality care. In closing, this bill delivers three important outcomes: it provides greater certainty for women and families about post-natal care; it supports choice at a critical moment in family life; and it strengthens our maternity system in a practical and responsible way. I commend this bill to the House.
Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour): Mr Speaker, thank you; and thank you to the Minister for his remarks. It’s good to hear a fulsome speech on a bill while the House is sitting in urgency. I want to take the opportunity to recount the background of the bill and some of the significant changes along the way.
: The Minister gave credit to Catherine Wedd, who initially held this bill as a member’s bill, but I should also add it was originally introduced in 2022 by Hon Louise Upston. It came to select committee last year, and I’d summarise the discussion about the bill at select committee as focused on two main implementation concerns. The first was the operational impacts of introducing an entitlement without consideration to implementation. The second thing was the cost. There’s been positive developments, since the select committee hearing, on both of those fronts.
: To elaborate a little, firstly, the Ministry of Health advised the committee that to implement this entitlement would cost $100 million in capital expenditure (CAPEX) to make sure that there were sufficient beds available for this, and then between $31 and $38 million a year in operational expenditure. The Health Committee also heard that absent that type of investment, there could be challenges in implementation. So for example, women taking up the right to this entitlement would occupy beds that might otherwise be occupied by others in greater need. They are very challenging decisions those managing those wards face, and wanting to balance those things would be quite challenging unless extra capacity was created.
: So it’s positive to see announcements in Budget ’26 that do address some of these implementation initiatives. Appropriately, then, this has been taken over as a Government bill, and the announcements in Budget ’26 included funding for these initiatives. The Minister gave the assurance that this investment matches the investment needed to deliver these entitlements. It’s worth breaking down what the Budget ’26 investments were, in that case. Firstly, contrary to the Ministry of Health presentation at select committee, all of the funding for this is operational expenditure. So there’s no CAPEX related to this initiative. We look forward to seeing the Amendment Paper, to understand whether capital expenditure is also expected as part of the implementation plan. Otherwise, we have to conclude that the entire plan for building new beds would be to use outsourced beds.
: We’re told from press statements that the entitlement will apply to new mothers only, for the first two years, so that’s the year starting from now and the year starting from July 2027. That’s funded through $1.6 million of operational expenditure each year—so in health terms, a very modest contribution in the first two years. We had the opportunity to go into the scale of this contribution of this funding at Estimates, and the Director-General advised that the funding needed was limited because new mothers—those eligible in the first two years—already occupy beds for 2.5 days. I think that was the number she gave when her statement was corrected in the House by the Minister; 2.5 days is currently the average length of stay for new mothers. So there’s a minimal need, we’re told, to increase the funding in the first two years because the increase in entitlement on average will be slight.
: So the substantial implementation of this commitment is really going to follow—well, 18 months after the election. It is a shame that opportunities to increase capacity in the maternity system weren’t taken during this term of Government so that the commitment could be implemented in a more fulsome way. That is to follow in years 3 and 4, so the years covered by Budget ’28 and ’29. In those years, $13.3 million is appropriated, and $17.9 million, respectively. So returning to the Ministry of Health modelling that they gave the Health Committee back when the member’s bill was considered, that’s half. So the assumption is half of women will take up this this entitlement. Look, modelling is based on assumptions, so we understand that not every health entitlement is taken up by everyone. But it remains to be seen if, for this entitlement, half is a reasonable expectation—or not. One might ask: how meaningful is it to describe it as it has been, as a right, if it’s only expected that half of people will take it up?
: Which takes me back to the stories that we heard from women, NGOs who work with women, and clinicians who work with women, in the select committee. We heard multiple stories about the wonder and happiness that a new birth, a new baby brings, a time that people really treasure and a time of closeness for family. We also heard stories of birth trauma and injuries, post-natal depression, challenge with family finances, challenge with travel around birth, and the juggle of caring for other children and the partners’ other work commitments. All of these pressures are on families, and there might well be reasons why families choose not to take up the full entitlement. I’ve seen many mums who are concerned about their other kid and their other children at home and therefore would rather be at home knowing that everything was OK there—even though if they didn’t have that commitment, they might well have taken up the opportunity to be in hospital longer.
: That was certainly how we felt after our daughter was born. We would rather be at home in an environment we were comfortable and familiar with, not in the busy hospital ward where all my former colleagues kept pulling back the curtain and saying hello, and where I had a far too in-depth knowledge of the number of hospital infections that get transmitted there. We got on public transport, waved our Snapper card and went back to my mother-in-law’s apartment in the city. And I’m excited that the almost 13-year-old who joined our family that day is going to wave her Snapper card and come to Parliament to hang out with her mum during urgency later on this afternoon.
: Anyway, families have other priorities. So it does make me think perhaps we should think broadly about the entitlements that we’re looking to support mothers with—and the Minister actually did mention these—that support provided in the community can be part of an important part of the equation. Maybe that is where our efforts for further expansion of care should go.
: My sister gave birth to my two nieces in the Netherlands, and they have a seven- to 10- day entitlement for post-birth visits in your home—so someone who’ll come and do the dishes and make sure you get a chance to have a shower and check that you’re OK and, also, sometimes identify when families are facing particular challenges that need other social services to be involved. My sister’s not like me; she’s quite a private person. I think she found having a Dutch lady come and visit her every day for seven days a little bit more intervention from the Government than she wanted. But it certainly would make a difference for many people.
Ingrid Leary: I hope it wasn’t because they’re Dutch!
Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL: No, Ingrid Leary, it wasn’t.
: We’re pleased to be able to vote for this bill today. We see it as positive that the Government has taken on funding challenges that were identified at select committee, and we take the Minister’s assurance that the funding is in scale with the entitlement on face value, and we commend the bill to the House.
LAN PHAM (Green): Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. I want to join my colleagues in acknowledging the Hon Louise Upston and Catherine Wedd in terms of the progression of this bill, and the Minister who was speaking to it earlier.
: I want to start by acknowledging that I’m sure lots of people in the Chamber today are feeling very tired, but the levels of tiredness and new levels of exhaustion are absolutely front of mind for me when speaking to this bill, because they were something that I’d never experienced before after the birth of particularly my first child, my son. I was so exhausted after maybe 20 or 21 hours of birth that when he was put on my chest after giving birth, I literally could not even raise my arms to put them around him.
: When I hear the comments about how critical and how vulnerable this time is for whānau and parents and families and babies, I absolutely have that front and centre. So I want to, firstly, do a massive shout-out to the midwives, the carers, the hospital staff, the specialists—to anyone who has been in this system and has had experiences, both good and bad. I acknowledge how critical they are and how formational those times are to, hopefully, a healthy, functional life ahead. I particularly want to shout out to my midwife, who was present for the birth of my children, Sheena Ross, in Christchurch, and the time that I spent in Christchurch Women’s Hospital, and then was very lucky to be able to give birth at home for my second one.
: Yes, this is positive, and I really appreciate that the Minister talked about the support for this bill being about the intent, because there’s no question that intent is really good. The thing is, there are so many aspects that come into it that mean that we need to make the intent real, we need to make it tangible, we need to fund it, we need to ensure that this isn’t just a rubberstamp and a glossy outer window—we need families and whānau to be able to walk into these places at this critical time and experience true support. I think what’s been really clear, in trying to understand and listen to the voices that have fed into this bill, is that we’re so far away from that and we really need to make steps towards achieving that.
: The positive things about improving breast-feeding support and the potential to reduce neonatal readmissions is absolutely positive. That potential for the positive influence on maternal confidence and emotional wellbeing is absolutely vital. As has been mentioned, the essential nature of the education and support that comes in that post-natal period is absolutely critical, particularly for first-time parents, when this is all new and different and they’re really in that learning phase.
: What I really want to emphasise with this bill, which we absolutely will be supporting, is the voices of those who understand this and who know and who are signalling careful consideration of the bill’s broader implications. I particularly want to note the joint statement that was put out by the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, the New Zealand College of Midwives, and the National Council of Women, because they talked about the risks with this. They talked about the risk that the policy could actually shift the provision of post-natal care from a model based on clinical need to one driven by entitlement. They talked about concerns about people being discharged before they’re actually ready, in order to accommodate those who might not actually need that support but are actually entitled to it.
: Within those comments, they made really clear the concerns about health system capacity. You know, we know, and it’s well established, that the country had 330 midwife vacancies nationwide as at 2024. Now, I don’t know what those more recent statistics are, but it is clear that this is a sector that is chronically underfunded and underpaid, and then we get caught up, within that, with the scrapping of pay equity, which means that that is going to continue. So, again, this is the call to really take this seriously. We know that where these shortages exist with midwives, this will simply be exacerbated with higher demand, and that’s absolutely a concern.
: The other thing that has been raised by the specialists in the know is by the Paediatric Society of New Zealand Te Kāhui Mātai Arotamariki o Aotearoa. They talk about the potential benefits and join others in supporting those with this bill, but they recommend new investment and clear investment in staffing and infrastructure—you know, they talk about how these services must be properly resourced rather than relying on reallocations from existing services. They also talked about the importance of expanded lactation support when it comes to breast feeding. These trained consultants are absolutely pivotal, and I remember and again want to acknowledge the amazing services that do exist, however stretched and however much they are managing to operate on such, such little resourcing.
: They also talk about the protection of neonatal care spaces and the fact that this increased post-natal bed occupancy should not come at the expense of vulnerable newborns needing specialist care. That is something that should be well understood, but the fact that even today, in 2026, they’re having to reiterate that and point it out just shows how vulnerable our system is and how we can’t take those basic things for granted.
: They also talk about the need to strengthen primary birthing units, and ensure that not only do they have the midwives available but the social work support necessary to actually care for babies and their whānau beyond the hospital settings.
: Finally, their plea is for that flexibility and that needs-based approach, because we know that people’s experiences vary so greatly from the absolute joy and positivity to ones of real, severe, lasting trauma, and the needs need to cater to that, and the investment and the funding absolutely needs to cater to that.
: We know that the bill requires Health New Zealand to ensure that sufficient maternity facilities are available, but, without additional investment, all this necessity could just lead to the shifting of already strained resources rather than actual system improvement.
: I again want to commend the intention of this bill. I applaud the people in this space who are making it really clear what the Government needs to do to make this real. My plea is just to actually back that up with funding and investment, listen to those voices, and ensure that new babies and whānau are truly at the centre of all of this.
ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Maureen Pugh): The question is that the motion be agreed to.
LAURA McCLURE (ACT): Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise in support of this bill. Having had two children of my own, I know how incredibly special but also challenging that time can be, particularly if you’re a new mum and things don’t go as planned. I think this is a really great bill. I think that we should have the opportunity or option to be able to stay in hospital or post-natal care. There have been many, many stories within my friend circles and within my family where people are being rushed out of hospital within like a couple of hours, and, you know, not ready for what comes next. We want to make sure that we do take care of our new mums.
: I think given that we’re talking about being a new parent, we’ve had three new babies in the ACT office in the last month. Our chief of staff has had a new baby, so we want to congratulate him; and we’ve also got the senior private secretary from Karen Chhour’s office, and Amelia and Jacob, a senior researcher in my office, welcomed baby Jude Edwards Butson-Gill—I wanted to get that right. Congratulations—the ACT party welcomes these new additions. And I just want to say that I commend this bill to the House. Thank you.
JENNY MARCROFT (NZ First): Thank you, Madam Speaker. It is absolutely a pleasure to stand and rise on behalf of New Zealand First in support of the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) (3 Day Postnatal Stay) Amendment Bill. The coalition agreement between New Zealand First and National was inked in November of 2023, and one of the commitments in that coalition agreement was to ensure proper funding for birthing units and maternity care, including providing for a for a three-day stay for new mothers. So this bill absolutely fulfils the commitment in our coalition agreement with the National Party, and we thank them for that.
: I’d also like to acknowledge that Catherine Wedd, who inherited a member’s bill from Louise Upston—I congratulate you also—was pushing on an open door to get her member’s bill once it was drawn from the ballot. And what a thrill it must be to actually have a member’s bill that you know is going to succeed. So well done to you, Catherine.
: The Health Committee, of which I’m a member, and I would like to acknowledge all of the committee members, had a great process—123 submissions on this bill; 20 oral submissions. One of the things that came through during that select committee process was that we were a little bit concerned with the language that was being used by the Ministry. So the Hon Casey Costello required the Ministry to use sex-based language—no more of the “pregnant people” or the “birthing parent” language. That was something which we felt was important during that part of the process.
: This is a great bill for new mums. Everyone who has had the opportunity, the pleasure, the pain and the suffering of being a brand-new mum—because some of that comes during that period of time—will appreciate being told by their lead maternity carer, because it’s really important, that, actually, as part of this bill, those lead maternity carers notify mums that they are entitled to this longer period of stay, up to 72 hours, should they need it.
: Just in conclusion, we are very thrilled to be part of a coalition that is delivering on our commitment because at the core, this bill supports family-centred policies, it promotes fairness and access to healthcare, and it addresses some of those gaps in the maternity services that are provided. These values are central to New Zealand First, with our mission of putting families and communities first. I commend the bill.
RICARDO MENÉNDEZ MARCH (Green): Thank you, Madam Speaker. The Green Party is supporting this bill in it’s a second reading. I want to acknowledge, like my colleague Lan Pham mentioned, that the intent of this bill is excellent. I think any bill that allows parents to have more time to access breastfeeding support, newborn checks, recovery care, and education before returning home is really important.
: I particularly wanted to reflect on why I think that, from an equity point of view, that extension could be particularly beneficial for some of our low-income communities. Prior to becoming an MP, I used to work a lot with mums, particularly new mums, many who were living in the likes of emergency housing, many who did not have a safe, stable home to go back to, mums who were transient and often moving between addresses even while pregnant. I acknowledge that for many, that additional time to recover is critical if they’re going back to an environment that is not yet stable and provides that financial stability. And so I think that additional day to literally recover, to be well before returning to those environments, it will make a difference. I say this not just out of vibes or personal experience; I say this because even the Government’s own statistics show that more children are growing up and birthed into households that just do not have enough to cover the basic essentials. This is what we call child material hardship rights. What we know is that new kids are currently being born into environments where the household just does not have enough.
: This takes us back to my colleague Lan Pham’s comments and plea to the Government to address issues in relationship to the resourcing that goes into staffing and making sure that we deliver this on the basis of need, and that we do more work to actually address those inequities that new parents are experiencing. Because, ultimately, as my colleague noted, the worst-case scenario we could see is that someone who actually has a high degree of need and is at risk of going back to a precarious material condition is not adequately served, simply because we’ve created a system where someone who may not need this as much is entitled too. I do think we should, nonetheless, work towards universalising the support and making sure that everybody can get it when they need it, but the funding needs to come alongside it.
: I wanted to comment, as well, on the Minister’s remarks in relationship to funding. I think too, like the Labour Party, that we will take those at face value and in good faith, because I do want to believe that the Government wants this policy to succeed. And we will be keeping a close eye as to whether the commitments from the Minister in relationship to funding will be met. I also want to encourage parliamentary colleagues to, perhaps, put more emphasis on fighting—and this is not so much to the National Party members—for the funding that is required and the conditions to be met so that every parent can thrive; rather than focusing on issues in relationship to language that, ultimately, in my view, make no material difference to the people who this bill is supposed to serve. I think the focus on that takes away from the feedback that submitters have rightfully given us, that there are concerns around funding. I think that’s what, I would say, communities would expect us to be focusing on. Because, ultimately, the language in relationship to whether we are inclusive of all genders or otherwise actually makes no difference to the staffing issues, the funding shortfalls, whether the beds are there or otherwise.
: But the Green Party will continue supporting this bill through its remaining stages. We will particularly be looking at, for example, exactly how the Government will look at engaging the community sector for the procurement of beds. I think, more broadly, we call on the Government to create the conditions so that every new parent has what they need to create a safe, thriving environment for the kids and for generations to come,  because I think, ultimately, the intent of this bill will not be matched if we continue having parents that go back home to houses that are cold, damp, and without enough kai to put on the table. Ultimately, no matter how education a parent may receive in that additional 24 hours, if they do not have the means to survive, they do not have then the resources to put in place, whatever they may have learnt in that additional time, and into practice. But, again, we are commending Catherine Wedd for continuing to fight for this bill, and other members who have brought this issue forward.
NANCY LU (National): I will always remember when I gave birth to my first daughter and fainted in the birthing room. It was all the nurses and doctors who were there to protect me, to help me, and, when I finally gained consciousness, then to learn, as a new mother, the amount of help that we needed in the birthing unit and in the hospitals.
: I absolutely commend this bill, and I commend the work of my colleague Catherine Wedd. This is the National Party’s way of fixing the basics: by providing the healthcare for our mums and babies, and building the future for all New Zealanders. I commend the bill to the House.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Thank you, Madam Speaker. It’s been interesting to listen to all the speeches, because, outside of two of the speeches so far, it’s been mainly women speaking, and I think this is a testament to having women in Parliament. I doubt that a bill like this would have ever reached this level of parliamentary process had there not been women championing it, and so I want to commend Catherine Wedd and also Louise Upston and all the people who have supported the bill and have enabled it to get here.
: This is an example of why we do need women in Parliament: because we do have very particular issues. For many years, the birthing experience has not been taken as seriously as it should, nor, indeed, maternal health generally. So, hopefully, this is the beginning of a lot of good stuff.
: I think the question for us the whole way through on whether to support to this bill has been whether the intent of the bill can be safely delivered. As the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall has said, there have been some developments since the introduction of the bill through the Budget process that gives us more confidence, including the $34 million funding that would go to providing a boost to maternity services. That doesn’t necessarily meet the capital and expenditure (CAPEX) requirements that we’ve heard about through the Ministry of Health, which came to $100 million, which is, essentially, about beds.
: But we have also heard assurances from the sponsoring member, Catherine Wedd, that the capacity would be provided through public and private providers, so that may answer the question, and, indeed, the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall said that based on all the maths and what has been detailed, it looks like it will mainly go to those outsourced, probably private providers. That raises a question for me about privatisation and the health service, because if we want to have universality and we want to have good maternal public services, in my view, the capital expenditure should be public, as well. I’m not sure that relying on private providers is a way forward. Nevertheless, that is what is intended, and that would seem to resolve that CAPEX issue in the short order.
: When we looked at safety, the questions in my mind while I was sitting on the committee were around the funding of beds—which I’ve just talked about—about workforce development, and we’ve heard this morning that there may be an Amendment Paper coming that is going to require a legislative commitment to that. I’ll speak shortly about how that might pertain to other facets of health law that we’re looking at today in the House.
: I think I also was keen to see what would be happening around rural health support, as well as the protection of high-acuity births. Now, when it comes to rural health support, we’ve seen, for example, GP funding decisions made lately that, on the face of it, look good for many practices, but actually disadvantage some communities, like the community of Wānaka, where they’ll take an effective 11 percent decrease in rural funding, and they already have very stretched maternity services. So my question is: how are places like that going to be able to support this mandated entitlement?
: There is also the question of the protection of high-acuity births. Given that there will be some mothers who will need more care than the three days that are now enabled, will they still get the levels of care and the length of stay in hospital that they need if there are other people who are sort of the first cab off the rank with their entitlements, particularly the new mothers?
: I do think that it is really important for new mothers to have those three days. I share the sentiments of colleagues around the House who have talked about the fairly surreal experience of birthing, particularly the first birth experience. I can say that in my situation, the people that were there, the wonderful people who supported—particularly the midwives—took on this kind of larger-than-life presence through the whole birthing experience, and when I went back to North Shore Hospital to thank them a few weeks later, I was amazed at how they had sort of reduced down to ordinary-sized people. In fact, I was a bit taller than the midwife, the Irish woman who supported me through my birthing experience, but, at the time, they just took on this huge presence. They were such an important part of the birth experience, and I also wanted to add my voice to thank those people who work in this really beautiful and critical part of the health system.
: When we look at the community provision of the delivery—going back to safe delivery—the Ministry of Health has said in its advice to the committee that those services are patchy. I think it’s important that we do look at that, and if there is going to be an Amendment Paper around workforce support, it would be great to see if it speaks also to the postcode lottery of birthing provision, because that is something that may not necessarily be addressed by something that simply addresses workforce development.
: I also am concerned about bed block. We know, for example, that the hospital service loses between $8 million and $12 million worth of beds a year, not at this end of health, but through seniors being unable to be released back into the community because they don’t have the appropriate enduring powers of attorney or care provision for those whose care they might be going back into. That is something that could be worked on to free beds up at that end.
: Bed block is, essentially, where somebody is taking a bed that might otherwise be available to someone with higher clinical need. We’ve heard about that previously in this debate. If we think about bed block in terms of maternity services, we’ve already got bed block around gynaecological services for women. We’ve got real workforce shortages in particular parts of New Zealand, including the West Coast, Northland, Tairāwhiti, and Wairarapa, and then, when you put into that picture the types of issues that can come up after a birthing experience which might not be the textbook experience that we’ve spoken about in the House today—that includes things like infection, injury trauma, feeding issues, very fragile babies, and also mental health issues—we cannot understate the significance of perinatal mental health and the importance of being able to provide for that.
: Now, certainly, being able to stay in the hospital longer might be one solution; equally, being able to get people back home into familiar surroundings might be the other solution, but all of those issues can create situations where mothers might need longer than the three days. It would just be reassuring to know that there isn’t going to be pressure on other women to release their beds, even though they have a three-day entitlement—there might be pressure on them to release their beds for the sake of women who are doing it really tough and are needing that extra level of care.
: We know that in 2029, the expected increase in the number of women who would use this entitlement will rise to 18,000. That’s a significant number of women, and so if we don’t have an equally significant uptick in the resourcing provided and the beds being available—not just relying on the community sector but knowing where those beds are, and whether they are available across the motu and not just in particular centres, is really important. What we don’t want to see is women wanting the three-day entitlement or feeling they need to take it and then finding that they have to have a birthing experience away from their own locale because they just simply cannot get that provision there. That would be another perverse incentive.
: Finally, I’d just like to talk about two things. One is the workforce development Amendment Paper, if that is, indeed, what is going to presented to the House in the committee of the whole House stage. I would welcome that. I also think there’s an opportunity in another bill that we’ll be discussing later on today—the Mental Health Bill—to equally put a legislative requirement for workforce development to be able to achieve some of the things that the bill has said that it is intending to achieve. Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): I present a legislative statement on the Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill.
ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Maureen Pugh): That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.

Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): I move, That the Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill be now read a first time. I nominate the Justice Committee to consider the bill.
: Too many New Zealanders are spending too long caught in the court system. For victims, delays mean waiting a year or more for a case to be resolved. For witnesses, it means uncertainty and repeated disruption. For defendants, it means cases hanging over their lives. For families, employers, and communities, it means the justice system is not working as quickly as it should. Timely justice matters, because justice delayed is justice denied.
: This Government is focused on practical changes that make the courts work better. This bill is a practical reform that improves access to justice, reduces delays, and makes better use of the resources that we already have. This bill expands the role of community magistrates so that they can deal with more straightforward matters from start to finish. It will reduce unnecessary adjournments, free up District Court judges to focus on more serious and complex cases, and will improve the public’s confidence that the justice system can deliver.
: Community magistrates are not new. The role was introduced in the late 1990s to increase judicial capacity to take pressure off the District Court judges. They were intended to deal with lower-level criminal matters, represent the communities that they serve, and help the courts to operates more efficiently. Community magistrates generally sit part time. They preside over certain lower-level matters in the District Court’s criminal jurisdiction. They are not required to hold a legal qualification, although many of them do. They bring practical experience, judgment, and community knowledge to the court system.
: But at the moment, they are not being used to their full potential. Too often, if a case reaches a point where a decision is needed outside of a community magistrate’s jurisdiction, it has to be adjourned and transferred to a judge. That means another court event, another delay, another day off work, another round of uncertainty for victims and other court users. It also means some cases are never scheduled before a community magistrate in the first place, because everyone knows that they might have to be transferred again later on. That’s not efficient, nor is it fair on court users, and it certainly is not the best use of judicial time and resource.
: This bill changes that. It will enable community magistrates to take guilty pleas for all cases except those tried in the High Court—that means murder, manslaughter—to preside over trials and determine guilt for offences with a maximum penalty of a fine, community-based sentence, or up to three months imprisonment; to order pre-sentencing reports for offences being referred to a District Court judge for sentencing; to make a greater range of bail decisions, where the defendant has pleaded guilty before a community magistrate; and make a greater range of administrative decisions, including transferring proceedings from one District Court to another and hearing unopposed limited driver licence applications.
: These are sensible, practical changes. They do not ask community magistrates to replace judges; they allow community magistrates to do more of the work that they were created to do so that judges can spend more time on cases that genuinely require a judge. It is expected that these changes will free up a net 5.2 District Court judge full-time equivalents. Put simply, this bill is, effectively, five judges for the price of none. This is good value for taxpayers, good for court timeliness, and good for victims who have waited too long for justice. The benefits will be felt across the justice system. When cases move faster victims get answers sooner. Witnesses are not left waiting indefinitely.  Defendants are not held in limbo longer than necessary. Remand pressure can reduce as cases progress more quickly. Judges can focus on the work only they are able to do.
: Expanding the role of community magistrates is sensible, but it must be done carefully. The public needs confidence that the cases will continue to be dealt with appropriately and consistently. This bill does not change the sentencing jurisdiction of community magistrates. Community magistrates will still not be able to impose imprisonment or home detention. Where a community magistrate considers that either of those sentences may be appropriate, the case must be transferred to a District Court judge, and that is an important safeguard.
: The bill also supports stronger leadership and oversight of community magistrates. Judge Moses has recently been appointed as the first Chief Community Magistrate, recognising the growing importance of community magistrates in the court system in providing judicial oversight for the role. The bill will make it so that there must always be a judge in this role. Budget 2025 also provided funding for three additional community magistrates and extra training to support them in their work.
: This bill is practical, it is targeted, it is common sense, and it makes better use of community magistrates. It frees up more than five full-time judges’ worth of capacity. It helps cases to move faster, it supports victims, it reduces pressure on the District Court, and it does all of that while maintaining appropriate safeguards. I commend this bill to the House.
ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono): The question is that the motion be agreed to.
CAMILLA BELICH (Labour): Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s a pleasure to be able to take a call on this bill, the Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill. This is something which introduces an issue that is a fundamental pillar of the justice system, and that is the premise that justice delayed is justice denied. No matter what the system we put in place is, if people are unable to utilise the systems we have, especially in criminal law, due to the fact that we don’t have the resourcing, that will result in delays.
: We know there are lots of issues with delays, many different issues for the people who have been charged, in terms of the pause that’s on their life until an issue is resolved—that might have implications on employment—and issues for victims in terms of wanting to get justice and understanding what will happen after an alleged crime has been committed. Also, we have practical concerns around the evidential basis of many of our criminal cases, as based on people being able to recall what happened. Of course, with the passage of time, no matter with the best will in the world or how traumatic that is, that does dissipate over a period of time.
: We’re pleased to be able to support this bill to the select committee. We’ll listen to what is said in select committee, and I hope that we will have the opportunity to hear from magistrates and judges. I know that that is probably not something they usually do, but this is specifically in relation to the work that they do; also the criminal bar, because they will have to be liaising with them as well.

: I was just discussing with my colleague how that works and the difficulty that often occurs when you’re deciding who is able to determine a case. : It was interesting reading the regulatory impact statement on this to see that numbers of cases in the District Court have actually fallen, but the number of procedural appearances—so the work of the District Court judges—has actually increased.
