Hon CHRIS PENK (Minister for Building and Construction): Thank you, sir. I present a legislative statement on the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill.
ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono): That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.

Hon CHRIS PENK (Minister for Building and Construction): I move, That the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
: The Transport and Infrastructure Committee has considered the bill and recommends that it be passed with amendments. I’m grateful to the people and organisations who made a submission on the bill and of course to the select committee itself, who took the time to hear those submitters and to consider improvements on the bill. Following the Canterbury earthquakes and royal commission of inquiry, the current earthquake-prone buildings regime was introduced.
: I just want to take a moment to acknowledge, as I’m sure all in this House would, the considerable tragedy, the loss of human life, that was entailed by those tragic events. And I don’t wish to bring you into the debate, Mr Speaker, but I will acknowledge that you more than most were familiar with the nature of the tragedy, and of course I commend and salute you for your work following that, of course, to bring that beloved region of yours back to more normal circumstances.
: All that said, of course, I think it’s fairly acknowledged that the introduced legislation at that time—albeit, of course, in good faith and balancing all the relevant considerations—has not worked entirely as intended. It has inadvertently imposed large costs on building owners and communities, including throughout New Zealand, without focusing enough on the buildings that present the greatest risk to people’s lives.
: This cannot continue, and so, even with the recent earthquakes in Venezuela providing a salutary reminder that we do need to prepare further for such events in New Zealand, nevertheless, we have decided that it is important to reform the earthquake-prone building regime to target or refocus on those buildings most likely to cause fatalities in an earthquake.
: The changes will remove barriers to strengthening high-risk buildings, making retrofits more affordable for their owners and better protecting people in and around them. Focusing effort and investment on the highest-risk buildings will ultimately save more lives than the current one-size-fits-all approach.
: Today I will briefly reiterate the bill’s key elements and summarise the key changes recommended by the select committee. As I say, we have decided to accept those changes.
: First, the bill narrows the systems scope so that it targets only high-risk buildings in medium and high-risk seismic zones. It introduces tiered remediation requirements, amends the definition of priority building, and provides greater flexibility through deadline extensions and lower-cost pathways for alterations and change of use.
: Only two types of buildings will remain designated as earthquake-prone buildings (EPBs): unreinforced masonry buildings and tall heavy material buildings. These are the buildings most likely to cause harm in an earthquake, and these will be only those located in medium- or high-risk seismic zones. Territorial authorities must identify and remove other building types from the EPB register in the three months from 1 July 2027.
: Meanwhile, buildings in Auckland, Northland, and the Chatham Islands will be out of scope. These areas have a scientifically determined lower seismic hazard than other parts of New Zealand. On Royal assent, therefore, earthquake-prone buildings in these areas will have that designation removed.
: At the same time, other provisions of the bill go through coastal Otago, including Dunedin and Oamaru and Stewart Island, will shift from a low to medium seismic zone to reflect the latest scientific understanding of seismic hazard in those places. Current earthquake-prone buildings (EPBs) there will retain their existing remediation deadlines and territorial authorities will have until 1 July 2032 to identify potential EPBs there.
: The bill also narrows the so-called identify at any time pathway for designating buildings as EPBs. Too many low-risk buildings have been designated as earthquake-prone using this pathway. So the bill, as introduced, narrows the pathway to cover only the post-1976, tall, heavy-material buildings that were constructed before 2027. This includes buildings akin to the CTV building in Christchurch. For buildings that remain EPBs, territorial authorities will determine their required remediation measures in accordance with the updated EPB methodology, issue EPB notices, and keep the EPB register up to date.
: The bill narrows the definition of “priority building”. Under the bill, only buildings that could fall on to a busy street or block a strategic transport route will qualify. Buildings that were priority simply because of their usage, such as hospitals or fire stations, will lose that status. Together, these changes provide clearer rules and a stronger focus on the buildings that matter most for public safety.
: The bill also introduces a tiered approach to remediation, replacing the current requirement to strengthen all buildings to 34 percent of the new building standard, commonly known as NBS. There will be two principal forms of remediation measure. Most unreinforced masonry buildings will need to mitigate their risk of facades falling on to people below. Multi-storey concrete buildings and large unreinforced masonry buildings will need targeted work to prevent those buildings collapsing. For unreinforced masonry buildings then that are one or two storeys high and located outside urban centres, no remediation will be required by a set deadline. But, at the same time, I note that owners will need to mitigate the risk of façade collapse if they want the building to be taken off the EPB register.
: EPB owners will be able to apply to territorial authorities for deadline extensions of up to 15 years, even if the original deadline expired before commencement. This will replace the current “up to 10 year” extension, open only to heritage EPB owners.
: The bill also supports lower-cost compliance pathways for owners carrying out seismic work or changing the use of a building. If the work only involves seismic remediation, no fire or accessibility upgrades will be required. Similarly, if an owner wants to change an EPB’s use, it would only need to meet its remediation requirement, rather than anything higher. Together, these changes provide more practical and cost-effective solutions, more time to comply, and fewer barriers for owners committed to making their buildings safer.
: The Transport and Infrastructure Committee has unanimously recommended amendments to address issues identified by submitters, officials, and the select committee itself. I welcome these improvements and again place on the record my thanks to the committee for their detailed examination of the bill. I note the chair, Mr Andy Foster, and I thank him and his colleagues who did such a careful and coherent job of understanding and in turn explaining the changes that have ultimately been made.
: In response to feedback from submitters, the committee clarified what areas are in “urban centres”, which helps to determine the remediation requirement of an unreinforced masonry EPB. For example, Wellington and Porirua are urban centres, whereas Featherston and Greytown are not. To acknowledge the unique barriers to remediation faced by various buildings, the committee added heritage status to the list of matters that territorial authorities must have regard to when determining whether or not to grant a deadline extension. Some submitters were concerned that the alternation provisions may allow for reduced building code compliance. For example, drilling stabilising rods through walls can increase the risk of fire spreading in one room to the next. The committee introduced a backstop into the bill to ensure that seismic work needs to be done in a way that doesn’t increase the risk of fire spreading or reduce disabled peoples’ access.
: The committee also amended the bill so that warning signs must be displayed on all earthquake-prone buildings, including those that are only recorded on the register or have a seismic work exemption. The committee updated the terms for the required remediation measures to façade risk mitigation and targeted retrofit. This will ensure that approaches to remediation mitigate risk but do not necessarily involve securing a façade or a full retrofit of the building can be used. This bill now also includes high-level descriptions of these measures.
: Some submitters were unsure how buildings with unusually tall storeys or part storeys will be treated—a fair question. The committee clarified that the thresholds for determining how many storeys high an EPB will be will be set out in the EPB methodology. One way that a building can be a priority building with half the remediation time frame is if it may impede a strategic transport route if it were to collapse during an earthquake. Submitters recommended that territorial authorities be allowed to revisit their strategic transport route—again, I think, a very sensible recommendation. The committee therefore amended the bill to empower territorial authorities—councils, in other words—to revise and remove strategic transport routes up to 1 July 2027. No new strategic transport routes may be added, ensuring that no building owners will be worse off.
: Last, in my remaining minute, the committee clarified the meaning of a building within scope. This makes it clearer which buildings are within scope of the system before the reader then looks to the EPB methodology for further technical detail. An unreinforced masonry building must have an exterior masonry wall and satisfy other criteria in the methodology to be within scope. A tall, heavy material building must have one or more significant elements, such as a roof or a floor, built using concrete or other heavy materials and satisfy any other criteria in the EPB methodology.
: Overall, in summary, the bill creates a more focused and workable earthquake-prone buildings system by targeting the buildings that present the greatest risk, introducing tiered and more cost-effective remediation requirements, and reducing barriers to remediation for building owners. For all those reasons, I commend this bill to the House.
SPEAKER: The question is that the motion be agreed to.
ARENA WILLIAMS (Labour—Manurewa): Thank you, Mr Speaker. This is an important bill and an important piece of reform that Labour continues to support, with specific reservations. I’m going to use this speech to set out what those things are. They will be parts that we consider are the most sensitive and are the least well-supported around the House. It is important that we come to consensus on these rules which impact on the long-term viability of buildings and not only those that are being built now but in expensive and costly remediations that are to come in the next five to 10 years. So it is important to flag where we have bipartisan support which is for a sensible set of rules for remediation of the highest-risk buildings, but to indicate that we do have reservations around how some of the exclusions have been applied, particularly around Auckland.
: Maintaining affordability has been our concern here. We want a building system and a built environment which is affordable, where remediations happen from either existing owners or there is an incentive for buildings to be sold to people who can remediate them. Because you do not want a situation like Wellington is experiencing now where some important civic sites and main streets have buildings which have not been remediated because the cost is very high and that continues to pose a risk to neighbours and to people on the street who walk past them. We want a system which incentivises that kind of remediation and where it is affordable in the public interest. So that is why we need some updates to these rules.
: We have vociferously opposed at every opportunity the exclusion of Auckland from the rules for remediation of risky buildings. Colleagues, let me explain what has occurred here. Cabinet has set out to create a set of rules where the highest-risk buildings around the country are the ones that get fixed. That makes sense. We shouldn’t fix buildings which are not posing a risk to peoples’ lives and are not posing a risk to the neighbouring buildings around them. Those rules require expensive fixes and so they should be something which is sensible. There is also a category of buildings under that that require being fixed—they need to be fixed. There shouldn’t be rules which force people to adhere to a certain time line. Building owners in that category should be able to make their own decisions about what kind of risk they will put up with and what kind of risk the building’s users will put up with.
: When I’m talking about these highest-risk buildings, some of those have been excluded from this bill. The way that these rules have been drawn is that if you have a very high-risk building in Auckland which is on the main street, it does not need to be remediated any more. The House must understand that by excluding Auckland, we have drawn lines on a map which mean that those remediations do not need to occur.
: Yes, you could have designed a system where the highest seismic risk regions were the way that we decided what sorts of buildings would be remediated. But that’s actually not what we’ve done. If you drew lines on a map, you might use, say, faults, and areas where say, an eruption around the Alpine Fault was going to cause regional risk and regional land movement. You might have drawn lines around volcanic movements in our shaky isles.
: But that is not the system we have used. We’ve used a system, which is perfectly sensible, whereby you identify the buildings which are at risk of movement in any kind of event like that and how much they are used. So a building that might move the same amount and might have the same kind of risk on the main street in Auckland is a different sort of risk to the one that’s on the West Coast and has two users a year for family weddings. That’s sensible.
: But addition, at the last minute, of an exclusion for Auckland does not fit with the uncontentious and unpolitical way of identifying risk here. It has overlaid a set of judgements that are, simply put, relatively political about whether Auckland should be included or excluded from the rules.
: I think that is the wrong decision. I think we will be back here in this House debating whether that has worked, because it is not a system that the public can have faith in, and it will test confidence and trust in our built environment system and whether central government stands behind the risk that we are asking Aucklanders to take on, not only as a community, but as individual business owners who, say, have buildings next to highly risky buildings and people who maintain other parts of built environment around them that are at risk because of this decision.
: This is not also a minor issue for Auckland. The majority of earthquake-prone buildings are in Auckland, despite many people’s assumptions about the earthquake-prone buildings being in Christchurch; that is a largely an area which has been through a pretty painful process of having to come up to speed with the rules that we required of them. People in Canterbury have done what they have been asked. They have fixed buildings; they have remediated buildings. For some people, have that has been at personal cost, huge personal investment of family savings. For many businesses, it has meant years of having to forward-fund capital investment in their buildings, but they have done that.
: This is an exclusion, now, of another region, in fact, where there are 1,400 earthquake-prone buildings, which was in the queue, and this Government has made a decision to exclude them. That decision will have lasting consequences for generations to come and is, frankly, being made at a time where that is possible for the Government to do it because it’s not in people’s minds.
: The deadline extensions powers in the bill have also been something that the committee worked very closely with, and, ultimately, that is something we do not support. There are shifting goal posts now in the bill, where deadline extensions of up to 15 years don’t come back to this Parliament. They are made away from public scrutiny. What does that mean? It means that building owners don’t have a clear indication of the time that they will need to make remediations in the rest of the country.
: For Wellington apartment owners, who are an important constituency when Governments of both stripes have considered this bill, they now do not have certainty of investment decisions. Little old ladies who live in apartments, and that’s their entire life savings, will be hugely impacted by this bill, and that is a very hard case.
: Labour’s answer to this was not one that National politics supported. It was to use public money to assist those private owners with their private property because we recognise that there is a no-fault element of this and that it would be inequitable to treat this in any different way.
: But there were other choice for the National Government to make, and simply kicking the can down the road is what is being done here in this bill. It’s a very difficult position to be putting those retirees, especially, but also first-home buyers, in, when they are now under water and find themselves without equity to invest in other properties that they would like to live in, especially in the current climate of the Wellington property market.
: The committee had some very useful discussions around the idea of addressing the need for assistance that those apartment owners faced, but, ultimately, Government has not proposed either an insurance product which would help them or a financial scheme which would allow them to sell and then to recover some of the costs for the Government’s coffers. That was what was in place 2022-23 under the Labour Government and that is not what the Government has announced.
: These rules in this bill should have been progressed at the same time as another scheme to properly spread risk between those who can afford it and those who can’t were introduced. Things like body corp rules are critical to getting this regime right. Those have also not been progressed at the same time.
: Ultimately, this is an area where reform is welcome. We need sensible rules for remediation, and the rules aren’t working for a sector which is struggling with the construction and the repair of these buildings right now. We do not have enough capacity in the system to fix all of the earthquake-prone buildings that we need to in New Zealand today. We needed a sensible way for the Government to direct when that work would occur and where.
: But the exclusion of Auckland wholesale should not have been part of the planning of that pipeline. If we’re serious about an infrastructure pipeline which works for people, we also need to consider the built environment and the private buildings which are associated with that—our construction sector needed to be able to plan that out well. There is also an extension in here which means that it might 10 years, it might be 15 years—nobody knows.
: So when we’re accountable to the people in our electorate who are looking at this Parliament and seeing an improvement of the earthquake-prone building rules, we all also have to know that the risk of earthquakes hasn’t gone away, that there are risky buildings out there which this bill doesn’t deal with. Simply sticking a notice on the door doesn’t deal with it, and we all need to wear that for our communities, where there is not just private risk, it is public risk—to our main streets, to the people who use the movie theatres, to the people who use the malls, all of this is something that this Parliament should keep a very close eye on because it does speed up building, but it also spreads the risk in ways we haven’t anticipated.
: Debate interrupted.

topicSummaries.topic: Vote Correction — Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill
topicSummaries.content: SPEAKER: Before I call the member, can I inform the House that the vote on the first reading of the Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill was incorrectly recorded as Ayes 91, Noes 20. The correct result is Ayes 101, Noes 20. The record will corrected accordingly.

: Debate resumed.
Hon JULIE ANNE GENTER (Green—Rongotai): Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Tēnā koutou e te Whare. I congratulate the Transport and Infrastructure Committee for their work on this bill and the very helpful report that came from it. My colleague Celia Wade-Brown is currently the primary member for the Greens on that committee, as I have to be on the Environment Committee for the Planning Bill. So I wasn’t there for the submissions on this bill, but I have a great interest in it, particularly as an electoral MP for Rongotai.
: Wellington City, which is mainly Wellington Central electorate and Rongotai electorate—both held by Green MPs—was significantly affected by the Kaikōura earthquake and by the changes to the earthquake building standards that were brought in following the Christchurch earthquake. So that was back in the prior term. I know the Speaker will remember this well, because I think he was involved at that time. I think that the changes that were made at that time were made for the very best reasons, which was to try to protect loss of life following the extremely damaging and tragic Christchurch earthquake.
: However, while Christchurch, in the recovery, received a significant amount of central government funding to rebuild horizontal infrastructure and a significant amount of support, Wellington has not really received that level of central government support. And yet, it’s had extreme damage to horizontal infrastructure like the pipes, which only became visible some years after the Kaikōura earthquake. Our town centres have really, really struggled with building owners who simply are not in a position to upgrade the building to make it functional. We have buildings in Newtown that have been just used as storage or sitting empty to perfectly good apartments on Riddiford Street above a commercial space empty because those buildings are not going to be repaired and it’s affecting the vibrancy of our whole town centre.
: So as a Wellington MP, I definitely had to support the changes proposed by the Minister. One thing that was great is sort of trying to make—firstly the prioritisation is not stopping a building from falling down, but protecting loss of life. That is really, really important.
: Secondly, there was kind of no awareness. I think council engineers were quite conservative in terms of putting things on the schedule. They would say a one-storey building that’s, say, a tennis club somewhere in Wellington, which doesn’t have people living in it, doesn’t have people working in it all the time, had to be upgraded, and it was the same test for a multi-storey residential building that had people living in it. Clearly, the risk is different for those infrequently used buildings that are single-storey versus a multi-storey residential building.
: We welcome these changes, but we still have some concerns. The primary concern from my point of view is that everywhere else that I’m aware of—at least, this is what I understood from briefings from officials, and coming from an earthquake-prone part of the world, in California—where there have been increases to building standards, there’s usually some central government or State-level support for helping building owners to fix their buildings to make them safer. So it’s unusual to massively put up the seismic standards and not provide any real support, which is, unfortunately, the situation we’ve been in—and there was a pathway for support.
: I have a constituent, an older lady who lives in a residential apartment in the eastern suburbs of Wellington, who went through this whole process with the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment to try and access the support for remediation to her apartment in the building, to access financial support, and had just gotten through all the bureaucratic hurdles when this Government and the Minister Chris Penk announced that they were not going ahead with that programme. So, suddenly, the money was taken away and it wasn’t available, which was incredibly stressful for a woman, if I recall correctly, in her late 70s or early 80s. During this period while the Government’s been working on this legislation, we still have not seen any financial support for apartment owner-occupiers come through. I know my colleague Arena Williams referred to this in Labour’s concerns around the bill. It is a major concern.
: While there will be fewer buildings that need to be remediated, there are lots of buildings—and there might be 40 residential buildings in Wellington, mostly owner-occupiers; some will be investment properties with renters in them, but mostly owner-occupiers. For those owner-occupiers, where is the financial support to undertake the remediation, especially given that property values in Wellington are not up, so borrowing to pay for that remediation might not be available to those apartment owner-occupiers.
: It would be useful if central government had a fund, even if it’s not grants—but it would be great if it included some grants and some loans, low-interest loans to assist owner-occupiers to fix their buildings so that, you know, they’re not at risk of death. We need them to fix these buildings—like, as a community, we need these buildings to be fixed, and we cannot rely on city council, which has already been, particularly in Wellington’s case, under so much pressure to upgrade its own buildings. It’s made a whole lot of recent projects in Wellington City Council far more expensive because of the complications of the seismic standards, which now are, in some cases, being removed. So they’ve already put a lot of money into this stuff. Ratepayers can’t be the ones bailing out everyone in the city. So I think there is very much a role in calling on Government to do something about this, to offer some sort of financial support.
: The other big concern is the exclusion of Auckland from the rules for remediation of risky buildings. I think, unfortunately, as we saw with Christchurch, sometimes the most damaging earthquakes are happening in places where we’re not expecting the earthquakes. My university geology professor I remember very clearly saying that if you’re in an earthquake-prone area, the place that’s most at risk of a catastrophic earthquake is a place where you haven’t had lots of little earthquakes, because the pressure has built up over a long period of time. So while everyone’s expecting it to be Wellington, you know, it might not be Wellington, and clearly a city built on a zone of volcanoes might be at risk. So we should probably not be excluding it, even if it seems cost-effective at the moment; it could end up being the wrong the wrong decision. So, concerned about Auckland’s exclusion. There are 1,400 earthquake-prone buildings in Auckland, and that’s the majority of the earthquake-prone buildings around the country. So excluding Auckland’s buildings that are highly vulnerable in seismic events is not the right decision based on the evidence available.
: We’re not going to oppose this bill, because we know that the other changes need to be made, particularly for places like Wellington, and we were assured by officials during the briefing that engineers were working on far more cost-effective solutions to effectively remediate buildings without having to completely redo the structure. You know, when you’re looking at those, like, 1940s concrete buildings, unreinforced masonry, there might be some more cost-effective solutions that address the issue without having to do everything that had been recommended prior. So that’s what we’re hoping to see.
: I mean, the reality is we are an earthquake-prone nation; we need to build accordingly. We also have higher costs of building, in some cases, and we have an economy that is struggling slightly. So I think working together to address the public risk of earthquake-prone buildings and the cost of that and to share that cost makes sense, especially when it comes to retrofitting older buildings, because people really appreciate those older buildings, you know, like, there’s a lot of really good design, and it would be a shame to have to knock them all down. As we’ve seen in Wellington, people aren’t knocking those buildings down; they’re simply not going ahead with the remediation because it’s not affordable. That means there’s not as much housing available in our city as we need, there’s not commercial space being utilised, and it’s sort of a negative, self-reinforcing cycle for our communities.
: One other point in the last few minutes: we will be moving an amendment in the committee of the whole House around fire safety and disability provisions, because we do think that’s really important. We do need those older buildings to address disability access and fire safety. Thank you, Mr Speaker.
SIMON COURT (ACT): ACT supports the amendment to the earthquake prone-buildings regulations. In 2016, David Seymour, ACT leader, was the only member of Parliament to vote against the legislation and the rules that we’re now repealing. Seymour said the rules would be arbitrary, there was a lack of cost-benefit analysis, and there would be huge cost to many building owners with little benefit either to private or public users. It was an attack on property rights. That’s what this Parliament voted for, 119 to one: an attack on people’s property rights by forcing owners to spend vast sums of money on buildings that they could not justify commercially or ever hope to recover. As a result, as Julie Anne Genter has just pointed out, there are many buildings that’ve never been remediated and never would’ve been under the rules we’re repealing today.
: Seymour said in 2016 these rules will cost a fortune, and since then we’ve heard heartbreaking tales about people who are, essentially, in their old age, living on a fixed income, unable to afford their share of the cost of remediation and living heartbroken, ruined lives as a result of the rules this Parliament’s repealing today, and the Government review of the rules agreed. They had imposed around or would impose around $8 billion in avoidable costs.
: ACT is proven right again, just like we were with the zero carbon Act—119 to one. We will be proven right. New Zealand will have to get the Paris Agreement changed for our benefit or we’ll have to leave. ACT was proven right about the firearms confiscation and the laws that the Labour Government brought in, 119 to one, and that is why Nicole McKee has to fix them with a new firearms Act. ACT is right more often than any of you—excluding you, Mr Speaker—
SPEAKER: Yeah, no, that’s right; I’m never wrong.
SIMON COURT: —care to admit.
SPEAKER: The member does need to come back to the bill. I know that, look, the advertorial stuff is interesting but not relevant to the bill.
SIMON COURT: ACT looks forward to seeing this bill progress through all stages to give New Zealanders with earthquake-prone buildings a chance. Thank you, Mr Speaker.
ANDY FOSTER (NZ First): Thanks, Mr Speaker. I rise on behalf of New Zealand First, and also having chaired the Transport and Infrastructure Committee, which considered this bill. I just want to say thanks to all the people who worked on this: the officials, the submitters, and, always, the great committee that it’s my pleasure to work with.
: This bill followed a public engagement process before the bill was introduced, which I think is a great process that’s all too rare, if I might say, by any Government. The bill reduces the overall requirement for earthquake strengthening, reduces the number of buildings, and reduces the extent of work required in many cases, but not all. It takes a tiered approach, first of all, starting with information. We did say, as a select committee, that we want to make sure that buildings that are earthquake prone, even if you don’t have to do anything with them, that at least there is a notice on those buildings to inform people—a simple notice. Partial and facade strengthening is another step, and then full treatment as well.
: The select committee tightened up on urban areas—for example, churches in fields where we didn’t seem it to be high risk. We tightened up on fire access so upgrade is no longer required, but you can’t make it worse. We agreed with the exclusion of low-risk areas: Auckland, Northland, the Chathams, etc. We did test that, though we told, very clearly, to the Opposition, there was a low benefit-cost ratio and that’s why they stayed excluded.
: The biggest issue, though, just very briefly, was the lifting of coastal Otago—so Dunedin and Oamaru—into the medium-risk area. There was a lot of concern by those communities about that. Those are areas with some of the most significant collections of heritage buildings, and New Zealand First thinks heritage is very, very important—the most significant collections of heritage buildings in New Zealand. Huge public benefit—what Simon Court was saying—and yet, in the bill for those, the strengthening is private. There’s a real concern about the economics of strengthening in both of those towns, but the bill actually reduces the impact on those communities. We did explore the details of those—things like the treatment of mezzanines, basements, two-storey buildings that are four storeys at the back, and so on. [Interruption] Sorry, am I interrupting the good folks over there? Do you want me to—
SPEAKER: No, Mr Foster. You were being interrupted and I’d advise those who were interrupting to contain themselves.
ANDY FOSTER: Thank you. You know, we go through an extensive process; we go through a serious select committee process. Don’t make the process a joke here.
: The assessment of coastal Otago, though—one of the challenges there is that coastal Otago is based on 160 buildings which have been assessed at the moment; I’m told by the folks in Dunedin Council that there are about 3,500 still to assess. So there is a serious issue there, which we are going to need to look at.
: If I can just finish off, just in terms of Wellington, Julie Anne Genter was absolutely right: Wellington got no support whatsoever as the effects of the Kaikōura earthquake slowly emerged, particularly on the water infrastructure. She’s also right about the parlous state of many of the apartment owners there. It is painful for them. They are trapped in that situation. There is no necessary answer in this; it’s something, again, we should look to see if we can find an answer for them—and it does blight areas.
: I’m going to leave it there, but just to commend the bill to the House, and thank everybody for the hard work that’s gone into putting it together.
SPEAKER: This is a split call—Tamatha Paul.
TAMATHA PAUL (Green—Wellington Central): Kia ora, Mr Speaker. Thank you to the previous speaker for sharing those insights, because, as we know, being based here in Wellington, where shakes are common, this is something that we’ve absolutely always got to be considering. We are going to be supporting this bill because it’s moving towards a more proportionate risk-based framework that better targets life safety and reduces unnecessary compliance costs, which was looking like a very big bill for Wellington. We’re glad that those costs might be spread out a bit more over time.
: We all saw those videos in Venezuela, watching all of those buildings come down, watching those buildings collapse on top of people, and just the misery that came about. Whenever there’s a major seismic event across the world, it does really remind us why we have to make sure that our buildings are safe and compliant, and why it is so important. I think New Zealand, in particular, has done a really good job of making sure that our buildings are safe and reinforced and that things like chimneys or stone masonry won’t fall down and crush people in the way that we saw in Venezuela. I think it’s really good that we’ve learnt the lessons from the tragedies that have happened. But, like the previous speaker said, in Wellington, after the Kaikōura earthquake, there was a lot of damage done in the city, especially to our main buildings that we rely on—like our Central Library; basically our entire Civic Square, and that’s only just getting open now, 10 years later. It would have been great to have a hand.
: I know, Mr Speaker, you did a lot of amazing work for the city of Christchurch following the big earthquakes, and I wish that we had a Gerry Brownlee in Wellington to help us hustle a bit more financial support—but it’s all right because we’re here now. I do recognise the previous speaker’s contribution—
Hon Matt Doocey: No, we’re keeping him in Canterbury.
TAMATHA PAUL: Damn it. I do recognise the previous speaker’s work, following the different quakes that we’ve had here in Wellington.
: My colleague the Hon Julie Anne Genter covered a lot of our position quite well. One thing that she mentioned towards the end of her speech is that we’re really hoping that, through the committee of the whole process on this bill, we’ll be able to get some amendments in here that make sure that disabled people or those with mobility requirements living in these buildings are able to safely enter and exit the building in the event of an emergency or an earthquake. We’re really hoping to work pragmatically with the other parties to implement those amendments, which will make this bill and these changes more fair and reflective of the fact that a quarter of our population are living with disabilities.
: Now, the other main point that I wanted to make in the short time that I have was around some of the constituents that I’ve met with in Wellington, particularly those people who are living in earthquake-prone buildings, who are on fixed incomes, who are in a really difficult financial situation due to some of the legislation that addresses those buildings that they live in. I just wanted to highlight some of the solutions that they are wanting in addition to some of this work. Obviously, this is about the legislation, but there are also some financial schemes or assistance that we might be able to consider, to assist some of those owners.
: Some of those recommendations include—and I’ve written to the Minister for Building and Construction early in the year to bring these to his attention—but we respectfully request that we include, within the earthquake-prone building system reform programme, a dedicated workstream which looks at owners of multi-unit residential buildings, recognising the distinct barriers faced by body corporates and homeowners. We ask that there are financial support settings that are workable for owners of multi-unit apartment buildings who must still undertake remediation, including arrangements that recognise fixed incomes, limited borrowing capacity, and the collective decision-making required under unit title and company share governance arrangements.
: Finally, we request that the Government provides certainty and transparency on timing, transitional arrangements, and implementation so that homeowners can plan, secure finance where necessary, and make informed decisions. So, really, just acknowledging that for some of the superannuitants who live in these buildings or disabled people who are on fixed incomes, they have less financial ability to make different financial decisions. Sometimes, they’ve put their lifetime savings into buying these apartments are now in this really tricky situation where they don’t have the money to remediate. My request is that we consider the financial assistance that might sit alongside this bill, which will mean that people living in seismic-prone areas can stay where they are. Kia ora.
Dr CARLOS CHEUNG (National—Mt Roskill): We had many submitters tell the committee how frustrating and confusing the current system is, especially in Auckland where the earthquake risk is relatively lower than in other parts of the country. This will provide a more practical and proportionate approach to manage earthquake-prone buildings. I commend this bill to the House.
TANGI UTIKERE (Labour—Palmerston North): Kia orana, Mr Speaker. Well, I have to say, the National Party member and the deputy chair of the Transport and Infrastructure Committee—I was expecting for the member to be a little more fulsome in the contribution. Usually, we hear about Mt Roskill, but clearly not today. So that is disappointing, but none the less, we will box on.
: As my colleague Arena Williams as indicated, the Labour Party will be supporting this bill this afternoon. That’s because we do agree that the earthquake-prone building system does need to be practical, it needs to be targeted, and it also needs to be focused on the buildings that do pose the greatest risk to life and, indeed, to safety. We acknowledge that when we step back and look at the current regime, it has placed some pressure on councils who have an active role in this particular space, on building owners, on communities, and particularly in regional communities and smaller towns where the costs of undertaking remediation can be, at times—not all of the time, but at times—disproportionate to the level of risk.
: We do think that an approach that is looking at a risk-based approach—one that is balanced—is perhaps a sensible one. It’s right that, when we’re looking at the approach for buildings around priority 4, those that are unreinforced masonry, those that perhaps are seen as vulnerable because of the structure containing concrete, and other areas where the seismic risk is perhaps higher than in other places, it is the best way to go rather than treating every single building in the same way despite those particular aspects as well. But, there still does need to be an expectation that, across the board, throughout the country, when we’re looking at things like this, the consideration for life and safety is paramount, and there should not be a dereliction of duty or responsibility in that regard. We must do this work, although we need to take a measured approach to it.
: I want to acknowledge the Transport and Infrastructure Committee. I want to acknowledge Mr Foster, who has made a contribution today. We’re acknowledging Mr Foster quite a bit. That’s because there are a few bills from the Transport and Infrastructure Committee as part of the urgency motion. I do want to acknowledge the work that the committee did do on this bill. I think the fact that it’s come back to the House with unanimous support, in terms of the report, is a direct indication to the work that colleagues have done. We did hear from a number of submitters, as you would expect for a bill like this, and also officials.
: As colleagues have touched on, the committee did receive some advice around areas in New Zealand that would be considered as low-seismic zones. The resultant action from the committee is that those three particular areas would no longer be subject to the earthquake-prone building regime at the level at which they entered into the regime, and that relates to Auckland, Northland, and the Chathams. Now, this has led to the view from the Labour Party that we oppose the exclusion of Auckland from this regime, and that is because there are, naturally, buildings in Auckland where there is still a risk. There is still a risk that those buildings present a significant life and safety risk if an earthquake were to take place. We do remain concerned that the Government has gone too far in excluding Auckland from this regime, because low risk does not mean no risk, and there continues to be high-risk buildings in places all around the country that would cause harm to life and safety following an earthquake.
: We know that, if we look at Auckland—and set aside Northland and the Chathams—Auckland is home to our largest population. It is our largest city by far. There are substantial levels of infrastructure in that part of the country, in existence and being built at the moment, and there are, as my colleague has said already, a significant number of buildings that have already been identified as earthquake-prone, in excess of 1,400. The select committee report identifies 1,544 Auckland buildings that are currently classified as being earthquake-prone that would no longer be covered by this particular law change. We do think that a complete carve-out of our country’s largest city, which has the most population in the country located in it—
Dr Carlos Cheung: Best city.
TANGI UTIKERE: —does create a gap in public safety and public confidence. Now, Mr Cheung says it’s the best city. Well, he could have told us about that in his contribution, but he’s given that opportunity up. We do think there was an opportunity for perhaps an alternative, where there could have been some middle ground, where Auckland could have still been subject to some provisions, maybe a lighter regime, who knows? That was certainly the preference rather than a complete removal from the regime in its entirety.
: Mr Foster has talked about coastal Otago and the protections that that would provide them. Now, this bill does move that area from a low- to a medium-seismic zone based on the updated information around hazards that is now available. The committee has inserted some transitional provisions so that there is a lack of disadvantage to existing building owners in that particular area. There are still the remediation deadlines that exist, but there is an opportunity for some time frames to be changed in that particular space, after the commencement around those medium-zone time frames as well.
: One change the committee has also made is around the definition of an urban centre. This bill will require a different approach for those that are in urban centres, for those that have unreinforced masonry, and why that is is because of the likely higher damage and threat to pedestrians moving about in urban areas, and vehicular traffic as well, that might also block or impede emergency vehicles seeking to utilise the roads, which we’ll talk about in a moment. The committee has narrowed the definition so that “urban centre” is not going to capture those smaller satellite towns that would be subject to some tougher requirements. Often, close to home for me, the Manawatū District Council is a regular submitter to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee when it comes to these sorts of matters. They would be considering, for their community, where they sit in terms of being an urban centre or not, and adopting the Statistics New Zealand approach as to what the definitions are—and that’s contained in the committee’s report—we think it’s a sensible way to go.
: As you’ll be aware, there are priority buildings that are identified that have, effectively, a shorter runway or a shorter period of time that the remediation work will need to be carried out. Now,  some regional authorities have gone through a process of identifying a large number of strategic transport routes, which means that any of those buildings that are priority buildings that have been identified as being positioned along those strategic transport routes will need to, effectively, create a quicker form of remediation. Why? Because, if an earthquake were to occur and those buildings were to collapse, that would impede the strategic transport network, and so there needs to be a quicker form of remediation around that.
: What has been brought to light, however, is that some authorities have perhaps been a little bit more loose around designation of those strategic transport routes, so the bill does provide for an option for councils to have a look, on a one-off opportunity, around their routes, sort of planning for transport, and to remove some routes if possible. It’s not an opportunity for councils to add, or controlling authorities to add, more routes in, but rather to sensibly, where possible, rationalise what that route looks like. When it comes to highways, Waka Kotahi - New Zealand Transport Agency needs to be included in that particular process.
: Just to wrap up, there are a number of other small changes, but they are changes that we think will make a difference. They’re things like the notices on buildings being a little bit simpler than they are currently. Hopefully they’ll be able to serve as a reminder and a guide to members of the public around what the particular state or assessment of an earthquake-prone building is, so that members of the public can make their own choices around that. At the moment, that is something that might need to be focused on through the regulations process. What this bill does is it changes it so that the chief executive of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment is able to sign off on that and that councils can go about making that happen. It’s a sensible change that will hopefully not create bureaucracy—another layer of bureaucracy—around that but will ensure that it is a very clear, simple direction to the public around what the state of the building is if they choose to go into that.
: Then, the final part is around the removal of some of the “Henry VIII” provisions. That was in response to the Regulations Review Committee, which is ably chaired by Arena Williams, that identified that aspects for the transitional purposes were no longer required, and so the committee was very happy to respond to that request from the Regulations Review Committee to change that.
: On balance, the Labour Party is supporting this bill this afternoon; however, with the caveat that we still believe the time frame and the exclusion of Auckland is an issue.
DAN BIDOIS (National—Northcote): This is a good bill, reflecting a risk-based approach to earthquake-prone buildings. It’s very good for Auckland. It’s all a part of this Government’s plan to fix the basics and build the future. I commend it to the House.
SPEAKER: We have a split call.
GEORGIE DANSEY (Labour): Tēnā koe e te Māngai o te Whare. Mr Speaker, firstly, it’s very good to see you in the Chair. I think the last time I spoke with you in the Chair was at my maiden speech, so let’s hope this speech is as heartfelt and good as that one.
: This is a very important bill that we’re speaking to today, the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill. I want to acknowledge the effects of earthquakes and the importance of getting this legislation right, as other speakers have spoken to.
: We are in a very earthquake-prone country, and we need to do really good and ongoing work on protecting people who deal with the repercussions of earthquakes across the motu and good work that’s going to protect the lives of people and our communities.
: We’ve all been affected by earthquakes. I acknowledge those living in cities who have been hugely affected by earthquakes. We all know the huge impact it has on communities, financially and otherwise, particularly the Christchurch earthquakes, which I know triggered a lot of work in this space. My colleagues have spoken of the impacts of that and I’m pleased to support this bill in order to get that legislation right so that we can protect our lives and our communities.
: We need to keep safety at the centre of our system when we are considering this bill. Reforms should focus on genuine risks and public safety must remain the overriding principle. So Labour supports targeting regulatory efforts at buildings that present the greatest risks to life, safety. As I mentioned, we have learnt considerable lessons from Canterbury, and other speakers have spoken to the Kaikōura earthquakes. Governments have a responsibility to protect people from avoidable harm.
: As other speakers have mentioned, although Labour supports this bill, we do not support the exclusion of Auckland, Northland, and the Chatham Islands from these reforms. Even though they have a low seismic hazard, Auckland doesn’t have a zero risk. We risk building a two-tiered system in our country by excluding Auckland. A low risk does not mean no risk. We need to ensure that we are protecting everybody. As other speakers have spoken to, Auckland contains approximately 1,400 earthquake-prone buildings—the majority of identified earthquake-prone buildings nationally. Excluding our largest population I don’t think is a smart move.
: I come from the sunny place of Hamilton. Hamilton and the Waikato also has a low seismic hazard risk. However, I wouldn’t want the Waikato and the place that I live to be excluded from these regulations, because, as I said, a low risk doesn’t mean no risk. In fact, Hamilton, as reported, is the largest urban centre with the lowest natural hazard risk. So a little plug there for the great city but also let’s not exclude areas. We need to make sure that we are protecting all our people and communities across the board in this legislation.
: The other point I wanted to quickly touch on was balancing affordability with long-term responsibility. As natural hazards increase, or natural disasters increase, in our country due to climate change, this is something we need to think about more and more in regard to earthquakes and personal liability but also in other natural hazards. I don’t think it’s something that gets enough attention—is how are people going to manage the personal, financial burden on them when a natural disaster affects them? I think that’s a missed opportunity, and I would have liked to see more support for our public in that space.
Dr HAMISH CAMPBELL (National—Ilam): Thank you, Mr Speaker. It is a great honour to stand up and speak on the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill. A lot of previous speakers have, Mr Speaker, flattered you with many great compliments, but I just want to acknowledge all the work that you did do for Christchurch after the earthquakes.
: This bill would make more pragmatic, tiered system, intended to better reflect the actual risk posed by individual buildings here in New Zealand. It would focus on mitigating the risk to life. Therefore, I commend this bill to the House.
Dr TRACEY McLELLAN (Labour): Thank you, Mr Speaker. I was a bit surprised that the previous speaker didn’t look at the clock and maybe think to speak for a little bit longer and we may have been able to go for lunch, but, nevertheless, here I am, on my feet, and I’ve got quite a lot to say. So I make no apologies for that snafu.
: The Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill—where do we start? Well, let’s start at point one. Labour supports the overall direction of this bill. Obviously, it’s been argued that the current earthquake-prone building system has imposed substantial and, in some cases, disproportionate costs on building owners and on councils and on regional communities. That is something worthy of some reconsideration. So this more targeted system, which focuses on the buildings themselves, the earthquake risk, and the locations that present the greatest risk and threat to life, we do believe is sensible.
: It’s not a perfect system. There are, as has been discussed, at least two or three major—well, when I say “major”, two or three very specific concerns that we certainly don’t agree with. That’s not what we would have done given the opportunity to do so. But a risk-based system that assesses genuine risk is something that we’re happy to support in this instance.
: But we simply don’t think that we can draw a line around Auckland and pretend that every vulnerable building—of which there were, I believe, 1,400, at least—on one side of a line are no longer a concern, because it doesn’t take away the concern, it just takes them off a statutory list of concern.
: So the central purpose, as has been said by almost everybody on this side of the House, who are, pretty much, the only people—apart from Andy Foster, who made a very interesting contribution—to have commented on what is a really important bill and we should have more to say about it. The most important principle that does have to be underpinning this legislation is that earthquake-prone buildings regulation exists primarily to protect people’s lives.
: As has also been noted, those of us from Canterbury certainly don’t need a reminder that earthquakes don’t just affect buildings; they affect people and they change lives. Within an instant, lives can be changed—and lost. Many Cantabrians, as I’m sure yourself, Mr Speaker, will remember walking past buildings that they had entered hundreds of times or driving pasts buildings, as I did just before the earthquake, paused at a set of lights because the lights were red—a very frequent place for me to be paused. Two hours later, that building was down and the person that was unfortunately paused at those lights on that occasion lost their life.
: So buildings that seem like innocuous bricks and mortar that serve the function of housing work, of housing people, conducting business, and all of those other activities that they afford us the opportunity to do aren’t just buildings if they are not designed in a way or if legislation and regulation don’t ensure that aspects of buildings aren’t a little bit more safer for the reality that they involve housing people and accommodating people who are not nearly as indestructible as we might somehow like to think we are.
: Labour, therefore, supports a greater focus that is in this bill on unenforced masonry buildings. That was certainly a big lesson from Canterbury—vulnerable concrete buildings, falling facades, and other known life-safety hazards.
: A more proportionate system, however, is, we do believe, a little bit more fairer for regional communities. The existing system tended to treat every building as if the community that it was functioning within presented the same level of risk. A small building in a low-risk town shouldn’t necessarily face the same obligations as a large, vulnerable, concrete building on a busy pedestrian route.
: I know that through the select committee process, that formula, those calculations have been taken into account to get to where we agree here: there were some aspects of that that Labour were in 100 percent in agreement with when it came to assessing that risk, but some of that was debatable and we put forward some alternatives. We don’t think that our position was necessarily the perfect one either, so we were happy to contend with this—acknowledging that the cost of strengthening has exceeded, for some people, the value of the building itself, and also acknowledging the stress and the uncertainty that lots of people have faced, wondering how they would be able to now making those buildings compliant under the previous regime.
: However, proportionality must not become an excuse for an indefinite inaction. That is a huge problem. Extensions should be available where owners are making genuine progress, and we absolutely believe that, but not simply to push difficult decisions another 10 or 15 years further into the future.
: Ultimately, we actually do want to be able to take this opportunity to say we live in an earthquake-prone country; there are certain well-known risks; given our recent history, we have been afforded the opportunity to look into and to research and to have experts and engineers on this, that, and whatever, design and innovate some possible solutions to make our lived environment a lot safer. So we should be moving with a certain pace to be able to afford our own selves the opportunity for that.
: As has been mentioned, excluding Auckland, we think, is entirely the wrong approach. I do understand the rationale behind it, and we listened intently to various people raising their methodology behind how they came to that decision or how they came to provide us with that advice. I still don’t think it’s the right thing to do. I think even if we think about the situation where we’re discussing Auckland as if it’s one homogenous area, just by virtue of the fact that it has some boundaries and we’ve created a made-up, essentially, boundary—and that’s what we call Auckland. But even within Auckland itself, there are different geological considerations, and we just think that with a little bit more time we may have been able to work with the Government to maybe reach a compromise on how we could have got the best of both worlds.
: But we accept that Auckland does have a lower seismic risk, we acknowledge that seismic hazard is not the only part of risk calculation, however, and a light-tough framework could have been retained, we think, which would have left highly vulnerable buildings—lots and lots of highly vulnerable buildings still could have been identified, recorded, and subject to some targeted obligations, which I think was probably the place that we should have ended up.
: I also do want to acknowledge the earthquake notices. I think both Andy Foster and my colleague Tangi Utikere mentioned these, in so far as it’s one of the things I remember the most from select committee. Sometimes it’s the little details. The earthquake notices that you put on a building—just because there’s no remediation required for that building, we didn’t think that that should remove the need to have a properly displayed notice. People should still know that, yes, the building’s got some issues; no, not enough to have required the full suite of treatment in terms of remediation—I still want to know what those issues are and then I can make my own informed choice about how much time I may choose to spend in that building.
: In closing, Labour supports this bill because it is targeted and more proportionate in a genuinely risk-based system. We do think that we probably do need this now as a pragmatic step forward. We support this bill at second reading while continuing, obviously, to argue for a more consistent national safety framework and better support for those people that are expected to carry out some of the costs to their own homes, including the apartment dwellers. Ultimately, we all want safer communities.
SPEAKER: Members, the time has come for me to leave the Chair. The House will resume at 2 p.m.
: Sitting suspended from 1.04 p.m. to 2 p.m.
SPEAKER: The House is resumed. We’re dealing with the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill. There’s one call—Dr Vanessa Weenink.
Dr VANESSA WEENINK (National—Banks Peninsula): Thank you, Mr Speaker. It is an honour to speak on this bill. The Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill actually makes a very sensible and sensitive balance between respecting the legacy of those who lost their lives in the Christchurch earthquakes and being able to recover and move on from those events and future ones. This is just another way that National is fixing the basics and building the future. I commend the bill.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Mr Speaker?
SPEAKER: Point of order?
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN: No, sorry, I’m taking Te Pāti Māori’s call.
SPEAKER: No, we’ve lost the opportunity there.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN: Sorry, point of order. My understanding of Appendix E of Standing Orders is that you lose your chance for first reading but for second and third reading we do have the opportunity to bid for a Te Pāti Māori call at the end, should no one else take that call.
SPEAKER: Yeah, OK—way you go.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I rise on behalf of the Green Party to also take a call on the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill. I do want to commend the Transport and Infrastructure Committee on the thorough work they’ve done in this bill, but particularly the chair of the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Andy Foster as well.
: I do want to start by saying that I agree with what everyone has said in terms of the need for us to look at this and exactly how this interacts with local authorities when it comes to the strengthening. Of course, we have seen the impact of earthquakes, both in terms of Ōtautahi Christchurch but also here in Te Whanga-nui-a-Tara Wellington. I think, as my colleagues both Julie Anne Genter and Tamatha Paul as local electoral MPs of Wellington have expressed, this is something that is of great concern. Even as someone from Tāmaki Makaurau Auckland, this is something that is important for us as well.
: The main areas of this—and I think this is an interesting bill, because we’ve seen quite a number of such bills in the building and construction space which allow for some narrowing of the methods available to territorial authorities for identifying new earthquake-prone buildings after the initial identification period. Some of these—particularly some of the high-risk buildings—could be identified after the initial period. I think, when we’re looking at a bill such as this and the kind of flexibility it allows, it also allows for a more nuanced approach. So for those particular buildings, especially if they are older buildings, to be able to have the time to upgrade to a certain extent.
: I think, from an Auckland perspective, I believe—and I need to just double check—some of these changes when it comes to Auckland are something that I am a little bit concerned about. This is where you get changes in Auckland, Northland, the Chatham Islands, and coastal Otago where those in a low seismic zone will no longer be designated earthquake prone. I think that is a concern because there is the possibility anywhere in Aotearoa, being on a faultline, has that kind of potential. I know personally in various electorates—Auckland Central as well as Epsom—that there are buildings that would be considered earthquake prone under the old regime, but I think under the new regime their fate will change to a certain extent. I think that that potentially is important for local authorities to actually monitor and territorial authorities to monitor as well, just because of the potential impact that comes to human lives, should something happen. I can think of particularly along Newton Road between Auckland Central and Epsom that has certain buildings that previously were designated, as there was on Manukau Road.
: But overall, this is a bill that the Green Party does support. There are various elements in there that we’ll be interested in asking the Minister further about. History suggests he’s also a very engaging Minister who I’m sure will be able to let us know the detail of some of these.
: One last thing I want to touch on in terms of this particular bill—and this is something that has been going through various bills. I mentioned that we have seen quite a few of these types of building bills, particularly around earthquake-prone buildings—which is on the Henry VIII powers that it presents. Because this is something that has been noted by various members as well as other committees of the kind of Henry VII clauses that we are seeing manifesting in some of the building bills. They are important, some of them are required, but again some of those in general would have sunset clauses. But then how that gets managed and how that Henry VIII clause manifests is something that, I think, as a House we should continue to monitor and is something that we’ll be asking the Minister on as well.
: Also, I think, with that, there are some areas, like I mentioned, with a level of nuance that need to be unpacked further. But overall we understand the requirements for this bill and we understand the necessity it presents, particularly for people in Wellington. Finally, I do want to acknowledge, Mr Speaker, your role as a previous Minister in the work that you did in the Ōtautahi earthquakes.
: Motion agreed to.
: Bill read a second time.

topicSummaries.topic: Vote Correction — Offshore Renewable Energy Bill
topicSummaries.content:
MIKE DAVIDSON (Green): I seek leave to correct two votes taken during the committee stage of the Offshore Renewable Energy Bill. In order to correct the Green Party’s vote on the closure motion for Part 4, which should have been 14 votes opposed and on Hon Dr Megan Woods’ tabled amendments to Amendment Paper 571, which should have been cast as 14 in favour.
SPEAKER: Leave is sought for that purpose, is there any objection? There appears to be none. The record will be corrected accordingly.

Hon MARK MITCHELL (Minister for Emergency Management and Recovery): Thank you, Mr Speaker. I present a legislative statement on the Emergency Management Bill (No 2).
SPEAKER: That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.

Hon MARK MITCHELL (Minister for Emergency Management and Recovery): I move, That the Emergency Management Bill (No 2) be now read a second time.
: Mr Speaker, while you’re in the seat, I just wanted to acknowledge you. As a member of the National Party backbench when we were hit by the awful Christchurch earthquakes, I got to observe your tireless work as emergency management Minister leading the recovery for Christchurch. I just want to think, reflect, and mourn on those that were lost, but also now recognise that Christchurch is a thriving city that is a joy to visit and to see how far they’ve come since that event. I want to acknowledge you, because I got a front-row seat that helped inform me in terms of what I needed to do when I took on the role of emergency management Minister. So thank you for that work.
: I’d like to thank the Governance and Administration Committee for its work to consider this important piece of legislation. I’m pleased to see the select committee was unanimous in its recommendations. This reflects the collaborative cross-party approach that we need to strengthen our emergency management system. In my view, like national security, emergency management should be bipartisan. I want to thank all of the parties that have worked hard and had input into the development of this bill.
: I also want to acknowledge the submitters on the bill. Their input has improved the bill and will also feed into its implementation and other operational improvements. Emergency management is relevant to every person in New Zealand. Submitters’ insights are important to supporting the whole-of-society approach to emergency management we need to adopt as a country.
: The Government’s objectives for reform are to strengthen the role of communities and iwi Māori in emergency management; provide for clear responsibilities and accountabilities at the national, regional, and local levels; enable a higher minimum standard of emergency management; minimise disruption to essential services; and ensure agencies have the tools to do their jobs effectively when an emergency happens.
: The majority of submitters supported this intent. Where submitters sought changes, it’s clear the select committee has given those views careful consideration, and, in many cases, has recommended changes to the bill as a result. These amendments have strengthened the bill, and the Government will be taking them forward. There are some changes I want to highlight, because I see them as particularly helpful in supporting improvements on the ground.
: The bill as reported back extends civil liability protections to official responders when they’re taking precautionary actions immediately before an emergency. These protections will also cover the likes of volunteers and civil contractors when they’re acting under official direction. Concern about civil liability before a state of emergency is declared should not create hesitation to act, because hesitation can result in avoidable damage. At worst, it may cost lives. I welcome the select committee’s recommended changes on this issue, and I thank the submitters who raised it. The committee has also recommended creating a formal link between regional emergency management plans and the long-term planning process under the Local Government Act. Good planning is fundamental to driving action on the ground across the four Rs of risk reduction, readiness, response, and recovery.
: While there was already an expectation that local authorities would implement their emergency management responsibilities through long-term plans, making this link explicit and clarifying how a multi-council planning process should flow into individual councils and their long-term plans was important. Emergency management committees are intended to achieve economies of scale and integrated management of hazards and risks, but they can only be successful if all councils play their part. Linking regional emergency management plans and long-term plans will ensure that committees’ decisions translate into action.
: This change reinforces a key shift the bill is making to put more emphasis on the emergency management role of individual councils. Related changes include creating specific roles for regional emergency management committees and their local authority members, making mayors primarily responsible for declaring states of local emergency and recovery transition periods within their own districts, requiring every territorial authority to have a district controller and district recovery manager with a clear line of accountability to the council’s chief executive, and giving territorial authority chief executives an explicit mandate to coordinate resources provided by other agencies in the lead-up to and during an emergency over that longer-term recovery. In late October last year, severe weather events coincided with the local body elections. Because new mayors had not yet been sworn in, I needed to declare states of local emergency over Southland and Canterbury.
: The committee has recommended a sensible change to address this gap, enabling mayors to be sworn in early on a temporary basis to declare a state of emergency or transition period. This will enable local declarations to continue to be made locally and avoid potential delays in the emergency disruption communications if the emergency is disrupted because of communications between the affected council and the Minister.
: When it comes to improving our resilience to emergencies, this bill is only part of the picture. Councils also hold many tools to address specific hazards under the planning, building, and biosecurity legislation. To name just a few: like under the current Act, emergency management committees are expected to use these tools to support their emergency management responsibilities. I’m pleased to see that the select committee has recommended making the connection between these responsibilities clearer by creating a requirement for emergency management committees and councils to consider whether functions, duties, and powers in other relevant legislation would help meet their emergency management responsibilities.
: New Zealand is one of the most exposed countries to natural hazard risk in the world. I’m sure I don’t need to convince the House about the need for a strong emergency management system. This need is reinforced by every severe weather event, let alone when we consider our most serious risks, like the Alpine Fault. It’s critical we have legislation that sets us up to manage these risks. At its core, New Zealand’s approach to emergency management is based on three key principles: (1) we consider all hazards, natural and man-made; (2) we manage the risk from these hazards by taking action across the four Rs: risk reduction, readiness, response, and recovery; and (3) all parts of society have a role to play in emergency management: central government, local government, communities and businesses, iwi and hapū, and individual households.
: Overall, this bill will better enable our emergency management system to achieve this intent, and deliver the improvements identified through past inquiries and reviews. For that reason, I want to thank, again, the select committee and all of the submitters for the critical role you have played in improving this bill.
: The Emergency Management Bill (No 2) will provide stronger foundations for New Zealand to meet the growing risk we face as a country, and I commend it to the House.

: The bill also updates the governance arrangements for our regional emergency management organisations, including renaming civil defence and emergency management groups as emergency management committees. : Another slight point of difference is governance. Labour believe that the strongest emergency management system is one that empowers regions while ensuring national coordination where necessary. This bill shifts the balance towards centralisation. It introduces new ministerial powers, binding national rules, and compliance orders enforceable through courts. While there will certainly be occasions where national leadership is essential, we must remain connected to our local leaders who know their communities so well, they know their rivers so well, they know their whenua so well, they know their roads so well, and they know their bridges so well. I want to acknowledge, too, the training and professional development that has gone on throughout our communities. Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Speaker. As we heard from both of the previous speakers, this is a bill that is important and very much needed, and the Green Party also supports this bill. I want to first acknowledge the Governance and Administration Committee for considering this bill and all of the members on that committee for doing a very thorough job of it.
