As mentioned before, the bill would replace the existing Civil Defence Emergency Management Act and then build this new legislative framework by this bill in terms of the 2023 Government inquiry into the response to the North Island severe weather events. In terms of the 2023 events, what we have seen from that, both in terms of the Auckland anniversary floods that affected areas such as Auckland Central, Epsom, and Mount Albert more severely, as well as areas over the shore, and the responses that MPs have had on that, but also personally having relatives on the East Coast and in Napier, Tokomaru Bay, Tolaga Bay, was going to those areas and seeing the ongoing impact, even to this day, that Cyclone Gabrielle had in those kinds of areas. This is something that very much is facing Aotearoa New Zealand on the whole.
: I think, with that, it’s really important for us to address the first major issue that we have in this House, which is around climate change and how we are responding to both climate mitigation and also climate adaptation. Of course, this is something that the Green Party in particular is very interested in and would like to follow through in having this conversation, with any Government, and on this bill and during the committee stage in particular. Now, the reason for that is because what we have seen is an increase. What we normally have seen to be once-every-hundred-year events are now annually, and our local authority simply—our people, our communities, our society—is not at this stage prepared to handle that kind of level of frequency. Right now, we’re seeing more extreme weather patterns all around the world, most recently with the heat waves in France hitting record highs again. We’re seeing that happening every year. We just declared that El Nino is here in Aotearoa and the impact that that, potentially, will have in the coming months.
: So climate change is absolutely an important focus when we’re looking at the way we look at emergency management, of course, with all of the other natural disasters on the bill we have just spoken on, the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill, on other forms of natural disasters like earthquakes. With that kind of setting the scene, it’s important then to ask: it’s very well to have a bill such as this, but what is the level of resourcing that is needed to be able to undertake and actually do what is set out as a legislative framework to its full effect and give credit to what we’re trying to do here today?
: For example, one of the things we have raised and we are concerned about is that in Budget 2024 we did see that ring-fencing for the Climate Emergency Response Fund has been taken back and nearly $1 billion has been wiped from that fund to subsidise other parts of that Budget. What we have seen is that the marae resilience fund is drying up, even though marae play such an important role in an emergency response. I want to give a specific shout out to the marae that supported the local communities, our tourists, our visitors—not just Māori but everyone who was in the communities in the climate-charged extreme weather we saw in the Bay of Plenty earlier in the year. All of these are important considerations as we progress this bill further through the House.
: What we have also seen is that the Government has given record investment and record funding to Defence but, proportionately, we have not seen the personnel, particularly when it comes to civil defence, receiving a proportion of that record increase in Defence. Again, we feel like, if we’re really talking about emergency management and emergency response, there is a little bit of an imbalance in terms of what we see as a legislative framework and what we’re seeing in action from a resourcing perspective. Another important aspect of that resourcing is what we have seen most recently here in Te Whanga-nui-a-Tara, in terms of the sudden flood that we saw only a few months ago, which has also left many, many of our families here in Wellington in hardship. I do want to give a special acknowledgment to our local Green MPs, Julie Anne Genter and Tamatha Paul, for the role that they played—as all electorate MPs do in the event of an emergency, when it comes to the emergency response.
: One of the things we did see, through a series of these emergency events that we’ve seen since the beginning of this year, was a record number of local states of emergency being triggered; yet what we don’t see is the corresponding response from, for example, the Minister of Social Development (MSD) when it comes to the civil defence payment. There has to be constantly this battle with MSD to trigger the civil defence payment, because, if a local authority doesn’t ask for it, it’s not triggered—whereas, when people are in hardship, particularly when we were looking at a local state of emergency or national state of emergency, those civil defence payments should be automatically triggered rather than people having to ask for that. That all comes down to the package of what the Greens would really like to see when it comes to resourcing.
: Another area that I want to touch on is the disproportionate effect that this will have on certain communities. Two communities that come to mind in particular are our disabled communities and our seniors communities, as we saw when it came to Cyclone Gabrielle a few years ago. We noticed that when it comes to seniors, when it comes to the disabled, there was no really good record—particularly for civil defence personnel, for firefighters, for those who were on the front line—to know if a particular family or people that they were evacuating actually required those kinds of additional specialised support. It’s really good to see this particular bill having a specific mentioning and acknowledgment of the importance of those disproportionately affected communities.
: With that kind of legislative framework—towards the policy framework, again—it comes down to what sort of resourcing we need. What kind of collaboration with hapū, with iwi, with disabled communities, with seniors, and with our elders are we expecting to see, to ensure that these sorts of things are being addressed, so that we are not in a position where older people are left stranded at home because those people who are on the front line don’t know that they require additional support—wheelchair access and all of those things?
: Finally, I think another important area when it comes to the idea of emergency management is that the idea of schools and also communities being local hubs in the event of emergency management is absolutely crucial. From the perspective of schools, we have seen that schools have also recorded an incredible rate of needing additional support from the Ministry of Education as a result of school property damage, which has also meant that our schools couldn’t open as well. This is, again, something that we’d really like to see: how can we build up schools’ resilience as a local hub? We’re looking at even more than what the Government has put in this year’s Budget when it comes to solar panels on schools, as well as the ability for schools to have things like industrial grade kitchens and the broader school lunch availability that’s done locally. That way, in the event of an emergency, the schools can also be a source or hub for the local communities as well.

CAMILLA BELICH (Labour): Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s a pleasure to take a call on the Emergency Management Bill (No 2).
Arena Williams: On behalf of the ACT Party!
CAMILLA BELICH: Yeah, on behalf of some party in the coalition Government. : I don’t think a bill like this will ever be perfect, and you’ve heard from colleagues, including our spokesperson Cushla. She’s lived this in her community. She’s lived through disasters. She’s volunteered. : There will, obviously, always be things that can be better with this bill. It’s not exactly the same as the bill that was introduced by, I think, Kieran McAnulty or Kiri Allan under the last Labour Government, but there are very similar aspects to it and the tenor of most of the improvements has remained the same. It also, very importantly, has learnt from the 2023 events that we had with Cyclone Gabrielle and with the Auckland flooding. This is an unusual area. I’m sure the Minister will agree that this couldn’t be more serious, because we’re talking about life and death—getting it right is important, and we have to do everything we can to make the response as safe as possible—but, in a response, you never see a better side of New Zealand than when people are responding to an emergency. People are hopeful. They’re optimistic. They muck in. They help their neighbour.
: I just think this is where New Zealanders really shine in these situations, and it’s unfortunate that it’s so often tinged with a great sense of loss. Often we see that sense of loss and that feeling—once the original emergency has subsided, we see that sense of loss. I want to have an upbeat speech because I’m really positive about this bill, but we have had some terrible disasters, and the Mauao situation with the slip was just so utterly tragic, and I want to acknowledge Tom Rutherford there as well for his commitment to the response there.
: That was extremely difficult for the community and I think something for the entire country to acknowledge, the danger of slips. This is an area that I was working in. To be fair, I feel that this is much more prominent now, in my mind, in terms of assessing the risks of disaster than it had been. In many ways, it’s similar to how I hadn’t fully appreciated the risk of flooding and rain until the Auckland floods as well. So we do learn from these situations, but we do have to stand alongside families. I will never forget that service where the families were there. That was incredibly moving and I think a real testament to the community in Mount Maunganui, to come together to support those families. Just wanting to acknowledge, obviously—whenever we talk about these tragedies, we have to acknowledge the families who are the ones affected and we do what we can as elected members to support people.
: So this bill has changed a little bit since it was first introduced, and there are a couple of areas that the select committee changed that I think deserve mentioning. There had been a few changes that it’s become apparent were needed as the bill was really progressing through the House, and one of those ones was enabling mayors to be sworn in early. Now, this is a really interesting one because we had a situation where mayors have a very important role in our emergency management system, leading the response. We had a few situations where it wasn’t quite clear, because it was during an election period, which mayor we were meant to be relying on. That’s not really OK because in emergencies you do need a leadership structure. You need a hierarchy of when decisions are made and you need those decisions to be made, if they are decisions that should be left for someone who’s elected democratically, to be made by that democratic representative. So I think the ability to enable mayors to be sworn in actually might seem like an unusual thing, but, actually, because we have events so often in New Zealand, that probably will be something that does come up again.
: I think enabling people to be co-opted is also additionally an important aspect of making sure that all of the skills are there on an emergency management committee, because sometimes you might have some communities that do have that expertise and there’s more often than not a wealth of expertise, but you might not have all the skills. So enabling that is also really important, too.
: There’s also a slight change in requiring engagement and representatives of iwi Māori, and Cushla Tangaere-Manuel spoke to that earlier. This was an area which has changed a little bit since the bill that the last Labour Government put in place. So the rules in relation to engagement with Māori are not as strong as they were under our proposal. So it’s good to see that this proposal encouraging engagement is there as well.
: I don’t think this is a political thing or anything that anyone would disagree with, that the response from iwi Māori and marae in disasters is exceptional throughout the country, and it is built into the way that marae are set up. For a country that experiences these events, they’re set up perfectly to respond to the events. I don’t think that’s an accident; I think that’s to do with the way that tikanga have evolved and the way that marae have evolved in order to deal with events over the time. So we just see again and again marae, iwi, and hapū standing up. I think what we haven’t been as good at in this House in the past, and I hope with this bill we can get better at it, is not just expecting that and saying thank you and moving on. It’s actually resourcing those marae to be able to do, with their leadership that actually respond, in the best way that they can, the way they want to with our support, and not only taking when we’re in need, but actually supporting those marae to step up and do the job that they have always done in New Zealand, you know, well before any of us were here and will do well after all of us are gone as well. So that is a really important thing too.
: The issues around climate adaptation are important. This isn’t a bill that solves all of the future issues associated with extreme events. There are issues which are still on the table, and I know the Minister’s been working on a joined-up system in relation to making sure that people in different parts of New Zealand, when there’s a disaster in another area, can step up and use the same operating system, and, actually, we can utilise a much bigger workforce because of that common operating model. That’s tricky work. It’s expensive. There are a lot of existing operating models. But I think that that work is something that I would encourage the Minister to continue with and I know he has been doing that in the latest Budget.
: The other issue is with climate mitigation. Of course, that’s so interlinked with a lot of this emergency management work. There is more to do in that space, and we have to acknowledge the fact, as a country, that we will be, especially with the confirmed El Nino weather pattern that we’re having, having these systems and these issues again and again. So this bill is a great step in the right direction. It was built on the work of this Government, this Minister, and previous Ministers, and it will be something that future Governments will work on in the future. All we can do is take the best advice, do the best we can, and make sure we do everything we can to keep New Zealanders safe in emergencies. I commend this bill to the House.
SIMON COURT (ACT): Thank you, Mr Speaker. ACT supports this bill and the necessary changes, in particular extending protection from civil liability to persons with functions, duties, or powers under the bill, who considers an imminent threat of an emergency and take preventative or precautionary actions, actions designed to limit the impacts of the emergency on people and property.
: This is because during the 2023 Cyclone Gabrielle and other similar flood and storm events, people with decision-making power have often felt reluctant to take the necessary measures. Putting an excavator into a river to clear debris comes with risks of prosecution under the Resource Management Act (RMA). Putting an excavator or a bulldozer on to a beach to clear a river mouth comes risk of prosecution under the RMA. So it is important that new defences are established in this law so that when individuals, private people who might have a digger or a dozer, want to get in and do something to stop the flood damaging property or potentially harming people’s lives, they can do it. So, on that basis alone and for many other reasons, ACT commends this bill.
ANDY FOSTER (NZ First): Mr Speaker, thanks. I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to speak on this bill, proud of the work that we did as the Governance and Administration Committee. I just want to pick three things very quickly. The first one of them, as Camilla Belich has already said, was empowering mayors during that interregnum period, between an election and being formally sworn in, to actually declare emergencies. That was a real issue that arose last year and was something that the mayor certainly raised with me. So we fixed that. That’s great.
: Second one is being able to take, as Simon Court just said, a proactive action where there is an emergency looming. Think about the Wairoa River Bar. Action wasn’t taken quick enough—Wairoa flooded. Also Lakes Forsyth and Ellesmere—again, floods caused by the lack of proactive action. This will empower that.
: The third one is the Minister said the new clause 43A is clearly linking between councils’ emergency management powers. If you’re the emergency management controller or you’re the chief executive of a council or a mayor of a council, you’ve also got powers under the Resource Management Act, etc. to link those two together. We’ve got to stop building dumb things in dumb places. That was one of the issues for Christchurch City Council. It didn’t want to have development in what is now the red zone. It got forced to do that. We’ve got to empower councils to avoid having dumb things built in dumb places.

Likewise, Gisborne—if it’s an emergency in Te Araroa, why does it affect Gisborne city? So we think that needs to be thought through. Otherwise, great bill. I commend this bill to the House.

Hon LOUISE UPSTON (Minister for Social Development and Employment): I present a legislative statement on the Regulatory Systems (Social Security) Amendment Bill (No 2).
DEPUTY SPEAKER: That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.

Hon LOUISE UPSTON (Minister for Social Development and Employment): I move, That the Regulatory Systems (Social Security) Amendment Bill (No 2) be now read for a first time. I nominate the Social Services and Community Committee to consider the bill.
: This amendment bill is an omnibus bill that amends legislation administered by the Ministry of Social Development and the New Zealand Defence Force. Specifically, the bill makes a number of minor policy and technical changes to the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001, the Social Security Act 2018, and the Veterans’ Support Act 2014, and repeals the Family Benefits (Home Ownership) Act 1964. This bill is intended to improve the provision of social welfare benefits. The amendments in the bill will update statutory provisions, address regulatory duplication gaps and errors, and bring legislation up to date with public expectations. The bill will reduce the chance of regulatory failure and unintended consequences that harm the wellbeing of New Zealanders. The changes are small and do not warrant stand-alone bills, but together the changes will ensure greater effectiveness and efficiency of the social welfare system.
: The first minor policy change is to extend the sustainable employment trial for supported living payment recipients from 26 weeks to a maximum period of 104 weeks. The supported living payment is a benefit payable to people who are permanently and severely restricted in their capacity to work because of a health condition, injury, disability, or because they are totally blind. The purpose of the sustainable employment trial is to encourage and support supported living payment recipients who want to move into employment or increase their hours of work to establish whether they can sustain that employment and cease receiving the benefit.
: Feedback from health and disability stakeholders and international evidence indicates that the fear of losing the supported living payment entitlement can be a significant barrier to work and that 26 weeks is not long enough for some recipients to test their ability to work. Furthermore, increasing hours of work incrementally over a longer period better supports people to sustain employment and become independent. Extending the sustainable employment trial to two years will therefore improve incentives for supported living payment recipients to work as much as they can, leading to a better financial position and improved wellbeing outcomes for those who can participate.
: The second policy change is to ensure that residents of the Realm countries of Niue, Cook Islands, and Tokelau cannot use social security agreements to meet the residence requirements for New Zealand superannuation and veterans’ pension. Social security agreements are bilateral treaties between Governments that provide for the reciprocal payment of social security benefits and pensions. These agreements are intended to apply to the residence of the two agreement partner countries. However, the Ministry of Social Development has advised that a court would likely find that some of New Zealand’s social security agreements could apply to people applying for New Zealand superannuation or veterans’ pension while resident in the Realm countries.
: Social security agreements are not intended to apply to residents of the Realm countries. Realm countries do not have the resources to participate in the cost-sharing aspects of social security agreements. Instead, New Zealand superannuation special portability provisions are extended to the residents of the Realm. Therefore, the bill will amend the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001 and the Veterans’ Support Act 2014 to exclude the application of social security agreements to Realm country residents.
: The third minor policy change will enable people who are live organ donors to be eligible for an emergency benefit payment equivalent to the rate of the supported living payment. Currently, a supported living payment recipient who is caring for a person who would otherwise require hospital or residential care is not eligible to receive supported living payments should they be recovering from surgery for a live organ donation. This is because they are not caring for someone while they are recovering from surgery, which is a criterion to receive the supported living payment—caring. Instead, they are transferred on to the emergency benefit while they are in their recovery period and can only receive the rate of the equivalent main benefit that they would be entitled to, which is either the jobseeker support or sole parent support. This anomaly in the supported living payment does not align with the Compensation for Live Organ Donors Act 2016, which is designed to remove financial deterrents to the donation of organs by live donors. Therefore, the bill will establish explicit legal authority to pay emergency benefit to clients at the same rate that they were receiving on the supported living payment on the ground of caring for another person for a period of up to 12 weeks after the donation.
: As I noted earlier, the bill also contains minor technical amendments. These minor amendments are mostly related to the Social Security Act 2018 and the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001. Rather than go through each technical amendment, let me highlight the common themes behind the changes. The majority of the proposed amendments will address errors or omissions found following the rewrite of the Social Security Act 1964 to the Social Security Act 2018. Other changes are aimed to improve the provision of social welfare benefits and strengthen the performance of the social security system. There are also changes which will repeal redundant legislation. For example, the bill will repeal section 190A of the Veterans’ Support Act 2014, which has been replaced by section 127 of the Legislation Act 2019.
: In conclusion, it can be difficult to find time on the parliamentary calendar for repairs and maintenance of existing legislation. This amendment bill is a vehicle for smaller regulatory fixes to be progressed in a timely and cost-effective way in order to improve the provision of social welfare benefits. I commend this bill to the House.

Hon WILLOW-JEAN PRIME: Now, coming to the bill that we have before us in July 2026, the disclosure statement says that it’s important that the legislative framework for social development is fit for purpose, and, as the Minister outlined in her legislative statement, this is about ensuring that we are maintaining the currency of our legislation. : The reason why I’m focusing on clause 10 is that we know, in this country, there’s about 20,000 people, according to the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment’s (MBIE) estimates, who are without a visa here. My parents were parents affected like that. They were not from any kind of inheritance. They had no money behind them. They were, in fact, in a little town called Kawerau, which some of my colleagues know well. They were able to buy a house under that scheme. So, in some ways, I’m going to be sad to see that gone from the statute book, because I think it’s a really interesting idea and it made a big difference in New Zealand. And we do, after all, have a housing crisis.
: I also wanted to just mention the part of the bill that talks about extending the sustainable employment trial. Now, this looks to me like a really good part of the bill. It’s for people who are recipients of benefits—supported living in particular—based on medical grounds. They are able to work 15 hours at the moment, for a period of up to 26 weeks, without losing that entitlement. But then it stops. It actually puts people into a situation where the international evidence suggests that people are worried to go and do that work because they’re worried that that benefit, that backstop, will stop. What is good about this legislation is that it extends the sustainable employment trial to 104 weeks, and that just seems like a really good idea. People are moving into work. It gives them a capacity to do that. That looks like a very good part of the legislation.
: Another part of this legislation is the extension of benefit entitlements to people on supported living payments who are caring for live organ donors. My recall is that there’s another part of this Act that dovetails in with that and looks after people in that situation in a way that hasn’t been possible until now. Now, it did say in the notes that I’ve received that nobody’s actually been put in that terrible position of not getting that kind of cover as a caregiver until now, but it’s really nice that we’re getting ahead of it and we’re making sure that we’re not disincentivising that at all.
: One other thing I just noticed in the bill, in clause 16, is that the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) may grant a child disability allowance for a child with a serious disability if someone is caring for them. I was really interested to see that it’s somebody who’s in a private home and there’s an accommodation part of that as well. I like to see that kind of discretion being given to MSD. I think we take away too many discretions, and that can cause real harm. The people who are working in these departments—it’s great if they’ve got the capacity to do something in a humane way and support people. I look forward to seeing this bill in my select committee.
DANA KIRKPATRICK (National—East Coast): Thank you, Madam Speaker. This of course is the Regulatory Systems (Social Security) Amendment Bill (No 2). It is a small—well, it is a complicated bill, actually, for the Social Services and Community Committee. But, basically, it’s small tidy ups and non-controversial fix-its, and I commend the bill to the House.
GEORGIE DANSEY (Labour): Kia ora. It is good to take a call on the Regulatory Systems (Social Security) Amendment Bill (No 2). I acknowledge that this is a technical-change bill, but, as the previous speaker mentioned, it is complicated for the Social Services and Community Committee. So I look forward to that process.
: I wanted to start, really, by acknowledging all of the people involved in the Ministry of Social Development (MSD)—all of the people that work there and all of the people that receive the support of the Ministry of Social Development. It’s a huge ministry that does very, very valuable work, and it’s good to tidy up some bits and pieces to make sure that the ministry is operating at a level that is manageable for staff and those accessing the services. I see this bill as fixing up some of those minor policy changes and technical amendments, which will hopefully go towards a more effective use of MSD for all those involved.
: The legislation that is being affected: New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001, the Social Security Act 2018, and the Veterans’ Support Act 2014, as well as the repeal of the Family Benefits (Home Ownership) Act 1964. And these changes will make sure that the legislation is fit for purpose for the Ministry of Social Development. The ministry, when it’s most effective, ensures that people receive the right support at the right time, improves individual wellbeing, and strengthens communities across New Zealand. And this bill I see as making it easier for MSD to perform its duties.
: I think it’s an important time for us to be having this discussion. You know, outside of this bill, MSD is in the news around targets, in their use of targets for staff, which could be used to see as gaming the system in emergency housing and putting pressure on staff to reach their targets in order to reach the approval of management.
: The issue there is what’s happening with the data and if people are being processed through the system as they should into emergency housing or if they are pushed off in other directions and what pressure staff might feel in order to reach those targets. That’s not something that we want, and it’s something that we need to make sure that people are getting access to—affordable housing in whatever case that might look like—while also being a very effective service and not taking too much time to get people the support that they need. And this is a good bill in order to tidy up some of those.
: It would be good to see this Government go a lot further than they have in regards to support within MSD, and I hope to see a subsequent bill that addresses the huge inequities in our society concerning people’s access to housing, as I mentioned earlier. But this bill, with its minor policy changes, will do that. I hope that it allows the ministry to promote its value of getting people into employment and independent through jobseeker assistance, training, and employment programmes and also goes further to protect children and families by connecting people with services that will improve their wellbeing and safety.
: I wanted to, just before I finish, speak a little bit to the differences between the first and the second version. Other speakers have spoken to their concern around what happened with the first version and why we’re in urgency now on the second version, so I won’t go over that again. But there are some differences in the legislation between the first and the second version, particularly around the Accommodation Supplement under clause 15, the new clause 17, clause 21, and a new clause 24. Labour does support this bill, and I look forward to hearing back after select committee.
SUZE REDMAYNE (National—Rangitīkei): Look, this bill makes minor technical policy amendments to help ensure the legislation is fit for purpose. It’s all about fixing the basics so we can get on with building the future.
: Motion agreed to.
: Bill read a first time.

DEPUTY SPEAKER: The question is, That the Regulatory Systems (Social Security) Amendment Bill (No 2) be considered by the Social Services and Community Committee.
: Motion agreed to.
: Bill referred to the Social Services and Community Committee.

topicSummaries.topic: Discharge and Referral to Select Committee
topicSummaries.content:
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): I move, That the order of the day for the second reading of the Regulatory Systems (Courts) Amendment Bill be discharged and the bill be referred to the Justice Committee for consideration of Amendment Paper 635 in my name.
: Motion agreed to.
: Bill referred to the Justice Committee.

Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): I present the legislative statements on the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill.
DEPUTY SPEAKER: Those legislative statements are published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.

Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): I move, That the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
: I am pleased to speak to these bills in the House again today. As I noted in my first reading speech, the regulatory system amendment bills are one of the ways that this Government maintains and repairs existing legislation and ensures that our regulatory systems deliver for New Zealanders. At a high level, these two bills reflect the Government’s commitment to delivering fit for purpose regulation and to improving access to justice. They will have a significant impact on the regulatory regimes that govern tribunals and occupational regulation, enhancing their effectiveness and efficiency while improving consumer protection and the quality of justice legislation.
: The Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill makes practical improvements to tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies. It removes barriers to justice by allowing successful applicants in the disputes tribunal to recover their filing fee from the respondent where it is appropriate. It strengthens the regulation of the private security industry by providing more effective information-gathering powers to investigate breaches. It also streamlines appointments and employment arrangements for tribunal members to ensure these bodies operate efficiently.
: The Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill strengthens protections for both consumers and regulated professionals while reducing unnecessary compliance costs. One important change allows conveyancers’ professional undertakings to be enforced in the High Court, just as lawyers’ undertakings already are. This promotes competition in the conveyancing market and benefits consumers.
: The bill also removes a disproportionately harsh penalty that automatically disqualifies real estate agents from practising for five years simply because they failed to complete continuing professional development or pay fees on time. That issue has been recognised by the profession for many years, and this bill delivers a more proportionate response. At the same time, the bill strengthens the Real Estate Authority’s ability to investigate unlicensed trading and ensure licensee’s meet their obligations, improving consumer confidence in the industry.
: Both bills have benefited from the select committee process, and I would like to thank the Justice Committee and the Education and Workforce Committee for their careful consideration, along with everyone who made submissions. Their constructive feedback has resulted in sensible improvements.
: The Justice Committee has clarified the role of the Complaints, Investigations and Prosecution Unit when dealing with complaints about unlicensed private security operators. The Education and Workforce Committee has recommended that the Real Estate Authority’s new powers be exercised on a reasonable basis and clarified that provisions relating to unsatisfactory conduct apply only where behaviour is connected to a licensee’s professional role and affects public confidence in the profession. These are practical improvements that make already sensible bills even stronger.
: I also thank officials and the Parliamentary Counsel Office for their work in developing these bills. Whether someone is taking a claim to the Disputes Tribunal, buying a home through a conveyancer, or working as a real estate agent, these reforms will make our regulatory systems fairer, more efficient, and easier to navigate. They demonstrate this Government’s commitment to good regulatory stewardship, maintaining the laws we already have, reducing unnecessary compliance, and improving access to justice and ensuring regulations work for the people they are meant to serve. I commend these bills to the House.
CAMILLA BELICH (Labour): Thank you, Madam Speaker. It’s a pleasure to be able to take a call on not one but two bills at the same time, the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill. These bills cover quite a few different things, and I’ll talk about them both briefly. Essentially, as I understand, there was a programme that went through where four regulatory systems amendment bills administered by the Ministry of Justice were looked at, and I think this goes alongside the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Courts) Amendment Bill, which we’ve just had re-referred to select committee prior to this.
: For anyone getting papers from the Table, be very careful about which regulatory systems bill you pick up, because there are three on the Table—well, at least two or three on the Table at the moment.
DEPUTY SPEAKER: Very good advice.
Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall: So considerate.
CAMILLA BELICH: Thank you. I have looked at these bills—and I’ve looked quite carefully just to check, as a good Opposition spokesperson should do—and they do appear in all my analysis to be minor and technical, and I was unable to kind of find any fish-hooks in either of them so far.
: The interesting—well, interesting for me; maybe not for anyone else. I was on the Education and Workforce Committee but, sadly, just missed hearing the submissions on the occupational bill, and now I am on the Justice Committee, but I also missed hearing the submissions on the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill. It does appear that both select committees have done a thorough job in looking through these proposals and have made some sensible changes as well, which I think the Minister touched on.
: I do note, from the Table—and I just quickly looked at them, so I may not have taken my own advice on noticing which regulatory system all the amendments related to! I did notice some amendments there from the Minister too, so I’m sure, when we get to the committee stage, she’ll explain what those amendments are and what they do. Again, we have looked at those, and they do appear to be minor and technical, along the lines of what these bills are meant to do.
: Just briefly on both bills, I’ll start with the tribunals bill, which we will move on to look at more closely in the committee stage. It is a bill that’s structured in a way that we will be able to have a much closer look at in the committee stage, too, because it is an omnibus bill that does amend, I think, five different bills: the Disputes Tribunal Act 1988, the Motor Vehicle Sales Act 2003, the Parole Act, the Private Security Personnel and Private Investigators Act, and the Unit Titles Act 2010. We’ll be able to look at those in a little bit more detail at this time.
: I suppose one criticism is that I’m not 100 percent convinced these are very urgent bills. We are in urgency. In the real world, it’s a Friday; here, it’s still 30 June, a Tuesday. We are a little bit unconvinced about the urgency of these, considering they are, as the Minister said, minor and technical. None the less, that is not my call to make, so we will look through them.
: Just to finish off on the tribunals bill, this bill does make a number of changes to those Acts that I did state before. I suppose, notably, a few things about that bill are the fact that you can get a filing fee back for the Disputes Tribunal. I think that’s a good change. I think people are probably surprised that that wasn’t already something you could claim back, and, obviously, it’s a disincentive for people to seek justice through the Disputes Tribunal, so I commend the Minister for bringing in that change. There are some interesting changes to private security. I mean, that always is something you do look at more closely, and so we will have some questions for the Minister around some of those changes. They do seem reasonable, though.
: Then, to move to the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill, this has three major policy proposals: the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act, the Prostitution Reform Act, and the Real Estate Agents Act. There are some sensible changes there as well. I think the Prostitution Law Reform Act changes are around the people who are able to hold a certificate to operate a brothel and making sure that there’s alignment between that and the Crimes Act and the Misuse of Drugs Act, which I think appears to be sensible. It also allows some changes to the Law Society’s complaints mechanism, which I think appears to be sensible. For example, there’s discretion given to the Law Society, rather than an automatic referral of a complaint. I think you can also see the potential value in that.
: There’s a new name in this as well, for the Real Estate Agents Authority is now the Real Estate Authority, which I think sounds better. I can’t make much more comment than that. I don’t know why they decided to change it. They did also decide to change the membership of the now—well, soon after this passes—Real Estate Authority, so  that the chairperson doesn’t have to be a lawyer. As a former lawyer, I support opening up leadership opportunities for non-lawyers. That’s also a good change. They do, importantly, have to have a lawyer on the authority, but it just doesn’t have to be the chairperson—so there we go; hopefully, everyone will remember that. There’s also some discretion in relation to licences for real estate agents, and I know, in emergency situations, sometimes licences lapse, and so those changes have been made following events that we all lived through with Cyclone Gabrielle and the Auckland floods. Anyway, there’s some further discretion there.
: We will have the opportunity to look at these bills separately. It’s kind of an odd situation talking about two bills at a second reading—two different select committee processes; two different sets of recommendations—and then we’ll have two totally separate committee stages. We will be able to look at that more closely, but I think, just reflecting that this is also the job of this House, not everything we do here is on hugely controversial pieces of legislation or pieces of legislation that we feel very passionate about. The fact that we’re all here on a Friday doing this work because it makes the law of New Zealand work better should be commended. With that in mind, I commend both of these bills to the House.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise on behalf of the Green Party of Aotearoa to speak to these two associated bills, the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill.
: I want first to address some of the context around these two bills. As we see with the regulatory impact statement—and I think, from the previous contribution by my colleague Georgie Dansey, I now can’t look at “RIS” in the same way without thinking it’s “rizz”. But I do believe that these two bills very much do have rizz, despite the fact that they may come across as being reasonably boring.
Tom Rutherford: That’s a test of generations.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN: Thank you, Tom Rutherford. As a millennial, I very much appreciate that particular shout out.
: I think, in terms of the context, this is a broader suite being brought by the Minister around the regulatory systems justice package. Now, we have just heard previously that as one part of this package, the Regulatory Systems (Courts) Amendment Bill is being recommitted into the select committee stage, and we’ll be interested to have further opportunities to analyse that particular bill.
: The other bills that are part of this package that actually extended beyond simply a regulatory systems bill were the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Amendment Bill and the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism (Supervisor, Levy, and Other Matters) Amendment Bill (AMLCFT) bills, and those two bills previously were also associated. I am looking forward to the committee stage for these two bills, and hopefully we won’t have the same hilarious, I guess, incidents we had with the two AMLCFT bills, where we kind of crossed over a little bit, and that was much to this House’s enjoyment in general.
: In terms of the two bills that we have here—the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill—it is also important to understand that often we do have a lot of these regulatory systems bills. We just saw the first reading of one on social development and a few days ago in calendar days—but not so much in House days, because it’s still Tuesday here in the House—we saw the Regulatory Systems (Primary Industries) Amendment Bill. It’s always what we consider as sort of housekeeping bills to update our legislation overall in a collaborative, non-partisan way. Because for a lot of these—as we understand—as primary legislation, the only way to amend them is through Parliament and through this House. These are a way for us to group a lot of that together, and we have other mechanisms around some of the other updates as well—statutes amendment bills being a really great example of that.
: I’m going to start with the first bill, actually, which is the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill, which was heard by the Education and Workforce Committee. Now, I do want to say that originally the Green Party opposed this bill, but after going through the select committee stage—and this is particularly due to the Real Estate Agents Act 2018. We did have some concerns around this part of the bill, but I just also want to acknowledge the Minister during the select committee process for her transparency in terms of responding to our questions, which has reassured us that the particular ways around the registration or in terms of unsatisfactory conduct, after hearing from the officials, is something that is more severe than any other professions that we have seen. I think in order for us to maintain that consistency, we were happy with what we’ve heard both from the officials but also from the Minister regarding this particular section.
: We did look at some of the comparable jurisdictions around de-registration, whether it is conveyors, whether it is from other professions, lawyers, etc. Again, upon balance, from what we’ve been told by the officials, it is something that is more on the other extreme end. We are happy with where that particular part has landed, so I think overall, in terms of both regulatory systems bills, the Green Party will be supporting both. I think when we did the first reading of this, it is quite unusual in general for a political party to oppose a regulatory systems bill and we didn’t do that lightly. But, again, like I said, we are happy with where we’ve landed.
: Just in terms of the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill, it is important to note that other than the Real Estate Agents Act, there are also other additional parts that have been touched on that this bill encompasses as well—lawyers and conveyors being one of them. We will be just checking a few more things with the Minister as we go through the committee stage, but also noting that for this bill, the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill, but also for the tribunals, the Ministers do have some additional amendments to this, which we’ll be able to hopefully check with the Minister during the committee stage as well. I think at this stage, both of them, in terms of updates, also seem reasonable, but I just want to be able to make sure, since we’re only seeing these two quite recently.
: The other bill that I want to touch on, the second bill we’re looking at, the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill—there are sort of five parts to this. Again, we’ve seen just previously when we are talking about whether it is the Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill or I mentioned previously in terms of the Judicature (Timeliness) Legislation Amendment Bill, it is a way for us to look at how we’re able to ensure that we have timeliness. I think overall, whether it’s tribunals, whether it’s community magistrates, in a lot of the conversations we’ve had, what is important from our perspective and from the Greens’ perspective is number one in terms of some of the delays we’re seeing in our justice system but also in terms of some of that access.
: Again, some of the things we’re seeing here, particularly with regards to the Disputes Tribunal Act and also the Parole Act, for example, hopefully, once these bills are passed through the House, we’ll see some changes that will allow us to have more of an impact in terms of the ability for people to access justice in different ways, of course noting, as we discussed with the previous bills with the community magistrates, whether it’s the disputes tribunal—because, again, we’re not looking at it from the lens of higher courts, from District Court and above, and with greater powers come greater responsibilities. It will be important for us to see how we’re able to also balance the better access to justice with some of the outcomes that we see as a part of these changes.
: I do want to touch on one particular aspect of this. For both bills, as we’re going through the select committee and we’re hearing from the officials—I mentioned before we heard from the Ministers and also heard from the submitters—we have also made amendments as a part of a select committee. I was glad to be sitting on both the Education and Workforce Committee as well as the Justice Committee for these two bills to be able to consider this. But I think one of the things I want to just quickly touch on is the Private Securities Personnel and Private Investigators Act. This is an interesting and significant improvement that we’re making which allows for that greater transparency of the function of the Complaints, Investigation Prosecution Unit, which allows for the preparation of reports about complaints against unlicensed or uncertified persons when it’s being requested by a licensed authority.
: The last thing I just wanted to touch on—and this speaks to most of the regulatory systems bills we’re seeing in general. These two bills were referred to the committee 16 months ago. The two reports basically came back to the House about a year ago and we only have the opportunity to speak on the two bills now. Although they may not be prominent politically, like I said, they are important bills for this House. I think we should also, as a House, consider if there are better ways for us to be able to put up these bills without having to wait for a year to be able to update them. With that, we commend this bill to the House.
TOM RUTHERFORD (National—Bay of Plenty): Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s a privilege to stand and speak on the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill. I welcome the direction the Minister has given around referring the Regulatory Systems (Courts) Amendment Bill back to the Justice Committee. We will obviously consider that in further depth as that bill progresses, but I support both of these pieces of legislation and I commend them to the House.
JAMIE ARBUCKLE (NZ First): Thank you, Mr Speaker. I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to support the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill in its second reading. I sat on the Justice Committee that heard the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill. We only received seven submissions, two of them being oral. They were very minor and technical changes. They didn’t require extensive discussion from the committee, and I commend it to the House.
SPEAKER: This is a split call—Steve Abel.
STEVE ABEL (Green): Thank you, Mr Speaker. I stand to speak on the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill. These are not things I have any particular expertise in. I just had a brief look through the impact statement and to be very frank, reading these bills, it’s one of those instances where it’s witheringly boring. There’s nothing of real excitement here except to say it is essential for us as a Parliament to go through and sort out pieces of legislation like this to make sure that they are serving their purpose: having the effect of removing barriers, in the instance of the tribunals bill, to the access to justice; clarifying and resolving inconsistencies and gaps in legislation; better enabling statutory authorities to conduct their prescribed functions; and ensuring independence of tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies. The quasi-judicial bodies is quite interesting.
: The bill would amend the following Acts and associated secondary legislation: the Disputes Tribunal Act, the Motor Vehicle Sales Act, the Parole Act, the Private Security Personnel and Private Investigators Act, and the Unit Titles Act 2010. I cannot trouble the House to speak any further on these except to say that we do support them and we support the principle of these sorts of amendments, so the Green Party commends these bills to the House.
PAULO GARCIA (National—New Lynn): Thank you, Mr Speaker. We are fixing the basics by strengthening the ability of occupational regulators to protect consumers. By increasing the efficiency of the regulatory regimes, we are building the future. I commend this bill to the House.
Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB (Labour—Christchurch Central): Thank you, Mr Speaker. I’m surprised that people think that these are merely technical bills. I want to speak to the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill. Look, there are actually two quite important points to make here. The first one is in respect of undertakings of conveyancers. Now, in 2006, the law was changed to allow for this new profession of conveyancers, essentially to create competition in the market with lawyers for real estate transactions. One of the advantages it turns out that lawyers had that no one realised was that the courts would enforce undertakings.
: Now, an undertaking is often used in conveyancing transactions, and I can actually remember using them when you get halfway through a transaction and you’ve forgotten something. You might be like, “Oh, I forgot to get that document signed, but I undertake that I will deliver you a signed copy of that document. It’s sitting on my desk.” or whatever. The courts would take that to be a binding and enforceable promise. If your lawyer didn’t comply with it, not only could you be sued in court for it but it would be a professional breach. That didn’t exist in respect of conveyancers.
: In new section 38A, inserted by clause 5, the framework says that undertakings given by conveyancing practitioners are enforceable. That’s what the heading says, but it’s not what the section says. What it says in new section 38A(1) is “An affected person may make an application for summary judgment in relation to an undertaking” That’s all very good, but it’s kind of narrow because you should be able to make any kind of application on the basis of an undertaking, including an application to the High Court under its general jurisdiction.
: Now, it’s recognised that the District Court doesn’t have jurisdiction over lawyers in respect of undertakings, but you can basically go to the High Court in respect of a general undertaking by lawyers and get them enforced or injuncted or damages, whatever you like, any way you like. Summary judgment is a very narrow procedure which proceeds only on affidavits, so I’m perplexed as to why, if you’re suing a lawyer for an undertaking, you can use the whole jurisdiction of the High Court, but if you’re suing a conveyancer, you’ve only got summary judgment. That’s one.
: The second one is actually even more concerning. It might be that this needs to go back to select committee because it’s about the complaints service for lawyers. As it happens, I have some experience in this, because in a former job I was, in fact, the legal complaints review officer, which was essentially an appellate role from Law Society complaints standards committees. One of the challenges of complaints frameworks is a flood of shall we just say meritless complaints, for one reason or another. They might just not understand the rules and they’re just wildly wrong or they had unrealistic expectations or they could be vexatious or any other number, or it could have been 10 years ago. That was another one we used to see.
: The way the complaints system works is you send your complaint to the Law Society and then the Law Society kind of triages it. Sometimes they have a phone call, but by and large, if you want to complain, it then goes on to a standards committee, which is a group of lawyers and some non-lawyers as well to resolve it, even if it’s a vexatious or trivial or extremely old and stale complaint. What new section 135A, inserted by clause 7, does is it says that the complaints service itself can turn around these extremely low-level complaints.
: I can see why you didn’t send that to the Justice Committee, because there would have been a good bit of discussion around whether an administrator—because that’s what it is; probably a skilled one, but an administrator in the Law Society or the Society of Conveyancers—gets to turn around these complaints and say, “I think that’s too old.” “I think that’s too trivial.” “I think that’s without foundation.” or “I think that’s vexatious.” But that’s where we’ve got to.
: My concern actually goes a bit further, because in my experience as the legal complaints review officer, as with most complaints services, most of my time was spent dealing with either some very difficult lawyers or very difficult complainants. If you really want to upset a vexatious complainant, the best thing to do is to tell them their complaint is trivial or vexatious and turn it around at the first hurdle. What I am almost certain will happen here is that these will be challenged. Now, the difficulty is, as I see it, there is no way to challenge this complaint within the Law Society framework, within the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act framework. If you go to the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act, in the depths of it at about section 210 or something, it says that a person can complain to the legal complaints review officer about any final decision at a standards committee.
: The problem is this never got to the standards committee. This is a decision—and it’s final, because they’ve said that we’re not going to take it further to the standards committee, so you’ve got no right of appeal or review to the legal complaints review officer. So what will a vexatious litigant do? A vexatious litigant will take a judicial review. The whole idea of this system, which is entirely funded by levies on lawyers, is to be low cost, quick, and effective—it hasn’t always been either of those things, but that’s the idea—dispute resolution system for lawyers’ complaints.
: I do think there’s a missing part here. I actually get the motivation behind complaints services being able to turn around complaints. I’m not sure it’s a good idea, but I understand why the Minister has taken that route. Certainly, one of the challenges with lawyers’ standards committees is they take too long because they can become overwhelmed with the volume of complaints. But if you’re going to have an administrator—a faceless administrator if you like; not even a public servant but an employee of a private organisation—turning around complaints on the basis that they are meritless for one reason or another, then you had better be very careful about how you go about that. It may well be, and I’m hoping—and I see the Minister is in the House, and good on her for being here—that officials will be taking an interest in this debate as well and will be scratching their heads and thinking, “Oh, maybe we should have thought about that.”, because we know—and the Minister, who is the Minister for Courts, has been working hard on relieving the burden on the courts, including the High Court.
: A judicial review on the back of a complaint which doesn’t have merit—you’ve got to remember, if you’re going to judicially review this, you don’t have to prove that your complaint was right; you only have to prove that it wasn’t without some merit; that the decision made internally to extinguish the complaint was not appropriate; that it should have been given a hearing at the next stage. In fact, the grounds upon which they can do it are set out quite clearly: trivial, frivolous, vexatious, “The complainant does not have a sufficient personal interest.”—that’s often an opposing person. A disgruntled husband complaining against the wife’s lawyer is a common one you’d see—those sorts of things. The grounds are there, and you’ve got grounds to go, “Well, they’re wrong about that. I do have an interest which is sufficient, and I want to argue my case about that.”
: There’s actually a lot to be thought about there, and these complaints processes are tricky, but they do have to comply with natural justice. What we have here is, essentially, an administrative decision maker making a quasi-judicial decision without any right of appeal or recourse. When you frame it in those terms, we’ve got something of a problem. We’ll be exploring that a bit later on. Thank you for your time.
Dr HAMISH CAMPBELL (National—Ilam): It’s a great pleasure to rise and speak on the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill. These bills are part of a package of three bills in the regulatory systems justice amendment bill package, each focused on improving a different part of the justice system: the courts’ occupational regulation and tribunals. They improve access to justice by removing unnecessary barriers and making tribunal processes fairer and more accessible. Therefore, I commend the bills to the House.
SPEAKER: This is a split call—Georgie Dansey.
GEORGIE DANSEY (Labour): Tēnā koe e te Māngai o te Whare. I’m standing to speak on the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill. These bills are a package of four regulatory systems amendment bills administered by the Ministry of Justice.
: I’d like to start my contribution by challenging the previous speaker Steve Abel on his comments about these bills being boring. I think he just hasn’t read them in depth enough, because I’m sure my colleague the  Hon Duncan Webb thinks these are the most interesting things he’s ever seen in his life.
SPEAKER: Come on, I think you should give the House a proper reference if you’re going to make them.
GEORGIE DANSEY: Ha, ha! I’ve actually had the pleasure of speaking on a number of regulatory systems amendments bills, and you always learn new things about different areas of our society. I’ve spoken on boxing and contact sports in the past, and I’m pleased to speak on these too, because I think they do have some very valuable content in them.
: I think that getting our justice system processes right, which we’re very far from at this point, having an accessible and fair justice system, should be an absolute priority for any Government, of any stripe, who sits in this House. Anything we can do to make the justice system more accessible and more fair for people accessing the system is paramount. I hear stories constantly, as I’m sure other members do, around the barriers to accessing justice for people in New Zealand, whether that be financial or otherwise. In these two bills, there is some content that I see as improving that access to justice.
: I’ll talk about both, but I wanted to speak firstly about the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the technical changes. This bill will improve the operations and efficiency of tribunals. I thought it was pronounced “quas-ee”, but the Hon Duncan Webb just said “quas-aye”—
Hon Dr Duncan Webb: “Po-tay-toes”, “po-tah-toes.”
GEORGIE DANSEY: OK, “po-tay-toes”, “po-tah-toes.” OK, because I didn’t want to put my foot in it and say the wrong word in front of the Hon Duncan Webb!
Hon Rachel Brooking: What about the Rt Hon Gerry Brownlee?
GEORGIE DANSEY: I’m so sorry—I’m so sorry. Rt Hon Gerry Brownlee, Mr Speaker, I want to say the right words in front of you. And this is my third speech in front of you now. Back to the bill—in two minutes.
: This bill will improve the operations and efficiency of tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies by removing barriers to accessing justice, and it will clarify and resolve inconsistencies and gaps in the legislation. Of the quasi-judicial bodies, I think it’s interesting to see which ones are having changes to them: the Disputes Tribunal, the Motor Vehicle Disputes Tribunal, the Private Security Personnel Licensing Authority, the Complaints, Investigation and Prosecution Unit. I think it’s important that these bodies remain independent and can make independent decisions, because they affect the rights, responsibilities, and interests of all people.
: One of the pieces of legislation that caught my eye and that I thought was interesting was the change that will give the Disputes Tribunal referees the ability to order a respondent to pay the filing fee back to a wholly or partly successful applicant. If a party is successful, they will now be able to claim back that filing fee. As is in the notes, this will make a specific difference for people who don’t have a monetary outcome to their claim, because that filing fee is something and it could cause a grievance to a successful applicant in that space. This is one way that access to justice and fairness in the justice system is being changed through the changes in this bill. In some cases, the filing fee could be a significant portion of what the applicant receives, and so I think it’s an important change. I commend these bills to the House.
SUZE REDMAYNE (National—Rangitīkei): Thank you. Look, the benefits of these non-controversial bills have been well traversed, so I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate my friend and colleague Tom Rutherford, who was elected the chair of the Justice Committee on Monday. We wish you all the best. Go well. I commend the bills to the House.
DAN ROSEWARNE (Labour): Thank you, Mr Speaker. I’d to rise and take a call on the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill and just echo my colleague’s sentiment around how exciting these bills are. The Hon Dr Duncan Webb’s contribution was exceptionally exciting. For those members of the public that have just tuned in to watch these bills progress, I will attempt to cover off some of the key points with this legislation.
: These bills focus on improving systems that people interact with every day. They make changes to tribunal processes, occupational regulation, complaints procedures, and licensing arrangements, so that those systems operate more effectively and efficiently. Both bills have now completed the select committee process. The Justice Committee considered submissions on the tribunals bill and heard oral evidence from submitters. The Education and Workforce Committee received a larger number of submissions on the occupational regulation bill and heard evidence from a range of interested parties as well. The committees received advice from officials, support from the Office of the Clerk, and assistance from the Parliamentary Counsel Office as they worked through the details of both pieces of legislation.
: Labour supports the changes that have emerged from that process, and these bills are part of a wider programme of regulatory systems legislation administrated by the Ministry of Justice. The purpose of that work is not to revisit major policy decisions that Parliament has already made. The purpose is to identify parts of the legislation that can be improved through experience and feedback from regulators and professional bodies, and people like tribunal users and those responsible for administrating these systems on a daily basis, and it’s an important part of Parliament’s role. No regulatory framework stays perfect for ever. Over time, gaps emerge, inconsistencies develop, language becomes dated, and administrative processes no longer reflect how a sector actually operates. So, periodically, Parliament needs to revisit these settings and make improvements, and this bill does just that.
: The committee process demonstrated that point. Submitters raised practical issues, officials provided advice, and members tested the provisions that are before us, and the result is legislation that is stronger than what it was when it was first introduced. One of the themes running through both bills is public confidence. Whether somebody is dealing with a lawyer, engaging with a real estate professional, lodging a complaint with a regulator, or appearing before a tribunal, they need confidence that the rules are clear and that institutions involved have the ability to carry out their responsibilities properly. Confidence is built in different ways. Sometimes it comes through strong professional standards, sometimes it comes from effective complaint systems, sometimes it comes through regulators having access to information that they need to investigate concerns, and sometimes it comes through accessible dispute resolution processes that ordinary New Zealanders can use without excessive cost or complexity. Across these two bills, we see examples of all those things.
: The Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill focuses on three key areas: lawyers and conveyancers, the real estate sector, and provisions within the Prostitution Reform Act. Its purpose is to strengthen consumer protection, improve efficiency, remove inconsistencies, and reduce those unnecessary compliance costs across all of those systems.
: One of those significant changes concerns the Lawyers Complaints Service. Under this bill, complaints can be made subject to an initial assessment process before being referred to the lawyers standards committee. The legislation identifies circumstances where no further action may be appropriate, including where complaints are trivial, frivolous, or, as the Hon Dr Duncan Webb mentioned in his contribution, vexatious, made in bad faith, or excessively delayed, or where another remedy might very well exist. That intention is pretty straightforward. Complaints systems work best when resources are focused on matters that require investigation and resolution. Every profession depends on public confidence, and maintaining that confidence requires complaints processes that are both robust and efficient.
: The bill also contains significant reforms relating to the Real Estate Authority. The real estate sector plays a major role in the lives of New Zealanders; everyone knows that. For many families, purchasing a home is the largest financial commitment they will ever make, and there’s an expectation that professional standards will be maintained and that regulators will have the ability to investigate concerns where those standards may not have been met. The legislation strengthens the authority’s ability to obtain documents relevant to investigations. During select committee considerations, amendments were recommended to ensure that the authority must have reasonable grounds before exercising those powers and to clarify the circumstances in which relevant documents may be sought from those parties holding information relevant to an investigation. The bill also updates a number of licensing provisions. It allows licences to be renewed up to 12 months, I think it was, after expiring. It provides mechanisms that recognise the experience and knowledge of practitioners returning to the profession. These are practical changes that simplify administration while maintaining the expectations around competence and professional standards.
: There are also a number of amendments, as mentioned earlier, to the Prostitution Reform Act. Those changes update the references to criminal offences so that legislation continues to reflect the developments elsewhere in criminal law while preserving the existing policy intent around disqualification from holding a certificate, essentially.
: Taken together, the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill strengthens consumer protections. It improves the operation of complaints systems and provides regulators with clear tools to fulfil those responsibilities.
: Now, turning to the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill, the purpose of that bill is to improve the operation and efficiency of tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies, remove barriers to accessing justice, and address legislative inconsistencies to better support statutory authorities in carrying out their functions. One amendment relates to the Disputes Tribunal. As has already been traversed in the House today, the bill allows the tribunal to order reimbursement of filing fees where an applicant succeeds wholly or partly in their claim. For many New Zealanders, the Disputes Tribunal is the most accessible way to resolve disagreements without entering the formal court. The system was designed to provide a relatively low-cost and straightforward avenue for dispute resolution. The ability to reimburse filing fees recognises that, where somebody has pursued a legitimate claim successfully, there may be circumstances where reimbursement is appropriate. The legislation also preserves incentives for parties to reach settlement, recognising the value of resolving disputes before they require a formal determination.
: The bill also includes amendments relating to the appointment of referees. Those provisions formalise the assessment process used for appointments and reappointments, providing a more consistent mechanism for selecting people to carry out those very important roles. The quality of decision making within the tribunal depends heavily on the quality of those making those decisions, so transparent and credible appointment processes are very important. For that reason, I commend the bill to the House.
MILES ANDERSON (National—Waitaki): Thank you. Mr Speaker. This bill is about fixing the basics and building the future. I commend it.
Hon JAMES MEAGER (Minister for Hunting and Fishing): Thank you, Mr Speaker. Now, I won’t take a long call, but I just want to note my own congratulations for the new chair of the Justice Committee, Tom Rutherford. They seem to keep getting better and better and better as the term goes on. With that, I think the leadership shown by the Justice Committee is in good hands, and I commend this bill to the House.
: Motion agreed to.
: Bills read a second time.
SPEAKER: I declare the House in committee for consideration of the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill.

topicSummaries.topic: Part 1 Amendments to Disputes Tribunal Act 1988
topicSummaries.content:
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): Members, the House is in committee on the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill.
: We come first to the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill, and we begin with the debate on Part 1.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Madam Chair, for the opportunity to open the committee stage of the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill. I’m pleased to say that there was broad support across the House for this bill at its second reading, and I look forward to hearing the views of the other parties as we debate this bill.
: The bill amends five Acts to improve the effectiveness and the efficiency of tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies by reducing barriers to accessing justice and better enabling statutory authorities to investigate and regulate the industry. The amendments will, among other things, give disputes tribunal referees the ability to order a respondent to pay the filing fee to a successful applicant, to simplify the appointment process for disputes tribunal referees and Motor Vehicle Disputes Tribunal adjudicators, and provide a new information-gathering power to the unit responsible for private security investigations and prosecutions. These improvements will support the maintenance and continuous improvement of tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies, and this will help to ensure that the tribunal system is accessible and fit for purpose.
: I also wish to draw my Amendment Paper 353 to the attention of the House for consideration during this committee stage. This Amendment Paper is straightforward. It only makes some minor technical changes to ensure the provisions read as intended. I’m happy to take questions on the bill as we go through the committee.
Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan: Madam Chair.
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): Yes—just before I call Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan, I was just going to say that I omitted to say, before the Minister made her introduction, that Part 1 of the debate is on clauses 3 to 8A, “Amendments to Disputes Tribunal Act 1988”. The question is that Part 1 stand part.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Madam Chair. I think I want to start by, in some ways, slightly disagreeing with my colleague Steve Abel. I think the regulatory systems bills are some of the most interesting bills in terms of the committee stages, and I always found my engagement with the Minister, in particular, to be really enlightening, and it’s just, in general, a really good way to learn about the different kinds of legislations that we do have in the broader context of our legislative package here in Aotearoa New Zealand. They are quite exciting, in my opinion, but that’s just me.
: I want to start by looking at clause 4 for the Disputes Tribunal Act, “Section 8 amended (Selection of candidates for appointment or reappointment as Referees)”. I’ve got two questions for the Minister to begin with, and this also touches on the Minister’s Amendment Paper 353. I’m noting that, in both cases, what we have seen—sorry, this clause 4, subclause (2)—is a shift between using “shall” to “must”. Now, from a legislative drafting perspective, my understanding is that both fulfil the same requirement.
Hon Rachel Brooking: No: “shall” is out of date.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN: Well, that was my question, the Hon Rachel Brooking. Can I just check with the Minister: are the changes here simply an update from using “shall” to “must” in general? And, if that is the case, are these the only instances in this bill where we’re seeing the change from “shall” to “must”? If not, then why weren’t there—as far as I can see—a complete package of changes from that? Maybe I am old-school, but personally I’m a fan of “shall”. That’s my first question.
