: My second question to the Minister: one of the things we heard as part of the select committee stage, and I have to refresh my memory a little bit with the departmental report, is around independence when we’re looking at the appointment of referees—noting that the chief executive, in this case, appoints them, and what we’re seeing with this particular section is that it removes the notice period for people to be able to submit names to the appointment or reappointment as referees. But what I’m curious to know is, my understanding of the process is that the chief executive appoints the assessment panel; does the assessment panel then appoint the referee or the assessment panel recommends the appointment of the referee to the chief executive, who then reappoints or appoints the referee? Those are my two questions. Thank you, Minister.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Madam Chair. To speak to the member’s first part, about the “shall”, the “must”, and the little—what’s going on over there, I do actually agree with the member, Rachel Brooking. It is quite important when you use “shall” and when you use “must”, and we are making these minor amendments, really, to just have consistency and clarity when the wording is used, and, of course, that’s why we’re making that small amendment. The member asked why it wasn’t changed originally: these are small little words that often get picked up as officials start going through amendments that came about from select committee and realise, “Oh, actually, a ‘shall’ must be a ‘must.’” That’s why that change is there.
: In regard to the suitability of appointed—the referees side of it, as well: what I am told is that the disputes tribunal candidates currently require a nomination by a community member in order to be appointed. The amendment will remove that requirement from the disputes tribunal referee appointment process. The disputes tribunal has a strong appointments process to ensure that the referees are well suited to being appointed, so this change is only simplifying that process. The candidates are still required to name three people who will, indeed, referee as to their character and their capability to be a referee with the assessment panel. That’s all that is changing there; the process itself, after that, is continuing to stay the same.
CAMILLA BELICH (Labour): Thank you, Madam Chair, and thanks to the Minister for her engagement. It’s good to have some analysis of that Amendment Paper, which does cover clause 4, so it’s even in the right place in this debate, and I do agree with—
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): That’s always helpful.
CAMILLA BELICH: That’s right. I do agree with Lawrence Xu-Nan that, actually, for a committee stage, these omnibus regulatory system bills are designed in a way that does make it easier to scrutinise and, also, we get to look at different things.
: Sticking with the disputes tribunal amendments in Part 1—and my colleague has spoken to clause 4—I want to look at clauses 5 and 6. I’ve got three questions. The first question is on clause 5. Clause 5 inserts new section 43(5). This is in relation to the filing fee, which is probably one of the major changes in the disputes tribunal; that the respondent may get the applicant’s filing fee paid in whole or part. I wanted to know if this is specifically drafted in a broad way so that it can be up to the discretion of the referee as to whether it’s paid based, basically, on merit, because it might be that the claim is majority unsuccessful but one tiny part of it is successful and, I suppose, in that instance, a filing fee could be ordered. So, any guidance the Minister had—I mean, that’s a possible issue of future statutory interpretation, possibly; Duncan Webb may have some further thoughts on that. Anyway, that was my first question.
: The second question I had was following on from that in (6)—so that would be new section 43(6) that is inserted by clause 5. In this, it states that the agreement to pay the filing fee cannot be made—I think—if there’s a settlement agreed. Now, I wanted to just clarify for the Minister that that this isn’t intended to be a prohibition if there’s a settlement made, but, if there was a settlement made, it would be assumed that the settlement would cover the filing fee. That would be my usual understanding.
Hon Dr Duncan Webb: Yep, $450.
CAMILLA BELICH: Yes. Is that how much it is?
Hon Dr Duncan Webb: It can be—up to.
CAMILLA BELICH: Up to $450. I think that’s also an important clarification for statutory interpretation, so that it would be allowed to be part of the settlement, not prohibited from that. It would be great, actually, to have some statement or advice from the Minister on there.
: My third question—I will move on; others may have further questions on clause 5, but I don’t. On clause 6, I looked back to the original Disputes Tribunal Act, which this deletes section 59 from. That section is about the entitlement of referees to be considered an employee for the purposes of accident compensation. That just seems to be a wholesale deletion of that. I’m not sure if it’s covered somewhere else or what the thinking was behind that, but obviously that would probably be of a concern to referees if they weren’t entitled to ACC—they currently are entitled to ACC as an employee. There may be some context that I’m missing there—maybe it’s inserted somewhere else—but I’d be grateful for some clarification on those three questions.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Madam Chair. I thank the member also for her questions. In regard to the changes in clause 5, we are not inserting a new section 43; we’re just amending section 43. This is in regard to the respondent paying the applicant the cost of any filing fee, wholly or partly successful. The member asked about when a settlement agreement is made and whether or not the referee can then determine whether or not to make a payment. This is actually allowing the referee to be given discretion in order to make such orders. The member was quite right when she indicated there could be a settlement where there is a monetary involvement, but there could also be a settlement where there isn’t. It could be just the handover of a property or something like that. That would then allow, even when there is a settlement, the referee to be able to have that discretion on whether or not to give full or even partial remittance of that filing fee, so just giving them that ability to do that. I hope that answers both the questions on Part 5—please come back if I haven’t.
: On clause 6, the deletion in regard to the ACC, we’re repealing that employee provision because the referees around all the other tribunals are contractors and as contractors they pay their own ACC claims. In this particular tribunal, half of them are not contractors. We’re just looking for consistency with all the other tribunal adjudicators where they are all contractors and they all pay their own ACC. At the moment in this one, we’ve have got half paying ACC and half not—half being employees. We just want to ensure that they are all on the same wave length there and they’re all doing exactly the same thing, which is contracting and paying their own ACC levies.
Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB (Labour—Christchurch Central): Thank you, Madam Chair. Thanks to the Minister for Courts for the engagement there. I want to talk about clause 8, and in particular I want to talk about clause 8(2), which is always a tricky one because it says “Revoke rule 36(1).” so you have to go to the rules to find out what it actually does. Rule 36 is about the recruitment process, if you like, for disputes tribunal referees. In fact, 36(1) is the first step. It provides two things: that there should be advertisements in the area that you’re looking for them—interestingly, it doesn’t say “newspaper advertisement”; it just says “advertisement” so it could be anywhere, could be an electronic advertisement—and also to be publicised by such other means as the secretary considers necessary, kind of a general discretion.
: Firstly, it would seem odd to remove the clause which says “Go out and publicise that you are looking for dispute tribunal referees.” I accept that there’s always going to be a discretion. There’s no prohibition on doing that. But I would have thought that in what is essentially the Public Service—quasi-judicial officers—that you actually want to go out publicly. Because the other process—and this is what the legal profession has done for centuries—is to look towards people you know. That is to say people like you, who are your mates, and ask them. That’s not always good.
: But the other thing is section—or clause, rule, whatever you like—36(1), which actually sets the scene for getting candidates, because it says: “For the purpose of encouraging the nomination, as candidates for appointment as Referees, of men and women from diverse backgrounds and diverse ethnic and age groups, the chief executive shall”—and then it goes on to say advertise. I’m wondering if that’s the reason that was removed, because the Government doesn’t want to emphasise the need for a—and, in fact, disputes tribunal referees, although there are mainly lawyers, they are generally a diverse bunch of people. To be honest, I can’t see why you’d remove that clause. It’s innocuous, it does some useful work, and it gives a theme. If it was the diversity bit that you didn’t like, you could just get rid of that and say, “For the purpose of encouraging the nomination of competent people.” But you still want to have a requirement that it be a public process rather than a closed one—a shoulder-tapping exercise. I’d actually really appreciate the Minister responding as to why rule 36(1) is being revoked.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Madam Chair. In response to the member on clause 8, the clause 8 change in there is a consequential amendment because of the changes that we’re making in clause 4. I’m just advised there is still a publicly advertised advertisement that goes out for this, but it relates to the changes that are made by clause 4. It’s consequential. It removes the requirement for the disputes tribunal candidates to be nominated a community member and to be appointed. All it is, really, is a consequential amendment to the change that we’re making in clause 4 to amend that section 36, and there is still some form of advertisement.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Madam Chair. Just following up from what the Minister for Courts is saying, I think there is another important aspect of the Hon Dr Duncan Webb’s question around the requirement for the diversity component of that.
: But the question that I have there is around, like we said before, when we’re looking at the expanded role of referees—or we talked about community magistrates before and a number of other ones. They don’t go through some of the similar processes we see with the appointment of judges. Whether you’re self-representing or have a lawyer present is another matter, but I think one of the things I’m thinking of, particularly as we’re seeing an increase in, for example, Asian populations here in Aotearoa New Zealand who have also started seeing an increasing number of cases going through all stages of our courts. I just wanted to check in terms of, for the candidates or for the appointment of referees—because we do hear from Asian lawyers a number of these sort of nuances within our court system not being understood or accessible to the Asian population, particularly if English is a second language and you are requiring a translator, etc. I just want to check: from an appointment perspective, what are the considerations the Minister has, either in the existing rules or some of the changes we’re seeing here that would take into consideration the nuances of the cultural diversity that we see, not necessarily in the appointment body or the referees themselves, but the broader society in general? That being my first question.
: The second question is I want to check with the Minister going back to what the Minister said regarding clause 6, which is consistent between the disputes tribunal referees compared to some of the other tribunal referees who are self-employed and disputes tribunal referees are being employees as opposed to being self-employed. I want to check with the Minister: if they are self-employed, what then would be the financial implication for them when they are paying for ACC as a self-employed person? Because, for example, when we’re looking at some of the questions we asked as a part of the select committee process, we do see that if you are self-employed—for example, if section 59 is repealed—at different earning levels you will be seeing the referees having quite a bit higher levy than you have to pay for ACC.
: I want to check with the Minister if this is something that has already been consulted on with existing referees—some of the feedback you’ve heard in terms of now that they are self-employed, there will be additional costs to them in terms of paying for their ACC levy. To give an example, when we’re looking at one of the bands—let’s say if you’re earning $25,000, the existing is $362.50. But then if section 59 is repealed, you need to add in the ACC Work levy, the Working Safer levy, and those additional levies which make it up to $410, which is $471.50 including GST, which is quite a bit higher than $362.50. I just want to check with the Minister on what the feedback is that she has received regarding the increase in ACC cost.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): I was talking a little bit through the member’s questions, so if I have not addressed or do not address all of his questions, I invite him to stand and ask again. Before I start, I’d just like to make a correction to something I said about clause 5, which is the ability for the adjudicator to be able to award the filing fee after a settlement. I made mention, apparently incorrectly, that if there is a settlement, the adjudicator could determine whether or not to pay the filing fee back, and I’ve got that wrong. If there is a settlement, it is the settlement in itself, and a filing fee will not be paid in that instance. That will be up to the adjudicator, just to make sure that there is fairness. This is why the adjudicator is given some leeway there to be able to make the decisions. The referee cannot award a filing fee on top of an agreed settlement. The settlement would cover all matters. If the referee thought that was unfair, they could choose not to endorse it and make the filing fee go to that person instead.
: With the referees, again, at clause 6—this is about the ACC. As I mentioned, this is about consistency. It’s to ensure that all tribunal referees—not just tribunal referees in this area; that tribunal referees across the entire tribunal sector are all contractors, and they all pay their own ACC levies. I do have some figures that are there, but it’s creating a fairness so that they are all paying the same amount; you’re not having some pay one amount and others pay another amount. You want all of them across all the tribunals in the court system to be able to be paying that same amount. That’s why we’re looking for that consistency.
: To the member’s first question, the policy intent at the time was to ensure that a referee was a person who had standing in the community and that they were nominated by the community. That was, in a way, to try and create the diversity of referees, but the requirement is not being used as intended. There’s not been an independently nominated referee under this system in many, many years. I understand that in practice, there’s a public call for expressions of interest, and this is what I meant by continuing to advertise. As part of that, each candidate has to find a nominee.
: This proposal would remove a provision that was introduced to increase diversity among the pool of referees; however, we do note that there is now a greater mix of gender and age groups amongst the referees that we have. Additionally, the Disputes Tribunal has other mechanisms to encourage ethnic diversity, such as the establishment of the Māori referees committee and the establishment of the Pasifika referees committee. I did ask my officials: do we have Asian referees committee? Not yet. Maybe that is something that future Governments can look to.
CAMILLA BELICH (Labour): Thank you, Madam Chair. Thanks to the Minister. It’s been said before, but we really do appreciate the constructive engagement on some of these issues.
: I think the Minister has answered my questions in relation to the earlier questions I had in relation to clauses 5 and 6. The only kind of quick follow-ups that I would want to add are—I understand about the settlement having to cover everything. I think it’s really good to have that direction, because if a settlement didn’t cover a filing fee—for example, it often happens in settlements that perhaps you forget around that filing fee. It could be someone who’s entirely successful—or the application fee or whatever it’s called; yeah, filing fee. I mean, my view would be that the most equitable way would be—obviously, the situation we want to avoid is that we wouldn’t want it to be paid twice. We wouldn’t want a settlement amount to cover the filing fee and then for it to be paid separately again, because that wouldn’t, obviously, be fair. But if a settlement covers the filing fee, then, of course, there shouldn’t be an order. Probably, in an ideal world, the ability to make a filing fee order if the settlement didn’t cover that would be, probably, better.
: But I think having clarity for those people in the Disputes Tribunal is important, and that’s why I’m glad that we’ve had these questions. They’ll be on the record if anyone is interested to look at that in the future. They’ll have clarity that, as I understand it, if there is a settlement, that needs to be fulsome, and it needs to include any application for the reimbursement of a filing fee. If that’s wrong, please let me know, but otherwise I think it’s good to have that on the record.
: In terms of ending the employment, I do take the point around consistency, but I do wonder, for the group of referees who are currently considered employees, have there been discussions with them around the changes in terms of them doing their own ACC? They wouldn’t be entitled to KiwiSaver. Obviously, employment has a totally different rights profile from contracting. The fact that we’re doing this by statute is significant, and I just wanted to know if there had been any thought and put into that and also if there’s any consequential raise in the amount of remuneration that they would receive. Obviously, it’s not, maybe, a huge amount, probably, for what they’re receiving, for them to pay their own ACC, but that will be a cost that they’re facing that they don’t currently have to face.
: I think in relation to that part, which is still Part 1, that’s probably all the questions that I have, so up to the Minister. If anything I’ve said is wrong, it would be good to have clarification. Otherwise, that’s all.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): I think the member has its spot on in regard to the settlement side of it. My apologies for saying the incorrect thing in the first place, but I think that we’ve got to a place where we’ve both been able to make it quite clear for anybody that will be listening.
: Again, when we come back to the ACC, we’ve really got to make it so that it’s fair on every tribunal referee. When you have some paying one rate and a few paying another, it’s not fair on the others that are paying less or more than anyone else. As I’ve mentioned before to the Green member, this is really about having consistency across all tribunal referees and adjudicators throughout the country so that they are all paying the same amount dependent on whatever their wages are. Some work part time, some work full time, and those amounts themselves will change depending on what their income is and who they work for.
: I will point out as well: some tribunal referees and adjudicators are on multiple different tribunals. Some are paid, I guess, as a contractor, and some are being paid another way. It’s actually going to make it easier for those people that are multiple referees or adjudicators to be able to contract back to the ministry instead of having two different versions of how they go about paying ACC. I come back again to the consistency in ensuring that all adjudicators are paying ACC levies as contractors to the Crown.
Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan: Madam Chair?
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan—just recognising it’s a smallish part, so we’re just into final points of clarification on this part.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Yep. One final question from me—a short question, and maybe a short response from the Minister. Are the Disputes Tribunal referees the only ones, then, who are currently still employees—everyone else is a contractor now?
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): To be fair, I’m actually not aware of whether or not they are. I’m looking at just what’s in front of me, and this is the tribunal that we’re dealing with. I suspect that if we have others like this, we would pull it into a future regulatory standards bill. But this one is talking about tribunals. No one else has come in, so I suspect this may be the only one, but I’m not 100 percent sure.
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): The question is that the Minister’s amendments to Part 1 set out on Amendment Paper 353 be agreed to.
: Amendments agreed to.
: Part 1 as amended agreed to.

topicSummaries.topic: Part 2 Amendments to Motor Vehicle Sales Act 2003
topicSummaries.content:
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): Members, we come now to Part 2, the debate on clauses 9 and 10, “Amendments to Motor Vehicle Sales Act 2003”. The question is that Part 2 stand part. Dan Rosewarne.
DAN ROSEWARNE (Labour): Thank you, Madam Chair.
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): I know your interest in Holdens will be driving something here.
DAN ROSEWARNE: Thank you for your contributions so far, Minister. My question is in relation to clause 10, which amends section 82 of the Motor Vehicle Disputes Tribunal, and replacing section 82(3)(a) with subparagraph (a) there. The questions we need to ask here are probably pretty much what the people of New Zealand would want to know. A lot of us buy vehicles, some are second-hand vehicles, we drive them off the lot, and there might be a catastrophic failure—an engine might blow—we might enter into that Motor Vehicle Disputes Tribunal process. I suppose a lot of Kiwis at home would want to know: how would this amendment here improve the motor vehicle dispute process for consumers?
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Madam Chair. It’s a good question; I thank the member for it. This is actually going to help speed up the process. At the moment, the Motor Vehicle Disputes Tribunal adjudicators all need to have a current practising certificate. That makes it quite difficult to get people with a current practising certificate to put their hand up to even be adjudicators. This change will mean that they won’t need to have a current practising certificate but they do still need to be legally qualified. You might have, for example, a retired lawyer who doesn’t have an active practising certificate but is still legally qualified. They need to have at least five years’ experience in law—a minimum of five years’ experience—to be considered for this role. This means it’ll be less restrictive and it’s going to help reduce delays in the appointment process. Of course, if we can reduce delays there, then we help reduce delays in the tribunal itself.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Madam Chair. I just want to check with the Minister for Courts one question on clause 10. My understanding of clause 10 is currently the adjudicator has to have a practising certificate for at least five years, and that’s kind of the baseline requirement. But this particular one allows it to be not retrospective, but it allows a barrister or barrister and solicitor to have a past practising certificate that has now lapsed but then they are able to continue to be adjudicators. So you’re looking at maybe a greater pool of people who could be adjudicators maybe, and also now the five years no longer need to be consecutive. I guess my question number one is: does it allow there to be a greater pool of adjudicators as a result of this? Also, has there been any work done? Because it wasn’t, I think, even something we considered as a part of the Justice Committee. Does it affect the quality of the adjudication that you might see if solicitors, for example, their certificate has lapsed and maybe they were a barrister or solicitor 30 years ago for five years and they technically now meet this requirement? Has there been any work done on the quality as well?
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Madam Chair. As mentioned earlier, it’s more about trying to get these adjudicators in. They don’t need to have had necessarily just completed five years with the practising certificate—they need to have a minimum of five years’ legal experience. This is where you can get those retired people that come in. They will be appointed based on their abilities. The panel that appoints those individuals will have to look at who those individuals are. It doesn’t really matter whether or not they’ve just retired recently or retired 10 years ago. They have that legal experience behind them. I would have thought that if they retired or left five years ago or 10 years ago, they would have had a lifetime of experience, no doubt. But they still need to fit the criteria for the panel that will appoint them and make sure that they are fit for that. I guess the question that I was asked is: does it increase the pool? It will hugely increase the pool, and it means that we can have more adjudicators in a timely fashion and get people through the system quicker.
: Part 2 agreed to.

topicSummaries.topic: Part 3 Amendments to Parole Act 2002, and Schedule
topicSummaries.content:
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): Members, we come now to Part 3, the debate on clauses 11 to 16—“Amendments to Parole Act 2002”—and the Schedule. The question is that Part 3 stand part.
CAMILLA BELICH (Labour): Thank you, Madam Chair. The Parole Act changes are interesting and I’ve been looking through them to try and understand the purpose—and I’ve got the Parole Act here in front of me as well. I just wanted to ask the Minister for Courts: it appears to me that the main thrust of these changes—and I’m looking at clause 13 and also the new Schedule, which is inserted in clause 14. When I looked at the Parole Act as it currently stands, I think the salaries for members of the Parole Board were set by the Higher Salaries Commission. I’m reliably informed by my colleague that that has been defunct for a while. I wanted to know if that’s correct, and, if so, how have the salaries been determined of the Parole Board? Or is it just something that’s been in a static waiting period until this bill comes into place? That’s on clause 13. That was, I think, in 13(2) the replacement of section 122(1). It seems to refer to the deletion of the Higher Salaries Commission or the reference to that.
: I also discussed this with my colleague Dr Duncan Webb, who by the way—and this is referring to the previous section—would fulfil the criteria of someone who could be appointed to the Motor Vehicle Disputes Tribunal board, as would I and many other former lawyers on this house. That shows you how wide the pool could be under that previous part, but I don’t have a question about that—it was just a comment.
: In this bill, clause 13(3), which replaces section 122(2), also reflects the fact that a judge could be on the Parole Board and not have it affect their terms and conditions. I understand from my learned colleague that that is quite a usual clause to be put in. I was going to ask a series of questions about, “Why is this? Is this relating to a particular individual?”
Hon Dr Duncan Webb: Who is it? Who’s the awkward judge?
CAMILLA BELICH: Ha, ha! Yeah. If the Minister could confirm if Dr Duncan Webb is right: that it is simply a usual clause to have in this and not related to a single individual.
: I suppose the last question I had around the Parole Act at the stage—unless anything major arises—is just in relation to the Schedule, which I think comes into this section?
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): Yes, it does.
CAMILLA BELICH: Yeah. So that’s the Schedule right at the back of the bill, and that appears to me to be a transitional provision. That may assist with my initial question around the Higher Salaries Commission, but just wanting to know basically a sequence of what’s happened—obviously the Higher Salaries Commission not being effective and then us not passing this bill, and then what will happen once this bill is passed in relation to that responsibility for remuneration in clause 13(1), then going back to the actual Parole Board itself.
: I would be grateful if the Minister could kind of allay some concerns around the separation in terms of the Remuneration Authority being separate from the Parole Board and then making sure that that is separate. I may have answered my own question with that, but that does appear to be a sufficient separation in the determination of the people who receive the salaries and the people who actually set them.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, and I will clarify for the member and speak to clauses 13, 14, and the Schedule there. Currently, we have four roles on the New Zealand Parole Board where their fees are being determined by the Cabinet Fees Framework. The others, who are members of the judiciary, have their remuneration determined by the Remuneration Authority. The amendment will ensure that the Remuneration Authority considers all of the remuneration for all members, because it’s inappropriate for the Cabinet Fees Framework to be looking at the fees network for what could possibly be judges that come through. It must be independent, so that’s why we’re making that change.
: The member is also quite right that the schedule is like a transitional part, because, while we make that change, we need to ensure that those four members of the Parole Board continue to be paid until we get this into force. Clause 14 is amending that schedule to make it transitional to ensure that they continue to be paid while that takes place. The Remuneration Authority is not empowered to make an official remuneration determination until the bill’s commencement date, and that’s why we need to have that transitional period through there. I hope that answers the question.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you for that, Minister. I think, just to follow up, I have never heard of the Cabinet Fees Framework before. One of the questions asked was about the fact that—sorry, this is clause 13(2). What has been replaced—what was previously there—is “Higher Salaries Commission”. Can I just clarify: is the Higher Salaries Commission part of the Cabinet Fees Framework? Does it sit under the Cabinet Fees Framework? I understand the other parts that the Minister for Courts said, in terms of consistency with the Remuneration Authority, but it’s just the current clause and what the Minister said—I don’t know if they are the same thing. That’s all.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): I’d not even heard of that until the member stood up and actually talked about that. All I’m aware of is that they’re currently paid under the Cabinet Fees Framework and this is why we need to change it, to make sure they come under the Remuneration Authority, to ensure that there is that distance, especially between the executive and the judiciary.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Madam Chair, thank you. While the Minister for Courts gets some guidance, I would be quite interested because that’s what it currently says in section 122(1) of the Parole Act. Can I just check: if it’s the Cabinet Fees Framework—we know that the Remuneration Authority is independent, and that’s also good in terms of consistency. Is the Cabinet Fees Framework also, then, an independent thing, or does it get determined “dependently”, I guess? I don’t know how else to phrase that. Is the Cabinet Fees Framework determining their own remuneration, whereas the Remuneration Authority sits outside of all that? I don’t know if that actually makes any sense!
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Madam Chair. No, I didn’t quite get that, sorry. The question that the member Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan is asking me is going a little bit further than what’s actually in the bill, and I’m sure that the member could probably Google that question and get the answer to it. What I’m looking to do is ensure that everybody is paid under the same network, which is the Remuneration Authority, rather than the Cabinet Fees Framework, especially in order that, if there are judges on the Parole Board, they do not come under the executive framework, that they come under an independent one.
: Part 3 agreed to.

topicSummaries.topic: Part 4 Amendments to Private Security Personnel and Private Investigators Act 2010
topicSummaries.content:
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): Members, we come to Part 4, the debate on clauses 17 to 39, “Amendments to Private Security Personnel and Private Investigators Act 2010”. The question is that Part 4 stand part.
Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB (Labour—Christchurch Central): Thank you, Madam Chair. As we move through this Act, I think we’ll probably be through it relatively soon. I want to skip a lot of the technical stuff in the first sections, which appears to be largely wording, and get to new section 73AAA, which is “Complaint against unlicensed persons, etc”.
: I can certainly understand why there should be a power to make complaints about people who are behaving as if they are licensed security personnel or private investigators. I guess my question, really, relates to subsection (3) of that new section 73AAA, because, under subsection (2), it says that a constable can file a complaint with the authority or another person with the leave of the authority. I can kind of understand why that would be the case, although, in many ways, I’m not even sure that is appropriate—perhaps a justification of why leave is needed.
: Then, in subsection (3), it says the Licensing Authority “may” grant leave—I emphasise that word on purpose—only if the authority is satisfied the complainant has an interest greater than the general public and that it’s not frivolous or vexatious. I can imagine, if you’re at a pub and someone thinks you’ve misbehaved and you get thrown out and it turns out that the person isn’t a licensed security guard, and they should have been, and they acted inappropriately, you should then be able to complain on the basis that they were acting as a security guard when, in fact, they weren’t a security guard. But, I guess, my real point is this—and it may well be in law that the Licensing Authority is obliged to allow you to complain if you’ve got a legitimate complaint. So, rather than saying that the Licensing Authority “may” grant leave, in fact, that shouldn’t be discretionary. The Licencing Authority “must” grant leave where it is satisfied that they have a greater than ordinary interest and it’s a legitimate good-faith complaint.
: Private investigators are another thing: if someone’s conducting themselves and presenting themselves as a private investigator, it gives some sort of authenticity to them. People who then deliver up information to them, thinking they’ve got a legitimate and responsible investigation under way, have, essentially, a right to make that complaint rather than a mere discretionary possibility at the hands of the Licensing Authority. I guess, once again, it’s the question about an administrative discretion going a little bit wide.
: I guess my next thread, possibly third thread, is: if they don’t get the right to make that complaint—if they are wrongly refused that right—what can they then do? They are my questions.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Madam Chair. If you’d bear with me, Madam Chair, I actually have an answer which might help the member Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan. It’ll be very, very quick. I’m told that the Higher Salaries Commission was replaced by the Remuneration Authority, so that might help us with an understanding there.
: In regard to the member Dr Duncan Webb’s questions, currently, the Licensing Authority cannot explicitly accept complaints about security personnel who are or might be in breach of requirements to hold a licence or certificate of approval under the Act. However, in practice, it does accept those complaints, because this is important to ensure that we keep public confidence in the private security industry.
: This clause will explicitly confirm the Licensing Authority’s ability to accept those complaints. It will remove any ambiguity and assist the Licencing Authority in carrying out what is its statutory functions.
Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan: Madam Chair?
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): The question is that the Minister’s amendments to Part 4—
Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan: Madam Chair?
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): Sorry, no one called.
Hon Dr Duncan Webb: He did.
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): No, I’m sorry. We went through this yesterday.
Hon Dr Duncan Webb: You didn’t look.
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): No one called with their voice. The question is that the Minister’s amendments to Part 4 set out on Amendment Paper 353 be agreed to.
: Amendments agreed to.
: Part 4 as amended agreed to.

topicSummaries.topic: Part 5 Amendments to Unit Titles Act 2010
topicSummaries.content:
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): Members, we now come to Part 5. Part 5 is the debate on clauses 40 and 41, “Amendments to Unit Titles Act 2010”. The question is that Part 5 stand part.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): With this particular part, I want to check with the Minister in terms of clause 41, section 176 amended. I want to check because, from what I can see in the original version No. 1 of this bill, as well as the departmental report, it is still not entirely clear what is trying to be achieved with this particular clause around unit title disputes. Particularly, I think, the part that says: ”Without limiting subsection (1), rules made” and ”apply in respect of the hearing and determination of a unit title dispute by a Tenancy Tribunal.” So I think, if the Minister wouldn’t mind, just to sort of highlight on this particular part in relation to what we’re seeing in the context of subsection (1), I’m assuming section 176, subsection (1).
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Madam Chair. The existence of the Residential Tenancy (Unit Title Disputes) Rules 2011, they seem to be currently not very clear and there is some confusion about whether different documents service provisions in another Act should apply. So this proposal will make it clear that the rules exist and apply to how documents should be served for unit title disputes. So this is going to improve clarity and ease the use of the Act. It also makes absolutely no operational changes.
CAMILLA BELICH (Labour): Thank you, Madam Chair. I’m just bringing these unit titles up as we speak, but—
Hon Phil Twyford: Through a loud voice.
CAMILLA BELICH: So I’m using my loud voice; thank you, colleagues, for that.
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): Can I just make it clear that usually when we start a committee stage, I look to both of—or any Opposition parties that are here. But once we go on, if there’s silence, I’m assuming that no one’s taking the call.
CAMILLA BELICH: Thank you. I just had a question around the Unit Titles Act. The unit titles are a part of our residential property system—and obviously the Unit Titles Act is not one of the oldest Acts that we have. But I just wanted to know, in terms of the future of unit titles, you said that there wasn’t anything that was actually changing the substantive policy intent on this, but was there any advice received on whether this would be something that would be more likely to continue as it is into the future, or is there kind of a view around the nature of how unit titles are looked at. The reason I raise this is in Auckland, for example, we had, for a period of time, a number of different legal ways that ownership was recorded within our kind of wider Torrens system that have now kind of fallen out of favour. So the cross-lease system obviously continues and is still something which is a valid form of legal ownership of land, but it has—this is a generalisation—fallen out of favour with the way that the councils have utilised their powers there. In terms of unit titles, I just wanted to know if that was something that had been thought of in terms of updating that piece of legislation.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): This particular amendment is purely about making sure that there are clear rules that exist—rules that do apply to how documents are served. This is about, now, that service for the unit titles disputes at the moment is not clear. So all this section is doing is making sure that those that are serving documents under this particular section are very clear about how it is that they are meant to do that. That’s all that I have been advised on.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Madam Chair. I just have one final question on this section, and I thank the Minister for that response. Can I just check, in terms of what the Minister says and the clarity provides, because it makes references to the rules made under section 116 of the Residential Tenancies Act, are those existing rules now applicable here or does it in fact empower this section then to go and make additional rules under section 116 of the Residential Tendencies Act?
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): It’s purely saying that there are rules; that there’s currently rules and they must apply.
: Part 5 agreed to.
: Schedule agreed to.

CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): Members, we come now to our final debate, clauses 1 and 2, the debate on “Title” and “Commencement”.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Madam Chair. I actually just have a very, very short question for the Minister. I think—if it’s okay with you, Madam Chair—this will apply to this bill and also the next one that we are going to committee stage on, which is around the fact that there has been a delay. Although the commencement date is the day after Royal assent, there has been a delay since when this got reported back from the select committee. I believe, like I mentioned in my second reading, it’s been about 12 months since being reported back from that. Can I just check with any of the changes in this bill particularly, is that something that those various agencies etc., that are responsible for this, are already working towards updating it? Have they updated it and are waiting for it to go live the minute this gets Royal assent, or will they only start to work on some of the additional processes that we’ve mentioned here once it’s gone live? That’s my question on commencement.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Madam Chair, thank you. The commencements are for these five different areas of legislation that are being changed here. I do know that in the following bill that’s going to come, there are different commencement dates. I’ve not been told that there are different dates for these particular five; what I have been told is that the Act will come into force the day after Royal assent. So therefore I would presume that the ministry is all ready to go, and the moment that we get Royal assent we will be able to implement this. One thing I will say: yes, there has been a delay between when this came back from select committee, but I think that speaks very soundly to the large number of bills that this Government is putting through the Justice Committee. In fact, I’m aware that the number of bills that’s gone through the Justice Committee by Minister Goldsmith and myself actually outweighs every other bill that’s gone through every other select committee. So the reason why we have a delay here, even though it’s very important, is it’s a priority.
: Clause 1 agreed to.
: Clause 2 agreed to.
: Bill to be reported with amendment.

topicSummaries.topic: Part 1 Amendments to Lawyers and Conveyancers Act 2006
topicSummaries.content:
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): Members, we now come to the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill. We begin with the debate on Part 1. Part 1 is the debates on clauses 3 to 11, Amendments to Lawyers and Conveyancers Act 2006. The question is that Part 1 stand part.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Madam Chair, thank you for the opportunity to open the committee stage of the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill. I’m pleased to say that there was broad support across the House for this bill at second reading, and I look forward to hearing the views of the other parties as we debate the bill. This bill amends the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act, the Prostitution Reform Act, the Real Estate Agents Act, to increase protections for regulated professionals, such as real estate agents, and for consumers of those regulated services. The amendments will, among other things, enable the undertakings or professional commitments of conveyances to be enforced in the High Court in the same way that lawyers’ undertakings are; to remove a disproportionately harsh punishment for real estate agents who failed to complete their continuing professional development or pay their fees on time; and to ensure that the Real Estate Authority has the investigative powers that are required to investigate allegations of unlicensed trading and ensure licensees are meeting their obligations.
: These improvements will support the maintenance and continuous improvement of the occupational regulation regimes to ensure that regulated services are performed with reasonable care and skill, and promote and protect the interests of consumers. I also wish to draw to attention my Amendment Paper 636 to the House for consideration during this committee stage. This Amendment Paper makes minor and technical changes to the current drafting in the bill, including an amendment to ensure the policy intent of one of the changes is achieved.
: I also note that there are two Amendment Papers to this Amendment Paper in regard to clause 25. These are technical amendments. I am hopeful that the parties across the House got a copy of this beforehand—I did ask my office to get it to you. These are minor amendments that were picked up at the very last minute by the Real Estate Authority. They are just technical amendments—wording changes. They thought that they would take the opportunity to get to this while they could, and I can speak more to that once we get to clause 25. In the meantime, I’m happy to take your questions.
Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB (Labour—Christchurch Central): Thank you, Madam Chair. I know the Minister for Courts was in the House at the second reading, so she knows, essentially, what I’m going to say. I will just ask one question at a time.
: My first question is about undertakings by conveyancing practitioners. This is clearly a very good reform, because if you are going to do conveyancing on an even par with lawyers, you need to have enforceable undertakings. The question is whether we’ve now got a second-rate undertaking regime because of subsection (1) of new section 38A, inserted by clause 5, which says, “An affected person may make an application for summary judgment in relation to an undertaking”. It just strikes me that it should simply say, “An affected person may make an application to the High Court in relation to an undertaking given by a conveyancing practitioner”, because summary judgments are a kind of particular form of proceeding where there is no oral evidence. In fact, if you are seeking to enforce a solicitor’s undertaking, you’re actually relying on the inherent jurisdiction of the court to discipline solicitors, who are in fact officers of the court.
: Now, I accept that conveyancing practitioners simply don’t neatly fit into that, but I would have thought that by saying “undertakings by conveyancers are enforceable” and “the application to enforce them may be made to the High Court”, that would have been all you’ll need. Now you’ve got to have this unusual procedure, and I guess the challenge is—because summary judgment application is in fact an application which says, “Look, it’s obvious we don’t need to go to full trial; we can do a quick-fire procedure”. If you lose that, it then usually turns into an ordinary proceeding in which you then go and have a full trial. It’s actually unclear, and it’s just unclear to me why summary judgment was thought as appropriate. Here are two questions: why isn’t it just “apply to the High Court”, and what happens if you do this and you lose your summary judgment application?
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Madam Chair. I understand that the member was not on this particular Education and Workforce Committee, so I appreciate the question. I hope I can answer it well enough.
: The amendment will enable conveyancers’ undertakings to be summarily enforceable in the High Court, similar to how lawyers’ undertakings are currently. I understand that registered conveyancers transact around 280 purchases annually. For each one of these transactions, conveyancers pay up to $500 in additional solicitor costs as a direct result of banks refusing to instruct conveyancers, and these costs are passed on to the consumers. The change in this clause will improve the confidence of banks, lawyers, and consumers to work with conveyancers and bring down the costs for consumers. I also note that this amendment was strongly supported by submitters at the select committee stage. This will help give effect to the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act, which had the aim of increasing competition for conveyancing services and driving conveyancing costs down.
Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB (Labour—Christchurch Central): Yeah, look, I got all that. I basically said that at the beginning when I outlined what an undertaking was, and those are great notes written by officials, but the question is this: why does it say that they must take a summary judgment application and not an ordinary application, and if it has to be a summary application, what happens if they lose that summary judgment application?
Hon PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atatū): Thank you, Madam Chair. I’m very keen to hear an answer to the Hon Dr Duncan Webb’s question about why the provisions in this bill, essentially, provide a sort of second-rate or lightweight option for people who want to enforce the undertakings given by a conveyancer. That hasn’t been answered, and as someone who was on the Education and Workforce Committee—
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): I think Dr Webb’s also waiting for the answer to a question, and the Minister is taking advice, so does the member have a further—
Hon PHIL TWYFORD: Yes—as someone who was on the committee, I would say that this matter was never raised by the officials, by submitters, or by any of the committee members, so I’m glad that Duncan Webb has raised it at this time.
: I wanted to ask some questions. Assuming that this matter can be resolved—
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): Yeah, we’ll just wait for an answer on this matter. Move on, and then we can come back.
Hon PHIL TWYFORD: You want to wait for the answer? OK, sure.
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): No, I’m happy for you to keep going.
Hon PHIL TWYFORD: OK. Assuming that that matter can be adequately answered, I’m interested in what thought the Minister for Courts has given to monitoring whether banks will alter their practice following the commencement of this provision, given that we’re trying to improve confidence in conveyancers’ undertakings; whether there’s been any estimate made of the reduction in settlement delays or transaction costs that are likely as a result of this change; and whether or not there will be any operational guidance provided to practitioners or to lenders if this provision enters the law.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): I do not know the answer to the members’ questions, and the officials have advised me that they don’t have an answer to that either, because this is a minor change that relates specifically to new section 38A, which is being inserted here by clause 5. The question that’s being asked is talking about hypothetical situations that have not been considered when just trying to progress through what would be a standard, minor, technical-type change to this.
: The members are asking legal questions about what if or why would we not do it somewhere else. The reality is that we have been asked to—the Government is looking to progress changes in this area in this way, and I have detailed the reasoning for that. I’m not in a position to be able to answer extended questions, because they actually don’t relate to what it is that we’re trying to change right here.
Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB (Labour—Christchurch Central): I must say, I find it extraordinary that on a question about why a summary judgment procedure was adopted and not an ordinary procedure, which is the wording of the legislation, why officials can’t answer that beggars belief. If they came here today thinking that this was a formality, well, they’ve got the wrong end of the stick. It might be late in urgency, but we expect the Government to be able to answer questions and justify their position. The fact that it went through a select committee process is neither here nor there; this is the committee stage of the House of Representatives, so I hope I’ll get a better response when I talk about new section 135A, inserted by clause 7. Again, I raised these questions at second reading on purpose. I thought, “If I raise it here, at least officials will get an hour or so’s notice so that they will know it will be raised at committee stage, and they won’t be caught by surprise and be ferreting around.” My question is about section 135A, which allows complaints about lawyers to be summarily dismissed by a Law Society administrator where they are trivial, vexatious, or stale, or on a number of other grounds. My question, fundamentally, is this: if we’re going to have an administrative shutting-down of complaints against lawyers, what is the recourse for that person to have that decision reviewed?  Can they ask either the standards committee to have a look at it or the Legal Complaints Review Officer to have a look at it? Or will they be forced to clog up the high courts by taking it on judicial review?
: Now, can I say I support this reform intent—that is to say that complaints that are clearly meritless should be able to be turned away at the first point of contact, where otherwise they would clog up the select committee system, which is a body of six or seven or more people, including lawyers. But they make mistakes. These are not lawyers, necessarily—they may be, but they don’t have to be—but they are, ultimately, part of the internal administrative machinery of the Law Society and they should be subject to some oversight. Look, in terms of the law, I know what the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act says: you can seek a review from the Legal Complaints Review Officer for a standards committee decision, not an internal Law Society administrative decision. So we’ve got a problem.
: I hope the Minister isn’t going to say, “Will there be another administrative review?” because that is just giving two problems of the same kind. I do think that there’s a lack here; this section should have said that: “the complainant can seek a review by the standards committee of that decision.” Now, it would still go to the standards committee, and I accept that, but it still acts as an effective filter for 80 or 90 percent of these meritless claims. It’s also the case that some of these claims thought to be meritless, may not be. The administrator may make mistakes, and we need to have an ability for that review process. And, as I said in the second reading, telling someone who is a problematic or querulous complainant or a vexatious complainant that they have no merit, they’re a waste of time, and their vexatious, and we’re not even going to look at your complaint, we’re not even going to send it to the committee of lawyers, is the first way to really upset them. I know from experience that these people will not give up and they will go to the highest level and clog up our higher courts if we don’t give them a safety valve within in the process itself. So I hope we’ve got some better advice on this question.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Madam Chair. One thing I’m going to start off by saying is I do not, in any way, appreciate that member attacking the officials who work really hard to do the work that this Government asks them to do, especially the sheer volume of work that this Government has put through them. I would expect that member to stand up and apologise to the officials for what he has said about them, because if that member wants to say anything, you should be saying it to me and leave the officials out, because that, I think, is a very low blow.
: We are looking at these minor changes, and the member is asking for information that goes outside of that and the consequences that goes outside of that, from officials who do not have that information.
Hon Kieran McAnulty: It’s not his fault you don’t know. For goodness’ sake!
Hon NICOLE McKEE: And it’s not their fault.
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): OK. I don’t think we’re going to go into a slanging match between everybody. What Dr Duncan Webb actually said was he was surprised, given the time that had passed, that he’s unable to get the answer that he wanted in that time frame. Now, we’re going to give the Minister an opportunity to say what she was going to say at this point in time. In the absence of an answer, we’re not at the end of this committee stage and we still have some time in the dinner break, but bearing in mind that written questions are an option but can only be asked about policy intent and they can’t go for legal opinion.
: So let’s just work this through. I know that Dr Webb was looking for time before and we may be able to get some time here. We may or may not get an answer. I can’t guarantee that the answer that the member’s looking for will come, but this is where we are.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Madam Chair. I’m going to go through parts of clause 6 and clause 7 in an attempt to answer some of that member’s questions. With clause 6, which is amending section 135(1), this is introducing the discretion for the Law Society’s complaint service to refer those complaints to the standards committee in clause 6, and it will enable the triage process, that has been introduced by clause 7 of this bill. The assessment grounds for the triaging would be the same grounds by the standards committee when they are considering complaints. The triaging decisions—the change was supported by submitters, although some suggested that the triaging criteria for the standards committee should come with a right of review. The review and appeal rights are not provided in similar triaging decisions of comparable regulatory bodies such as the Teaching Council, for example. I don’t think review in this case is necessary or appropriate.
: Creating a right of review would shift current inefficiencies to an earlier part of the process. If a complainant was to seek a review of the triaging decision, they would need to apply for a judicial review—I know the members spoke about that just before. That is, however, thought to be an appropriate pathway. The Government is confident that the Law Society will have appropriate guidance and policy in place to make well-judged positions.
Hon Phil Twyford: Madam Chair.
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): If there’s a clarification on this, I’ll take it before the dinner break. If it’s a new question—
Hon Phil Twyford: It’s not a new—
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): —it’s not a new question.
Hon PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atatū): Does the Minister think that judicial review is appropriately affordable and accessible for ordinary citizens who might find themselves in a dispute with the Law Society over the handling of a complaint?
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Whether it’s affordable or accessible will come down to the individual and their case. What it is, for that member, is a pathway.
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): Members, the time has come to break for dinner. The committee will resume at 7 p.m.
: Sitting suspended from 5.57 p.m. to 7 p.m.
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): The House is resumed. Members, before the dinner break, the committee was debating Part 1 of the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill. This is the debate on clauses 3 to 11, “Amendments to Lawyers and Conveyancers Act 2006”. The question, again, is that Part 1 stand part.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): In answer to the Hon Dr Duncan Webb’s thoughts earlier, over the dinner break I have had this from my officials: currently the affected person must enforce an undertaking through a separate proceeding in tort, contract, or estoppel, or, alternatively, a deed of undertaking that would need to be relied on, providing the process for enforcing breaches summarily will be simpler and more efficient for the affected person, and use less court and judicial resources. This will extend the range of pathways available to pursue breaches. The change will also improve the confidence of banks to rely on undertakings from conveyancers. If an unaffected person is unsuccessful with their application for summary judgment, the usual court processes apply. If the Hon Dr Duncan Webb is happy with that answer, I implore him to come back down to the Chamber and apologise to the officials that he abused before he left.
Hon PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atatū): On clauses 6 and 7, the administrative triaging that we were talking about before the break, I wanted to know from the Minister what consideration she’s given to the trade-off of efficiency against public confidence, in light of the exchange we had earlier in the select committee and now in the Chamber. We support administrative triaging, but I think these are real questions that arise from some of the evidence that we had at the committee.
: The Law Society and the Law Association are obviously strongly in favour of this, but they would be because they have a direct benefit, a direct gain, from the efficiency that this will deliver. But not everyone agreed. One submitter argued that complaints should never be dismissed administratively, that there should be some form of independent review, and that concepts such as “frivolous” and “vexatious” required greater definition. Now, ultimately the officials and the committee rejected those recommendations, but I would like to know from the Minister whether or not she has considered the possible lack of public confidence in a process that is, effectively, as was characterised earlier, an administrative employee having the ability to, basically, knock these complaints out with no real accessible right of review other than a judicial review.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Do I have confidence that this is the right way forward? Yes, because the advice that I’ve been given says that. As I mentioned before we went to the dinner break, the Government is confident that the Law Society will have appropriate guidance and policy in place to make well-judged decisions.
: I also mentioned the assessment grounds for triaging would be the same grounds used by the Lawyers Standards Committee when considering complaints, and they are also set out in section 138 of the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act, “Decision to take no action on complaint”. I’m just going to go through those grounds very quickly. These grounds are from subsections (1)(a) to (f), paragraph (a) being “the length of time that has elapsed between the date [and] subject matter of complaint … or (b) the subject matter of the complaint [being] trivial; or (c) the complaint [being] frivolous or vexatious or is not made in good faith; or (d) the person alleged to be aggrieved does not desire the action be taken or, as the case may be, continued; or (e) the complainant does not have sufficient personal interest in the subject matter of the complaint; or (f) there is … another adequate remedy or right of appeal”.
: Now, with these grounds that have been met, I think it very clearly sets out what those boundaries are before you get to that point of judicial review. So, yes, I do have confidence that I believe that we are on the right pathway here.
Hon PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atatū): Thank you, Minister. Further to that, does she expect that the Law Society will be transparent about the handling of complaints under this new mechanism? For example, is there any expectation that they will publish annual statistics showing the number of complaints received, the number triaged, the grounds relied upon, and the complaints referred to the standards committees? Is there any expectation that there will be an ongoing audit to ensure that the triage decisions are being made consistently?
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Because this is a regulatory standards bill, which is looking to make just small and minor amendments, we have not gone into every single clause with what is expected of organisations such as the Law Society, but one would hope that we need to get into a position where there is transparency across agencies, whether they be Government agencies or not, in order for the public to have confidence. So one would encourage transparency from all organisations that need to implement the law in some way or another. How they go about doing that, though, is up to them.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair. Thank you for that response, Minister, and I do appreciate the Minister for going over some of the questions, for a more detailed response, over dinner. That’s very much appreciated.
: Before dinner, Minister, you mentioned something around the changes we’re seeing both in terms of clause 8 but also in terms of clauses 5 and 7 around the guidelines that are going to be developed. Some of the guidelines have been developed alongside this, and this is also something we’ve seen from the submitters as well that is very much welcomed, but then there needs to be further guidelines on that.
: I want to check with the Minister whether this is something, again, as we’re seeing with this particular bill, with some of these new additions like undertaking to be enforceable—whether either the Ministry of Justice or the appropriate, I guess, collective agency committee have already started working on some of those guidelines that the Minister referred to.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): My purpose here is to do some small technical amendments. Guidelines is not something that is under my purview, but if you’re going to have any implementation work correctly or work well, you would expect an agency or organisation to be able to get that information out to the users in order for them to be able to work efficiently. But the creation of guidelines is not under my purview.
TANGI UTIKERE (Labour—Palmerston North): Thank you, Mr Chair. Can I just ask a question of the Minister that relates to clause 7; this is in relation to new section 135A. The Minister has identified that in terms of the ability to either take no action—it seems to me that there are only two options, either for a referral of the complaint for further consideration or indeed no action. Now, the Minister has identified those particular specific criteria that relate to no action. One of them is in relation, it seems, to time; the period of time that’s elapsed. In a circumstance where there is an active referral that’s being considered, obviously one wants to, potentially, in the interests of natural justice, reach a conclusion at a time that is sufficient and not sort of drawn out so much.
: When the Minister identifies the length of time that has elapsed between the date on which the matter of the complaint arose and the date that the actual complaint was made, where in the scheme of things is the quantum of time set in terms of action being taken around what the next step is? So it’s not about the amount of time from actually receiving the complaint, but the period of time from when the complaint is received and when the next step to either refer it or otherwise is taken.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Mr Chair. I am advised that the length of time that has elapsed between the date of when the subject matter of the complaint arose and the date of when the complaint was made is such that an investigation of the complaint is no longer practicable or desirable.
TODD STEPHENSON (ACT): I move, That debate on this question now close.
TANGI UTIKERE (Labour—Palmerston North): Thank you, Mr Chair. I thank the Minister for her answer. In terms of being practicable, what sorts of factors would lend themselves to that consideration? It is quite a significant thing as to whether a complaint is heading down that path of referral or not. When she says practicability, practicableness, what sort of things is she envisaging? I know that, in terms of providing some guidance around what that might mean, it would be important.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): As I mentioned before, it is not for me to issue what that guidance is. What is practicable or desirable will come down to those that need to make those decisions, based on the cases that are before them. My role here is to make minor and technical amendments to law in order for them to operate well. The question that I am now being asked is almost a type of operational question which I have no control over.
TOM RUTHERFORD (National—Bay of Plenty): I move, That debate on this question now close.
: A party vote was called for on the question, That debate on this question now close.
: New Zealand National 48; ACT New Zealand 11; New Zealand First 8.
: New Zealand Labour 30; Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand 10; Te Pāti Māori 4; Ferris; Kapa-Kingi.
: Motion agreed to.
: Part 1 agreed to.

topicSummaries.topic: Part 2 Amendments to Prostitution Reform Act 2003
topicSummaries.content:
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Members, we now come to Part 2. This is the debate on clauses 12 and 13, “Amendments to Prostitution Reform Act 2003”. The question is that Part 2 stand part.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair. I just have a short question for the Minister for Part 2, clause 13, “Section 36 amended”, noting that the current section 36 of this particular Act, “Disqualification from holding certificate”, already has burglary, robbery, extortion/blackmail, and money-laundering within that. Can I just check this is simply because the section numbers have changed around, and this is just to update the section numbers?
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): I thank the member for his question. Section 36 of the Prostitution Reform Act 2003 lists quite a wide range of offences, and many of them are out of date. They haven’t been updated since 2003. The amendment updates to the Prostitution Reform Act also correct out-of-date sections that are in the Crimes Act 1961 and also the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975. We’re basically just updating, adding to those, and updating those references to those particular two bills.
TANGI UTIKERE (Labour—Palmerston North): Thank you. Thanks to the Minister for that. In light of that response, these regulatory bills don’t come around that often, but when they do, they span quite widely. Is she confident that this process has captured all of the relevant updates in relation to the Prostitution Reform Act? It is a piece of legislation that’s been around for more than 20 years. Is she comfortable that there are no further other options that might need to be addressed?
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): At this stage, the answer to that is yes. This change is about ensuring that the Act is not only up to date but it still sticks with its original policy intent as well. Correctly referencing the relevant offence provisions that are in the Crimes Act 1961 and the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975 will ensure that the correct disqualifying factors are applied in that licensing process. At this stage, I do believe that we have caught up, so to speak.
: Part 2 agreed to.

topicSummaries.topic: Part 3 Amendments to Real Estate Agents Act 2008
topicSummaries.content:
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Members, we now come to Part 3. This is the debate on clauses 14 to 36, “Amendments to Real Estate Agents Act 2008”. The question is that Part 3 stand part.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair. Part 3 is, as far as this bill goes, the most substantial part of this bill. It is also the part with the Minister’s amendment, which I’ll come to shortly, because I do have a few questions on the Minister’s amendment, but I’m not quite at clause 25 just yet.
: My first two questions are for clause 18. The first one is clause 18(2), replacing section 13(4)(b). This is the new criteria that’s been added in terms of the membership of the authority. I’m guessing it’s just simply moving what is in subclause (1) to a different area, I guess—is that what is being done there?
: The second question I have is—
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Could you repeat the clause again, sorry?
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN: OK. I will restart, very briefly. Clause 18(1), which is deleting “and that member must be a lawyer of not less than 7 years’ legal experience”—is that just simply moving that into a different section, which is now 13(4)(b), being my first question, and are there any implications with that?
: The second one is the repeal of section 13(5)—again, I don’t think this is something we looked at specifically, and it’s not in version one of this bill—which is consultation with the Real Estate Institute of New Zealand (REINZ). Can I just check with the Minister: why do REINZ no longer need to be consulted? That’s the part that’s being repealed in clause 18(3). Does REINZ even still exist?
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Mr Chair. At the moment, the chairperson of the board needs to be a lawyer with not less than seven years’ experience. What we’re doing is replacing section 13(4) with a new provision that requires at least one of the members of the board to be a lawyer with at least seven years’ experience. Effectively, what we’re saying is it doesn’t have to be the chair that has that, but somebody on the board has to have that.
: The reasoning for that is it’s actually really hard to find a lawyer with seven years’ experience who wants to put their hand up to be here. In fact, I would like to do a bit of a shout-out to the current member, because the chair with seven years’ experience at the moment actually wants to resign and hasn’t been able to do so because we can’t replace that person with another lawyer. We’re, effectively, saying someone on the board, please have seven years’ experience—well, you’re going to need to have seven years’ experience, but you don’t need to be the chair. The chair just needs to have a year’s legal experience.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you for that, Minister. I will move on to clause 19. Clause 19 is also the part where the select committee has actually made some changes around the power to require specified documents. I just want to check in this section, when we are looking at that—and I believe I’m looking at clause 19, new section 24A(2). In that—yes, it is (2). Can I just check that still allows for the contravention, for example, which is not listed in (1), around things like privacy, etc.? Just checking that the authority, when requesting “any person to supply the Authority with any specified document”, is also exempted from certain other principles, like the information privacy principles, for example.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Mr Chair. Clause 19 actually makes a few new subsections. The member mentioned 24A(2), but there’s also 24A(3) and 24A(4). What I think I might do is just talk to the changes that we’re making all together. The Real Estate Authority has limited ability at the moment to gather information to support any investigations into breaches of the Act, regulations, or practice rules, and into unlicensed trading. This clause, clause 19, which is inserting the whole of new section 24A, establishes a new power to require documents from licensees and other individuals to facilitate those investigations that they wish to undertake. This change will enable the regulator to better fulfil its functions and better support the consumer protection purpose that is within this Act. The provision is complemented by the introduction of an offence for failure to comply with such a request. We do that in clause 28, with the maximum penalties of $50,000 for a company and $10,000 for an individual. I will just point out, too, that those penalties are consistent with other similar offences in the Real Estate Agents Act. I’ll just throw that in there while I can.
: The select committee did make some recommendations, including amending clause 19 to clarify that the Real Estate Authority must have reasonable grounds to believe to initiate the power. It also recommended amending the test for exercising the power to make it consistent with the exercise of other existing powers by the authority under the Act. These changes also make it clear that the reasonable grounds to believe applies to situations involving a licensee’s conduct, not only a person who may be engaging in unlicensed trading.
: The select committee, at this clause, also recommended amending the scope of the authority’s ability to require documentation so it could be applied to any person. This ensures that the relevant documentation could be obtained from any parties that may not be involved in illegal activity but who may have relevant information about others. Then, new section 24A(4) has been inserted to clarify that people or organisations can only be required to supply a specified document that is or has been in their possession or in their control. So, for the member, clause 19 and new section 24A and its insertion really is about providing the authority with that ability to be able to get that information in the best way that they can in order to make their judgments.
Hon PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atatū): Thank you, Mr Chairman. Further on clause 19, I thought it might be worth noting for the committee that the Law Association supported the objective of this section—of strengthening investigations—but it did raise a number of concerns, including the breadth of the power, the threshold for issuing notices, and privacy implications. The Privacy Commissioner came along to the committee and also accepted that there was a sound policy basis for the investigative power to require documents but stressed that it should be accompanied by appropriate limits, particularly in relation to the later use and disclosure of personal information obtained under this new power.
