: As the Minister pointed out, the committee did strengthen the threshold for reasonable belief, but I don’t think you could say that the committee actually accepted the other proposals that were made by the Privacy Commissioner—for example, around what operational guidance would be provided, the privacy concerns, and reporting and transparency. I want to ask the Minister: why did the Government conclude that the existing safeguards in the bill are sufficient, given that critique by the Privacy Commissioner? The Privacy Commissioner supported the proposal only on the basis that there would be appropriate limits on subsequent use and disclosure of personal information. Where are the safeguards? What limits are there? It’s not clear to me, so I’d be interested to know from her where those safeguards are, if they do exist. Finally, in this contribution: does she expect that the authority will publish operational guidance governing the use of these powers that they’re been given?
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Mr Chair. What I have been advised is that this particular provision of this clause will come into effect eight months after the Royal assent of the bill, giving sufficient time for the agency to be able to prepare what I would expect to be guidance to those, because there is a bit of a change here. The delay of that eight months after Royal assent for implementation of this, I believe, would be in order for them to be able to get the House in order and ensure that everybody understands what their obligations will be; perhaps guidelines, as well. As I’ve mentioned earlier, I’m a big fan of transparency and I would explicitly hope that those that have to abide by this will understand exactly what it is that they need to abide by. It’s not a place to put those details into this form of legislation, but one would expect that if people are going to abide by the laws, they need to understand what those parameters are.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair. Thank you for that response, Minister. I think my colleague Phil Twyford may have additional questions for clause 19, but I want to ask a question around clause 20, just noting to you, as well, Minister, that I may have a follow-up question on this once we get to the commencement part, which I don’t think I want to discuss at this stage.
: The only question I have for this section—this is the part that, from our perspective, we had the greatest issues around, but then we have, like I said, had some of these being teased out during the select committee stage. Looking at it again, one of the things I want to check is about clause 20, “Section 36 amended”, subclause (2), inserting new paragraph (f), in the case of an individual whose licence was cancelled and is applying for a licence within 12 months—they’ve completed that. But, let’s say, should a person complete any required continued education within 12 months but they didn’t apply for a licence or re-licence within that 12-month period, are they again no longer eligible, as well? Is the criteria that you have to apply for it within 12 months, not the continued education part?
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): My  understanding is that we have a series of real estate agents that have a qualification, and we have a series of older real estate agents who actually aren’t qualified, but they have a whole lifetime of experience. The requirements when people reapply is that they need to have a qualification, and we’re ensuring that those that don’t have the qualification but have adequate experience don’t miss out on continuing their job.
: Now, that 12-month delay that is allowed actually came about as a result of Cyclone Gabrielle. It was a time when people had other things going on, and they couldn’t put in their application. When we think about natural disasters, of which we’re having a few in New Zealand, we need to be mindful that people just actually might not be able to get in and do their application at the time when they need to. There’s two things going on there: one is allowing those without qualifications but with experience to carry on; and the other is, with that 12-month extension, allowing those in predicaments to actually have that bit of extended time to apply.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you for that, Mr Chair. Thank you for that, Minister. That actually does answer my question, because I did wonder where the 12 months came about, and force majeure happens, events happen, and I think that’s reasonable.
: I’m actually, if it’s OK, going to move on to—and other members may have questions in between—the Minister’s Amendment Paper 636 but also the two tabled amendments that are on that amendment. The question I have for the Amendment Paper is: when you look at new clause 25, “Section 54 amended”, the “Cancellation of licence”, in terms of the specific phrasing, it states, “is convicted … of a crime … involving dishonesty”, etc., and what we see in new section 54 (i)(i) and in new section 54 (i)(iii) and (iv)— I’ve actually seen that in some of the other legislation as well. Is that just simply updating this part that’s sort of recently been captured in this bill and updating it to be consistent with some of the things I see already in other legislation, being my first question.
: My second question is around the Minister’s two tabled amendments. On the first, I thank the Minister for actually communicating with us ahead of time with these ones and with a little bit of explanation for both. I think the amendment itself looks fine, but I was more interested in a process question, which I believe, in the correspondence, it talked about this coming from the Real Estate Authority quite late and they only just picked up on it. I want to check, in terms of the process for such tabled amendments, is it that the authority would contact the Minister and the Minister saying, “These are some amendments.”, then the Minister contacts either the Parliamentary Counsel Office or the officials and going like, “Does this look OK?”, and then it goes into a tabled amendment? I just want to check, do officials need to being involved in any other process? Because I assume that the authority is not the officials.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Mr Chair. I’ll start off with just talking about the first Amendment Paper in the way that it relates to clause 21. With the main Amendment Paper—Amendment Paper 636—it adjusts this clause to align with new section 54(i)(ii), which was added by the Amendment Paper, and then the member’s not actually asking me about the two Amendment Papers to the Amendment Paper, but rather the process of it.
: The way that it has operated is that my understanding is the Real Estate Authority, last minute, just went through and started having a look at the bill and the Amendment Paper and then realised very quickly, and at the last minute, that a clause had dropped off. I think that was section 54, which we are putting in there now—section 54(k), going by memory. That had accidentally been deleted, and nobody had picked that up. The officials were contacted by the Real Estate Authority, not my ministerial office. The Real Estate Authority went straight to the officials. The officials would in turn have gone to the Parliamentary Counsel Office to check, is that a drafting error, which it was confirmed, and then it was put back in as section 54(k).
: Of course, they then found the other one—section 54(i)(v)—as well, which is just a small amendment that they also picked up at the time that they were going through. I do appreciate that it is late notice, but I also appreciate the fact that the Real Estate Authority did find this and it’s not something we will then have to add into another regulatory standards bill in the future or next term. We were just taking the opportunity to fix that, and again, my appreciation to the Real Estate Authority for picking it up.
Dr VANESSA WEENINK (National—Banks Peninsula): I move, That debate on this question now close.
Hon BARBARA EDMONDS (Labour—Mana): Thak you, Mr Chair. Just wanting to take a question in relation to the Minister for Courts’ Amendments Paper 636, specifically clause 25, which amends the provisions around the cancellation of licence. I’m not quite sure whether the changes in the cancellation of licence actually would fit within the scope of a regulatory systems bill given, actually, it’s bringing in other clauses to cancel a licence. For example, obviously, with regulatory systems bills, they’re usually just technical changes. However, the new clause brings in a whole series of different ways that the cancellation of a licence can be undertaken.
: Under section 54 of the Real Estate Agents Act right now, a registrar can cancel the person’s licence if they die, which makes sense obviously; if the person gives written notice to the registrar, which, obviously, if they’ve given up doing real estate; if the person has failed to maintain the prescribed qualification—that’s good, they’ve got to keep their qualifications to maintain their licence; if the person has failed to complete any continuing education—obviously, there’s professional development requirements as part of that; a couple of other sections—section 99 and section 110—in accordance of those; if the licence was granted on the basis of any false or fraudulent representation or declaration made orally or in writing; or if the person has failed to pay any prescribed fees or levies. Other than section 54(g), I can kind of understand where the insertions under the Minister’s Amendment Papers, which is around false or fraudulent representation, kind of still fits within that scheme. Hence why I think, perhaps, this is why it’s been allowed under the regulatory systems amendment bill.
: But specifically, my questions for the Minister are in section 54(i)(ii)—“if, during the term of the licence, the person is convicted of an offence under … the Fair Trading Act” and it sets out a whole lot of sections in the Fair Trading Act. For example, section 12A is around unsubstantiated representation; section 14 of the Fair Trading Act is in relation to false representation and misleading conduct in relation to land—that makes absolute sense; section 17 is offering gifts and prizes and not providing them—again, that’s sort of a misleading offence; section 19 is in relation to bait advertising—again, that makes sense, if want to keep your real estate licence, you shouldn’t be doing bait advertising; section 20 of the Fair Trading Act is referral selling; section 21 is demanding or accepting payment without intending to supply a product; section 21C is prohibition on assisting right to payment with respect to unsolicited goods or unsolicited services; section 22 is in relation to misleading representations about certain business elements; and section 24 is around pyramid selling schemes.
: I can understand why all those particular sections allow the regulator to cancel the person’s licence, but my question is actually in relation to the sections of the Fair Trading Act which are missing. That’s my question to the Minister, because if you look at that grouping between sections 12A to 24 of the Fair Trading Act, and if you work through the ones that are not included, they also have a similar theme to both the current section 54(g) of the Real Estate Agents Act, as well as the fair trading list. For example, section 23 of the Fair Trading Act, basically, is around harassment and coercion. If you’re a real estate agent, I would hope you’re not harassing and coercing a vendor to potentially buy the house. My question is around why section 12 of the Fair Trading Act is not included. That’s in relation to cancelling their licence if they have misleading conduct in relation to employment. Misleading conduct in relation to employment is quite important. Obviously, for some real estate agents, they are actually employees.
: My other question is, why not section 13? Section 13 of the Fair Trading Act is about false or misleading representations in respect to the supply of possible goods. There is some weight to those three particular sections of the Fair Trading Act that have been missed out as a potential reasoning for the cancellation of licence. I just want to ask the Minister whether her or officials had considered those three particular provisions of the Fair Trading Act and as to why they were not included as a reason to cancel a licence.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Mr Chair. The member went quite extensively into clause 54(i)(ii) and laid them all out, but we’re not making any changes there. The Amendment Paper would replace clause 25 to adjust the amendments to section 54. The original wording of clause 25 would not achieve the policy intent to clearly allow the registrar to cancel a person’s licence if they meet the grounds that would prohibit them from holding a licence. The replacement to clause 25 makes more explicit the grounds for cancelling a person’s licence during the term of a licence, which mirrored the disqualifications from holding a licence in the Act now.
: The Amendment Papers that we’re making include section 54(k), which I had just spoken to with the other member from the Green Party. The second amendment, to section 54(i)(v), makes a technical amendment to just adjust that section to refer to an agent’s licence. This better aligns the grounds for cancellation of a licence in this section with the current prohibition in section 37(2) for holding an agent’s licence. This amendment will mean that section 54(i)(v) applies to the cancellation of an agent’s licence. The member’s gone into an area that I don’t think actually correlates with what we’re doing here.
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Dr—the Hon Barbara Edmonds.
Hon BARBARA EDMONDS (Labour—Mana): That’d be nice, without the PhD—but anyway, thank you, Mr Chair. When the Minister responded that it’s in relation to the original, did you mean when the bill was introduced—the original bill—or the one post - select committee?
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): I will say that it relates to probably what was in that original bill. My officials can come and correct me if I am incorrect.
Hon BARBARA EDMONDS (Labour—Mana): Thank you, Mr Chair, and thank you, Minister, for getting your officials to check that, because, if I understand that it is the bill as introduced, this is a new section under the Real Estate Agents Act 2008. That whole section 54(i), inserted by clause 25, is new because the Real Estate Agents Act currently only those to section 54(h). So it is an insertion—obviously an insertion that would have been put in the bill as introduced, but the question still remains: it provides a list of particular offences under the Fair Trading Act. Why have those other three offences, which is also under the Fair Trading Act, been omitted? What is the policy reason for them being omitted, even if it was the original bill, because currently it is a new amendment to the Real Estate Agents Act 2008?
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): I thank the member for her question and seeking further clarity. I hope that I can give some of it here, now. Now they’ve not come up to me to say that I was incorrect, and they might do soon, so if they do, I will stand up again. My understanding—you’re quite right. Section 54(i) is a new section requiring the register to cancel the licence “of a licensee company, 10 working days after the licensee’s sole agent licence is cancelled…unless a temporary licence holder or a new [sole] agent licence holder has been appointed for the licensee company.”
: So, I think, rather than having the huge list of it, it’s just allowing them that ability to be able to do that. The amendment paper would replace clause 25 to adjust the amendments in section 54, which makes me think that it that’s it is—
Hon Barbara Edmonds: In addition to it.
Hon NICOLE McKEE: Yes.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair. Thank you for that, Minister. I’ve got two additional questions, and that’s on clause 27 and clause 28. Again, others may have other clauses in regard to the Minister’s amendment. For clause 27, can I just get clarification from the Minister that the intent over here is that what we’re now seeing in this replacement section 72(b), paragraphs (i) to (iii), will now be relevant for just the licensees conduct in general, not specifically to do with the real estate agency work. Which means that if the licensee, for example, carries on with their day-to-day work, going to the supermarket, etc., and something happens and their conduct falls short of the standards that a reasonable member of the public is entitled to expect, that then would now fall under this particular clause. Would that be a reasonable example—checking with the Minister? That’s my first question.
: My second question is on clause 28. Now, this new section 146A inserts not only an offence but also a fine. The fine is quite high. My understanding in terms of that is it may possibly be outdated—do not quote me on this—or that it offers a general understanding that fines should be no more than $1,000, because the thing with the fine is, there’s no way for anyone to respond. It’s not like, you know, upon conviction, you get fined; it’s just you get a fine. So $10,000 and $50,000 is what I would have thought is quite high and above some of the advice I have seen.
: Can I just check that with—I have not gone through the entirety of the Real Estate Act, but does this come out from some other parts of the Real Estate Act that matches this particular one, which is why you are able to mirror it for that consistency? Because, otherwise, I would also assume that this is quite new.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Mr Chair. To the member, the change that we’re making in replacement section 72, inserted by clause 27, to expand the definition of “unsatisfactory conduct” is to make sure that real estate agents will be accountable for a broader range of conduct, not just the conduct while carrying out real estate agency work. To give you an example of that, it will include, say, aggressive or abusive behaviour during cold-calling people, or a licensee acting inappropriately towards a client maybe, after a transaction has concluded. At the moment, it’s about the business that they’re doing, but we’re saying, well, actually, you need to behave well, broadly.
: The member talked about a fine—well, it’s actually an offence, so it’s not like it’s an infringement fee; it’s an offence. The reason why it’s so much—$50,000—for a company and $10,000 for an individual—is because those penalties and those amounts are consistent with other similar offences, as the member mentioned, within the Real Estate Agents Act.
Hon PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atatū): So on clause 27, I remember the Law Association, at the committee, supported this, but they questioned whether or not the drafting provided sufficient certainty. They accepted the arguments about consumer protection, about the need for professional discipline, but they submitted that there was insufficient legal certainty. So, further to the Minister’s response to Lawrence Xu-Nan’s question, I’m interested in whether or not her interpretation of the draft would be that real estate agents could be held accountable for behaviour completely outside their work as a real estate agent—so, not cold-calling potential customers or whatever, but committing a crime when you’re out shopping or watching your kid’s football game, or bringing yourself into disrepute in some way that doesn’t relate at all to your work as a real estate agent. I’m interested in if she could answer that question.
: Secondly, how does she expect licensees to know where the boundary lies for unsatisfactory conduct? Because just a plain reading of the provisions doesn’t provide that. Perhaps the Minister could give us some examples of behaviour that would count under this provision as unsatisfactory conduct. Further to that, does she expect that the authority will publish guidance for real estate agents so that they can have some understanding and some clarity?
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): I gave some examples just before to the member from the Green Party, so I’ll say that I’ve already delivered that, and I will carry on because I’ve answered your last question first. I’ll now move back to your first question then. My understanding is that the select committee actually raised those concerns as well, because submitters had raised concerns about what actually makes up that unsatisfactory conduct. In response to that, I understand that there are tests of unsatisfactory conduct in the clause that have been clarified. A clearer link has been drawn between unacceptable conduct by a licensee and their profession to emphasise that this test is about upholding consumer confidence in the real estate profession. So as there is a test, I would expect that that test would be made known to the real estate agents in order for them to understand and have knowledge about how to comply.
TOM RUTHERFORD (National—Bay of Plenty): I move, That debate on this question now close.
TANGI UTIKERE (Labour—Palmerston North): I just have two areas that I’d like to ask the Minister questions about. The first one is a brief one. It’s a response to her to Dr Xu-Nan’s question about having a lawyer as a chair, basically. I accept the Minister has said that history has proven that it’s apparently quite difficult to attract someone into that role. If that is the reason, Minister, was there any thought than to, perhaps, not completely removing that requirement for the chair’s role, but maybe allowing the Minister to make the appointment of the chair with preference given to someone who has that particular qualification in terms of a minimum number of years as a practising lawyer? That’s the first question.
: The second one in relation to clauses 20 and 21 in Part 3. This is about the entitlement to a licence and the prohibition on someone from being licensed. In clause 20, which seeks to amend section 36, it identifies the various things that need to be considered for someone who has had a track record of having a licence being cancelled, and it seems to me that in new section 36(1)(f) in clause 20(2), it talks about someone who has had their licence cancelled within the previous 12 months and who has, basically, undertaken a process of professional development. Further down, in new section 36(2)(d) in clause 20(4), it’s around the registrar being satisfied that, actually, the applicant can demonstrate a sufficient level of knowledge and experience of agency work.
: In clause 21, it talks about the prohibition on someone who, in the previous five-year period, has had a licence cancelled, and so my question to the Minister is this. Clause 20 is all about those sorts of qualitative considerations around what someone’s record might look like. New section 37(1)(d)(i) in clause 21 is very definitive in that it’s a five-year threshold. Minister, are you satisfied that five years is appropriate, and, if so—or if not, I guess—were there any other considerations as to what that particular time frame would be? How did five years get landed upon?
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): I’d note that perhaps the member wasn’t in here when I answered these questions before, and so I’m happy to go through them again.
Tangi Utikere: This part? I’ve been here for this part.
Hon NICOLE McKEE: Yeah. Both the questions that you’ve just asked me, I’ve actually answered, but I’m happy to answer them again for you. With regard to the requirement about the chairperson having seven years’ legal experience, we had mentioned how it’s hard to find a person. We’re not actually removing that from the board, at all. We still want a person with seven years’ experience, if we can find it, to sit on the board—
Tangi Utikere: Just not as chair?
Hon NICOLE McKEE: —but just not as chair. Effectively, I had spoken about how the current chair with seven years’ experience has been wanting to resign, but we have nobody who is able to replace the dear lady. Her name is Denese Bates, and she does a wonderful job for the real estate agents, but she does want to retire. There is nobody there to replace her, and so we’d like to be able to replace her with someone that has the legal experience, but not so defined as it currently is.
: Now, if someone else comes along and they happen to have seven years’ legal experience, we can in the first instance at least get them on to the board, and maybe they could eventually end up in that chair role. It’s just trying to make sure that we have a spin of people that can continue, and the Real Estate Agents Authority can continue in that respect.
: In regard to clause 21, the five-year prohibition following grounds for cancelling a licence is really, really extensive, and there is no other organisation or agency that has that sort of penalty. We’re looking to remove that five-year stand-down period as an automatic consequence for not completing compulsory personal development or for failing to pay the annual suspension fee, and, again, this can also come down to people just having a time where they can’t even get in and do their reapplications, etc., for other things like, say, Cyclone Gabrielle, as I had mentioned before.
: Again, I will just point out that this will come in eight months after Royal assent in order to ensure that we have it all set up and ready to go in the Act, and so that we are not taking away what could often be a lifetime of work. Real estate agents are often in that job for decades before failing to do something as simple as not doing a particular course or not paying a particular fee at any one time, and, as I’ve mentioned, it’s a punitive and disproportionate consequence when you compare it to so many other professions which don’t have anything anywhere near a five-year suspension.
PAULO GARCIA (National—New Lynn): I move, That debate on this question now close.
: A party vote was called for on the question, That the debate on this question be now closed.
: New Zealand National 48; ACT New Zealand 11; New Zealand First 8.
: New Zealand Labour 30; Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand 10; Te Pāti Māori 4; Ferris; Kapa-Kingi.
: Motion agreed to.
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): The question is that the Minister’s tabled amendments to Amendment Paper 636 be agreed to.
: Amendments to the amendments agreed to.
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): The question is that the Minister’s amendments to Part 3 set out on Amendment Paper 636 as amended be agreed to.
: Amendments as amended agreed to.
: Part 3 as amended agreed to.

CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Members, we now come to our final debate: clauses 1 and 2. This is the debate on clauses 1 and 2, “Title” and “Commencement”.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair. I’m signalling that I have just two short questions on this, and they’re all to do with clause 2(1), which is on the commencement date for Part 3.
: Of my two short questions, No. 1 is this. Minister, you mentioned that the poor person who has been the chair of the authority now wants to step down. Does that mean that they have to wait eight months before they can step down because this part doesn’t come into effect for eight months? That’s my first question.
: My second question is to do with how this interacts with clause 20. We did talk about the fact that if a person’s licence is cancelled, they can reapply within 12 months, and yet the commencement is in eight months’ time. If the commencement is in eight months’ time, does that mean that a person who is within that eight months—because there’s no retrospectivity, as far as I know. So if a person whose licence was cancelled within that eight months, the old rules still apply, and it’s not like in eight months’ time, they have four more months of leeway to go to make that up within 12 months—if that makes sense. Those are my two questions for this.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): My officials and I had the same thought on this, but they’re just going away to double-check and will come back. But there is a delay just in Part 3—which is the real estate agents area—for eight months, and if Denese Bates KC is listening to this, we are of the opinion—
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Shout-out to Denese.
Hon NICOLE McKEE: Shout-out to Denese. She’s going to be there for another eight months unless we do find somebody with that seven years’ experience. But the delay of the commencement is because there is some updating of IT systems, forms—which we were talking about earlier—and training programmes that need to be implemented, and the information on their website also needs to be updated. Unfortunately, the chair side of it is in there too, and so, hopefully, Denese Bates KC will stay on for eight months, and unless we—
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): You might have some answers now.
Hon NICOLE McKEE: Clause 18 in Part 3, which amends the membership of the Real Estate Agents Authority, will, however, come into force on the day after Royal assent, as an additional time for the implementation of that particular clause is not required. Denese Bates KC, if you’re listening to this, you can heave a sigh of relief—and I most certainly am—and I hope that that answers the member’s question.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Just checking with the Minister: I had a second part of that question around the reapplication of the licence within that eight months. I understand that the Minister might be seeking some advice, and, Mr Chair, I just wanted to get clarity. That’s my only question. If the Minister is able to get that advice and wants to tie it in to her third reading speech, so to speak, I’m fine with that. I just would like an answer to that—that’s all.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Mr Chair. No, that notification that I had there was saying that it’s only that clause that will be implemented straight away. Everything else will be eight months away, and so—yes—it will take eight months for everything else.
Hon BARBARA EDMONDS (Labour—Mana): Thank you, Mr Chair. It is quite an important question, so if I just practically work through it, because this does become important, particularly in the transition period. So, for example, section 54(d), as amended by clause 25, won’t come into effect until March next year. So therefore, “if the person, at any time, ceases to be able to hold a licence on 1 or more of the grounds [that are now] set out under section 37;”—for example, if tomorrow they cannot meet any of those motions, doesn’t matter; it gets to March—this won’t come until effect until March next year, so that notice period of over month is well superseded—therefore, if it means that with the 12-month period, which Dr Xu-Nan referenced, does that mean—April, May, June, July—by July next year, which is 2027, that’s when that cancellation comes into effect, or is it not for another 12 months from March 2027? So it’s just that clarity around when that is.
: If the Minister, as you said correctly, that’s when section 54(d) comes into effect, March next year, technically, based on the question by Dr Xu-Nan, it won’t be until March 2028 that that person’s licence can be cancelled.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Mr Chair.
Hon Barbara Edmonds: Not 23 July.
Hon NICOLE McKEE: Yeah. I understand the member’s question, and it probably goes a little bit further than what I’m able to answer. When I looked at the notes that I have, the reason why we have that eight months requirement is to update the IT systems, forms, training programmes, and information on their website. I suspect that information on the website, training forms, information that goes out to the real estate agents, will detail exactly how they will roll that out.
: One thing that we have made clear to the real estate authority is to try and ensure that any changes that they make are for the benefit of the real estate agents, hence why we’re removing that five-year suspension as well, because we really just needed to update this.
: I think, in the bigger scheme of things, my expectation is the real estate authority would work with an individual depending on what that circumstance is. To give you an example, if that member did something that was really out of order, one would expect them to be suspended and not have to go through the—
Hon Barbara Edmonds: Not wait until those provisions come in.
Hon NICOLE McKEE: —yes, not wait until those provisions—but if it’s something that, perhaps, could be addressed when those provisions come in, there could be the ability, perhaps, for the real estate authority to suspend their decision until that comes in. But it’s very hard to ascertain exactly when or what, because there will be so many variations to what they have to deal with.
: Clause 1 agreed to.
: Clause 2 agreed to.
: Bill to be reported with amendment.
: House resumed.

topicSummaries.topic: Report of Committee of the whole House
topicSummaries.content:
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Madam Speaker, the committee has considered the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and reports it with amendment. The committee has also considered the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill and reports that also with amendment. I move, That the report be adopted.
: Motion agreed to.
: Report adopted.
DEPUTY SPEAKER: The Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill are set down for third reading immediately.

Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): I present the legislative statements on the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill.
DEPUTY SPEAKER: Those legislative statements are—what are the words?
Tom Rutherford: —published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
DEPUTY SPEAKER: —there we go. Those legislative statements are published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.

Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts): Thank you, Madam Speaker. I move, That the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill be now read a third time.
: I’m pleased to take this final call on two practical bills that improve the way parts of our justice and regulatory systems operate. These bills are not about creating unnecessary new layers of regulation, they’re about maintaining the laws we already have, fixing known problems, removing disproportionate penalties, and making sure our regulatory systems work better for the people who use them.
: The Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill improves access to justice and supports the effective operation of tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies. It allows successful applicants in the disputes tribunal to recover their filing fee from the respondent where it is appropriate.
DEPUTY SPEAKER: You can get another Minister to read it out for you.
Hon NICOLE McKEE: Yes, if you wouldn’t mind.
Hon LOUISE UPSTON: That is a sensible change. People who have had to enforce their legal rights should not be left bearing unnecessary costs when they have been successful.
: The bill also strengthens oversight of the private security industry by improving information gathering powers. This will help detect and deter people operating outside the rules. It also makes practical changes to appointments and employment arrangements for tribunal members so these bodies can operate more consistently and efficiently.
: The Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill improves the occupational regulation system for both professionals and consumers. It allows conveyancers’ professional undertakings to be enforced in the High Court, as lawyers’ undertakings already are. That will support competition in the conveyancing market and give consumers more confidence in the services they use.
: It also removes an overly harsh penalty that disqualified real estate agents from practising for five years for failing to complete continuing professional development or pay fees on time. That kind of penalty is out of proportion to the breach. This bill replaces it with a more sensible and balanced approach. At the same time, the bill strengthens the real estate authority’s ability to investigate unlicensed trading and ensure licensees are meeting their obligations.
: I thank officials in the Parliamentary Council Office, for their work on these bills. I commend these bills to the House.
DEPUTY SPEAKER: Just for the Hansard record: that was the Hon Louise Upston. The question is that the motion be agreed to.
GEORGIE DANSEY (Labour): Thank you, Madam Speaker. Well, it was just an hour, maybe two hours ago that I was here speaking on the second reading of these two great bills: the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill.
: In the intervening time we’ve had a committee stage and I’ve had dinner—fish and chips; fish and chip Friday—but the point I’m making, is the fact that it’s been such a short time, and here I am speaking now, on the third reading, is the way that this legislation is moving through Parliament at such a rapid pace under urgency.
: The need for us to have a process that is robust ensures that the legislation receives the public attention that the public may want to give the legislation—it treats proper scrutiny as an inconvenience—allowing robust debate around this legislation. So it is disappointing to be back here two hours later, in the third reading, to discuss these two important bills, which I would have liked to have more time to consider, as would my colleagues, and I’m sure the public would have appreciated some more time to consider these bills. Nevertheless, I will continue. These bills are a package of four regulatory systems amendment bills administered by the Ministry of Justice. Look, we acknowledge the challenges in our justice system—
Simon Court: Read it better, Georgie.
GEORGIE DANSEY: What do you mean “Read it better”? Read what better?
Simon Court: Your speech.
GEORGIE DANSEY: I was thinking that, maybe, members on the Government side would take an actual call on this. I challenge—
DEPUTY SPEAKER: I would actually challenge the member to speak to the piece of legislation, please, because we’ve just had quite an extensive two hours on the committee stage, so there’s plenty to talk about.
GEORGIE DANSEY: There is plenty. Thank you, Madam Speaker. First of all, I’ll talk about the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill. Within here, there are some technical changes. There are technical changes that will amend the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act 2006, the Prostitution Reform Act 2003, and the Real Estate Agents Act 2008. The aim is to strengthen the ability of occupational regulators to protect consumers, increase efficiency, and remove inconsistent or redundant provisions.
: What I wanted to start talking about was the amendments within the Law Society which give the complaints service discretion rather than requirement in referring complaints against lawyers. This has been hashed out a little bit across the board, and the pros and cons of this part of the legislation have been discussed. It is still not completely resolved, and I think there are still questions around who’s making the decision as to whether a complaint progresses through and how that decision was made and then around what the repercussions are if, say, the complainant’s complaint is dismissed but they don’t think their complaint should be dismissed—what process they would go through? Those are still questions we have, and if we had had more time, those could have been addressed.
: One of the benefits of this legislation—and I see the intention of it is to increase how quickly complaints can be resolved. As we all know, all facets of society will get complaints about the way things are done, and some of them have basis, and some of them don’t. Not having to go through a full investigation process for every single complaint is surely going to benefit the Law Society. When we’re talking about justice, we have to talk about a fair process and fair access to justice. If we can make things more efficient within the system, which in turn frees up resources and people to concentrate on the important things when it comes to administering justice, then that has got to be a good thing—as long as we are doing so in a way that doesn’t limit access at all and is a robust process.

Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): I present a legislative statement on the Mental Health Bill.
DEPUTY SPEAKER: That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.

Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): I move, That the Mental Health Bill be now read a second time.
: It’s a privilege to be standing here today for the second reading of the Mental Health Bill. I’d like firstly to start by thanking the Health Committee for all their hard work—ably led by the chair, Sam Uffindell—in examining this bill. Can I say, from the start, that I think it’s vitally important for tangata whaiora that this bill comes back with full cross-party support. I’d also like to thank the people who took the time to make a submission and engage with the select committee process—particularly those who shared their personal experience. It is a deeply personal thing to share your own experience, so thank you for your bravery. I do want to acknowledge all those with lived experience.
: The committee considered submissions from 358 individuals and groups. Those submitters brought a range of perspectives, including those who have experience of compulsory treatment, those with family with lived experience, clinicians, academics, and mental health organisations. I’d also like to thank the 89 people who spoke directly to the Health Committee to share their views. I’d also like to acknowledge those who bravely came forward to share their stories in the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Historical Abuse in State Care and in the Care of Faith-based Institutions. It is important that we carry their voices, not only tonight but through any work looking into how the State cares for people when they need it the most.
: I want to reiterate that this bill will demonstrate meaningful and significant progress by contributing towards at least 10 of the abuse in care recommendations, relating primarily to care safety and monitoring. All of you have helped shape a Mental Health Bill that goes beyond compulsory treatment, as we know it today, and that, instead, firmly places a person at the centre of their care and empowers people to make decisions about their own care.
: While most in New Zealand who access specialist mental health and addiction services are not subject to the Mental Health Act, over the course of a year, around 11,000 people receive compulsory care. In an ideal world, we would not need compulsory mental health care; however, we need a system in place for New Zealanders experiencing mental distress at a level that does require intervention to support their recovery. This bill strikes a balance of a future focus on safe and effective mental health care for people who require that State intervention, while having the right safeguards in place to ensure people’s rights are upheld and protected. This bill will be a critical safety net for those experiencing severe mental distress who are unable to make decisions about their own mental health care. I do want to reiterate tonight that it is intended to be used as a last resort only.
: The submissions received on this bill represented a variety of views. This is an important piece of legislation, and I expected there to be views across the board on key areas in the bill to assist the Health Committee’s consideration. It has been heartening to see that, of the individuals and groups that commented on the general policy intent of the bill, the majority were supportive. People recognise that we need compulsory care in some form; however, there were divergent views on what people felt this should look like.
: I’m also encouraged by the support from submitters for the introduction of compulsory care principles, the supported decision-making provisions, and establishment of new roles and processes to safeguard those under compulsory care. This includes independent support persons and advocates, nominated persons, and collaborative care teams. These are integral to the shifts I want to see under this new legislation.
: There were some key changes made through the select committee process. These include introducing a “dignity of risk” principle. This aligns with the legislation’s purpose of promoting decision-making capacity. I believe it’s critical that the legislation recognises a person’s right to take reasonable risks to achieve personal growth, self-esteem, and overall quality of life.
: Terminology is really important to how people see themselves and how people are treated. I’m pleased to see the Health Committee has made changes to the term “patient” to instead be “person under compulsory care”. This change responds to submitters who said the term “patient” is stigmatising and can reinforce power imbalances between someone seeking support and professionals. Submitters also said it reinforces a paternalistic approach to care, which we want to move away from.
: Offences and penalties are important enforcement tools in the legislation. The royal commission of inquiry raised the need for appropriate and significant penalties for failures to comply with standards of care. I’m very pleased to see that the select committee has made changes to modernise the offences and penalties in this legislation, with a more structured regime as well as more tools for the regulator to use to support greater compliance with the Act.
: However, I also recognise that many people who submitted on the bill had concerns about specific areas—in particular, the use of restrictive practices such as seclusion and the use of electroconvulsive therapy, or ECT. People also want strong safeguards for care of those under 18. As I spoke about in the first reading on this bill, these practices have a history of inappropriate use, abuse, and overuse.
: I want to be very clear that I remain committed to seeing the reduction and elimination of seclusion. However, it is critical that this is done in a way that minimises the risk of unintended consequences. In particular, I would not want to see an increase in other inappropriate practices such as chemical or physical restraint. The bill strengthens requirements on the use of seclusion to drive the change needed to reduce and eliminate seclusion. The bill prohibits seclusion for children and young people. This is an incremental but significant step towards elimination that I am proud of, but I’m aware that there’s going to be a big shift for mental health workers, and it is important that we manage this change safely for both children and young people as well as staff.
: I do want to acknowledge that the Health Committee has made a number of improvements to further strengthen provisions relating to seclusion to ensure there are stronger protections and greater monitoring of progress. The committee received a wide range of views about ECT, from being an effective, life-saving treatment in modern clinical practice through to wanting it banned. The committee has also recommended a range of improvements to make sure there are greater safeguards on the use of ECT, including for people under 18.
: From the submissions received, the Health Committee has recommended changes that will improve clarity and ensure greater safeguards for those subject to the Act. The word I want to emphasise here is “balance”; the bill aims to strike a balance between placing limits on people’s rights when there is a need to intervene to provide care and ensuring that this intervention is only done when absolutely necessary and in a way that protects and upholds an individual’s rights.
: In closing, I acknowledge that there are diverse views on this piece of legislation, which were heard through the select committee process. Developing this bill has involved careful balancing of all of those views.  I believe the bill represents a meaningful step forward, and I’m pleased to present it to you today. The bill will enable supported decision making, safer practice through stronger protections for people subject to legislation, and care that is provided in the least coercive way—that is therapeutic and responsive to a person’s needs. I hope to see continued cross-party support on this important bill. I commend this bill to the House.
DEPUTY SPEAKER: The question is that the motion be agreed to.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Today, there was a press release that was issued, and anyone who saw TV ONE news would have heard of what has been happening at Wakari Hospital, where the Ombudsman said, “I’m deeply disturbed by what our inspectors found. What they observed at Ward 10A were some of the worst practices we have observed anywhere”. People who are at Wakari Ward 10A or who were there have been kept under the Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act 2003 and the Criminal Procedure Act 2011, but, also, the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992.
: The Wakari Hospital developments that have been occurring in Dunedin, very close to my electorate, are a stark example of why we need reform in this area. I welcome the fact that we have a new bill before us. I agree that it would be great to have cross-party support, and I guess it depends on how one measures that. If it’s just on votes, then yes, this is cross-party support. But we really do feel, on this side of the House, that despite the small changes that we were able to make at select committee, it is a bit of a wasted opportunity to make a transformational change to a bill that probably won’t be able to come before the House for another 10 or 15 years.
: If I look at what the Ombudsman said had been happening at Wakari Hospital to our intellectually disabled mental health patients, in one instance, a person was tied down on a bariatric or evac-mat to move them across the ward. This was causing physical and mental harm to the person, who suffered carpet burns as a result. Inspectors also found that one person had been secluded in their bedroom for around 18 months with an almost complete lack of meaningful human contact and no access to the outdoors. There were restrictions on dental care and people being denied access to their own money. Staff were observed incentivising good behaviour by rewarding people with access to basic necessities, including dental treatment or the use of a toilet. There was unlawful administration of medication, and serious and significant failures.
: I am heartened that, after my calls for an independent inquiry into this—and after not being able to get an urgent debate in the House, unfortunately—the Ministry of Health has accepted the Ombudsman’s recommendation to undertake an independent investigation into the treatment and conditions of people at Ward 10A. That ward is now closing down for that particular purpose, and I would really like to acknowledge the Ombudsman for taking so seriously the work that they’ve done, or that he’s done. I’d like to acknowledge the staff and the PSA union, who’ve worked under incredibly difficult conditions given the structure and the environment that they’ve been working in and the harm that some of them have endured. I’d like to acknowledge Health New Zealand for acting very quickly on the Ombudsman’s recommendation, which was the only thing, really, that they could have done, given the seriousness of that.
: But, also, patients and former staff who reached out to me and shared their story, even though they were shattered by their experiences, and some of them who were just too scared to go through official channels. On that note, I’d really like to acknowledge Matthew Littlewood from the Otago Daily Times, who has done an excellent job in bringing this to light.
: This is the reason why we need reform in the mental health sphere and the Mental Health Bill—and it’s no small bill: it’s 168 pages, 221 clauses, and two schedules. We’ve had an amendment today, a five-page Government amendment, which tells me that we do have some scope in the committee stage to really forensically look at this. There were submissions that indicated that the process was quite rushed, and there are examples in the bill of typos and questions which would indicate that has happened, and so it would be useful for us to use this time to go through the bill.
: The main point I would like to make is that we are supporting it, because the 1992 Act—that’s a long time ago—is absolutely not fit for purpose, but this modern framework does fall short of the transformational reform that was envisaged by the He Ara Oranga report. Where we see the opportunities are around implementation, workforce planning, and accountability that don’t seem to have legislated safeguards. We also would have preferred to see stronger protections for Māori, disabled people, children, young people, and other vulnerable groups. We would have liked a greater emphasis on voluntary participatory care wherever possible, particularly given the evidence we heard at select committee about the way that participatory care contributes to recovery for people journeying through mental health, versus the absolute lack of evidence that compulsory care orders enable recovery—and yet, they seem to be the norm currently.
: We definitely would like to see the bill contain a strong commitment to ending seclusion. We are happy with where we landed on electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). It is a vexed issue, and we do see that there could be still some further strengthening, but we do acknowledge that there are some very limited examples where ECT is appropriate.
: We are very happy that there have been some small changes—and I would say they’re small, compared to the ones that we would have liked to see—made with the presumption that birthing parents and newborn babies should remain together unless separation is necessary for safety purposes. But, today, we’ve seen this Amendment Paper come into the House, which is really limiting that again, and so we’d like to go through that quite closely to find out whether our change that we had advocated for in select committee actually has any meaning left to it for our birthing parents.
: We also are happy that there’s been an acknowledgement of and our recommendation adopted that Labour advocated for, which was children and young people being able to travel with a trusted adult between facilities in what can be a very traumatising journey. That has been adopted without change, so that’s good. The dignity of care provision that the Minister referred to is fantastic but, actually, was a hygiene factor for us. That is something that should have been in the original drafting of the legislation. Nevertheless, it’s good to see it in there.
: I do want to acknowledge the Minister, actually, for giving us the opportunity to be reacquainted with the bill just a couple of nights ago and, also, be able to suggest some of our amendments to him in case he would entertain them. I think that’s a very useful final check to go through. Nevertheless, I have got about 40-odd amendments on the Table, and these are not single-word changes or frivolous. These are very thought-through amendments that we believe, on this side of the House, would panel-beat the bill into something that would actually be transformational. We do hope that the House gives them due regard. We would also like to see the giving-effect of Te Tiriti o Waitangi happen in a way that is in the totality of the bill, not just in the particular limited circumstances that have been mentioned, and we will be going through that in the committee stage.
: We acknowledge that the bill does limit seclusion to a degree, but I’d like to point out to any media who are watching this that we’re in quite different places around seclusion on this side of the House. When I was being asked to do media reports a couple of weeks ago, I was surprised that media thought that there was a sunset clause on seclusion. That is not the case. There is simply a five-year legislative review. We would have liked that to have been a sunset clause and, at least—at the very least—two-yearly reviews for the House to be able to consider whether we’d move to a place of resourcing where we could do that.
: The Minister has mentioned that under-18-year-olds won’t be subject to seclusion, and that’s a good outcome that we support, but there’s a contradiction, then, in the bill, because the Minister has said the reason for not sunsetting seclusion is because it will encourage other forms of restraint unless there’s resourcing. What I’m hearing from that is that, perhaps, our children and young people are in a more vulnerable position as a result, and we would like to interrogate that with the Minister. We did have evidence of places that had been able to eliminate seclusion and we are questioning why that can’t happen if there’s a commitment to resourcing—and yet, the Minister and the Government members have shied away from any kind of legislative commitment to resourcing, which is really the fundamental problem with the bill.
: There’s a number of other things that we would like to see, but, in conclusion, we do support the bill, because we cannot remain under the 1992 Act. The story that I told you at the beginning of this is an evolving story. It is huge. It is terrible in the context of abuse in care, and it is terrible because it involves our most vulnerable, marginalised, and invisible people in society. We want to see a bill that has more participation, more human rights at the centre, and stronger implementation, accountability, and safeguards. Thank you.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise on behalf of the Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand to also support the Mental Health Bill in its second reading. Now, I do want to acknowledge both the Minister and also the previous speaker, Ingrid Leary, on this particular bill. I will lay out some of the concerns on this side of the House, though we do support it. I think it’s important to highlight some of the context around this and also some of the positions and also some of the areas we want to engage with the Minister on during the upcoming committee stage.
: In terms of this bill, as mentioned previously, this is a bill that replaces an incredibly outdated piece of legislation, the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992. A lot of this came from the 2018 report He Ara Oranga, which was delivered, I believe, to the Minister of Health at the time in December 2018. I think this is a really important starting point that this bill came from. The Minister has already laid out some of the conversations that have been heard during the select committee stage, even though I wasn’t a part of that. I do want to thank all of the members on the Health Committee for taking part in that process, and, particularly, I want to thank all of the submitters who came along, as always, and shared their personal stories and experiences with this bill, particularly when we’re looking at compulsory care.
: It’s also important, I think, to contextualise a lot of this with the example that my colleague Ingrid Leary just gave before around the broader context that we saw just over the last year and up until very recently with the royal commission of inquiry into abuse in care and how we’re still seeing some of those really quite severe and horrendous experiences that people are experiencing in compulsory care, which, I think, by any standard as a New Zealander and by any standard internationally, from a rights-based perspective, is unacceptable.
: I also want to address the fact that one of the things that did come through the select committee as a part of this process—and, particularly, it was raised by the Ombudsman, was the fact that for such a significant bill and such a significant change, there wasn’t sufficient time given to hear from submitters in an appropriate way. I think that’s really important, bearing in mind that the first reading of this bill was in 2024, and it was referred to the select committee, where it had, I think, by select committee standards, quite a long period that was open for submissions; I believe it was about two months. But, over this period, the report from select committee came back on 17 April 2025—that is over 14 months ago—and we’re now just hearing this bill for the second time now. I think, in hindsight, potentially, with the blessing from the Minister, that select committee could have actually had a longer time to consider this bill and to hear from submitters in a way that is appropriate and that uses different forms to engage with submitters, as we have seen in various other bills that have happened in the House recently.
: Now, on to the actual content of the bill, there are eight parts, and we’re looking forward to engaging with the Minister on all of them, but I want to address a few areas that are of significant concern for the Greens. I think the previous speaker has already mentioned the fact that there is still a review period and not a sunset clause for seclusion, even though I think the Minister has laid out that, in certain areas, children and young people, I believe, will no longer be under seclusion, which is an important step. At the same time, seclusion, as we heard from the example before, is something that is deeply traumatic and is actually simply not good for anyone’s wellbeing, mental or physical. Yet it is disappointing to see that there has been no sunset clause on a seclusion commitment in here, whereas I think the Greens would have liked to see a five-year sunset clause, which would have shown that there is some form of commitment around this particular practice.
: Now, the other thing that is really important from our perspective is this idea that if we are looking at some of the international standards and if we’re looking at the disability convention and also the rights of tangata whaiora and disabled people and neurodivergent people, we would like to move towards something that is more rights-consistent and that considers the mental and physical wellbeing of these people, where we can start moving towards an area where we can maybe look into replacing compulsory care with a voluntary care order. Again, this is something that the Greens would like to see, as voluntary care orders should be the default, not an option. We are going in a way that best emphasises and also takes into consideration the ability for people to rehabilitate, to recover, and also, like I said before, that considers people’s wellbeing as a starting point before we move into the need for compulsory care. That is something that, for example, the Greens would also like to see, with voluntary care as the default, as opposed to going to more extremes with compulsory care.
: I already mentioned before that one of the areas that the Greens has the greatest concern around is, again, the implications that this will have for disabled people and for neurodivergent people and how this would interact and how this would be moving towards a system that will allow them to have more dignity and allow them to maintain their rights and freedom to a greater extent. Like we have said previously, this bill is a significant improvement from the 1992 bill, which is why we do support it.
: I also think it’s really heartening to hear from the Minister and also in the engagement from the Minister that we hope that we can move to a stage where we can do better and be able to provide more funding. This is something that I’m hoping that the Minister will be able to consider as well, both in terms of the amendments by my colleague Ingrid Leary but also my colleague Kahurangi Carter, who is our mental health spokesperson, who is also engaging with the Minister as well on this bill. We have also a few amendments on this as well that we would like to engage with the Minister on as part of the committee stage.
: There are, obviously, other parts in this bill that I think deserve mention as well. I think this is something that, again, to the best of the select committee’s consideration, there have been amendments to this bill in a way that may have changed some of the aspects further. One of the areas that the Minister has already mentioned and that I think was one of the things that I, in one of the rare opportunities when I subbed in on the Health Committee, did actually hear from the experts, is around the electroconvulsive therapy, or ECT. I think that is something that, from our perspective, we’re still cautious about. We know that is something that the ministry has considered can be an effective treatment for depression, mania, catatonia, and other serious neuropsychiatric conditions. But, again, it’s one of those things where, from our perspective, we would like to see other mechanisms in place and only use this as an absolute last resort.
: Again, with those kind of things, particularly from an international convention perspective, what we want to avoid is any sort of therapy or any sort of care, compulsory or otherwise, that would amount to torture. This is something that I think everyone in this House but also something that, for example, OPCAT, which is our obligation under the Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture, will possibly be interested in as well. This is something that our NPMs, the national preventive mechanisms, such as the Ombudsman, Oranga Tamariki, and the Human Rights Commission, would have oversight or some checks and balances on as well. That is just one example that I want to give, on top of everything else I mentioned, that we would like to have more conversations with the Minister on.
: Like I said, the Green Party does support this bill. We do have a few amendments that we want to engage the Minister on, but we are looking forward to the upcoming committee stage. With that: yes from the Greens; we support the Mental Health Bill.

And through that select committee process, there has been quite a lot of amendments and changes, and most of them have strengthened the bill, but while we do support it, we still don’t think it has gone far enough.
