: I would like to just, I guess, touch on a couple of the points that the Greens still have concerns about. Obviously in the commentary, there’s a joint differing view with Te Pāti Māori, and a lot of the concerns we have, we also shared with the Labour Party as well. We’re very committed, and I know the whole House is committed, in trying, with the importance of improving mental health and how that’s handled. There’s always going to be some differences, and we’ll continue to try and strengthen that and improve the outcomes that we get. It’s really important that when we make the decisions, we do it for all of us.
: So, obviously, one of the major concerns we did have, which has been outlined a number of times, but I think it’s really important to continue to outline, is around seclusion Obviously, there’s a review of that in five years, but for the Greens, we would have liked to see that have a sunset clause. Seclusion, as we know, is a harmful and traumatic practice. We do know that there is an issue and you couldn’t go straight to removing that straight away because of workforce issues, but we believe with having a sunset clause in there, and giving that time and ensuring that the staffing levels that were put in place would cater for what was required, we could actually move to it, and having that sunset clause in there would put a definite time limit in there to ensure the resources would be put in place to ensure that happened. I’d just like to note that, obviously, while we as a political party believe that that sunset clause should be in place, that view has been shared by a lot of other people around the motu, and so we really do hope that we can move in that direction.
: Another area that we recorded in our differing view was to replace compulsory care with volunteer care orders. We also spoke around neurodivergent children as well, and some proposed changes around clause 6, that voluntary care should be the default, with compulsory care used only when absolutely necessary, and for the shortest duration.
: I would like to note that part of the clause was to strengthen—I guess, when you look at what happens with mental health, Māori are disproportionately affected by mental health, and it was really important and good to see that there was a Treaty clause in there which would actually, hopefully, help in that space.
: Once again, I would like to reiterate that the Greens support the Mental Health Bill. We still have concerns and we look forward to working on that further as we go through the committee of the whole House stage, which, as I said, is coming up very, very shortly. So on that note, I commend this bill to the House.
Dr HAMISH CAMPBELL (National—Ilam): It’s an honour to rise and speak on the second reading of the Mental Health Bill. I do just want to acknowledge New Zealand’s first Minister for Mental Health, Matt Doocey, and for the work he has done to bring this bill to the House. This bill is replacing the 1992 Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act, which no longer aligns with modern mental healthcare. Therefore, I commend this bill to the House.
Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour): Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s a privilege to rise to take a call on this bill, which has been a long time coming following on from the He Ara Oranga review, and then work by successive Ministers in the Labour Government, and now the National Government. It’s great to see it in the House.
: I do have to admit that the select committee hearings feel like quite some time ago now, and it is a shame that such a landmark piece of legislation is being debated under urgency, meaning that we’re not hearing full calls from the other side. This is really important, and I can’t think of much other legislation that has the same human rights impact in the health sector. It was with that lens that I went into the select committee hearings, from which I had my involvement when I was briefly the Minister—well, my engagement with the bill as Minister was brief compared to the other Ministers who have shepherded this bill.
: The 1992 Act I would characterise as having the test of who could be placed under compulsory care in the Act, and then the main defence of the person’s human rights under the existing Act is largely through processes of review that are structured throughout the course of the person’s treatment and the time periods at which they must occur. This Act takes a very different approach to upholding the rights of people who are subject to the compulsory treatment clauses of the Act. So, for a start, compulsory treatment should only be used to improve the person’s mental health. So it’s not an opportunity to improve other elements of the person’s health—they still have to consent for that—or their social circumstances. I think that’s important to remember because sometimes some mental health conditions do mean that people’s living circumstances can deteriorate.
: The bill requires that the least restrictive option be used. Voluntary care options should be always preferred to compulsory care, and compulsory care should only be used for as short a period as possible. There’s also the reassessments of whether compulsory treatment can be used. Those are positive developments.
: In addition, there are some new and innovative concepts that clearly can be done, but it’ll be interesting to see how these practices interact with the law and how, ultimately, people’s care and human rights are affected. This includes the creation of mental health advance directives. That is something viewed favourably in many of the submissions that we received on the committee. But advance directives of all sorts have limitations, and I hope they are not too easily set aside by busy care teams who wonder if the circumstances in which the advance directives were set are no longer in place. There can be good reasons why they’re not followed, and so I hope that we are able to live up to the aspiration in the bill in terms of how we implement those.
: I think the appointment of nominated persons to stand up for the rights of the person in compulsory care is as important, as well as the practice of wellbeing meetings. These are practices that may well be being used across the health system already, but they are not mandated. Overall, I think those would be good things.
: I think one of the things about the involvement of family and whānau in someone’s care is that, at times, and I guess under the current Act, treatment teams can confuse, and we all as a society can confuse—well, excessive concern about respecting someone’s privacy might lead to the non-inclusion of family members, in some situations. So I think the bill’s presumption is that family member involvement is a good thing and will mean that people have greater access to the supports that they will depend on when they are no longer in compulsory care, and also during the time that they are in compulsory care. So I think that’s positive.
: The requirement for independent support people to advocate for the person under the Act and assist them with participating in decision making and exercising their rights is another really, really positive innovation in the Act.
: There are some areas where rights have been strengthened as well. People have to be able to understand their rights, and there’s also an entitlement to use aids like mobility and other communication aids, under the Act. I mean, it’s kind of unbelievable that we don’t say that, but, of course, if you’re dependent on a device for your hearing, your communication, your mobility, and not having the ability to get that for yourself, it is important that those things are specified.
: I was pleased my colleague Ingrid Leary and I were able to lead a discussion on the committee about the right for a birth parent under compulsory care orders to be able to stay with their baby unless there is a safety risk. I think the presumption that a mother and their baby should not be separated is an important one.
: The other area where I paid a lot of attention as the Minister briefly responsible for this bill, and then in committee, was the use of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). In both of those capacities, I held serious questions about whether or not one day we’ll look back on the use of electroconvulsive therapy and regret that we permitted it. It’s not an area of medicine that I have any expertise in, so I was pleased that the select committee gave us the opportunity to gather evidence and to hear from experts on that; we heard from experts at length. We accept the conclusion of expert evidence that it is still a practice that is beneficial for some people and can be done in a humane way. I’m pleased, however, that there are increased protections in this bill around the use of ECT, particularly on people under the age of 18.
: So, all in all, there is a lot to be positive about in this bill.
: I do want to mention our concern about the continued use of seclusion. Seclusion has been eliminated in some parts of our health system in New Zealand, and good on the teams who have worked really hard in their facilities and hospitals to make that the case. They should be really proud, and we should be really proud as a country if we were able to do away with that.
: Resourcing and workforce are always challenges in the health system, and there are always difficult choices about where we place resource and what we prioritise. We have an opportunity in this bill to say that seclusion is something that we would like to make a priority, and to make that staffing to ensure that seclusion is no longer used, a priority.
: In my remaining time, I want to tell you why I’m so convinced that that is important. Actually, a Labour Party member who I met through my work in the party in recent years came and talked to me about it two or three years ago. She had had an experience of compulsory care. She described the experience of seclusion and how traumatic it was. I suppose, as a former clinician, I always approach that question from the prism of “But was it justified because otherwise you would hurt yourself?”. But, actually, in talking to her, I realised that it wasn’t justified, because she no longer trusts those people who could provide care for her in the future because of the experience of such a traumatic thing at the hands of people who were meant to be caring for her. For that reason, that is my one reservation about this bill, but there are a lot of other positive developments in it, and I commend it to the House.
Dr CARLOS CHEUNG (National—Mt Roskill): This bill is a significant step forward in modernising compulsory mental health care. It puts patients at the centre of decisions about their own care, strengthens protection and safeguards, and improves access to efficient mental health and addiction support. Therefore, I commend this bill to the House.
GEORGIE DANSEY (Labour): Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s a hard, hard bill, the Mental Health Bill. It’s a big topic. I’ll start by thanking the Minister and the Health Committee for the work that you all did in this space, and as my colleague the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall has alluded to, the previous Government started the work in this space. This is a really significant improvement on the current Act. As other speakers have spoken to, Labour supports this bill. However, we’d like to see this bill go further and make more transformational reform.
: This is a really personal one for me because 11 years ago I lost my brother-in-law who was under compulsory care. The coroner found that the care facility had not cared for him adequately and that resulted in his death. There were multiple downfalls at multiple stages of his care, and multiple times when the ball was dropped. Had there been more effective processes around that facility, then he would, hopefully, still be here today. That kind of loss, obviously, has a lifetime impact on family and whānau members. I’d like to acknowledge everyone else in New Zealand who has lost someone in these circumstances, and really send my aroha to you and the lifelong impacts that this has.
: So, really, for me, speaking on this bill—it’s quite deep. I am really pleased to be able to contribute in this small way, and so much thanks to those that have done the real mahi in this space, because this will make a real difference. I appreciated the Minister’s comments around the compulsory psychiatric assessment being the last resort only. I appreciate that, and hope in implementation that that is the case. We need to have a human rights approach to this and that it is the last resort when we require compulsory care, obviously taking into account the health of the person and those around them.
: I would like to talk about some of the aspects where we would hope to go further. In regard to He Ara Oranga report, the Government inquiry into mental health and addiction, really, this report falls short of the transformational reform that the report envisioned and the real matter of human rights for people in this space. We would have liked to see a greater emphasis on voluntary participatory care, and supported decision-making, where possible, and where the therapeutic evidence supports this. We also would have liked to see more in the implementation workforce planning and accountability, which still remains a significant concern, in particular, the workforce planning.
: From my experience in the system, there were multiple people who didn’t have the training required to do the job to look after the people they were required to care for in quite acute health situations. I would like to see a real emphasis on training for people working in the system, in whatever space they’re in, as healthcare workers. We need to make sure that they are trained and also paid effectively—#EqualPay.
: So, thank you. Labour supports this bill. I hope to see more, and I will continue to advocate for more safeguards around compulsory care in the future. I commend this bill to the House.
Dr VANESSA WEENINK (National—Banks Peninsula): It is an honour to speak at this historic point in the journey that New Zealand has been on in the care for people who are experiencing mental health crises and mental health ill-health. This takes us forward. The Minister has done excellent work, along with the committee, and I commend the bill to the House.
Dr TRACEY McLELLAN (Labour): Thank you, Mr Speaker. I, too, rise to take a call on the Mental Health Bill at this second reading. It’s very appropriate that Labour supports this bill because it is essentially updating—well, it is replacing a very outdated law that we simply can’t continue to operate under: the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992. A lot has changed since 1992. Certainly, the way that society as a whole conceptualises the difference between mental illness, mental health, and mental wellbeing, and a lot of improvement in our understanding—and in our expectations—of what people care could and should expect from their mental health system.
: As has been noted, the law was written more than three decades ago. It no longer reflects the modern understanding of human rights, of supported decision-making and how that can be possible, not just in an idealistic way but in a therapeutic way, and something not just to strive towards but something that can be inculcated into something even as complicated and as important as treating mental illness and mental wellbeing.
: It also no longer reflects our modern understanding of disability rights and cultural safety, or the importance of involving whānau in care, and all of those other things that, since 1992, we have prided ourselves in this country of improving. So we do think this bill was a substantial improvement.
: I’d like to acknowledge the Minister for his work. I’d like to acknowledge the Health Committee for all of the work that they have done. I wasn’t on that committee, but even just listening tonight, you can see the nature of the robust questioning that would have happened, the nature of the genuine and inquisitive inquiries that would have been offered only with the absolute intentionality to do the very best by this bill and the very best by the people who would be most impacted by this bill. I’d also like to acknowledge, no doubt, all of the officials and the people with expertise who submitted, people with lived experience, because only with that breadth of input could we make necessary improvements.
: Whilst I say that the bill has made substantial improvements—as we’ve heard, it follows the He Ara Oranga and the royal commission into abuse in care—I do agree also with my colleagues that it does also feel somewhat of a missed opportunity. I understand the tension between fixing something that needs to be fixed because it is outdated and no longer reflects society’s expectations, and the tension between doing something that is much more transformative. That has been the decision that has been made. Would we have made, potentially, a different decision? Yes, probably so, but we do respect where we’ve landed, but it is incumbent upon us to make those notes.
: The bill introduces, as I said, a more modern rights-based framework and places a greater emphasis on participation, which we know, therapeutically, is actually a really important factor in the efficacy of any kind of treatment regime, particularly when people are under all sorts of stressors, as is often the case in this domain, but ultimately, always need to be treated with dignity, and voluntary care should always be the goal, so that direction is welcome. We fundamentally believe that compulsion should never be the default simply because there is a lack of time, staffing, or resources.
: It’s on that point that I do just want to take a moment because that, for as long as I can remember, has always been a justification, an excuse, a perfectly decent and reasonable explanation—however we want to term it—but for as long as I can remember, a lack of time, staffing, and resources has always held up a different way of doing things in mental health. I’ve worked with many nurses in particular who have worked in mental health, and my goodness, they really do an amazing job. I have worked with nurses who work in all sorts of health sectors. Whilst some people, for instance, might assume that some aspects of nursing are harder than others, I can absolutely tell you that the people that work in mental health have a very unique perspective, and they work incredibly hard under very difficult circumstances, and often face quite personal issues in terms of their own safety in those areas. We shouldn’t be allowed to use a lack of staffing as a means by which to have lower expectations of what the system could look like.
: A right written into legislation, ultimately, is only as meaningful when a person can actually exercise it. We do implore, along with our support of this bill, much more focus on increased staffing and even things like increased capital spend, because I’ve seen several facilities that just simply are not designed for what they’re being utilised for, and even just basic layout can pose really, really significant risks to people’s safety, including staff. Without those foundations, there is a risk that the language of this law changes—which it will through the passage of this bill—but people’s experience of the system doesn’t necessarily change if it’s not resourced properly.
: We have also touched on tonight, and both of my colleagues on this side of the House have, I think, spoken quite eloquently about the need to have a genuine plan to end seclusion, and Labour supports New Zealand’s commitment to eliminate seclusion. This bill doesn’t go that far. It doesn’t turn that commitment into a credible plan. We acknowledge that annual reporting is important, that the five-year legislative review is better than no review at all, but neither of those things actually amount to a commitment to end seclusion in practice. I acknowledge that that’s a resourcing issue as much as it is an educative and a legislative process, but Labour certainly does believe that the legislation should set a goal of ending seclusion. Even within five years would be a reasonable goal to require a proper systems phase-out plan. That matters because ending seclusion can’t simply be directed from Parliament. It requires, as I’ve said, the investment in workforce capacity first and foremost, therapeutic environments as I’ve mentioned, and appropriate building designs, specialist training, and alternative models of care. All of those things are possible. All of those things are well-advanced in terms of knowledge. There are just some pieces missing to the puzzle, and that is appropriate resource.
: With regards to electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), I’d like to echo my colleagues’ reservations and their comments that they made about the process and about making the Health Committee’s ability to be able to make some leeway on what the bill as drafted had in it. I would also like to note that ECT can be a really emotive topic, and it’s one of those things that we’ve heard, quite rightly so, a lot of horror stories over the years. It absolutely is something that has been used abusively over many, many years. It is an area that I’ve had a little bit to do with through my personal background, and I have seen it also be put to incredibly good therapeutic use. When it’s considered as a treatment of last resort, it actually can save lives. I think that this bill does strike a right balance between acknowledging the therapeutic qualities and the necessities that still exist for ECT, but also having much more robust safeguards around when it should be used and on who that should be used too.
: Labour will support this bill. We absolutely acknowledge the fact that the 1992 Act is old and not fit for purpose. The bill moves us closer to the goals that I think many of us, regardless of what side of the House we sit on, would agree is an ultimate outcome and an ultimate goal of a much, much better mental health system, and we are therefore happy to commend it to the House.
GREG FLEMING (National—Maungakiekie): [Authorised reo Māori text to be inserted by the Hansard Office.]

DEPUTY SPEAKER: The Mental Health Bill is set down for committee stage immediately.

CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Members, the House is in committee on the Mental Health Bill. Before we begin debating this bill, I will note that Government Amendment Paper 648 on this bill was released at 12.45 p.m. today. I remind members of Speaker Brownlee’s ruling earlier in the sitting that committee stages are always going to proceed slowly when substantive Government amendments are released on the day that the bill is in committee. While I am satisfied that the majority of the amendments in this Amendment Paper are minor and technical, there are some that, on the face of it, appear to be more than minor. The committee stage is always an opportunity to correct matters in a bill, but it is not good practice to release a Government Amendment Paper so close to the beginning of a committee stage, and I will take this into account to enable members to properly scrutinise its contents.
: We come first to Part 1. Part 1 is the debate on clauses 3 to 11—“Preliminary provisions”—and Schedule 1. The question is that Part 1 stand part.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Thank you very much, Mr Chair. Can I begin by just acknowledging what you’ve read around the Amendment Paper. I think, in fairness to officials, genuinely, they thought the bill would be up tomorrow afternoon, so putting it up today was going to be a day early. But I think you pointed out, quite rightly, that it could have been in a bit early, so I do accept that.
: It is good to be here to debate the Mental Health Bill and Part 1. The bill, as we know, has already been out for extensive public consultation before it was introduced to the House, and is a critical piece of legislation for people experiencing severe mental distress. Part 1 of the bill sets out the foundation for this bill to support a shift towards a rights-based and recovery approach to mental health care; to establish a modern, rights-based framework that promotes decision-making capacity, safeguards rights, supports recovery, and protects the safety and wellbeing of people and their communities.
: It’s a key principle in this bill that voluntary and least restrictive practices be used. However, with the exception of extending all rights to voluntary mental health care consumers, the scope of the bill is about the rights of people who are subject to compulsory care, including assessment and treatment. In this part of Part 1, we’re introducing a new decision-making capacity criterion, ensuring compulsory care is only available when a person has seriously impaired mental health, is experiencing serious adverse effects, and lacks decision-making capacity about their mental health care. The compulsory care principles in Part 1 require care to be therapeutic, least restrictive, supportive, and responsive, and to recognise the dignity of risk.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Thank you, Mr Chair. I take on board the direction that you’ve given us around the Amendment Paper today. I understand that when we met with the Minister the other evening, he was of the mind that the bill would be in the House tomorrow. Having said that, this bill has been sitting on a dusty shelf for many months, and so there was plenty of time for that amendment to come before the House.
: I thought it may be useful, as I look at Part 1, clause 3, the purpose clause, to just also provide a little bit of an architecture about how we intend to prosecute the bill, because it is a very big and significant bill, as has been said. I want to frame that around the purpose as it’s articulated in clause 3(a), which talks about promoting the decision-making capacity. I will note that it talks about promoting decision making, not safeguarding, so there is a threshold there that the bill purports to put into place. Many of my questions around this very first section are, really, whether that threshold is indeed met or whether those words are appropriate.
: You will find, Mr Chair, from our side, that many of our questions will be in Part 1, including the definition section, because that will help to inform the rest of the debate. There will be some questions in Part 2 and probably the fewest questions in Parts 3 to 8, including very little, if anything, in the schedules. But we also would like to debate the amendment that’s before the House, because that is indeed around one of the changes that Labour members had put forward and it does appear to have reduced in scope the protections afforded in there.
: When I look at clause 3, there are two things I would like to prosecute, perhaps in a couple of contributions. The first one, really, is around process. It was mentioned in the second reading speeches, but it’s important to bring it up here, just around the time constraints that we’ve had to look at this comprehensive bill. It’s not just us who are saying it. The Ombudsman said at point number 3 of his submission that this is a very short time frame for commenting on such a significant piece of legislation. He also talked about time frames not being appropriate, given key stakeholders included people with lived experience, the mental health workforce, and wider disability community. He mentioned their rights to be involved through the United Nations (UN) Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities’ concluding observations on the second and third periodic reports of New Zealand, and also the UN recommendation to New Zealand that development process for the new legislation actively involves persons with disabilities, particularly persons with psychosocial disabilities. Again, I refer to the word “promote” in the purpose in Part 1 that I am referencing there.
: The second issue is that the Ombudsman talked about how this was being compounded by a lack of accessible formats such as Easy Read and/or other accessible and engagement tools. We also found that the advice to the Health Committee, while the officials worked really hard, did feel very rushed and it didn’t cover many of the items raised by submitters. In the end, we drafted a table of 50 areas for discussion and debate, and we had to fight very hard just to have substantive discussions about recommendations, and for many of them we didn’t get to do that. The time frame was extremely tight, and we don’t believe on this side that it did justice to the issues raised by the submitters. Some areas, including forensic mental health, including incarcerated people, got very little, if no, attention, and there’s a whole section of the bill devoted to that that appeared to have been lifted and shifted. It would be good to be able to scrutinise that before it is to come into law.
: My questions around process are, really, to ask the Minister: why was the select committee phase of the bill rushed, particularly when it appears to have been languishing—not even on the Order Paper, actually—off the Order Paper and on a shelf for some months, when that could have been valuable time for people to submit? Why were submissions open on 25 October last year for just six weeks, which, if one were cynical, one would say that was just before Christmas. The committee acknowledged the tight turn-around, and Labour asked for an extension. The extension was only until 20 December 2024, so during a very busy time before Christmas. I probably am a bit cheeky asking if that was deliberate, but it does give us pause to wonder why those time frames are chosen.
: Just a few more questions on this: why couldn’t submissions have been extended until Parliament resumed in February so people could at least have had the summer period to read the bill and get their heads around it?
: While I have the floor, I’ll just also make the point that there seems to have been very little attempt to reach out to disabled communities and neurodivergent communities to solicit their views on the bill in a way that could have afforded them much-needed protections. We have drafted amendments around that, and we heard really compelling evidence from people who were mainly their representatives rather than necessarily their own voice, although there was evidence from some groups as well. But if we think about the context of the young neurodivergent girl who was mistakenly placed under the current Act and given sedation, that is an example of what can go horribly wrong under the Act if we don’t have the right safeguards in place.
: I’ve got some more to say about the substance, and I’ll just go into one point around this, still on clause 3, which is that one of the most significant goals of the bill relates to decision-making capacity, including a shift from the current emphasis on risk aimed at eliminating compulsory care. But it involves treatment irrespective of consent, and if someone lacks capacity in a certain area, then proper process must be followed. It seems to be that although there is lip service in clause 3 in talking about promoting the decision-making capacity—and there are other parts of the bill that talk about that—we don’t see in the functioning of the bill that substituted decision-making will be a last resort. It feels like there aren’t ways to do that, and it also feels like there’s a kind of blanket approach to capacity rather than a decision-by-decision basis, which is the modern approach to mental health philosophy.
: The questions I have around that are: why does the bill take an approach regarding restoration of capacity, which is a binary approach and doesn’t seem to follow best practice? Wouldn’t the purpose of the bill be better served by ensuring that safeguards are in place to support the full exercise of decision-making capacity? Is there a financial reason why those changes haven’t been made? Ultimately, it might take more investment into the mental health sector—and I do appreciate that; I don’t say that glibly, because it could be a major investment—and yet, if the bill is trying to achieve that, then, perhaps, workforce development and resourcing and legislative safeguards around delivery would be the way require the delivery of that, rather than making it contingent upon the capacity for the Public Service to do that. There will be other questions that really look at the decision-making capacity and the full exercise of that when we come to clause 9 of the bill.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Thank you, Mr Chair. Look, to start off, I think we’ve all agreed that this is an important bill, right? So we can get up and grandstand, or we can actually get into the issues. I mean, to raise for five minutes the issues of select committee when, obviously, select committees are independent of Ministers is, probably, quite a disappointing first call from the Opposition spokesperson, and I think it says a lot. That Opposition spokesperson should actually—
Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall: What! For goodness’ sake.
Hon MATT DOOCEY: Well, no, you can’t have it both ways. They are independent of Ministers, and, actually, the select committee was a standard process. You can’t have it both ways—and, actually, as that member will also know, because it happened under her last Government, there was a full public consultation on this policy of this bill by Andrew Little before it came into the House, and there’ll be many members here who probably haven’t debated a bill before that went through such a thorough process before it came to the House. I don’t want to hear, “Oh, well, it could have been transformative.”  I mean, quite frankly, that’s what the problem was under the last Government in mental health, when it was all about transformation, and look where it got them, right? So, actually, everyone has worked hard on this bill—every party—and the public has been fully consulted; and it turns up to the House in very good shape. Not only that, it had an expert advisory panel that fed into it. So, yep, we’re going to debate the points of this bill, but let’s do that.
Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour): I want to try and get back a semblance of collegiality in this debate. As the Minister has acknowledged, this is a bill started under our Government and completed under theirs. It is incredibly important, it is historic, and it deals with issues that touch on the human rights of some of the most vulnerable people in New Zealand. I think it behooves us to approach—yeah, as I said— this debate with collegiality. It is late. It’s probably, while we’re talking about mental health, worth reflecting that everyone’s probably quite tired. Why don’t we write some elements of behaviour off as that and try and get off on a different foot?
: I think it is fair, for a bill that deals with human rights, for the Opposition to have some concerns about the amendment that we are about to debate. It is an amendment that takes a decision made by the select committee and that affects the rights of mothers to be with their children and changes it substantially. I won’t, in this contribution, pose questions about that, because we’re not up to clause 38A yet, but I think it is an important procedural point to raise that it appears to be a substantial change to an issue that is a very important issue, made under urgency and without the opportunity for the public to consult on this. We will have questions about that, and I understand from my colleague that the nature of this change—we only learned about it when we saw the Amendment Paper. It is not how I would like to participate as a parliamentarian—to be discussing the rights of mothers to be with their babies when I’ve only seen it very recently. That’s not good.

This does tie in to amendment Paper 644. Again, this is to do with the kind of support that’s expected and the community support commitment that is expected after involuntary hospitalisation becomes voluntary, which, again, shifts us—hopefully—from a high level of compulsory treatment to avoid cases of seemingly indefinite compulsory care. I wanted to check whether the Minister would be interested in those, and I still have further questions on both clauses 5 and 6.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Thank you. Just on the fact that the Minister won’t clarify, in the bill as it currently, the issue around “person under forensic compulsory care”, I think it is good for us to work out which bit of legislation takes precedence. As I say this, I’m thinking again about the incidence, at Wakari Hospital, of people who would be potentially under both the Mental Health Act currently but also the Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act.
: If someone is a special care recipient under section 2 of the Intellectual Disability Act and they also have a mental disorder, which statutory regime will now take precedence, and how does that compare to the current Act? Can the Minister identify any circumstances in which a person could potentially fall under both bits of legislation, given the changes and the fact that we’re not going to clarify that now in the definition section? And, if so, what safeguards exist to ensure that people aren’t inadvertently moved from protections available under the Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act and into the mental health regime? As I say, they sound a bit nitpicky and a little bit conceptual, but they’re very, very real right now, given what’s happened at Wakari Hospital and is mentioned in the Ombudsman’s report. It is worth us understanding the interplay of those two pieces of law.
: Going back to the Armed Forces Discipline Act, where I talked previously about “Court Martial”, Part 10 continues to apply under transitional provisions, and yet we don’t have “Court Martial” anywhere else or in any other reference to the Armed Forces Discipline Act, except under Part 10 of that Act. I’m wondering if it’s just an oversight and if we should still remove that from the definition section, or why is it that it doesn’t appear to be anywhere else in this bill?
: Then, finally, we’ve covered the medical health professionals—the New Zealand Health Plan; it would be great to understand from the Minister where we are with it. I believe that there has been a draft and there may be a strategy due for finalisation, but it would be good to know when the plan will be published under the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act or if the Minister can let me know if it has been published. I haven’t been able to find it, but it may have been.
Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall: Yes, it has been.
INGRID LEARY: The Pae Ora mental health one?
Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall: No, the health plan.
INGRID LEARY: The health plan. Sorry, I’m just—oh, no, that was 2025. I’ll leave that, then, because my colleague is telling me that doesn’t apply. So that’s fine. We covered that one off. I think that’s just about all from there. Then if we go to clause 5, which is the Treaty clause—I will sit down and let someone else take a call while I gather my thoughts. Thank you.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Thank you very much, Mr Chair. I just wanted to respond to the member Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan. He’s referencing Amendment Papers 644 and 645 in the name of Kahurangi Carter. Amendment Paper 644, to require measures to support transition from compulsory to voluntary mental health care, looks to add a new compulsory key principle requiring “appropriate measures”, and, for that reason, we would not support that. It would be unclear what “appropriate measures” actually refers to in definitional terms, and it would not be appropriate to include it in the principles of the bill.
: Amendment Paper 645 introduces a commitment to provide community care. Look, I understand the intent of the proposal, ensuring those who come out of, potentially, hospital inpatient compulsory care can be joined up with community care. The issue with that proposal is then that you would create, potentially, a new entitlement or preferential access through that route, as well. What I think we all can agree on for community care is that the decisions for referral should be undertaken through established clinical assessment and service eligibility and prioritisation, which currently exists.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair. Thank you for the response, Minister. I have to say, it’s very refreshing to get such a detailed response to any Amendment Paper, so I appreciate that. Just picking up from what the Minister is saying—and I’ll get on to the community part—I understand there are currently existing processes, and I acknowledge the Minister’s point around preferential care.
: I want to check in terms of clause 6 around “Compulsory care principles”. I’m looking now at subclause (1)(b) regarding the “Least restrictive application”. One of the things that I raised, as well, in my second reading speech is that we want to move in a direction where compulsory care is a last resort. Can I just check if that is in line with the interpretation here under clause (6)(1)(b), which is “be applied in the least restrictive manner”? Would that still imply that compulsory care is being used, but just less restrictively, and that there are different hierarchies of restrictiveness when it comes to compulsory care? But, also, over here in subparagraph (i), the bill mentions that “voluntary care options should be actively offered and preferred”. Can I just check if “preferred”, in this case, would also imply it’s the default starting point for that, and then the level of severity, I guess, depending on diagnosis and the requirement for the person needing compulsory care?
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Thank you for that question from Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan. I think, when you look at the purpose of the Act, especially around the compulsory care principles, it does state around the therapeutic purpose, and I think that is very important in the context of the discussion here.
: Not only therapeutic but the least restrictive application as well. What we do find with voluntary care options is that, quite often, they can be the most therapeutic and the least restrictive.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): On the definitions section, this is just a quick note to say that we did have a long discussion about the wording of tāngata whaiora, and some of the Government members didn’t like the definition, but we have it defined in the bill as “people with lived experience of mental distress”. I am interested to understand from the Minister whether speaking of distress rather than mental illness is appropriate or how does he see that, because mental distress tends to be a short duration—less gravity; less, perhaps, diagnosed as a medical illness, and not necessarily a clinical kind of definition—so would it be better to say “mental illness” or would it perhaps be better to have a te reo word that defines what tāngata whaiora is so that we don’t have to try and have this kind of transliteration?
: When I go to the Treaty of Waitangi clauses, there were a number of submissions on that, and the biggest impression I had was that there seems to be a commitment to Te Tiriti in an overall sense but that it doesn’t feel like it applies in the delivery of service to tāngata whaiora. I wonder if the Minister would entertain tabled amendment 1.50.06, which says, “in clause 5, after subclause (1), insert ‘that persons exercising powers and functions under this Act must actively support equitable outcomes for Māori and enable Māori participation in decisions affecting the care of Māori receiving services under this Act.’”
: If we look again at the promotion of decision-making capacity in clause 3, that would seem to align really well. Alternatively, there is my tabled amendment 3.04.01, which just says that, under the heading, “Every person performing a function or duty or exercising a power under this Act must give effect to the principles of Te Tiriti.” I know that the current wording talks about giving to effect as the bill, but it doesn’t actually require anything of the people delivering services, so that could be another way to do it.
: We did have the opportunity to meet the other evening, and I was hoping that the Minister would take on board my tabled amendment on clause 6, which is around disabled and neurodivergent people. We heard that they are implicitly protected in the bill, but I do have tabled amendment 3.04.01, which would explicitly ensure that disability, neurodivergence, and different styles of communication would not be treated as evidence of impaired decision-making capacity. Just another plea to the Minister: I know it didn’t make it over the line the other evening, but this would be of great comfort to our disabled and neurodivergent communities, because, often, with the way that they can present, it is assumed that they are suffering some kind of mental health event when it is actually a form of their expression and communication.
: I know the Minister’s going to stand up and say, “Yes, it’s implicit in the bill.”, but disabled and neurodivergent people do not get the protections. We know that they are overrepresented in all of the abuse in care scenarios, and so having an explicit mention as per my tabled amendment would be really helpful. The other one, which would be also something that I would have thought the Minister would support because he is a champion of lived experience, is to actually recognise the value of lived experience wherever reasonably practicable. We could do that with my tabled amendment 8.00.01. We could put that into clause 6(1)(c). Then we could actually, after clause 211, have the director-general actually have a plan and a statutory requirement to take into account advice from people with lived experience of compulsory mental health care, some of whom we heard at the committee stage, but also including appropriate Māori, Pacific, disabled, and youth lived experience—again, the most marginalised communities.
: Under clause 6, I have tabled amendment 1.50.09 to include the words “including whānau and cultural support”, which would be to specify what kind of support is referenced in the definition section. That would make sure that support was available to the person, including whānau and cultural support, housing, income, education, employment, and so on—all the things that people might need to get onto their journey of recovery. That would then apply the principle of least restrictive care and it would also require some investment into resourcing.
: Mr Chair, if I can keep going with these amendments, we’ll get through them really quickly?
CHAIRPERSON (Greg O'Connor): Well, yes, that’s a good idea to finish them off. We’ll go through them; it would be a nice way to finish your contribution.
INGRID LEARY: Thank you. I’ve got an amendment under clause 8, tabled amendment 15.00.11: which would be, “after the words ‘Seriously impaired mental health’, insert the words ‘without evidence that those matters are contributing to a serious impairment of mental functioning’.” This is another safeguard. We’ve heard that there’s quite a binary position in the bill about people either lacking capacity or not, and yet we heard from expert submitters that those judgments should be made on a decision by decision basis because mental capacity fluctuates. Putting this amendment in clause 8(2) would help to move us into the 21st century when it comes to best practice around how we determine mental impairment and capacity so that it’s no longer binary but more a journey, and appropriate supports can be put in at each gateway.
: We also have two amendments on clause 9 which are, again, safeguards for people with intellectual disability, which is that they cannot be presumed to lack capacity to make decisions about their mental health care solely because they have an intellectual disability or a neurological or brain condition. We have seen the Wakari Hospital incident. We have also heard evidence from people where they are the most vulnerable, and just having that safeguarding would be something that would give those communities confidence.
: Finally, the “Meaning of capacity to make decisions about mental health”: we could capture all of that in assessing capacity, to say that reasonable steps must be taken to support the person to make or communicate their own decision before determining that the person lacks capacity; so it’s a kind of active or proactive duty of care on officials to take the person as they are before them. Yes, it’s implicit across the bill, but it doesn’t really apply individually on a case by case basis where somebody may be taken at face value rather than for their particular situation or circumstances.
: Finally, in clause 12, I suggest amending advance mental health directives so that a copy of the statement that is given must be provided to the person. They must be consistent with that person’s wishes and to the person’s support network and to the independent advocate. This is around giving them reasons why their advance directive might not be followed. We heard a lot about advance directives and people wanting them to be taken more seriously and to be on hand, rather than them just being discarded, and having a duty of care on those choosing not to follow them—probably for good clinical reasons. It would be prudent to have that in writing so that there is a process to safeguard their rights.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Alrighty, hey, let’s get into this; alrighty. We have tabled amendment No. 6 from Ingrid Leary wanting to insert additional requirements around equity and participation for Māori. I would not support that, because there are already overarching principles in the bill, recognising the Treaty of Waitangi—
Hon David Seymour: It’s “Wai-taa-ngi”.
Hon MATT DOOCEY: —Waitangi; apologies—and requiring care to be responsive and meet cultural needs as well. Another tabled amendment—1.50.09—expands the principle to housing, income, education, employment, counselling, and peer support to be available to the person. I would not support that, because, as we do know, care planning already requires a holistic assessment for the person and the support that is required under the bill as well.
: There were some quite technical questions/statements, I suppose, around the interface between the Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act 2003 (IDCCR) and the Mental Health Act. No compulsory care order may be made if the person is under IDCCR. If on an ID order, to become under the Mental Health Act, the ID order needs to be suspended.
: The next one I have here from Ingrid Leary talks about inserting into the bill compulsory care principles relating to disabled and neurodivergent people. I would not support that, because the compulsory care criteria in the bill already ensures that disability, neurodivergence, and different communication styles are supported.
: I have another one here. I’m not sure whether it’s got a number on it, to be honest. Well, the response to it is—the request in the amendment here, I think—sorry, Mr Chair, is that 150.05?
CHAIRPERSON (Greg O'Connor): It might relate to the time it was received.
Hon MATT DOOCEY: Oh, OK. Do we get a number on these, or—it’s not the tidiest, is it? OK. Looking to insert “A health practitioner exercising powers or performing functions under the Act must have appropriate competence, training, and experience in the assessment, diagnosis, treatment, and care of people”—I wouldn’t support that, because, as the member would know, that’s already covered by HPCAA, or the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act, which provides for processes to ensure all practitioners remain within their competency as well.
: Then we have this other one. Maybe that’s number four, do you think, Mr Chair?
CHAIRPERSON (Greg O'Connor): Four, yes.
Hon MATT DOOCEY: OK, that’s helpful. To insert “The person under forensic compulsory care means a person described in section 113”—that’s interesting. I would not support that one. Drafting practice is that the definition section is reserved for definitions throughout the bill.
CHAIRPERSON (Greg O'Connor): Lawrence Xu-Nan. We’re getting near the end here, so quite substantive now.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): I’ve got just a few short questions following on from a previous one. Just the first short question is on clause 6(2). I just want to check, when we’re looking at who determines whether the compulsory care principles have been reasonably practicably met, who would the burden of proof be on? It does mention specifically courts and tribunals. I think that’s an important question: is it up to those who are providing the compulsory care or those who are challenging the provision of that compulsory care? That’s my first question.
: My second question—I’m going to move on to clause 8. In clause 8(2), I have noticed that the select committee has made changes, and I do believe the changes are important and significant. However, what I’ve noticed also is that a large number of prohibited grounds for discrimination under section 21 of the Human Rights Act are not in there, so the likes of, for example, sex, ethnicity, physical disability, I believe, etc. Can I just check that, for example, when we’re looking at “a person cannot be assessed to have seriously impaired mental health on the basis of” this list, if it’s inconsistent with section 21 of the Human Rights Act, if someone challenges under the Human Rights Commission, how would that interact with this particular list?
: My final question for this contribution is clause 9, and in clause 9, I would like to know, when we are looking at “Meaning of capacity to make decisions about mental health care”, who would be the one assessing this? I also want to check, in terms of the definition, the definition doesn’t give an interpretation for what is considered a “sustained basis”. In this case, we see clause 9(1), line 16 of page 21, explicitly mentions “unless they cannot, on a sustained basis,”. Is there a specific duration? Is there a range of duration?
: Those are my three questions at this stage.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): There was a question from the member Ingrid Leary about the question of distress versus illness and how we would apply the bill to that. I suppose, when you look at compulsory care, it is not limited to a specific diagnosis, because there is a range out there about ensuring we provide timely care and support.
Dr HAMISH CAMPBELL (National—Ilam): I move, That debate on this question now close.

topicSummaries.topic: Part 2 Tāngata whaiora rights and support
topicSummaries.content:
CHAIRPERSON (Greg O'Connor): Members, we come now to Part 2. This is the debate on clauses 12 to 40, “Tāngata whaiora rights and support”. The question is that Part 2 stand part.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Thank you, Mr Chair. I don’t have a huge number of suggestions or questions on this part, but I do want to go into the community care orders, because what we currently have is a situation in New Zealand where we use a significant number of these orders, compared with countries that we compare ourselves to. They have a disproportionate effect on Māori in particular, and yet we have before us a bill that purports to strengthen the human rights of tāngata whaiora.
: There is international research-based consensus that compulsory community treatment is not effective in achieving its stated aims of reducing hospital readmission and improving mental health outcomes. Given that—and given that it is a significant breach of human rights—we’d expect a substantial amount of evidence of the benefit needed to justify these orders, but that evidence doesn’t seem to exist. In fact, in their submission, the FACTORS team, which included Professor Anthony O’Brien, concluded that, if the bill were to pass in its current form, it would be unlikely to have a significant impact on the current practice or on reducing the use of compulsory community care.
: My questions to the Minister are: does he know roughly how many people are currently on compulsory care orders? What evidence does he have that they actually work? Why is he so resistant, and why are his officials so resistant, to making community care orders voluntary? Is it do with a sense of moral panic or the assumptions from medical practitioners, who maybe haven’t seen the evidence, of wanting to do something that looks like they are being accountable and responsible for patients yet doesn’t seem to have the evidence to back up that they actually work? And is he aware of evidence that participation by patients in their own care in the community actually has a better chance of getting people on to the road to recovery? That is my first tranche of questions. I’ll continue so we can move through the bill.
: In section 13, there were submissions around the advance mental health directives and the status that they have, where there seems to be—again, I hate to use the words “lip service” because they do have some waiting, so that would be too cynical. What are his reasons for saying that section 13 can be overridden when the advance directive was made by the person when they had capacity? There may be good reasons, but it would be good to understand what they are because I think there is a sense that these community care orders provide a lot more human rights protection than what they actually do in practice. I’ll stop my questions there, and I’ll go into clause 17 later. Thank you.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Thank you, Mr Chair. Look, I think it’s well traversed with this bill that before it was introduced to the House, there was significant public consultation. On top of that, it had its own expert advisory group. It had a full select committee process. We’re here at 10 minutes to 12, so it would be good to get some questions specific to the clauses, not just general questions that, quite frankly, could have been answered—and probably were—several times with officials in the select committee. We are talking about community care. By definition, if you are not providing that, what sort of level of care are you providing some of the most vulnerable New Zealanders in a time of need? Now, if the member’s advocating that every person needs to then go into inpatient hospital care because there is no community care, then that’s an interesting proposition, because she’s just been going on for the last few days about Wakari and the issues we’ve got in there. The whole principle of this bill is to ensure that we have compassionate care for people at some of the most vulnerable times of their life, and it just, quite frankly, beggars belief that we are now still questioning whether we should have community care in New Zealand.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Thank you. The Minister has said that we traversed this in select committee. In fact, we didn’t really get much time to look at it. Just for clarity, we’re not suggesting that there wouldn’t be community care. The suggestion is that there would be assertive outreach with statutory resourcing and people being able to participate in their own level of care and that there would be a small number of cases of people who might need to be under compulsory care.
: The Minister didn’t answer any of my questions regarding evidence, but the numbers of people under compulsory care at any one time in New Zealand is around 6,000. The researchers who have done this— well-respected university researchers—have shown that around 50 people might need to be held under compulsory care. So the question is not whether to remove community care but whether to remove the presumption of having it be compulsory and, instead, to legislate and resource the care that would be needed for assertive outreach, to make sure that people could participate in their own wellbeing. I did say that very directly in relation to clause 12.
: I do have an amendment. I’m not going to read it out, but if the Minister was minded to read it, it is around giving effect to valid advance community care orders. I also have some other amendments, which I may as well go through now, since it is late. Another one is making sure that if somebody’s advance mental health directive is not used, then they would be able to get something in writing around that. I’ve got an amendment to clause 17 around attendance at hui by order, where people should be able to request that somebody else could come along, and there are insertions there in clause 17(4)(a) and (ca).
: I have an amendment around clause 23, “Independent supported person”, to make sure that when there are independent supported persons under the bill, they can’t be people working for Health New Zealand, the Ministry of Health, or their agencies. That is just, really, to reflect some of the arrangements that happen because there are so many organisations that have formal relationships through legal relationships that may not necessarily be seen as being independent.
: In clause 24, I’ve got an amendment around independent advocates—that we amend clause 24(2)(c) so that they will represent “the views, will, and preferences of persons under compulsory care”. That is to make sure that that person does have a distinct role, compared to a legal advocate, because we didn’t get any clarity from the Minister about what the different roles were in the definition section.
: I’ve also got another amendment under clause 24 around what those advocates could do—particularly in relation to electroconvulsive therapy and also seclusion—to strengthen safeguards there, because, as we’ve said, we don’t believe that there are enough safeguards in the bill as it is currently worded. Also, it is making sure, in clause 37, that a responsible practitioner must take all reasonable steps to ensure that a person is able to access independent advice as soon as practicable. That is something that was said to us at select committee would be good, and I don’t believe it was given due regard.
: Then we have some other amendments around the rights of children and young persons. A great deal of the evidence that we heard at select committee was around the fact that children and young people are, unfortunately, going into adult institutions. It’s happened under successive Governments. There isn’t any statutory resourcing requirement under this bill, and there is a requirement for children to be put into appropriate care where it’s available, but where it’s not available, there aren’t additional safeguards for them. We heard that there’s nothing to safeguard their educational development, their outdoor living space, the things that would make them feel nurtured and protected. The most we were able to get was the ability for them to be accompanied when they were being transported between facilities. So this amendment in clause 38—[Bell rings]
CHAIRPERSON (Greg O'Connor): The time has come for me to leave the Chair. I’ll allow the Minister to cogitate on those amendments overnight. The committee will resume at 9 a.m. Have a good evening.
: Debate interrupted.
: Sitting suspended from 11.58 p.m. to 9 a.m. (Saturday)

topicSummaries.topic: Part 2 Tāngata whaiora rights and support (continued)
topicSummaries.content:
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): Good morning, members. It’s Tuesday morning again. When we suspended last night, we were debating Part 2 of the Mental Health Bill. This is the debate on clauses 12 to 40, “Tāngata whaiora rights and support”. Just before I put the question to stand part and we start the debate, I just wanted to note that we spent some time in the committee on Part 1. CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): Members, we come now to Part 3. This is the debate on clauses 41 to 100—“Compulsory care”—and Schedule 1A. The question is that Part 3 stand part.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Thank you. I have been one of the people bringing the voices of some of those who spoke to us in the Health Committee into the debate, and I intend to do that where it is appropriate, in this section, if that’s alright with the Chair.
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): As long as it’s not long.
INGRID LEARY: Given the number of clauses in this rather large bill, we have been running fairly tightly, I would suggest, Madam Chair. If I look at clause 41 now, this is a clause that worries us, because it currently seems to extend powers to non-medical people to be able to make decisions around compulsory care. The questions I have are, really: what has been the basis of this, and has the ministry somehow included in its thinking whether it’s primarily intended to address workforce shortages rather than improve clinical care? I won’t go back into the questions that were raised in the definition phase, but, very clearly, there has been a broadening under some of the definitions of who can make decisions.
: My specific questions are: why does clause 41(2) allow any mental health practitioner to be appointed as a responsible practitioner rather than requiring a medical practitioner or a psychiatrist? What clinical decisions are they expected to make under the bill, and are those decisions appropriate to be exercised by someone who is not medically qualified? If they’re not a psychiatrist, who, ultimately, carries responsibility for the diagnosis, the treatment decisions, and the compulsory care reviews? What safeguards are there for the postcode lottery across different districts, where one director may appoint nurses or psychologists in one area, while, in a different area, somebody else might only appoint psychiatrists? If the Government intends psychiatrists ordinarily to perform this role, why is the expectation of that not reflected in the legislation? What evidence demonstrates that extending the role beyond medical practitioners improves patient outcomes?
: We do know that we have a shortage of psychiatrists, and that’s, indeed, across the mental health services. The Minister himself alluded to the associate psychologist role and the fact that they do not have clinical competence as currently assessed under the Act. We need to be really clear who is expected to be authorised under this provision and who will be accountable under this provision. Would the Minister look at my amendment 19A, which would tidy this up for him?
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Madam Chair, thank you very much. The substantive part of that line of questioning is around the member’s amendment, which I would not support. The change is unnecessary.
: The question was raised about the postcode lottery. Well, I would put the principle of the law that would prevent that postcode lottery, because the Director of Area Mental Health Services needs to be satisfied that the mental health practitioner being appointed has undergone the relevant training and competency. That is important, because only a competent and trained practitioner can properly operate within the scope of practice under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act.

: I am going to jump a little bit—noting that others may have questions before that—but I want to just mention clause 49, which is “Reduction and elimination of seclusion”. : Finally, there is the amendment from Kahurangi Carter, inserting new clause 49A, which is just to specify, around the prohibition on the use of seclusion, that a person under compulsory care must not be placed in seclusion. This is, again, something that the submitters have asked for.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Thank you, Madam Chair, and thanks to that member for those questions. The first two questions were more around, I suppose, how we operationalise the Act, which I think is a fair question. There’s one around the ratio and the access. This being an operational matter, the guidelines and secondary legislation will guide that practice. And also there was the question around size of the team and, I suppose, multi-disciplinary care planning teams. The size and make-up of a team is expected to reflect the needs of the person.
: To the more substantive question around seclusion, I think we’ve heard loud and clear that, as a direction of the country, we need to look towards removing seclusion in our mental health services. The first point I’d raise is it’s not necessarily a question of money. If you look at, potentially, some of the announcements of the last Government around funding into mental health, the data shows seclusion rates actually went up. The conclusion I’ve drawn from being Minister is not only is it about adequate resourcing—I’m not disagreeing with that—there is a particular focus needed on training and the workforce. I would like to share a reflection where I visited an inpatient facility, not far from here, that had actually reached zero seclusion because of a decision made by the clinical leadership team around the culture of the organisation. I think it’s incumbent on us, when we are aware that no comparable countries have achieved the removal of seclusion, that as we move towards potentially being the first country in the world, we ensure that we have the right plan.
: I’m comfortable that the regulations in the bill allow for ending seclusion. That’s why I do not believe there needs to be a sunset clause. What I’m also encouraged by is the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission’s recommendation around New Zealand’s first seclusion plan that Health New Zealand has accepted to be published in 2027. My expectation, with that plan, is that it would set out a road map of how we would achieve that and that it would then be incumbent on any Government of the day to ensure that we follow the road map.
: The final point I’d make is that the regulations allow for that and actually could be brought well forward from the five-year review and a lot earlier within the regulatory framework that this bill sets up.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Thank you, Madam Chair. I’m sure we’ll have a number of questions around the Minister’s response to that question on seclusion. I just want to tidy away the last clause that I want to look at before going on to clause 49, which is around care planning. The Minister himself, last night, raised the relationship between the compulsory care order and the person’s care plan under clause 43. It’s important because the compulsory care order authorises compulsory care but the advance directive or the care plan arrangement records a person’s wishes, preferences, and treatments. Understanding what parts of those will be given weight and when is really important.
: My questions are: does a compulsory care order compel treatment generally, or does it only authorise the compulsory care that is subject to the treatment safeguards elsewhere in the bill? If a person has an advance mental health directive refusing a particular treatment, how is that reflected under the care plan required under clause 43, and, if they do refuse, what legal effect will that refusal have? Where there is an inconsistency between a care plan and an advance mental health directive, which one of those prevails? And shouldn’t there be a requirement under clause 43 to distinguish between treatment that the person consents to, treatment authorised despite lack of consent under the Act, and treatment that has been expressly refused in an advance mental health directive?
: The reason I raise that is because we did hear evidence from people who had been subject to different treatments under the Act—some of them restraint treatments; some of them seclusion. Almost all of them universally talked about the increased trauma and the impact it had on their worsening mental health, and they also talked about not having a voice in the treatment that was applied to them. So, where we have an arrangement where that could be there in writing but there is also the prevailing clauses and powers in the bill, it’s really important to understand what the Minister’s expectation is around how that should prevail and what weight should be given to the wishes of the person receiving the treatment. After this, we intend to go on to seclusion as well.
HŪHANA LYNDON (Green): I just wanted to supplement on clause 43 of Part 3 by asking and inviting the Minister to provide an explanation around the role of the whānau of the whaiora who is in care. As we see in the care planning, there’s great detail in terms of the review, the way that notes and the plan need to be updated, the way that the service is being provided to the whaiora, but I haven’t seen, within this part of the legislation, any mention of whānau and what the role of whānau is in the care planning. Further, how is the whānau engaged and kept up to date in terms of care of their whānau member who might be within care at that time? Particularly in the transition component of this clause, where you’re moving from service to service, how is the whānau engaged and how do they maintain connection to the plan of care for their whanaunga or tangata whaiora? I also acknowledge that, maybe, tangata whaiora may not have whānau there in support, so what advocacy or what supports, external to the service, independent or otherwise, may be provided within this care planning process so that whānau or an independent person or agency is there walking alongside the patient in care? Kia ora.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): I thank that member for those questions. I think that the bill, quite rightly, as a part of some of the 10 recommendations, achieves the abuse in care recommendations of new roles, of independent roles, and of advocates as well.
: There was a question around involvement of the family, and I think a good example of that is around the new advance mental health directives, where a hui whaiora must be convened if a person under compulsory care does not have an advance mental health directive to assist with decisions about their care. My expectation is that where and as much as it’s appropriate, whānau would be involved; and if there was no whānau, then there would be the use of the new independent role in advocacy roles.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Turning to seclusion. We did have multiple submissions, including really strong submissions from the Mental Health Commission, page 10, clauses 47 to 50, and also the Ombudsman, pages 18, 19, 20—particularly point 88.
: The question that we have is it feels like there is a practicality kind of “we don’t have the resourcing to do this, but we might be able to one day”, and when I heard the Minister talk about a plan being ready in 2027, that sounds like we are inching at a snail’s pace to something that both the Minister has experienced and also we, on the select committee, had heard, has been able to be achieved in this country through planning, culture change, training and so on. So my questions are: if he’s saying that seclusion is an objective of the bill, why is he still declining to set an end date? Doesn’t he accept that if there isn’t an end date, there is less incentive to change the system? The whole point of statutory safeguards is to require systems to get up to speed with things like human rights protections and so on. And, particularly, if there had been a workforce training and resourcing statutory requirement, which is in my amendment, which I think the Minister is probably going to decline, in the workforce capability, then that would be really helpful, because it would set the Minister’s expectation. He’s said it’s his expectation, but there’s nothing in the legislation that reflects that expectation of the Minister. This would strengthen the expectation and make it very clear to the institutions what they need to do and there would be the requirement for there to be adequate funding.
: What evidence does he have that five years is the right amount of time to transition away from seclusion? The Minister will be aware of my tabled amendment that says, “at least have two yearly reviews”, so that we can put some kind of pressure on the system to show the direction of travel. What message does retaining an indefinite statutory power to seclusion send to those services who had managed to eliminate it? It’s not just in Wellington; there is one in Auckland as well.
: I’m curious to know if it’s the Government’s position that seclusion will always remain necessary somewhere in the system. I know there are different clinical and professional views on this, and I’d like to have on the Hansard what the Minister’s view is on that. I don’t have a position for or against it because I know there’s a lot of discussion and evidence, but it would be helpful to understand what the Minister’s own expectation is of that.
: If we’re not ready to move to seclusion, can he tell us what specific workforce, infrastructure or funding milestones remain outstanding? If services are not ready today, isn’t that why the transition period of five years, which does seem generous and does seem proportionate—isn’t that the right time frame to be able to get that in order?
: The final couple of points are really that he’s talked about regulation being able to be used in the bill to end seclusion, but, equally, there are force and search powers, in and clause 204, that also relate to those limitations on human rights. That worries us because we all know that any limitation on human rights should be in primary legislation. Wouldn’t it be better to lift and drop both of those elements into the bill? The sunsetting of seclusion as well as the limitations on people through force and search powers—once again, it is feeling like bad law making to be relegating that to regulation. I agree seclusion could be done through that, which is less problematic, but if we’re going to do that, we should have everything in primarily legislation, so we avoid the issues caused by clause 204.
: Finally, the Minister has talked about the fact that seclusion won’t apply to under-18-year-olds. That’s something we absolutely welcome. The reason that we’re given also for the non-ending of seclusion is that other restrictive practices that could be harmful, as harmful, or even more harmful to adults will occur as a result. Now, the Minister can’t have it both ways. If that is the logic relating to adults, surely that is the logic relating to young people—many of whom, we have established, are also in these adult secure mental health facilities. Against the backdrop of what we were discussing in the committee last night and with Waikari Hospital and the Otago Daily Times story this morning, I think it’s important, particularly, to hear the Minister’s view about whether there could be an unintended consequence in the way the bill divides up the rights of under-18-year-olds with adults as we discussed seclusion.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): There’s a bit in there, so I’ll step through it. I suppose we are slightly returning to Part 1. If I remind members that one of the principles in this bill is the principle of the least restrictive practice, the second is that this bill brings in quite significant safeguards. I’m confident that we are heading in the right direction as a country. When we came into office, seclusion rates had significantly increased, and the data shows that they have now significantly reduced. So we are on a direction as a country.
: As previously said, I’m confident that we’ve got the right regulatory framework to ensure that we continue that direction as we work with the mental health system.
