I’m acutely aware, as that member is, there is actually a wide-ranging number of views within the existing workforce, and other advocates within the system, that I think we need to bring along in that journey as well.
: There is a concern by some of the workforce around the risk of removing seclusion, and I think that does need to be acknowledged; and others, as was well-canvassed during the select committee stage, are concerned about the unintended consequences of seeing a reduction in seclusion but, actually, then seeing an increase in chemical and physical restraint as well.
: There was a question about why we are confident we can remove seclusion or prohibit seclusion in under-18s but not apply the same measure in over-18s. Well, the advice around under-18s is that it is a very small number of young people that are secluded. I’ve just got the number here: 32 young people across all inpatient services in 2023-24, compared to 561 adults.
: The point I’d make there is that it’s very emblematic of past Governments that think they can put an end date somewhere and it will just happen. I think what we’ve shown around the reduction and the prohibition of seclusion for young people in this bill is that if we take a targeted approach, we can continue to reduce the numbers. That’s why the regulatory framework allows for that and also New Zealand’s first seclusion plan.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Madam Chair. I just have one follow-up question on seclusion for the Minister for Mental Health, and then I’m going to move on to subsequent clauses. This is to do with new clause 49(1A), and it’s to do with reporting annually. Can I just check: as a part of that reporting, would the Minister have an expectation that the average hours and the maximum hours that a person spent in seclusion will also be reported as a part of that report, particularly consecutive hours?
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): That data is already collected. I think it’s a very important point, because it’s not only the unique numbers of people under care but it is the total number of seclusion events, the total number of hours in seclusion, and also the ability to identify where the seclusion is happening within each individual in-patient facility or wider setting as well. We’ve also got the reporting on population groups, because, as we do know, Māori are overrepresented in seclusion rates. That’s why I welcome the public reporting.
: Not only that, when you look at the seclusion regime that this is bringing in, there is a lot more requirement now on reporting. Services now have to report every time there is a seclusion, with the reasons why there is as well. That’s why this gives me comfort that, with the framework that this bill sets up, we can continue the direction of travel around reducing and, ultimately, eliminating seclusion.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you for that, Minister. I think that is really heartening to hear, and I think, in that, I also implied that there would be reporting on consecutive hours as well.
: I want to move on to clause 50, and this is on ECT, electroconvulsive therapy, and again it’s to do with reporting. I’m looking at clause 50(2): “The responsible practitioner must record the use …”. I wanted to check: with that recording, will they, again, record the frequency of the use on an individual? Again, it’s part of that broader, I guess, accountability mechanism. That’s my question.
: I know that others may have additional questions, but to signal to you, Madam Chair, my last question on Subpart 1 is on clause 52(1)(d), and that’s the right to repeal or review.
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): You may as well ask it now.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN: Yeah, I’m going to ask that now, and then, depending on the Minister’s response, I’m done with Subpart 1 and I’m happy to move on to Subpart 2.
: I want to check with the Minister: paragraph (d) says, “a Judge of the High Court …”. Can I just check whether it is only the High Court that is able to have the right to review this, and is there any sort of advice that the Minister has received on how frequently we would be looking at this anyway? Would it put a strain on the High Court system?
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Just to tie off those last questions around seclusion and electroconvulsive therapy, I think the member Lawrence Xu-Nan does raise an important requirement around reporting and publicly publishing that data. That’s something that I take quite seriously. That would be my expectation.
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): I’ll take a call from Ingrid Leary, but I have to say that, on this part, we just need to be focusing on changes—any changes—now.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Thanks, Madam Chair. I note that, in the definitions section, there doesn’t seem to be a definition of seclusion.
: In the Wakari Hospital incident, one of the things that has emerged is that people suffered serious seclusion that wasn’t recorded as seclusion, because of the circumstance of the building. I’m wondering if the Minister could respond to how we’re going to be able to capture those events under the bill, and whether he would entertain a definition of seclusion, to be able to make that something that institutions couldn’t wiggle out of because they don’t have a formal seclusion-type room.
: I do think, Madam Chair, we’ve only just started the questioning on electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). ECT is highly controversial, and I think it’s important for the public to know that we looked at this as a select committee really carefully and we’re pretty happy about—
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): I did hear questioning about ECT in last night’s session, so this is specifically around any amendments or adjustments.
INGRID LEARY: Sure. We’re pretty happy about where we’ve landed with safeguards, but we still think there could be additional safeguards. They’re only minor. One of them would be for the consent to be called “fully informed consent” and to take into account future side effects of ECT. The other one was something to ensure the independence of two psychiatrists, because sometimes psychiatrists can work together, or may not—they simply rubberstamp other people’s notes. There are amendments on the Table to that effect. Those are my questions on ECT. I do have more questions on this part, Madam Chair.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Thank you, Madam Chair. Look, the continual reference to Wakari—patients at Wakari are actually under different legislation, the Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act, so that is clearly out of scope. I have been advised that the seclusion definition is in secondary legislation, and that allows for the adjustment with new practices as well.
: I would like to say, in response to the question, that I do welcome the changes at select committee. I think, when you look at Part 1, the principles of the Act are ensuring that we do have safeguards. I welcome now the new safeguards, especially around the second opinions, also around the reporting as well—if you look at seclusion specifically, around having identified seclusion rooms as well. My view is that this bill gives more confidence around the existing practice of seclusion.
: Within electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), of course, there was a range of views at the select committee. I respect that. We heard from the Hon Ayesha Verrall in the second reading about her concern and whether we should prohibit the use of ECT, but actually, through the select committee process, the validation and the clinical evidence—but, of course, it is around the safeguards, and I welcome the changes made here today to ensure that we do have those better safeguards.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Going to clause 70, just a quick question: I know that the Mental Health Bill has been through the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act process, but has he specifically considered section 7 of the Human Rights Act, the requirement of the Attorney-General to bring into the House of Representatives any bill that could be deemed inconsistent or any provision, in relation to community care orders? In other words, what specific advice has he had on that?
: I turn now to clause 80. This is around what we heard could be a change in the threshold regarding the determinations that are made. In the previous bill, the practitioners were required to make determinations, and that language is not used in the current bill. There were submissions to suggest that that reduces the level of protection for tāngata whaiora. We know that “reasonable grounds to believe” has been removed from a lot of the provisions, which is really good, but we still don’t have a determination one. We have words like “in their opinion” rather than a determination, which would seem to have a higher clinical threshold. Can he explain if he is happy with that language and why he’s chosen that language rather than determinations?
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): The Minister’s just looking for something, Ingrid Leary, did you have another—Ingrid Leary, the Minister’s just looking up some answers. Did you have further questions?
Ingrid Leary: I’ll cede to Lawrence Xu-Nan at this point.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Madam Chair. I indicated I’m happy to move on to Subpart 2. I actually only have one question for Subpart 2, on compulsory care assessment. I think Schedule 1A is actually very clear in terms of the process. My only question is around clause 57(1)(a) specifically. This is page 48, line 15. Again, this is when we’re looking at the first assessment. I want to check with the Minister—again, you get the Director of Area Mental Health Services determining the mental health practitioner. Can I just check if that practitioner—I’m just checking, unless I missed it—is able to conduct that first assessment using audiovisual links? For example, I’m, again, thinking about distribution and distance to travel, etc., for rural and regional areas where it might potentially be quite hard to have access to a mental health practitioner to determine that first assessment. I want to the check with the Minister if there’s any consideration of how that could work.
: I now want to move on to clause 73. This is in Subpart 3, and this is page 56. The reason I want to speak to this clause—and my question and my next question—is to do with the Minister’s amendment on clause 73 and clause 81. I want to check with the Minister: in clause 73(3)(c), why has the term “proposed” been removed in the Minister’s amendment? Is it just simply to do with the fact—I’m just going to check that there is no explanatory note on this particular bit. Can I just check: is it because the care plan is already in effect, therefore it is not a proposed one, and that’s why that word was removed?
: My final question for this contribution is on clause 81, and this is to do with the Minister’s amendment as well. We’re looking at, possibly, the top of page 60, right after line 7, and that’s to do with if the responsible practitioner considers that a person under compulsory care meets the compulsory care criteria. It’s about the record that’s being sent. The Minister’s amendment added this new Director of Area Mental Health Services. I just want to check if there is anyone else who should also be sent a copy, assuming that this is quite a last-minute thing. For example, a person I could think of is—I just mentioned before in terms of the assessment that there is a requirement for the mental health practitioner to conduct an assessment, but I don’t know if the mental health practitioner needs to be also sent a report or if that is encapsulated under clause 81(3)(c) as the primary health care provider. Any clarifications on the Minister’s amendment for clauses 73 and 81 would be appreciated.
Ingrid Leary: Madam Chair.
Hon Matt Doocey: Thank you, Madam Chair—
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): Ingrid Leary—oh, sorry, the honourable Minister.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): There’s a few questions I’ll gather up there around the question of the section 7. The bill was vetted for consistency with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act and considered, in its entirety, to be consistent.
: There was a question from Ingrid Leary about the amendment in her name—number 80, if I understand that to be correct—about questioning the reference to “in their opinion”. I’ve been advised that the current reference “in their opinion” makes it clear that the status review decision requires careful assessment to form a reasoned opinion, not just an issued decision.
: The questions from Lawrence Xu-Nan, in only, respectfully, a way Lawrence Xu-Nan can, I think some of them by the end of it answered his own questions around clarification. If I don’t—
Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan: OK. That’s helpful.
Hon MATT DOOCEY: Ha, ha! If I don’t answer your questions, then do let me know.
: There was one around the practitioner being able to conduct first assessment using audiovisual links (AVL) as well. Clause 215 sets it out when AVL can be used.
: There was the question around who would be notified at certain points of the care planning process. Of course, there is the principle of confidentiality. The person under care can nominate people as well, and we expect when this bill is operationalised, we do have comprehensive care planning processes as well.
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): I was about to take a call from Ingrid Leary, so I’ll come back.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Thank you. Moving to clause 85, this is the subsection that talks about the expiry and extension of mental health care orders and, again, involves people making decisions that potentially have an impact on the human rights of those who they’re deciding about. Some of these do seem to be broader in scope than the current Act. Therefore, it’s important to ask questions about them.
: The first one is the first extension, which is six months. What additional safeguards, if any, are provided before a person’s compulsory care order is extended to the first six months, and how will the responsible practitioner make the determination about whether they should be under a compulsory care order or whether they’d be better supported through voluntary care? What weight must be given to evidence that the person has regained decision-making capacity or is engaging voluntarily? Does he expect the first extension to be the exception rather than the norm—it would be good to have that on the record—but also, if so, how will that expectation be monitored? There doesn’t seem to be anything in the bill around that, so it would be good to hear what kind of operational monitoring might be occurring.
: There’s also, in clause 86, second and subsequent extensions, where, after the first extension, the court can grant an order for up to 12 months, and the Government has increased the maximum duration of subsequent extensions to that level. The committee changed the wording to say for a period of “up to” 12 months, but it does create questions, because it means there’s a discretion. What factors does he expect the court to consider when deciding whether an extension should be, say, three months, six months, or the full 12 months? Wouldn’t it be important, if there is that discretion, which is implicit, to have some safeguarding wording around that?
: There are also questions about whether an annual judicial review is sufficient for monitoring those extensions. That means that once a year, there will be some kind of report done, but somebody could potentially just have the order extended over and over again without any kind of transparency or ability in the system to be able to see it as a milestone or a gate to reassess, so what’s in place in the bill to do that? Is there anything in clause 86 that requires the court to grant the shortest extension reasonably necessary, and, if so, can he point to that, please? How will he ensure that there will be consistency across different courts, because at the moment the legislation is silent on that?
: I guess we’re really wanting to see some direction from the Minister, given that there isn’t the safeguarding, necessarily, in the bill, of his expectations of how these two clauses, 85 and 86, will, in practice, be delivered.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Thank you. There were the statements made around decision-making capacity and the criteria for being placed under compulsory care. I’m confident they are explicit in the bill. The more substantive question at the end there around the 12 months with the care order—I would just point to the key principle of the legislation, the least restrictive practice, as well as the additional safeguards. What gives me great confidence and also why this meets 10 of the abuse in care recommendations is that there may be a 12-month order, but, of course, because of the requirement for a review every three months, if a person is deemed not to be required to be under the Act, then they won’t remain under the Act.
Hon Member: Madam Chair—Madam Chair.
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): Hūhana Lyndon. I said I’d take a call from Hūhana Lyndon.
HŪHANA LYNDON (Green): Kia aroha mai [ [sorry], Madam Chair—we skipped ahead, and I wanted to take us back to page 46 for a quick question with the Minister in regards to section 53, in the “Release from compulsory care”. It notes that at any time when a responsible practitioner considers that a patient under compulsory care does not meet the criteria for compulsory care anymore, that the person must be released immediately—ka pai. But then when there’s a disagreement that might occur, the case gets referred on to the Mental Health Review Tribunal. My question is, because we’ve heard data around both youth and overall adult, those who are retained within compulsory care, the monitoring function and the retention of data and reporting of how many contests or challenges around the review of release of release of care—is that recorded? Will it be made public, as a part of the reporting, to show the progress in the way that we are being robust in considering our retention of a person and release of a person from care?
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Thank you, Madam Chair. I think it’s actually a very important question about the Mental Health Review Tribunal. As I sketched out to the previous member’s question—around the three-monthly review and being discharged from the Act—where there is a disagreement, I suppose, from the person under compulsory care and the responsible practitioner, it does go to the review. So I’m happy to commit to that capturing of the data and publishing it. If that’s not happening already, then that will happen.
Dr CARLOS CHEUNG (National—Mt Roskill): I move, That debate on this question now close.
: A party vote was called for on the question, That debate on this question now close.
: New Zealand National 48; ACT New Zealand 11; New Zealand First 8.
: New Zealand Labour 25; Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand 10; Te Pāti Māori 4; Ferris; Kapa-Kingi.
: Motion agreed to.
CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger): Members, Mr Speaker has given permission for Tom Rutherford to help out in the Chair today, and so at this stage, while I move to go and do something else, I am going to ask Tom Rutherford to take the voting on this part. Thank you.
TEMPORARY CHAIRPERSON (Tom Rutherford): Alrighty. Thank you, members. The question is that the Minister’s amendments to Part 3 set out on Amendment Paper 648 be agreed to.
: Amendments agreed to.
TEMPORARY CHAIRPERSON (Tom Rutherford): The question is that Ingrid Leary’s tabled amendment replacing clause 41(2) be agreed to.
: A party vote was called for on the question, That the amendment be agreed to.
: New Zealand Labour 25; Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand 10; Te Pāti Māori 4; Ferris; Kapa-Kingi.
: New Zealand National 48; ACT New Zealand 11; New Zealand First 8.
: Amendment not agreed to.
TEMPORARY CHAIRPERSON (Tom Rutherford): The question is that Ingrid Leary’s tabled amendment inserting new clause 48A be agreed to.
: A party vote was called for on the question, That the amendment be agreed to.
: New Zealand Labour 25; Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand 10; Te Pāti Māori 4; Ferris; Kapa-Kingi.
: New Zealand National 48; ACT New Zealand 11; New Zealand First 8.
: Amendment not agreed to.
TEMPORARY CHAIRPERSON (Tom Rutherford): The question is that Ingrid Leary’s tabled amendment to clause 49 inserting new subclauses (1B) to (1D) be agreed to.
: A party vote was called for on the question, That the amendment be agreed to.
: New Zealand Labour 25; Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand 10; Te Pāti Māori 4; Ferris; Kapa-Kingi.
: New Zealand National 48; ACT New Zealand 11; New Zealand First 8.
: Amendment not agreed to.
TEMPORARY CHAIRPERSON (Tom Rutherford): The question is that Kahurangi Carter’s amendment to Part 3 set out on Amendment Paper 646 be agreed to.
: A party vote was called for on the question, That the amendment be agreed to.
: New Zealand Labour 25; Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand 10; Te Pāti Māori 4; Ferris; Kapa-Kingi.
: New Zealand National 48; ACT New Zealand 11; New Zealand First 8.
: Amendment not agreed to.
Dr Tracey McLellan: Point of order. I just thought I could draw your attention to photos being taken in the gallery, if you had any discretion to be able to do something about that.
TEMPORARY CHAIRPERSON (Tom Rutherford): I’m just taking some advice.
: Permission is needed to take photos, so if permission hasn’t been granted then I ask the member to refrain. But thank you for raising that and bringing it to my attention.
: Carrying on: Ingrid Leary’s tabled amendment inserting clause 49A is out of order as being of uncertain legislative effect.
: The question is that Ingrid Leary’s tabled amendment to clause 49 inserting subclauses (1B) to (1D) be agreed to.
: A party vote was called for on the question, That the amendment be agreed to.
: New Zealand Labour 25; Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand 10; Te Pāti Māori 4; Ferris; Kapa-Kingi.
: New Zealand National 48; ACT New Zealand 11; New Zealand First 8.
: Amendment not agreed to.
TEMPORARY CHAIRPERSON (Tom Rutherford): Ingrid Leary’s tabled amendment replacing clause 80(8) is out of order as not offering a serious alternative form of words.
: Part 3 as amended agreed to.

topicSummaries.topic: Part 4 Persons under forensic compulsory care and persons on restricted orders
topicSummaries.content:
TEMPORARY CHAIRPERSON (Tom Rutherford): Members, we now come to Part 4. This is the debate on clauses 101 to 135, ”Persons under forensic compulsory care and persons on restricted orders”. The question is that Part 4 stand part.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Thank you, Mr Chair. Look, I do want to sort of slightly get ahead of the questions in this part. The reason I say that is, actually, when you look at this part, it is one of the most consistent parts with the current Act—some of the least changes—and also, I would point to members that the new principles of the bill we are debating will now be brought into forensic care for the first time. I’m sure we’ll agree, when we think about our prisoners who experience psychiatric issues that need to be transferred out of corrections facilities into forensic Health New Zealand facilities, that we want to ensure that they receive the same level of care that people going in under the comprehensive Act.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair. I do have a few questions for Part 4, and it’s good to hear from the Minister for Mental Health that it’s the most consistent, which in some ways is also the more concerning because of the development in terms of our criminal and justice system. This part, in some ways, has more to do with justice as opposed to purely a mental health portfolio element.
Hon Matt Doocey: Mr Chair.
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Is this a point of order?
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Well, I’d just like to respond to that because, before we go off, it doesn’t have anything to do with justice. When a prisoner, if we use this as an example, is deemed needing psychiatric care, they come into a Health New Zealand forensic service, which is covered by this legislation. They’re solely covered by this legislation. I just want to reiterate that this part is the least change from the current Act and has no significant changes. I accept that there is an important discussion, maybe in a general debate, about how we better manage our prisoners in New Zealand, but I just wanted to point out the substantive of the clauses.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair. I think the Minister for Mental Health has jumped ahead in anticipation of what my question is going to be. My question starting with section 101 in terms of notice of admission. The reason I ask this is actually to do with the fact that we have just had a debate on the declaration of inconsistency when it comes to public protection orders and extended supervision orders. This particular section, I think, in reference to the Criminal Procedure (Mentally Impaired Persons) Act, was a specific component of the consideration when we’re looking at that declaration of inconsistency. I want to check with the Minister then, when we are looking at this section in particular, has the Minister received any advice on the potential contradiction with section 26(2), I believe, of the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act around double jeopardy. My second question is to do with clause 103—collection of biometric information. Now, the reason I’m asking questions around this is what the Minister said, that this is kind of mostly consistent—our Privacy Act has also changed quite substantially over the last couple of decades compared to 1992. I do want to check, when it comes to collection of biometric information, for example, how is that being stored and how is that being used? I do have some supplementary questions later on biometric information, but I want to check those two questions to set the premise around.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Thank you, Mr Chair. Just noting that I endorse what Lawrence Xu-Nan has said. The reason that we need to scrutinise this part of the bill is because it is indeed the most similar to the current law, which we know is not fit for purpose, so we will have questions about that. I’m not sure it’s appropriate. I hope the Minister for Mental Health is not going to stand up and require me to stand down in the middle of my contribution. I want to go to clause 112(4A), which is the new provision that was advocated for by Labour members at the Health Committee, which is, where a person under compulsory care is to be transported, they can request from the Director of Area Mental Health for him or her to permit a support person for the duration of the journey. It can be a retraumatising event for a young person, and subpart (b) says “the request may not be unreasonably denied”. Further in the provision ahead of that, there are planning and delivery elements about how that is to happen using Government transport. I just want to ask the Minister, would it be, in his opinion, an unreasonable denial of that permission if the young person was not able to make the request in a timely way? I’m thinking here of situations where somebody might be told on the day that they’re due to move, that they need to be transferred to another facility, and they simply don’t have time either to make the request or for that response to be received. Would that be considered an unreasonable denial of that new right for that young person?
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Thank you, Mr Chair. There’s a question by the member Lawrence Xu-Nan about the bill. It was independently vetted against the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act and found to be consistent.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair, and I’m just signalling to the Chair that I’m waiting for the questions around biometric information and how they are going to be used and stored against the new privacy principles. Again, I’m not seeing, in this particular section, that privacy is even mentioned, which is deeply concerning. I think the second question is, for example, with that—and again, this is something we’re seeing quite recently in some of the justice-related portfolios, and also immigration-related materials—in and around the use of biometric information. Can I check, is this being stored within the agency and are the agencies compelled to share such information? For example, because we’ve seen it with immigration, are they compelled to share that information with Five Eyes partners?
Dr TRACEY McLELLAN (Labour): Thank you, and thank you, Minister for Mental Health. I just want to reiterate a couple of quick points, and that is, when we have debated this bill in second reading before entering into this committee of the whole House stage, everybody noted that the current legislation is simply not fit for purpose. I also want to lend my voice to the fact that when we get to Part 4, which is what we’re on now—and we can see and then have that confirmed via the Minister’s opening remarks that this is essentially unchanged—it does raise legitimate questions that should be ventilated in this process now as to why the Minister feels as if, throughout policy development, throughout all other aspects of making changes to this legislation, that the forensic part of the operation of the Mental Health Act was deemed to be pretty much fit for purpose. Just needs a little bit of an update of language, because, certainly, from a prison perspective, and I appreciate the difference between this Act and the Corrections Act, but it is clear that there are many things that are not working in the health component of people that find themselves incarcerated into the corrections environment. I would like to hear—and this is a perfect opportunity for the Minister to be able to just walk us through, talk us through—why he feels that there wasn’t a need in this Part 4 to make any substantive changes that could have improved the way that this bill acts for real-life people in those environments.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Thank you, Mr Chair. Well, that’s because, as we’ve reaffirmed multiple times during this debate, the bill had full public consultation before it was brought into the House. I also took some comfort from the Health Committee in its recommendations or, potentially, lack of recommendations in this part. There was a question around privacy of Five Eyes concerns by the member Lawrence Xu-Nan. The answer there is no. The issues are here. The Privacy Act continues to apply for storage and sharing.
: There was a question around collection of information, and the biometric information is collected in accordance with the regulations as well.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): The Minister for Mental Health has mentioned full consultation. Can he confirm, then, that patients held under forensic legislation or in prison mental health settings were consulted as part of the drafting of this bill?
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): I can only reaffirm, and that was the advice, because, as we know, the full public consultation happened under that member’s last Government.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair, and thank you for that response, Minister, around the information privacy principles—IPP. Just to check, one of the directives that the Privacy Commissioner has submitted around that is to do with the fact that our IPP actually, in some ways, doesn’t cover the sharing of information, both individually but in also in terms of collective or bulk. I do wonder if the Minister for Mental Health could just confirm with me not just simply that this is something that has been checked through but that the Minister or officials have had a conversation with the Privacy Commissioner about this particular area. I think that would relieve a lot of our concerns as well.
: I do want to move on to clause 106, in terms of the detained person in need of care. This goes back to one of my earlier questions around public protection orders (PPOs) and extended supervision orders. In here, what you’re looking at is specifically a person who is detained in prison or a residence established under the Public Protection Orders Act. I just want to check with the Minister on what then would be the process of transferring someone from PPO to person under forensic compulsory care status, and if the Minister wouldn’t mind saying just how many of those are currently in the system.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Yeah, just to tie up the questioning around that, the Privacy Commissioner was consulted around the policy and made a submission.
Dr HAMISH CAMPBELL (National—Ilam): I move, That debate on this question now close.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Mr Chair, I just want to seek clarity from you. We’ve got some outstanding questions. If the Minister for Mental Health wants, we are happy to move on, but then if the Minister, in future parts, would be able to still respond to some of the current questions.
Hon Matt Doocey: I’m happy with that.
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): You’re happy with that?
Hon Matt Doocey: Yes.
Dr TRACEY McLELLAN (Labour): Thank you, and I appreciate the Minister for Mental Health’s previous answers; I just wanted to further dig into a little bit of context. The Minister said that the consultation had happened under the previous Labour Government, and that’s all very well and good, and obviously we’re very well aware that a lot of this work was initiated and instigated under a previous Government.
: The Minister has had the opportunity to add his two cents’ worth, so to speak, for lack of a better term, but the context is quite different now to what it was then in regards to forensic mental health, because the prison population has absolutely risen. There are clearly a lot more concerns about the forensic capacity within the prison system being able to cope with what is a booming prison population and all the requisite problems that that forces on other types of less forensic but still mental health responses.
: Has the Minister engaged in any further policy development or any kind of consideration of a very, very different environment to what it was three years ago, and how can he assure us that this even touches the sides in terms of an appropriate forensic mental health component of this bill?
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): As has been well traversed, this “repeal and replace”, which is a once-in-a-generation improvement of the Mental Health Act will equally improve care for those forensic patients that come outside the wire from Corrections into a forensic Health New Zealand setting.
: The question around, I suppose, capacity and ensuring we have the right number of beds: I would point the member to not only Budget 2025—$51 million specifically for more forensic mental health beds—and then Budget 2026 with $36 million specifically for more forensic mental health beds.
: Part 4 agreed to.

topicSummaries.topic: Part 5 Reviews, appeals, and judicial inquiries
topicSummaries.content:
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Members, we come now to Part 5. Part 5 is the debate on clauses 136 to 143, “Reviews, appeals, and judicial inquiries”. The question is that Part 5 stand part.
: Just before we move on to Part 5, and just to assist those of us at the table as well, many of us were not at the Health Committee, so it can be appropriate for you just to mention that in your address, and then we can sort of deal with that as that arises—but then also noting that we do have a Minister who is engaging, so it is possible that if you signal that you have a series of questions, you can just take a couple, I’ll take a beat, and if the Minister is going to engage, we can move forward that way as opposed to jamming 10 questions right at the end, which then makes it harder for us to track up here.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Mr Chair, thank you. I’m looking at the first clause in Part 5, clause 136, which is “Tribunal reviews of persons subject to compulsory care”. This records where a Mental Health Review Tribunal can review the condition of any person under compulsory care.
: We’ve had a bit of discussion in this House about whether compulsory care is appropriate in many settings, given that there’s no evidence of its therapeutic benefit. My question is on clause 136(4). It says that “If it appears that for any reason a status review … has not taken place, a Mental Health Review Tribunal may review the person’s condition”, etc. Given that this is a bill about safeguarding, wouldn’t it be better to have the word “must” there? Under this bill, people are entitled to those reviews of their compulsory care. What are the circumstances in which it would be ethical to not actually require that to occur, given all the direction of travel in this bill about the safeguarding of tangata whaiora?
: A similar question on clause 140, the “Application to revoke appointment of nominated person”. We’ve got a perceived safeguard there where, if “it considers that (a) the appointment is not in the best interests of the person under compulsory care; or (b) [they’re] unwilling to … participate”, or the appointment could have been obtained by some weird reason, a Mental Health Review Tribunal may basically revoke the appointment of that person. Now, again, if we’re really interested in the human rights of tangata whaiora, wouldn’t it be better just to change that word to “must”? The fact that there are reasonable grounds, that it’s not in the best interests, and that they have reason to believe that—they consider that—which means they have decided and landed on that view, means it would be untenable, from a human rights perspective to then enable the a Mental Health Review Tribunal the ability to overlook that. Tangata whaiora are sick of being overlooked. These are the very operational details of this bill that would make sure that wouldn’t happen.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair. I do have a couple of questions for this section as well, nothing that while it’s a smaller section, this is sort of one of the accountability measures and mechanisms that we have in this entire bill.
: I want to start by looking at clause 136(3). This is on page 93. I understand the clause in general when you apply to a tribunal, but I think this is quite an interesting clause where “a Mental Health Review Tribunal may at any time, of its own motion, review the condition of any person under compulsory care.” We’ve only seen a few of those instances in a tribunal or in a court setting. I do want to check with the Minister, what then would the criteria be or the circumstances that would encourage the tribunal to review of its own accord? That being my first question.
: My follow-up question is, usually when we see tribunals or courts, the tribunal itself cannot undertake any additional research. One of the few examples where we have the ability for tribunals to also undertake its own research is the Waitangi Tribunal. Can I check with the Minister if the Mental Health Review Tribunal is able to, in its own motion, review the conditions? It also implies that the Mental Health Review Tribunal can also undertake its own findings rather than just simply based on the submissions or the applications that they’re hearing. So those are my two questions to start with.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): I do believe that if the Minister is waiting to get some response, that’s totally fair, but we would be keen to at least get one engagement from the Minister for this part because we do have a couple of questions on this.
: I want to check with the Minister, when we’re looking at clause 139 subclause (5), this is page 98, at the conclusion of the review, the Mental Health Review Tribunal must record its findings stating the following—but what I want to check, and what is not clear, as far as I can see at this stage, is whether the conclusion of the review and the findings by the tribunal are binding or is that just simply a recommendation? If it’s binding, that’s clear; if it’s simply a recommendation, who then will take that recommendation further as a result of that?
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Thank you very much, Mr Chair. Just in response to those questions from Lawrence Xu-Nan: my expectation that the tribunal would use its authority to ensure that it does have all the relevant information about the review. If you’re asking the first question about their ability to seek and undertake their own activity to require that information, that would be my expectation. And to the latter: yes, because, ultimately, we want the tribunal to make a decision.
: Part 5 agreed to.

CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Members, we now come to Part 6. This is the debate of clauses 144 to 181—“Administration and public assistance”. The question is that part 6 stand part.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): I’d like to look at clause 164, “Appointment of Mental Health Review Tribunals”. We did have an amendment that landed on the Table at the eleventh hour, which has made a change to this, that says after clause 164(6), there should be an insertion about “nothing in this section prevents the appointment of a member of the Forensic Mental Health Review Tribunal to the Mental Health Review Tribunal.” In clause 164, we have a list of up to four appointees that can be made by the Minister; they include legal experts, health practitioners, people with lived experience and so on. Was the addition of this an afterthought where it is common practice for a forensic mental health review person to be on there and we’d just forgotten to put it into the bill? Or is there another reason why we’re having this late-stage amendment because it could conceivably raise issues of conflicts of interest insofar as the forensic mental health side of things being around forensic mental health versus mental health and not having the forensic elements. I’m wanting to understand, is it an oversight that’s already in common practice or are we trying to extend something here so that there is greater synergy but perhaps less transparency depending on how it’s safeguarded in the bill?
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Thank you, Mr Chair. I think it’s a valid question. Just to assure the members, it’s a small technical change that provides clarification.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair. I think this is a particular section that has quite a few amendments from the Minister, so I do want to go through some of them, and my colleague Ingrid Leary has gone through the first one around clause 164.
: I want to now move on to clauses 164 and 174. I, actually, then want to move on to clause 175—this is on page 113. Just to signal to you, Mr Chair, that we may have other questions, but we do want to address the Minister’s Amendment Paper 648 first. In clause 175, what we’re seeing is an insertion of two additional parts. I do want to check with the Minister—I see that in the explanatory note that he just says it provides us with more functions and powers, but he doesn’t actually address the fact of why the Minister considered that these are important to include last minute. So if the Minister wouldn’t mind to just elucidate the House on how this particular bit came about. I may have further questions based on the Minister’s response.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): If the Minister could just clarify, since he said it was a clarification: is it currently practice for that forensic member to be able to be on the tribunal under the current Act, and does that currently happen in practice?
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair. I will continue to look at some of the other sections, but I want to, now, first go back to an earlier section. This is something that is of interest and something we actually discussed yesterday in a separate bill, which is around fees and travel allowance—this is clause 172, page 112. The reason I want to look at this part is I want to check, as this came up in the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill, if the Minister wouldn’t mind just clarifying, the members on the Mental Health Review Tribunal, are they employees or are they contractors? Because that did come up yesterday, in terms of referees and adjudicators, and there is a level of consistency that’s expected that they’re all now going to be contractors and not employees. So if that if the Minister wouldn’t mind clarifying that, that would be greatly appreciated.
: I do want to check on a separate section of this bill and that’s more to do with the appointment of the Mental Health Review Tribunal. Can I just check, and again, this is something that came up previously. I’m looking at clause 168 subclause (2), which is that the “deputy of each member who is a lawyer must be a lawyer, and the deputy—”
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Sorry, are you looking at clause 160 now?
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN: 168.
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): 168. Alright.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN: Page 111. I do apologise. I’m jumping just a little bit, Mr Chair, because I want to check the Minister’s amendment first before going back to earlier sections.
: One of the considerations I had before is the capacity of the pool of people who are able to fulfil a particular role. That came up yesterday, I believe, as a part of the occupational regulation amendment bill. Can I just check, with the criteria that has been listed in clause 168 regarding deputies of members and also in terms of the criteria for the appointment of members in general, whether the Minister is confident that they are able to have the people who are able to fulfil all of those roles and particularly the role of, I’m assuming, that the tribunal will have a lead or a chair of some sort.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): The answer’s yes, I am confident.
: The question around the types of role being advised: independent statutory officers.
: The response to the member Ingrid Leary around “Is this current practice?”: as she will know, the Forensic Patient Review Tribunal was new, so no current practice.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Thank you. I’d like to turn to clause 181 around police assistance. This is a clause that lays out the powers that police have when they are attending an event and need to use powers of restraint, I guess. It’s really a policy question, Minister—a policy and resourcing question—about how you see this working given the direction of travel towards mental health response teams, which we applaud, and how this is going to work in effect because we are hearing lots of reports of police not attending situations and mental health workers having to put themselves in harm’s way, sometimes, to take people to hospital. They are clear they don’t want to have additional powers of restraint—that is not their core job. Their job is to support tangata whaiora and yet there are often powers of restraint needed. I can see these laid out in clause 181. How does he see this working where police are infrequently attending these events?
: We know that they are not necessarily declining to attend; often they’re just saying to mental health workers or families, “Call us back in 10 minutes.”, “Call us back in half an hour.”, “Let us know how you’re going.”, and workers are telling us in the end they’re just having to unilaterally make those decisions and try to get people into vehicles—sometimes for four- or five-hour drives to hospitals in rural areas like the lower South Island. It’s of great concern to mental health workers and I’m wondering if the provision could somehow be futureproofed, or does it need to have a reference to mental health response teams as a way of making sure we’re not back here doing something with an omnibus bill.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Yeah, look, I welcome that question by the member; it’s a very important topic. I suppose it starts to stray into the question of how we operationalise the bill. Something I’ve been very clear about with the police mental health change programme is that between Health New Zealand and NZ Police, they have new operating procedures. My expectation with this legislation is that it would inform those new operating procedures, because until there is surety that any changes between police and health can happen safely with new operating procedures then they are not green-lit.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair. I also have questions around clause 181 in terms of police assistance. I’m just noticing that this section does make a lot of references to other parts, and so I was hoping to wade into this section before I discuss this. One of the areas I’m not seeing, in terms of police assistance, is actually around clause 89. I understand that there are a lot of other sections here, and just to refresh the memory of the Chair and also the Minister for Mental Health, section 89 is around—
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Are you still on 181?
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN: I am on 181, but it refers to how then—are there any expectations, police assistance, when it comes to leave for a person subject to the hospital care? A responsible practitioner “may grant the patient person under compulsory care leave of absence from the hospital for a period specified”. But what I’m not seeing in both that section but also in this section is the fact that what happens when that person who is leaving will require police assistance. Because unless I’ve got it wrong, my understanding is it’s about a person who has leave from compulsory care going into the community, potentially for weddings, funerals, tangi, etc., with the care plan that everything that’s all considered. But also in those kinds of circumstance, in neither of these sections do I see a cross-referencing on awareness or an awareness to the police in case something does happen, so I just want to check with the Minister on whether that is a baseline expectation already: that the police may be assisting in the event of a leave, or whether that is actually not required as part of the care plan.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Yeah, look, a good question. I suppose where it gets slightly conflated when we talk more broadly about operations between police and health, that will be in response to those under the compulsory care Act, and of course those in mental distress who are not under the Act as well, but I think it points to more an operational issue. As you know with NZ Police and also health, the expectation when there may be a risk to the individual or others and how health work with police.
CARL BATES (National—Whanganui): I move, That debate on this question now close.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Just a final question on that—and thank you to the Minister for Mental Health for his answers—the wording of clause 181 is really interesting because it’s written passively around the words that somebody “is believed to be”. Then there’s the question of whether they should be under the Act. Currently one of the problems that we have is that it feels to mental health workers that the final decision about whether that person needs restraint or not is being made by police rather than by a clinician.
: I’m guessing that the wording is deliberately silent on that so that those protocols can be established, but I wonder if the Minister could just point to exactly where the determination will be made about in whose belief those decisions will be made. Because what we’re seeing is tangata whaiora falling through the cracks, family falling through the cracks, because the opinions of mental health workers are seeming, under the protocol, sometimes to fall secondary to the non-clinical decisions being made by police. Whose belief and on which protocol can that be put very clearly so that there is certainty for families and for tangata whaiora and mental health workers about who makes that decision?
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Yeah, important question and that’s why it’s important in this bill that there is clear criteria and principles under compulsory care and also the process of not only first but second assessment.
SUZE REDMAYNE (Junior Whip—National): I move, That debate on this question now close.
: A party vote was called for on the question, That debate on this question now close.
: New Zealand National 48; ACT New Zealand 11; New Zealand First 8.
: New Zealand Labour 25; Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand 11; Te Pāti Māori 4; Ferris; Kapa-Kingi.
: Motion agreed to.
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): The question is that the Minister’s amendments to Part 6 set out on Amendment Paper 648 be agreed to.
: Amendments agreed to.
: Part 6 as amended agreed to.

CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Members, we now come to Part 7. This is the debate on clauses 182 to 201, “Powers and offences”. The question is that Part 7 stand part.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): I’d like to go straight to the Amendment Paper that was dropped onto us very late in the piece, Amendment Paper 648. This does go to the question of police powers, which are important when it comes to human rights, and we have not been able to see this at the Health Committee. I notice that clause 182, “Police powers in relation to person appearing to meet compulsory care criteria in [a] public place”, has been changed and there’s an addition in there after 182, after line 35, to say, new subclause (7), “However, the constable must immediately release the person when the constable no longer has reasonable grounds to suspect that the person may meet the compulsory care criteria.” Then if they do that under new subclause (8), they must record the reasons for their suspicion of that and they must record their reasons for releasing them.
: This goes a little bit to the questions we had under the previous section, under whose belief is involved with persons making decisions about putting somebody under the Act. Whereas previously it appeared to be around police and health protocols, it’s very clearly spelt out in this amendment that this is on the constable.
: The question I had for Part 7 is whether the constable is the right person, and whether there needs to be any conferring or consultation with a health practitioner or others involved in that person. I know that it’s in a public place, but it does seem to be quite a burden that’s put on a constable who is not a clinical person.  My worry isn’t that the constable won’t release the person, because that could be exactly the right thing to do. My worry is that we’re starting to conflate clinical decisions that should be made by clinicians on to police, who are in charge of restraint and not clinical decisions.
: There’s also two different test levels in here, where it says that the constable “no longer has reasonable grounds”. So we’ve got the reasonable grounds test, which is a well-established legal test, but then we also have “record the reasons for their suspicion that the person may meet the compulsory care criteria”. There are two different thresholds there, and I wonder if the Minister could please explain why that language is different in the subparts rather than being consistent. Are they two different thresholds?
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): I’d just point the member to the principles of the bill. First, less restrictive practice; and, also, bringing in the new decision-making capacity—the acceptance that decision making can fluctuate and then applying less restrictive practice. This part of the bill points that out in the context of police.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): The second part, under Part 8, where they have reasons for suspicion, is a lower threshold than having the reasonable grounds in Part 7—it’s inconsistent. So is the Minister saying—
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Can you point to that clause? Sorry.
INGRID LEARY: This is in Amendment Paper 648, clause 182. Is it a lower threshold for suspecting that the person may meet the compulsory criteria? And then, is it a higher threshold being required in order for them to be released; and, if so, how does that accord with the principles of the bill?
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): No, but I would also expect police, where appropriate, to seek advice from DAOs, or duly authorised officers, to help inform their decisions.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair. I, too, want to speak to the Minister’s amendments set out on Amendment Paper 648, starting with clause 182. I’m just trying to get my head around the interactions between the Minister’s amendment and the existing process.
: Essentially, when we are looking at the amended clause 7, new clause 182(7) in the Minister’s Amendment Paper states that the constable who no longer has reasonable grounds must immediately release the person. That’s understandable; that’s fair. But we also see the same wording in clause 182, subclause (3). My understanding of the process is a constable finds the person; detains the person; then the constable, in subclause (6), may detain that person for six hours, or however long it takes to get an assessment under subclause (2); then the medical health practitioner examines the person; and then the medical health practitioner determines that, if the person does not meet the criteria, the person must be released under subclause (3); and then subclause (7) is that the person must be released.  Can I just check: why does it need to mention that the person is released twice? Once is by the medical health practitioner—but then that’s also in the passive voice—and the other one is by the constable. I’m just trying to get a sense of why we need to do that twice. What is missing in the interpretation between the two?
: My final question for clause 182 is around subclause (6), which is: why has six hours been the default selected for this part? Is it based on existing data of the maximum time it would take for the actions to be carried out, i.e., get access to some consultation or etc. from either an authorised person or a mental health practitioner?
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Thank you, Mr Chair, and I say respectfully to that member that I do enjoy, sometimes, his questioning when he poses the question and then goes through and actually follows through by answering the question, as well. I’m not saying that flippantly; I think it actually helps the debate of the House, and it’s better for clarification. I think he’s quite rightly identified the two different parts, because one refers to police and one refers specifically to the practitioner.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Just for clarity: that would only capture a situation where a mental health practitioner is authorised under the bill to restrain or hold on to somebody? We’re not now conferring those powers of restraint by somehow having to release points?
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Yes, I can confirm that.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Thank you. I have a question on clause 184, which is the “Power to sedate person when sedation urgently required”. I just wonder if it would be helpful to have an amendment—I haven’t drafted it up, but the wording would be very simple—where, under subclause (5), we could add the words “and police may not unreasonably withhold that assistance”. Now, we’ve seen that wording previously when a young person has asked the Director-General of Health for assistance to be transported and they want somebody to come with them, and the Director-General cannot unreasonably withhold that. The addition of these words would basically resolve the problem that we’re seeing at the moment, where mental health practitioners are turning up to events that can endanger themselves or—
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Just checking that you’re on clause 184?
INGRID LEARY: Clause 184, Subpart 5.
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Clause 184, Subpart 5. All right.
INGRID LEARY: —where health practitioners can turn up to events and they’ve been called by families. It’s high anxiety for everybody. They are aware they need to administer a sedative drug to be able to transport somebody, probably, to a secure unit. They’ve called police, and time and time again police are saying, “We’re not at the event yet; can you keep talking them to them? Can you keep trying to get them to come?” As I’ve said in my last contribution, it often leaves them with the distressing decision to travel unaccompanied in a potentially volatile or dangerous situation without police assistance.
: Changing these words under subclause (5) just to have “ police may not unreasonably withhold that assistance” means that there’s an expectation that police will turn up where a clinician has decided that a sedative drug is needed—but, also, it gives police the out that it’s not unreasonably withheld, so if there was something else that was occupying their time and they were all tied up, they could actually use that and there should probably be a recording of that decision. This would be incredibly helpful, because this status that we’re currently hearing from the front line of police not making a decision one way or other to turn up—this would clearly require them to do so where they can, or to be explicit where they can’t. That would give mental health workers more choices in situations where things can escalate really rapidly and where, currently, they’re feeling very vulnerable.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): I’d like to thank that member for that proposal of an amendment. It’s one that I would not support. I’d reinforce, within that clause and subpart, that by having the requirement it would be the expectation that that would then be operationalised between Police and Health New Zealand in their new joint working procedure.
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Before I take the next call, just to note that this is about penalties and offences. There’s a considerable amount of weight in this particular part, so having considered questions is a good thing for the process.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Thank you, Mr Chair. I’ll turn now to the offences under clause 190, which is about neglect or ill treatment of people. Again, recent events would say that this is something that may seem archaic, and yet it is all too often happening for us, not just in the abuse in care but very recent events, and we don’t now know how systemic this is around the country. So my question for clauses 190 to 199 is: when we’re talking about intentionality, is recklessness captured? What is the threshold? And if it isn’t captured, should it be captured, so that we can make sure we are really safeguarding our most vulnerable people?
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair. I want to first seek clarification from you. A few days ago, we heard the Chairperson’s guidance that the expectation is for us to have fulsome debates. As we’re moving through this bill, we do look at the operational elements.
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Is this a point of order?
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN: Yes, sorry. In that case, I will start with the point of order. Just if the Chair wouldn’t mind providing clarification—I do find it disruptive and concerning when the Government side is trying to shut down a debate for a very important part on offences. We haven’t repeated questions while speaking to the Minister’s amendments, and yet I just feel like it is actually inappropriate, based on the Chairperson’s guidance, and I seek your clarification.
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Well, we are dealing with penalties and offences, which does have a considerable amount of weight to it. We are open to considered questions, because of the importance of this particular part as well, and I’d like members to be aware of that. But also, it is possible to keep the question short as well so we can move through methodically.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN: Thank you, Mr Chair; I appreciate that.
: My first question is on clause 184(2). This is the only time I see in this whole section where “paramedic” is mentioned. However, we don’t see “paramedic” being mentioned in any other subsequent clauses, including the ability for a paramedic to call for police assistance, under subclause (4). Can I check with the Minister—my first question is: does this mean that paramedics do not have the ability to do that, or is the ability for a paramedic to call for police assistance covered under other legislation?
: My second question is around the Minister’s amendment to clause 187, “Powers of nurse if urgent assessment required”. Again, this to do with the fact that nurses must immediately release; that’s perfectly clear. But what we don’t see is, for example, similar insertions in clause 185 or clause 186. Can I assume that the Minister’s insertion in clause 182, that medical examiners need to immediately release and the police need to immediately release, covers subsequent sections.
: I note that the Minister said that I sometimes answer my own questions. If the Minister would just even like to nod, then I know that it’s covered.
Hon Matt Doocey: You’re doing well.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN: Cool, that’s helpful.
: I would like to move on now to the offences section. I want to start with clauses 190A to 190C. This is where a responsible practitioner commits an offence. I want to test two questions over here: based on what my colleague Ingrid Leary has asked regarding recklessness, are we looking at limited or strict liability here, being my first question? My second question is: it specifies an individual—i.e., the responsible practitioner—but what happens if there is an individual that is a part of a hospital system that is responsible but they’re not the company that is responsible? So, normally, we do see two tiers when it comes to fines or when it comes to offences or with a fine attached to it.
: Those are my four questions for the Minister so far, and just to very quickly recap, I asked questions around paramedics, questions around the Minister’s amendment to clause 187, and my two questions around clauses 190A to 190C.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Thank you very much, Mr Chair. Look, some of the questions, quite rightfully, around offences and penalties around neglect are quite timely. As we’ve stated, this bill meets 10 of the abuse in care recommendations. I would like to acknowledge the substantive work that the committee did on this part as well, which I think brings it up to a threshold that, actually, New Zealanders would expect as well. There are already regulation-making powers to create further offences, and, as we would expect under registration, they comply with the respective regulatory body for their workforce as well as the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): I would like to look at quite a problematic clause, in my view, clause 187, “Powers of nurse if urgent assessment required”. What this does is it has some pretty sweeping powers that nurses can apply, and also are expected to apply, and there are problems around both of those in situations that are probably evolving very quickly, I imagine. So it’s when someone’s been brought to a hospital and the nurse is having to assess whether they should be under the Act.
: The first question I have is that clause 187(1)(b)(i) states that “there are reasonable grounds to suspect that the person may meet …”. Previously, that was that they believed that the person “meets”. So these words have been changed and given more sweeping powers to the nurse, and subclause (1A) opens the door even further by saying that “In forming their belief that a person may meet the compulsory care criteria, the nurse can seek the advice of an authorised person”, in section 178. Section 178 basically just has an authorised person as being someone who is a kind of point of contact for the tāngata whaiora.
: What I see here is possible is that the first issue, really, is that a nurse who isn’t aware of the circumstances is possibly going to put very heavy weighting on the authorised person. There don’t seem to be safeguards around that, and we’ve got the diminishment of the threshold through the word “suspect” and “may meet” rather than the original words “believe” and “meets”. I’m not clear whether we actually saw that in select committee because sometimes we’re told these things are technical changes. But I’m sure, Mr Chair, you’ll appreciate that that does open, quite broadly, the powers of the nurse.
: The other bit that’s very problematic for me is then we have, in subclause (3), the words “The nurse may—(a) detain the person where they are … or (b) take the person to some other place”. This goes, again, to the real concerns that mental health staff and nurses have that they don’t normally have, unless it’s in the provisions of this bill, powers of restraint. And they don’t want them, because their job is to provide care and support, and when they now have a duty to detain a person—I mean, it’s not a duty; it says “may” —it’s going to put them in a really difficult position where they’re expected to do what’s, essentially, a policing function.
: We’ve heard some first responders, for example, talk about wanting to wear stab-proof vests, and other unions have said to us that that’s the last thing they want, that is not their job, that is not why they went into healthcare, and this really muddies the waters. So I’m wondering if the Minister can please respond to both of those concerns.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Thank you very much, Mr Chair. For nurses’ powers under clause 187, the nurse does not decide if the person comes under the Act. I also refer the member to looking at the recommended change, more specifically under clause 182, and how this update is to align with that.
: I come back to the principles of the bill, around least restrictive practice as a principle, but also the requirement that the nurse will need to record and report the reasonable grounds, and for that reporting to be provided to the Director of Area Mental Health Services.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair. I’m just noting that I am still on the offences section and I’m waiting for the Minister’s response regarding my two questions there, and also my questions on paramedics.
: I want to ask just one more question around this because what we are seeing, I’m assuming, is different severities between clauses 190A to 190C as well, where we’re looking at, in 190C, the words “knowingly provide”; in that case, we’re looking from a mens rea perspective of intention, I’m assuming—I just want to double check with the Minister if that is the case—whereas, potentially, clauses 190A and 190B, as per my colleague Ingrid Leary’s question, could be around recklessness, which has a much lower threshold if you’re looking at the hierarchy of mens rea.
: Broadly, if we’re looking at clause 193, clause 195, and clause 196—these are the clauses on page 125 and 126—others may have questions on the detail of those, but again, what we’re seeing across those is the inclusion of “an individual” and “for any other person”. I just want to specify in that case that “any other person” refers to a legal person but not necessarily an actual person, if that is the correct interpretation of that.
: My final question for this contribution is around infringement offences. While the other sections in terms of offences have a detailed amount of fines, what I’m not seeing in this section—and this is to do more around infringement notice—is that there hasn’t been an amount given for an infringement notice here. Is that intentional or is that covered under another Act? Those are my few questions for the time being.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Thank you very much. I mean, to answer that question specifically, we’ve tiered penalties when offences are set by regulations. Just going back, in fairness, I think we did move on from, was it clause 184 around paramedics?
Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan: Yes. Paramedics, yes.
Hon MATT DOOCEY: First and foremost, that clause in the context is emergency as well. In practice, paramedics should request advice and assistance from the authorised person. That’s covered under clause 178. Authorised persons can advise on steps under the Act and request police assistance if required. This is an important safeguard. It builds back to that primary principle of safeguarding.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Thanks. I’m a bit troubled by the Minister for Mental Health’s answer to my question on clause 187 and what this means for nurses, because as I understand the clause, it means a person comes to hospital, they’re not under the Act, they might be agitated, someone thinks they should be under the Act and they approach a nurse, and if he or she has grounds to suspect that they may meet the criteria and they can confer with somebody else who is not a clinician and they form that opinion, there’s two really problematic bits. One is that the nurse must arrange for a mental health practitioner to examine the person, so that’s a duty that they have to do. I get that that could be in the interests of the tangata whaiora, but if we couple that with the Minister’s response around “The nurse may detain the person” or “take the person”, that’s a huge burden on a nurse now to be detaining someone who isn’t under the Act.
: My question is, what power do they have to be able to use their discretion to detain the person? Because that is a fundamental restraint and power and infringement on another’s human rights. Is this going to stray into the territory of some kind of citizen’s arrest? Where is the authority for that detention that they would be exercising? Because although it says “may,” not “must”, there will be pressure on them to do it because of the application of subclause (2), which says, “the nurse must arrange”. The last thing they’re wanting to do is see the person leave the vicinity of their room or their hospital, and yet they now have to detain that person, probably from an ethical perspective, or to be able to meet the obligations of subclause (2). Without the previous amendment that I suggested about the police being present unless not reasonably being able to be there, what kind of work burden does this put on nursing staff, and does it make their job more unsafe?
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Thank you very much, Mr Chair. I suppose we are moving into an operational area as well, but there would be an expectation from the nurse to seek advice from the authorised officer. It is at times because it is publicly available or in the media when people leave environments and the ability to be detained or not.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair. Just seeking the Minister for Mental Health around some of the questions I had earlier regarding legality, some of the terminologies being used. I do appreciate the Minister’s response to my question around infringement notice. My next question is around clause 200, “Use of force”, and it’s just a simple clarification from the Minister that this particular one simply refers to “a person”. Can I check, in that interpretation, is the person—sorry, this is page 129, line 15, clause 200. In that case, does “a person” have to be any of the named ones we had before—a nurse, police, an authorised person, a medical or mental health practitioner, etc., etc.—or can it be a person of the public? Can anyone do this? Because it doesn’t specify. That’s just my clarification for this section specifically.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): I turn to clause 195, “False or misleading records”. If this is captured somewhere else in the bill, it would be really useful to know it. Apologies, I haven’t found it. But we had a situation in Dunedin where there were abuse in care records that were knowingly destroyed. As I read the bill and clause 195, I can see that there are fines for changing information or recording information misleadingly. I don’t see a fine for destroying the information belonging to people that may have been captured under the bill. That has been absolutely devastating for abuse in care people down in our way who found the process of applying for redress and going through the apology system and all of that incredibly difficult because they couldn’t access their own personal information. Somebody had destroyed it on the basis of bad legal advice, and there was some fallout about that, but I think it’s incredibly important that we do ensure that destruction of records is explicitly mentioned. As I say, I apologise if I have missed it, but from my reading of the bill it doesn’t seem to be explicit.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): I think that’s a fair question. We did traverse it slightly earlier in a different context, but the Act allows, through regulations, new definitions.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Point of order, Mr Chair. Thank you, Mr Chair. Just to seek your guidance—and this may cover later sections—that I’m personally quite happy with where we’re landing on Part 7 but noting there are some outstanding questions. I know the officials are also working incredibly hard and we very much appreciate the time spent here. If it’s OK with you, Mr Chair, for the Minister to answer my questions in a subsequent section.
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Just to respond to the point of order, the Minister has indicated, because the information is still coming, that those questions will be addressed possibly in Part 8, if that’s OK.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN: Yes, thank you.
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Is that all right? Have you got another question? Have you got on under Part 7 still?
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri): Yes, Part 7. Just based on what the Minister for Mental Health said about putting destruction of records into regulation, I’d just ask the Minister if he’d consider an amendment to make it a legislative matter, not a regulatory matter. It is of great importance, and if changing records can be in the legislation, I would imagine, for consistency, that destroying records should also be in legislation, not regulation.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health): Yeah, no, I wouldn’t support that, but I’m happy with the new regulatory powers.
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): The question is that the Minister’s amendment to Part 7 set out on Amendment Paper 648 be agreed to.
: Amendment agreed to.
: Part 7 as amended agreed to.

topicSummaries.topic: Part 8 Secondary legislation and miscellaneous provisions, and Schedule 2
topicSummaries.content:
CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono): Members, we now come to Part 8. This is the debate on clauses 202 to 221—“Secondary legislation and miscellaneous provisions”—and Schedule 2. The question is that Part 8 stand part.
Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green): Thank you, Mr Chair. I’ve been waiting seven parts for this particular part because regulations aren’t my favourite. I want to start by looking at the regulations that are expected in clause 212, noting that, I believe—oh, no, not for this particular bit.
: I just want to check some of this, particularly when we’re looking at paragraphs (ca) and (db), to do with prescribing fines, etc.—particularly when we’re looking at this whole area that has been listed. I’m wondering how those regulations will manifest, and I want to focus on one particular part of it, which is clause 202(1)(eb), which is “prescribing infringement offences for breaches of the regulations and prescribing infringement fees for those offences”.
