content.speaker: Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan
content.text: OK, cool. Just the clarification is helpful. Thank you.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DEBORAH RUSSELL (Labour)
content.text: After that confusion, trying to sort out the arcane rules of the way we do things around here, I wish to speak in support of my colleague Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan’s motion to extend the date by which the select committee must report back to 17 September 2026.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Maureen Pugh)
content.text: But that’s not actually—no.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DEBORAH RUSSELL
content.text: Oh. In that case—I really don’t understand what’s happened. It is just so complicated trying to sort my way through this. I do have a particular issue I wish to raise, so perhaps if I speak in support of Hon Dr Duncan Webb’s amendment, that might do the trick.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Maureen Pugh)
content.text: That would be useful.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DEBORAH RUSSELL
content.text: Thank you very much for your help with that, Madam Speaker. Look, I have no strong views as to the report-back date except that the four-week period is far, far too short, and I do support the Hon Dr Duncan Webb’s proposal of just having no report-back date so that the standard time applies.

The reason I support this is to do with the matter of consulting with experts and, particularly, with legal experts as to the desirability of this move. What I found in the various releases of papers from the Minister was that a bit of work the Minister had done had asked for consultation with experts and, in particular, with legal experts as to what the pros and cons were of this move of disallowing this tort and disallowing the particular court case and putting this statutory bar in place—litigation bar, whatever it is. I’m not a lawyer; I find it hard to find my way around these words.

Looking at the summary of the consultation with experts and the advice that was given to the Minister, it says that some experts think there might be some benefits of a statutory bar on emissions-related tort claims, but several other experts say it might be speculative. That was on the costs or benefits. Then, in terms of the design features of the statutory bar, some of them said it was going to be very, very difficult and then they said it should be drafted very, very narrowly. Some of them talked in terms of the policy and international implications, and they said that there were concerns raised about the absence of alternative legal remedies. In terms of constitutional perspectives, some noted that climate change is a complex social issue better addressed by Parliament than the courts—that would be the Minister’s view. But others said that, actually, the environment is a taonga and that blocking claims could breach the Treaty of Waitangi. So it’s a back and forth and a back and forth and a back and forth in terms of the legal expertise. Some experts thought that the removal of judicial scrutiny might erode public trust and corporate responsibility. Some thought that the concern about business confidence should be addressed with alternative approaches.

In other words, what I’ve got here from the picture of reading the advice to the Minister is that experts were divided. The difficulty was that in terms of the advice that was given to the Minister, there is no sense of which were the weightiest concerns; where there was the most agreement amongst experts; whether the officials, quite properly being careful about how they referred to these experts, said “some said this” and “some said that”, whether they mean nine were against the move and two were for it. That would “some” covers a multitude, or very few narrow.

Now, that’s a real problem for the select committee. It’s a real problem because, as a select committee, those of us who sit on it—or join the committee for the purpose of this particular bill—are going to have to try to work our way through the pros and cons of this move. We are going to need to consult the experts. We’re going to need to be able to quiz them. And importantly, we’re going to need to try to form some view of the weight of views from experts, where they are most held. Now, this very short select committee process, I think, won’t allow us to properly engage the experts. So we have some advice sitting here, where, frankly, we just don’t know what it really means—it said that plenty of people seem to think this is a bad move. Then we move on to the advice from the Minister’s own officials who consistently, in terms of their own advice, have advised the Minister not to do this. They said it’s the wrong thing to do.

As a select committee, somehow we’re going to have to pick our way through that. I think one of the only ways we are going to be able to do that is by having a talk to some of the experts ourselves. The trouble is we’re going to need submissions from those experts. Now, we’ve got people who regularly comment on the law for us here in New Zealand. In particular, we’ve got a number of academic experts who, on an ongoing basis, will put in submissions around some of the legal technicalities in the laws that are in front of us. I’m thinking about people like Dr Eddie Clarke, and I just have to think—who’s the guy down at Otago University who’s really good on this stuff?

content.speaker: Arena Williams
content.text: Andrew Geddes.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DEBORAH RUSSELL
content.text: Oh yes—Professor Andrew Geddes. There are a variety of others who actually often—

content.speaker: Arena Williams
content.text: Dean Knight.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DEBORAH RUSSELL
content.text: Dean Knight is another great—give us their expertise. You know, I hope those gentlemen are watching tonight, because actually, we’d like to hear from them. But I actually happen to know that it’s a busy time of the year, the semester is just starting up. They have other concerns—they’ve already been very busy submitting on other pieces of legislation. Yet, we are going to want their expertise, if they can lend it to us for this piece of legislation. I think that this very shortened report back of four weeks is not going to allow enough time for those people to write to us and to give us their submissions. I’m hoping—I’m hoping—that some of the experts who were consulted by the Minister’s officials a year or so ago might also come and lend us the value of their expertise, and so on. But again, getting those people in is going to be quite hard.

This shortened report back period is very, very difficult for the select committee. Some of our colleagues have previously talked about, in terms of the volume of work and so on, and obviously, well, there goes our recess. We’re all working anyway; it’s not exactly a holiday, is it? But it’s going to complicate things. But my genuine concern here is that we need more time to enable the select committee to consult experts and to form our own opinion on the merits of this law change. To really understand the implications of it and to be able to move beyond the interesting advice that has been given to the Minister earlier, but one which we really have no idea as to how to weight that advice. So for those reasons, I think that we do need to extend the time available to us for the select committee process. That’s the reason why I am supporting Dr Duncan Webb’s motion.

content.speaker: ARENA WILLIAMS (Labour—Manurewa)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I am speaking to the amendment proposed by the Hon Dr Duncan Webb, to extend the referral to the select committee. Four weeks is not a select committee process in the way that Parliament has generally understood the deliberative process, which is a part of the Constitution Act.

The reason why we should extend this process for this particular issue is that given the Minister has said it is simply because he wants to get this done quickly, I don’t think it really meets the standard for what giving a reason is intended when the Minister is meant to give a referral motion to the House. It is clear, then, that the worry from many Parliaments before us, that this use of a shortened select committee process to four weeks concentrates power within the executive in a way which was unintended, in using the deliberative processes within that Act, is quite clear. It was alluded to by the Minister, and confirmed then by the then executive, that that was the intention. Because there are other mechanisms that allow the executive to use this kind of concentration of their powers to move legislation quickly.

One is all-stages urgency—that is not this—but then there are other checks. If this bill was proceeding without a select committee process, it would be referred to the Regulations Review Committee for a review of the powers—not only in the primary legislation but also in its secondary legislation—to give due consideration to the kinds of impacts that primary legislation would have on not only the courts but the regulation-making bodies within our legal system. In some ways, that is a thorough check when you have a piece of primary legislation which does something like this, which has impact on secondary level decision makers. That’s not a part of this process, if it’s avoided because of the four-week select committee process. The four-week select committee process is then asking a select committee to do all of that—and all of the advice from officials and all of the submissions—at the same time. It doesn’t even have the robustness of some of the Parliaments that we like to compare ourselves to, let alone that they have an Upper House and a written constitution which courts can refer to when negotiating these kind of sub judice issues—which, by the way, we are generally discouraged from considering in this House.

These sorts of cases, where Parliament deliberately decides to legislate over the top of active proceedings, are particularly difficult when trying to negotiate the independence of the courts from the parliamentary system. But that aside, we have no way of actually checking that the courts will be properly empowered to undertake the work that they are otherwise given within our constitutional framework, given this four weeks select committee process. That’s why the referral to the select committee should last for the entire period. The entire period then allows not only those submitters to have their say but also advice from organisations like the Legislation Design and Advisory Committee. This is a group of well respected lawyers who practice in New Zealand’s constitutional system, and who regularly advise Cabinet, to be able to also make their submissions in public. That is their only chance to make their submissions in public, because they are not a body which would otherwise, say, take a position in the media against the Government; that is not something we want to be encouraging in our legal system. So using the select committee in that way is important for their access, to raise these issues.

It’s also part of Crown Law’s remit, that they would be able to give advice on those pieces of this legislation which impinge on individual’s rights. This is one where you might expect a Crown Law vet, because where there is one person impacted by legislation, or a small group of people impacted by legislation, that is often a good candidate for the Attorney-General’s view of whether individual rights are impacted by a particular piece of legislation. I think a good example of this happened in the last term, were 16 people were affected by a piece of Corrections legislation, and that was where Crown Law gave particular attention to the circumstances of each of those individuals. In this case, it is one individual whose rights are being impacted, and instead of legislating in the normal way—where one person’s rights would be impacted, which would be a private Act—the Government has chosen to do this using a public Act, which does warrant further scrutiny by Crown Law.

We’re also curtailing the ability of those groups, that act as sort of soft checks within our constitutional system, to do that. They do come back to my point, which is that to curtail the select committee’s role here, when we’re also dealing with a parliamentary system which doesn’t have an Upper House, doesn’t have those extra checks and balances—that any legislature that we would compare ourselves to when doing this kind of process to maintain the independence within Parliament and the courts—has. You have to have special regard to the role of the select committees in that deliberative process. But deliberative in the sense of the mechanics of Government, not just deliberative in the sense of parliamentary democracy. Deliberative in the sense that when you give the different arms of the legislature, of the Executive, of the court systems, their ability to respond to something which Government has brought to bear. Because the way that the courts do there is that there is time for Crown Law to represent the views of the Government within its deliberative processes. But there is no ability here for any of their advice to be presented in a public way.

So what does that mean? It means that it all has to happen behind the scenes. This is an issue of public trust and confidence in the system, because what we have here is a Government that has, through the use of different legal instruments in this term, had a number of instances where rights that had been taken to the court process, and in some instances to a second court process, have been curtailed.

An example of this was the ANZ-ASB case, which was heard by the High Court and which will continue to be appealed by one of the complainants. It was a case where Cabinet had made decisions which would have curtailed the rights of thousands of complainants to seek damages against their banks that was owed under consumer law, and the way that that select committee process played out is the perfect example of where a deliberative process actually brought those issues to bear.

Before the select committee got hold of that, it was quite unclear to the public what the changes proposed by Government would actually mean for those thousands of New Zealanders. But once it came to the select committee’s attention, and once there was a public forum where not only people but the other arms of Government, in Government departments—in that case, it was the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment and Crown law—and the Legislation Design and Advisory Committee (LDAC) was able to advise on what the effect of the use of Crown power in that way would mean for individuals. That was when it became clear that this would really undermine public trust and confidence in the way that the executive is using their power, and, ultimately, the executive sanctioned a different sort of use of that power which saw those complainants to be able to take their rights to the court.

That was a good thing. It was an example of an executive that listened, in that case, to the submissions made by the people and made by LDAC and Crown Law. It would not have otherwise happened if we had had four weeks in that case, and that was only six months ago.

I’m not raising the issues that we have debated in this House today that date back to 2009 about the Auckland super-city. I’m talking about just this year, when the Government listened to people who were raising their ability to bring proceedings in the court, as you can in any other Westminster jurisdiction like ours, when Parliament respects the role of the courts in the system and where you, as an individual, have rights that you want to seek against a large company. These rights are difficult to demonstrate and they are expensive to demonstrate. If you are somebody who wants to bring a case against Fonterra for these sorts of matters, you need to be very, very determined, and that is what we have here. It is a complainant who has sought to crystallise the rights that they think they have. To be able to pursue those, it has meant a huge amount of work and investment in this case, and so it’s right for the Government but also the Parliament, separately, to give due regard to that seeking of rights.

It’s an equity law. It’s the concept of coming to the issue with clean hands. We have that here with the plaintiff, who has done everything in their power to pursue rights that they should have under the law and to clarify those rights in the courts. For the Government to look over the top of that, you might expect that the complainant was not doing that with clean hands in that concept of equity law, and yet that is the case here. So it’s right for us to consider and properly debate the amount of time that the complainants and New Zealanders will be able to bring these matters to the committee.

There is one more issue that I wanted to raise with members. I started this contribution focusing on the Constitution Act, but there is also a decision for the Standing Orders Review Committee right now to determine how we deal with pieces of legislation which move very quickly through the four-week report-back period for select committees. In Parliaments past, attention has been given to all-stages urgency legislation, and we have a new rule in this Parliament where the Regulations Review Committee plays that sort of check and balance role that’s missing in our system to review legislation, which has a sort of wide-reaching impact, especially for regulatory bodies after it has passed. I want to raise—[Time expired]

content.speaker: GLEN BENNETT (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. As we stand here this evening in this room, where the calendar says it is 30 June, it actually is 2 July. The report-back date, obviously, is 30 July, and I have an amendment on the Table—which I will move shortly—about that.

I just really want to be really clear and come back to Speaker’s ruling 115/3, which is around where a Minister talks about a shortened period, and it says that they are to give the House a good reason, or to give a reason, I should say. As has been spoken about before, I think that that Speaker’s ruling is really important. I see the Minister is in the room and he’s more than—

content.speaker: Hon Member
content.text: He gave a reason.

content.speaker: GLEN BENNETT
content.text: He gave one sentence. I think was that the Government is keen to resolve something—that was the reason—which I think they should expand on and explain it a bit better, because having it completed in a timely fashion actually isn’t a good reason. The expectation we’ve heard from many a Minister in this House—because I’ve been through this process many a time in this Parliament, that other Ministers have taken the time to be thorough and thoughtful in terms of listing the reasons why a shortened report back time is needed, and I think we need to come to that.

What I heard from the Minister was the “what” and the “how” in referring to Standing Orders 193, 195, and 196, which is often talked about around sitting during any time except for question time, after 6 p.m., and that can be done when the  House sitting—all of those types of things, which are around the “what” and the “how”. But, actually, the “why” is the real challenge we have here.

I have the paper on the Table. I move, That the report-back date be replaced with “1 September 2026”. I don’t think that is unreasonable. The House will rise—is it 24 September, I believe, that the House will rise? That gives at least some time for some of the experts to engage with and spend some time thoroughly considering this legislation. I think it should be longer, but that is just, I guess, the fact of this Government that it moves at pace with legislation. We’re talking about, I think, 29 days for this—if I’m correct with my maths—and, generally, it is six months, and so 180 days is what normally would be expected when it comes to the select committee process in order for it to be thoughtful and thorough.

But if we look back, time after time, we’ve had report-back times of 71 days, we’ve had 28 days, we’ve had 43 days, 81 days, 83 days—it just goes on in terms of how shortened our report-backs have been when it comes to select committees doing what? Doing their job of engaging, trying to find the issues, trying to hear from the experts, and doing what is right to ensure that when the legislation ends up back in this House, it has, hopefully, been shaped in a way that, potentially, is more palatable. Sometimes, for us in Opposition, we don’t like the legislation, but I believe that we try to be as constructive as possible—knowing it’ll potentially pass—to try to make changes within the space of select committee in order to find a way through that will make the legislation less bad.

I really want to note this, and I say to the Minister that I don’t feel that the sentence he gave was enough of an explanation—hence that Speaker’s ruling makes it very clear that either they are welcome to get up and have a more fulsome explanation, or we will continue with the debate on the report-back time.

Four weeks is very short, and this is a serious change in terms of what is going on. I won’t go into too much more detail in terms of it, and I know my far more learned colleagues have mentioned things around the current court process that is being gone through, which is acknowledged in the legislation.
But my amendments sits on the Table. I have now put it forward, and I hope that this Parliament can discuss and can consider that.

content.speaker: Hon Members
content.text: Madam Speaker.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Maureen Pugh)
content.text: The question is—just a minute. There is an amendment being moved, and so I just want to make sure that I get the wording correct in putting that, just so that the House knows what we’re doing.
The question is that the amendment to the motion is agreed to. Glen Bennett’s amendment is now debatable, alongside the amendment and the motion.

content.speaker: RICARDO MENÉNDEZ MARCH (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker.
I move, That the motion be amended to replace the words “30 July 2026” with “17 September 2026”.

I support also the other two amendments that are being put on the Table, and I wanted to present a bit of a rationale for mine as well, which is—and I hope that the Government can take this with a conciliatory and good-faith approach. The 17 September date that I am proposing still leaves a week for this bill to be, basically, debated in its second and third reading as well as the committee of the whole House stage, which, in my view, would still meet both the intent of a good democratic process on something that has constitutional impacts as well as the Government wanting to fulfil its agenda—which, obviously, we disagree with.

I think with something so significant, an amendment like this one would allow a broader range of members of the public to be able to adequately contribute to the select committee process. Other members noted that otherwise, without the date being changed, you would have, effectively—well, some members calculated—potentially, a one-week submission period, which would not be good enough.

I wanted to touch on—and I haven’t seen it being touched on by others—who are we limiting by, effectively, creating a process where the submission period is so short? I would make the case that the very same people that are most impacted by climate change and climate policies are some of the ones that would likely be least able to find the avenues and the time, the resources, or have the ability to be able to make a submission, let alone actually, probably, do an oral submission to the select committee, if we are not to amend the motion. My amendment would allow the select committee to create a bit of a longer submission period for the committee as well as to have more flexibility over the period in which we hear oral submissions.

Now, when I talked about the demographics that I think the current motion, without amendments, would disproportionately negatively impact, I am thinking of people who have to work, for example, multiple jobs to make ends meet. When I have worked with constituents who deeply care about the legislation that this Government is putting forward, some of the feedback that I often receive is: “Well, I could submit, and I would love to be able to present to the select committee, but often the dates that are given to me conflict with the fact that I’ve got multiple responsibilities”—potentially multiple jobs—“to juggle.” I would assume that if this is a Government that backs working people, they would want to support an amendment that would enable the greater participation of working people, particularly those who are on lower incomes, have to work multiple jobs, and on top of that, potentially, juggle caregiving responsibilities.

The other group that I wanted to mention is disabled people. Disabled people—there’s quite a lot of literature that speaks about the fact that climate change will disproportionately impact disabled people. As we have seen in other select committees on bills that disabled people are disproportionately affected by, tight time frames really hinder adequate participation. If you want to create a process that is genuinely accessible, my amendment would enable a more fulsome select committee process that would allow that broader participation of people as well.

The other group is parents with young children and caregiving responsibilities to generations—they will be disproportionately impacted by this piece of legislation. Therefore, I think caregivers who are having to juggle caregiving responsibilities will not be so able to participate in the oral submission process that the current time frame would allow.

Again, to me, this speaks to and it’s sort of a bit of an attempt to offer an olive branch to the other side of the House when it comes to the process, not the substance of the bill, to genuinely commit to be able to include as many groups of people who will inevitably be impacted by the consequential impacts of this bill in the process. I would say that if what the Government wanted was to create a mandate, and they were confident that they had a mandate on this specific policy, they would want to invite and create a process where as many people as possible are able to contribute. I would assume that what they’re hoping for is that by the end of the process, the Government will find itself with a select committee report that tells them that the majority of submitters actually supported their bill. I think they can only achieve that, if they genuinely believe in that, by extending the select committee process to one that actually enables that broader participation.

I back the other amendments. I wanted to briefly speak on Duncan Webb’s amendment as well. One of the things that I find particularly concerning about the fact that we are able to sit in select committee while the House is sitting is that you end up cycling through quite a lot of members in that select committee. I know others talked about the impact on smaller parties, but I want to speak more to the fact that I don’t believe and I don’t think any party will claim that they’ve got a caucus full of people who feel fully competent and have expertise on this specific area of legislation, right? We want to enable our caucus members who do have expertise on this issue to be able to participate in all the select committee sessions while also being able to meet whatever other responsibilities they may have to their electorates, to their other portfolios, or just other party responsibilities that they have.

Without being able to have, I guess, just a bit of greater certainty of when the select committees are more likely to meet, I think you will likely end up with a process where you’ll have members sitting in and out of the select committee, where their participation will be through proxy contributions that are presented by the spokespeople to that member subbing in. I think that creates a process where collaboration is less likely to happen, where fulsome engagement with submitters is less likely to happen.

Finally, the other argument I would want to make to broaden this is that when you have quite shortened report-back dates, one of the things that you end up not really enabling is cross-party collaboration. When amendments are being proposed, for example, in the select committee process, it is normal that respective parties would want to take those amendments to their respective caucuses. When you have such a short report-back date, you really limit the number of caucus meetings that happen in that select committee process, particularly if there are recess weeks that are in between those. That means that even sometimes when you may find changes that you may want to propose, and you can tell that maybe other members of other political parties are in agreement as individuals, those amendments may end up stalling just by the nature of a really rushed process that does not allow for those members to consult with their party during their caucus meetings.

I think that would be a shame, if members want to work collaboratively around this bill—I don’t know if that’s the intent, but I would assume that we would want to enable as much of that as possible. My amendment would support allowing that to happen, if there is cross-party work to identify, for example, how this bill could be improved, or if in between, even, coalition parties, they find a way that they want this bill to better align with their Government objectives.

I hope that the Government is able to consider the 17 September report-back date in order to allow them to build a mandate of public support, as they assume, they claim, they have, as well as to have a broader range of population groups being able to present to the select committee on something that, ultimately, is of great significance to people of this country, as a country that I think has often had a big range of the population who ranks climate change as one of the issues that they care about. I would include in this people that do not vote for our political party. I would assume that across most of our political parties, voters and supporters of those parties care about climate issues as well. With that, I will end my contribution.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Maureen Pugh)
content.text: The question is that the amendment to the motion in the name of Ricardo Menéndez March be agreed to. The amendment is now debatable alongside the other amendments and the motion.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I want to go back to what the purpose of select committee scrutiny is, because what we have at stake here is quite significant. The fact that we are able to take fulsome arguments to debate the referral motion shows the level of seriousness that this Parliament takes about making sure that we follow process. Whether we’re going to get the outcome we want is a different question, but the very fact that we are having a debate on this shows that this is a significant matter, when we are wanting to truncate something that is inherently part of the lawmaking process.

If we look at the Standing Orders, Standing Order 338A talks about the purpose of scrutiny being “to hold the executive to account, to contribute to good governance for improved outcomes, and to strengthen confidence in public institutions.” I think it’s really important to mention that when supporting the amendment that the Hon Dr Duncan Webb proffered in the first instance, but otherwise also in the alternatives, those proffered since then, including the one by the Green member to extend the period out to September. There are a number of really significant words in that Standing Order that are worth looking at. I’d also like to point out to people at home who might be wondering what’s going on with this that the Standing Orders were amended. Standing Order 338A shows that this was an amendment at some point in time, where it was felt needed to clarify the significance and importance of select committee scrutiny.

Other members have touched on this when it comes to the question of the public interest and the public confidence in the parliamentary process. That is what is at stake here, along with the fact that the very matter that is being referred to select committee for a shortened period of time is not a trivial matter; it is a matter of great constitutional importance. While the Green member talks about climate change and the specific substantive nature of that and what that means, what I’m turning my attention to is the implications that that particular law would have on the broader lawmaking powers of this House and what it means constitutionally.

If we look at select committee scrutiny, the word “scrutiny” by its very nature means to scrutinise, to be forensic, to hold up into the light. It’s important that the committee has the time to do all the elements of that that it needs to, including, should it decide to, to appoint an independent adviser. Professor Andrew Geddis has been mentioned. But certainly with a matter of such great constitutional import—

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Maureen Pugh)
content.text: I’m sorry to interrupt the member. The two Green members are meant to be seated while you’re in the House, not wandering around talking. If you do want to have a conversation, please take it outside.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY
content.text: For a matter of such constitutional importance, it might well be the intention of the committee to get an independent adviser to understand the ramifications of what the particular bill would have on the broader area of constitutional law. For members at home, we do have statute law, like the laws that are made and passed in this House that are written down on bits of paper and that are scrutinised and go through a process. But we also have common law, which is known as tort law, and that is what this particular bill is looking to override.

Tort law has been what makes our country different and distinctive from the motherland, from the UK. We have developed our own tort law. We have seen that come under threat with the Treaty principles bill and we saw the level of response to that. We saw that people understood the significance of what was being proposed because Te Tiriti had become part of our tort law and suddenly there was this move to rewrite history and rewrite all the laws that were there and put it into a written law, and there was a huge backlash to that, quite rightfully.

Now, in a smaller sense, this is purporting to do the same thing. In that case, there may well be a huge public interest in what is attempting to be done, but we cannot gauge that with the effective one-week turnaround at the select committee. We cannot gauge what the impact will be, necessarily, on other parts of the law if we don’t have an independent adviser or the level of scrutiny that the Standing Orders require.

When I look at Standing Order 338A(2), it says, “For this purpose, select committees examine, assess, and express views about the executive’s strategy, policy, expenditure, administration, performance, and results.”  It is about scrutinising the executive.

Now, Sir Geoffrey Palmer has said that we’re the fastest lawmakers in the West. We probably are, perhaps apart from Fiji where I used to live, where they equally use urgency to a great degree, but in that environment where we are making laws so quickly and where there are numbers on the executive who outnumber the Opposition MPs, which is how our Westminster parliamentary system works, we want to ensure that the public don’t think of the select committees as just a rubber-stamping exercise. The disdain that the Government members are showing by flicking this off to a select committee for about a week shows that they don’t take the role of select committees seriously and that they don’t have regard, in fact, to the views of the public. They know they have the numbers to get this over the line and so it feels like their attitude is “Well, who cares, because we’re going to do this anyway.”

Now, that may or may not be their intention, but it is certainly the message that they are sending to members of the public. That does not instil confidence in the democratic process. If we look at other legislation that has passed—Arena Williams spoke about some of it. If we look at the protest on the parliamentary steps today about the disability bill, where that was done in a very quick way—we saw changes to Ministry of Social Development entitlements done under the House under urgency late at night. If it wasn’t for the forensic work of Opposition MPs, that may well not have had any level of scrutiny or any level of media highlight. That seems to be the point of this exercise.

If the Government wants to prove that that’s not the case, and if they have a good business case for sending this to committee to make this fundamental constitutional change, they should at least be confident in their business case or confident in the law they’re proposing and they should ventilate it and let it endure that scrutiny so that they can take the public with them.

I think we stand to lose a great deal in this House if they continue to show this level of disdain for lawmaking. We’ve had record numbers of sessions in urgency. We are becoming like a steam train when it comes to just pushing bills through. I had a meeting with a Minister today where the invitation at the meeting was if we could talk about bits where we could move faster through the committee stage. That is not the spirit of the parliamentary system that we should be encouraging and nor is it what we should be communicating to the members of the public who put us in this House.

Let’s not forget that. We are here, put into these positions by the people we serve. We are only here by their grace and only here by their trust and only here by their confidence. Every time we don’t follow process correctly or we show disdain for process, we are doing the middle finger to the public that put us here. No wonder they are losing faith in politics. No wonder young people are disengaging. It’s on all of us together to rebuild the confidence in the democratic process because that is a flawed process, but it is the best process that we have. When we go to do things that are going to reduce, using the words of section 338A, “the scrutiny to hold the executive to account, to contribute to good governance for improved outcomes”—every time we do that, we are losing the public’s trust and confidence.

I think that’s what this debate is really about. As I say, it’s not a trivial matter. We’re not wanting to put something to select committee that is an operational change. This is about a fundamental piece of constitutional law. Let us not forget the separation of powers. Let us not forget there is the Parliament, the judiciary, the executive, and, of course, the fourth estate, the media. There must be a balance of power of all of those. We have seen a diminishment, in my view, in this House through the waka-jumping law. We cannot afford to diminish it any further by treating select committee processes as a rubber-stamping exercise. We are in peril of falling into the type of democracies that have very low engagement across the world, including the US, which is in the 30 percent. In my electorate of Taieri, we enjoy something like an 89 percent turnout at election, but every year that is going down across the nation, and so there’s a lot at stake with this referral motion. It is not a simple matter. For that reason, I fully support the amendment by the Hon Dr Duncan Webb in the first instance and any of the amendments that push out the time to give people their say in the second.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DEBORAH RUSSELL (Labour)
content.text: Madam Speaker, thank you. I hadn’t intended to take another call, but I am going to take another call. I’m speaking at this time in support of Dr Xu-Nan’s amendment. Here is the reason that I am going to take this call. It’s because of an interjection from the Minister, who said, I think, something like he had offered perfectly good reasons for this shortened select committee process, but in the Minister’s speech, right the start of this referral debate, he said that we needed a four-week process because he wanted this business, this work done, this bill through the House on a timely basis.  There’s a hell of a lot of circularity in that argument. “We’re going to do it in a quick time because we want to do it in a quick time. We’re going to do it fast because we want to do it fast.”, is the essence of the Minister of Justice’s argument. I do submit that the Minister has, as yet, not offered a good reason as to why this particular piece of legislation should go through fast. I’m going to take his word that he wants it to go through fast because he wants it to go through fast, have a look at some of the dates that are sitting in the advice that has been given to him, and the process that has gone on until now.

It turns out that the work that the Minister wanted quickest kicked off in June last year. That’s the date of the first advice he got from officials on this, dated 4 June 2025, as to the ongoing process here. The process then was—and it’s set out in the Minister’s advice—that the officials would undertake some targeted consultation, they would brief him by 7 October, and some policy decisions were needed by 16 October. As it turned out, the officials got their briefing paper back to the Minister by, I think, 1 October—so they did very, very well—but I can’t tell when the Minister actually responded giving his policy decisions. It’s hard to know.

The point is that, in terms of this going to Cabinet, it didn’t get to Cabinet until March. That’s a real shame because they had been aiming, as far as I can tell, for this paper to get to Cabinet by mid-January or late January, maybe some ministerial consultation around there. This work that the Minister needs to get done so quickly, in the next four weeks, because he wants to get it done so quickly, because that’s his reason—he’s going fast because he wants to go fast—in fact, he was going quite slowly at one stage. Suddenly, now, the Minister, because he went slowly earlier this year, wants to go fast now because he wants to go fast now.

I just don’t think that’s a good enough reason. If there was genuine urgency behind this, the Minister would have been chasing this along all the way through, and we are now ending up with a shortened select committee process because the Minister was tardy in doing some of his work. Now, I appreciate that things get crowded in the Cabinet Office, that things get crowded in the Parliamentary Counsel Office, that there’s a whole lot of timing issues to consider, but I think the Minister needs to do rather better when asking the select committee to work fast because he has been tardy, to either be upfront about that or perhaps give us some better reasons as to why he wants the select committee to go fast on this.

In fact, there is no particular reason to go fast. The case that the Minister was concerned about was not due to be heard until April next year. There’s a bit of time in hand before that. There is no good reason to go this fast at this stage. We do not need to go this fast unless the Minister has some other reason for wanting this legislation to be through the House and finished before the election, but in that case, we still don’t need this reported back until, say, maybe the start of September. There’s a variety of dates that have been proposed, and the legislation could still get through the House were they to organise themselves properly.

The Minister wants to go fast because the Minister wants to go fast, the Minister wants to go fast because the Minister was tardy, and now there seems to be some other reason as to why we are going so lickety-split at this stage as to have this four-week process. I just invite the Minister to, I guess, fess up and give us some good reasons. As I’ve said, I’ve probably said all I’ve wanted to say in this debate. I probably won’t be participating in it again unless something particularly egregious is said. Madam Speaker, I do thank you for giving me this call, because I did want to make that challenge to the Minister.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Maureen Pugh)
content.text: Before I take another call, can I just remind members that, as with most debates, we’re looking for new material. The repetition of the need for speed is getting a bit tiresome, and also, the need for more time has been heard very well. I’m looking for new material.

content.speaker: ARENA WILLIAMS (Labour—Manurewa)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I move, That the motion be amended by adding the words “and the Justice Committee will open a briefing on the Climate Change (Tort Liability) Amendment Bill that will invite submissions for a period of six months” before the full stop.

The reason I make that amendment is it draws on a paper by the Rt Hon Geoffrey Palmer and his suggestion over the last six months, on reflection, following a lecture from the former Solicitor-General Una Jagose about the use of urgency and the way that we consider bills which proceed through urgency, and indeed, through the shortened select committee process. You heard my earlier submission on why we should extend the date, but failing that, it is my genuine suggestion to the Government and to the chair of the Justice Committee who is sitting here tonight. Congratulations on your appointment. I hope you take on this suggestion, which I hope will be given by the House as an instruction to you, but even if it is not given by the House as an instruction to you—

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Maureen Pugh)
content.text: No, the instruction to me.

content.speaker: ARENA WILLIAMS
content.text: Sorry, the instruction to the committee chair via the House.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Maureen Pugh)
content.text: Can I interrupt the member and remind her of Standing Order 129, which I read out before. A member who has spoken before on an amendment cannot move a new amendment.

content.speaker: ARENA WILLIAMS
content.text: Oh, I see. That would be my suggestion, now speaking to the original referral motion of the Minister. Given that that doesn’t need to be an amendment, I would simply say that, based on the Minister’s referral instructions, it comes to the House to consider what other practical measures the select committee chair might consider to enable some of the concerns of Opposition members to be properly heard.

My suggestion to the House is that it would be appropriate for the select committee to open a briefing that heard submitters for a period of six months, while also considering the bill that would be reported back in the shorter period. This is a suggestion that has been made by the Rt Hon Geoffrey Palmer in relation to bills that proceed through urgency—all stages—that another sort of bill would be introduced to a subject matter select committee instead of the Regulations Review Committee, so that even though it was presented back to the House in time for the executive to advance its legislative agenda, the select committee would still then be able to consider submissions, to be able to consider advice, and then to come to a reasoned view not only in its departmental report, advised on by the Minister’s advisers, but in its report to the House. As we know, often a select committee will come to a different view than the departmental report provided by the advisers. That is an appropriate part of the select committee process.

This novel method of opening an inquiry at the same time as hearing a bill would provide for that. It would also allow for a select committee to test what has been a suggestion by one of our preeminent scholars of our constitutional arrangements in New Zealand, the Rt Hon Sir Geoffrey Palmer, and whether this would work in an ongoing way, whether the House would be aided by select committees being able to review legislation in the normal way even when urgency is afforded. You can imagine that members on this side of the House would also be in a situation where, in Government, they might be able to use urgency for certain things—there are incentives for both major parties to be able to use it—but, in a new sort of arrangement where select committees could proceed at an ordinary pace, to be able to consider the submissions of submitters and also the advice from the department, you might then pick up things along the way, where a Minister can then consider those things. That is already the arrangement whereby these periodic checks by different parts of the legislature and the executive will check the legislation and will notify Ministers of changes they need to make.

Just today, we saw a Minister of primary industries in the chair in a committee stage, where he was presenting to the House a number of updates to primary industries legislation—23 pieces of legislation were being updated in that way. We already have a mechanism for Ministers to hear feedback, not only from the industries they are representing but also from the legal experts who come along and make these representations. This is the perfect way to make this a part of our ordinary constitutional framework whereby those things are formalised: people aren’t accessing the members of the executive via a back door or a fast track to access to a Minister but they are coming in through the front door, through a select committee process and making the representations to a select committee of nominally independent MPs from the executive who can consider those submissions separately.

That is an important part of the scrutiny process that New Zealand Parliament has. Many of us really enjoy that feature of the New Zealand Parliament, where someone can rock along to a select committee and make a suggestion and the law will reflect that. This is an appropriate way of building that into the system and still allowing an executive Government to, at times, require the House to move at pace and on its terms. There will always be a need for that in this system, and the tension here between speed and between proper scrutiny does not need to be arranged in the way that it is. We can have proper scrutiny of this bill, and we can have proper scrutiny of later bills. The process for a select committee to be able to do this can be enabled now via the inquiry or briefing process. Opening a briefing on a piece of legislation that is before a committee is well within its power. It does not need to be directed by the House to do so—although that is what the Minister should have included in his referral motion, and that is why I am making a speech on his original referral motion.

It is important that we consider here what the role of select committees is, because this Parliament has had some uniquely good select committees that have been great at grappling with, particularly, legislative detail. This is a Parliament where you can see, in the mix and the make-up of it, with minor parties being chairs of select committees and with engaged Opposition members being right in the detail of their portfolios, that we are capable of this and we always should arrange our select committees in a way where Ministers can look at a select committee and see a chair who they trust not only to scrutinise the legislation that they have before them but, also, to make changes to it.

This Government is one that has been in the habit of introducing legislation at the first reading before it is finished, and that is a process that our legislature is not designed for. If we want to continue to use it in that way, where legislation comes to the House at first reading in a way where the policy will be changed at the committee stage, then we have to have select committee chairs who can deal with that. We have to have a system that is robust enough to be able to hear from experts; for committee chairs to be able to seek guidance from the departments who are advising them, not the executive. That has to be clear, too, because a number of times in this Parliament, it has been unclear whether the department officials are advising the Minister or are taking instructions from the Minister, or are actually there to serve the committee, which is what the constitutional arrangement requires of them.

This is something that non-executive MPs must constantly defend, but this is a way which practically enables it. And so, I hope—it is my genuine hope—that the Justice Committee will open a briefing alongside this piece of legislation to be able to give the submitters their full due in terms of presenting their submissions on this issue. I don’t think it is an overlap; I think it is the appropriate thing to do in the circumstance. People are sophisticated enough to know that they are not only submitting on a bill but they also need to submit to a briefing that is a wider inquiry about the policy statements in the bill and what is written. That kind of process should be genuinely cross-partisan, because that is the only way that this will continue to work—that executive Government will be able to get away with using the legislative system in this way, where undeveloped policy positions come to the House in the form of legislation at the first reading and they are finished by the end.

We have seen, a number of times, that Ministers have amended things at the last minute. There are also changes that should be made by the Standing Orders review about that. Those should be fully debated with no time limitation on them, and that was reflected in the Speaker’s comments on Tuesday about that kind of debate. This is similar to that, where you have an unfinished policy statement that is introduced to the legislature by a Minister open to feedback and criticism, and so, we should give it the appropriate time at the select committee stage, as well as allowing a department and the other organisations within Government that want to contribute to it to be able to submit to the select committee through a briefing.

Local Government (System Improvements) Amendment Bill
Second Reading

content.speaker: ANDY FOSTER (NZ First)
content.text: Look, I’m delighted to get to this point of finally being able to speak on this bill, because it’s the third time I’ve actually been the next speaker up on this particular bill. It’s taken a long time to get to this point, but it’s great that we got here.

The Government’s got quite a number of initiatives in respect of local government going on at the moment. We’ve got this bill, we’ve got regional deals, we’ve got the rates cap proposal—which we’ve talked about, but no legislation yet—and then we’ve got all the structural reform announcements which have been made.

It’s interesting: I’ve spoken to probably most councils’ mayors, and often chief executives as well, over the term of this Government. Sometimes it’s the ones before the last local body election; sometimes it’s the ones after; sometimes both. I’ve never seen as much interest and as much enthusiasm as I have seen now, in terms of exploring amalgamation. So the Head Start announcement is potentially a good nudge. But I have talked to a lot of mayors also since the structural reform announcements a few weeks ago, and while there’s wide agreement about getting rid of regional councils, there is real concern about the time frame which is being announced there—real concern about those time frames—and also that feeling of: is this the last chance for councils to be able to put a Head Start proposal before some sort of backstop stick is applied?

There’s also concern about the place of community consultation, which is absent from those documents: the protection of local voice, the ability to be able to do the numbers, the effect on rates, debts, and so on. Those numbers really matter; they matter in terms of the choices that councils and communities should be able to make. There is this idea that every council must have a dance partner—the rural-urban split: most of the rural areas don’t particularly want to be taken over by their neighbouring urban areas—and the ability for bigger-population councils to, effectively, apparently take over small ones.

There’s also a lot of desire to see a greater clarity about the rationale, particularly around the idea—and I think there’s a lot of scepticism about this idea—that bigger will be better and bigger will be more efficient. That has also come from the likes of the New Zealand Initiative and the Infrastructure Commission. So my appeal in all of this is that central government needs to work much closer with local government, and in a respectful way, as we go through any reform proposal.

All of that said, this bill, and all of these other initiatives, have a big, clear focus on rates—on affordability. That is absolutely right and absolutely understandable. Across New Zealand, between 2022 and 2025, that triennium of councils, we saw and we paid unprecedented increases in rates across the country. I understand the cumulative average was something like 34.4 percent, which is absolutely unaffordable and unsustainable. Inflation during that time—admittedly, that was Consumers Price Index, not Local Government Cost Index—was 13.7; way, way, way above inflation.

Consequently, rates have become a very significant component of the inflation rate. It’s interesting: in the debate that was going on a few weeks ago on this particular reading, Labour and the Greens seemed to want to continue with that trajectory. That is unsustainable, and I suggest they think again about that.

In my 30 years in local government in Wellington, generally I saw people saying, “I want more and more services.”—more and more services. That’s really frustrating for a fiscal conservative like me. They never ask for water services, incidentally, but now what I’m hearing is that that’s changed. In some places, I’m hearing real fear that people will be forced out of their homes and will certainly have to make decisions about what basic services they, in their lives, and have to forgo to pay the rates and the water bills. So I reject completely the assertions which are made, particularly by the Green Party, that this bill is not thinking about people; it is.

The question I would ask local government is: has it shown the same discipline that Government has shown in terms of its expenditure—right-sizing and ensuring value for money? Some councils are much better at this than others. Often it’s the smaller ones who are better at doing it. So if we are going to make councils bigger, then I wonder whether some of that discipline of being close to community will be lost.

This bill’s encouragement to focus on core service intends to bring rates down. I understand that the intention is that a rates cap would also apply to core services. It is a point there that councils are really concerned about, because they’re concerned that there’s a real tension between rates capping and asset management, and I think that argument is a real one, and we need to think about that very, very carefully. Local government would often say they just need more money; I don’t accept that without seeing, first, a serious improvement in delivery efficiency and better prioritisation, because rates and water charges are unaffordable for property owners.

I would ask the question of what we can do as central government to reduce costs that local government faces, and therefore the rates bills—for example, the seismic costs, with the earthquake-prone building legislation which we will consider, hopefully, later today; traffic management costs; health and safety costs; audit costs; and representation reviews, which, hopefully, they won’t have to do if we’re going through these changes in terms of structure. So we should be looking very thoroughly at all the burdens central government places on local government.

So in terms of this bill, it focuses on core services and on performance. We made a few changes to the core services; I won’t go through that. Being a core service, of course, still leaves councils to decide on the quality and the quantity of those core services. The big question is about rates capping and the application of those rates caps to core assets and the maintenance of those assets. That’s a real concern for councils. We know that there’s been under-investment in infrastructure for a very long time. Applying rates caps in that way could make that even worse, so we’ve got to be very careful about that, because, of course, Government is in a glasshouse on this score as well.

I’m going to just touch on two final things now. One of them is that in this bill, we have the idea of the reappointment time frame for chief executives in councils. At the moment, it’s five years plus two years, so without going to the market, you can do five plus two. The proposal here is to go five plus five. It was originally going to be the same day that we were considering this bill—we did the Public Service Amendment Bill, and what we did there is we said that you cannot reappoint a Public Service chief executive without going to the market: so five years and no right of renewal. So we’re going in completely opposite directions with local government chief executives as we are with central government chief executives. So we will have an amendment on that when we get to the committee of the whole House. At least consistency would be a good thing, because we are being completely inconsistent.

The other issue, which I know there are amendments about—and they will come up in the committee of the whole House—is the issue of unelected members voting. That’s become a much, much bigger issue. I know that the ACT Party has put some amendments up there. We will also have an amendment along those lines about delegations from councils to committees. I think that we do need to make some changes in those areas.
We are supporting the bill, we think it could be improved, and we do have some questions about the wider reform programme and the coherence of that reform process. I commend the bill to the House.

content.speaker: Tamatha Paul
