content.speaker: CELIA WADE-BROWN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I rise to speak against this bill, the “Local Government”—so-called—“(System Improvements) Amendment Bill”. It claims to improve local government, but it strips away the purpose—[Interruption] Sorry, Mr Speaker, there seems to be more people having debates—

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: Yes, gentlemen down there, I can hear that conversation from here—it’s just a bit too loud.

content.speaker: CELIA WADE-BROWN
content.text: Thank you.

I really want to, first of all, thank all the mayors, not just the ones in this room, and the councillors and the Chairs and the staff for the huge amount of work that’s done by councils, often closely with their communities, iwi, volunteer groups, business groups, and so forth.

Mr Foster and I lived through local government before the four wellbeings were in the legislation—during then, and then when they were taken away again. Frankly, in practice, it made little difference. We did go through the most painful core services review, when we justified all the things that we were doing anyway. But it was very long-winded and it was open to challenge in the courts. So I think it’s quite contradictory, with one hand, to take away the four wellbeings, and, with the other hand, to leave the core competencies there.

I want to focus on two particular contradictions that I think this coalition Government is putting on local government. The first contradiction is in the area of economic development, particularly tourism. I think that all parties in this House think that sustainable tourism is a good way to earn a living, is an interesting way for people to learn about different places, to get out into the beautiful outdoors—before it’s all mined—and just learn about cultures. You’ve got the Pounamu Pathway on the West Coast, for example—fantastic.

content.speaker: Hon Mark Patterson
content.text: Provincial Growth Fund—thanks, Celia.

content.speaker: CELIA WADE-BROWN
content.text: That is also supported by iwi, and it is also supported by the councils. I think you’ll find that the museums are supported by the councils across the rohe.

Let’s take another example, then—Wellington: I expect some of the people here, from both sides of the House, will go to the World of WearableArt. They might enjoy Wellington On a Plate. But economic wellbeing has been removed from the purpose of councils. That’s not tidying up legislation; that’s setting up local government to fail.

The recent tourism strategy, which I actually think is a good tourism strategy, looks at what different. Whether it’s going to be local government or central government, or whether it’s Tourism New Zealand or the regional tourism organisations, it gives everyone a bit of a place to play together, but it’s completely in contradiction to the changes to the Local Government Act. Every tourism-reliant district is expected to plan infrastructure, manage visitor pressure, and market and promote their area, but you’ve just taken away the statutory basis for doing that.

The second contradiction is very close to my heart, and it is the removal of environmental wellbeing. We’ve just heard Minister Potaka putting the portion of the international visitor levy into Auckland’s predator-free area. That is led by Auckland. You’ve got unitary councils, regional councils, city councils—and the most recent speaker was a great proponent of Zealandia. But, oh no, we’re not going to have environmental wellbeing here. Well, how did the Otago Peninsula get rid of possums? It wasn’t central government; it was local government, and you are just cutting them off at the knees. There is a lot of talk about localism, but this bill does the opposite.

content.speaker: TIM COSTLEY (National—Ōtaki)
content.text: The National Party wants to see rates stop going up. We want to make them more affordable, and that’s why we’re refocusing the purpose of local government.

I just want to make one point: section 12 in the Act states—I’ve heard councils quote this—that “For the purposes of performing its role, a local authority has—(a) full capacity to carry on or undertake any activity or business, do any act”. That is true in the context of performing what their purpose is in section 12. This came up in the select committee, and it’s really important that we get this in the Hansard. They can perform any activity to the extent that it allows them to fulfil the purpose, which is good quality local infrastructure and public services, and regulatory functions that are cost-effective. We must make sure that hierarchy is understood and is captured in the Hansard, and, with that, I commend it on that point.

content.speaker: TANGI UTIKERE (Labour—Palmerston North)
content.text: Kia orana, Mr Speaker. Well, I find it fascinating that the member Tim Costley, who has just resumed his seat, is the National Party lead and the deputy chair of the Governance and Administration Committee—the very committee that considered the submissions and prepared the report for this bill—and the member did not take much time to explain the issues that has led to the bill coming back. It’s not as if he had a shortage of time—there was plenty of time left on the clock, as well—and so that is very disappointing.

This is a terrible bill. It is an absolutely terrible bill from a Government that spouts a lot about localism. We think about the election, when they campaigned with this sort of magic word known as “localism”, but they really don’t actually know what it is. They do not know what it is.

Before I delve in a little bit deeper, I do want to acknowledge all of those 536 submitters who took time to submit on this bill. Many of them were actually councils from around the country among the 35 organisations that were able to front up to the committee.

But this is an example of a Government bill that clearly indicates that Christopher Luxon continues to be out of touch. It’s been some time, actually, that this bill has been sort of languishing on the Order Paper. Perhaps he would have had a little bit of time to think about whether this was a good move or not. Clearly, he has not bothered to change his mind. This is nothing more than a power grab by this Government to have centralised control out of Wellington, and it is very much undermining local communities and local democracy all around this country.

I want to acknowledge that the local government sector at the moment are going through an interesting time. They are going through a period of reform that has not just all come at once but, cumulatively, there has been something after something after something that they have been expected to continue to have to deal with. But this bill, overall, really does represent a backward step for local democracy and a backward step for community wellbeing.

Local government, in terms of its purpose, will be refocused under this bill, which will remove the four wellbeings. Like our colleague Celia Wade-Brown, I too was around the council table prior to the introduction of these four wellbeings, and I can tell you that when they came into being, they made the decision making focused, and, actually, you were able to identify what was important for your community in those areas.

Let’s just be very clear about what it is that this Government seeks to change. They seek to remove the social wellbeing consideration. Those are things like housing opportunities, pools, recreational facilities, parks, libraries, social services, and community centres. They seek to remove the cultural element of wellbeing. What’s that about? Well, it’s about, again, libraries, museums, art galleries, iwi engagement, and engagement with other aspects of community life. They seek to remove the environmental component of wellbeing. What’s that about? Consents, regulatory regulation, waste minimisation, waste treatment—fundamentals for what it is, in terms of council land and council life. Then, finally, they seek to remove the economic wellbeing. Well, what’s that about? Economic development in terms of an agency and how that’s delivered, tourism opportunities, having good conferences come to your city, making money, and people spending in terms of retail opportunities as well.

This is a Government that is signalling that, actually, we don’t want councils to specifically, in legislation, focus on those four aspects of wellbeing. What they want is a completely narrow focus on infrastructure, which is important, and on the regulatory functions, which is also important. But what is not important to this Government is a broader view and an understanding that vibrancy, community connection, and democracy are important things that should be considered and be active around council tables all around this country.

They don’t seek to embrace vibrancy, they don’t seek to look towards the needs of being a resilient community, and they don’t seek to think about climate adaptation and all of those sorts of things. So it’s a very one-track mind when it comes to this Government.

I have to say that what’s really disturbing is that this is a bill that went through a select committee process. Once it’s gone through that process and the select committee has returned its report to the House, we now learn that the Government want to go further and they want to strip away the voting rights of committee members who have been appointed to committees around council tables. We are talking about individuals who, as a collective, represent iwi, Māori, young people, and rural communities, and one other thing that they haven’t quite actually latched on to is the many councils who appoint skilled-set individuals around audit and risk because they identified that that is a particular skill set that needs to be around the council table. But they have failed to address that.

Now, why is it that this Government has not actually put those considerations through the select committee process? Instead, they’ve come through the back door, once this committee has reported back to this House, and have failed to allow councils in the community to have a say on whether they think that is a good idea or not. That is absolutely disgraceful.

It’s disgraceful, and a sham when it comes to a Government wanting to support councils and the need for local democracy. If they knew that they were going to do this, why did they not put it into the package of items that was considered by the select committee and that members of the community were able to actually submit on? I know why they have neglected to do that: it’s because they knew—and they know, now—that they are on the wrong side of that particular ledger. They are on the wrong side of that particular ledger.

When it does come to the committee stage, it will be interesting to actually see what’s in that Amendment Paper. We heard from Mr Foster that he’s got his own ideas about what should and shouldn’t be in that Amendment Paper, and it’ll be interesting to see what actually comes through in terms of that particular process.

This is a bill that is a very clear message to communities and to local government as a sector that the Government actually don’t care about how you do business. They don’t care about the decisions that you make to reflect your communities. They forget the fact that they, like us, have been elected into public office by the community. You wouldn’t think it—you wouldn’t think it. So it’s very disappointing that the Government are heading down this particular pathway, as well.

A lot of the commentary seems to be around what in the Government’s mind are nice-to-haves, and, of course, roads and footpaths and waste management—all of these sorts of things are important. No one is suggesting otherwise.  But so too are community facilities, so are social services in our communities, so are libraries, so are museums, so are opportunities to strengthen community connection and local democracy and decision making. This is a Government that’s, basically, saying, “Well, we don’t really care about that sort of stuff.” They seem to be saying that the reason for all of this is cost-of-living pressures. Since when has this Government ever taken cost-of-living pressures seriously? When has this Government ever taken cost-of-living pressures seriously? Never, and they never will. They had a Budget, in recent memory, when they had an opportunity to do something about that, and they failed to do exactly that.

I want to touch on one other point, because it is important. The process is all important. One change in this bill is a change that will allow access to information by elected members. Look, I’m comfortable with that—we need to have elected members getting the information they need—but it is interesting that an anomaly has been identified by Dr Dean Knight. I know his name has already been mentioned in the House tonight. I understand that there are other Government parties that are aware of this. The change is that the governing body—i.e., the council—is able to now make decisions on access to information that’s held by the local authority. The problem with that is that, because the decision is being made by a council, there is no avenue for an elected member to go to the Ombudsman to challenge that information. It is a discrete issue, but it is an important one, and I do hope that the Minister and the Government have taken that on board, to initiate a change, because it will be important. If not, we’ll certainly make sure that, through the committee stage, we are able to do that.

To conclude, again, this is a very strong signal from the Government that they are not interested in local community. They’re not interested nor serious about local democracy. This is a bill that simply prioritises conformity and control on the part of the Government rather than actually looking at genuine improvements that would make a difference. The Government should be focused on strengthening local democracy, strengthening local voice, strengthening the opportunity for communities to be connected with their decision makers, and vice versa. Instead, what we constantly get from this coalition Government is a barrage of direction that is one that signals they’re not actually serious about local government. They want to make life harder for households as a result, rather than easier, and it’s on that fundamental basis that we oppose this bill. We will continue to do so beyond the second reading.

content.speaker: Hon Dr SHANE RETI (National—Whangārei)
content.text: This bill takes pragmatic steps to strengthen the performance, accountability, and fiscal discipline of local government. I want to acknowledge the work of the Governance and Administration Committee and commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: ARENA WILLIAMS (Labour—Manurewa)
content.text: Mr Speaker, ngā mihi o te wā Matariki ki a koe [greetings of the Matariki season to you]. How good is Matariki? So good! To everyone who’s enjoying Matariki around the country at the moment, and their councils, who are putting on a great Matariki in the town square, putting on a light show, these guys want to cut it. They want to cut pools, they want to cut parks, they want to cut libraries, they want to cut our community sectors, but they can’t even be honest in a bill like this. Instead, they want to take the nice part of the politics for them. They want to be tough and say we’re going to be rough on rates, but then they want the mayors, they want the councils, and they want the councillors out in their communities right now, defending the ruthless cuts they have had to make to meet their rates targets.

It is outrageous that, at the moment, around the country, councils are doing this great work. They are celebrating te ao Māori and the amazing tradition that we have in our Pacific voyaging nation, of Matariki, the heliacal rising of the stars of the Pleiades, and yet these guys won’t even be honest: that it makes them so uncomfortable that councils are doing this important community work that they will introduce a law to stop them from doing it. They won’t even be honest about that, because this is a law which messes with the Auckland Council, and that is something I cannot abide.

We hear all of the Wellington members on that side of the House get up and say, “Well, actually, we need to recognise the hierarchy here.” I really want every mayor in the country to know that this legislation is going to make them wear the community feedback about those public services that are important to their communities being cut. Not only that, we’re going to introduce an amendment at the committee stage that will make it even harder for their elected representatives to have a truly representative council table. Shame on this Government for not backing the elected members and their communities. They are National councillors, they are National mayors around the country, and this Government is so ideologically committed to centralisation that they will dump on their own people around the country to do it. Shame on them, and I hope they are dealt to at the ballot box at this election and at the local elections, for all of those councillors elected on a blue ticket who put up with this nonsense.

What are we really dealing with here? The Auckland super-city legislation is 16 years old. I know that because they have been talking about it in this House twice today. In 2009, the Minister, Rodney Hide, sat in that chair in a committee stage that lasted four days and he was defending more centralisation for Auckland. This Government continues that despite, at various times since then, seemingly opposing it. This is Wellington reorganising Auckland’s affairs under that Act once again—

content.speaker: Tamatha Paul
content.text: Kāpiti Coast.

content.speaker: ARENA WILLIAMS
content.text: Kāpiti Coast is doing it. He’s telling them what the hierarchy will be under him.

It’s a reorganisation which no Aucklander has asked for. No Aucklanders asked for this reorganisation that is ideological nonsense. It’s an onslaught of reorganisation, and as my colleague Tangi Utikere has said, it’s a power grab for centralised control. The National Government said they would do exactly the opposite when they sought election around the regions. They know this is unpopular, because they know this does not work. They should have learnt the lessons since 2010, when they reorganised Auckland and we had the bizarre situation where the Auckland mayor couldn’t even set his own parking fines. He had to come to Wellington and ask for that power. This is more of the same.

Has it been good for the Manukau City Council, which lost its assets and has had such an under-investment in its parks and playgrounds that $17 million would need to be invested in that region alone to bring it up to speed in, in terms of the west and the north? No. Has it worked for the west, which had to give up some of its environmental assets and lost its regional parks? No. Has it been good for the north, which had to contribute so many services and get on the same level as the other services in the Auckland Central area? No. It has not worked for Aucklanders, and this continues much of the same.

Unelected power is a problem in our democracy, but it is not found around the board table in the form of the audit and risk chair or the iwi Māori representatives who go to work and represent their communities; it is found in lobbyists and those people who have unrestricted access to this Government about this kind of ideological change that nobody asked for. That is the unelected power that this Government should be sorting out, but what are they doing? Dumping on Māori, dumping on the poor old accountant who is giving up his time to do this public sector appointment for less than he is worth. It is outrageous that this Government has picked that target.

This is a stupid bill that they should dump, let alone push it through an urgency at a time when no one is watching what they are doing. Well, I tell you what, the councillors who are elected under a blue banner know what you’re up to. The councillors who are elected under a red banner will take their places.

content.speaker: PAULO GARCIA (National—New Lynn)
content.text: Too many times around the country, councils have spent far more than people consider are things about core activity for local government. This bill establishes the new regulatory framework for water services delivery. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: Hon JAN TINETTI (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I am the current chair of the Governance and Administration Committee, and this is not a bill that has been there since I have been chair. I had to go back, thinking, “Well, that’s been quite some time now”, and I had one bill that I was overseeing when I came in as chair. I thought, “How long has this bill been sitting back on the Order Paper?”

I went back to have a look and to read the submissions and to read the departmental report. I see the departmental report came back to the committee in October 2025, which tells me that this has been sitting on the Order Paper for a heck of a long time. Suddenly, here we are in urgency, with some sort of rush that we need to see this bill go through, and I’m not really certain why. This bill is very detrimental for our local government. It is another hit that they are getting from central government, which is incredibly disappointing, and what I want to outline here, from what I can read from the departmental report and from the submissions that I’ve made, is that there’s a real sense that there’s a populist approach that’s being taken here, and an ideological approach, rather than one that’s based in reality and the evidence that local government are seeing on the ground.

I know that people have already mentioned this in their contributions, but I just wanted to make certain that the people who submitted were acknowledged for their submissions for this bill. You know, for bills that sit outside of some of those bills that we see, like Treaty principles bills that have hundreds of thousands of submissions, this isn’t too bad in the number of submissions that it garnered, considering that a lot of people don’t understand what the bill does.

There were 536 written submissions, and 35 of these submitters provided oral submissions between 8 and 15 October last year. As I said, they probably have even forgotten that they did that because they haven’t heard what’s actually happening with the bill. Four hundred and sixteen submissions were from individuals and 120 were from organisations; of those organisations, 40 were from local authorities. That was a little bit surprising to me because we’ve got more local authorities than that but it was good to get a reasonable percentage of those local authorities that were submitting.

I just want to mention this figure: out of those 536 submissions, 74.4 percent of those submitters did not support this bill. When I went through and had a look at the reasons for it, I could see the desire of local authorities and of individuals to build strong communities, and that they see that this bill will take that away from them being able to make those choices and decisions, to be able to build those strong communities that will lead to the empowerment of all of the demographics that sit within those communities.

We’ve already heard, here, from my colleagues, that this bill shrinks the focus and the role of local Government down to such things as pipes, roads, and rubbish, and then ignores the wider needs of the communities. I’m really concerned about that, as are many of the submitters that came through in the Governance and Administration Committee. When I read them, I started to think about localised context that I could see that would be at risk, from my own perspective. I’m thinking about communities such as our disability community in Tauranga, for example, who would be completely disenfranchised under this bill. I know that some of my colleagues on the other side of the House who are sitting here this evening—and we’ve had a discussion around this in a car ride that we actually we shared—disagree in many of these areas, but I think if you want to put your side, take your calls to have that side, but I want to put my side here too. As I say, we’ve already traversed this quite a lot.

The disability community in Tauranga have been well supported by our local council, even down to having their own committee that they can see what is right for them as the city and as a community and how they can be more empowered to participate freely within that community. They’ve been able to manage things like an amazing disabled changing area on the Mt Maunganui beach, which is paired with a wonderful mat that can get them down to the water very easily, that the council has supplied. That means that they can do everything that able-bodied people can do within that particular small part of our community. They can go and enjoy the beach, and it is an amazing beach that they can enjoy.

Going through the submitters at select committee, there was definitely a fear that that could be taken away under this narrowing of the focus of councils, in this bill. So we’re absolutely isolating really, really vital parts of our community and that is of concern. Why do they have that fear? Because they’ve seen it before; they’ve seen these four wellbeings go and come back and they know that when they’ve gone in the past, it has not been good for them. That came through loud and clear when I read those submissions that came through at select committee.
The other area, when I was reading this report, that I put my localised context in—and I do put my hand up here because I’ve got my husband involved in the Merivale Community Centre—

content.speaker: Sam Uffindell
content.text: He does a great job, too.

content.speaker: Hon JAN TINETTI
content.text: But I thought—thank you, from the other side; I’m very proud of the work that he does, too. I have seen in very recent times, as has my colleague on the other side of the House, a brand new centre that the council got in behind and funded for that community. Merivale is the lowest socio-economic demographic community within the Tauranga boundaries, in fact it’s the whole of the western bay; it is that lower socio-economic community. For 32 years, the community centre which is central to that community operated out of a not-fit-for-purpose State house, and the council could see the potential of what that community centre could do if they had a purpose-built facility, so they funded an absolutely brilliant new centre.

That centre opened in October last year—ironically, the same time that this departmental report came back to the Governance and Administration Committee. Since that time, that community centre has been able to offer support to their community that they haven’t been able to offer before. Because they’ve got a private consult rooms, they’ve been able to have different groups such as Oranga Tamariki, such as financial mentors, such as health doctors and free nurses come into the centre. They have seen more people come into that centre than what they have ever seen in the past. They have had more people and been able to support more people into jobs than what they have been able to do in the past. They have had more young people come through into their rangatahi and youth programmes than what they’ve ever had in the past, and they have been able to support the young people and their families, which they’ve never been able to do. They’ve always worked really hard to do that, but they’ve never been able to do it at the level that they’ve had now. That’s all because the council was able to make a localised choice and decision to support that community with this purpose-built facility.

Why I tell this story is that when I read this departmental report, it seems to me that narrowing the focus of the councils is not going to enable something like that to happen in the future, and that is of huge concern. That is what people who submitted on this bill, whether they were heard orally or not, were absolutely 100 percent concerned about. They know that those marginalised communities will be the most impacted from this piece of legislation. If that doesn’t concern everyone in this House, there is something wrong because we are here to make a difference in people’s lives, and that’s a positive difference that we are here.

Getting people into work, getting people the support that they need because there is a purpose-built facility is surely something that each and every one of us agree with. If councils can’t do that because of the choices that we have made—or you have made, I should say; the choices that the other side have brought in through their legislation—please put a lens to that and ask yourself if that is right, because in my opinion that is probably an unintended consequence that many on the other side of the House have not thought about.
We’ve got a chance to get it right; we’ve got a chance to get it right in the next few stages. Please think about that for all people in our community. Kia ora.

content.speaker: Hon MELISSA LEE (National)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. This Government is focused on fixing the basics and building the future, and what that actually means is that we want councils to get back to basics, focusing on essentials like water services, infrastructure, roading, and rubbish, so ratepayers can see real results for what they actually pay. I commend the bill.

content.speaker: SHANAN HALBERT (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Heck, what a bill that’s before us this evening. When I look at this, I can’t believe that in such a short time, within only 2½ years, the National Party, last election, was campaigning on localism—on localism—about ensuring that Auckland had its voice, and here we are with the bill in front of the House today, in second reading, where, once again, it is clearly Wellington telling Auckland how to suck eggs. It’s Wellington telling Auckland how to run their council.
Anyone that is a representative in Auckland is going to know that this is not going to go down well with Auckland Council or with Mayor Wayne Brown. I wonder—

content.speaker: Hon Paul Goldsmith
content.text: He’s not your friend.

content.speaker: SHANAN HALBERT
content.text: Yes, he is my friend. I wonder if anyone has spoken to him to tell him, actually, the impact of this bill on our council, our decision-making processes, and our communities. Where I live, in Northcote, there’s a bunch of questions that have been raised by my local board.

When you remove the four wellbeings, you start to remove the environmental focus that’s important for our community—organisations like Kaipātiki Project, like Pest Free Kaipātiki. Members over the other side need to answer what is going to happen to them when we look down the road and this Government says that you can only focus on roads and rubbish, council, because you’re “fixing the basics”. Well, whose measuring sticks are those basics? It’s not the measuring stick of our people in Auckland. It’s not the measuring stick of our communities. You ask anyone. They want great facilities for our kids to go to. They want wonderful sport and recreation facilities and pools. They want an environmental focus. They want spaces and places and recreational areas where you can go to as a family, but most of all where you can be a community.

When I hear this Government talk about more accountability, here it is again, Wellington telling Auckland how to suck eggs, how to do their business, what’s good for Auckland. It’s another example where this Government has broken promises. Remember this: they promised to fix the economy; they haven’t done that. They promised to provide respite with the cost of living, and things have got more expensive under their watch. They promised localism, and this bill doesn’t deliver that.

Of course, the big question mark that’s around at the moment is about representation—unelected representation on committees. What’s the motivation there, National Party—what’s the motivation there? Anyone that sits on a governing body knows about the importance of having key skills to make good decisions for your organisation—whether that’s cultural, whether that’s business skills, whether that’s accounting skills. That happens in any organisation.

content.speaker: Arena Williams
content.text: Why are you picking on the accountants?

content.speaker: SHANAN HALBERT
content.text: But let’s be clear: it’s not just about the accountants, is it? It’s not just about the accountants. This isn’t just about the ACT Party. This is about the National Party. This is about the National Party’s decisions of removing localism, taking it away, and ensuring that Māori have less of a voice around decision-making tables.

It’s important that every MP in the National Party that is based in Auckland, you’ve got a few groups to stand up to, to communicate your message to, over the coming months. By God, it’s going to be good on the hustings, because you’ll be going around there and you’ll have to explain yourselves why you’re giving up on our local pools. You’ll have to stand up to iwi, to urban Māori, and tell them and explain yourselves why you don’t want them around the committees and influencing and informing decisions. You’re going to have to do that, and I’m looking forward to that.
To this National Government and the ACT Party and their failure to deliver for our communities: bring it.
