Bill read a second time.
Crimes Amendment Bill
Legislative Statement

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice)
content.text: I present a legislative statement on the Crimes Amendment Bill.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
Second Reading

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice)
content.text: I move, That the Crimes Amendment Bill be now read a second time.

One of the core pledges of this Government when we came into office 2½ years ago was to restore law and order. That is the work of generations and is certainly the work of all New Zealanders—to fix the basics and build a future where people feel safe in their communities. That has been an unerring focus of this Government for the last 2½, years, and this bill, the Crimes Amendment Bill, is about putting victims at the heart of our justice system, and it strengthens consequences for crime. It builds on work that we’ve done bringing back real consequences for crime through changes to the Sentencing Act and three strikes, but it also moves its focus to dealing with matters around retail crime.

I want to thank the Justice Committee for its careful consideration of the bill—very hard-working committee—and extend my hand across the aisle to work and contributions on the other side. The committee received 233 submissions on the bill, and I want to thank all the submitters and the time that they put into it.

So what does it cover? Coward punch—what it does there is it recognises the horrendous nature of these so-called coward punches, where people come and attack somebody from behind, with no warning, to the head and can turn a life upside down. The bill targets perpetrators of these attacks by adding three coward punch offences to the mandatory sentencing framework of three strikes and maximum penalties for coward punches causing grievous bodily harm increasing to eight and 15 years depending on the intent. The coward punch manslaughter offence defines this category of violent offending and responds to the need for greater denunciation.

The Act will be another tool for police in their response to violent crime. While I’m sympathetic to calls for even tougher responses around, say, minimum sentences, that can’t be accommodated within the confines of this crimes bill, but it’s something that people can give consideration to over time.

Now, the committee also notes that the Government’s capping of sentence discounts is already increasing sentences for coward punch offenders and will make it more likely that fewer of such offenders would be eligible for home detention, for example. I’ll continue to monitor the impact of the recent sentencing reforms on penalties imposed for coward punch cases. I also intend to put an Amendment Paper to better address this issue at the committee stage.

The second area is around citizen’s arrest. There has been a lot of discussion around that matter. We are recognising that we’ve had provisions in place for a long time for things happening at night after 9 p.m., but during the day it’s been a different regime. We were concerned about instances, particularly in the retail crime sector, of people walking off with trolleys full of food, not paying, people seeing that, and undermining public confidence in law and order in our community. We wanted to make it clear that people, security workers for example, can grab hold of somebody and hang on to them, with very clear instructions that they need to immediately call the police and follow the instructions of the police.

There have been a lot of comments about this, and I just want to make the point, of course, that nobody is compelled to do anything. Everybody will make a judgment based on the circumstances of the time, and whether they think it’s safe to get involved or not. Businesses can decide whether they’ll have protocols around this, or not, but we heard a very strong call, particularly from small, family-owned dairies and retailers who wanted to have another tool available to them to deal with what continues to be a real problem in the retail crime sector.

Another one is shoplifting. This bill brings in an infringement regime for shoplifting. At the moment, if you steal a small amount of goods from a shop, the only option is to arrest that person and send them off to court. That’s quite a high threshold. Our concern was, well, the outcome of that is that a lot of people tend to, in practice, get away with it and face no real consequences. An infringement regime provides an opportunity for a police officer to bring an instant consequence such as a fine, such as a speeding ticket situation, so that there are immediate consequences. It doesn’t replace our theft offences, but it’s another tool for police to use.

Finally, our human trafficking offences are strengthened by this bill. As one submitter noted, these reforms are long overdue and warmly welcome. They’ll help close loopholes and better equip law enforcement to hold traffickers accountable, and that’s what we’re prepared to do there. As a result of consultation with agencies, I intend to take a step further with an Amendment Paper which will remove requirements around the Attorney-General’s consent for cross-border trafficking offences.

Finally, the bill brings in tougher consequences for people who attack first responders, those Kiwis who go racing into danger—our prison officers, constables, ambulance staff, firefighters—and with intent-to-injure offences added to the mandatory sentencing framework for three strikes. All of these, collectively, bring a continuation of this Government’s effort to restore real consequences for crime and to push back against the tide of retail crime that we saw when we came into power 2½ years ago. We’ve made great progress as a country. People do feel safer in this country, but we’re very conscious that there is much, much more to do, and this legislation will continue that effort.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: The question is that the motion be agreed to.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s good to be able to speak on this bill. I have to say, there are many good intents in this bill, but the way it has been put forward for this Parliament has been extremely disorganised and frustrating. The Minister of Justice just stated that he was grateful for the help of the Justice Committee, and I do want to commend the select committee. We did work hard on this bill, and prior to my arrival on it too.

This is a law, but I have to say, there is no order in it. I have criticised the Government for a lack of evidence in their approach to criminal legislation, or justice legislation, and I have to say, in this instance, I would settle for some analysis, because a lot of the provisions in here, unfortunately, won’t deliver for victims and may actually make the situation worse. It does cover a lot. I’ll try and make sure that I go over everything, but we do have a bit of a timeline here.

First of all, we had this proposal—this covers a lot of different amendments, and it is an amendment to the Crimes Act. Well, that is our first flag that something is not going quite right, because we have the police providing advice, before this was introduced by the Minister, saying that they didn’t think there was a need for the coward punch offence. That’s not to take anything away from the families and the victims of coward punches. We know that a lot of the reason this law has come to the House is through the advocacy of families in tragic situations where unspeakable and inexcusable crimes have been committed against people who have, in many instances, lost their lives. There are two offences in this bill—one around manslaughter and one around grievous bodily harm—that relate to coward punches. Sadly, the flags were there that this, potentially, as a solution, as a way of addressing some of the tragic instances that had occurred, may not be the best vehicle for addressing that.

We also had Crown Law noting that serious offending in relation to wounding with intent is already dealt with, in relation to assault on first responders. We have two very august organisations—Crown Law and the Police—raising concerns before this was even taken to Cabinet. Then we had the introduction, and in good faith, we supported the bill to select committee to see if we could work through some of the issues there, even though there were a lot of things that we were very concerned about. We did have, immediately after the introduction, an amendment sought straight away, and that was because the amendment that the Minister wanted was actually under the Summary Offences Act and not under the Crimes Act, and was therefore not within the scope of the original bill. There’s some serious disorganisation here in the Minister’s office that, unfortunately, has led to a number of issues not being dealt with in a way that would have led to the smooth running of this particular bill.

Then we have a number of issues that are raised in the bill. I want to make sure that I mention the trafficking offences, because this is something that we are very supportive of. In fact, the wording in the legislation is very similar to a member’s bill I had in my own name in the ballot. I support it. I think that they’re overdue, and I know a colleague from the National Party, Greg Fleming, had a member’s bill in his name and this was adopted as a Government bill. I am extremely supportive of these trafficking offences. The Labour Party is supportive of this. We’ve taken other measures through the joint Modern Slavery Bill to show how committed we are to updating our law in relation to modern slavery. On their own, that would be something that we would support wholeheartedly. These changes are overdue, and we commend the Government for bringing this aspect of the Crimes Amendment Bill to the House. However, it has been, sadly, through disorganisation, overshadowed by some of these other aspects of this bill, which have been brought to the House.

This does cover a lot of different issues. We’ve got the citizen’s arrest. Now, this was due to, as the Minister said, people in small businesses like dairies wanting to have citizen’s arrest power. Sadly, during the select committee process, we heard a number of businesses not very supportive of this because of the conflict that it may have with the Health and Safety at Work Act. Although these are meant to allay some of the community’s concerns, some of the very businesses that this particular provision was targeted at were not happy with those provisions. I think there are potentially issues that will arise. Obviously, we already have citizen’s arrest provisions which are in place, and this bill looked to strengthen them.

We’ve mentioned the coward punch offences. This was extremely problematic for the committee. We are worried, and we did receive advice, as we have noted in our publicly available report, that it may be that fewer offenders who have committed a coward punch are actually convicted of that offence under these new provisions. This is what I mean when I say that of course victims should be the central concern of Parliament’s attention when we look to change the Crimes Act, but, in this instance, we have a provision which, on the advice of many submitters and officials, looks to mean that there may potentially be fewer successful convictions for this type of offence. I know that’s not the intent of the Government, but, sadly, that is the advice we received, so we can only reflect what has actually happened in this instance.

We also had quite a bit of advice around first responders. Now, of course, I think there would be a general understanding that if people are injured in their job as a first responder, if they are targeted because they are being a first responder—if people are at work and they’re injured as a result of being at work, I have sympathy for the fact that the people who commit that offence against those workers should be held to account. We did have a bit of a discussion about, could we extend that? Could it be people in the course of their duty? Could it be anyone who was helping someone else in the course of their work? But that was not accepted and we weren’t able to broaden that out, so that offence sits there as an additional offence—whether that’s necessary or not, or whether it could have been worked up to be the slightly more fulsome offence, we were not able to get agreement around that.

Then we look at the theft offences. Now, this is something that looks to be a simple change but actually has some quite extreme consequences for the country. Just before I talk about that, on the coward punch, we are expecting—and it was foreshadowed by the Minister—further amendments on that particular provision to be brought to the House at committee stage. This goes back to my original point that the Minister either has not thought through how the law is going to work or hasn’t taken advice on how this law should work in a way that is actually going to achieve its objectives.

This is not us saying that we are opposed, in any ideological sense, to taking law and order seriously or having people held to account for their crimes. It’s actually a more fundamental thing with this law, in that it actually hasn’t been drafted in a way that works to meet its objectives. That’s partly because some of the offences should have been in the Summary Offences Act. If they were, then maybe we could have more of a pure debate on the relevance and whether those particular offences were something that we either agreed with or didn’t agree with. But as we have it, what we have is actually a mess. The work hasn’t been done. It had been brought to the House last year and it still has not been able to be fixed, because of these fundamental issues with the bill.

We’re expecting a new amendment; that is regretful. I think we’re all working hard and we’ve said in good faith that we will put up amendments to try and fix aspects of this bill. I don’t want colleagues on the other side to think that we are washing our hands of this. We want the best law possible for New Zealand. Unfortunately, this law is a total mess, and we will put up amendments on that.

I do want to just say: the theft offences have changed the fines, but one of the things that have changed is that—basically, for stealing anything, you can go to prison for a year. The result of that is the number of female prisoners is expected to surge by 63 percent in the next decade. That is a huge change as a result of what appears to be quite a minor change in this bill. It’s very disappointing to see this, because these are not violent offences. We know what the effect of incarceration, especially of mothers, has on families, and we don’t have the prisons to support these people.
We can’t support this bill at this stage because it’s a total mess and it will make things worse for victims and New Zealand.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. The Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand will not be supporting the Crimes Amendment Bill. We didn’t support it through first reading and, after select committee, we’re even more convinced that it’s a terribly—well, most of this—it’s a terribly-drafted piece of legislation. There are obviously some parts of this bill, as the previous speaker has alluded to, that we could have supported in isolation: the exploitation offences, for example, in particular, is an area that is much needed, in terms of what we heard from the feedback from submitters. I want to start by discussing that before I move on to some of the more problematic aspects of this bill.

I think, when we’re looking at exploitation offences, what we’re not seeing as a part of this bill is the fact that there are no additional protections. You know, we talk about victims and the rights and the protection of victims, but this bill itself—and I haven’t seen any other bill that’s been introduced that will discuss what are some of these better protections for victims. Some of the things have been called for by submitters were non-punishment for crimes committed as a result of being trafficked; protection visas; resourcing to access legal and specialist trafficking services and rehabilitation programmes; a national strategy plan—one that is resourced—to allow for the underlying drivers of vulnerability to trafficking, such as poverty, housing security, family violence, and lack of access to education opportunities, which led to some of these dependencies we see in migration. That is one area that we, in isolation, could have supported.

I want to discuss some of the other areas, and I’ll start by the citizen’s arrests. Now, this is an incredibly controversial aspect. This bill not only extends the scope of citizen’s arrests, I believe, in section 35 of the Crimes Act, but, more importantly, it applies now to every single crime under the Crimes Act. They have also—despite, even, the advice from the ministerial advisory group—not included an age limit for that. So, yes, there is a chance where people, in the heat of the moment—I think in the heat of the moment is the best time for them to have rational judgments when it comes to citizen’s arrests. So what we’re going to be seeing is kids who are going to be handcuffed, because you can use mechanical restraint as a part of that.

That’s not all of the crimes under the Crimes Act. You know what is a crime under the Crimes Act? Common assault. You bump into someone without consent—bam! You could be citizen arrested. You witness an employer stealing from you—bam! You can be citizen arrested.

content.speaker: Hon James Meager
content.text: That’s not common assault. You need intention.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
content.text: No—if you read the bill, the Hon James Meager, you will know that all of those are now captured under this bill, because there is now no longer a limit when it comes to certain offences or even a year threshold, because common offences—which, by the way, is section 196 of the Crimes Act, I believe—is considered under a citizen’s arrest.

content.speaker: Hon James Meager
content.text: Absolutely, bumping into someone is not common assault. It requires mens rea.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
content.text: Well, you know what? In the heat of the moment, you can rationalise that with a person who is going to be arresting that member for conducting a common assault.

What is more egregious about the citizen’s arrests is the fact that literally everyone, except for the Minister’s precious Ministerial Advisory Group for Victims of Retail Crime—a group of people that, by the end of it, was basically left with two, who had no experience in criminal law, no experience when it comes to understanding the complexity of the criminal system. In their report, they themselves said that “One of our weaknesses is having no legal expertise to make a decision on this element.”—despite the opposition from former members of that ministerial advisory group from Retail New Zealand, from Business New Zealand, and even from the Police, who submitted and said that this is not going to be good for people.

Like the previous speaker said, we already have citizen’s arrests, and one of the biggest challenges we’re seeing now with people who conduct citizen’s arrests is that, after a certain period of time, if the police don’t arrive, they have to let them go, so you enter this awkward situation that you have just escalated a situation, arrested someone, and the police, for whatever reason, couldn’t turn up and you have to let them go. We’re now going to be seeing more of that, which is where the previous speaker said that there are then serious concerns from a health-and-safety perspective, because—whether you like it or not—under the new bill, even these would potentially be considered critical risks to the employees of that retail store. ACC—we’re going to be seeing more payouts as a result of that. These are the things that this bill has not thought through.

I want to move on, now, to the one-punch attack, coward punch, or strike to the head and neck. This is a complex section and I am disappointed that the Justice Committee said “We agreed to take this part out because we’ve heard from officials that our culpable homicide regime is delicately balanced and the way that we have put this in this bill is not going to work. So we said that we are going to take it out.” Then at the eleventh hour they put it back in. That meant that the Opposition, the rest of us have to go and essentially redraft our differing view because that’s how late it was; go back and redraft our differing view to highlight our concern with this reinsertion of the one-punch attack, because it wasn’t appropriate to put it under the Crimes Act.

Now we hear from the Minister that there is going to be a new amendment coming through in the committee stage. I would like to remind that Minister of the guidance given by the Speaker, which is: if you now know that it’s going to be available, release it now and make sure it’s available; don’t release it two hours before the committee stage. That’s more something for the Minister himself to consider in terms of that particular amendment bill.

The other things that we wanted to hear is, yes, this absolutely is a concern. We have heard from victims and we have heard from their families and we absolutely acknowledge the pain and suffering that people have to go through as a result of this. But what we are not seeing, for example, is how this is going to work with existing legislation. We know that there is no opportunity, for example, for the reinstatement of the three strikes legislation to see how that is going to work with this particular bill, being one example of that. Like the previous speaker has said, this—and the unworkability around this—has meant that there are going to be issues within the criminal system when it comes to how they are going to be able to process or work through this unwieldy piece of legislation. It’s going to create additional confusion for the jury, which could potentially even lead to acquittal.

The next thing I want to touch on, and the final bit I want to touch on for this particular reading, is the second part of retail crime, which is a very unorthodox way of introducing another part that doesn’t have a purpose to this bill—the Amendment Paper 436—and they expect the Governance and Administration Committee to include it as a part of this particular bill. Again, as the Minister himself has said, could have been introduced as a separate bill, yet they’re trying to add it in here.

Overall, there are very few parts of this bill that are going to work in action. The Green Party reinstates that if we are going to address the issue of crime, we must address the drivers of crime, whereas this Government cares about the victims but will only care when there’s a victim in the first place. Well, here is our revolutionary idea: how about if we ensure we have a system where there are no victims in the first place? The way that we can address that is by providing the very basics that are the fundamental right of every single person here in Aotearoa New Zealand. We are going to be seeing a reduction of crime if we provide sufficient housing, not in the case of the move on order the Government is introducing. We can have reduction in crime if you have better mental health services, better education as opposed to disengagement of the youth. So the Green Party will not support this bill.

content.speaker: TODD STEPHENSON (ACT)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Look, it gives me great pleasure to rise on behalf of ACT and speak on the Crimes Amendment Bill. In ACT, we really want to make sure that we can unlock New Zealand’s potential—

content.speaker: Hon Member
content.text: It doesn’t mean you have to lock everyone up.

content.speaker: TODD STEPHENSON
content.text: —but that is very difficult if your business is being attacked by a criminal. It’s very difficult if you don’t feel safe to walk down your own street, and so ACT, as part of this Government, continues to be focused on law and order. I want to say to the Green member: we’ve actually made great advances in reducing victims of crime over the time of our Government.

This bill does a number of things, and I’m not going traverse them all, but it does actually increase a new theft around offence, and we heard about that; it’s particularly when you’re doing something that’s threatening. We’ve got the important changes around the penalties around slavery and dealing with human trafficking, and there’s new offences around theft, the ticketing regime, so again—and now raising the monetary thresholds. Again, a lot of this is to do with dealing with retail crime, which is a huge problem.

There’s a couple of other important things in here. One is the new assault offences for first responders, so those people in our community—ambulance officers, fire personnel who are actually just going about their job, trying to do their job, either putting out a fire, picking up someone who’s been injured, and making sure they’re looked after. The other new offence in here is this one of a coward punch. There’s been a little bit of commentary on this tonight, and this was actually an offence, along with the first responders, that was part of the New Zealand First and National coalition agreement. The Justice Committee did spend a lot of time looking at this and it did become obvious that the coward punch, which is a horrendous crime and actually deserves its own offence and a proper penalty to go with it, was something that we actually wanted to do something about.

Unfortunately, yes, we probably needed to do it not just in the Crimes Act but in the Sentencing Act. That became apparent that we could just be creating an offence without any real teeth. Now I’m not one to be deterred, so I looked at a way of dealing with that; I put forward an amendment to the Justice Committee which would ensure there was an eight-year minimum sentence for a conviction of a coward punch. ACT will be tabling that again when we get to the committee of the whole House, because it is important. Just because it wasn’t in our coalition agreement doesn’t mean that we can’t improve this bill and make sure that we are actually delivering the sentences that community wants.

That’s what ACT is committed to: making sure the sentences for criminal acts actually reflect what the community wants. We’ll not only be supporting this bill, we will be working with our coalition partners to improve it as much as we possibly can. I commend it to the House.

content.speaker: Hon CASEY COSTELLO (Associate Minister of Police)
content.text: Mr Speaker, with your indulgence, I’d like to just take a moment of my time to recognise the 40th commemoration of the sinking of the Lady Elizabeth II on 2 of July 1986, which saw the loss of two serving police officers, Constable Glenn Hughes and Senior Sergeant Phil Ward, and recognised the incredible bravery of the pilot Peter Button, who along with his son, saved the two other police officers. I just thought it was worth mentioning in the House. Thank you, Mr Speaker.

I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to speak on the Crimes Amendment Bill and would note, first of all, that New Zealand First will be invoking the agree to disagree on this piece of legislation. The Crimes Amendment Bill encompasses a few pieces of work and is important to the delivery of the National and New Zealand First coalition agreement, significantly in terms of the coward punch culpability and the first responders’ protection. New Zealand First has long advocated for the coward punch legislation. We have been lobbying for this for quite some time and it is the reason that we included it in our coalition agreement.

We note that every effort has been made to make that an effective piece of legislation, but only creating a new offence technically meets the coalition agreement commitment, but it is at strong risk of creating an offence that is, effectively, window dressing. We know there is significant concern about the sentencing of coward punch assaults and deaths. Without minimum mandatory sentencing, we are not changing the dial. New Zealand First’s differing position has been outlined in the select committee report and we will make amendments in the committee stage of the House. We acknowledge ACT’s efforts in this space also.

Similarly, New Zealand First’s commitment to protecting first responders, as included in the coalition agreement, specifically talked about including mandatory sentences. . The current legislation does not meet this agreement. We fully appreciate the complexity and the impact of minimum mandatory sentences, but we acknowledge that it is not without precedent in New Zealand law and believe we can do better.

It is the position of New Zealand First that being tough on crime means drawing a clear line in the sand about what we as a society will tolerate and where greater protection is essential. Allowing those who attack individuals without any ability to defend themselves, causing grievous bodily harm and often death, the protection of being able to say that it was just one punch—which means that there is lighter sentencing or less seriousness applied—is unacceptable.

The risk that someone dies from a single punch and then you have the ability to claim a degree of innocence in your assault because it was just one punch is just unacceptable, and we have to send a stronger message. The reality is that the coward punch is a planned, intended assault on someone who is attacked in a way that removes the victim’s ability to defend themselves. Our laws should respond appropriately.

Similarly, anyone who attacks a first responder—the people that we send in front of us when others step back deserve protection. Anyone who crosses the line and attacks a first responder should know the seriousness of the minimum mandatory sentence that will be applied for that assault.

We in this House should be providing the assurance to our front line that we know what we expect of them, and they should expect more of us. For this reason, we will be invoking the agree to disagree provision. But I would highlight that that is not the only clause of the bill and, as has been spoken to, there are a number of clauses and conditions within this legislation, some which we support strongly. The changes around the sentencing and the conditions around the exploitation and trafficking offences are important, and we acknowledge that. The removal of the Attorney-General as a decision maker is also critically important. We need to be bringing more trafficking convictions and prosecutions, and this will make the pathway simpler.

But we do, with caution, acknowledge the increasing powers of arrest capable for citizens. Our concern is reflecting on the fact that the clear message that we are sending is that you can arrest. As New Zealand First is a strong advocate for protecting our front-line workers, the hard-working Kiwi battlers that are working in our businesses, we want to be assured that there will be no compulsion or obligation on anyone to act and invoke a power of arrest. We also are cautious about the level of responsibility that has been placed on police officers to, over the phone, give direction or make conditions, and how they will be compelled to respond in the response to someone who’s been arrested. We believe that this can be operationalised and there will be work done to make that happen, but we are cautious of the impacts of this and how it impacts our front-line workers and our retailers and our employees that are working in businesses.

In summary, this is a complex piece of legislation, as has been outlined. We do support and we will support the bill through to the committee stage, but we are cautious about the impacts and we are critical of the final conclusions that have been reached around the first responder protections and the coward punch legislation. Thank you, Mr Speaker.

content.speaker: TAMATHA PAUL (Green—Wellington Central)
content.text: Well, I’ve only got five minutes, and there’s a lot in this bill. I think the overarching criticism that we have of this bill which means that we can’t support it is that it just—if making something a crime stopped it from happening, we wouldn’t have the levels of abuse and violence, family violence, and sexual violence that we have in this country. Whenever there is a bill that introduces a new offence or a new type of crime or that increases the penalties for certain types of crimes, the way that we assess that is—there’s multiple measures, but one of them is to ask whether this is identifying a genuine gap in legislation that doesn’t already exist. An example of that is that we, obviously, supported the stalking law because that was a really big gap in the law which meant that lots of people were not able to get justice and were not able to have any action being taken by police or by the courts.

The problem that we have with this bill is that there are—to give credit where credit is due, there are parts of this that we do support. There are acts set out in this bill that we fully support being recognised and identified, because they represent a gap within legislation. However, there are also some really concerning parts of this bill, as well, and we think that it’s a disservice to those victims and those communities who have been impacted by some of these types of crimes to designate it as a crime, but to not go any further to address the root causes of those crimes.

I think one of the biggest examples in this bill is that it increases penalties around shoplifting. As my colleague Camilla Belich raised, the amount of women that we see cycling through courts and the corrections system, with their most serious offence being shoplifting, is just such a waste. I’ve spoken to these women before, and I can assure you that for many of these women, it’s not because there’s a thrill in stealing and it’s not because they want to hurt anybody; it’s because they’re starving. They’ve got no money, they can’t feed themselves, and they can’t feed their kids, and nobody in this room understands how it feels to be so hungry that you have to resort to something like that. I promise you that locking somebody up for that, and these small amounts that we’re talking about, is not going to solve any of their issues. In fact, it’s going to create a life cycle of going in and out of the justice system and costing the State so much more than it will ever cost any of those retailers for the things that are stolen.

One thing that I really wanted to highlight is the citizen’s arrest bill. The fact that there are no age limits and that this could impact children reminds me of Bruce Emery, who murdered a kid, Pihema Cameron, who was tagging on his fence, and that is the consequence of people taking matters into their own hands. Let’s all admit that we don’t have the skills—very few people have the skills—to de-escalate a situation, but particularly if it involves children, and I think about some of the youth crime waves that we’ve seen, noting that youth crime is at a low—

content.speaker: Hon Dr Duncan Webb
content.text: Point of order, Mr Speaker. Oh, no—sorry. Well, I’ll explain myself. It appeared that there wasn’t a Minister in the House, but it turns out that James Meager was scratching his shoe.

content.speaker: TAMATHA PAUL
content.text: Anyway, where was I? Can I get an extra minute for that interruption?

I think about the fact that this young man, this 15-year-old kid, lost his life because someone took matters and justice into their own hands when someone was breaking the law, and somebody lost their life because of that. That is something that we need to reflect on. I think it’s a pretty big red flag if the police themselves—the people who are meant to respond to these citizen’s arrests—don’t support the bill. But it’s also concerning when the advisory group that made these recommendations had all but dissolved by the end of it, and then we’re taking the word of Sunny Kaushal. I’m trying to understand why this Government is so intent on listening to this guy when he has no legal experience. He doesn’t understand the criminal justice system. He’s—

content.speaker: Hon Priyanca Radhakrishnan
content.text: Paying him to shut him up.

content.speaker: TAMATHA PAUL
content.text: Yeah, exactly. He’s come and spoken to us at the Justice Committee and what was so evident to me was that this was a guy that does not understand what he’s talking about, and he has this massive political influence and it will impact lives. When people are assaulted, whether that’s the shopkeeper enforcing the citizen’s arrest or the person that is shoplifting, this Government will have to answer to those consequences and to any harm that is created by such irresponsible lawmaking.

content.speaker: TOM RUTHERFORD (National—Bay of Plenty)
content.text: We are a Government focused on fixing the basics and building the future, and in this space, we are prioritising greater justice for victims and stronger consequences for offenders. As a former volunteer firefighter myself, we were the ones running towards danger, day in, day out. My brother Ben, who is a police officer in this country, puts on his uniform to protect the country, and what we can do as legislators is protect them to do their job every single day. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB (Labour—Christchurch Central)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. This bill is a hotchpotch. It’s got one good section, or a couple of good sections, around modern slavery and under-cover police officers, which are good improvements, but you can’t wrap this in a couple of good sections, because the rest of it is hopelessly bad.

If we start with citizen’s arrest—nobody wants this. The only person who wanted this was the scone-eating ministerial group into retail crime, who were a total waste of money and came up with all of these crazy ideas, including allowing dairy owners to use mechanical restraints to arrest shoplifters. Now, the police are well aware of the fact that you have to be carefully trained to detain someone and that if you’re going to detain someone, you have to know what to do next. If you detain someone and it turns out you’ve done it wrong, they’re going to be a little upset, but you’re going to have to let them go. Even if they were shoplifting and the police say, “Look, we’re a bit busy with a much more serious crime. We can’t attend. You’re going to have to release them.”, what happens at that point is very complicated and actually quite dangerous.

We certainly don’t want people in retail situations to have some kind of expectation that they will be not just security guards but police officers and arrest and detain people who they find shoplifting, because it’s not their job and it’s not safe. The retail association, the police know that, the supermarkets know that, so it’s no surprise that the overwhelming majority of submissions said, “That’s a bad idea.”

Then we come to this creation of a new offence, the strike to the head or neck. It’s really problematic, and, in fact, it’s ironic, and I’m not sure if I regret it or not, but here we had an offence that was so unworkable, and, in fact, would, in its original form, have had the effect of more acquittals—more people getting off scot-free. What the original proposal was was this: you had the coward punch offence, a surprise attack to the head or neck. The irony is this: if someone walks past someone at a bus stop and pushes them in the chest and they fall over and crack their head and die, that’s not a coward punch, but if they slap them in the face and they fall over and crack their head and die, that is a coward punch.

Look, let’s be clear: when people engage in violent behaviour, this side of the House agrees that the law should come down on them. There should be an appropriate response which does all of those things that the criminal law should: denounce, punish, deter—all of those kinds of things. But here we had the perverse situation where this was going to be very hard to prove. You had to prove that the blow was unexpected. If two people are in an argument, at what point does a blow become unexpected? If one person pokes someone in the chest, and the other person punches them in the face, is that unexpected? I don’t know, but a jury would have to answer that question, and chances are that they’d say, in many cases, no, it’s not unexpected; that is a predictable outcome of an argument of that nature. Here’s the really perverse thing: as drafted, that would have meant an acquittal, and they would get off scot-free.

If you charge someone with manslaughter, all you have to prove is a base level of negligence and a death, and once you prove those two things, you get a conviction, and the rest of the argument is about how serious it is. That’s the law as it stands today and prior to this coward punch coming into force. You could look at the full range of offending, from an unprovoked attack to a stupid but accidental death, and that also would be a manslaughter. Under the coward punch law, people who were acquitted would walk scot-free and be unpunished for killing someone if you couldn’t prove all the elements of the offence.

That’s why, against perhaps my better judgment, in select committee, I pressed for an amendment which included an alternative charge, which is new section 171B. Now, that should be a Criminal Procedure Act question, but we had to kind of shoehorn it in here, which allows an alternative verdict of manslaughter. But, I mean, it’s silly, because the truly stupid thing about this offence is that the penalty for coward punch is the penalty for manslaughter. It is exactly the same, but harder to prove. It’s a truly stupid—there’s no other way to put it—stupid, complicating, unnecessary piece of legislation.

Then we have the theft—that’s a very serious offence, but turning towards something which might seem less serious is the theft provisions. I want to talk about the infringement offences of theft. Theft, in section 219 of the Crimes Act, is really clearly defined. It has three basic elements: take property, dishonestly, with the intent of permanently depriving someone. That’s, basically, the three elements in theft.

This new offence, removing property from retail premises without payment, is really specific. You’ve got this retail premise element, but then all you have to do is take property. There is nothing else. There’s no mental element required. What is more, you are presumed to have committed this infringement offence. You have to raise a defence. You have to show that, in fact, you had a reason to take this property.

This is really problematic, because you realise how this—what this is aimed at is things like large stores using facial identification, and they might recognise you and identify you, perhaps even wrongly. How are you notified that this charge is laid? By an email. Now, I don’t know if you’ll check your emails or if summaryoffences.govt.nz is in your spam folder, but that’s how you’re notified, and then you’ll get a conviction for this infringement offence. It’s a reversal of the onus of proof, and the procedural safeguards around it are fundamentally non-existent. It’s a really problematic piece of legislation. Essentially, that theft infringement offence has a presumption of guilt and a procedure which is serviced by email, and then if you don’t turn up to court, a conviction, essentially, is entered against your name for that offence.

Then we had the first responders provisions, which are neither here nor there. Assaults against first responders are serious. We already recognise in sentencing that assaults against first responders are serious, and that’s entirely appropriate. But the interesting thing was that there was real difficulty in the committee—and this went across all parties, I think—identifying who, in fact, were first responders. Some are easy—your firefighters and your ambulance drivers, your police officers. But one of the ones that was left out that was really concerning to me was another group of people with statutory powers and obligations, and that was Māori wardens. Now, all of a sudden, they fell on the other side of the line, and why that is, I just couldn’t say, because they have a very significant role, particularly at events on marae but elsewhere, in keeping order, attending to incidents, and basically being statutory security officers for tangata whenua. Yet that committee wasn’t persuaded that they should also get the protection if they’re assaulted in the discharge of their duties of this more serious offence.

There’s a lot to be said for this. Yes, the increased sentences for slavery and the upgrading of the slavery provisions are appropriate. But we can’t support a bill with incoherent offences, offences where the onus is on the defendant to prove their innocence, and giving citizens powers which don’t, in fact, protect people; they put citizens at risk. This is a hotchpotch bill of knee-jerk reactions, and it’s pretty typical of this Government’s approach to justice policy.

content.speaker: PAULO GARCIA (National—New Lynn)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. With this bill, criminals will soon face stronger penalties for attacking first responders, for coward punches, for human trafficking, and for retail crime.
The bill ensure that victims’ interests are at the centre of the justice system. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: This call is a split call.

content.speaker: DAN ROSEWARNE (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Labour opposes this bill and remains concerned about the way the legislation has been put together.

This is a bill that covers everything from human trafficking to citizen’s arrest powers, assaults on first responders, shoplifting, and the proposed coward punch offence. Some of those measures are sensible, some deserve support, but then others raise some serious concerns. The difficulty is that instead of bringing these issues to the House in separate pieces of legislation, the Government has bundled them together into one large bill and then tried to rush it through. When we are dealing with the public safety, criminal offending, and people’s rights, you know, Parliament should take time to get this absolutely right.

Let me start with the areas where there is broad agreement: Labour supports the changes relating to human trafficking and people smuggling. These offences involve some of the most vulnerable people imaginable. The amendments modernise our law and better reflect the reality of modern exploitation and slavery. That’s a worthwhile and necessary change.

We also acknowledge the intent behind stronger protections for our first responders and corrections officers. Nobody should be assaulted while carrying out their duties in the service of the public. But part of this bill, which has attracted some of the strongest criticism at select committee, was the proposed coward punch offence. And like every member of this House, I acknowledge the families who have lost loved ones through these senseless acts of violence. One punch can end a life, and one punch can leave a family grieving for ever. Those families do deserve to be heard. Coward punches are probably the one thing that worries me most as a dad. When my son—he’s 15 years old—does go out with his mates, that does worry me.

A victim, a victim’s family, can have their lives ended or changed forever as a result of a second of stupidity on the part of an offender. But Parliament also has the responsibility to make good law. The evidence presented to the committee raised very serious doubts about whether the proposed offence would actually achieve what the supporters hope it would achieve. Officials advised the committee that the offence, as drafted, would be harder to prosecute in existing manslaughter provisions. And why was that? Because prosecutors would have to prove additional elements. They would need to demonstrate not only that the assault caused death, but also that the victim had little or no opportunity to defend themselves, and that creates an extra hurdle in prosecution.

Several submitters pointed out that the existing offence of manslaughter already covers this conduct. Both offences carry the same maximum penalty, as the the Hon Dr Duncan Webb mentioned, of life imprisonment. So the obvious question becomes: what practical problem is this new offence actually solving? In fact, officials warned that it could actually create new problems. A jury could be faced with multiple overlapping options: murder, manslaughter, manslaughter by strike to the head or neck. And so, rather than simplifying matters, this bill risks making them even more confusing.

Even more concerning is the possibility that the additional elements in the new offence could make a conviction harder to secure. A prosecutor might choose to proceed under the new offence. If one of those extra elements cannot be established beyond reasonable doubt, the prosecution could fail. Officials acknowledged that the legislation does not fit neatly with existing provisions that allow alternative verdicts. That means that there’s a real risk that the law introduced to secure more accountability, could actually produce fewer convictions. And this should concern every member of this House.

Labour’s position on this is straight forward: If there’s a problem with sentencing outcomes for these offences; yeah, let’s debate sentencing. If there’s a concern about whether the courts are properly recognising the seriousness of these crimes; then yeah, let’s consider sentencing law. But creating a parallel manslaughter offence that officials themselves have warned may be confusing, difficult to prosecute, and potentially counterproductive is not sound law making for. So, for that reason, we do not support this bill.

content.speaker: DAN BIDOIS (National—Northcote)
content.text: The Crimes Amendment Bill is a good bill. It helps us restore law and order and ensures that there are real consequences for those that break the law. It’s all a part of this Government’s plan to fix the basics and build the future. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: HELEN WHITE (Labour—Mt Albert)
content.text: Thank you. I was really impressed by the speech tonight from the the Hon Dr Duncan Webb, who had been on the committee and really explained to me why he considered the situation, with regard to coward punch changes, were so wanting. What it made me think was that there is a theme through most of this legislation, despite the fact that it’s a cluster of different changes. And that theme, really, is one that I’ve come to understand in this job, that you have to be weary of law change for the sake of signalling to the community, when, actually, that’s all you’re doing. You’re not putting the resource in where it’s necessary. Instead, there is an attempt to bluff, really, with the public, and tell them that more is going on than is.

Now, it doesn’t mean that some of this law that Labour is opposing isn’t going to do damage, and it doesn’t mean that some of the law, we’ve already said, will do good. I want to focus on that for a minute, the issue of bluff, because I think it’s a very dangerous game to play with the public. When we say that we’re going to do things, we’re going to make lives safer for them, but what we’re actually doing is giving them a piece of paper, a law change, but we’re not putting in the resource that’s necessary.

Now, years ago, and not that many years ago, I got hit in the back of the head by somebody—just out of the blue. When that happened, there wasn’t enough response, as far as I was concerned, that was immediate, from the police force—because they were under-resourced. Actually, what I wanted, as somebody who had that happened to me, was I wanted somebody to make sure that the person who did that didn’t do it to anyone who was old or, basically, understood the consequences of what she had done. That kind of follow up, from our police force, that requires real people. It didn’t really require a change in the law. it required resourcing. I would have been very happy to have heard that that young girl, who did that, had been apprehended and had been put into a process of reconciliation with her actions. That’s nothing to do with punishment, etc. It’s got to do with preventing it happening to somebody she could have killed. I was just lucky, in some ways, I was older, I was healthy, and I wasn’t in a situation where I was really hurt by it—but I was pretty shaken up.

Now, I think that’s something I want to take to some of these other changes because that also informs the way I see the stuff about citizen’s arrest. In my area, we’ve had quite a lot of issues at things like Countdown with the stealing of food, etc., and we’ve had a terrible tragedy in my area, at somewhere called Rose Cottage Superette—it’s a little dairy and it’s quite isolated—where the worker ran after someone who had stolen something from the shop and they were stabbed and they died. It’s a terrible thing that happened Actually, I don’t want that worker to be in a position where they are suddenly arresting somebody in that situation because they’d be arresting a pretty violent individual and it would put them in danger—as it did. So I’d rather that the police dealt with that.

What the police have told me about the concern that they have over this, when we’ve talked about the realities of it, is they can’t get there anyway. If somebody arrests someone in a shop for an action like shoplifting, the police can’t get there. Just imagine what it’s going to be like when somebody arrests somebody who’s a bit dodgy and they’re holding on to them and the police don’t come—they don’t come straight away; they don’t come in half an hour. Well, what’s the outcome? What is going to happen? We definitely need to make sure that it’s the police dealing with that situation. It’s absolutely a blind spot to think that is, somehow, miraculously resolved by somebody without those skills, without that kind of defensive training and the training in actually dealing with people who are quite often pretty messy individuals. We need it to land right with those police officers, not with those other citizens who need protection. They don’t need empowerment in that way. It’s being dressed up as empowerment. It’s not empowerment; it puts people at risk.

I was talking to a liquor store owner who just had a robbery. All this talk of these things have stopped—they have not. This was not very long ago. There was this liquor store owner who had had somebody come in and take a whole load of stuff and he was very scared. I said, “You wouldn’t do the citizen’s arrest stuff?” And he said, “No, there’s absolutely no way I would.” He knew that to do that would put him at risk, and it would; it would put him at risk. I ask this Government: is that really the answer, or is the answer actually making sure that we are resourcing the police to do their job and protecting our citizens? Isn’t that the much better approach here?

I want to talk about some of these other things that have been promised to New Zealand tonight. How true are they? Let’s talk about the shoplifting tickets. It seems absolutely bizarre to me that, while the Government’s talking about being tough on crime, it’s walking away. It’s saying, again, “Not us. It’s just an administrative issue. Someone can send out an email and ticket somebody who’s stolen something.”—“It’s in the ether. That’ll do.” It will not do. It doesn’t solve the problem whatsoever. The person has still taken the item, and I totally take on board that it’s pretty, pretty bizarre to think that an email ticket for a proposed crime, which has no other testing in it, is an answer to this problem. The answer is that we stop people doing this sort of thing. I agree with that. I’m actually probably tougher on crime on this one than the people purporting to be. That’s an answer, but the answer is not to ticket them.

At the moment, we have really weird approaches to things like this. This law is one of them, where we say we want to be tough on crime, but then we want to do, what? Ticket people. I mean, I just don’t think that there’s many members of the community out there that are going to be satisfied with this one, because this is walking away. It’s corporatising the problem, and it totally ignores the reality of people’s situations.

I’ve dealt with two of the more, in some ways, smaller items in this bill, and I want to acknowledge one, before I finish, that I think is a good one. I want to leave on a good note. I really want to make sure that people understand that I fully support the amendments here that are about trafficking. Trafficking is very misunderstood; it has been for a long time. One of the amendments here means that there is a much greater possibility of prosecuting for trafficking where all the elements of the offence happen in New Zealand. Trafficking absolutely happens in New Zealand—all elements—and it’s great to see this particular change coming in. See, that’s a real one. That means more bad situations are dealt with. That’s in the hands of the police. It empowers them to do their job.

I also just really love the one which protects police officers who are going out and finding out about child exploitation, and there’s a much higher threshold. I love that because it’s a modern-day terrible problem, and we have to deal with it. That’s a good thing. I’m not anti dealing with real and serious crime; I’m for it. I just think that this is a patronising, silly bill, in lots of ways, and I wish we were dealing with the real things tonight and we could have added a few more things than that were real and meaty.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: The member’s time has expired.

content.speaker: SUZE REDMAYNE (National—Rangitīkei)
content.text: This bill is about putting victims at the heart of our justice system. It’s about consequences for serious offenders. We’re fixing the basics and building the future.

content.speaker: Hon GINNY ANDERSEN (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s a pleasure to take a call on this bill and to highlight some of the concerns that have been raised right throughout the select committee process. I’d like to focus my contribution on the citizen’s arrest provisions. I think it’s really important that we reflect back to the regulatory impact statement, which is really good. It goes to the heart of what the problem is that we are trying to solve with this legislation. As we know, Paul Goldsmith appointed Sunny Kaushal for about $925 a day to come up with some ideas on how to fix these problems. Funnily enough, the same ideas were provided to our Government for free, but this Government paid over $3 million for them. The main thing he came up with, which is the same thing he told us, was that providing more certainty may result in greater bystander intervention, increased confidence for retailers, and is intended to help bring about more certainty and consequence for retail offenders. However, in the regulatory impact statement, it does note that submissions to the ministerial advisory group have revealed that the causes of hesitancy to intervene largely exist outside of the Crimes Act. That’s the one that we’re amending right now.

These perceptions of police resourcing, actually having a police officer able to turn up, and the fact that this type of offending sometimes has a lower priority in police in terms of when they responded. The problem we’re trying to fix is that police don’t tune up, and the solution of this Government is that it will enable citizens to do that on behalf of police.

When we asked police what they think of this, funnily, they don’t like it too much. They think it’s quite dangerous and, in fact, we might get many situations around New Zealand where someone has taken the law into their own hands—and they can actually restrain them under this as well. Under the Minister’s option, the use of restraints are now permitted. That would be cable ties or, potentially, handcuffs—cuffed to a shelf. A member of the public can cuff and restrain somebody, but, as Paul Goldsmith described in his oral question in the House this week, they’re meant to hold them until the police arrive. You’re meant to ring up the police and get some real time instructions about administering the restraints and how to detain the person until, potentially, the police arrive.

Now, one of the main points that was raised by Retail New Zealand, I believe, when they submitted against this provision—that’s a major retailer representative across New Zealand; the people who are helping small businesses—they don’t want this, because their concern is that, if someone who has been aggressive and then restrained by the small-business owner, if the police do not in fact turn up, as we’ve seen often is the case, and, as we also know, because this Government hasn’t reached their 500 more police officers as promised, we don’t have extra police bouncing around to be able to come and turn up to this situation. Then the small-business owner is in the unenviable position of having to release the offender in their shop when they already agitated. There is a real concern that they will cause increased instances of harm within our community, increased violence, and actually put at risk those members of the small-business community when they are working in their environments. When there has been reporting on this from local media and ethnic communities, particularly in Auckland, which have been impacted by the sharp increase in retail crime, many of those small-business owners do not want this. They think it will put themselves in harm’s way, and they are really concerned that there is potential loss of life down the track.

I’m going to return and finish with the regulatory impact statement. It’s always good to have evidence in these things, isn’t it; because if we’re changing the law, we should have some good evidence to understand why we’re doing this. The Ministry of Justice was unable to provide or access any material evidence to substantiate the ministerial advisory group’s policy problem, nor was it possible to gather any evidence from agencies in relation to arrests and defence of property. In the whole conclusion from the Ministry of Justice, they’re unable to provide any evidence as to why they are doing this.

The other point I’d like to finish off with is the ministerial advisory group’s—that’s Sunny Kaushal—rationale that increased certainty, with respect to when the public can intervene and what level of force is permitted, will enable and empower the public to intervene, which will then deter criminal offending. We’ve got no cops, we’ve failed our 500, and we’re hoping that some small business owners might put their life on the line to intervene to try and get the crime rate down. Well, that’s a sorry story of a Government that’s given up and talks about victims of crime, when in reality, they are just creating more by this harmful legislation.

A party vote was called for on the question, That the amendments be agreed to.
