content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: This bill is set down for committee stage next sitting day.
Land Transport (Revenue) Amendment Bill
Legislative Statement

content.speaker: Hon JAMES MEAGER (Associate Minister of Transport)
content.text: on behalf of the Minister of Transport: I present a legislative statement on the Land Transport (Revenue) Amendment Bill.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
Second Reading

content.speaker: Hon JAMES MEAGER (Associate Minister of Transport)
content.text: on behalf of the Minister of Transport: I move, That the Land Transport (Revenue) Amendment Bill be now read a second time.

Mr Speaker, colleagues, this bill is yet another step in the evolution of our land transport funding system and it meets our changing circumstances and upholds one of the fundamental principles of how we fund land transport in New Zealand. That principle is that vehicle users should contribute fairly in proportion to the use that they undertake on our roads. Since we centralised our roading system in the 1920s—planning came a bit later—this principle has continued to underpin how we fund and pay for our roading network. However, the system is now under increasing pressure. As our vehicles have become more fuel efficient, and we start to drive more and more electric vehicles, the traditional method of collecting revenue from our petrol excise duties and our fuel taxes has dropped while our transport investment demands have continued to grow.

To better support sustainable transport investment, we must ensure that the tools we collect for revenue are sustainable, fair, and fit for purpose. To achieve this, the bill advances the Government’s revenue action plan by proposing amendments that reform the tolling network and modernising the road user charges system. This bill does two key things: it looks at how we toll in a modern day and age, and it reforms our road user system.

First, to tolling. We’ve actually got a long history of tolling in New Zealand. We’ve been doing it for over 100 years. The Auckland Harbour Bridge was built by tolls. The Lyttleton Tunnel was built by tolls. Tauranga have a few, so there are some people here who are familiar with how they work. What tolling does is it helps us to bring forward investment and build the roads and infrastructure that New Zealand needs sooner. It means the users who benefit most from new roads contribute most to those roads. We currently have toll roads in New Zealand, as I mentioned before, and we now want to progress our roading system plan, so we need to make sure we have the revenue to match those ambitions. It is about fixing the basics of our transport system so we can build a future where New Zealanders can get around our routing network in a quick and efficient manner.

The bill does a number of things around tolls. It has gone through the select committee process, and I’ll outline a few of the changes that have come through in a moment. It does allow for the tolling of existing roads where the users benefit from new roads on the same corridor, so that we can take a revenue approach across an entire tolling scheme rather than just on new sections of the road. Road users out there should be aware that the requirement for a feasible, untolled, or free route will remain. Of course, nothing is free in life. Those so-called free roads are still paid for by our road users. However, there will be an untolled alternative to all of our tolled roads. The bill will also enable heavy vehicles to be restricted from using unsuitable alternative routes, but only in specified circumstances.

Finally, we’re also updating the rules to toll concessions to make it easier to partner with the private sector to deliver the infrastructure we need. Taken together, these changes will ensure tolling is a more effective tool to help fund new roads, including our roads of national significance, those that deliver the infrastructure that New Zealand needs.

The second key thing this bill does is it looks at the road user charge system that we deal with in our modern day State, and it recognises that some changes are needed to be made. We need to modernise the system. We need to keep the system fair. We must ensure it’s ready to go for a shift in the future of all light-petrol vehicles onto the road user charge system. Our current system was designed in the 1970s. It is admittedly a bit clunky. It’s a manual process that relies on us to monitor our own odometers, pre-purchase road-user charges (RUC) in thousand kilometre blocks, and display teeny tiny little paper licences on our windows.

I’ve already said many times in this House how annoying those little bits of paper are, particularly when they fall down the dash, and a zealous parking officer comes along and gives you a nice wee donation to make to the local council or to the local NZTA because you haven’t put the right sticker in the right place. This bill does away with those stickers around road user charges. It removes the requirement to display, carry, or produce a RUC licence. In an electronic age, a paper licence should not be a strict requirement where people are paying bills, not to put paper in the front of the windscreens. The bill updates the definition of an electronic distance recorder to address some current restrictions and allow for more flexible, cost-effective approaches to recording distance.

In a bold modern move, it allows us to have more flexible regular payment systems, so that, instead of that thrill we get when we’re driving along the road and we realise we might be running out of road user charges soon, and we’d better pull over to the side of the road, jump on the NZTA website, and buy another thousand blocks to get us around the countryside a bit more, we’re going to be able to create some new options for some more regular payments to make it a little bit easier to deal with that. Yes, we will no longer get that thrill of driving and seeing the odometer tick over and wonder when that next thousand block will kick in. But maybe—just maybe—it might make it more helpful and easy for us to run our lives as we’re going around the countryside.

We are also aiming to change the road user charge retail landscape in general. We’re going to make it easier for other providers to help manage the road user charge system, particularly as we move to a system where all petrol vehicles will be on it at some point. Of course, that makes sense, because as our fuel efficiency increases in our petrol vehicles, we’re going to be using less fuel on the road. That is good, obviously, for our emissions, but it does impact our revenue streams. We’ve got to make sure that those vehicles still have an impact on the road. We’ve still got to make sure they still contribute to the impact on the road that they make, and we’ll be doing that in the future through road user charges rather than fuel tax.

The Transport and Infrastructure Committee made a number of changes that I’m sure members will go through today. I would like to thank the hard-working and industrious Transport and Infrastructure Committee. I want to thank the 47 written submissions from interested groups and individuals, and the 12 individuals that came to the select committee to provide their views. It did result in a number of changes throughout the process that, hopefully, this House will agree to today. I’ll very, very quickly go through them.

The committee has recommended some changes to refining the rules for tolling existing roads on the same corridor as new roads. They’ve tightened when toll revenue can be used for alternative routes. They’ve strengthened the rules for restricting heavy vehicles on alternative routes, and some changes around road-user charges. The updated bill provides that the approval of each alternative payment scheme is a regulatory decision for the RUC collector, rather than requiring Cabinet approval through secondary legislation, which would be a long and lengthy process. The bill now provides the power to set prescribed administration fees for NZTA as well as a separate service fee to cover the agency’s expenses. The bill removes the need for separate approval processes and enables the NZTA to become a provider from the date the Act commences.

Finally, Mr Speaker, I know you’ve been looking forward to this part of the speech: the end of it. The bill clarifies the power of the RUC collector to monitor and review providers, including any agents or contractors they engage. This change responds to those submitters who had concerns about the importance of oversight for third parties that collect land transport revenue and handle road user information.

I would like to thank everyone who has contributed towards the development of this bill. This is a practical and important bill that takes us one step closer to a fairer and more sustainable transport revenue system. I look forward to the contributions across the House. I’m sure they will be fulsome and exciting, just as exciting as it is to see the odometer tick over as we travel around the countryside over the next few months. I commend the bill to the House, and I look forward to its passage forthwith.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: The question is that the motion be agreed to.

content.speaker: TANGI UTIKERE (Labour—Palmerston North)
content.text: Meitaki maata, kia orana, Mr Speaker. Well, it’s great to have the Associate Minister of Transport with such optimism and a lengthy contribution. I do hope that his colleagues who are seated near him take a leaf out of his book and share their own views when it comes to this very important piece of legislation.

The Labour Party will be supporting this bill this evening because it is a bill that seeks to modernise our road funding tools, and that is somewhat overdue. There were many concerns that were raised in the first reading opportunity when this bill came before the Parliament, but where we have landed is that, through the select committee process, we are comfortable that many of those issues have been addressed by the the select committee, and I do intend to touch on a number of them this evening.

I want to acknowledge colleagues on the Transport and Infrastructure Committee. It is a hard-working committee, and I think this particular bill is a fine example of the committee working through a process to deal with some of the issues that had been identified at first reading and to get some consensus and change, to the point where a lot of the issues that we’d identified we worked through as a team, with the support of the advisers. I want to acknowledge the advisers that were supporting and advising the committee through this process.

This is an omnibus bill. As the Minister has already identified, it seeks to address two particular areas, and they relate to the road tolling rules that exist under the Land Transport Management Act, and that is about, effectively, road tolling. The second one is in relation to the Road User Charges Act of 2012 around the changes to the RUC, or the road-user charges system.

It is important to note, though, that the changes that exist within this particular bill are the enabling components to allow changes to the RUC system to roll that out across the fleet, noting that that is not something that will happen overnight. It is something that empowers the ability to make some change, and, again, colleagues on this side of the House will touch on that, no doubt, as well.

Currently, the law really only allows for the tolling of existing roads—so they’re not new roads, but existing roads—in what are fairly limited and constrained circumstances. Now, what this bill does is it allows the Minister of Transport to offer up tolling options on a particular stretch of road if two particular conditions are met. The first was around existing and new roads being part of the same corridor. That was a particular issue that the committee spent a lot of time on—and I’m thankful that they did to ensure that we got that corridor definition right. The second was that the users of existing roads need to receive a benefit from a new road in a particular area, as well. Now, the problem was that as it stood when the committee received the bill, there were no definitions around what a roading corridor is, nor were there specified definitions around the benefits that might flow or that might follow.

I want to turn to the benefits first. The benefits were an area where the select committee did introduce a number of changes, and those were that for users on an existing road, there must be one of four benefits that need to be received. One is that there are savings in terms of travel time savings—so a reduction in the time that it would take to travel from point A to B. Secondly, there is the issue of safety—so there would be safety benefits. Often, it is quite difficult for this current Government to consider safety benefits when it comes to transport, but we’ve got that in there, none the less. The third one is around travel time reliability—so the functionality of the particular roading network or the roads that are in question here. The final one touches on resilience, which is something that is a constant consideration in terms of the roading network moving forward. The Minister could consider any other benefits that might exist, but there must be at least a link to one of those four specified benefits in order for a tolling proposal, effectively, to be on the table.

The other one is the definition of corridor, and it’s something that I touched on in my first reading contribution. The select committee was of the view that there needed to be a clearer and more direct definition as to what a corridor actually meant. This is because the use of corridor is very commonplace in terms of transport context, and we wanted to make sure that we were able to get it right and that we had a definition that ensured that unrelated roads near a tolling proposition could not be tolled as part of a roading corridor.

The select committee made changes to this bill to provide that two roads are, effectively, in the same corridor if they have a clear functional relationship but also an operational relationship. The functionality bit is around where the roads would be commonly used together by road users as part of one single journey, as opposed to separate ones, and that journey from point A to B would be achieved, effectively, by ensuring that there was a single journey there.

The example that was used by the committee was someone who was travelling from Wellington to, perhaps, Kāpiti or vice versa, and whether or not using Transmission Gully versus using the coastal route of State Highway 59 would be part of the same roading corridor. It’s often unusual for a select committee to put a map in its report, but that is exactly what the Transport and Infrastructure Committee decided to do—

content.speaker: Hon James Meager
content.text: It’s tiny.

content.speaker: TANGI UTIKERE
content.text: —to provide a little—it is tiny, but when you’re reading it larger, you’ll see that it has the information that is needed.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: I did notice the map.

content.speaker: TANGI UTIKERE
content.text: Thank you, sir. Therefore, in considering this issue, you can’t move between A and B—those two routes—on a single journey, and so it’s not considered a roading corridor for the purposes of tolling. So the map itself is pretty helpful. The other part in terms of it being operational is around ensuring that there is a connection between the flow of traffic and the traffic management on one road supporting or influencing the other.

There still needs to be a realistic and feasible alternative route for any tolling road under these proposals, and I think that is a very clear distinction that needs to be made. If a road is up for tolling, there needs to be an alternative one that is feasible and easy to be accessed.

In terms of the maintenance side of things, it’s really important that, at the moment, the law only allows for revenue from a toll to be used on a new road. The change that was initiated through this process was that it would allow for toll revenue to be gathered to be used on the maintenance and operational costs of alternative routes.

Now, Mr Assistant Speaker Tuiono, you are very familiar with Te Ahu a Turanga, the Manawatū Tararua replacement highway. That is not a new road; that is a replacement road, and whilst this Government tried to whack a toll on the local community for that, the good people, the folk of the Manawatū, the Pohangina, and the wider Tararua area, stood up against that. Why? Because it’s not a new road; it’s a replacement road. That is important to acknowledge in this context, because the Saddle Road, which is familiar to many, really took quite a hammering and a battering as a result of it being an alternative route and heavy vehicles having to utilise that.

Now, what this bill does is it does initiate some change so that it could be possible for revenue that is generated from the use of a toll to be channelled towards the maintenance and operational costs of an alternative route, if the Minister forms the view that the pressures in terms of funding are such that the local road-controlling authority would not be in a position to be able to fully fund or meet the costs of that. It is a particular point of distinction that is important, nonetheless.

I want to just finally touch on the RUC component because these are some changes that will enable—over time, not overnight—the transition of the entire fleet towards road-user charges. What’s really important is that that process is smooth.

Now, the Minister, interestingly, in his contribution tonight talked about the sense of maybe anxiety when you get towards a particular 1,000 RUC mileage, and you realise that you need to actually buy another 1,000. Well, the problem is that if we’re going to transition or enable transition across the whole fleet, a lot of people can’t afford to buy 1,000 kilometres. So this is also accepted as part of this process that there needs to be flexibility in the new regime to allow for, yes, different ways of payment, but also making sure that we’re not just going to have a minimum purchase of 1,000, because that would cut out quite a number of households who continue to do it tough. So I’m really cognisant of while we’re bringing in these changes, there does need to be a lens over ensuring that equity considerations are front and centre; that technology is utilised; and that it is able to work out well.
We are supportive of this bill; we think that it does provide some opportunities, but also there needs to be a level of cautiousness as we continue to work through it.

content.speaker: CELIA WADE-BROWN (Green)
content.text: The Green Party knows that a balanced, sensible transport system can connect and enrich our communities and protect our environment and reduce the cost of living. At the moment in Aotearoa New Zealand, we are really car dependent, and it costs us all far too much, especially with the recent costs of diesel and petrol.

For households who are doing it tough in a cost of living crisis, they are spending thousands and thousands on car travel that people could ill afford. That’s one of the many reasons that the Green Party has consistently pushed for less urban sprawl and more intensification, and there has been some work across the floor on improving that in some places.

I think it’s important to remember that not everyone can drive. There are people with certain disabilities, there are children, there are people who can’t actually even afford a vehicle. So this is not a recipe necessarily for more and more roads and more car dependence.

The reason that we support this bill is that it brings the costs of the roading system closer to the people that use it. But we do have some issues to resolve—not with this bill—but with some of the wider transport funding. It is really clear, not just through the National Infrastructure Plan, that we need much more investment in maintenance before so many new, shiny roads are built.
If you look in the Wairarapa, the Tūranganui Bridge—the only route to Ngawi and Cape Palliser for locals and tourists alike, again, has had problems with the climate-charged rainfall events.

I have to say that we can change this system to a much better one, and this bill is a small step in the right direction. It was a pleasure, as my colleague Tangi Utikere said, to be on the Transport and Infrastructure Committee, and I commend the chair, my colleagues, the submitters, but particularly the officials, and, yes, it is great to have a commentary that has a picture in it; I think we could do this more often, to be clearer.

Coming back to what the consequence of more direct pricing will be, it’s also, potentially, a disincentive for people to drive as much. Now, there are some jobs and there are some transport areas where it is absolutely essential to travel by road—no argument with that—but there are also some places where, with some investment in alternatives, we could make it more cost effective, more relaxing, less congestion, and better for people’s health. I am slightly frustrated that the tolls cannot be used to improve any alternative modes of transport, any other choices, but that’s something that could relatively easily be changed.

I also echo Tangi Utikere’s point that we have to be careful where we do and don’t toll. He mentioned Te Ahu a Turanga, between Ashhurst and Woodville. It is conceivable that one of the other roads, whether it’s the Saddle Road or it’s the Pahiatua Track, maybe, at some point, it will become only, pretty much, a tourist road. I mean, it’s been wonderful investment in that.

The map is useful in defining corridors, but what it doesn’t do is talk about the share between local government and central government. If you look at that map, we’ve got State Highway 1 now going through Transmission Gully. I was going to ask, “Hands up who’s driven Transmission Gully?”, but maybe I won’t. But the green road, the coastal road, which is at considerable risk of inundation, which is one of the reasons Transmission Gully was built, remains a State highway. So it will still be the Government that does the funding of that State highway through the Government policy statement and New Zealand Transport Agency. There are other circumstances where a new road comes in and central government says to the council, “Oh, have a road.” “Well, great, we’ve got a new asset” is not what is likely to be said by people who are facing rate caps and other pressures.

One huge improvement is that some of the toll revenue can be used on the maintenance of the old road that local government has to do. The Minister, when he introduced the bill tonight, talked about us having a centralised system, but our transport system is not that centralised. Most roads, local roads—the rates are paying for at least half of the costs of roading. Whether it’s the bitumen, the culverts, the bridges, the signage, the traffic lights—all of those things are often the realm of the ratepayer and the local council.

I think it’s another example of having to work out the relationship between central government funding and local government funding, not just passing on the obligation to keep a road open. Because even if it’s not going to be the major transport route anymore for stock trucks or for tradies or whatever, often people live along those smaller roads that have been bypassed by the new roads and, therefore, there will need to be continued maintenance.

I would like to have seen more investment in this year’s Budget in things like rural school buses, rail—I mean, it’s ridiculous. The number 200 bus in the Wairarapa which links up the five towns doesn’t run after about 5.30 in the evening. That really constrains people who, perhaps, don’t have their own car, can’t afford a car, can’t drive because of some visual disability. Now there’s a whole lot of people that are not served just by cars, whether they’re on toll roads or other roads.

I also think this bill makes it a little clearer that the costs of new roads and their planned maintenance should not really be subsidised by everybody else. So I would like to thank the members of the select committee, the submitters, and the very knowledgeable advisers who helped us improve this bill, and the Greens are happy to support it.

content.speaker: SIMON COURT (ACT)
content.text: ACT supports this bill for one simple reason: New Zealanders have a huge aspiration for better infrastructure, better roads, being able to connect businesses with ports, businesses with customers, and people who simply want to get to work or be able to get their kids to school on time. One of the major problems we have right now is that our aspiration for our roading network is not matched by our aspiration to fund it. There is a huge gap between the roads we need, the roads many of us know that are important to support growth, and our ability to fund them through the road-user charges, through fuel excise duty, and through Crown contributions. As a result, in 2026, 30 or 40 years behind the rest of the world, New Zealand has accepted it’s important that we introduce changes to our tolling regime so that the roads that can be funded partly or, really, wholly, by charging those who use the roads through tolls, mean that we can actually fund and deliver roading projects that connect communities with work, with education, and with opportunity in a way that our current system does not allow.

That is why ACT is proud to support the bill. The bill includes provisions to specify user benefits. For too long we’ve had different groups saying, “Oh, the toll is too much—people won’t use the road.” In the new way of working, there’ll be some very clear tests as to how we demonstrate those benefits. We’ve also heard concerns that where roads are tolled, alternative routes will become congested or not funded at all. Let’s be clear: when we’ve built four-lane major highways like Transmission Gully, like Pūhoi to Warkworth, there is an overwhelming preference to use the new, better road.
When I first started working in Auckland, I used to go to Ōrewa—a small beachside town just north of Dairy Flat.

content.speaker: Joseph Mooney
content.text: Yup. I went to high school there.

content.speaker: SIMON COURT
content.text: State highway 1—Joseph Mooney—potential Minister for Space in a future Government. He said he used to go to school there. He will know that 15,000 vehicles a day used to ride in between the ice-cream shop and the fish and chip shop and the beach on State highway 1. Stock trucks used to drop effluent all along the main highway—truck and trailers. It was impossible for a community like Ōrewa to reach its potential without shifting 15,000 vehicles a day off that road. The tolled alternative route that most Aucklanders and anyone leaving Auckland heading north has accepted without question for decades now has enabled that beautiful community of Ōrewa to connect the community with the beachfront and all of that amenity. That is one of the benefits of improving the way that we fund and judge infrastructure.

We’ve also heard concerns about, “Well, what about heavy vehicles?” The transport sector is concerned that they will be forced to use toll roads and pay more than they currently are to use the existing State highway network. Well, let’s be clear: if your truck is running on the State highway network, you’re paying road-user charges per kilometre of travel, but you’re running through townships like Kumeū in north-west Auckland or other places around the country where you are paying the fair share of the roading cost, but that does not possibly compensate for the opportunity cost that that community is suffering from having thousands of heavy vehicles running down its main street every day. It makes sense to say, “You should and must use an alternative tolled heavy vehicle route that has been built specifically, that has been engineered specifically, for your purpose.

So while we understand that many heavy vehicle operators are concerned about the costs, I must say that there is a huge benefit. New Zealand Inc. benefits. We understand your concerns and the cost you face, but it’s important we shift to user must pay for the benefit. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: ANDY FOSTER (NZ First)
content.text: Thanks, Madam Speaker. I rise on behalf of New Zealand First and as the chair of the Transport and Infrastructure Committee which considered this bill. I just want to start off just by saying thanks to all the submitters, the officials who we’ve already heard did a fantastic job, and the select committee which, as always, operated really collegially to tackle the bill, and I want to thank them all.

The Minister and Tangi Utikere in particular have both laid out what the bill’s all about, so I don’t have to do any of that, but I did want to touch on a couple of things. The first one of them is that the bill obviously advances the road-user charges (RUC) system digitisation and so on. It helps modernise and sets us up for moving from fuel excise duties to RUC—that’s all very good. But there’s two areas I particularly just wanted to focus on: first of all there’s the tolling bit and secondly the heavy vehicle bit.

So in terms of tolling, it was interesting that we heard a mention from the Minister about tolls being used to bring forward new roads. The Manawatū Tararua Highway, which was used as an example, I think, by Tangi Utikere, was one, actually, where that wasn’t true because the road was nearly complete when the idea of a toll was suggested and the community went ballistic. We actually agree with the community in that situation and said that we weren’t particularly happy with that either. That would have been somewhat disingenuous, to put it mildly, to put a toll on then. So it was a good result that it is not a toll road.

But we spent a lot of time as a select committee looking at this issue of existing roads being tolled, because that’s not the case at the moment. As Tangi Utikere has said, we spent quite a bit of time trying to define this thing of a “corridor”, because corridor was not defined in the bill when it started out. We used the example there in that little map there with Transmission Gully and Centennial Highway. Now, that wouldn’t have worked anyway because there’s not a free feasible road down through that part of the North Island.
But I do want to give you one illustration where it could occur. If we had a second harbour crossing in Auckland, we decide to toll the new one—

content.speaker: Hon Dr Deborah Russell
content.text: Third one—there’s already two crossings.

content.speaker: ANDY FOSTER
content.text: Yeah, if we had another bridge, another tunnel, and we decided to toll the new one, and you had not got a definition of corridor, you could then say, “Actually, because we’ll get diversion from the new one to the old one, which we don’t really want to do, we could toll them both because there’s”—you could argue—“a feasible route around the outside of the harbour through the western part of Auckland to come back there.” It would mean that, with the definition of corridor that we’ve got in there, you couldn’t actually do that. So I think that’s an important definition and it was good to spend a little bit of time on that.

The second bit we talked about in terms of tolling was the issue around local government and the transfer of—sometimes, Wayne Brown said, when we put a new State highway in and we say to local government, “Well, you can have the old one.”, the local government goes, “Well, that’s great because we’ve got to maintain it with all the rates you’re going to cap us on, etc., etc., etc!” Of course, then local government’s saying, “Well, can the new road help to fund the existing one?” So that’s what that conversation is about. But I did want to just say that I have been party to a local road being given to the State. It was quite a few years back and I managed to persuade the New Zealand Transport Agency that it would be quite a good idea if State highway 1 didn’t stop at the Basin Reserve but carried on to the airport, which has probably saved ratepayers an absolute fortune over many, many years.

The second point I wanted to make is just regarding the issue of heavy trucking. We heard from the trucking industry that they did not want to be in a situation of being forced to use a new toll route and potentially for those tolls to be particularly significant—in other words, imposing a significant cost on them. So we were very, very careful with the circumstances under which that might occur, and they are set out there: heavy vehicles being unsuitable for an alternative route, which is exactly the kind of thing that Simon Court was talking about. If you’ve got a new route which has been urbanised and beautified—all that sort of thing—to create a lovely place for people to be, you don’t want to have a whole lot of heavy trucks going through there. So it would be reasonable to say that we actually want you to go on to the new route. That’s exactly what’s happened in the Orewa example that you talked about, and there’s issues around significant maintenance costs and so on.

The one bit, though, that I did want to highlight on that, just before finishing, is that the Minister’s got to be satisfied. We’ve said the Minister’s got to be satisfied that adequate consultation has occurred before issuing a restriction notice. We also specifically put in—this was one that I was particularly keen to put in there—the definition of “adequate consultation”.

Just for—some of us have been around a little while. There’s a Court of Appeal decision going way, way back to 1993, which set out exactly what consultation is. It basically says that you cannot have a firm decision, a firm position, at the beginning; you’ve got to have an open mind; you’ve got to listen authentically to the feedback you get; you’ve got to allow time for that feedback to be given; and you’ve got to give adequate information to consider adequate options. That is something that is really, really important in any good consultation process. One of the things that annoys people—no end—is when consultation is inauthentic.

So we put that in there, and maybe that’s just a little message to say what consultation should be all about. That’s what we said should occur in this instance with heavy vehicles, but it should occur in terms of all consultation that we do and all consultation that local government does. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: This is a split call—Mike Davidson.

content.speaker: MIKE DAVIDSON (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise on behalf of the Green Party. We cautiously support this bill. We did not support it to the select committee, but, obviously, I’d like to acknowledge the work of the select committee, the transport and environment select committee. They must have done something right, because we’re now—

content.speaker: Dr Carlos Cheung
content.text: Transport and infrastructure.

content.speaker: MIKE DAVIDSON
content.text: Sorry, yes. Thank you very much—the Transport and Infrastructure Committee. I should put my glasses on when I read things—because we now do support it. We did have some concerns around the private enterprise of policing and tolling roads, and through that process, they have been sorted in a way. But we still have, I guess, some concerns around the use of tolling. At the same time, we have been a long-time campaigner of more direct pricing of road use. Road pricing can actually be an extremely effective tool to move people more effectively around our network.

I think, at the same time, we need to remember that if we just focus on moving people via cars, we’re never going to get anywhere as a society, because it doesn’t take long for those roads to be clogged up again. The more roads we build, the more people drive, the quicker it gets clogged up and another road gets built and it never ends. When, actually, if we look at alternative means of moving people, whether that be through bussing, walking, or biking, we actually create space on our existing roads for people that need to travel by car.

You only have to look at roads during school holidays when we don’t have people taking their children—or high school students, university students driving—to their education, to see how much quieter it is on the roads. It doesn’t actually take a huge shift to actually create a significant reduction on people using our roads. If we actually want to look at trying to make our dollar stretch further in our transport space, we should be looking at how we actually can have less people driving instead of more people driving.

I do find it interesting when, obviously, the Minister spoke about the tolls being used to build the new roads. We know with Christopher Luxon’s $15 billion worth of roads—a few roads across the country that most New Zealanders won’t use—the tolls aren’t going to pay for them alone. They need a lot more investment. Once again, I reiterate my point: if we just invest in roads, we’re going to get nowhere as a country. We do know that cars not only just create congestion, which creates productivity issues, but it also has significant emission issues, which causes health issues as well. So, the more we actually move into different forms of transport, the better we are as a country.

One of the things that I would like to focus on in my remaining 90 seconds is, obviously, the idea of the tolling of the new roads and the corridor effect as well. I look at Woodend Bypass, and, obviously, the impact on State Highway 1, which will have a reduction of cars. Just by that is Tuahiwi, and anyone that doesn’t know Tuahiwi, it is the heart of the mighty Ngaī Tūāhuriri and, obviously, it’s quite close to Woodend. I have seen the modelling that shows that the tolling will actually impact Tuahiwi. We’ll see more vehicles going through Tuahiwi, and I’m sure the Minister is aware of Tuahiwi and knows where Tuahiwi is and how narrow the road is.

It would be a real shame if, actually, it sits outside corridors and we actually start seeing an increase of transport and traffic going through that fantastic place. So it would be great to know that we’re not going to see issues happening there. There’s the Woodend Bypass; some like it, but there are some significant concerns that may come from it if not addressed properly.

As I said at the start of my call, the Green Party does cautiously support this. We have always been a strong party that has supported the use of road-user charges, so it’s good to see the National Party following our lead. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: Dr CARLOS CHEUNG (National—Mt Roskill)
content.text: This bill ensures that New Zealand has a more sustainable and reliable way to fund transport infrastructure. It creates a more flexible tolling framework, sets clear rules for toll pricing, and allows toll revenue to fund both new and existing roads. It is a great bill. It is fixing the basics and building the future. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DEBORAH RUSSELL (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. Let me start with a couple of thoughts, which I promise you are completely related to this.

First of all, I just want to remind Andy Foster, who made the mistake—and other people do it—and who said that we need a second harbour crossing in Auckland. We have two harbour crossings already. There is the State Highway 1 route across the harbour bridge and there is the State Highway 16 and 18 route up around the top of the harbour through West Auckland across Upper Harbour. So I just invite Andy Foster to abandon his Wellington-centric view and understand how Auckland actually operates.

The second is a story about tolling, which only some people in this House may remember, and it may well be the stuff of urban legend—though it is in Wikipedia, therefore it must be true. It goes back to the days when there was a toll over the Auckland Harbour Bridge. People who have driven over the bridge will have seen, particularly heading north, that after you come off the bridge, the road widens considerably. There used to be a series of toll booths there. A few of us can remember driving through there and our mum or our dad, probably, because we wouldn’t have been driving ourselves back then, handing over the 20 cents or the 50 cents for the toll. Of course, people who lived north of the harbour bridge and had to commute over every day for work resented that toll.
Now, come 1980, there was a by-election in the East Coast Bays seat. The person who was standing for the by-election was Don Brash.

content.speaker: Hon Erica Stanford
content.text: That’s right.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DEBORAH RUSSELL
content.text: That’s right, indeed. But legend has it that Rob Muldoon did not like Don Brash. Now, you’ll recall that in 1980, Rob Muldoon was Prime Minister and Minister of Finance—he liked having his control over everything. So a few weeks out from the by-election, legend has it that he lifted the tolls on the Auckland Harbour Bridge so that all the voters in East Coast Bays were really angry at National, and, rather that voting for Don Brash, they voted for Gary Knapp instead, and brought another Social Credit MP into the House.

content.speaker: Hon Erica Stanford
content.text: A dark stain on our history.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DEBORAH RUSSELL
content.text: Ha, ha! I see that the current MP for East Coast Bays knows this story well.

Tolls have often been a point of contention in New Zealand. We seem to think that we ought to be able to drive everywhere on the roads for absolutely free, and we forget that roads need to be paid for and that we need to find a way of paying for roads which is equitable, which reflects the usage of those roads, that kind of spreads the load. Roads are, in many ways, a good socialist institution, where we spread the cost over many of us and we all derive benefit from it.

We pay for roads in a variety of ways: we do use some tolls; we use some central government funding; we use our fuel taxes; we use road-user charges; and, of course, we use rates. So there’s a whole mix of funding that goes into roading. It does seem to be fairly important that we get that mix right and that we ensure that—

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: There’s too many people standing on the right side of the House. Sit down please.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DEBORAH RUSSELL
content.text: —not too much of the load is borne by one purported part of the community rather than another.

We also know that we need to upgrade and develop our roading infrastructure in New Zealand. We know that one way of funding some of these new roads that we do need is through tolls. If people think that we don’t need new roads, I wish to point them to the glory of the Hamilton bypass, where one can just drive straight past Hamilton—very sorry to my Hamilton colleagues. Also, the difference that Transmission Gully has made to Wellington; to the Taupō bypass, years and years ago; and the way we’ve been able to, of course, bypass Huntly: these are all good things. They make for efficient roading networks and they enable people to travel about this country and enable freight to travel about this country. The trick is how to pay for them and what is going to be the most effective way of paying for them. Tolls do seem to help there.

So we welcome the changes in this bill, where we are looking at enabling tolling in various ways along road corridors, not just a particular road. This seems to be a sensible change. In terms of the work that has been done around the benefits from roads in a roading corridor, I think it’s been very helpful that the select committee has spelled out some of the benefits that must be demonstrated to show that a new road could be tolled. Whether it’s a saving in time or safer roads or more reliable travel time or a resilient structure, these are all benefits from a good roading network.

I’m looking at those ways that this select committee has worked on the rules around tolling and have, I think, come up with some pretty good solutions. I know we’ll need to keep an eye on it in terms of equity and on fairness, but that’s our job as a Parliament, so we will continue to do that.

I do want to speak about some of the issues around the road-user charges, which is the other major change which is sitting in this bill. As we all know at the moment, some drivers pay road-user charges via their fuel excise and some pay road-user charges via the road-user charge. Now, the fuel excise is becoming less and less effective. We have more electric vehicles, less fuel being consumed—we hope—and so less fuel excise being collected. It’s a problem that is widespread around the world. Many, many jurisdictions collect something like a fuel excise and use it to fund their roads. That particular source of road funding is dropping as people move towards electric vehicles, so we do need to find a way to ensure that all vehicle users contribute to the cost of the roads.

At the moment, one of the things that doesn’t work so well around road-user charges—around paying for that—is a heap of us pay for it via petrol, and the amount of petrol we use is taken as a proxy for the distance we travel and as a proxy for the impact of our vehicle on the roads. Now, it’s an imperfect proxy. So if we could move away from that, that’s a good thing to do. The particular changes that are being made for the fuel excise and the road-user charges mean that, in time, we will all be paying road-user charges instead of, we hope, paying that cost for our roads via the fuel excise. I think that’s a fairer way of doing things. It’s a more accurate way of doing things. The technologies are starting to exist so that we can measure very accurately the distances that vehicles travel and therefore ask for the appropriate amount of road-user charges.

There are a couple of equity issues or issues around payment there. One of them was touched on by one of the earlier speakers. At the moment, a person who’s paying road-user charges—that’s a person who’s driving a diesel vehicle usually—those road-user charges are bought in 1,000-kilometre blocks. That’s a chunk of money. It’s all very well if a person can pay that quite easily, but there are families for whom that is not possible, so we do need to be able to pay for those road-user charges in smaller chunks.

The other issue I’m worrying about, though—and this will be one for us as a Parliament to keep an eye on—is that once we start collecting road-user charges separately from paying for fuel—remember that portion of funding is currently collected through the fuel excise—once we ask people to start paying a separate bill, it may well become a deferrable bill. At the moment, a person who goes to fill up their car automatically pays the amount of fuel excise. I’m sure they notice the cost of petrol, but they don’t notice the particular amount that is the fuel excise. Once we separate that amount out and ask for it to be paid separately, it is like any bill that can be paid with a bit of discretion from people putting off paying their power bill to putting off paying their rent and so on. There are some bills that can be put off. We need to make sure we have a mechanism so that people pay their new road-user charges not in big chunks of 1,000 or so, but on an as-you-go basis and that there is a simple mechanism for collecting that from people as they go; not too much in arrears. Otherwise, I fear we could add to some of the problems we already have with people ending up in debt and ending up in desperate circumstances because of their accumulated debt. So that is something else for our Parliament to keep an eye on.
Having said this, this is a good bill. It takes us further down towards better funding for our road system, and we commend it to the House.

content.speaker: DAN BIDOIS (National—Northcote)
content.text: This is a good bill and it literally helps us build the future for our country. I wish to thank the select committee for their work on this bill, and I commend it to the House.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: Dan Rosewarne. I look forward to hearing about the Woodend Bypass! Just a prediction!

content.speaker: DAN ROSEWARNE (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I wasn’t going to mention it, but now I might have to—I might have to. I rise to speak on this bill in its second reading. Labour will be supporting this bill, not because we agree with every part of it necessarily but because the select committee has done a good job in improving it. A number of concerns were raised by submitters, and they’ve been addressed. The bill comes back to this House a lot better than the one that was introduced—that’s for sure.

There are two broad parts to this legislation. The first one deals with tolling, and the second one modernises the road-user charges system. On road-user charges, there’s quite a bit to this bill that makes sense. The current system still relies on processes that belong in another era. The bill removes the requirements for paper licences. It enables digital administration and allows for flexible payment options. It also opens the door to new technology and service providers.

It was great that the Minister actually had a really good analogy around the paper option being a relic of the past. I still have a car that—I would like that paper option. I wouldn’t really like to touch it. I’ve got a 1976 HJ Holden Kingswood. I did bring this up in the first reading, but once I get started on these kinds of things, I can’t stop. It actually has Michelin tyres, so the Government will be really happy about that. In fact, they probably subsidise them in some way, although it didn’t feel like it when I paid for them and chucked them on to the car. But anyway, the odometer on that has actually gone around the clock a couple of times, so that no doubt will have to be a consideration if we stick to the old style. But don’t get me started on old Holdens—I’ll be here all night otherwise.

I’ll get back to the bill. This bill is designed to prepare for the future transition of petrol vehicles into the on-road user charges system. Some really good changes. People expect the Government systems to work efficiently, they expect them to be easy to use, and if technology can reduce compliance costs and make life easier for motorists, that’s something that’s worth supporting. The select committee also spent a lot of time considering issues around privacy, competition between providers, and access for people who still prefer the traditional ways of paying, particularly for classic cars—I’ll just add that in there again. Those are all matters that deserve ongoing scrutiny as the system develops.

The more contentious part of this bill is tolling. Tolling is always a difficult decision because most people would rather not pay an extra charge to use the road, and that’s understandable. But Governments also have to be honest about the fact that major transport infrastructure projects do cost money, and communities often want projects delivered sooner rather than later. So the question has never really been about whether tolling should exist; the question is about when it is appropriate, what safeguards should apply, and whether people are being treated fairly.

There’s also much in the select committee’s work focused around corridor tolling, concerns about how toll revenue could be used, and concerns around giving Ministers too much discretion in the future. Those concerns led to a number of changes, including tighter definition arounds corridor tolling, clearer safeguards, consultation requirements, and stronger limits on how some of these powers can be exercised. Those improvements are important because public confidence matters. If people are expected to pay tolls, they need to know that there’s clear rules around where tolling can occur and how those decisions are made.

I’ll inject my Woodend Bypass here: so for people in north Canterbury, this project is often talked about—it’s been talked about for years. Anyone who has sat in traffic through Woodend, anyone who runs a business that relies on freight moving efficiently, and anyone who travels that route regularly understands why that bypass is needed. There’s a strong case for getting it built: it will improve safety, it will improve travel times, it will improve the reliability of an important route into Christchurch.

Supporting the Woodend Bypass doesn’t necessarily mean supporting the toll on the bypass. Interestingly, tolls were only actually recently raised about the bypass, which has caught the community off guard. So we definitely support it being built, but I’m not convinced that local community members should be paying that toll. I commend the bill to the House.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: The member’s time has expired.

content.speaker: Dr HAMISH CAMPBELL (National—Ilam)
content.text: It is a great honour to rise in support of the Land Transport (Revenue) Amendment Bill. This bill will help create a fairer, simpler, and more modern transport funding system, ensuring New Zealand will be ready for the next generation of road building. Therefore, I commend it to the House.

content.speaker: Dr TRACEY McLELLAN (Labour)
content.text: Madam Speaker, thank you. I also would like to make a contribution on the Land Transport (Revenue) Amendment Bill—probably a little bit longer that the previous speaker, but let’s just see what happens.

Transport funding obviously needs to catch up with how New Zealanders actually travel. This has been described in various contributions tonight as a bit of an overdue, modernisation bill. For that reason, Labour continues to support it.

I just want to run through a few points, but in summary of that and in anticipation, the current road-user charges (RUC) system has been described on several occasions tonight as being a system that is stalled, paper-based, very cumbersome. I think the Minister, in his first reading, talked about the little piece of paper that can easily be lost down the dash. It does seem a little bit antiquated to still be relying on a ticket, so to speak, to prove that you’re, essentially, allowed to be on the road—and all of the stressors and logistics around maintaining such an old-fashioned system. So we’re happy to see this included in this bill.

The bill also talks about the future transition of petrol vehicles into the RUC system. Again, the Minister and various other contributors have talked about, I suppose, the sustainability of funding as we look forward. We’ve heard contributions talk about the need for it to be a much more user-pays system, and the fact that, with more and more EVs on the road, it’s inevitable that we’re going to move to a RUC system. Increased fuel efficiency—all of those things contribute to that. Essentially, modern technology, flexible payment options, and a much more efficient funding system are all sensible reforms, which is a big part of the reason Labour continues to support this bill.

We support modernisation, but only if it’s accompanied by things like fairness. It’s got to have decent transparency. Most importantly, it must maintain public confidence. That’s an issue that has to be maintained not only during this legislative process, as we have worked on this bill and we will inevitably watch it turn into legislation, but also as the regime is maintained in the future. A transport funding system, as I said, needs to be modern, it should be efficient, but, most importantly, it also needs to be trusted. Those three things need to go together—cue the select committee process, and that certainly was the starting point for our considerations.

Whilst this bill was in the select committee, it was improved, and there were several improvements made to the bill, many of which have been touched on tonight. Some have been elucidated in a lot more detail. I’m going to run through them from my perspective, as a member of the select committee and the experience I had as we not only discussed this bill but we were in a somewhat unique position, because select committees aren’t always made up of people who bring individual expertise—and they shouldn’t need to be—but on this particular occasion, we had a select committee that was made of people who brought a wealth of either individual expertise or individual experience in this realm. I think that it made the select committee process, for someone who doesn’t possess that expertise, all the more richer. I felt like I learnt quite a lot.

In regard to the types of things that we discussed and the improvements that we made, we were initially concerned that this bill gave the Minister very broad powers to toll existing roads. The term “corridor” wasn’t particularly well defined, and, as it turns out, it needed to be. Again, as someone from a lay perspective, who didn’t necessarily realise how important that was, it didn’t take long for people like Simon Court, who has a lot of lived experience and loves a good road, and it didn’t take long for people like my colleagues Tangi Utikere and Andy Foster and Celia Wade-Brown, who have a wealth of experience in local government, to be very firm on the fact that a lot of this needed a little bit of fixing up. So I felt very privileged to be privy to that process.

content.speaker: Arena Williams
content.text: Great select committee.

content.speaker: Dr TRACEY McLELLAN
content.text: Yes. In terms of the corridor, it needed to have, as was said earlier, both a functional and an operational relationship. We almost got to the point where it would be somewhat of an exaggeration to say there was “acting out”, but we almost got the point where, with that wealth of experience, both practical and through local government, several examples were raised of roads and alternate routes and alternate roads and toll roads and the functional and operational relationships—when I say “almost an exaggeration”, it was minus the car and it was minus leaving the select committee room. But it really did make you feel like you were there—a little bit frustrating at times, but I think it was well worth it to get to the place where we got.

There was also no clear test for when an existing road could be tolled. Through the process, I think that those definitions were well worth the time. It removed, also, the vague reference to “efficiency”, which could have expanded tolling far too far. That’s exactly how a select committee process should work. Concerns were raised—and I do want to acknowledge all the submitters. I think there were 47 submissions and 12 oral submissions, and they were very much appreciated. It’s exactly how the select committee process should work: concerns were raised, evidence was heard, and the legislation was made all the stronger because of it.

In line with those sentiments of gratitude to the members of the select committee and the submitters, I also do want to acknowledge the officials who did have to put up with a huge number of questions and clarifications.

The new RUC system is a major structural change, and it’s a major part of this bill. What happened through this bill and through this process is it separates the New Zealand Transport Agency’s regulatory role from the retail providers, and the Minister provided some more examples of that; creates approved third-party RUC providers; allows subscriptions and post-payment systems, which we’re all in favour of; and, as I said, prepares for a much more nationwide RUC system in the future.

Through those discussions, we also, certainly from the Labour Party perspective, wanted some assurances—and were given them—around issues of privacy, around issues of consumer protection, transparency, and accountability, as we discussed those. Because of those improvements, obviously, Labour continues to be comfortable supporting this bill.

In this case, many of the concerns raised through the submission process were not only practical but they were quite technical. Tolling remains fair, because our consideration was that tolling must remain fair and not just a means by which to collective revenue, particularly at this time in history as we find ourselves in quite a prolonged situation where the cost of living really is biting a lot of people. So it seemed particularly pertinent that we weren’t introducing something that was just going to be used as another way to raise revenue. Because tolling’s still quite controversial. We don’t have a long history of it. I think Simon Court talked in his contribution about New Zealand being decades behind other countries when it comes to this issue, but that doesn’t mean that we’re really necessarily for it without that public trust. I think that that’s really important that that is done.

Of course, New Zealanders are under significant financial pressure, as I’ve said, and we have to make sure not only through this process but as this is implemented and as things will change in the future that transport funding never loses sight of the equity issue. Because not everybody can afford tolling. There will be consequences to a regime that does too much too quickly or that doesn't keep equity in sight.

Labour supports this bill because the funding ultimately does need to be moved into the 21st century. Modernisation shouldn’t be the ultimate goal if it doesn’t also include fairness, transparency, and public trust. Those changes that have been made through this process continue to give us confidence and therefore I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: Miles Anderson—what’s your road?

content.speaker: MILES ANDERSON (National—Waitaki)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I don’t have one.

content.speaker: Tim Costley
content.text: The road less travelled!

content.speaker: MILES ANDERSON
content.text: “The road less travelled”—that’s correct. Look, this is a very sensible bill. It’s obviously focused on fixing the basics and building the future. I commend the bill.
