Infrastructure Funding and Financing Amendment Bill
Legislative Statement

content.speaker: Hon JAMES MEAGER (Associate Minister of Transport)
content.text: on behalf of the Minister for Infrastructure: I present a legislative statement on the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Amendment Bill.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
Second Reading

content.speaker: Hon JAMES MEAGER (Associate Minister of Transport)
content.text: on behalf of the Minister for Infrastructure: I move, That the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Amendment Bill be now read a second time.

I’d like to start this contribution by thanking all of those involved in getting this bill to the second reading. To the members of the Finance and Expenditure Committee for their careful consideration of this bill, to the members of the public who took the time to provide both oral and written submissions: thank you to you all. Your input has helped to strengthen and improve this bill and it is greatly appreciated.

The rationale for this bill is as follows: we need to increase the effectiveness of the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act. That is a key component of pillar two of the Government’s Going for Housing Growth programme, which is focused on making improvements to infrastructure funding—you might say fixing our infrastructure funding network—and making improvements to the financing tools to help get more housing and the future of New Zealand’s housing built.

Under the status quo, councils and developers do face significant challenges to fund and finance the enabling infrastructure for housing. This Government and hopefully this House wants to move to a future state where funding and financing tools will enable a responsive supply of infrastructure where it is commercially viable to build new houses. This will shift market expectations of future scarcity, bring down the cost of land for new housing, and improve incentives to develop land sooner instead of holding it for land banking. This is a necessary step to help fix our housing crisis.

First, some background. The Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act was first established in 2020 as an alternative means to fund and finance infrastructure needed to support urban growth. It was a good idea and it had good intentions. However, the Act has fallen short of delivering additional infrastructure needed to respond to growth. To date, only three levies have been authorised. So this bill has the purpose of removing unnecessary barriers to using the Act to improve its viability for a range of infrastructure projects and to make the levy development and approvals process simpler and more streamlined.

The bill makes changes to streamline that levy approvals process. Currently, there’s an extensive process required for applicants to have a levy approved, and that can be a barrier when trying to use the Act. This bill will streamline the process and improve certainty for developers by simplifying requirements for levy proposals and recommendation reports, simplifying the mandatory considerations that the Minister of Housing must take into account when assessing the levy and improving certainty for developer-led proposals.

The bill also broadens the scope of the Act to improve its flexibility and viability for a range of infrastructure projects. This will better reflect the developer-led use of the tool and enable the Act to be used for transport projects delivered by agencies—for example, the New Zealand Transport Agency and KiwiRail—as part of a funding stack for transport infrastructure investment where it benefits property owners.

The bill also makes changes to enable the Act to be used for water infrastructure investments delivered by new water organisations established through the Local Government (Water Services) Act 2025 and allows for those water organisations to act as the responsible levy authority. In addition, the bill replaces the definition of community infrastructure so it is not required to be owned or controlled by a territorial authority. This broadens the potential use of the Act to therefore include community infrastructure that is owned or controlled by a third party, rather than that vested in a territorial authority. There are a number of other changes that the bill makes that are very, very important, but they are the key ones outlined so far.

In December last year, the bill was referred to the Finance and Expenditure Committee, so it’s been a while to get to this stage, and we’re hoping that it’ll progress with pace tonight. The bill received submissions from 60 interested groups and individuals and the select committee heard oral evidence from six submitters at hearings in Wellington and some via video conference. The select committee examined the bill and recommended that it be passed with amendments to a number of clauses, which the Government supports in full.

To strengthen consideration of affordability, the select committee proposed a change so that when the relevant Minister is assessing the affordability of a levy, they will also need to consider the cumulative affordability of the levy when combined with existing levies, rates, and water services charges. That’s sensible change, and I’m glad the select committee offered it forward.

In respond to feedback from iwi and Māori, an amendment is proposed to require levy proposals to include details of any consultation undertaken, including with affected landowners, iwi, or hapū. This will enable the recommender—that’s the person who assesses levy proposals and writes the recommendation report—and the responsible Minister to consider any consultation that has occurred, including any impacts for Māori raised during consultation as part of overall decision-making on the levy proposal.

An additional safeguard has also been added to the accelerated recovery mechanism to require a special-purpose vehicle to seek a court judgment for Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act (IFF Act) funding and financing costs before the special-purpose vehicle may apply to the registrar for the sale of undeveloped land. This new step would introduce an independent assessment of the amount of IFF Act funding and financing costs the special-purpose vehicle has determined needs to be repaid, and ensures that there is a judgment issued before sale proceedings may be commenced.

A number of further technical amendments have also been proposed by the committee to improve the workability of the bill, and, of course, we all agree with them wholeheartedly and look forward to their passage and acceptance in the second reading.

In conclusion, the changes in the bill and the bill itself will make the Act far more viable and flexible so that councils, developers, and other infrastructure providers can get on with fixing the basics of our housing crisis and building the infrastructure that our growing communities need. I commend it to the House.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: The question is that the motion be agreed to.

content.speaker: ARENA WILLIAMS (Labour—Manurewa)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. This is a sensible bill. It is a Labour Party idea that has come to fruition. Some good ideas survive elections. It is something that will get more pipes laid in the ground, get more roads built, get more houses going up, that is why we continue to support it. Even though there are some policy choices in here which would not have been our choices, we are serious about the housing crisis, and that makes us serious about infrastructure.

The test for this will really be whether it enables, in the next decade, in the lives of my kids and their kids, more infrastructure to be built faster and to be built, hopefully, as we spread the risk differently, cheaper, more affordably, and in the right place.

As the housing Minister said when he appeared at his scrutiny week hearing before the select committee—that is, all of these changes are important, but anything that’s not improving the planning system is just tinkering around the edges. This is tinkering; at least it is tinkering in the right direction, and I’m going to tell you how the select committee also tinkered with it.

It is building on Labour’s original framework, which was essentially acknowledging that we already have special-purpose vehicles as an ordinary part of Government funding and financing. Something like the City Rail Link is a special-purpose vehicle that exists—I think it’s a limited partnership that draws on not only council governance but also central governance and is able to access financing at its own rate and has its own risk balance on its books. Those are usually creatures of special legislation. This sets up a framework of legislation which can be used for anything.

We are debating this piece of legislation tonight because the Government doesn’t have its own special-purpose vehicles to build roads and to build pipes to pass new legislation, but don’t worry, we’ll pass a special rule book to deal with it in future when they do have some infrastructure proposals for us to consider in this House.

The way that it’s meant to work did have some exclusions. Some of those, you can imagine, were really important to Labour politicians, and they’re still really important to Labour politicians. One of them was the way that consultation would apply to an area of land which included Māori land. Māori land, now, under the new provisions, can be brought into a scheme, but it’s been excluded by the Minister from the ability to accelerate recovery.

There are two special rules going on here. One is, what sorts of rules can be included in the new regime where security and value of the land is being changed. From ACT Party perspective, you introduce a levy-making power over land, and the value of that land changes. That is a regulatory taking in their eyes, but that is allowed by this bill—in fact, it is enabled by this bill.

In the original formation of this bill, it was impossible for Māori land to be included in that, and I’ll tell you why. In a New Zealand Court of Appeal decision called the Mangatu case, Māori land was held to be differently valued for the purposes of the English common law that we associate with our Torrens system in New Zealand that governs land value.

I’m very proud of that case. It is my whānau that took that case, Mangatu is my land: an area the size of Hamilton City that my whānau, over six generations have reclaimed their rangatiratanga over, first started by my great-great grandmother Waioeka for whom my daughter is named.

In that case, the Court of Appeal agreed with the claimant and said that because Māori land is governed in such a way, that sale is tightly restricted and there’s a pool of purchasers that is smaller, and that there are additional governance and administration costs associated with owning Māori land, that it should not be rated in the same way. Most recently, the Government has a set of 2019 guidelines that set out how it should be rated. That’s relevant, because when you consider the different value in our common law that’s associated with Māori land, when you are going introduce a new levy-making power for Government over that land, you would also expect the rules to recognise that common law position.

This bill has brought Māori land into this scheme. It is possible now for it to be included in an area that which will be relevant for things like Watercare’s new wastewater and sewerage treatment facilities that are being built out in Māngere. Māngere is one of the few areas in Auckland with a significant proportion of Māori land, including Ihumātao. That would have been a reason why it would have been difficult, say, for this provision to be used under the old formulation that will be included in the new formulation of the bill.

That has been excluded from the provision, which makes it really valuable. Any private equity financier that looks at the arrangement and sees that they cannot claim against Māori land—that will give them pause, and it is an appropriate kind of protection for Māori land, given that it is very hard to sell and shouldn’t be easy to claim against if you’re a financier looking to recover your amount by selling land. Those are pretty broad provisions that will require the sale of land, and it is appropriate that they are restricted in this way by this legislation.

Some of the changes that the committee has made deserve some level of scrutiny at this stage. One of the issues that the committee rightly pointed to was raised by the Regulations Review Committee about the regulation-making powers in section 29 that relate to the setting of levies. It’s a pretty broad power, and it’s broad by design, but it does function much more like a taxation-making power in that, currently, the formulation is that any area of land can be levied by the special-purpose vehicle. It may be on top of rates, and may be on top of other charges which are being charged for the same thing.

An example of this would be in a water infrastructure setting, some of some rates and some value within a rateable value of land is being paid for water infrastructure, but to set up something like the Wellington sludge factory, you might have otherwise included a consideration for that in your rates, but then there is also this extra top-up charge levied against those property owners that’s appropriate for that kind of future-focused infrastructure, but it was given particular consideration here because it is a very broad power.

The officials when asked that question by the committee came back with pretty comprehensive advice on why that was appropriate and why it was also comparable to international jurisdictions. The committee has relied on that advice, and it is worth understanding that the committee did turn its mind to this broad levy-making power is much more akin to a taxation-making power.

The second thing which is worth bringing to the attention of the committee is the findings it made and were shared by all members around consultation with Māori. The officials asked the committee, “Can we engage with stakeholders? Can we go out, given that this has been introduced pretty quickly by the legislature and we haven’t done that consultation with iwi-Māori groups?”

When they did that, one of the particular issues that came up was, when the levy is set by the special-purpose vehicle (SPV), the SPV might not have any requirements on it to go out and consult, so that is now included. Especially given that now there is a change to the way that those SPVs might not be set up where you might not have Government, which has duties under Te Tiriti o Waitangi; you might not have local government, either, which has duties under Te Tiriti o Waitangi by its delegated constitutional arrangements from the Crown; you might have something which is running that SPV which doesn’t have those underlying constitutional duties. So having that requirement to consult is useful—

content.speaker: Simon Court
content.text: We just need the pipes. We don’t care about the constitution.

content.speaker: ARENA WILLIAMS
content.text: The ACT Party has just one trick. Simon Court says, “Just build the pipes. We don’t care about te ao Māori.”

The point is that if you are levying citizens, you should tell them clearly, and that is a principle of the ACT Party—I think they used to have that in their constitution. But obviously not. Obviously if you’re a Māori landowner, then it is fine to have a regulatory taking and to pay an extra levy which is more like a tax—is it? Oh, he’s lost for words now.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: He won’t be soon!

content.speaker: ARENA WILLIAMS
content.text: Ha, ha!

The next part that the committee raised, which is important just to note, is the right to challenge the validity of the levy. The committee considered this carefully, and the reason for that—I’m going to sound like an ACT Party member now—is that when local government and central government delegate their power to somebody who is not the Government to charge a levy to the citizenry, we should be very careful about that, and that shouldn’t be done by officials; it should be done by a power which is really, really clear.

content.speaker: Simon Court
content.text: User pays—say it!

content.speaker: ARENA WILLIAMS
content.text: The member is heckling me; he’s saying, “User pays”. Yes, users should pay, but levy makers shouldn’t use the coercive power of the State against citizens who can’t stand up to them if they are not, in fact, elected. A party that believes in elected members and elected power and would go so far as to remove the Independent Māori Statutory Board from the Auckland super-city should believe that; they should at least have some conviction in their principles, but they do not tonight.

So, with that, I am very happy that we have cross-partisan and bipartisan support for a sensible infrastructure bill. Even if the ACT Party can’t quite work out tonight what they think about it, we will press on to build the houses, build the roads, and put the pipes in the ground regardless of the ideology on that side of the House.

content.speaker: FRANCISCO HERNANDEZ (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise on behalf of the Green Party to speak on this bill. I think the thing that’s really important to guide this conversation is the sorts of numbers that we know are around the infrastructure sphere. We know that we do have an infrastructure deficit of around $200 billion, and we know that it’s going to cost around $1 trillion to fix it over the next 30 years. So a bill like this that enables settings to help us address those deficits is a positive thing.

We do agree with some of the words that have been said by the two previous speakers. In particular, we agree with the nods to cross-partisanship and bipartisanship that were given by the first speaker, James Meager, and also, then, Arena Williams. Working together in a cross-party way is a good way that we can help address, in a cross-party way, the infrastructure deficit and the gaps that do exist. The infrastructure plan that was signed off, I think, a few weeks ago did have forewords from both Opposition parties. So that was an encouraging sign.

Now, this bill does some things that we do support. One of the top things that it does is to reduce and simplify requirements for levy proposals and recommendation reports. That’s a good step forward. Reducing and simplifying the mandatory considerations that the Minister must take into account when assessing a levy is also a positive step forward, from our point of view. We do think that’s really important because as either the first or second speaker said—or maybe they both said it—only three projects actually managed to get into the levy under the previous legislation. So simplifying it and making sure that it’s more accessible is a pretty good step forward.

One of the things that we emphasise that is also a good step for this bill is the broadening of the purpose beyond just addressing local authority financing. We do regard that as a positive thing. We do think that it’s good to be able to use other transport projects such as that delivered by the New Zealand Transport Agency or KiwiRail or for other water infrastructure.

content.speaker: Hon Member
content.text: He loves it!

content.speaker: FRANCISCO HERNANDEZ
content.text: Well, we’ve articulated the things we do like about the bill, but you know, I do need to say the things that we do have concerns about on this current bill.

Now, while we did support the enactment of the original Infrastructure Funding and Finance Act in 2020, you know, on a case by case basis, in general we might prefer it if development contributions are borrowed by local and central government, but we do acknowledge that the additional tool could serve an additional purpose. But we are a little bit sceptical about potential things that don’t protect endpoint public ownership or things that might allow for securitisation of public infrastructure. So we are a little bit cautious.

content.speaker: Tim van de Molen
content.text: Stop reading your speech!

content.speaker: FRANCISCO HERNANDEZ
content.text: Well, I’m not reading the speech. There’s no speech that I’ve written. That’s the problem—I’m making it up as I go. I wish I had a speech that was pre-written. I wish I had the pre-written speech. I’m just reading these notes.

The things that we do find concerning that I do need to stress are the things around the requirements to assess the levy affordability for proposals supported by developers. We also find a little bit concerning—well, we do support better ways to fund and finance infrastructure, and we do support the overall intent of the bill. We do have some concerns that it might enable private developers or Crown entities to proceed with ill-considered projects and lock people into unaffordable payments. Now, that has been characterised by some members as unnecessary barriers, but it’s possible that some projects might not necessarily stack up.

I think some of the submissions articulate a lot of the concerns that we’ve expressed around the potential for this bill to, essentially—it does enable financing, and that is an important part of it, but as New Zealanders for a Democratic Economy put it in their submission, sometimes things that are limited in financial scope can be limited in imagination and outlook. We do agree with their concerns that it operates from the assumption that the dominant factor in formulating public infrastructure necessarily should rely on market mechanisms. We do think that a broader bill that considers what kind of public infrastructure might be most conducive to the public good might be better in terms of considering things like sustainable development, in terms of national wealth, in terms of workers’ wealth, workers’ rights, ecological limits, and long-term planning. But the problem is that this financing is only one aspect of a potentially broader project for national development that we need to undertake.

We do think that this bill will accelerate infrastructure delivery, but we are concerned that it does so in the process of shifting risk, cost, and control away from community and democratic oversight towards the more financialised structures, which might serve to obscure or evade public scrutiny; that is something that we did put in our differing view. It is a concern that I think we should articulate again at this stage.

We do like the fact that this bill does allow infrastructure to be financed through long-term levies attached to land titles. In general, the idea of making people pay for things that benefit them, that might potentially benefit their property or land values, is a good thing. Ultimately, things like developer contributions are potentially a good mechanism, especially for capturing the value that might be captured in this land. That mechanism, basically, effectively, socialises private development costs across time.

But we do have, as I’ve said, some concerns, and one of them is, again, the embedding of infrastructure funding within the special purpose vehicles, which raise money through private finance and recover costs through levies. We do think that that might lead to things like shifting financial control to private lenders and things like shifting decision making away from democratic institutions. And under the more traditional models, public infrastructure builds traditionally sit within accountability frameworks that can be held accountable and are sort of auditable, or have some mechanisms that enable scrutiny of it.

So, for example, under the current public provision model, ratepayers can seek information, Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act (LGOIMA) their councils, and, ultimately, ratepayers can have the ultimate veto—being able to remove their councils if they don’t like what they’re doing.

It’s the same principle that governs central government as well. If you have questions about a project, you’re able to make an Official Information Act request or, ultimately, if you don’t like a project that’s been approved, you have the ultimate veto of being able to de-elect a Government.

content.speaker: Mike Davidson
content.text: Happening 7 November.

content.speaker: FRANCISCO HERNANDEZ
content.text: Yes, exactly. These mechanisms which do enable more public-private partnerships is something that might potentially lead to less accountability. And our concern about the special purpose vehicle (SPV) model is also about the embedding of the commercial logic into the heart of infrastructure delivery. We do know that the special purpose vehicles have a legal duty to maximise returns for their investors over things like the public good. We do think that the public good is something that should have the overriding consideration. We’re not necessarily opposed to SPVs inherently, as short-term measures or things that might alleviate the infrastructure burden, which is real and is only growing, but examples of this are not hypothetical. There’s no guarantee that the stormwater systems that will be built to the standards that we need to enable long-term public infrastructure or adaptation. We do know that community centres might face pressure to commercialise.
Thank you so much. I’ll yield the floor now.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: Simon Court. I’ve been waiting for your right of reply.

content.speaker: SIMON COURT (ACT)
content.text: As the co-sponsor, along with Minister Chris Bishop, the Minister for Infrastructure, this Infrastructure Funding and Financing Amendment Bill has the potential to fix a real infrastructure blockage. New Zealand needs more homes, but homes need pipes, roads, stormwater, transport links, and power. Because without that infrastructure, houses are delayed, they’re made more expensive, or never built at all. That has been New Zealand’s problem for too long.

Land has been rationed by planning rules, councils have been constrained by debt limits, and funding tools have been too slow, too costly, and too hard to use. Developers have been ready to build, buyers have been ready to buy, but the infrastructure system has too often said “no”. This bill helps turn “no” into a “yes”. It’s part of the Government’s Going for Housing Growth programme: to free up land, improve infrastructure funding and financing, and to give councils better incentives to support growth. That’s exactly the principle we need: growth should pay for growth. The people who benefit from new infrastructure should contribute to its cost over a reasonable time.

Private capital, investors, should be able to respond to demand, but the Act has not worked as intended. That’s why we’re amending it. Only three levy proposals have been authorised. That’s not a lack of need; that is a failure of process and, dear I say, a failure of will. New Zealand Initiative’s report, Finance Freedom, makes the same point. New Zealand’s housing shortage starts with pipes and roads. Where councils cannot fund growth infrastructure, planning rules, councils end up rationing growth that forces up the price of housing. Families pay the bill. The answer is a second finance channel: private investors funding infrastructure and future residents repaying that cost over time. That is what this bill supports.

In 2022, I visited Texas and Colorado, including Dallas and Denver. I saw how special purpose vehicles, like those enabled under this Act, support housing growth and development. This year, where the United States has reached its 250-year milestone, there is much to learn from our state-side friends as to how to unlock growth and deliver housing at an affordable price. They do not wait for every pipe, road, and utility connection to be funded through an overloaded council balance sheet. They define the growth area, finance the network, build ahead of demand, and recover the cost over a reasonable time from properties that benefit. That is not theory; that is engineering discipline that is what New Zealand needs right now.

We do not need to copy Texas or Colorado wholesale, but we should learn the lesson. When people want to build homes, when private capital is willing to finance the infrastructure, Government and councils should not be the blockage. This bill removes the blockage. It simplifies the mandatory considerations for approving a levy. It requires levy and infrastructure authorities, including councils, to provide endorsements where statutory requirements are met. If the legal test is satisfied, a council should not be able to stall a project simply through enforcing process. It also extends the eligibility for infrastructure delivered by the New Zealand Transport Agency and KiwiRail and new water service organisations.

The select committee has improved the bill. I support these technical changes. These changes protect levy payers, as Arena Williams pointed out—it’s an important consideration—but they keep the tool workable. This bill is not about Government building everything; it is about Government setting clear rules so infrastructure can be financed and funded where people need it. We will not fix housing by signalling intention alone. We will fix it by freeing up land, cutting delays, funding infrastructure, and letting people who want to pay for it build the stuff we need. I commend it to the House.

One of the key things, and I think it was traversed a little bit last night as well, was this SPV, special purpose vehicle, arrangement. You know, the name is on the tin. What I find really amusing about when we’re all in agreement here is that we have to take a slightly different approach to things, and that’s what the philosophers call a heterodox approach. In other words, we listen to everybody, and we all agree, and we’re going to get there in the end—as I heard last night, which is really nice.
The SPVs: the Nats claimed it, then Labour claimed it, and then ACT claimed it, and the Greens were—

Sir Bob Harvey was the chair. It was, really, an SPV, a special purpose vehicle. It wasn’t just about housing; it was the development of the waterfront, it came from the Auckland City Council, and then it was rolled over into the new Auckland Council. And, oh, by the way, everyone that keeps calling Auckland a city, I’ll just remind you that, actually, it has a regional part. If you really look at the understanding of regional development, it is a city region. But, anyway, I traversed that a little bit.

Waterfront Auckland was time-limited, it was for a special purpose, and, here’s the kicker, it was public investment that catalysed private investment. That’s what these things do. Waterfront Auckland being time-limited was rolled into Eke Panuku, which is now the Auckland Urban Development Office. It fulfilled the purpose—so congratulations to Sir Bob Harvey for a job well done. It’s not just about housing; obviously, that’s one of the jewels for Auckland. There’s the waterfront and the work that was done there.

Let’s just get to the Green Party member’s concern about special purpose vehicles. What are we trying to do here? Special purpose vehicles: well, it’s on the tin. The special purpose vehicle here is about, if you like, private benefit and public good.

content.speaker: Tom Rutherford

content.speaker: Dr DAVID WILSON

content.speaker: Tom Rutherford
content.text: No one’s listening.

content.speaker: Dr DAVID WILSON
content.text: I’ll get to that in a second. But, unfortunately, Tom, you’re not my whip. Ha, ha! Yes, it’s a balancing act, and it takes skill and experience. I’m still trying to find a little bit of that here! I’ve been in this kind of job and this kind of process many, many times before, and it’s all about leveraging for the public good or for the community’s benefit. That is the essence of economic development. That’s how you do it.

I’ve seen a lot of snake oil salesmen, in my time, coming with really good projects where they want public money, and you’ve really got to sort those ones out. If you ask a simple question to any proponent: what’s in it for the public? What’s in it for the ratepayer? What’s in it for the taxpayer?—in any project. That’s the whole purpose of this. That’s the whole purpose. I’ve also seen leaders in the private sector—to the Green Party member’s concerns about SPVs—such as Sir Ron Carter, Sir Stephen Tindall, Sir Eoin Edgar. There’s a reason they’re sirs: because they had the community at their heart, just like Bob. Bob did a good job. Whatever that is and however you make those arrangements, what I like about the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Amendment Bill is that there are some guardrails there to ensure that the public gets the benefit out of these things, and we implement in the proper way.

So, yes, back to the bill, sometimes councils are under the real pressure to provide infrastructure where rates are insufficient—for example, those ones that are heavily touristed or are under pressure from rapid growth. It’s about unlocking New Zealand’s infrastructure potential, infrastructure funding and financing. The model is good. And, may I remind the House, that things like the Provincial Growth Fund and the Regional Infrastructure Fund do this all the time; it’s not new. We need this balancing act, and we need the guardrails. We, as New Zealand First, commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: MIKE DAVIDSON (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. What a good morning to everyone. It’s such a lovely morning. I hope everyone got a good sleep last night. It’s a bit of a shame to hear New Zealand First—all they want to do is have a go at the Green Party, when all we do is just care. We care.

content.speaker: Dr David Wilson
content.text: I was taking care of your concerns.

content.speaker: MIKE DAVIDSON
content.text: And I thank you, Dr Wilson. It was actually a little bit disappointing to hear your coalition partners just telling you to hurry up the whole time while you were trying to alleviate our concerns with this bill. It feels like there’s a few little cracks happening over there.

I will get back to the bill. It is good. It is a privilege to stand up on behalf of the Green Party to speak to this bill. We know, when this was first enacted back in 2020, we supported the bill, and, obviously, it hasn’t been hugely successful since then. I actually do recall as a city councillor the ability—if we’d had a special purpose vehicle, some of the things we could have actually achieved. We know that there are concerns when you do some of these significant infrastructure projects—the impacts they do have on councils and, therefore, ratepayers—so having a mechanism to ensure that doesn’t happen and move that issue away from ratepayers is actually a sensible thing. Ensuring that we do have an ability that enables good public investment is actually very, very good. Through this process, the Greens have been working hard to ensure that actually what we do get is an outcome that is beneficial to the public and enables growth that can pay for itself in a way that is sustainable.

We still do have some concerns about where we’re at. I think we’ve got to be a little bit careful, because we know, when we’re looking at growth paying for growth, there are issues that do impact councils significantly from that attitude. But, obviously, we can create these mechanisms that remove that.

I’m always concerned when we look at growth just for the sake of growth and ensuring that it’s commercially viable, when, actually, what we need to really make sure is that it’s not just commercially viable but also, just as importantly, stacks up environmentally, because we do know that growth for the sake of growth is not sustainable. We cannot just keep having urban sprawl.

There’s potential, when we create these bills that enable more development, that that development can occur in the wrong place; that will end up having impacts on future generations, future councils that have to actually pay for the cost of where we build. It is really important that we get our urban planning right and we have financial structures that actually enable it to happen. We need to make sure that we control where it does happen. Our natural resources are finite, and we cannot abuse that. If we do, we are failing future generations. What I have seen from this term of Government is a Government that just keeps doing that same—

content.speaker: RYAN HAMILTON (National—Hamilton East)
content.text: This bill literally unlocks infrastructure growth, just like Te Awa Lakes north of Hamilton. We’ve got a $50 million Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act loan to unlock 2,500 houses. This is about fixing the basics and building the future, literally.

content.speaker: Dr TRACEY McLELLAN (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker, and aren’t we peppy this morning, on this real Friday—perpetual Tuesday?

content.speaker: Hon Todd McClay
content.text: You mean last Friday wasn’t real?

content.speaker: Dr TRACEY McLELLAN
content.text: Ha, ha! Labour supports the Infrastructure (Funding and Financing) Amendment Bill, as was very eloquently noted last night, when we started this debate, by my colleague Arena Williams. However, she did raise some concerns, and I want to go through those a little bit today as well.

Infrastructure funding matters—we know that—but who ultimately pays matters just as much, and I want to highlight some of those concerns. Ultimately, we support better tools for unlocking housing and infrastructure. We know that New Zealand needs to unlock our infrastructure. We’ve got a huge deficit that we need to figure out better ways of grappling with. We know that too many developments have been delayed because things like the pipes, the roads, and other sorts of essential services don’t get funded upfront.

Financing infrastructure is never cost-free. The key question in this particular bill is who carries that cost and where is it transparent, and whether, actually, households can genuinely afford it. I agree with my colleague Mike Davidson: sometimes, we do have to think about the nature of growth. This bill does create a model that makes funding easier, but it cannot be used as an excuse to simply shift costs on to families already dealing with rates increases, mortgages, and everyday expenses in the cost of living. Ultimately, we can’t solve one affordability problem by simply shifting and creating a problem somewhere else.

The infrastructure levies, we acknowledge, can help new houses to get built, which is a good thing, but those levies remain attached to a property, sometimes for 20, 30, 40, 50 years. A developer or a current owner may support the levy because it makes a project easier to proceed with initially, but it’s often the future homeowners who are the ones who are going to make those payments. They almost certainly wouldn’t have been involved in the original decisions, so they might not fully understand the long-term costs when they purchase that property. Labour’s concern is that removing the affordability assessments, which has been done in some circumstances, could make a house appear more affordable upfront, which is alluring, but it does leave the new owner with a substantial ongoing charge.

The other thing that we are concerned about is the expansion into transport, and that raises some unresolved questions. One of the most significant changes is allowing this type of financing model to be used more widely for transport projects, including projects that have traditionally been led by national transport agencies for national transport infrastructure, and therefore funded through those national mechanisms. Labour doesn’t want this bill to become, essentially, a backdoor to fund things that have traditionally been funded by central government—just shifting it on to local government and, therefore, local communities and ratepayers. This concern is even sharper when, obviously, the Government is also proposing a cap to rates. Some of that doesn’t quite add up, and I think that that does require a little bit more scrutiny. Obviously, the councils could be expected to collect new infrastructure levies via this model, whilst also having a restriction placed on them about how they could fund their own essential services. That contradiction, I think, remains unresolved via this process.

I think the other important factor to take note of is that local communities and councils absolutely have to retain a meaningful voice in this process. The bill significantly narrows the circumstances in which a council can refuse to endorse a levy. In practice, this means that councils may be required to support a levy unless collecting it would put rate collection at risk. What does that necessarily even mean? The process around that remains a little bit opaque. Whilst we, again, support the streamlining of a process, we think that communities deserve some proper information and, actually, some genuine consultation so that they can have confidence that not only are their views being taken into account but the ultimate outcome is a good one.

The select committee, we believe, has strengthened protections around some of the forced land sales, which was a really important topic. As has been noted last night and this morning, the bill as introduced gave special purpose vehicles (SPV) a very broad power where development failed. An SPV could have sought the sale of undeveloped land based largely on its own assessment—sometimes, possibly, without even the requisite necessary information to make that independent process very clear to the landowner, to challenge the debt, which is an important part of that process.

My colleague Arena Williams talked a little bit last night about the situation that Māori land owners would find themselves in, and the fact that they absolutely deserve more than a tick-box consultation during this process. It’s a different set of circumstances with unique and sometimes complicated but bespoke considerations. Any piece of legislation that we enact needs to account for that properly so that we don’t create unintended or even intended negative consequences down the track.

Going back to the SPV, the select committee has recommended that that vehicle must first obtain a court decision, a court judgment, before it can apply for a forced sale, and that seems absolutely sensible to us, and congratulations to those people on that select committee that made that happen. We welcome that amendment; it was important to go through that process. It restores, ultimately, judicial oversight and protects natural justice, which is always absolutely important, and it ensures that the amount claimed can be properly tested before someone risks losing their land. You can imagine all the various situations where that could occur. A forced land sale is always a stressful and unfortunate situation, and there absolutely has to be public confidence that that’s done properly.

The affordability must be assessed cumulatively, not levied by levy, and that was another important consideration for the select committee. Households don’t experience rates, water charges, infrastructure levies in isolation; they experience it as one combined bill. They get their rates notice, they perhaps pay it annually, they pay it quarterly—whatever—but they get their rates notice, and not that many people go through it line by line and pontificate about the contribution that each thing makes to its overall rating. But that is how they experience the rating system.

Labour therefore welcomes the select committee’s recommendation that the Minister must consider the cumulative impact of a new levy alongside existing rates, water services charges, and other levies. This responds, we think, directly to concerns raised about double-dipping. Even just saying the word out loud—no one likes the concept of double-dipping. We’ve had various examples of that over the years. It feels, hence, like the fact that someone’s doing something to you that you didn’t realise was happening, and there’s nothing worse than feeling like you’re getting a bit ripped off.

In this particular example, where people may be charged several times for overlapping infrastructure costs—and you can imagine how potentially complicated some of that levying could end up being—it’s really important that that safeguard be there. Labour will obviously continue to argue for affordability protections and make sure that they are applied consistently, including for future homeowners, who are the ones who are ultimately going to bear these costs, but we support building houses. We think unlocking the potential to ensure that the pipes, the roads, and all those other services are financed out-front—because we acknowledge that that is often the sticking point for growth and development, and therefore we support this bill.

content.speaker: DAN BIDOIS (National—Northcote)
content.text: This is such a good bill. I’m going to commend it to the House.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB (Labour—Christchurch Central)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. This bill does build on an excellent initiative of the last Labour Government—

content.speaker: Hon Member
content.text: Is that Helen Clark’s?

content.speaker: Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB
content.text: —because we’ve always recognised the need for well-planned and well-funded development. This bill essentially improves in some respects the—

content.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall
content.text: Oh, now they have opinions over there—saying they can’t give speeches!

content.speaker: Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB
content.text: Why are you heckling me? Ha, ha! It improves in some respects the infrastructure framework that we put in place. In fact, here in Wellington, if I recall correctly, the sludge plant is funded exactly by this framework.

I think we do need to remember that, essentially, what this does is it allows a funding stream to repay what is usually commercial lending. By having a statutory framework, it gives some assurance to any lender that there will be a long-term source of income to finance interest costs and principal repayments, but it is still, essentially, borrowing for infrastructure. There is no magic way to come up with this cash—we’ve got to come up with it from somewhere. This is simply deferring and stretching out the repayments, usually across 30 or 50 years. As my colleague noted, someone’s got to pay. This framework essentially puts those costs on ratepayers and property owners across the long term. It’s not some magical way to get infrastructure for free, but it does smooth the costs out.

Having said that, there is some concern that we’re seeing a Government that wants to cap rates on the one hand for a cheap political win, but, in fact, this will simply impose other costs on ratepayers. It’s a little bit of the old magic cup—moving the costs around. Let’s be upfront about this, and it’s quite right that we need to be very careful about making sure that the overall costs imposed on homeowners in particular are affordable, because we’ve set up a new water system and we’ve seen water rates going up pretty significantly. We’ve got a framework of levies already. We’ve got special rates—in Christchurch there’s a special rate being imposed for some rebuild work. Then we’ve got this additional levy. Here in Wellington, we’ve had some accounting errors with the sludge levy where that’s caused some issues as well. It’s all costs, and if we do have infrastructure funded this way, it will increase, essentially, the bill of ratepayers. It’s just another way for rates to go up, so we’ve got to keep an eye on affordability.

I do want also to just express a little bit of concern about the watering down of protections for Māori land. Obviously, development does benefit Māori land, but we need to be cautious that we don’t think that just because we’re building some infrastructure plant or roading which benefits Māori land, we’ve got an untrammelled right to levy that land. Consultation on those projects is very important. In fact, as I understand it, previously, Māori land owners, iwi, and hapū were required to consent, but now, once you’re across a certain threshold, it can be imposed on them. In terms of tino rangatiratanga, that’s a bit of a concern, because Māori land—how it’s rated and how it’s dealt with and how it’s held—has always kind of been the last bastion of autonomy for Māori. This is just encroaching on it a little bit. I’m concerned about these small encroachments. I’m sure there’ll be more to be said about that.

The other thing, I guess, that I’d just like to say is the dangers around failed projects, because exactly what amounts to a failed project? A lot of these projects take a long time. They might not take off—look at Rolleston; didn’t take off overnight, but it took off eventually. We’ve got to be really cautious about leaping to a conclusion that there’s been a failure, when, in fact, all that’s needed is more time. I understand the select committee had a look at that—that’s good—but caution is required there. But, overall, it’s building on a good Labour initiative.

content.speaker: TOM RUTHERFORD (National—Bay of Plenty)
content.text: It’s time to get this done. I commend it to the House.

content.speaker: TANGI UTIKERE (Labour—Palmerston North)
content.text: Kia orana. Good morning, Mr Speaker. Look, it’s a pleasure to rise and speak in support of the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Amendment Bill. This was a bill that has been reported back to the House via the Finance and Expenditure Committee. I’m not a member of that committee, but I did have an opportunity to sit in on some of the submissions and, indeed, some of the advice in terms of the committee’s consideration on this bill. The report-backs are currently in front of the House.

There were 60 submissions. I think it was around about half a dozen who did front up and appear in front of the select committee. I do want to acknowledge the officials, particularly what was the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development and the Office of the Clerk, and obviously the Parliamentary Counsel Office as well.

We support this bill because we do recognise the need for good tools in order to fund and deliver infrastructure. The funding is the important part, as is the delivery. As my colleague the Hon Dr Duncan Webb has already indicated this morning, this was a bill that was introduced under the previous Labour Government. Naturally, we have had a look at this and have continued to support it, based on what we see currently in front of us.

New Zealand has, as we know, a bit of an infrastructure deficit in this country. What we do need is practical ways to unlock growth for housing, for further growth, and obviously for resilience, which is why we, as a team, do support the Infrastructure Commission’s National Infrastructure Plan and obviously the response that was provided by our infrastructure spokesperson, the Hon Kieran McAnulty, who did provide a forward as part of that. We are serious about the need around tackling the infrastructure deficit in New Zealand. Part of that is looking at how things are funded and how things are financed as well.

The question is not whether infrastructure should be built; it must be built in this country. We’ll go on to talk a little bit around what some of those particular parts of infrastructure will be in a moment, but whether the funding model is fair, whether it’s affordable, and whether it is transparent is what we have been looking at when we have considered this bill. Funding models are important, yes, but it’s not just an approach where some can be effectively introduced without consideration around where the transparency lens is. Colleagues have already touched on that in earlier contributions as part of this bill, as well.

Infrastructure financing absolutely should help communities to grow, but it shouldn’t just be about moving costs from one balance sheet to the other. We do need to understand that these decisions have an impact on households and on household budgets. That’s why ensuring that infrastructure projects go through the Infrastructure Commission’s independent insurance assessment process is really, really important. The reason why that is important is because, if we are looking at the funding opportunities and how things will be financed, knowing that a project actually stacks up through an independent lens is going to ensure some certainty and longevity for the project. I do hope that the Government, in terms of thinking about the wider brief of infrastructure, do consider that as well.

The important thing is when we, I guess, look at this particular bill, and some might see that as a form of streamlining a particular process—what is important is that that doesn’t soon become a euphemism for simply removing safeguards that need to be in place to make sure that there are checks and balances; that there isn’t a reduction in engagement with community as to how that might work, or, indeed, a weakening of accountability for when these decisions are made and when they’re taken; and that there is accountability as a key part of that. For Labour, we have been constructive in this space. We support the objective of enabling infrastructure—good infrastructure—infrastructure that connects communities but that also stacks up, and we will continue to scrutinise the detail. That is certainly a responsibility.

One of the changes that the select committee did make—and it’s one that the Labour Party were very, very keen on—is this issue of cumulative affordability. It’s something that my colleague Dr Tracey McLellan has touched on, and that is looking at affordability through the lens of not just whether in isolation these costs and items can be afforded or not, but actually an acknowledgment of the fact that households get a number of calls on their household budget. The Minister, in considering any sort of levy proposal, whether to advance that or not—one of the changes that has been made is that the Minister needs to consider that proposal alongside the existing levies, the existing rates, the existing costs that are already in place; the existing water charges that Dr Webb has touched on.

We’ve called for that change, and it’s good to see that that is a change that has been included in here. It means that the consideration as to whether a proposal should succeed or not, or even be put on the table, will have those cumulative considerations on households and their budgets made before those future decisions are actually taken. While a levy may, in a traditional sense, sit outside traditional rates, for families, that is still another bill that is coming through the door. That’s why there is a real need for there to be that active consideration.

One of the aspects that the select committee did spend a little bit of time on is the requirement for consultation with those landowners who would be affected by a proposal, and also with iwi and hapū as well. I want to acknowledge the officials who, under the direction of the select committee, did spend quite a bit of time going through this. Permission was granted for them to go out and consult concurrently at the same time that the select committee was considering this bill, and on page 5 of the select committee’s report, this arose out of concern that engagement needed to occur with iwi Māori organisations and other individuals around levy areas or charges that may affect Māori land, for Māori land that is subject to the Treaty settlement process, and also acknowledging the fact that infrastructure decisions that may be taken may affect Māori land. It’s pleasing to see that a result of that is a change to the bill that will require there to be active consultation, and the requirement also indicates and shows the lengths that have been taken to ensure that that consultation has been disclosed with the affected parties, with iwi, with hapū as well, and that that’s part of the whole process.

I want to just make some brief comments on transport because part of the focus of this bill is to allow for the funding, potentially, of transport infrastructure that leads to growth opportunities. In terms of transport infrastructure, we all know that this Government has a $56 billion suite of roads of national significance, and that number continues to grow. They accept that they need to reprioritise and reassess that, to rescope those projects, because right now they have a $30 billion fiscal hole in terms of that plan. One could say that that’s why they’re perhaps looking at any funding and financing opportunity around transport infrastructure to meet that .

We need to be very clear that this is not to be seen as an opportunity to grab every single bit of coin and every dollar that is out in the community to fund transport projects that do not stack up. For the sort of shift in this space to allow transport agencies like Waka Kotahi, NZ Transport Agency, to trigger projects that may result in local levies, it is important that that transparency at the local level still exists. It is important that the accountability for the decisions that have been taken by those that make those decisions still exists, and it is important that the consultation and accountability exists there as well.

Our concern is not with enabling infrastructure per se. Our concern, and my concern in the transport space, is with who pays for these projects. Who decides where these projects are going to go? Do they stack up through that independent lens, and are those costs affordable over time? What is very clear, under the current Government, is that their roads of national significance are not affordable, they are not funded, they are not going to be delivered anytime soon, and so they need to go through a process of reprioritisation, and we all wait as to when that is going to happen. We all think that there’s not going to be a Government policy statement on land transport before the election. That would be the first time in more than two decades that that has been the case. We do hope that the Government is serious about focusing on transport infrastructure, and moving forward we’ll continue to keep watching.

content.speaker: NANCY LU (National)
content.text: This bill is part of National’s plan to fix the basics, to unlock growth potential, and to build a future for New Zealand, particularly when most of the submitters have supported this bill. I commend it to the House.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I think this is a really interesting bill, because I think, overall, when it comes to public infrastructure and also facilities, there are some good aspects to this bill. I think one of the things in particular, as we heard from previous speakers on this bill, is around the ability or the streamlining of this in terms of the levies regarding infrastructure funding and financing (IFF).

This bill is an omnibus bill. While it’s intending on making the existing IFF models more usable, flexible, and viable by making it easier for such infrastructure projects—and I think we’ve heard some of those, and I will discuss more in terms of both housing, urban development, as well as transport to be funded—there are definitely still additional kinds of concerns that the Greens have regarding how this is going to work in other respects, particularly whether this is a way for the Crown, for example, to wash some of its responsibilities and look at further privatisation rather than putting in public funding. I think this is something that we mentioned and were looking at as a part of the select committee process—that this bill will allow for something like that to proceed with ill-considered projects and lock people into unaffordable repayment.

What’s really interesting, I think, in the context of this bill, is that what has been characterised as unnecessary barriers to uptake of the IFF may actually be that projects don’t stack up and shouldn’t be built in the first place. I think the previous speaker Tangi Utikere has mentioned some of the unaffordability when it comes to roads of national significance. I think, when we’re looking at some of the billions and billions of dollars that have been proposed on some of those, the burden it would have on both local government ratepayers as well as taxpayers, it is a concern. For a lot of those, I think we can agree, if we put them into other areas such as public transport, or even more varied things and diverse modes of transportation, like cycling and also rail, we’d potentially see better use for money. I think there are great potentials for this bill, but it’s the implementation that is going to be interesting to see as we develop.

I think one of the other things around this bill, when we’re looking at the levy aspect, is something that I think in general we’ve seen the Audit Office being quite interested in, in terms of some of the nuances between whether we would consider this a levy, consider this a fee, or consider it as a tax. This is something we have discussed across quite a few varied bills here in the House this term, and I think some of this blurriness potentially has piqued the interest of the Audit Office, as we see in some of their latest reports.

In this particular case, when we’re looking at the levy-making power, and particularly when we’re looking at, for example, the cumulative affordability concerns and the fact that one of the new sections, section 27—which will be interesting to unpack with the Minister more during the committee stage coming up—will simplify the mandatory consideration that the Minister must make when taking into account before recommending a levy order be made. I think it’s also important—and this is something that I think deserves further unpacking during the committee stage—when we’re looking at that levy-making power, looking at where some of that levy-making power is and where some of that levy is going to go.

As I mentioned before, if the levy, for example, were looking at specifically going towards the same remit and within the same scope of a particular agency or particular local authority, that potentially is useful. It’s helpful. However, what I’ve seen, for example, in some of the other changes—let’s say the waste minimisation bill—where the levy has now been used more broadly, in terms of the scope of other areas or the general operations of a particular local authority or agency, is not a very good use of a levy, and that’s something that should rightfully be funded by the Crown. We’ve also seen some changes to immigration where a levy has been used to supplement health and education, which also defeats the purpose of a levy. I think those are interesting to consider in the upcoming committee stage.
Motion agreed to.
Bill read second time.
Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) (3 Day Postnatal Stay) Amendment Bill
Second Reading

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Associate Minister of Health)
content.text: on behalf of the Minister of Health: Thank you very much, Mr Speaker. I move, That the Pae Ora (Healthy Future) (3 Day Postnatal Stay) Amendment Bill be now read a second time.

This bill is about guaranteeing women the choice of a minimum of three days of post-natal in-patient care after childbirth to ensure all mothers and babies get the support they need during this vitally important time. This Government believes that every child deserves the best-possible start in life. That start does not begin weeks or months after birth; it begins immediately, in those first precious days, when mothers are recovering from childbirth and families are learning to care for a newborn together. This bill responds directly to what women and families have told us about their post-natal experiences. They’ve told us that greater certainty and support in the early days following childbirth is needed. We know that quality early post-natal care can shape positive long-term outcomes well beyond the hospital stay.

It is for these reasons that this Government is proud to back this bill with significant new funding delivered in Budget 2026. We are committed to ensuring that this legislation is matched with the investment needed to deliver it. This new funding of $34.4 million over four years increases maternity system capacity so mothers can confidently choose up to three days of in-patient post-natal stay knowing it will be supported by the beds and the workforce required to do this safely.

First-time mothers will be the first to benefit. Starting immediately, up to 2,000 new mothers per year will be able to access a three-day post-natal stay within the first two years, utilising existing capacity. As access is expanded to all mothers after three years, we anticipate that up to 18,000 mothers per year will be able to access a 3-day post-natal stay.

I want to acknowledge the original sponsor of this legislation. How good, Catherine Wedd. This bill began its life as a member’s bill grounded in a genuine concern for the post-natal experiences of women and families. This Government made the decision to adopt the bill because we agreed with the fundamental importance of guaranteeing three days of in-patient post-natal care for all women if they choose to access it.

I also want to acknowledge and thank the Health Committee, specially chaired by the very hard-working Sam Uffindell, for its consideration of this bill and for the work it has done through the select committee process. I also want to thank the many individuals, the midwives, and other health professionals who took the time to make submissions and share their experiences. There was widespread support for the intent of the bill and for the principle that post-natal care should be a stronger and more consistent part of our maternity system. That feedback reflects just how significant the post-natal period is for families across this country.

Taking this bill forward with the support of my colleague the Hon Casey Costello also delivers on a clear commitment in the National - New Zealand First coalition agreement to strengthen maternity services and post-natal support for women. Crucially, it’s a practical and compassionate step that puts women and their wellbeing at the centre of our health system.

I intend to table an Amendment Paper as part of its adoption as a Government bill. The Amendment Paper will include transitional arrangements, requiring Health New Zealand to have a plan setting out how it will progressively build its capability and capacity across New Zealand to deliver this entitlement to all mothers. It also builds in more time to ensure that the system can safely deliver the entitlement to all women.

This is about increasing maternity services to mothers and babies in a responsible, well-managed, and well-funded way. The Budget allocation of $34.4 million over four years will address the workforce and capacity constraints the system is currently facing. I look forward to consideration of this Amendment Paper when this bill is debated in the committee of the whole House.

The bill established a clear entitlement that women can access three days of in-patient post-natal care if they choose, rather than leaving that decision uncertain or inconsistently applied. In doing so, it supports better outcomes for mothers and babies and reinforces that post-natal care is a valued and essential part of that maternity journey.

It does not mandate that women stay in in-patient care for three days. Many women will continue to choose to return home earlier, supported by community-based services and their families, just as they do now. What this bill does is ensure that women who would benefit from staying longer have that option available to them without ambiguity or inconsistency.

For some families, particularly first-time parents, the early post-natal period can feel overwhelming. There is a great deal to learn in a very short space of time. Having the option of additional support, monitoring, and reassurance within an in-patient setting can make a meaningful difference to confidence and wellbeing. Some women have told us they would have welcomed more time in in-patient care—more time to recover physically, more time to establish breastfeeding, more time to receive advice, and reassurance before returning home. Others have reported leaving hospital within 48 hours, even though they did not feel ready because they were unsure whether staying longer was an option. This uncertainty adds pressure at a time when families already have a great deal to manage. The bill removes the uncertainty and replaces it with clarity and confidence. This bill respects that different families will make different choices about what is right for them, and it ensures the system is better equipped to support those choices.

This legislation is not the only change. The Government has a broader programme of work to strengthen the maternity system and ensure it can deliver high-quality post-natal care in a sustainable way. Health New Zealand is already taking action to build and support the maternity workforce needed to deliver the strengthened post-natal care set out in this bill. This includes targeted recruitment initiatives, including international recruitment where appropriate, as well as return-to-practice support to help experienced midwives and clinicians re-enter the workforce safely and confidently.

I also understand that retention matters just as much as recruitment, particularly in districts facing ongoing workforce pressures. Supporting and retaining skilled staff is essential to maintaining safe services, continuity of care, and good outcomes for mothers and babies. That is why I’m focused on backing the maternity workforce and ensuring they’re supported to do their jobs well.

The community sector will have an important part to play in the implementation of this bill. Primary maternity units run by both the public and community providers, including the private sector, will expand the range of in-patient post-natal care options available to mothers, including care that is closer to home. Mothers may remain in hospital, where hospital level care is required, or transfer to a primary maternity unit once that level of care is no longer needed, depending on their preferences and clinical need. Having a broader range of options, both public and private, reduces pressure on hospital facilities while continuing to deliver safe and appropriate post-natal care to woman and babies.

Taken together, this work underpins the delivery of this bill and will support its long-term success. It reflects my commitment to ensuring women and their babies receive safe, timely, and appropriate care when they need it. I want to acknowledge the midwives and other health professionals who care for women and babies every day. Their experience and advice has been central to shaping the approach set out in this bill. They understand better than anyone the importance of post-natal support and the need for careful, well planned implementation. I thank them for their professionalism, dedication, and ongoing commitment to high-quality care. In closing, this bill delivers three important outcomes: it provides greater certainty for women and families about post-natal care; it supports choice at a critical moment in family life; and it strengthens our maternity system in a practical and responsible way. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour)
content.text: Mr Speaker, thank you; and thank you to the Minister for his remarks. It’s good to hear a fulsome speech on a bill while the House is sitting in urgency. I want to take the opportunity to recount the background of the bill and some of the significant changes along the way.

The Minister gave credit to Catherine Wedd, who initially held this bill as a member’s bill, but I should also add it was originally introduced in 2022 by Hon Louise Upston. It came to select committee last year, and I’d summarise the discussion about the bill at select committee as focused on two main implementation concerns. The first was the operational impacts of introducing an entitlement without consideration to implementation. The second thing was the cost. There’s been positive developments, since the select committee hearing, on both of those fronts.

To elaborate a little, firstly, the Ministry of Health advised the committee that to implement this entitlement would cost $100 million in capital expenditure (CAPEX) to make sure that there were sufficient beds available for this, and then between $31 and $38 million a year in operational expenditure. The Health Committee also heard that absent that type of investment, there could be challenges in implementation. So for example, women taking up the right to this entitlement would occupy beds that might otherwise be occupied by others in greater need. They are very challenging decisions those managing those wards face, and wanting to balance those things would be quite challenging unless extra capacity was created.

So it’s positive to see announcements in Budget ’26 that do address some of these implementation initiatives. Appropriately, then, this has been taken over as a Government bill, and the announcements in Budget ’26 included funding for these initiatives. The Minister gave the assurance that this investment matches the investment needed to deliver these entitlements. It’s worth breaking down what the Budget ’26 investments were, in that case. Firstly, contrary to the Ministry of Health presentation at select committee, all of the funding for this is operational expenditure. So there’s no CAPEX related to this initiative. We look forward to seeing the Amendment Paper, to understand whether capital expenditure is also expected as part of the implementation plan. Otherwise, we have to conclude that the entire plan for building new beds would be to use outsourced beds.

We’re told from press statements that the entitlement will apply to new mothers only, for the first two years, so that’s the year starting from now and the year starting from July 2027. That’s funded through $1.6 million of operational expenditure each year—so in health terms, a very modest contribution in the first two years. We had the opportunity to go into the scale of this contribution of this funding at Estimates, and the Director-General advised that the funding needed was limited because new mothers—those eligible in the first two years—already occupy beds for 2.5 days. I think that was the number she gave when her statement was corrected in the House by the Minister; 2.5 days is currently the average length of stay for new mothers. So there’s a minimal need, we’re told, to increase the funding in the first two years because the increase in entitlement on average will be slight.

So the substantial implementation of this commitment is really going to follow—well, 18 months after the election. It is a shame that opportunities to increase capacity in the maternity system weren’t taken during this term of Government so that the commitment could be implemented in a more fulsome way. That is to follow in years 3 and 4, so the years covered by Budget ’28 and ’29. In those years, $13.3 million is appropriated, and $17.9 million, respectively. So returning to the Ministry of Health modelling that they gave the Health Committee back when the member’s bill was considered, that’s half. So the assumption is half of women will take up this this entitlement. Look, modelling is based on assumptions, so we understand that not every health entitlement is taken up by everyone. But it remains to be seen if, for this entitlement, half is a reasonable expectation—or not. One might ask: how meaningful is it to describe it as it has been, as a right, if it’s only expected that half of people will take it up?

Which takes me back to the stories that we heard from women, NGOs who work with women, and clinicians who work with women, in the select committee. We heard multiple stories about the wonder and happiness that a new birth, a new baby brings, a time that people really treasure and a time of closeness for family. We also heard stories of birth trauma and injuries, post-natal depression, challenge with family finances, challenge with travel around birth, and the juggle of caring for other children and the partners’ other work commitments. All of these pressures are on families, and there might well be reasons why families choose not to take up the full entitlement. I’ve seen many mums who are concerned about their other kid and their other children at home and therefore would rather be at home knowing that everything was OK there—even though if they didn’t have that commitment, they might well have taken up the opportunity to be in hospital longer.

That was certainly how we felt after our daughter was born. We would rather be at home in an environment we were comfortable and familiar with, not in the busy hospital ward where all my former colleagues kept pulling back the curtain and saying hello, and where I had a far too in-depth knowledge of the number of hospital infections that get transmitted there. We got on public transport, waved our Snapper card and went back to my mother-in-law’s apartment in the city. And I’m excited that the almost 13-year-old who joined our family that day is going to wave her Snapper card and come to Parliament to hang out with her mum during urgency later on this afternoon.

Anyway, families have other priorities. So it does make me think perhaps we should think broadly about the entitlements that we’re looking to support mothers with—and the Minister actually did mention these—that support provided in the community can be part of an important part of the equation. Maybe that is where our efforts for further expansion of care should go.

My sister gave birth to my two nieces in the Netherlands, and they have a seven- to 10- day entitlement for post-birth visits in your home—so someone who’ll come and do the dishes and make sure you get a chance to have a shower and check that you’re OK and, also, sometimes identify when families are facing particular challenges that need other social services to be involved. My sister’s not like me; she’s quite a private person. I think she found having a Dutch lady come and visit her every day for seven days a little bit more intervention from the Government than she wanted. But it certainly would make a difference for many people.

content.speaker: Ingrid Leary
content.text: I hope it wasn’t because they’re Dutch!

content.speaker: Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL
content.text: No, Ingrid Leary, it wasn’t.

We’re pleased to be able to vote for this bill today. We see it as positive that the Government has taken on funding challenges that were identified at select committee, and we take the Minister’s assurance that the funding is in scale with the entitlement on face value, and we commend the bill to the House.

content.speaker: LAN PHAM (Green)
content.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. I want to join my colleagues in acknowledging the Hon Louise Upston and Catherine Wedd in terms of the progression of this bill, and the Minister who was speaking to it earlier.
