I want to start by acknowledging that I’m sure lots of people in the Chamber today are feeling very tired, but the levels of tiredness and new levels of exhaustion are absolutely front of mind for me when speaking to this bill, because they were something that I’d never experienced before after the birth of particularly my first child, my son. I was so exhausted after maybe 20 or 21 hours of birth that when he was put on my chest after giving birth, I literally could not even raise my arms to put them around him.

When I hear the comments about how critical and how vulnerable this time is for whānau and parents and families and babies, I absolutely have that front and centre. So I want to, firstly, do a massive shout-out to the midwives, the carers, the hospital staff, the specialists—to anyone who has been in this system and has had experiences, both good and bad. I acknowledge how critical they are and how formational those times are to, hopefully, a healthy, functional life ahead. I particularly want to shout out to my midwife, who was present for the birth of my children, Sheena Ross, in Christchurch, and the time that I spent in Christchurch Women’s Hospital, and then was very lucky to be able to give birth at home for my second one.

Yes, this is positive, and I really appreciate that the Minister talked about the support for this bill being about the intent, because there’s no question that intent is really good. The thing is, there are so many aspects that come into it that mean that we need to make the intent real, we need to make it tangible, we need to fund it, we need to ensure that this isn’t just a rubberstamp and a glossy outer window—we need families and whānau to be able to walk into these places at this critical time and experience true support. I think what’s been really clear, in trying to understand and listen to the voices that have fed into this bill, is that we’re so far away from that and we really need to make steps towards achieving that.

The positive things about improving breast-feeding support and the potential to reduce neonatal readmissions is absolutely positive. That potential for the positive influence on maternal confidence and emotional wellbeing is absolutely vital. As has been mentioned, the essential nature of the education and support that comes in that post-natal period is absolutely critical, particularly for first-time parents, when this is all new and different and they’re really in that learning phase.

What I really want to emphasise with this bill, which we absolutely will be supporting, is the voices of those who understand this and who know and who are signalling careful consideration of the bill’s broader implications. I particularly want to note the joint statement that was put out by the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, the New Zealand College of Midwives, and the National Council of Women, because they talked about the risks with this. They talked about the risk that the policy could actually shift the provision of post-natal care from a model based on clinical need to one driven by entitlement. They talked about concerns about people being discharged before they’re actually ready, in order to accommodate those who might not actually need that support but are actually entitled to it.

Within those comments, they made really clear the concerns about health system capacity. You know, we know, and it’s well established, that the country had 330 midwife vacancies nationwide as at 2024. Now, I don’t know what those more recent statistics are, but it is clear that this is a sector that is chronically underfunded and underpaid, and then we get caught up, within that, with the scrapping of pay equity, which means that that is going to continue. So, again, this is the call to really take this seriously. We know that where these shortages exist with midwives, this will simply be exacerbated with higher demand, and that’s absolutely a concern.

The other thing that has been raised by the specialists in the know is by the Paediatric Society of New Zealand Te Kāhui Mātai Arotamariki o Aotearoa. They talk about the potential benefits and join others in supporting those with this bill, but they recommend new investment and clear investment in staffing and infrastructure—you know, they talk about how these services must be properly resourced rather than relying on reallocations from existing services. They also talked about the importance of expanded lactation support when it comes to breast feeding. These trained consultants are absolutely pivotal, and I remember and again want to acknowledge the amazing services that do exist, however stretched and however much they are managing to operate on such, such little resourcing.

They also talk about the protection of neonatal care spaces and the fact that this increased post-natal bed occupancy should not come at the expense of vulnerable newborns needing specialist care. That is something that should be well understood, but the fact that even today, in 2026, they’re having to reiterate that and point it out just shows how vulnerable our system is and how we can’t take those basic things for granted.

They also talk about the need to strengthen primary birthing units, and ensure that not only do they have the midwives available but the social work support necessary to actually care for babies and their whānau beyond the hospital settings.

Finally, their plea is for that flexibility and that needs-based approach, because we know that people’s experiences vary so greatly from the absolute joy and positivity to ones of real, severe, lasting trauma, and the needs need to cater to that, and the investment and the funding absolutely needs to cater to that.

We know that the bill requires Health New Zealand to ensure that sufficient maternity facilities are available, but, without additional investment, all this necessity could just lead to the shifting of already strained resources rather than actual system improvement.

I again want to commend the intention of this bill. I applaud the people in this space who are making it really clear what the Government needs to do to make this real. My plea is just to actually back that up with funding and investment, listen to those voices, and ensure that new babies and whānau are truly at the centre of all of this.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Maureen Pugh)
content.text: The question is that the motion be agreed to.

content.speaker: LAURA McCLURE (ACT)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise in support of this bill. Having had two children of my own, I know how incredibly special but also challenging that time can be, particularly if you’re a new mum and things don’t go as planned. I think this is a really great bill. I think that we should have the opportunity or option to be able to stay in hospital or post-natal care. There have been many, many stories within my friend circles and within my family where people are being rushed out of hospital within like a couple of hours, and, you know, not ready for what comes next. We want to make sure that we do take care of our new mums.

I think given that we’re talking about being a new parent, we’ve had three new babies in the ACT office in the last month. Our chief of staff has had a new baby, so we want to congratulate him; and we’ve also got the senior private secretary from Karen Chhour’s office, and Amelia and Jacob, a senior researcher in my office, welcomed baby Jude Edwards Butson-Gill—I wanted to get that right. Congratulations—the ACT party welcomes these new additions. And I just want to say that I commend this bill to the House. Thank you.

content.speaker: JENNY MARCROFT (NZ First)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. It is absolutely a pleasure to stand and rise on behalf of New Zealand First in support of the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) (3 Day Postnatal Stay) Amendment Bill. The coalition agreement between New Zealand First and National was inked in November of 2023, and one of the commitments in that coalition agreement was to ensure proper funding for birthing units and maternity care, including providing for a for a three-day stay for new mothers. So this bill absolutely fulfils the commitment in our coalition agreement with the National Party, and we thank them for that.

I’d also like to acknowledge that Catherine Wedd, who inherited a member’s bill from Louise Upston—I congratulate you also—was pushing on an open door to get her member’s bill once it was drawn from the ballot. And what a thrill it must be to actually have a member’s bill that you know is going to succeed. So well done to you, Catherine.

The Health Committee, of which I’m a member, and I would like to acknowledge all of the committee members, had a great process—123 submissions on this bill; 20 oral submissions. One of the things that came through during that select committee process was that we were a little bit concerned with the language that was being used by the Ministry. So the Hon Casey Costello required the Ministry to use sex-based language—no more of the “pregnant people” or the “birthing parent” language. That was something which we felt was important during that part of the process.

This is a great bill for new mums. Everyone who has had the opportunity, the pleasure, the pain and the suffering of being a brand-new mum—because some of that comes during that period of time—will appreciate being told by their lead maternity carer, because it’s really important, that, actually, as part of this bill, those lead maternity carers notify mums that they are entitled to this longer period of stay, up to 72 hours, should they need it.

Just in conclusion, we are very thrilled to be part of a coalition that is delivering on our commitment because at the core, this bill supports family-centred policies, it promotes fairness and access to healthcare, and it addresses some of those gaps in the maternity services that are provided. These values are central to New Zealand First, with our mission of putting families and communities first. I commend the bill.

content.speaker: RICARDO MENÉNDEZ MARCH (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. The Green Party is supporting this bill in it’s a second reading. I want to acknowledge, like my colleague Lan Pham mentioned, that the intent of this bill is excellent. I think any bill that allows parents to have more time to access breastfeeding support, newborn checks, recovery care, and education before returning home is really important.

I particularly wanted to reflect on why I think that, from an equity point of view, that extension could be particularly beneficial for some of our low-income communities. Prior to becoming an MP, I used to work a lot with mums, particularly new mums, many who were living in the likes of emergency housing, many who did not have a safe, stable home to go back to, mums who were transient and often moving between addresses even while pregnant. I acknowledge that for many, that additional time to recover is critical if they’re going back to an environment that is not yet stable and provides that financial stability. And so I think that additional day to literally recover, to be well before returning to those environments, it will make a difference. I say this not just out of vibes or personal experience; I say this because even the Government’s own statistics show that more children are growing up and birthed into households that just do not have enough to cover the basic essentials. This is what we call child material hardship rights. What we know is that new kids are currently being born into environments where the household just does not have enough.

This takes us back to my colleague Lan Pham’s comments and plea to the Government to address issues in relationship to the resourcing that goes into staffing and making sure that we deliver this on the basis of need, and that we do more work to actually address those inequities that new parents are experiencing. Because, ultimately, as my colleague noted, the worst-case scenario we could see is that someone who actually has a high degree of need and is at risk of going back to a precarious material condition is not adequately served, simply because we’ve created a system where someone who may not need this as much is entitled too. I do think we should, nonetheless, work towards universalising the support and making sure that everybody can get it when they need it, but the funding needs to come alongside it.

I wanted to comment, as well, on the Minister’s remarks in relationship to funding. I think too, like the Labour Party, that we will take those at face value and in good faith, because I do want to believe that the Government wants this policy to succeed. And we will be keeping a close eye as to whether the commitments from the Minister in relationship to funding will be met. I also want to encourage parliamentary colleagues to, perhaps, put more emphasis on fighting—and this is not so much to the National Party members—for the funding that is required and the conditions to be met so that every parent can thrive; rather than focusing on issues in relationship to language that, ultimately, in my view, make no material difference to the people who this bill is supposed to serve. I think the focus on that takes away from the feedback that submitters have rightfully given us, that there are concerns around funding. I think that’s what, I would say, communities would expect us to be focusing on. Because, ultimately, the language in relationship to whether we are inclusive of all genders or otherwise actually makes no difference to the staffing issues, the funding shortfalls, whether the beds are there or otherwise.

But the Green Party will continue supporting this bill through its remaining stages. We will particularly be looking at, for example, exactly how the Government will look at engaging the community sector for the procurement of beds. I think, more broadly, we call on the Government to create the conditions so that every new parent has what they need to create a safe, thriving environment for the kids and for generations to come,  because I think, ultimately, the intent of this bill will not be matched if we continue having parents that go back home to houses that are cold, damp, and without enough kai to put on the table. Ultimately, no matter how education a parent may receive in that additional 24 hours, if they do not have the means to survive, they do not have then the resources to put in place, whatever they may have learnt in that additional time, and into practice. But, again, we are commending Catherine Wedd for continuing to fight for this bill, and other members who have brought this issue forward.

content.speaker: NANCY LU (National)
content.text: I will always remember when I gave birth to my first daughter and fainted in the birthing room. It was all the nurses and doctors who were there to protect me, to help me, and, when I finally gained consciousness, then to learn, as a new mother, the amount of help that we needed in the birthing unit and in the hospitals.

I absolutely commend this bill, and I commend the work of my colleague Catherine Wedd. This is the National Party’s way of fixing the basics: by providing the healthcare for our mums and babies, and building the future for all New Zealanders. I commend the bill to the House.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. It’s been interesting to listen to all the speeches, because, outside of two of the speeches so far, it’s been mainly women speaking, and I think this is a testament to having women in Parliament. I doubt that a bill like this would have ever reached this level of parliamentary process had there not been women championing it, and so I want to commend Catherine Wedd and also Louise Upston and all the people who have supported the bill and have enabled it to get here.

This is an example of why we do need women in Parliament: because we do have very particular issues. For many years, the birthing experience has not been taken as seriously as it should, nor, indeed, maternal health generally. So, hopefully, this is the beginning of a lot of good stuff.

I think the question for us the whole way through on whether to support to this bill has been whether the intent of the bill can be safely delivered. As the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall has said, there have been some developments since the introduction of the bill through the Budget process that gives us more confidence, including the $34 million funding that would go to providing a boost to maternity services. That doesn’t necessarily meet the capital and expenditure (CAPEX) requirements that we’ve heard about through the Ministry of Health, which came to $100 million, which is, essentially, about beds.

But we have also heard assurances from the sponsoring member, Catherine Wedd, that the capacity would be provided through public and private providers, so that may answer the question, and, indeed, the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall said that based on all the maths and what has been detailed, it looks like it will mainly go to those outsourced, probably private providers. That raises a question for me about privatisation and the health service, because if we want to have universality and we want to have good maternal public services, in my view, the capital expenditure should be public, as well. I’m not sure that relying on private providers is a way forward. Nevertheless, that is what is intended, and that would seem to resolve that CAPEX issue in the short order.

When we looked at safety, the questions in my mind while I was sitting on the committee were around the funding of beds—which I’ve just talked about—about workforce development, and we’ve heard this morning that there may be an Amendment Paper coming that is going to require a legislative commitment to that. I’ll speak shortly about how that might pertain to other facets of health law that we’re looking at today in the House.

I think I also was keen to see what would be happening around rural health support, as well as the protection of high-acuity births. Now, when it comes to rural health support, we’ve seen, for example, GP funding decisions made lately that, on the face of it, look good for many practices, but actually disadvantage some communities, like the community of Wānaka, where they’ll take an effective 11 percent decrease in rural funding, and they already have very stretched maternity services. So my question is: how are places like that going to be able to support this mandated entitlement?

There is also the question of the protection of high-acuity births. Given that there will be some mothers who will need more care than the three days that are now enabled, will they still get the levels of care and the length of stay in hospital that they need if there are other people who are sort of the first cab off the rank with their entitlements, particularly the new mothers?

I do think that it is really important for new mothers to have those three days. I share the sentiments of colleagues around the House who have talked about the fairly surreal experience of birthing, particularly the first birth experience. I can say that in my situation, the people that were there, the wonderful people who supported—particularly the midwives—took on this kind of larger-than-life presence through the whole birthing experience, and when I went back to North Shore Hospital to thank them a few weeks later, I was amazed at how they had sort of reduced down to ordinary-sized people. In fact, I was a bit taller than the midwife, the Irish woman who supported me through my birthing experience, but, at the time, they just took on this huge presence. They were such an important part of the birth experience, and I also wanted to add my voice to thank those people who work in this really beautiful and critical part of the health system.

When we look at the community provision of the delivery—going back to safe delivery—the Ministry of Health has said in its advice to the committee that those services are patchy. I think it’s important that we do look at that, and if there is going to be an Amendment Paper around workforce support, it would be great to see if it speaks also to the postcode lottery of birthing provision, because that is something that may not necessarily be addressed by something that simply addresses workforce development.

I also am concerned about bed block. We know, for example, that the hospital service loses between $8 million and $12 million worth of beds a year, not at this end of health, but through seniors being unable to be released back into the community because they don’t have the appropriate enduring powers of attorney or care provision for those whose care they might be going back into. That is something that could be worked on to free beds up at that end.

Bed block is, essentially, where somebody is taking a bed that might otherwise be available to someone with higher clinical need. We’ve heard about that previously in this debate. If we think about bed block in terms of maternity services, we’ve already got bed block around gynaecological services for women. We’ve got real workforce shortages in particular parts of New Zealand, including the West Coast, Northland, Tairāwhiti, and Wairarapa, and then, when you put into that picture the types of issues that can come up after a birthing experience which might not be the textbook experience that we’ve spoken about in the House today—that includes things like infection, injury trauma, feeding issues, very fragile babies, and also mental health issues—we cannot understate the significance of perinatal mental health and the importance of being able to provide for that.

Now, certainly, being able to stay in the hospital longer might be one solution; equally, being able to get people back home into familiar surroundings might be the other solution, but all of those issues can create situations where mothers might need longer than the three days. It would just be reassuring to know that there isn’t going to be pressure on other women to release their beds, even though they have a three-day entitlement—there might be pressure on them to release their beds for the sake of women who are doing it really tough and are needing that extra level of care.

We know that in 2029, the expected increase in the number of women who would use this entitlement will rise to 18,000. That’s a significant number of women, and so if we don’t have an equally significant uptick in the resourcing provided and the beds being available—not just relying on the community sector but knowing where those beds are, and whether they are available across the motu and not just in particular centres, is really important. What we don’t want to see is women wanting the three-day entitlement or feeling they need to take it and then finding that they have to have a birthing experience away from their own locale because they just simply cannot get that provision there. That would be another perverse incentive.

Finally, I’d just like to talk about two things. One is the workforce development Amendment Paper, if that is, indeed, what is going to presented to the House in the committee of the whole House stage. I would welcome that. I also think there’s an opportunity in another bill that we’ll be discussing later on today—the Mental Health Bill—to equally put a legislative requirement for workforce development to be able to achieve some of the things that the bill has said that it is intending to achieve. So if we can do it for this bill—and I’m hoping we will—then I’m really looking forward to seeing what transpires with the Mental Health Bill and the conversations I’ve had with the mental health Minister around that.

Finally, looking at the wording for women, the New Zealand First member mentioned that the wording had been changed. Now, that could be problematic. I note that in the original bill the word “mother” is not defined. There are intersex people who can have babies, and also families like my sister’s family, where you have two mothers. If the birthing mother or birthing parent isn’t defined, arguably in this bill, the other mother would be entitled to all of those entitlements as a mother. So that could raise a problem. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

content.speaker: Dr CARLOS CHEUNG (National—Mt Roskill)
content.text: First of all, I want to acknowledge my colleague Catherine Wedd for her hard work and continued advocacy on this service, because this is a very important service. That three-day post-natal stay is about giving every new mum and baby the best possible start. Those few days are critical for recovery, bonding, and identifying any early health conditions.

One of the issues raised by the submitters was how this would be funded. I’m pleased to report to the House that Budget 2026 has allocated $34 million over four years to support this service. This Government is fixing the basics and building the future.

content.speaker: Dr Tracey McLellan
content.text: Madam Speaker.

content.speaker: Catherine Wedd
content.text: Madam Speaker.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Maureen Pugh)
content.text: This is a split call, and the call goes to Tracey McLellan.

content.speaker: Dr TRACEY McLELLAN (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. See, I almost relented because of Catherine Wedd’s connection with the bill.

Thank you, Madam Speaker, for the chance to say a few brief words about this bill. I’d like to start and echo the acknowledgments and the congratulations of the members who have shepherded this bill through. I try not to have magical thinking and I try not to conflate luck with random occurrence, but I also have to acknowledge that Catherine Wedd has been very successful in getting bills drawn from the tin. I have no doubt that that success has contributed to the inevitable pathway that this bill has taken.

Labour is supporting this bill because, ultimately, we support the principle behind the bill. We do think that new mothers and babies should be able to stay in hospital for longer, should they need that support. I know that there’s a great deal of variance in the type of support that people opt for or that people are comfortable with, but I think the backstop to all of that should always be a universal health system that is prepared to support people when they genuinely need it the most, should that be of their choosing, and no one should ever feel pressured. We’ve heard lots of stories, both during the course of this debate and in our own lives, of people that have felt really, really discombobulated at the concept of being told that they can’t have that support in a medical setting after they’ve given birth to their children, and so we acknowledge that.

I do note, as my colleagues on this side of the House have introduced during this speech, that a right written into law only means as much as the support and funding behind it and the mechanisms by which to turn something on paper into actual delivery. I do also acknowledge—as my colleague the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall said earlier—that there has been some additional funding. Because of the relatively new information that has come through during the select committee process, that has made us feel a little bit more comfortable about this bill.

I also note, however, that as part of that funding, there is a real lack of capital funding. What that could mean ultimately is not just for the bigger questions in the health system in terms of universality and of public health as a public good, but I wouldn’t like to see us become over-reliant more and more on the private sector to provide this particular provision for women and babies.

Aside from funding issues, which we do have concerns about, I also want to acknowledge the fact that the bill could potentially—and it is something that we do need to be mindful of and keep an eye on—put already stretched maternity services under even more pressure. I want to take the opportunity to acknowledge the amazing midwives and the super-amazing nurses and everybody that works in the health system—and particularly in maternity services—for choosing to perform a role that traditionally has been under-regarded and under-resourced, and has faced decades and decades of always having to advocate for themselves to the nth degree to have their voices heard for the stellar work that they do. As we’ve said, a change like this is not just about beds; it is also about making sure that those human resources, who are the difference between a safe environment and an unsafe environment and who carry huge risk for us, are well resourced and able to do the job to the best of their ability and to work to the top of their scope.

The ministry also during the select committee process warned that hospitals may have to make room for a legal entitlement by making different choices. We have to be really vigilant that we monitor and make sure that the implementation of this bill is able to monitor that and make sure that some people aren’t being deprioritised to make way for people who have a legal entitlement, because it would be a shame for this bill to end up being simply a snapshot window-dressing. We do want to make sure that it results in a good outcome, and it’s in line with Labour’s previous work. It was Labour that changed ACC to make sure that we included birth injuries, and so we continue to support this bill.

content.speaker: CATHERINE WEDD (National—Tukituki)
content.text: Look, I rise with great pleasure to support this three-day stay bill, which, of course, started as my member’s bill. It’s wonderful to see the progress in the House here today and see the cross-party support that we have for this really important issue where we want to, obviously, give mums and families across New Zealand better post-natal care.

It’s wonderful, of course, to hear a few birthing stories here today. It certainly humanises the House, because we all understand how special those first moments are after giving birth, and it’s really important that you bond with baby.

This bill enables mums and families to three days of post-natal care. It’s a legal entitlement. I’ve advocated strongly for this, and it’s wonderful to see that we are implementing it here today. This is about strengthening maternity care across New Zealand, and so I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: HELEN WHITE (Labour—Mt Albert)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I went into this select committee just once, and it was on the bill that Catherine Wedd had put up. So the first thing I want to do is acknowledge Catherine’s work and the work of Louise Upston in this area, and then I want to talk about my experience of coming to terms with the ask.

My experience was that I actually worked as the lawyer for the midwives for quite some time, and so I was aware in the area of health—and it’s not my speciality, at all—of the issues around maternity care and the crisis in the workforce there. So my first thoughts when I looked at this bill were: is it going to push other things out? I thought about that really very seriously in the following few weeks. I thought that I was picking up a kind of scarcity mentality that is actually quite a dangerous feature of politicians, where we’re too worried about the consequences of what we’re doing to do something that’s, essentially, something we should be asking for as women. Then I thought about some of the real risks.

There are real risks here. For example, one of the risks I think that was mentioned when I was in the select committee was the issue about the discharge of others in order to allow people into the beds because they had an entitlement—so this would be someone who might need it more. That story was something that did resonate with me because my first child had been born and my doctor had wanted me out of the hospital very, very quickly. It turned out that within hours, my baby was in the Special Care Baby Unit and then the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit, which is basically intensive care. I had no experience of children at all, so would not have picked up the symptoms which were quite a serious pneumonia if I had been at home.

So I totally appreciate those pressures, but I also say to those sceptical of this particular bill: it’s almost impossible to know what people’s needs are in those early stages. I wouldn’t have known as a young, new parent what I needed out of the system. So that kind of standardisation of three days of expectation of care and listening and help with things like breastfeeding is an incredibly important expectation for women. Often women don’t ask. Actually, my experience of being a young mother is that there’s a lot of pressure that comes on from other people—and generationally—to tough it out, that you’re not strong enough. There’s a lot of judgment out there, and it’s really important that there is a universal offering to people. I also think that’s what the State’s for. I think it’s really important that the State says to young parents, “We’re going to look after you. This is an incredibly hard job and we’re going to look after you and see you through this process.”

So while I do think there’s a risk that the money comes from other parts of the system, I think that that initial commitment to getting to know a young parent and getting to support them and being more attentive in that early time is really helpful. I remind a lot of the grandparents listening that my mother—I think that there was almost a forcing to stay for 10 days at that point. That’s what our system used to give us—10 days. My mother bucked against it like anything. It was also the kind of system where she was fighting very hard to have her husband in the theatre while she was giving birth because there was a lot of dictatorialism in the system. Hopefully that’s gone. We’re not talking about forcing women to have this particular nurture in a way that we would have in the past—that’s fantastic—but it’s incredibly important we offer that kind of support.

Now, one of the concerns I also had was that there would be—and I remember this happening, actually, to my brother and his partner. There was an offering of, “If you go home early, we’ll give you this, that, and the next thing.” I think it was a nappy service and various other things. I think we have to be really careful about those economic bribes, out of this system, and I know it will be tempting to do it. So I wanted to put on the Hansard record my concern and my plea to people managing this particular expectation: please think about the economic consequences of that.

As a young parent, I would have probably wanted the things that were being offered in that circumstance, because I had no money. I remember going home with my first baby, and it was this weird situation where we had no money in the bank, we had a child who was actually at that point still in intensive care, and we had no real income, because I didn’t even have parental leave at that point at all, so we were down to really minimal money. I wasn’t considering myself at all on the bread line, but there was nothing there, and the irony was I opened my fridge and there was a giant fish in there that was a beautiful salmon. My father-in-law, who wasn’t really good at feelings, had translated all his love into this giant salmon. I remember being very hungry, because when you give birth, you get really hungry, and I’d been through the trauma of having my child go straight into intensive care and I had to come home without him. Very few people in that system, despite absolute goodwill, had really looked after things like my need to eat.

I remember in those first few hours, things went wrong and my needs went totally out the door and, quite frankly, I felt like a train had run over me. Then I was being asked to manage an incredibly difficult situation. So I can see the nods on the other side of this House, and I know lots of us have those stories and it’s really important that it bonds us all. A lot of people out in the real world, when I get to the door, ask for cross-party work. They ask for it over and over again. Sometimes that gets dismissed in here, when, in fact, 80 percent of what happens in here we should have in common. So it’s really nice to have this law come up where we can find that common ground in the universal need to care for people in that situation.

Before I finish and go back to one thing, just to cheer everyone up, I wanted to talk about the value of parenting in our society. We have plummeting levels of parenting going on out there and that is directly connected with how hard it is to be a parent these days. We can see that it has become very economically burdensome for people to have kids. The fact that you have to try and get a home when the amount that it costs to do so is outrageous in comparison to the amount that I had to pay for my first home. I just told you that I went home with no money. So parents that are in that situation now are actually paying quite a high economic price. We need to wrapround parenting and actually give it more weight than we do in our policy making.

Now, I promised that I’d finish on a really high note, and this is a very personal one. Yesterday, my son Max, who’s the child that I talked about right now, turned 31 and he’s in England. He’s just been through Cambridge University and I’m so proud of him. I’ve got to say I’ve been so wrapped up in here recently. We’re an urgency, etc. But this is the first time in my life I almost forgot his birthday. I was talking to someone saying my son’s 30 and I realised that, actually, it was his birthday here and in England. I just managed to scrape in before he knew I’d forgotten his birthday. Thank you.

content.speaker: Dr VANESSA WEENINK (National—Banks Peninsula)
content.text: It is a pleasure to take a call on the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) (3 Day Postnatal Stay) Amendment Bill. Three days may not sound like a long amount of time but, actually, when you have a new child, making sure that you are settled and to routines is very important, and not having to rush is a great step.

When I was having my son, who’s now 21, I decided to leave after two days—well, a day and a half, actually—because there was no space for me. I hope that we can get this implemented and that everyone can do as they need.

content.speaker: Hon JAN TINETTI (Labour)
content.text: Madam Speaker, it is my son’s birthday today so I would like to—

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Maureen Pugh)
content.text: Sorry, I didn’t see you stand up, but I didn’t forget your first acknowledgment that you wanted the call.

content.speaker: Hon JAN TINETTI
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. People have been sharing their birth stories, and I would like to acknowledge that my son was born in Grey Base Hospital 30 years ago today. He is my youngest and I would like to start by saying “Happy birthday, Zak”. It is related to what we’re talking about, because he is my youngest. My oldest was born 18 months prior to Zak, but in Invercargill. Totally different stories and totally different things that happened to me at that time. Now, 30 years ago—and this is why I think that this bill is going back in time, in a way, because 30 years ago, we had five days, as of right, if we wanted to choose those five days to stay in hospital. I think you might remember those days, Madam Speaker, that we did have the opportunity to choose five days to stay in hospital, and it was our choice.

Now, when my oldest was born, things were sweet. Everything went well. Within 72 hours, I went home—and chose to go home. I thought that was what I was going to do when my youngest was born in Greymouth. I thought, I’ve got an 18-month-old at home, I need to go home. I’d had a brilliant pregnancy and, actually, had a brilliant birth, so this is not about a traumatic birth story.

content.speaker: Hon Dr Duncan Webb
content.text: Thank you.

content.speaker: Hon JAN TINETTI
content.text: Thank you, Dr Duncan Webb. So I had an 18-month-old at home, and 12 hours after my youngest was born, my husband was diagnosed with a very rare form of cancer, and my world fell apart. I thought I had to go straight home 12 hours after that birth. I had an amazing midwife who said, “You’re not going home. You have the right to choose five days. You need to take those five days, because things are going to get tough for you. You’ve got a mother-in-law at home that’s looking after everything. You need to get your head in order because your world has changed and it has fallen apart. You have a brand-new baby; hormones are running; you have an 18-month-old; you’re going to crumble if you go home.”

I had that midwife make that fantastic decision for me because I had the right to be able to take the five days. And it was an amazing five days, because I was able to bond with that new baby, and that was so important. If I had gone home to the trauma that was sitting in my house at home, that bonding wouldn’t have happened the same. And so, 30 years later, I have a wonderful young man who I’m so proud of. I was able to have that time without any pressure on me.

Here we are, 30 years later, debating for the right for three days’ stay. You know, we lost something along the way as women—we lost something along the way. We’re here, in this Parliament, fighting for this back. I know that that’s what submitters told us during select committee.

This is the right thing to do. This is the right thing for women. Catherine Wedd, I totally commend you for taking up the bill from Louise Upston. People are right: you have so much luck at getting bills drawn out of the biscuit tin.

content.speaker: Tom Rutherford
content.text: You don’t have to remind us.

content.speaker: Hon JAN TINETTI
content.text: By the way, Mr Rutherford, I’ve had just as many bills drawn out of the biscuit tin, so we’ll call that as an even.

This is such an important one. I’m pleased that we’ve got cross-party support. Yes, there are implementation issues; we’ll work through those. Both sides of the House—whoever is in Government—will work through those. This is good for women. This something that gives us that choice back. It is something that I just feel is inherently right for us to do, knowing my own story, knowing what I lived through. But I’m not the only one; people have talked about their own stories. There are things that happen and go wrong in that process every single day.

Women need to have the right to be able to make the choice to stay or have an amazing midwife who can help them make that choice so that they have that ability to bond with that beautiful baby and then, 30 years later, they’ll be standing there telling the world how proud they are of that child. Thank you, Madam Speaker. I commend this to the House.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Maureen Pugh)
content.text: I remember the 10-day stays, actually. Happy birthday, Zak. The question is that the motion be agreed to.
Motion agreed to.
Bill read a second time.
Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill
Legislative Statement

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: I present a legislative statement on the Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Maureen Pugh)
content.text: That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
First Reading

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: I move, That the Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill be now read a first time. I nominate the Justice Committee to consider the bill.

Too many New Zealanders are spending too long caught in the court system. For victims, delays mean waiting a year or more for a case to be resolved. For witnesses, it means uncertainty and repeated disruption. For defendants, it means cases hanging over their lives. For families, employers, and communities, it means the justice system is not working as quickly as it should. Timely justice matters, because justice delayed is justice denied.

This Government is focused on practical changes that make the courts work better. This bill is a practical reform that improves access to justice, reduces delays, and makes better use of the resources that we already have. This bill expands the role of community magistrates so that they can deal with more straightforward matters from start to finish. It will reduce unnecessary adjournments, free up District Court judges to focus on more serious and complex cases, and will improve the public’s confidence that the justice system can deliver.

Community magistrates are not new. The role was introduced in the late 1990s to increase judicial capacity to take pressure off the District Court judges. They were intended to deal with lower-level criminal matters, represent the communities that they serve, and help the courts to operates more efficiently. Community magistrates generally sit part time. They preside over certain lower-level matters in the District Court’s criminal jurisdiction. They are not required to hold a legal qualification, although many of them do. They bring practical experience, judgment, and community knowledge to the court system.

But at the moment, they are not being used to their full potential. Too often, if a case reaches a point where a decision is needed outside of a community magistrate’s jurisdiction, it has to be adjourned and transferred to a judge. That means another court event, another delay, another day off work, another round of uncertainty for victims and other court users. It also means some cases are never scheduled before a community magistrate in the first place, because everyone knows that they might have to be transferred again later on. That’s not efficient, nor is it fair on court users, and it certainly is not the best use of judicial time and resource.

This bill changes that. It will enable community magistrates to take guilty pleas for all cases except those tried in the High Court—that means murder, manslaughter—to preside over trials and determine guilt for offences with a maximum penalty of a fine, community-based sentence, or up to three months imprisonment; to order pre-sentencing reports for offences being referred to a District Court judge for sentencing; to make a greater range of bail decisions, where the defendant has pleaded guilty before a community magistrate; and make a greater range of administrative decisions, including transferring proceedings from one District Court to another and hearing unopposed limited driver licence applications.

These are sensible, practical changes. They do not ask community magistrates to replace judges; they allow community magistrates to do more of the work that they were created to do so that judges can spend more time on cases that genuinely require a judge. It is expected that these changes will free up a net 5.2 District Court judge full-time equivalents. Put simply, this bill is, effectively, five judges for the price of none. This is good value for taxpayers, good for court timeliness, and good for victims who have waited too long for justice. The benefits will be felt across the justice system. When cases move faster victims get answers sooner. Witnesses are not left waiting indefinitely.  Defendants are not held in limbo longer than necessary. Remand pressure can reduce as cases progress more quickly. Judges can focus on the work only they are able to do.

Expanding the role of community magistrates is sensible, but it must be done carefully. The public needs confidence that the cases will continue to be dealt with appropriately and consistently. This bill does not change the sentencing jurisdiction of community magistrates. Community magistrates will still not be able to impose imprisonment or home detention. Where a community magistrate considers that either of those sentences may be appropriate, the case must be transferred to a District Court judge, and that is an important safeguard.

The bill also supports stronger leadership and oversight of community magistrates. Judge Moses has recently been appointed as the first Chief Community Magistrate, recognising the growing importance of community magistrates in the court system in providing judicial oversight for the role. The bill will make it so that there must always be a judge in this role. Budget 2025 also provided funding for three additional community magistrates and extra training to support them in their work.

This bill is practical, it is targeted, it is common sense, and it makes better use of community magistrates. It frees up more than five full-time judges’ worth of capacity. It helps cases to move faster, it supports victims, it reduces pressure on the District Court, and it does all of that while maintaining appropriate safeguards. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: The question is that the motion be agreed to.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s a pleasure to be able to take a call on this bill, the Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill. This is something which introduces an issue that is a fundamental pillar of the justice system, and that is the premise that justice delayed is justice denied. No matter what the system we put in place is, if people are unable to utilise the systems we have, especially in criminal law, due to the fact that we don’t have the resourcing, that will result in delays.

We know there are lots of issues with delays, many different issues for the people who have been charged, in terms of the pause that’s on their life until an issue is resolved—that might have implications on employment—and issues for victims in terms of wanting to get justice and understanding what will happen after an alleged crime has been committed. Also, we have practical concerns around the evidential basis of many of our criminal cases, as based on people being able to recall what happened. Of course, with the passage of time, no matter with the best will in the world or how traumatic that is, that does dissipate over a period of time.

We’re pleased to be able to support this bill to the select committee. We’ll listen to what is said in select committee, and I hope that we will have the opportunity to hear from magistrates and judges. I know that that is probably not something they usually do, but this is specifically in relation to the work that they do; also the criminal bar, because they will have to be liaising with them as well.

Thanks to the Minister for bringing a practical change to help delays in the system. I’m sure that, hopefully, we can find a way to implement this in a way that doesn’t affect due process. I’m sure there will be issues that will be raised around due process. In New Zealand law, magistrates, as I understand, are not required to be lawyers. They’re not required to be legally trained, although many are legally trained—many are former lawyers as well. I understand we’ve got around 20 in New Zealand at the moment. This change is, really, just to let them be able to hear a wider range of cases.

I was just discussing with my colleague how that works and the difficulty that often occurs when you’re deciding who is able to determine a case. We heard from the Minister that the community magistrates will be able to hear any cases that have, as a maximum penalty, three months in prison, but they would not be able to, themselves, sentence for imprisonment. There will be a bit of a tricky way of making sure that that process is smooth. For example, if a community magistrate was hearing a case and did determine that, possibly, a sentence of imprisonment or home detention was appropriate, they would then have to allow a District Court judge to sentence in their place. That would be, possibly, two appearances in court or in front of a community magistrate; whereas, perhaps, under the previous system, there would have been only one. However, I suppose the likelihood and the way that this particular bill would work would be the fact that many, many cases are determined that don’t result in a home detention sentence or imprisonment. Assuming that that continues, there would likely be, hopefully, a slightly sped up process in the District Court.

It was interesting reading the regulatory impact statement on this to see that numbers of cases in the District Court have actually fallen, but the number of procedural appearances—so the work of the District Court judges—has actually increased. I suppose this is something that will look to address that. There will be issues around—and there are issues raised around—trust and confidence in the process. I think that will have to be something that we will need to work through and assess. I do think this is something that should probably be reviewed after a period of time, once it’s been in place, to see if it’s effective and working. I also think there is an important role for the very busy Justice Committee. Obviously, it is the appropriate committee for the Minister to send it to, but we do have a lot of bills. I know that the Justice Committee will do its due diligence on making sure that this is a good bill, and I commend it to the House.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I also rise on behalf of the Green Party of Aotearoa to support the Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill to select committee. I also want to acknowledge the Hon Nicole McKee, as well, for allowing us the opportunity to have a conversation on this particular bill.

Now, I think, across the House, this is something that we agree on—that, when it comes to access to justice, the idea of core timeliness is the important one. We have seen a number of those bills coming through the House that the Green Party has supported, including the High Court changes, including the Judicature (Timeliness) Legislation Amendment Act, and also the Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill.

I think there are a couple of interesting things to touch on in this case. I think that both of the previous two speakers have covered a number of them, but just to highlight some of the key areas, we do see that community magistrates can fulfil an important function in our legal system when it comes to the ability to undertake more case reviews, the ability to hear more bail cases, and, basically, alleviate some of the burdens we see on the District Court judges, and the District Court in general.

The previous speaker, Camilla Belich, has already mentioned that it’s interesting to see in the regulatory impact statement that, although the number of cases in the District Court has fallen—I believe by about 15 percent over the last six years—there are still significant delays that impede access to justice for complainants and defendants. We are hoping that this is something that, potentially, could move in a direction that allows there to be more timely access to justice.

However, of course, for us in the House, although we have this understanding of the principle of comity—that both the legislature and judiciary, in particular, in this case, are independent and should be operating independently—their expertise in this area, and the ability for us as a select committee to hear from experts, is an important one. In that case, we do encourage people from the judiciary, those who are involved within the community magistrates system, or legal experts who are involved in that, to submit to the best of their ability during the select committee process, so that we’re able to hear a balanced view of how this works in practice. Again, very few of us in the House have had that level of in-depth experience in the judiciary.

The other couple of things I want to touch on with regard to this bill is when we are looking at this—and I think the previous speaker, Camilla Belich, has already mentioned that a community magistrate doesn’t necessarily have to be a trained lawyer or have that kind of legal background, although it is preferred and many of them do.

Also, I think another important angle when we’re looking from a select committee perspective—that we should keep in mind—is the fact that across all levels of our criminal justice system, we do see an overrepresentation of Māori, and we do see an overrepresentation of Pasifika. This is something that, through a number of hearings, whether it’s Estimates week or annual review week or long-term insights briefings, etc., is one of the key focuses for both the Minister of Justice and also the Justice Committee.

I think this is an important moment, when we’re looking at the broader landscape of the judiciary, which includes community magistrates. As we’re seeing some of these cases manifest, the expanded scope of power comes with the expanded scope of responsibility. With that, what then are the requirements or considerations around cultural competency and culturally appropriate advice or judgments or consideration of cases—whether its bail, whether its criminal, or whether its others—before the community magistrates? I think this is something that we would like to hear more about during the select committee process, and particularly from officials, on how that side is going to work and what are some of the resources and considerations that have already been given.
With that, the Green Party does support this bill, and we look forward to considering it in the Justice Committee.

content.speaker: TOM RUTHERFORD (National—Bay of Plenty)
content.text: Thank you very much, Mr Speaker. It’s great to see some universal support coming from across the House on what is really very simple and fixing an anomaly around community magistrates being underutilised in our justice system and expanding the powers they have so they can hear more cases in the District Court end to end, which is ultimately going to free up District Court judges to progress more complex trial work. I commend it to the House.

content.speaker: JAMIE ARBUCKLE (NZ First)
content.text: Thank you. I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to support the Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill. As we know, community magistrates were created in the late 1990s, but they remained underutilised. New Zealand First has always campaigned on getting tough on crime and fixing the flaws in our justice system. I look forward to the select committee and the submissions on this bill. I commend it to the House.

content.speaker: TIM COSTLEY (National—Ōtaki)
content.text: National are fixing the basics and building the future. Law and order is so important. It is important that we take it seriously and move these cases through the court. I commend it to the House.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB (Labour—Christchurch Central)
content.text: Kia ora, Mr Speaker. I do think it’s worth spending a little more time reflecting on what this bill does. As you’ve heard, we do support this bill, but there will be some important points to consider at select committee.

Community magistrates are not legally qualified. At their inception, they were instituted as a model of, essentially, community-based justice—that is to say, people who knew the community, were part of the community, making decisions about minor offending within that community. I endorse that view, but we do need to be cautious—so we’re supporting this with some caution—about expanding the jurisdiction of magistrates to more serious offending. I will be interested to interrogate exactly what kind of decisions magistrates can make, in respect of what kind of offending, because justice delayed is justice denied but an outcome which is unjust is also problematic.

Whilst we can train them—lawyers aren’t the be all and end all of the justice system; don’t get me wrong there. We can train up non-lawyers to have some legal capacity, and we see that in the Disputes Tribunal—although, in fact, most of them are lawyers. In fact, if you look at community magistrates, the fact of the matter is—and I’d be interested in the statistics on this—many of those are lawyers as well, who are doing this, essentially, as a side gig or a retirement gig or something along those lines.

Now, I do think that, in terms of community magistrates directing traffic, that is a good idea—that is to say, doing case management, preparing things for trial, and addressing some bail hearings. That is a good thing. I think the regulatory impact statement is a little ambitious, or it perhaps overestimates the impact of this. For example, it suggests, on page 21, that there will be fewer people on remand in prison as a result of this. I find that highly unlikely given the jurisdiction of the community magistrates. The cases that go to community magistrates are by definition low-level offending where imprisonment is very, very unlikely indeed. It’s unlikely that by speeding up these cases in particular you’re going to be taking people off remand. They’ll certainly be on bail and therefore under the supervision of Corrections, in a sense, and Police, but, in fact, remand is unlikely to really have much of an impact.

If you like the professionalisation of community magistrates, I think that’s a good thing. There’s the suggestion—or the intention—that there be a chief magistrate by law and that that person be a District Court judge. That’s a very senior lawyer. The good thing about having a chief of a bench in that sense is that they can give direction and have a certain degree of mana, so when people aren’t getting things quite right, they can have that chat and say, “Well, look, that’s not how we deal with people” or “That’s not an appropriate process.” That’s actually a really good thing. The head of bench—the Chief Community Magistrate—will be networked with other heads, so they’ll be no doubt in touch with the head of the District Court and other judicial officers. It’s actually about creating a structure that builds capacity.

Community magistrates are a good thing, but I guess, with the expansion of them, we’ve got to be careful that we’re not doing this simply because it’s cheap. At the same time, I’m aware that community magistrates are remunerated on a very modest scale. It’s certainly not anywhere near what a judge is paid. It’s a bit more than an honorarium. I think it’s around $450 a day, but I’d have to be educated on that. You see that that’s not a huge amount for that kind of work.
It’s a good initiative that we’ll support and give it a good working over and yet again another piece of legislation going to the Justice Committee.

content.speaker: PAULO GARCIA (National—New Lynn)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Community magistrates already exist. The bill expands their jurisdiction to facilitate access to justice—and not just for the expanded jurisdiction but also for District Court judges. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: DAN ROSEWARNE (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s a pleasure to rise and take a call on the Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill at its first reading. We have two special guests in the House there. We have Andrew Bayly. He’s actually recently departed as chair of the Justice Committee, so I’d like to acknowledge his service. Then we have the new chair of the Justice Committee, Tom Rutherford. He was actually appointed yesterday, and he’s off to a good start. It’s good timing that they’re both there this morning.

Labour will be supporting this bill at its first reading. It’s a practical bill aimed at helping the District Court work more efficiently. The Government’s own explanation is straightforward. Criminal cases are taking too long to move through the courts. Community magistrates are not being used at their full potential right now, and this legislation is designed to make better use of an existing part of the justice system.

I think most members of this House would agree that delays in the justice system help nobody. They don’t help victims waiting for a case to be resolved; they don’t help defendants, whose lives are, effectively, on hold while matters work their ways through the courts; and they don’t help public confidence in the justice system. If we can safely reduce unnecessary delays and unnecessary court appearances, that is something Parliament should be willing to consider.

Community magistrates have been part of our court system for many years. They were established to provide additional judicial capacity to allow District Court judges to focus their time on the more serious and more complex cases. Yet the legislative statement makes clear that restrictions on their jurisdiction mean that they are often underused. Cases can end up being passed back and forth between community magistrate and a judge, creating extra hearings and additional delay.

One example is where somebody wishes to plead guilty. At present, a community magistrate may have to refer the matter to a judge before that guilty plea can be formally dealt with. The bill allows community magistrates to take guilty pleas for category 1, 2, and 3 offences, order pre-sentence reports when needed, and make limited post-guilt bail decisions before the case goes to a judge for sentencing. The intention is to remove unnecessary steps and avoid multiple court appearances where one would do.

The bill also expands the ability of community magistrates to manage and hear lower-level criminal cases. In particular, it allows them to hear those minor offences, as mentioned, and we see merit in that approach. Importantly, this is not a proposal to give community magistrates more power and to send more people to prison. The legislation specifically leaves imprisonment and home-detention decisions with District Court judges. Where a community magistrate considers that a sentence of imprisonment or home detention may be appropriate, the matter must still go before a judge.

The bill also includes some fairly practical changes that will allow community magistrates to deal with certain unopposed, limited licence applications and to transfer proceedings between court locations where all parties agree and jury trials have not been elected. These may not be headline-grabbing changes, but they reduce paperwork, reduce court events, and save judicial time, so they’re absolutely worth considering through the select committee process.

Another feature Labour welcomes is the requirement for a District Court judge to be appointed as a principal community magistrate. If community magistrates are being entrusted with additional responsibility, judicial leadership and oversight becomes even more important. The bill recognises that and provides a framework for it.

Now, supporting this bill at first reading does not mean giving it a free pass. The justice system is one of the most important institutions in our democracy and changes to our judicial powers and court processes should always be tested carefully. Labour expects the select committee process to examine whether the right safeguards are in place.
On that note, it’s an important bill, and I look forward to it going through the select committee. I commend it to the House.

content.speaker: Dr HAMISH CAMPBELL (National—Ilam)
content.text: Excellent. Thank you. It’s a great honour to rise in support of the Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill. This bill will support timely access to justice in the District Court; therefore, I commend it to the House.
Motion agreed to.
Bill read a first time.
Referral to Select Committee
