content.text: The question is, That the Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill be considered by the Justice Committee.
Motion agreed to.
Bill referred to the Justice Committee.
Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill
Legislative Statement

content.speaker: Hon SCOTT SIMPSON (Minister of Statistics)
content.text: on behalf of the Minister for the Environment: I present a legislative statement on the Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
First Reading

content.speaker: Hon SCOTT SIMPSON (Minister of Statistics)
content.text: on behalf of the Minister for the Environment: I move, That the Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill be now read a first time. I nominate the Environment Committee to consider the bill.

New Zealand is undertaking significant transformations regarding how we protect, conserve, and restore our natural environment, how we sustainably use our resources, and how we mitigate and adapt to climate change. However, to understand the impacts that our activities have on the environment and to respond accordingly, we need a comprehensive, reliable, consistent data and information base.

In 2015, the Environmental Reporting Act was enacted to do exactly that: to establish a trusted, reliable, and independent environmental reporting regime. Since then, we have completed four cycles of environmental reports. The Act has made significant improvements to the previously ad hoc way New Zealand reported on the environment; however, we need to extend its functionality and flexibility so that trustworthy data and information is at the heart of decision making.

In 2019, the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment released a report raising concerns about gaps and inconsistencies in environmental data. The commissioner noted a reliance on passively harvested data and information collected under other pieces of legislation and a lack of a coordinated environmental monitoring and reporting system. The high frequency of report production placed the Ministry for the Environment and Stats NZ on a never-ending treadmill of report-making. These often recycle old, patchy, and inconsistent data collected using a myriad of disparate monitoring practices. We have a significant opportunity now to address the Parliamentary Commissioner’s concerns, so in this piece of legislation a number of changes are being put forward.

The Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill before the House represents a commitment by the Government to quality environmental data and information. The bill will refocus reporting content and time frames. It aligns roles and responsibilities, and a more active collection of environmental data and knowledge. The bill ensures improvements to environmental reporting are safeguarded for the future. These include making data available to the public and decision makers when it is ready, rather than when a report is merely published. It also means expanding the reporting and setting up an interim strategic, in-evidence panel.

The bill will require the Secretary for the Environment to publish a State of the Environment report every six years, independent from political interference. This will achieve a more appropriate balance between reporting timeliness and the rates of change in our environment. The bill stipulates that the first State of the Environment report must be published in 2031.

The Pressure-State-Impact framework embedded into the Environmental Reporting Act has been expanded to include drivers and outlooks. Drivers describe the long-term social, demographic, economic, and environmental factors that cause pressure on the environment. Outlooks describe how the environment may change in the future based on projections and trends. Their ongoing inclusion will render a more complete picture and bring New Zealand more in line with international best practice.

The report must continue to describe changes to the state of the environment over time and how it measures against national and international standards. In addition, they can now report on progress towards Government priorities and limits, goals, and policy outcomes set in other legislation. This could include, for example, reporting on limits as proposed in the Natural Environment Bill and any measures set as part of the climate adaptation system, including managing the risk from natural hazards.

Between the six-yearly State of the Environment reports, a commentary report must be published at least once every 12 months. One of the foundational objectives of the bill is to ensure reporting flexibility. Commentaries report on an issue or topic that sits across one or more of the five environmental domains. The five domains of air, land, fresh water, marine, and atmosphere and climate will remain. All must be reported on at least once in the commentary reports between the State of the Environment reports. However, the amendments recognise that commentary reports may cut across different domains. This change allows for more flexible reporting, which better addresses the urgent needs we face.

The bill introduces a new requirement for the Secretary for the Environment. In consultation with the Government Statistician, the secretary will produce a priorities report within six months of every State of the Environment report. The report will discuss environmental data, monitoring, and research. It will also list recommended indicators and priority areas for improving data and evidence.

Several technical advisory groups have provided expert advice on the preparation of synthesis and domain reports over the years. This bill will, however, amend the Environmental Reporting Act to require the Secretary for the Environment, in consultation with the Minister for the Environment, to appoint a strategic evidence panel. The panel will provide independent advice to the Secretary for the Environment on matters related to environmental data monitoring and reporting. The bill also clarifies the roles of the Secretary for the Environment and the Government Statistician. The bill proposes clear roles and also stipulates where consultation between the two organisations is required, such as setting environmental indicators or producing data and evidence priority reports.

Finally, to bring together all the proposals and drive a cohesive, robust and fit-for-purpose reporting system, the purpose statement has been extended. The current purpose statement simply stipulates that the purpose of the Act is to produce national environmental reports. This has been clarified to align with the underlying policy to inform New Zealanders on the state of the environment and to support evidence-based decisions. This bill responds directly to a review of New Zealand’s national reporting regime. It improves efficiency of our reporting regime, making useful improvements to the frequency of reports, and does so without compromising their timeliness, impact, or independence. Therefore, I commend the Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill to the House.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: The question is that the motion be agreed to.

content.speaker: Hon RACHEL BROOKING (Labour—Dunedin)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker, for this opportunity to speak on the Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill. I thank the Minister for that fulsome speech in describing what some of the differences are between the bill and the Act that it’s amending. I do note that both of them are quite little Acts—well, a little Act and a little bill.

content.speaker: Catherine Wedd
content.text: Unlike our other ones.

content.speaker: Hon RACHEL BROOKING
content.text: And that is right. The chair of the Environment Committee is noting that it’s quite different from the Planning Bill and the Natural Environment Bill that the Environment Committee is currently looking at. But that does not diminish their importance at all. It is, of course, very important that all of that other stuff is based on good evidence and good data. We’ve heard from across Parliament, the importance of that data and that we’re not doing it quite right.

The Hon James Shaw—in, I think, his capacity as an associate environment Minister—was working on amendments to the Environmental Reporting Act when he was the Minister, and we see in the departmental disclosure statement a reference to consultation that happened in February and March 2022, which, of course, was in the last term of Government. Subsequent to that, obviously the Government changed, and I have been asking the previous Minister for the Environment what happened to that work, because it seemed to be bipartisan-type work that surely this Government could have been getting on with. The response was always that something was happening; so it is, though we’re now in 2026, good to see the something. Of course, it would be useful to know the differences between that work, that the Hon James Shaw was consulting on in 2022, and then what happened with the targeted engagement that happened in 2024.

This departmental disclosure statements says that, “Following the revision of the amendments by the current Government, the Ministry undertook targeted engagement with the regional sector advisory group in 2024. Feedback received was supportive of the proposed amendments. In February 2025, the Ministry undertook departmental consultation on these amendments, including separate engagement with the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment.” It is very important that the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment is involved, because he, the Rt Hon Simon Upton, has been saying to anybody who will listen, for some time, about the importance of data and that we need to make significant changes on what we do and also how we account for this in the scrutiny that we do in Parliament. He’s also spoken a lot and is doing written letters about the need for a federation of information as well.

What does this bill do, and how is it different to the current Act that it is amending? We know that the frequency of these reports—the requirement for the state of the environment reporting—is reduced. We also know, as the Minister has just said, that data will be available when it’s ready, and that can be very useful for the reasons that the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment is concerned in. There’s also, as the Minister noted, this change in purpose, which I think is important, because it does include there “to inform New Zealanders about the state of the environment and support evidence-based decisions that lead to effective and enduring environmental stewardship”. That seems like a good purpose to me. And there’s this new panel as well. We see that in Part 2 clause 14, there is a Strategic Evidence Panel established. That is to provide advice on a particular matter, if requested by the Secretary, or they may provide advice to the secretary on their own resolution. The panel consists of a group of at least seven, but no more than nine, with a three-year term, appointed by the Minister.

Just as I wrap up, Labour is supporting this bill to go to select committee because we are interested, and Government members might like to inform the House about the differences between what happened in that 2022 consultation and the 2025 consultation. I look forward to hearing thoughtful submissions on this important but small piece of legislation.

content.speaker: LAN PHAM (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. This morning at breakfast time, my daughter was reading a book that she got from the school library about baby turtles. Simultaneously, my phone was showing me a headline about green sea turtles. It was recalling a story about a green sea turtle that was found on a beach in Sydney, that was sick, and that was taken in by a rescue centre at a zoo. That baby green sea turtle pooed plastic for six days. What that made me wonder was whether my daughter would experience green sea turtles when she gets to my age. I recall the privilege of being on Rangitāhua, on Raoul Island, in the Kermadecs, and seeing green sea turtles around there. They are around New Zealand, but it made me wonder whether they’ll continue to be.

Why I wanted to start this contribution with that is because it is so important—and it was so great hearing the Minister’s comments just before—that we know and understand what is happening with our natural environment. Most importantly, he talked about how we respond accordingly. The reason that the Green Party will not be supporting this bill today—

content.speaker: Catherine Wedd
content.text: Why?

content.speaker: LAN PHAM
content.text: —is because we need to know and understand and respond accordingly to the stats, the figures, the information that is in front of us. And to illustrate my point about that—because I can hear Government members saying, “Why? Why?” The reason is because our latest domain report, which is the exact reports that are dictated and mandated under this Act, was Our Freshwater 2026 report. That told us that between 2020 and 2024, 44 percent of New Zealand’s total river length was not safe for swimming. It told us that more than half of our rivers are polluted. It told us most of our lakes are in poor health and that groundwater in many areas is increasingly unsafe to drink. It also told us that the area of land used for dairy farming almost tripled between 2002 and 2022.

The associated increase in cows across the country increased 71 percent nationally between 1990 and 2023, from 3.4 million to 5.9 million. The modelling tells us that the long-term decline of that, when it comes to river and freshwater quality since 1990 were closely associated with how much farming and forestry—but particularly the intensity of farming—there was upstream.

Now, what is really concerning about this is this is what we were told in 2026. If we agree with this bill and we put this bill through, the next reporting would not be until 2032. The reason why the Green Party cannot support this is because, even despite the fact that James Shaw, our previous co-leader, was part of the development early on, the landscape has changed so much. We cannot afford, as New Zealanders, to not be reminded of this stuff. If we’re not reminded in these domain reports, how many of us are going to notice the absence of green sea turtles when we’re out in the ocean, when they’re already so rare to see. We are not up for that.

What we are up for is actual protection, actual response, where we turn this tide in environmental. Because with this Government, the brakes are off, we’re in a race to the bottom, and New Zealanders deserve and expect so much better. We can do so much better. The Government should know this. We want to see them respond. We want to see them act. The information is right in front of them. Just use it.

content.speaker: SIMON COURT (ACT)
content.text: Firstly, I have to disabuse the member, the environmental catastrophist Lan Pham, about the fate of the sea turtles. The Department of Conservation (DOC), on their own website, says: “The status of this species is least concern”. DOC are the least concerned they could possibly be about it. They also say that green sea turtle sightings have increased around Northland and that if seas actually warm due to climate change, these sea turtles that don’t breed in New Zealand might actually decide to breed in New Zealand. There could be a net benefit from climate change that New Zealand could become a breeding colony for these sea turtles.

Let’s get back to the bill. This is a fantastic bill. It streamlines environmental reporting, and actually, increases to the time between reports so that more information can be developed is useful. There’s no point in having a three-yearly hop-in, stop-in on environmental conditions. We do need to let good policy and good environmental controls take effect. Thank you, Mr Speaker.

content.speaker: JAMIE ARBUCKLE (NZ First)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to support the Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill. This bill is consistent with the New Zealand First manifesto commitment to support an evidence-based approach to complex environmental issues. We are also proud to see the establishment of the strategic evidence panel, which will provide the independent expert advice needed to safeguard our reporting programmes. On that, I commend the bill to the House.

content.speaker: CATHERINE WEDD (National—Tukituki)
content.text: I rise to support this bill. In order to protect an enhance our environment, we need good data to do that. We need good reporting. It’s really disappointing to hear that the Green Party is not supporting this bill, because, to enhance the environment, we need good data. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: GEORGIE DANSEY (Labour)
content.text: Tēnā koe e te Māngai o te Whare. I’m rising on behalf of the Labour Party to speak to this bill. Look, the Labour Party supports good reporting. We support good reporting across the board, because reporting informs everything that we can do and what we can achieve in legislation in Parliament.

We support this bill—with caution. Caution because of what this Government has done in regards to the environment over this term. Over the last two-and-a-half years, we’ve seen this Government deprioritise the environment. So in a way, I’m proud of this Government for finally doing something that could help the environment after a long list, two-and-a-half years, of deprioritising it.

Look, Labour’s supportive of the aims of the bill in regard to reporting because we know that there are data and reporting gaps in the legislation. We’re interested to see how this goes in select committee and getting into the detail about what this reporting will look like and how it is going to be effective in caring for our environment. We will look carefully at this bill through the select committee process. I don’t sit on this select committee, but I know that my colleagues will do a good job of that.

I think one of the aspects of this is the importance of robust and credible environmental data and research, which is the intent of the Environmental Reporting Act 2015. For 10 years since that Act was enacted, feedback has been that we need more efficiency and more flexibility within the Act. So I look forward to the robust discussions throughout the select committee in that space.

I wanted to talk a little bit about something I read in the departmental disclosure statement regarding the regulatory impact statement (RIS). So there was a regulatory impact statement provided for this bill, which is great, but some of the notes in the departmental disclosure statement, which I’d just like to refer to, was that the Ministry for Regulation did not provide an independent opinion on the RIS, but there was feedback from—the Ministry for the Environment Regulatory Impact Analysis Panel has reviewed it, which is good. But there was a part there that I found interesting in regard to the way that the RIS—and when I first came to Parliament and heard “RIS”, I thought it was “RIZ” and I always wondered what the “Z” stood for, but it’s actually “S”. So it should be pronounced “riss” but I think “riz” sounds much better. So we’ll go with “riz”.

This is the point from the departmental disclosure statement that I wanted to mention. “While the [RIS] is generally clear and concise, it would benefit from additional evidence in the options analysis and cost-benefit analysis under each proposal … the RIS could have gained more from a broader public consultation … [it could] provide a … robust foundation for decision-making and enhance the overall effectiveness of the statement.”

The point there is that our RIS doesn’t quite meet the standard that I would expect. Since coming to Parliament, I’ve learnt how important it is to read the RIS, understand the RIS, to come speak in the House on it. It’s such an important document, and it’s a shame that, over the past little while, under this Government and under the Ministry for Regulation, the RISs haven’t been up to scratch, and I think this speaks to it.

We had a briefing from the officials from the Ministry for Regulation who talked to us about the new RAS and CAS that we’re getting. So the regulatory analysis summary, which is going to replace the RIS, and the point I want to make here is just—oh, sorry. The CAS is the consistency accountability statement—the RAS and the CAS. The RAS is going to replace the RIS, and I hope that that means we have a more robust process in ensuring that we get the information that we need to consider bills in the broader context. Thank you.

content.speaker: GRANT McCALLUM (National—Northland)
content.text: Well, if you’re going to make good environmental decisions, you need good data. This bill will help deliver it. It was ironic that it’s been developed, in part, by James Shaw in the past, and to have the current Green Party think that it’s not relevant to have good data says it all. They have really disappeared into a deep, dark hole. They don’t care about the environment, and, therefore, they don’t deserve to be called a Green Party. I commend this bill.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DEBORAH RUSSELL (Labour)
content.text: This bill has indeed had a very long gestation. Looking through the regulatory impact statement, we see that part of what kicked it off was, way back in 2019, a report from the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment saying that we actually did need better environmental reporting in this country. We have a great deal of respect for the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment—on all sides of the House, I think—especially for the current commissioner, appointed by Labour and the appointment continued by National. He’s a former National Party MP and I think a man of great intellect and insight and is doing a good job for us. And then, in 2022, the Hon James Shaw, someone for whom I have a great deal of respect, also kicked off the policy process on this to work us towards getting better environmental reporting.

Having had this very long, long gestation, it does seem odd that we now have to introduce it into the House in the closing months of this Parliament under urgency. It does seem a shame that the former Minister for the Environment couldn’t have gotten it into the House sooner. We’d have liked to have had the opportunity to examine it in this Parliament and get the whole legislation sorted out for the next Parliament. However, that’s the way things go sometimes.

I want to talk about a number of things with respect to this bill. I just want to direct the members’ attention to the purpose statement, which is being amended. It says it’s to “inform New Zealanders about the state of the environment” and “to support evidence-based decisions that lead to effective and enduring environmental stewardship”.

It does raise quite an interesting issue, and that’s the issue of whether having better information actually does lead to better action. It’s a long-discussed point. You know, the ancient philosophers thought that a person who knew the good thing would do the good thing, but David Hume quite correctly pointed out that you need, actually, motivation not just the information. I think that’s where we’re seeing a little bit of a gap in the debate on the different sides of the House. We know that good information is great to have. It’s great to improve the quality of information. But then people actually need to act on it, and that’s a different matter. So while we applaud this process of improving the information we’re getting, the real test that we hold the Government to is what action they take based on it.

In terms of whether or not this is going to be better information, going back to the regulatory impact statement and the history of this bill and that 2019 report from PCE—the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment—did recommend some changes. The improvements—and some of the improvements have been undertaken anyway in a non-legislative process—included focusing the broad purpose of environmental reporting, including incorporating drivers and outlooks into the reporting framework. There was a science advisory panel established to help with the formation of these environmental reports, and further clarifying the roles was built in via policy processes within the Ministry for the Environment and so on, rather than doing it as a matter of legislation. The risk is that if it is just—I shouldn’t say “just” done—done within a Government department without legislative authority, then it doesn’t carry on. It can be changed subsequently.

I was particularly interested in the science panel because, looking at the legislation, one of the things the legislation does is it does establish a strategic evidence panel. The purpose of that panel is to provide independent advice to the Secretary for the Environment on environmental data monitoring and reporting. And the members of that panel need to hold relevant expertise on matters related to environmental data monitoring and reporting.

I’d like to see the committee examine that a little. In particular, I want to see science expertise on that panel. I’m looking to see if there’s a way that we can put that into the legislation rather than just leaving it up to the Secretary for the Environment. So something for the select committee to look at, and I’ll be interested to work on that committee if possible.

content.speaker: DAVID MacLEOD (National—New Plymouth)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. The quality of decision making is dictated by the information that it receives. This very small bill makes amendments the Environmental Reporting Act 2015. It does exactly that, by improving the data, improving the information that is received by decision makers, and that’s a good outcome. I commend the bill to the House.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill be now read a first time.
New Zealand National 48; New Zealand Labour 34; ACT New Zealand 11; New Zealand First 8.
Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand 14; Te Pāti Māori 4; Ferris; Kapa-Kingi.
Motion agreed to.
Bill read a first time.

Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill
Legislative Statement

content.speaker: Hon CHRIS PENK (Minister for Building and Construction)
content.text: Thank you, sir. I present a legislative statement on the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
Second Reading

content.speaker: Hon CHRIS PENK (Minister for Building and Construction)
content.text: I move, That the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill be now read a second time.

The Transport and Infrastructure Committee has considered the bill and recommends that it be passed with amendments. I’m grateful to the people and organisations who made a submission on the bill and of course to the select committee itself, who took the time to hear those submitters and to consider improvements on the bill. Following the Canterbury earthquakes and royal commission of inquiry, the current earthquake-prone buildings regime was introduced.

I just want to take a moment to acknowledge, as I’m sure all in this House would, the considerable tragedy, the loss of human life, that was entailed by those tragic events. And I don’t wish to bring you into the debate, Mr Speaker, but I will acknowledge that you more than most were familiar with the nature of the tragedy, and of course I commend and salute you for your work following that, of course, to bring that beloved region of yours back to more normal circumstances.

All that said, of course, I think it’s fairly acknowledged that the introduced legislation at that time—albeit, of course, in good faith and balancing all the relevant considerations—has not worked entirely as intended. It has inadvertently imposed large costs on building owners and communities, including throughout New Zealand, without focusing enough on the buildings that present the greatest risk to people’s lives.

This cannot continue, and so, even with the recent earthquakes in Venezuela providing a salutary reminder that we do need to prepare further for such events in New Zealand, nevertheless, we have decided that it is important to reform the earthquake-prone building regime to target or refocus on those buildings most likely to cause fatalities in an earthquake.

The changes will remove barriers to strengthening high-risk buildings, making retrofits more affordable for their owners and better protecting people in and around them. Focusing effort and investment on the highest-risk buildings will ultimately save more lives than the current one-size-fits-all approach.
Today I will briefly reiterate the bill’s key elements and summarise the key changes recommended by the select committee. As I say, we have decided to accept those changes.

First, the bill narrows the systems scope so that it targets only high-risk buildings in medium and high-risk seismic zones. It introduces tiered remediation requirements, amends the definition of priority building, and provides greater flexibility through deadline extensions and lower-cost pathways for alterations and change of use.

Only two types of buildings will remain designated as earthquake-prone buildings (EPBs): unreinforced masonry buildings and tall heavy material buildings. These are the buildings most likely to cause harm in an earthquake, and these will be only those located in medium- or high-risk seismic zones. Territorial authorities must identify and remove other building types from the EPB register in the three months from 1 July 2027.

Meanwhile, buildings in Auckland, Northland, and the Chatham Islands will be out of scope. These areas have a scientifically determined lower seismic hazard than other parts of New Zealand. On Royal assent, therefore, earthquake-prone buildings in these areas will have that designation removed.

At the same time, other provisions of the bill go through coastal Otago, including Dunedin and Oamaru and Stewart Island, will shift from a low to medium seismic zone to reflect the latest scientific understanding of seismic hazard in those places. Current earthquake-prone buildings (EPBs) there will retain their existing remediation deadlines and territorial authorities will have until 1 July 2032 to identify potential EPBs there.

The bill also narrows the so-called identify at any time pathway for designating buildings as EPBs. Too many low-risk buildings have been designated as earthquake-prone using this pathway. So the bill, as introduced, narrows the pathway to cover only the post-1976, tall, heavy-material buildings that were constructed before 2027. This includes buildings akin to the CTV building in Christchurch. For buildings that remain EPBs, territorial authorities will determine their required remediation measures in accordance with the updated EPB methodology, issue EPB notices, and keep the EPB register up to date.

The bill narrows the definition of “priority building”. Under the bill, only buildings that could fall on to a busy street or block a strategic transport route will qualify. Buildings that were priority simply because of their usage, such as hospitals or fire stations, will lose that status. Together, these changes provide clearer rules and a stronger focus on the buildings that matter most for public safety.

The bill also introduces a tiered approach to remediation, replacing the current requirement to strengthen all buildings to 34 percent of the new building standard, commonly known as NBS. There will be two principal forms of remediation measure. Most unreinforced masonry buildings will need to mitigate their risk of facades falling on to people below. Multi-storey concrete buildings and large unreinforced masonry buildings will need targeted work to prevent those buildings collapsing. For unreinforced masonry buildings then that are one or two storeys high and located outside urban centres, no remediation will be required by a set deadline. But, at the same time, I note that owners will need to mitigate the risk of façade collapse if they want the building to be taken off the EPB register.

EPB owners will be able to apply to territorial authorities for deadline extensions of up to 15 years, even if the original deadline expired before commencement. This will replace the current “up to 10 year” extension, open only to heritage EPB owners.

The bill also supports lower-cost compliance pathways for owners carrying out seismic work or changing the use of a building. If the work only involves seismic remediation, no fire or accessibility upgrades will be required. Similarly, if an owner wants to change an EPB’s use, it would only need to meet its remediation requirement, rather than anything higher. Together, these changes provide more practical and cost-effective solutions, more time to comply, and fewer barriers for owners committed to making their buildings safer.

The Transport and Infrastructure Committee has unanimously recommended amendments to address issues identified by submitters, officials, and the select committee itself. I welcome these improvements and again place on the record my thanks to the committee for their detailed examination of the bill. I note the chair, Mr Andy Foster, and I thank him and his colleagues who did such a careful and coherent job of understanding and in turn explaining the changes that have ultimately been made.

In response to feedback from submitters, the committee clarified what areas are in “urban centres”, which helps to determine the remediation requirement of an unreinforced masonry EPB. For example, Wellington and Porirua are urban centres, whereas Featherston and Greytown are not. To acknowledge the unique barriers to remediation faced by various buildings, the committee added heritage status to the list of matters that territorial authorities must have regard to when determining whether or not to grant a deadline extension. Some submitters were concerned that the alternation provisions may allow for reduced building code compliance. For example, drilling stabilising rods through walls can increase the risk of fire spreading in one room to the next. The committee introduced a backstop into the bill to ensure that seismic work needs to be done in a way that doesn’t increase the risk of fire spreading or reduce disabled peoples’ access.

The committee also amended the bill so that warning signs must be displayed on all earthquake-prone buildings, including those that are only recorded on the register or have a seismic work exemption. The committee updated the terms for the required remediation measures to façade risk mitigation and targeted retrofit. This will ensure that approaches to remediation mitigate risk but do not necessarily involve securing a façade or a full retrofit of the building can be used. This bill now also includes high-level descriptions of these measures.

Some submitters were unsure how buildings with unusually tall storeys or part storeys will be treated—a fair question. The committee clarified that the thresholds for determining how many storeys high an EPB will be will be set out in the EPB methodology. One way that a building can be a priority building with half the remediation time frame is if it may impede a strategic transport route if it were to collapse during an earthquake. Submitters recommended that territorial authorities be allowed to revisit their strategic transport route—again, I think, a very sensible recommendation. The committee therefore amended the bill to empower territorial authorities—councils, in other words—to revise and remove strategic transport routes up to 1 July 2027. No new strategic transport routes may be added, ensuring that no building owners will be worse off.

Last, in my remaining minute, the committee clarified the meaning of a building within scope. This makes it clearer which buildings are within scope of the system before the reader then looks to the EPB methodology for further technical detail. An unreinforced masonry building must have an exterior masonry wall and satisfy other criteria in the methodology to be within scope. A tall, heavy material building must have one or more significant elements, such as a roof or a floor, built using concrete or other heavy materials and satisfy any other criteria in the EPB methodology.

Overall, in summary, the bill creates a more focused and workable earthquake-prone buildings system by targeting the buildings that present the greatest risk, introducing tiered and more cost-effective remediation requirements, and reducing barriers to remediation for building owners. For all those reasons, I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: The question is that the motion be agreed to.

content.speaker: ARENA WILLIAMS (Labour—Manurewa)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. This is an important bill and an important piece of reform that Labour continues to support, with specific reservations. I’m going to use this speech to set out what those things are. They will be parts that we consider are the most sensitive and are the least well-supported around the House. It is important that we come to consensus on these rules which impact on the long-term viability of buildings and not only those that are being built now but in expensive and costly remediations that are to come in the next five to 10 years. So it is important to flag where we have bipartisan support which is for a sensible set of rules for remediation of the highest-risk buildings, but to indicate that we do have reservations around how some of the exclusions have been applied, particularly around Auckland.

Maintaining affordability has been our concern here. We want a building system and a built environment which is affordable, where remediations happen from either existing owners or there is an incentive for buildings to be sold to people who can remediate them. Because you do not want a situation like Wellington is experiencing now where some important civic sites and main streets have buildings which have not been remediated because the cost is very high and that continues to pose a risk to neighbours and to people on the street who walk past them. We want a system which incentivises that kind of remediation and where it is affordable in the public interest. So that is why we need some updates to these rules.

We have vociferously opposed at every opportunity the exclusion of Auckland from the rules for remediation of risky buildings. Colleagues, let me explain what has occurred here. Cabinet has set out to create a set of rules where the highest-risk buildings around the country are the ones that get fixed. That makes sense. We shouldn’t fix buildings which are not posing a risk to peoples’ lives and are not posing a risk to the neighbouring buildings around them. Those rules require expensive fixes and so they should be something which is sensible. There is also a category of buildings under that that require being fixed—they need to be fixed. There shouldn’t be rules which force people to adhere to a certain time line. Building owners in that category should be able to make their own decisions about what kind of risk they will put up with and what kind of risk the building’s users will put up with.

When I’m talking about these highest-risk buildings, some of those have been excluded from this bill. The way that these rules have been drawn is that if you have a very high-risk building in Auckland which is on the main street, it does not need to be remediated any more. The House must understand that by excluding Auckland, we have drawn lines on a map which mean that those remediations do not need to occur.

Yes, you could have designed a system where the highest seismic risk regions were the way that we decided what sorts of buildings would be remediated. But that’s actually not what we’ve done. If you drew lines on a map, you might use, say, faults, and areas where say, an eruption around the Alpine Fault was going to cause regional risk and regional land movement. You might have drawn lines around volcanic movements in our shaky isles.

But that is not the system we have used. We’ve used a system, which is perfectly sensible, whereby you identify the buildings which are at risk of movement in any kind of event like that and how much they are used. So a building that might move the same amount and might have the same kind of risk on the main street in Auckland is a different sort of risk to the one that’s on the West Coast and has two users a year for family weddings. That’s sensible.

But addition, at the last minute, of an exclusion for Auckland does not fit with the uncontentious and unpolitical way of identifying risk here. It has overlaid a set of judgements that are, simply put, relatively political about whether Auckland should be included or excluded from the rules.

I think that is the wrong decision. I think we will be back here in this House debating whether that has worked, because it is not a system that the public can have faith in, and it will test confidence and trust in our built environment system and whether central government stands behind the risk that we are asking Aucklanders to take on, not only as a community, but as individual business owners who, say, have buildings next to highly risky buildings and people who maintain other parts of built environment around them that are at risk because of this decision.

This is not also a minor issue for Auckland. The majority of earthquake-prone buildings are in Auckland, despite many people’s assumptions about the earthquake-prone buildings being in Christchurch; that is a largely an area which has been through a pretty painful process of having to come up to speed with the rules that we required of them. People in Canterbury have done what they have been asked. They have fixed buildings; they have remediated buildings. For some people, have that has been at personal cost, huge personal investment of family savings. For many businesses, it has meant years of having to forward-fund capital investment in their buildings, but they have done that.

This is an exclusion, now, of another region, in fact, where there are 1,400 earthquake-prone buildings, which was in the queue, and this Government has made a decision to exclude them. That decision will have lasting consequences for generations to come and is, frankly, being made at a time where that is possible for the Government to do it because it’s not in people’s minds.

The deadline extensions powers in the bill have also been something that the committee worked very closely with, and, ultimately, that is something we do not support. There are shifting goal posts now in the bill, where deadline extensions of up to 15 years don’t come back to this Parliament. They are made away from public scrutiny. What does that mean? It means that building owners don’t have a clear indication of the time that they will need to make remediations in the rest of the country.

For Wellington apartment owners, who are an important constituency when Governments of both stripes have considered this bill, they now do not have certainty of investment decisions. Little old ladies who live in apartments, and that’s their entire life savings, will be hugely impacted by this bill, and that is a very hard case.

Labour’s answer to this was not one that National politics supported. It was to use public money to assist those private owners with their private property because we recognise that there is a no-fault element of this and that it would be inequitable to treat this in any different way.

But there were other choice for the National Government to make, and simply kicking the can down the road is what is being done here in this bill. It’s a very difficult position to be putting those retirees, especially, but also first-home buyers, in, when they are now under water and find themselves without equity to invest in other properties that they would like to live in, especially in the current climate of the Wellington property market.

The committee had some very useful discussions around the idea of addressing the need for assistance that those apartment owners faced, but, ultimately, Government has not proposed either an insurance product which would help them or a financial scheme which would allow them to sell and then to recover some of the costs for the Government’s coffers. That was what was in place 2022-23 under the Labour Government and that is not what the Government has announced.

These rules in this bill should have been progressed at the same time as another scheme to properly spread risk between those who can afford it and those who can’t were introduced. Things like body corp rules are critical to getting this regime right. Those have also not been progressed at the same time.

Ultimately, this is an area where reform is welcome. We need sensible rules for remediation, and the rules aren’t working for a sector which is struggling with the construction and the repair of these buildings right now. We do not have enough capacity in the system to fix all of the earthquake-prone buildings that we need to in New Zealand today. We needed a sensible way for the Government to direct when that work would occur and where.

But the exclusion of Auckland wholesale should not have been part of the planning of that pipeline. If we’re serious about an infrastructure pipeline which works for people, we also need to consider the built environment and the private buildings which are associated with that—our construction sector needed to be able to plan that out well. There is also an extension in here which means that it might 10 years, it might be 15 years—nobody knows.

So when we’re accountable to the people in our electorate who are looking at this Parliament and seeing an improvement of the earthquake-prone building rules, we all also have to know that the risk of earthquakes hasn’t gone away, that there are risky buildings out there which this bill doesn’t deal with. Simply sticking a notice on the door doesn’t deal with it, and we all need to wear that for our communities, where there is not just private risk, it is public risk—to our main streets, to the people who use the movie theatres, to the people who use the malls, all of this is something that this Parliament should keep a very close eye on because it does speed up building, but it also spreads the risk in ways we haven’t anticipated.
Debate interrupted.
