content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s a pleasure to take a call on the Emergency Management Bill (No 2).

content.speaker: Arena Williams
content.text: On behalf of the ACT Party!

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH
content.text: Yeah, on behalf of some party in the coalition Government. However, I am genuinely pleased to take this call, because this is a portfolio that I previously held for the Labour Party for over two years. I was pleased to work with people across the House, including with the Minister, and I want to acknowledge the Minister for his work. I was trying to think of all of the different emergencies that we happened to be attending at different times throughout the last two years, and there were quite a few. It’s always a stressful time for a community, but I know that having your leadership there has always been appreciated every time you’ve been there. Thanks for being inclusive.

I know that it’s a desire of the Parliament to have this bill pass, and also it has gone across Governments as well, because some of these changes were first suggested even as early as, and some of the lessons learnt in this bill came from instances like, the Christchurch earthquake. So, this has been a long time coming. We’ve had a problem, really, in New Zealand that we’ve kept having disasters. We keep learning from them, and we’ve been trying to change the legislation, so actually to get this here to second reading is a big achievement. It was a pleasure too—I didn’t make it through the whole select committee process but I did hear all of the submissions, and it was really good to get it through that stage and hear the different submissions.

I don’t think a bill like this will ever be perfect, and you’ve heard from colleagues, including our spokesperson Cushla. I’m immensely proud to see her in her role as emergency management spokesperson for Labour, because she’s really passionate about it and also because she’s lived this. She’s lived this in her community. She’s lived through disasters. She’s volunteered. She’s knows the pressure that comes from living in a community that is at the mercy of weather and climate change, and she gets in there and she mucks in and she knows what it’s like to be there on the ground. I think she’s really well-placed to do this work.

There will, obviously, always be things that can be better with this bill. It’s not exactly the same as the bill that was introduced by, I think, Kieran McAnulty or Kiri Allan under the last Labour Government, but there are very similar aspects to it and the tenor of most of the improvements has remained the same. It also, very importantly, has learnt from the 2023 events that we had with Cyclone Gabrielle and with the Auckland flooding. This is an unusual area. I’m sure the Minister will agree that this couldn’t be more serious, because we’re talking about life and death—getting it right is important, and we have to do everything we can to make the response as safe as possible—but, in a response, you never see a better side of New Zealand than when people are responding to an emergency. People are hopeful. They’re optimistic. They muck in. They help their neighbour.

I just think this is where New Zealanders really shine in these situations, and it’s unfortunate that it’s so often tinged with a great sense of loss. Often we see that sense of loss and that feeling—once the original emergency has subsided, we see that sense of loss. I want to have an upbeat speech because I’m really positive about this bill, but we have had some terrible disasters, and the Mauao situation with the slip was just so utterly tragic, and I want to acknowledge Tom Rutherford there as well for his commitment to the response there.

That was extremely difficult for the community and I think something for the entire country to acknowledge, the danger of slips. This is an area that I was working in. To be fair, I feel that this is much more prominent now, in my mind, in terms of assessing the risks of disaster than it had been. In many ways, it’s similar to how I hadn’t fully appreciated the risk of flooding and rain until the Auckland floods as well. So we do learn from these situations, but we do have to stand alongside families. I will never forget that service where the families were there. That was incredibly moving and I think a real testament to the community in Mount Maunganui, to come together to support those families. Just wanting to acknowledge, obviously—whenever we talk about these tragedies, we have to acknowledge the families who are the ones affected and we do what we can as elected members to support people.

So this bill has changed a little bit since it was first introduced, and there are a couple of areas that the select committee changed that I think deserve mentioning. There had been a few changes that it’s become apparent were needed as the bill was really progressing through the House, and one of those ones was enabling mayors to be sworn in early. Now, this is a really interesting one because we had a situation where mayors have a very important role in our emergency management system, leading the response. We had a few situations where it wasn’t quite clear, because it was during an election period, which mayor we were meant to be relying on. That’s not really OK because in emergencies you do need a leadership structure. You need a hierarchy of when decisions are made and you need those decisions to be made, if they are decisions that should be left for someone who’s elected democratically, to be made by that democratic representative. So I think the ability to enable mayors to be sworn in actually might seem like an unusual thing, but, actually, because we have events so often in New Zealand, that probably will be something that does come up again.

I think enabling people to be co-opted is also additionally an important aspect of making sure that all of the skills are there on an emergency management committee, because sometimes you might have some communities that do have that expertise and there’s more often than not a wealth of expertise, but you might not have all the skills. So enabling that is also really important, too.

There’s also a slight change in requiring engagement and representatives of iwi Māori, and Cushla Tangaere-Manuel spoke to that earlier. This was an area which has changed a little bit since the bill that the last Labour Government put in place. So the rules in relation to engagement with Māori are not as strong as they were under our proposal. So it’s good to see that this proposal encouraging engagement is there as well.

I don’t think this is a political thing or anything that anyone would disagree with, that the response from iwi Māori and marae in disasters is exceptional throughout the country, and it is built into the way that marae are set up. For a country that experiences these events, they’re set up perfectly to respond to the events. I don’t think that’s an accident; I think that’s to do with the way that tikanga have evolved and the way that marae have evolved in order to deal with events over the time. So we just see again and again marae, iwi, and hapū standing up. I think what we haven’t been as good at in this House in the past, and I hope with this bill we can get better at it, is not just expecting that and saying thank you and moving on. It’s actually resourcing those marae to be able to do, with their leadership that actually respond, in the best way that they can, the way they want to with our support, and not only taking when we’re in need, but actually supporting those marae to step up and do the job that they have always done in New Zealand, you know, well before any of us were here and will do well after all of us are gone as well. So that is a really important thing too.

The issues around climate adaptation are important. This isn’t a bill that solves all of the future issues associated with extreme events. There are issues which are still on the table, and I know the Minister’s been working on a joined-up system in relation to making sure that people in different parts of New Zealand, when there’s a disaster in another area, can step up and use the same operating system, and, actually, we can utilise a much bigger workforce because of that common operating model. That’s tricky work. It’s expensive. There are a lot of existing operating models. But I think that that work is something that I would encourage the Minister to continue with and I know he has been doing that in the latest Budget.

The other issue is with climate mitigation. Of course, that’s so interlinked with a lot of this emergency management work. There is more to do in that space, and we have to acknowledge the fact, as a country, that we will be, especially with the confirmed El Nino weather pattern that we’re having, having these systems and these issues again and again. So this bill is a great step in the right direction. It was built on the work of this Government, this Minister, and previous Ministers, and it will be something that future Governments will work on in the future. All we can do is take the best advice, do the best we can, and make sure we do everything we can to keep New Zealanders safe in emergencies. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: SIMON COURT (ACT)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. ACT supports this bill and the necessary changes, in particular extending protection from civil liability to persons with functions, duties, or powers under the bill, who considers an imminent threat of an emergency and take preventative or precautionary actions, actions designed to limit the impacts of the emergency on people and property.

This is because during the 2023 Cyclone Gabrielle and other similar flood and storm events, people with decision-making power have often felt reluctant to take the necessary measures. Putting an excavator into a river to clear debris comes with risks of prosecution under the Resource Management Act (RMA). Putting an excavator or a bulldozer on to a beach to clear a river mouth comes risk of prosecution under the RMA. So it is important that new defences are established in this law so that when individuals, private people who might have a digger or a dozer, want to get in and do something to stop the flood damaging property or potentially harming people’s lives, they can do it. So, on that basis alone and for many other reasons, ACT commends this bill.

content.speaker: ANDY FOSTER (NZ First)
content.text: Mr Speaker, thanks. I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to speak on this bill, proud of the work that we did as the Governance and Administration Committee. I just want to pick three things very quickly. The first one of them, as Camilla Belich has already said, was empowering mayors during that interregnum period, between an election and being formally sworn in, to actually declare emergencies. That was a real issue that arose last year and was something that the mayor certainly raised with me. So we fixed that. That’s great.

Second one is being able to take, as Simon Court just said, a proactive action where there is an emergency looming. Think about the Wairoa River Bar. Action wasn’t taken quick enough—Wairoa flooded. Also Lakes Forsyth and Ellesmere—again, floods caused by the lack of proactive action. This will empower that.

The third one is the Minister said the new clause 43A is clearly linking between councils’ emergency management powers. If you’re the emergency management controller or you’re the chief executive of a council or a mayor of a council, you’ve also got powers under the Resource Management Act, etc. to link those two together. We’ve got to stop building dumb things in dumb places. That was one of the issues for Christchurch City Council. It didn’t want to have development in what is now the red zone. It got forced to do that. We’ve got to empower councils to avoid having dumb things built in dumb places.

The one other thing that I wanted to just mention is a large disagreement on the bill and one small issue, and that is the smallest area in which you can declare an emergency. We think it should be less than a ward. I mean, if you think of areas like Dunedin, if you’ve got an emergency in South Dunedin, why do you need to declare that emergency in Middlemarch as well? Likewise, Gisborne—if it’s an emergency in Te Araroa, why does it affect Gisborne city? So we think that needs to be thought through. Otherwise, great bill. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke with a split call.

content.speaker: HANA-RAWHITI MAIPI-CLARKE (Te Pāti Māori—Hauraki-Waikato)
content.text: Tēnā rā koe e te Pīka, otirā tēnā rā tātou e te Whare. E tū ana ahau ki te waha i ngā kōrero mā Te Pāti Māori i tēnei rangi mō tēnei o ngā pire.
[Thank you, Mr Speaker; indeed, greetings to all of us in the House. I stand to give voice to statements on behalf of the Māori Party today regarding this particular bill.]
Papaki tū ana ngā tai ki Mauao
I whakanukunukuhia, e whakanekenekehia
I whiua reretia e Hotu a Wahinerua ki te wai
Ki tai wiwī, kia tai wawā
Ki te whai ao, ki te ao mārama
Tihei mauri ora.
[The waves beat continuously against the rocky cliffs of Mauao,
They tried to shift the canoe forward and aloft.
Wahinerua was thrown overboard there by Hotu,
Into the swirling waters, the roaring ocean
To emerge into the world of light
It is the breath of life!]

Ko te take e tū ana ahau ki te waha i ngā kōrero, ki te whakahōnore, ki te tuku whakawhetai atu ki ngā whenua o Mauao. Kātahi anō au ka tae mai i Tauranga Moana, i te rohe o Tauranga, i te mātakinga o ngā tamariki puta noa i te motu e tū ana ki ngā whakataetae ā-motu, Te Tāwharau o ngā Waka, ki ngā kapahaka o te motu. And i te ata tonu au i tuku au ngā whakawhetai ki te maunga, ki a Mauao.

[The reason I stand to give voice to these statements is to honour and give thanks to the lands of Mount Maunganui. I have only just arrived from Tauranga Moana, from the Tauranga region, from watching children from across the country standing in the national competitions, Te Tāwharau o ngā Waka, at the national kapa haka competitions.]

Nō reira, I start my speech with acknowledging that I’ve just flown in from Tauranga this morning from the national kapa haka competition throughout the motu, and acknowledging the land slide at Mauao that I was able to go to this morning. I just want to mihi to all of the civil defence and mihi to the Minister. I acknowledge that there have been over 21 states of emergencies in this country alone this year, and I do want to acknowledge the Minister for his team and making sure that different MPs, like myself, were aware of what’s happening with the National Emergency Management Agency crisis and response team. That’s been really helpful for electorates as well.

The fact that we’ve had 21 local states of emergencies this year this year alone, due to climate crises—that could be floods, that could be landslides, that could be weather events, and also knowing that El Niño has just been confirmed as the state of Aotearoa.

In the first reading, Te Pāti Māori supported this bill with recommendations of implementing a Te Tiriti clause and also specific resourcing for funding to marae. From listening to some of the written submissions that were given in the select committee process, iwi Waikato-Tainui speaks from the strength of 68 marae, intergenerational planning, and a vision grounded in mana motuhake. When emergencies hit, it is not Wellington bureaucracy that first knows which kaumatua need support, which marae can open, which roads are cut off, which whanau are isolated, which whenua is vulnerable, or which awa is rising. The National Iwi Chairs Forum speaks from the collective authority of iwis across the motu, iwi working together to protect our people. Many other iwi submitters know deeply what emergency means. They carry responsibilities as kaitiaki over lands, waters, islands, and communities. Their knowledge is not theoretical; it is lived, it is local; it is intergenerational.

So, for us, it’s also making sure that there is specific funding given to marae prior to a weather crisis event, not after the fact. For many of us, that’s actually what happens: we’re given funding after a weather event has happened. I was able to go to Ōtorohanga during the flooding crisis at the beginning of this year, and the amount of people that marae have—whether they are Māori, non-Māori, community groups, community halls, churches. We also had the museum that was flooded during their time. There were also local schools flooded at that time, and coming together as a community, marae were going through the night and through the day. We would be doing that even if we had a dollar or a million dollars, and we’ll continue to do that.

I think it’s unfair that marae usually carry the brunt with nothing. Being able to be properly resourced, whether it is a flood, whether it is a slip—it’s from the road cones to getting a cups of tea, to housing people overnight, to getting showers for people. It varies all across, and koirā te tikanga o te marae []. E tupu ana ahau i roto i tēnei momo āhuatanga i roto i ngā Koroneihana []:that is the purpose of a maraeI grew up in this kind of paradigm in the Coronation ceremonies you just turn up, and you house people, and that, often, doesn’t come with any money whatsoever. But when you have 21 states of emergency consistently throughout the year, that’s what we’re asking for. Tēnā rā koe e te Pīka.

content.speaker: MIKE DAVIDSON (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I arise on behalf of the Green Party to speak in support of the Emergency Management Bill (No. 2). I just want to acknowledge the Minister and the work that you have done—I actually really appreciate you staying through these speeches as well—and the impact of the emergencies we have been seeing across the country. I also want to acknowledge the Governance and Administration Committee, which I am a member of, and the work that we have done, and also my Green colleague, Mr Hernandez, who is the portfolio holder for emergency management and has done a lot of the heavy lifting for us in the Green Party as well.

For the Greens—and we support it—we do have a couple of concerns. The bill’s not perfect, and it’s never going to be perfect, but then you can’t let that get in the way of saying that’s it’s actually really good, and therefore that’s why we support it. There are a number of clauses in here that do actually create really good outcomes.

The bill did seek to strengthen the role of iwi Māori during emergency management, which is really good. I did move an amendment to ensure that the costs that they incur were actually reimbursed directly to them. Unfortunately, it was supported by the Labour colleagues that sit on the select committee, but it didn’t pass. They can get reimbursement, but it has to go through local government, which I think is just a bit of a shame because as we heard just before, we have seen 21 emergencies this year. Every time there is an emergency, they open up their doors so quickly and they provide so much in the time of pain. They do that no matter how much money they have. It’s a shame that they still have to go through this truncated way of actually getting money, which could have been, I think, better streamlined. So that is a bit of a concern.

I also just want to highlight something that the Christchurch City Council said. I’m from Christchurch and I worked for the Earthquake Commission at the coal face. I was a Christchurch city councillor, and a resident of Christchurch, obviously. We’ve been through a lot through earthquakes, through fires, through floods, and the mosque attack. I’ve seen the impact of these disasters, these situations, and, actually, how people rise, their communities rise, and the importance of having good emergency management in place.

One of the things that does concern me, and it came from this submission from the city council, was that, once again, it’s the potential of increased costs to city councils and district councils with emergency management that this could put on them at a time when councils themselves are going through quite significant reform and obviously looking towards having rate capping—what pressure this will put on them, and the fact that, for them to do this properly, they need to ensure that they have the support of central government to increase that workforce capacity and financial resourcing to do it. For too long, central government has put pressure on to local government without the resources to go with it to do the job properly.

It is really good to see, at a time of an election, when we have a mayor elect, that they now have that ability to declare those states of emergency. That was obviously a significant gap in the legislation that created a significant workload for the Minister, so it’s really good that that has been sorted.

Another thing I just wanted to note was, obviously, the change to ensure that animal welfare is addressed, which I actually think was quite an important thing to do, to ensure that people can enter properties to ensure that the welfare of animals is looked after in these emergencies, and they’re not just left to suffer. It was really good that that was actually sorted out.

As I said, the Green Party had put forward a different view; that does not mean we don’t support this bill. We absolutely agree with the intention, and therefore, we do support it. There are some concerns around how we ensure that we mitigate against the impacts of climate change and adapt, because it is not going to get better; it will get worse. We can’t just keep having to react every time we have an emergency, because they’re going to keep coming and we need to ensure that we’re actually doing our bit to be more prepared. Kia ora.

content.speaker: Hon MELISSA LEE (National)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. This bill replaces the Civil Defence Emergency Management Act 2002. I’d like to acknowledge the Minister in charge, the Hon Mark Mitchell, who has done an amazing amount of work on this. This House is in unanimous agreement and I think it’s wonderful that we can pass this bill through this stage. I commend the bill.

content.speaker: LEMAUGA LYDIA SOSENE (Labour—Māngere)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Firstly, I’d like to say that we support this bill. I want to acknowledge the Minister for his work and especially the inclusion of many members across the House, and in particular those who’ve experienced the need for emergency management. We support this important step in strengthening the emergency management system, because also communities must have their say before an event actually happens.

The progress of this bill could have been faster and stronger, had the Government not scrapped Labour’s original bill, which had been through extensive policy development and public select committee process. Because there have been a number of events across Aotearoa. For some of us, we have been heavily involved, and it’s really important that we acknowledge the partnership of iwi Māori, but also all of the first responders and those in the civil defence space.

It’s important that the efficiency of emergency response is understood. We’re really pleased to see that iwi Māori, in terms of those specific communities, are around the table. I do want to acknowledge a number of speakers on this side of the House who have firsthand experience. For us in Auckland, some of us on the Auckland Anniversary weekend, we had experienced being in the thick of that specific event on that day. So the importance of acknowledging the communities that responded and all the emergency responders, in this bill it’s really important that we identify the specific elements.

I want to acknowledge the select committee members that I was able to listen to the submitters. We were able to collaborate and debate on the specific elements that we wanted to bring forward because of our experience firsthand in different weather events around the country, but also the importance of arriving at the recommendations in select committee that will be able to respond. I do want to acknowledge, too, and reflect back to the event that I was involved in. We were on the motorway on the night of the Auckland Anniversary floods, and we were trying to get through as many people in Auckland were, because what you saw before you was a weather event and absolute chaos. So when you don’t have a system for who is making the call—whether it’s the Mayor of Auckland or a person in charge—this bill addresses that there needs to be very clear communication as to who is responsible for making that call and then spreading it across Aotearoa in whatever shape or form.

What was important in that event? On that Friday evening it was peak hour traffic and people were trying to get across Auckland, children needed to be picked up from daycare, people were finishing work, absolute chaos on the motorway, and people wanted clear leadership and clear information as to what to do. I go back to that time because it was one of those events where we recognised and I’ve heard across the House many colleagues talk about specific events. I can absolutely attest that in that Auckland Anniversary event when Auckland was gridlocked there was just chaos. It was important that we were waiting for the instruction from the Mayor of Auckland at the time, and for whatever reason it wasn’t made until a few hours later. This bill seeks to strengthen that there is really clear communication across the country when a disaster or when a weather event happens.

The importance of the bill and its purpose cannot be underestimated. We were very interested as select committee members that iwi Māori would get the recognition that they deserve because I have seen time and time again in different weather events that take place, iwi Māori and hapū just set themselves up. I want to acknowledge the role that they play. They just get on with the job. I do want to acknowledge their leadership, their aroha for communities, and many times when the emergency management system is not set up adequately, they just respond. I am thankful that we are here now in addressing this bill. So we will be supporting it.

Within this bill, communities need the confidence that there is a framework that is robust, that there is clear communication, that also communities understand—and I’m talking about diverse communities. Because some of the communities when we had to respond as a local team do not speak English. So please don’t make the assumption that when bills from this House are recommended and passed through every stage of the process, there’s the next step that diverse communities need to understand the processes, who makes the call, and who is responsible to communicate that to the community.

I just want to go back to the importance of weather events in big urban places like Auckland, like South Auckland. We saw through that process a number of very good people come forward and offer what they had to help those who were vulnerable and did not know what to do. We had elderly who would not leave their houses. They had to be carried out because they were very frightened and they were very afraid. What we need to understand as a community is the trustedness that vulnerable communities put into officials and people from different responding agencies. So I want to acknowledge those too. I specifically want to acknowledge SPCA in Māngere. Why? Because we had some people in our local community who would not leave their homes, even though they were flooded, because they weren’t going to leave behind their four-legged animals. So I do want to acknowledge them for their role and also the request that they made to the different services of the day.

The bill modernises the civil defence management framework. There were many lessons that have been learnt from Cyclone Gabrielle, the flooding on Auckland Anniversary, and events like Cyclone Hale. We heard from another of our colleagues that just this year alone there have been 21 weather events. So as we’ve heard, the system needs to have strong legislation that then people are very clear across Aotearoa in terms of who makes that call in responding and the resource is really important.

As you heard my other colleague talk about why we were supporting that iwi Māori and hapū would have a very effective and efficient system, but also work alongside the emergency management system. We weren’t supported in terms of a National Māori Emergency Management Advisory Group. I just want to put it out there in terms of the recognition and the acknowledgment of an advisory group that iwi Māori can sit on because they do their thing and they do it very well. Sometimes the connections channels don’t necessarily work, but it’s important that that is acknowledged through this bill and that it is strengthened, so that the people of Aotearoa in different communities and different diverse groups have the acknowledgment and the understanding that the bill will be very clear in terms of its recommendations.

The bill provides full recognition in terms of emergency management. It’s really important that when you’ve got executive groups that there is a clear understanding of the coordination of that. Because, importantly, it provides clarity around national, regional, and local responsibilities, and that it strengthens those planning mechanisms and gives the National Emergency Management Agency the tools to improve the response and readiness. There are specific aspects for those affected communities that they know who to go to, where to go to, and there’s a clearness of the channels of communication that come through. So those specific aspects are really important and they are fully supported by Labour. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: Hon Dr SHANE RETI (National—Whangārei)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I too want to acknowledge the courage and the contribution from our front-line responders to emergency management and also acknowledge the back office, particularly the staff and scientists at MetService and Earth Sciences New Zealand and commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: Hon Phil Twyford—this is a split call.

content.speaker: Hon PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atatū)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. Well done to the Minister, Mark Mitchell, for shepherding this bill through the House in a way that has attracted such wide support across the Parliament. It’s really good to see. It strikes me that this strengthening and modernising of our emergency management framework—the whole system, really—is kind of one of a handful of very, very pressing tasks that the country has as we try to equip ourselves for an era of climate change. Working out what to do about our transport network is another one. Managed retreat to reduce future risk for people and property is another. This is certainly one really important transition we have to make.

Other than the specialists, we all really reach for our own personal experience to try to make sense of these issues, and for me the relevant experience was as a local MP being right in the middle of the anniversary weekend floods in 2023, which had a huge impact in West Auckland. In my electorate alone, there were about 300 homes that had catastrophic flooding, with water knee or waist high inside the house; those homes made uninhabitable; and, on the night, many life-threatening situations, with old people and the disabled being kind of carried out of their homes by people through very high waters in the street.

One of the things that really struck me in the immediate days after the anniversary weekend floods was how little the emergency services actually touched the lives of the people who were affected. By and large, people were basically left to their own devices. I mean, obviously, ambulances and police and first responders and fire were out there, and there were some evacuations going on, and so on, but for a tiny proportion of the number of people affected. The great majority of people were left entirely on their own.  Maybe that’s just the way it is. Maybe that’s the way it has to be. I don’t know. But I was shocked by that.

The other thing that I recall and know from those early days, and actually in the weeks that followed, was that both Government agencies and—in West Auckland we’re blessed with this incredible network of community agencies—social sector groups, together they all mobilised. Carmel Sepuloni, a neighbouring MP and also the Minister for Social Development then, was at the welfare hub there. It was truly impressive, actually, to see Government agencies and the NGOs working together, providing income support, food, clothing, and an array of different social services. That was a very impressive part of the immediate post-disaster response.

I wanted to say something else about the cross-party consensus. I think it is extremely important. Citizens having confidence that Governments will respond both with efficiency and integrity and in an accountable way is extremely important. As parliamentarians and anyone in Government, it is at our peril if Government doesn’t deliver for citizens in times of emergency. There are many examples, not really in New Zealand but internationally. I think of Hurricane Katrina in New Orleans. The political backlash when Governments don’t do a good job and aren’t there to protect their citizens in moments of need can be pretty formidable.

I wanted to make just a brief comment about the importance—not only in Labour’s process in the bill that we had but in this bill and in the Government’s inquiry that they did that informed this bill—of marae. It says something about this unique institution in New Zealand society. It strikes me as an interesting analogy in COVID, when it was very clear that the Ministry of Health—central government—couldn’t reach down into the community to deliver the vaccination programme and was reliant on marae and Māori organisations and community-based primary health organisations. This is another example, I think, of how critical marae are for the delivery of emergency services, and it’s great to see that being recognised so fulsomely in this bill.

content.speaker: PAULO GARCIA (National—New Lynn)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. The Emergency Management Bill (No 2) replaces the Civil Defence (Emergency Management) Act 2002, ensuring that we are fixing the basics on dealing with significant emergencies that affect multiple regions all at once. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: It’s my understanding from Mr Speaker that Labour had an earlier call and have forfeited this call.

content.speaker: TIM COSTLEY (National—Ōtaki)
content.text: I just want to commend the Minister on the way he’s built a team and cohesion around delivering this plan, just as the National Party focused on building the future resilience. This is a key part of that. I commend this bill to the House.
Motion agreed to.
Bill read a second time.
Regulatory Systems (Social Security) Amendment Bill (No 2)
Legislative Statement

content.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON (Minister for Social Development and Employment)
content.text: I present a legislative statement on the Regulatory Systems (Social Security) Amendment Bill (No 2).

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
First Reading

content.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON (Minister for Social Development and Employment)
content.text: I move, That the Regulatory Systems (Social Security) Amendment Bill (No 2) be now read for a first time. I nominate the Social Services and Community Committee to consider the bill.

This amendment bill is an omnibus bill that amends legislation administered by the Ministry of Social Development and the New Zealand Defence Force. Specifically, the bill makes a number of minor policy and technical changes to the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001, the Social Security Act 2018, and the Veterans’ Support Act 2014, and repeals the Family Benefits (Home Ownership) Act 1964. This bill is intended to improve the provision of social welfare benefits. The amendments in the bill will update statutory provisions, address regulatory duplication gaps and errors, and bring legislation up to date with public expectations. The bill will reduce the chance of regulatory failure and unintended consequences that harm the wellbeing of New Zealanders. The changes are small and do not warrant stand-alone bills, but together the changes will ensure greater effectiveness and efficiency of the social welfare system.

The first minor policy change is to extend the sustainable employment trial for supported living payment recipients from 26 weeks to a maximum period of 104 weeks. The supported living payment is a benefit payable to people who are permanently and severely restricted in their capacity to work because of a health condition, injury, disability, or because they are totally blind. The purpose of the sustainable employment trial is to encourage and support supported living payment recipients who want to move into employment or increase their hours of work to establish whether they can sustain that employment and cease receiving the benefit.

Feedback from health and disability stakeholders and international evidence indicates that the fear of losing the supported living payment entitlement can be a significant barrier to work and that 26 weeks is not long enough for some recipients to test their ability to work. Furthermore, increasing hours of work incrementally over a longer period better supports people to sustain employment and become independent. Extending the sustainable employment trial to two years will therefore improve incentives for supported living payment recipients to work as much as they can, leading to a better financial position and improved wellbeing outcomes for those who can participate.

The second policy change is to ensure that residents of the Realm countries of Niue, Cook Islands, and Tokelau cannot use social security agreements to meet the residence requirements for New Zealand superannuation and veterans’ pension. Social security agreements are bilateral treaties between Governments that provide for the reciprocal payment of social security benefits and pensions. These agreements are intended to apply to the residence of the two agreement partner countries. However, the Ministry of Social Development has advised that a court would likely find that some of New Zealand’s social security agreements could apply to people applying for New Zealand superannuation or veterans’ pension while resident in the Realm countries.

Social security agreements are not intended to apply to residents of the Realm countries. Realm countries do not have the resources to participate in the cost-sharing aspects of social security agreements. Instead, New Zealand superannuation special portability provisions are extended to the residents of the Realm. Therefore, the bill will amend the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001 and the Veterans’ Support Act 2014 to exclude the application of social security agreements to Realm country residents.

The third minor policy change will enable people who are live organ donors to be eligible for an emergency benefit payment equivalent to the rate of the supported living payment. Currently, a supported living payment recipient who is caring for a person who would otherwise require hospital or residential care is not eligible to receive supported living payments should they be recovering from surgery for a live organ donation. This is because they are not caring for someone while they are recovering from surgery, which is a criterion to receive the supported living payment—caring. Instead, they are transferred on to the emergency benefit while they are in their recovery period and can only receive the rate of the equivalent main benefit that they would be entitled to, which is either the jobseeker support or sole parent support. This anomaly in the supported living payment does not align with the Compensation for Live Organ Donors Act 2016, which is designed to remove financial deterrents to the donation of organs by live donors. Therefore, the bill will establish explicit legal authority to pay emergency benefit to clients at the same rate that they were receiving on the supported living payment on the ground of caring for another person for a period of up to 12 weeks after the donation.

As I noted earlier, the bill also contains minor technical amendments. These minor amendments are mostly related to the Social Security Act 2018 and the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001. Rather than go through each technical amendment, let me highlight the common themes behind the changes. The majority of the proposed amendments will address errors or omissions found following the rewrite of the Social Security Act 1964 to the Social Security Act 2018. Other changes are aimed to improve the provision of social welfare benefits and strengthen the performance of the social security system. There are also changes which will repeal redundant legislation. For example, the bill will repeal section 190A of the Veterans’ Support Act 2014, which has been replaced by section 127 of the Legislation Act 2019.

In conclusion, it can be difficult to find time on the parliamentary calendar for repairs and maintenance of existing legislation. This amendment bill is a vehicle for smaller regulatory fixes to be progressed in a timely and cost-effective way in order to improve the provision of social welfare benefits. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: The question is that the motion be agreed to.

content.speaker: Hon WILLOW-JEAN PRIME (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker, for the opportunity to take a short call on the Regulatory Systems (Social Security) Amendment Bill (No 2).

I do want to remind the House that this bill was first introduced on 30 April 2024 but was discharged. I think we can all remember what happened at the time, and I think some of us found it quite ironic that that was the case—that the Minister for Social Development and Employment didn’t turn up to work that day. But here we are, apparently in a timely and more cost-effective way, making these amendments through an omnibus bill under urgency because this was discharged back on 23 July 2024. I’m not sure why it is that we are in July 2026, now fixing up this error that was made.

content.speaker: Jenny Marcroft
content.text: Check your email.

content.speaker: Hon WILLOW-JEAN PRIME
content.text: Oh, it might be Gmail—that’s what you all use on that side, isn’t it? [Interruption] Anyway—this is going to be easy, to fill my five minutes.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: OK. Order! Order! The member’s made her points now. We’ll come to the bill.

content.speaker: Hon WILLOW-JEAN PRIME
content.text: Kia ora.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: Thank you.

content.speaker: Hon WILLOW-JEAN PRIME
content.text: Now, coming to the bill that we have before us in July 2026, the disclosure statement says that it’s important that the legislative framework for social development is fit for purpose, and, as the Minister outlined in her legislative statement, this is about ensuring that we are maintaining the currency of our legislation. It does make minor policy changes and minor technical amendments, and the idea is that the changes are intended to improve the provision of social welfare benefits and the functioning of the overall social security system and that it will make it easier for the Ministry of Social Development to perform its duties.

There are some changes from the original bill to what we have before us now, and I’ve looked at the updates between the first and the second versions. Again, they are largely minor and technical corrections, cross-reference fixes, but there are a couple that have meaningful structural difference—for example, clause 15 with the accommodation supplement. Then we have a new clause 17, which amends section 304A, and that is a cross reference. Then we have minor drafting changes. I note, from listening to the Minister’s speech and also reading the legislative statement that has been tabled, that all of those changes are outlined there, and there’s quite a list. That, essentially, is the main point about this—to fix up these minor and technical changes.

One thing I did want to point out for the House, from the disclosure statement, is just the point around the consistency with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act. In there, there was advice to the Attorney-General. It was noted that the amendment “prima facie limits the right to freedom from discrimination on the grounds of family status. However, it also noted that ‘Social security legislation necessarily targets limited government assistance to those most in need of it. Assistance and obligations on those receiving it are then tailored to suit individual circumstances. Eligibility for benefits and obligations on beneficiaries are inherently discriminatory as they are based on drawing distinctions on many prohibited grounds.’ The advice goes on to say that ‘We consider the amendment serves the important objective in minimising the use of limited government assistance to support people who are unlawfully or temporarily in New Zealand’” and therefore concludes that it “appears to be consistent with the rights and freedoms affirmed in the Bill of Rights Act.”

I think it’s important to point that out, and one of the things I was thinking about when I was reading this is that this is in the case of what is provided for in legislation versus what might be provided for in letters of expectation or performance management of staff members in making discretionary decisions. This is clearly—and I’m less concerned because this is clearly—about what is in legislation.

I don’t have much more to add other than these are largely minor and technical amendments for consistency and to ensure that we have the overall functioning of the social security system, and that it’s easier for the Ministry of Social Development to perform its duties. Kia ora.

content.speaker: RICARDO MENÉNDEZ MARCH (Green)
content.text: Thank you so much, Madam Speaker. The Green Party is supporting the Regulatory Systems (Social Security) Amendment Bill (No 2) at its first reading. I did want to take the opportunity to comment on the context of why we are debating this bill just now. I think there is something to be said about the fact that, if the Ministers applied the same standards they do to beneficiaries, they would probably be on the red or yellow light in the traffic light system, as beneficiaries often are put if they fail to meet some of their obligations or requirements. But, here we are today, and I do want to echo that these bills are intended to address small, non-controversial changes that ideally would garner cross-party support—tidy-ups; things that may have not been identified. I notice and echo the comments from the Minister for Social Development and Employment that it seems like some of these changes have to do with omissions that were not codified in the rewrite of the Social Security Act that was finalised in the first term of the previous Labour Government.

This was supposed to be a policy-neutral rewrite, and I guess it raises a question, for example, with the changes in clause 10. From what I have read, it seems like this is just codifying existing practice. I’d be keen to understand the legal basis for that practice, seeing as that wasn’t carried over in the rewrite that occurred in 2018, and that is something that we are interested in being able to unpack in the select committee stage. What was the legal basis for the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) to continue that practice, seeing as it wasn’t carried over in the 2018 rewrite? That, to me, is something that raises some questions, and I note that, obviously, this was part of what was analysed—not so much the sort of legality of continuing the practice but whether it limited any of the rights and freedoms affirmed in the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act. There’s some commentary in there, as well, that will be worthwhile unpacking in the select committee stage.

The reason why I’m focusing on clause 10 is that we know, in this country, there’s about 20,000 people, according to the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment’s (MBIE) estimates, who are without a visa here. Many of them will have connections to people who are eligible for a benefit. Many of them will also be having family members and children that were born here in this country—children who have never been or lived in another country at all. Therefore, I guess there’s a question of, for example, whether the provisions and codifying the previous practice that was applied under the Social Security Act 1964 is contributing to material hardship for those families and for the children involved.

The reason why I say this is that the codification of the existing practice relies on calculating both people’s assets and incomes together but then the person receiving a single rate of a benefit. What that means is that the threshold to qualify for a benefit, when it comes to the calculation of joint incomes and assets, is pretty low. You don’t have to earn a lot as a couple to fully lose your eligibility to a benefit. I guess it would be useful to understand whether MSD, for example, has any data or information on how many people have not been able to access a benefit due to the provisions in clause 10 that are being codified through this bill. This is, I guess, one of the bits of the legislation that I would hope gets a little bit of further scrutiny, because the fact that we have had the rewrite of 2018 for about eight years now and this kind of being left out, in what was supposed to be a policy-neutral rewrite, raises questions of exactly how MSD has been applying, for example, the approach of giving someone the rate of a single person while also at the same time calculating both people’s incomes and assets for the purpose of eligibility criteria.

I would invite people who tend to work with undocumented migrants to submit to the select committee so that we can understand exactly how this will apply to a demographic that is often more vulnerable to exploitation, who often are more vulnerable to financial stress, and who, ultimately, are part of our communities and our societies. Like I said, many of them are raising family members who would have been born here and know no other country.
With that, we are supporting this bill, and we look forward to being able to unpack some of the less non-controversial bits of this amendment. Thank you very much.

content.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR (ACT)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. The ACT Party is supporting the Regulatory Systems (Social Security) Amendment Bill (No 2). This bill is intended to improve the administration of social welfare and is intended to fix technical errors and omissions. It does not make any significant underlying policy setting changes.

The Minister has already described the changes that this bill makes. They are minor policy changes. Otherwise, they are just omissions that are being corrected—drafting errors that are being corrected. The ACT Party really believes in ensuring that our laws are kept up to date, they are clear, and they are fit for purpose, and Parliament should not be waiting for any big problems arising from these kinds of errors in our legislation. It’s really important that we fix these things as soon as possible, so I commend the bill to the House. Thank you.

content.speaker: JAMIE ARBUCKLE (NZ First)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to support the Regulatory Systems (Social Security) Amendment Bill (No 2). This bill is to fix a number of common-sense fixes, correcting errors, clarifying rules, and removing redundant laws. I commend it to the House.

content.speaker: JOSEPH MOONEY (National—Southland)
content.text: I rise to speak on this bill. This is a sensible bill that will simplify the legislation and make it fit for purpose and operate effectively by making minor policy and technical amendments and ensure that we are fixing the basics so that we can build the future of this country. I commend the bill to the House.

content.speaker: HELEN WHITE (Labour—Mt Albert)
content.text: Madam Speaker, thank you. This bill is coming to my committee, and I’m pleased to see it come.

content.speaker: Dana Kirkpatrick
content.text: Our committee.

content.speaker: HELEN WHITE
content.text: Our committee, in fact. Absolutely, I’ll correct that. There are some great people on the Social Services and Community Committee, and we will take it extremely seriously. It is one that is a cluster of quite technical changes. It is one that will take a little bit of getting our heads around, in terms of some of the things that are in it, but it will also be a real opportunity for us to look at the system we have and make it better.

I wanted to go through some of the things about the bill that have caught my eye. I was interested that we were repealing the Family Benefits (Home Ownership) Act 1964. Now, many people watching will remember—if they’re old enough—that many of our parents got their first home through this Act, which was the capacity to take the family benefit, bundle it up, and then it was coupled with, I think, a 3 percent interest rate on the home loan. My parents were parents affected like that. They were not from any kind of inheritance. They had no money behind them. They were, in fact, in a little town called Kawerau, which some of my colleagues know well. They were able to buy a house under that scheme. So, in some ways, I’m going to be sad to see that gone from the statute book, because I think it’s a really interesting idea and it made a big difference in New Zealand. And we do, after all, have a housing crisis.

I also wanted to just mention the part of the bill that talks about extending the sustainable employment trial. Now, this looks to me like a really good part of the bill. It’s for people who are recipients of benefits—supported living in particular—based on medical grounds. They are able to work 15 hours at the moment, for a period of up to 26 weeks, without losing that entitlement. But then it stops. It actually puts people into a situation where the international evidence suggests that people are worried to go and do that work because they’re worried that that benefit, that backstop, will stop. What is good about this legislation is that it extends the sustainable employment trial to 104 weeks, and that just seems like a really good idea. People are moving into work. It gives them a capacity to do that. That looks like a very good part of the legislation.

Another part of this legislation is the extension of benefit entitlements to people on supported living payments who are caring for live organ donors. My recall is that there’s another part of this Act that dovetails in with that and looks after people in that situation in a way that hasn’t been possible until now. Now, it did say in the notes that I’ve received that nobody’s actually been put in that terrible position of not getting that kind of cover as a caregiver until now, but it’s really nice that we’re getting ahead of it and we’re making sure that we’re not disincentivising that at all.

One other thing I just noticed in the bill, in clause 16, is that the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) may grant a child disability allowance for a child with a serious disability if someone is caring for them. I was really interested to see that it’s somebody who’s in a private home and there’s an accommodation part of that as well. I like to see that kind of discretion being given to MSD. I think we take away too many discretions, and that can cause real harm. The people who are working in these departments—it’s great if they’ve got the capacity to do something in a humane way and support people. I look forward to seeing this bill in my select committee.

content.speaker: DANA KIRKPATRICK (National—East Coast)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. This of course is the Regulatory Systems (Social Security) Amendment Bill (No 2). It is a small—well, it is a complicated bill, actually, for the Social Services and Community Committee. But, basically, it’s small tidy ups and non-controversial fix-its, and I commend the bill to the House.

content.speaker: GEORGIE DANSEY (Labour)
content.text: Kia ora. It is good to take a call on the Regulatory Systems (Social Security) Amendment Bill (No 2). I acknowledge that this is a technical-change bill, but, as the previous speaker mentioned, it is complicated for the Social Services and Community Committee. So I look forward to that process.

I wanted to start, really, by acknowledging all of the people involved in the Ministry of Social Development (MSD)—all of the people that work there and all of the people that receive the support of the Ministry of Social Development. It’s a huge ministry that does very, very valuable work, and it’s good to tidy up some bits and pieces to make sure that the ministry is operating at a level that is manageable for staff and those accessing the services. I see this bill as fixing up some of those minor policy changes and technical amendments, which will hopefully go towards a more effective use of MSD for all those involved.

The legislation that is being affected: New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001, the Social Security Act 2018, and the Veterans’ Support Act 2014, as well as the repeal of the Family Benefits (Home Ownership) Act 1964. And these changes will make sure that the legislation is fit for purpose for the Ministry of Social Development. The ministry, when it’s most effective, ensures that people receive the right support at the right time, improves individual wellbeing, and strengthens communities across New Zealand. And this bill I see as making it easier for MSD to perform its duties.

I think it’s an important time for us to be having this discussion. You know, outside of this bill, MSD is in the news around targets, in their use of targets for staff, which could be used to see as gaming the system in emergency housing and putting pressure on staff to reach their targets in order to reach the approval of management.

The issue there is what’s happening with the data and if people are being processed through the system as they should into emergency housing or if they are pushed off in other directions and what pressure staff might feel in order to reach those targets. That’s not something that we want, and it’s something that we need to make sure that people are getting access to—affordable housing in whatever case that might look like—while also being a very effective service and not taking too much time to get people the support that they need. And this is a good bill in order to tidy up some of those.

It would be good to see this Government go a lot further than they have in regards to support within MSD, and I hope to see a subsequent bill that addresses the huge inequities in our society concerning people’s access to housing, as I mentioned earlier. But this bill, with its minor policy changes, will do that. I hope that it allows the ministry to promote its value of getting people into employment and independent through jobseeker assistance, training, and employment programmes and also goes further to protect children and families by connecting people with services that will improve their wellbeing and safety.

I wanted to, just before I finish, speak a little bit to the differences between the first and the second version. Other speakers have spoken to their concern around what happened with the first version and why we’re in urgency now on the second version, so I won’t go over that again. But there are some differences in the legislation between the first and the second version, particularly around the Accommodation Supplement under clause 15, the new clause 17, clause 21, and a new clause 24. Labour does support this bill, and I look forward to hearing back after select committee.

content.text: Look, this bill makes minor technical policy amendments to help ensure the legislation is fit for purpose. It’s all about fixing the basics so we can get on with building the future.

Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill
Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill
Legislative Statement

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: I present the legislative statements on the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: Those legislative statements are published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
Second Reading

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: I move, That the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill be now read a second time.

I am pleased to speak to these bills in the House again today. As I noted in my first reading speech, the regulatory system amendment bills are one of the ways that this Government maintains and repairs existing legislation and ensures that our regulatory systems deliver for New Zealanders. At a high level, these two bills reflect the Government’s commitment to delivering fit for purpose regulation and to improving access to justice. They will have a significant impact on the regulatory regimes that govern tribunals and occupational regulation, enhancing their effectiveness and efficiency while improving consumer protection and the quality of justice legislation.

The Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill makes practical improvements to tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies. It removes barriers to justice by allowing successful applicants in the disputes tribunal to recover their filing fee from the respondent where it is appropriate. It strengthens the regulation of the private security industry by providing more effective information-gathering powers to investigate breaches. It also streamlines appointments and employment arrangements for tribunal members to ensure these bodies operate efficiently.

The Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill strengthens protections for both consumers and regulated professionals while reducing unnecessary compliance costs. One important change allows conveyancers’ professional undertakings to be enforced in the High Court, just as lawyers’ undertakings already are. This promotes competition in the conveyancing market and benefits consumers.

The bill also removes a disproportionately harsh penalty that automatically disqualifies real estate agents from practising for five years simply because they failed to complete continuing professional development or pay fees on time. That issue has been recognised by the profession for many years, and this bill delivers a more proportionate response. At the same time, the bill strengthens the Real Estate Authority’s ability to investigate unlicensed trading and ensure licensee’s meet their obligations, improving consumer confidence in the industry.

Both bills have benefited from the select committee process, and I would like to thank the Justice Committee and the Education and Workforce Committee for their careful consideration, along with everyone who made submissions. Their constructive feedback has resulted in sensible improvements.

The Justice Committee has clarified the role of the Complaints, Investigations and Prosecution Unit when dealing with complaints about unlicensed private security operators. The Education and Workforce Committee has recommended that the Real Estate Authority’s new powers be exercised on a reasonable basis and clarified that provisions relating to unsatisfactory conduct apply only where behaviour is connected to a licensee’s professional role and affects public confidence in the profession. These are practical improvements that make already sensible bills even stronger.

I also thank officials and the Parliamentary Counsel Office for their work in developing these bills. Whether someone is taking a claim to the Disputes Tribunal, buying a home through a conveyancer, or working as a real estate agent, these reforms will make our regulatory systems fairer, more efficient, and easier to navigate. They demonstrate this Government’s commitment to good regulatory stewardship, maintaining the laws we already have, reducing unnecessary compliance, and improving access to justice and ensuring regulations work for the people they are meant to serve. I commend these bills to the House.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. It’s a pleasure to be able to take a call on not one but two bills at the same time, the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill. These bills cover quite a few different things, and I’ll talk about them both briefly. Essentially, as I understand, there was a programme that went through where four regulatory systems amendment bills administered by the Ministry of Justice were looked at, and I think this goes alongside the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Courts) Amendment Bill, which we’ve just had re-referred to select committee prior to this.
For anyone getting papers from the Table, be very careful about which regulatory systems bill you pick up, because there are three on the Table—well, at least two or three on the Table at the moment.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: Very good advice.

content.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall
content.text: So considerate.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH
content.text: Thank you. I have looked at these bills—and I’ve looked quite carefully just to check, as a good Opposition spokesperson should do—and they do appear in all my analysis to be minor and technical, and I was unable to kind of find any fish-hooks in either of them so far.

The interesting—well, interesting for me; maybe not for anyone else. I was on the Education and Workforce Committee but, sadly, just missed hearing the submissions on the occupational bill, and now I am on the Justice Committee, but I also missed hearing the submissions on the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill. It does appear that both select committees have done a thorough job in looking through these proposals and have made some sensible changes as well, which I think the Minister touched on.

I do note, from the Table—and I just quickly looked at them, so I may not have taken my own advice on noticing which regulatory system all the amendments related to! I did notice some amendments there from the Minister too, so I’m sure, when we get to the committee stage, she’ll explain what those amendments are and what they do. Again, we have looked at those, and they do appear to be minor and technical, along the lines of what these bills are meant to do.

Just briefly on both bills, I’ll start with the tribunals bill, which we will move on to look at more closely in the committee stage. It is a bill that’s structured in a way that we will be able to have a much closer look at in the committee stage, too, because it is an omnibus bill that does amend, I think, five different bills: the Disputes Tribunal Act 1988, the Motor Vehicle Sales Act 2003, the Parole Act, the Private Security Personnel and Private Investigators Act, and the Unit Titles Act 2010. We’ll be able to look at those in a little bit more detail at this time.

I suppose one criticism is that I’m not 100 percent convinced these are very urgent bills. We are in urgency. In the real world, it’s a Friday; here, it’s still 30 June, a Tuesday. We are a little bit unconvinced about the urgency of these, considering they are, as the Minister said, minor and technical. None the less, that is not my call to make, so we will look through them.

Just to finish off on the tribunals bill, this bill does make a number of changes to those Acts that I did state before. I suppose, notably, a few things about that bill are the fact that you can get a filing fee back for the Disputes Tribunal. I think that’s a good change. I think people are probably surprised that that wasn’t already something you could claim back, and, obviously, it’s a disincentive for people to seek justice through the Disputes Tribunal, so I commend the Minister for bringing in that change. There are some interesting changes to private security. I mean, that always is something you do look at more closely, and so we will have some questions for the Minister around some of those changes. They do seem reasonable, though.

Then, to move to the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill, this has three major policy proposals: the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act, the Prostitution Reform Act, and the Real Estate Agents Act. There are some sensible changes there as well. I think the Prostitution Law Reform Act changes are around the people who are able to hold a certificate to operate a brothel and making sure that there’s alignment between that and the Crimes Act and the Misuse of Drugs Act, which I think appears to be sensible. It also allows some changes to the Law Society’s complaints mechanism, which I think appears to be sensible. For example, there’s discretion given to the Law Society, rather than an automatic referral of a complaint. I think you can also see the potential value in that.

There’s a new name in this as well, for the Real Estate Agents Authority is now the Real Estate Authority, which I think sounds better. I can’t make much more comment than that. I don’t know why they decided to change it. They did also decide to change the membership of the now—well, soon after this passes—Real Estate Authority, so  that the chairperson doesn’t have to be a lawyer. As a former lawyer, I support opening up leadership opportunities for non-lawyers. That’s also a good change. They do, importantly, have to have a lawyer on the authority, but it just doesn’t have to be the chairperson—so there we go; hopefully, everyone will remember that. There’s also some discretion in relation to licences for real estate agents, and I know, in emergency situations, sometimes licences lapse, and so those changes have been made following events that we all lived through with Cyclone Gabrielle and the Auckland floods. Anyway, there’s some further discretion there.

We will have the opportunity to look at these bills separately. It’s kind of an odd situation talking about two bills at a second reading—two different select committee processes; two different sets of recommendations—and then we’ll have two totally separate committee stages. We will be able to look at that more closely, but I think, just reflecting that this is also the job of this House, not everything we do here is on hugely controversial pieces of legislation or pieces of legislation that we feel very passionate about. The fact that we’re all here on a Friday doing this work because it makes the law of New Zealand work better should be commended. With that in mind, I commend both of these bills to the House.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise on behalf of the Green Party of Aotearoa to speak to these two associated bills, the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill.

I want first to address some of the context around these two bills. As we see with the regulatory impact statement—and I think, from the previous contribution by my colleague Georgie Dansey, I now can’t look at “RIS” in the same way without thinking it’s “rizz”. But I do believe that these two bills very much do have rizz, despite the fact that they may come across as being reasonably boring.

content.speaker: Tom Rutherford
content.text: That’s a test of generations.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
content.text: Thank you, Tom Rutherford. As a millennial, I very much appreciate that particular shout out.

I think, in terms of the context, this is a broader suite being brought by the Minister around the regulatory systems justice package. Now, we have just heard previously that as one part of this package, the Regulatory Systems (Courts) Amendment Bill is being recommitted into the select committee stage, and we’ll be interested to have further opportunities to analyse that particular bill.

The other bills that are part of this package that actually extended beyond simply a regulatory systems bill were the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Amendment Bill and the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism (Supervisor, Levy, and Other Matters) Amendment Bill (AMLCFT) bills, and those two bills previously were also associated. I am looking forward to the committee stage for these two bills, and hopefully we won’t have the same hilarious, I guess, incidents we had with the two AMLCFT bills, where we kind of crossed over a little bit, and that was much to this House’s enjoyment in general.

In terms of the two bills that we have here—the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill—it is also important to understand that often we do have a lot of these regulatory systems bills. We just saw the first reading of one on social development and a few days ago in calendar days—but not so much in House days, because it’s still Tuesday here in the House—we saw the Regulatory Systems (Primary Industries) Amendment Bill. It’s always what we consider as sort of housekeeping bills to update our legislation overall in a collaborative, non-partisan way. Because for a lot of these—as we understand—as primary legislation, the only way to amend them is through Parliament and through this House. These are a way for us to group a lot of that together, and we have other mechanisms around some of the other updates as well—statutes amendment bills being a really great example of that.

I’m going to start with the first bill, actually, which is the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill, which was heard by the Education and Workforce Committee. Now, I do want to say that originally the Green Party opposed this bill, but after going through the select committee stage—and this is particularly due to the Real Estate Agents Act 2018. We did have some concerns around this part of the bill, but I just also want to acknowledge the Minister during the select committee process for her transparency in terms of responding to our questions, which has reassured us that the particular ways around the registration or in terms of unsatisfactory conduct, after hearing from the officials, is something that is more severe than any other professions that we have seen. I think in order for us to maintain that consistency, we were happy with what we’ve heard both from the officials but also from the Minister regarding this particular section.

We did look at some of the comparable jurisdictions around de-registration, whether it is conveyors, whether it is from other professions, lawyers, etc. Again, upon balance, from what we’ve been told by the officials, it is something that is more on the other extreme end. We are happy with where that particular part has landed, so I think overall, in terms of both regulatory systems bills, the Green Party will be supporting both. I think when we did the first reading of this, it is quite unusual in general for a political party to oppose a regulatory systems bill and we didn’t do that lightly. But, again, like I said, we are happy with where we’ve landed.

Just in terms of the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill, it is important to note that other than the Real Estate Agents Act, there are also other additional parts that have been touched on that this bill encompasses as well—lawyers and conveyors being one of them. We will be just checking a few more things with the Minister as we go through the committee stage, but also noting that for this bill, the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill, but also for the tribunals, the Ministers do have some additional amendments to this, which we’ll be able to hopefully check with the Minister during the committee stage as well. I think at this stage, both of them, in terms of updates, also seem reasonable, but I just want to be able to make sure, since we’re only seeing these two quite recently.

The other bill that I want to touch on, the second bill we’re looking at, the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill—there are sort of five parts to this. Again, we’ve seen just previously when we are talking about whether it is the Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill or I mentioned previously in terms of the Judicature (Timeliness) Legislation Amendment Bill, it is a way for us to look at how we’re able to ensure that we have timeliness. I think overall, whether it’s tribunals, whether it’s community magistrates, in a lot of the conversations we’ve had, what is important from our perspective and from the Greens’ perspective is number one in terms of some of the delays we’re seeing in our justice system but also in terms of some of that access.

Again, some of the things we’re seeing here, particularly with regards to the Disputes Tribunal Act and also the Parole Act, for example, hopefully, once these bills are passed through the House, we’ll see some changes that will allow us to have more of an impact in terms of the ability for people to access justice in different ways, of course noting, as we discussed with the previous bills with the community magistrates, whether it’s the disputes tribunal—because, again, we’re not looking at it from the lens of higher courts, from District Court and above, and with greater powers come greater responsibilities. It will be important for us to see how we’re able to also balance the better access to justice with some of the outcomes that we see as a part of these changes.

I do want to touch on one particular aspect of this. For both bills, as we’re going through the select committee and we’re hearing from the officials—I mentioned before we heard from the Ministers and also heard from the submitters—we have also made amendments as a part of a select committee. I was glad to be sitting on both the Education and Workforce Committee as well as the Justice Committee for these two bills to be able to consider this. But I think one of the things I want to just quickly touch on is the Private Securities Personnel and Private Investigators Act.
