This is an interesting and significant improvement that we’re making which allows for that greater transparency of the function of the Complaints, Investigation Prosecution Unit, which allows for the preparation of reports about complaints against unlicensed or uncertified persons when it’s being requested by a licensed authority.

The last thing I just wanted to touch on—and this speaks to most of the regulatory systems bills we’re seeing in general. These two bills were referred to the committee 16 months ago. The two reports basically came back to the House about a year ago and we only have the opportunity to speak on the two bills now. Although they may not be prominent politically, like I said, they are important bills for this House. I think we should also, as a House, consider if there are better ways for us to be able to put up these bills without having to wait for a year to be able to update them. With that, we commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: TOM RUTHERFORD (National—Bay of Plenty)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s a privilege to stand and speak on the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill. I welcome the direction the Minister has given around referring the Regulatory Systems (Courts) Amendment Bill back to the Justice Committee. We will obviously consider that in further depth as that bill progresses, but I support both of these pieces of legislation and I commend them to the House.

content.speaker: JAMIE ARBUCKLE (NZ First)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to support the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill in its second reading. I sat on the Justice Committee that heard the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill. We only received seven submissions, two of them being oral. They were very minor and technical changes. They didn’t require extensive discussion from the committee, and I commend it to the House.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: This is a split call—Steve Abel.

content.speaker: STEVE ABEL (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I stand to speak on the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill. These are not things I have any particular expertise in. I just had a brief look through the impact statement and to be very frank, reading these bills, it’s one of those instances where it’s witheringly boring. There’s nothing of real excitement here except to say it is essential for us as a Parliament to go through and sort out pieces of legislation like this to make sure that they are serving their purpose: having the effect of removing barriers, in the instance of the tribunals bill, to the access to justice; clarifying and resolving inconsistencies and gaps in legislation; better enabling statutory authorities to conduct their prescribed functions; and ensuring independence of tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies. The quasi-judicial bodies is quite interesting.

The bill would amend the following Acts and associated secondary legislation: the Disputes Tribunal Act, the Motor Vehicle Sales Act, the Parole Act, the Private Security Personnel and Private Investigators Act, and the Unit Titles Act 2010. I cannot trouble the House to speak any further on these except to say that we do support them and we support the principle of these sorts of amendments, so the Green Party commends these bills to the House.

content.speaker: PAULO GARCIA (National—New Lynn)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. We are fixing the basics by strengthening the ability of occupational regulators to protect consumers. By increasing the efficiency of the regulatory regimes, we are building the future. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB (Labour—Christchurch Central)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I’m surprised that people think that these are merely technical bills. I want to speak to the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill. Look, there are actually two quite important points to make here. The first one is in respect of undertakings of conveyancers. Now, in 2006, the law was changed to allow for this new profession of conveyancers, essentially to create competition in the market with lawyers for real estate transactions. One of the advantages it turns out that lawyers had that no one realised was that the courts would enforce undertakings.

Now, an undertaking is often used in conveyancing transactions, and I can actually remember using them when you get halfway through a transaction and you’ve forgotten something. You might be like, “Oh, I forgot to get that document signed, but I undertake that I will deliver you a signed copy of that document. It’s sitting on my desk.” or whatever. The courts would take that to be a binding and enforceable promise. If your lawyer didn’t comply with it, not only could you be sued in court for it but it would be a professional breach. That didn’t exist in respect of conveyancers.

In new section 38A, inserted by clause 5, the framework says that undertakings given by conveyancing practitioners are enforceable. That’s what the heading says, but it’s not what the section says. What it says in new section 38A(1) is “An affected person may make an application for summary judgment in relation to an undertaking” That’s all very good, but it’s kind of narrow because you should be able to make any kind of application on the basis of an undertaking, including an application to the High Court under its general jurisdiction.

Now, it’s recognised that the District Court doesn’t have jurisdiction over lawyers in respect of undertakings, but you can basically go to the High Court in respect of a general undertaking by lawyers and get them enforced or injuncted or damages, whatever you like, any way you like. Summary judgment is a very narrow procedure which proceeds only on affidavits, so I’m perplexed as to why, if you’re suing a lawyer for an undertaking, you can use the whole jurisdiction of the High Court, but if you’re suing a conveyancer, you’ve only got summary judgment. That’s one.

The second one is actually even more concerning. It might be that this needs to go back to select committee because it’s about the complaints service for lawyers. As it happens, I have some experience in this, because in a former job I was, in fact, the legal complaints review officer, which was essentially an appellate role from Law Society complaints standards committees. One of the challenges of complaints frameworks is a flood of shall we just say meritless complaints, for one reason or another. They might just not understand the rules and they’re just wildly wrong or they had unrealistic expectations or they could be vexatious or any other number, or it could have been 10 years ago. That was another one we used to see.

The way the complaints system works is you send your complaint to the Law Society and then the Law Society kind of triages it. Sometimes they have a phone call, but by and large, if you want to complain, it then goes on to a standards committee, which is a group of lawyers and some non-lawyers as well to resolve it, even if it’s a vexatious or trivial or extremely old and stale complaint. What new section 135A, inserted by clause 7, does is it says that the complaints service itself can turn around these extremely low-level complaints.

I can see why you didn’t send that to the Justice Committee, because there would have been a good bit of discussion around whether an administrator—because that’s what it is; probably a skilled one, but an administrator in the Law Society or the Society of Conveyancers—gets to turn around these complaints and say, “I think that’s too old.” “I think that’s too trivial.” “I think that’s without foundation.” or “I think that’s vexatious.” But that’s where we’ve got to.

My concern actually goes a bit further, because in my experience as the legal complaints review officer, as with most complaints services, most of my time was spent dealing with either some very difficult lawyers or very difficult complainants. If you really want to upset a vexatious complainant, the best thing to do is to tell them their complaint is trivial or vexatious and turn it around at the first hurdle. What I am almost certain will happen here is that these will be challenged. Now, the difficulty is, as I see it, there is no way to challenge this complaint within the Law Society framework, within the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act framework. If you go to the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act, in the depths of it at about section 210 or something, it says that a person can complain to the legal complaints review officer about any final decision at a standards committee.

The problem is this never got to the standards committee. This is a decision—and it’s final, because they’ve said that we’re not going to take it further to the standards committee, so you’ve got no right of appeal or review to the legal complaints review officer. So what will a vexatious litigant do? A vexatious litigant will take a judicial review. The whole idea of this system, which is entirely funded by levies on lawyers, is to be low cost, quick, and effective—it hasn’t always been either of those things, but that’s the idea—dispute resolution system for lawyers’ complaints.

I do think there’s a missing part here. I actually get the motivation behind complaints services being able to turn around complaints. I’m not sure it’s a good idea, but I understand why the Minister has taken that route. Certainly, one of the challenges with lawyers’ standards committees is they take too long because they can become overwhelmed with the volume of complaints. But if you’re going to have an administrator—a faceless administrator if you like; not even a public servant but an employee of a private organisation—turning around complaints on the basis that they are meritless for one reason or another, then you had better be very careful about how you go about that. It may well be, and I’m hoping—and I see the Minister is in the House, and good on her for being here—that officials will be taking an interest in this debate as well and will be scratching their heads and thinking, “Oh, maybe we should have thought about that.”, because we know—and the Minister, who is the Minister for Courts, has been working hard on relieving the burden on the courts, including the High Court.

A judicial review on the back of a complaint which doesn’t have merit—you’ve got to remember, if you’re going to judicially review this, you don’t have to prove that your complaint was right; you only have to prove that it wasn’t without some merit; that the decision made internally to extinguish the complaint was not appropriate; that it should have been given a hearing at the next stage. In fact, the grounds upon which they can do it are set out quite clearly: trivial, frivolous, vexatious, “The complainant does not have a sufficient personal interest.”—that’s often an opposing person. A disgruntled husband complaining against the wife’s lawyer is a common one you’d see—those sorts of things. The grounds are there, and you’ve got grounds to go, “Well, they’re wrong about that. I do have an interest which is sufficient, and I want to argue my case about that.”

There’s actually a lot to be thought about there, and these complaints processes are tricky, but they do have to comply with natural justice. What we have here is, essentially, an administrative decision maker making a quasi-judicial decision without any right of appeal or recourse. When you frame it in those terms, we’ve got something of a problem. We’ll be exploring that a bit later on. Thank you for your time.

content.speaker: Dr HAMISH CAMPBELL (National—Ilam)
content.text: It’s a great pleasure to rise and speak on the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill. These bills are part of a package of three bills in the regulatory systems justice amendment bill package, each focused on improving a different part of the justice system: the courts’ occupational regulation and tribunals. They improve access to justice by removing unnecessary barriers and making tribunal processes fairer and more accessible. Therefore, I commend the bills to the House.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: This is a split call—Georgie Dansey.

content.speaker: GEORGIE DANSEY (Labour)
content.text: Tēnā koe e te Māngai o te Whare. I’m standing to speak on the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill. These bills are a package of four regulatory systems amendment bills administered by the Ministry of Justice.

I’d like to start my contribution by challenging the previous speaker Steve Abel on his comments about these bills being boring. I think he just hasn’t read them in depth enough, because I’m sure my colleague the  Hon Duncan Webb thinks these are the most interesting things he’s ever seen in his life.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Come on, I think you should give the House a proper reference if you’re going to make them.

content.speaker: GEORGIE DANSEY
content.text: Ha, ha! I’ve actually had the pleasure of speaking on a number of regulatory systems amendments bills, and you always learn new things about different areas of our society. I’ve spoken on boxing and contact sports in the past, and I’m pleased to speak on these too, because I think they do have some very valuable content in them.

I think that getting our justice system processes right, which we’re very far from at this point, having an accessible and fair justice system, should be an absolute priority for any Government, of any stripe, who sits in this House. Anything we can do to make the justice system more accessible and more fair for people accessing the system is paramount. I hear stories constantly, as I’m sure other members do, around the barriers to accessing justice for people in New Zealand, whether that be financial or otherwise. In these two bills, there is some content that I see as improving that access to justice.

I’ll talk about both, but I wanted to speak firstly about the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the technical changes. This bill will improve the operations and efficiency of tribunals. I thought it was pronounced “quas-ee”, but the Hon Duncan Webb just said “quas-aye”—

content.speaker: Hon Dr Duncan Webb
content.text: “Po-tay-toes”, “po-tah-toes.”

content.speaker: GEORGIE DANSEY
content.text: OK, “po-tay-toes”, “po-tah-toes.” OK, because I didn’t want to put my foot in it and say the wrong word in front of the Hon Duncan Webb!

content.speaker: Hon Rachel Brooking
content.text: What about the Rt Hon Gerry Brownlee?

content.speaker: GEORGIE DANSEY
content.text: I’m so sorry—I’m so sorry. Rt Hon Gerry Brownlee, Mr Speaker, I want to say the right words in front of you. And this is my third speech in front of you now. Back to the bill—in two minutes.

This bill will improve the operations and efficiency of tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies by removing barriers to accessing justice, and it will clarify and resolve inconsistencies and gaps in the legislation. Of the quasi-judicial bodies, I think it’s interesting to see which ones are having changes to them: the Disputes Tribunal, the Motor Vehicle Disputes Tribunal, the Private Security Personnel Licensing Authority, the Complaints, Investigation and Prosecution Unit. I think it’s important that these bodies remain independent and can make independent decisions, because they affect the rights, responsibilities, and interests of all people.

One of the pieces of legislation that caught my eye and that I thought was interesting was the change that will give the Disputes Tribunal referees the ability to order a respondent to pay the filing fee back to a wholly or partly successful applicant. If a party is successful, they will now be able to claim back that filing fee. As is in the notes, this will make a specific difference for people who don’t have a monetary outcome to their claim, because that filing fee is something and it could cause a grievance to a successful applicant in that space. This is one way that access to justice and fairness in the justice system is being changed through the changes in this bill. In some cases, the filing fee could be a significant portion of what the applicant receives, and so I think it’s an important change. I commend these bills to the House.

content.speaker: SUZE REDMAYNE (National—Rangitīkei)
content.text: Thank you. Look, the benefits of these non-controversial bills have been well traversed, so I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate my friend and colleague Tom Rutherford, who was elected the chair of the Justice Committee on Monday. We wish you all the best. Go well. I commend the bills to the House.

content.speaker: DAN ROSEWARNE (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I’d to rise and take a call on the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill and just echo my colleague’s sentiment around how exciting these bills are. The Hon Dr Duncan Webb’s contribution was exceptionally exciting. For those members of the public that have just tuned in to watch these bills progress, I will attempt to cover off some of the key points with this legislation.

These bills focus on improving systems that people interact with every day. They make changes to tribunal processes, occupational regulation, complaints procedures, and licensing arrangements, so that those systems operate more effectively and efficiently. Both bills have now completed the select committee process. The Justice Committee considered submissions on the tribunals bill and heard oral evidence from submitters. The Education and Workforce Committee received a larger number of submissions on the occupational regulation bill and heard evidence from a range of interested parties as well. The committees received advice from officials, support from the Office of the Clerk, and assistance from the Parliamentary Counsel Office as they worked through the details of both pieces of legislation.

Labour supports the changes that have emerged from that process, and these bills are part of a wider programme of regulatory systems legislation administrated by the Ministry of Justice. The purpose of that work is not to revisit major policy decisions that Parliament has already made. The purpose is to identify parts of the legislation that can be improved through experience and feedback from regulators and professional bodies, and people like tribunal users and those responsible for administrating these systems on a daily basis, and it’s an important part of Parliament’s role. No regulatory framework stays perfect for ever. Over time, gaps emerge, inconsistencies develop, language becomes dated, and administrative processes no longer reflect how a sector actually operates. So, periodically, Parliament needs to revisit these settings and make improvements, and this bill does just that.

The committee process demonstrated that point. Submitters raised practical issues, officials provided advice, and members tested the provisions that are before us, and the result is legislation that is stronger than what it was when it was first introduced. One of the themes running through both bills is public confidence. Whether somebody is dealing with a lawyer, engaging with a real estate professional, lodging a complaint with a regulator, or appearing before a tribunal, they need confidence that the rules are clear and that institutions involved have the ability to carry out their responsibilities properly. Confidence is built in different ways. Sometimes it comes through strong professional standards, sometimes it comes from effective complaint systems, sometimes it comes through regulators having access to information that they need to investigate concerns, and sometimes it comes through accessible dispute resolution processes that ordinary New Zealanders can use without excessive cost or complexity. Across these two bills, we see examples of all those things.

The Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill focuses on three key areas: lawyers and conveyancers, the real estate sector, and provisions within the Prostitution Reform Act. Its purpose is to strengthen consumer protection, improve efficiency, remove inconsistencies, and reduce those unnecessary compliance costs across all of those systems.

One of those significant changes concerns the Lawyers Complaints Service. Under this bill, complaints can be made subject to an initial assessment process before being referred to the lawyers standards committee. The legislation identifies circumstances where no further action may be appropriate, including where complaints are trivial, frivolous, or, as the Hon Dr Duncan Webb mentioned in his contribution, vexatious, made in bad faith, or excessively delayed, or where another remedy might very well exist. That intention is pretty straightforward. Complaints systems work best when resources are focused on matters that require investigation and resolution. Every profession depends on public confidence, and maintaining that confidence requires complaints processes that are both robust and efficient.

The bill also contains significant reforms relating to the Real Estate Authority. The real estate sector plays a major role in the lives of New Zealanders; everyone knows that. For many families, purchasing a home is the largest financial commitment they will ever make, and there’s an expectation that professional standards will be maintained and that regulators will have the ability to investigate concerns where those standards may not have been met. The legislation strengthens the authority’s ability to obtain documents relevant to investigations. During select committee considerations, amendments were recommended to ensure that the authority must have reasonable grounds before exercising those powers and to clarify the circumstances in which relevant documents may be sought from those parties holding information relevant to an investigation. The bill also updates a number of licensing provisions. It allows licences to be renewed up to 12 months, I think it was, after expiring. It provides mechanisms that recognise the experience and knowledge of practitioners returning to the profession. These are practical changes that simplify administration while maintaining the expectations around competence and professional standards.

There are also a number of amendments, as mentioned earlier, to the Prostitution Reform Act. Those changes update the references to criminal offences so that legislation continues to reflect the developments elsewhere in criminal law while preserving the existing policy intent around disqualification from holding a certificate, essentially.

Taken together, the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill strengthens consumer protections. It improves the operation of complaints systems and provides regulators with clear tools to fulfil those responsibilities.

Now, turning to the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill, the purpose of that bill is to improve the operation and efficiency of tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies, remove barriers to accessing justice, and address legislative inconsistencies to better support statutory authorities in carrying out their functions. One amendment relates to the Disputes Tribunal. As has already been traversed in the House today, the bill allows the tribunal to order reimbursement of filing fees where an applicant succeeds wholly or partly in their claim. For many New Zealanders, the Disputes Tribunal is the most accessible way to resolve disagreements without entering the formal court. The system was designed to provide a relatively low-cost and straightforward avenue for dispute resolution. The ability to reimburse filing fees recognises that, where somebody has pursued a legitimate claim successfully, there may be circumstances where reimbursement is appropriate. The legislation also preserves incentives for parties to reach settlement, recognising the value of resolving disputes before they require a formal determination.

The bill also includes amendments relating to the appointment of referees. Those provisions formalise the assessment process used for appointments and reappointments, providing a more consistent mechanism for selecting people to carry out those very important roles. The quality of decision making within the tribunal depends heavily on the quality of those making those decisions, so transparent and credible appointment processes are very important. For that reason, I commend the bill to the House.

content.speaker: MILES ANDERSON (National—Waitaki)
content.text: Thank you. Mr Speaker. This bill is about fixing the basics and building the future. I commend it.

content.speaker: Hon JAMES MEAGER (Minister for Hunting and Fishing)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Now, I won’t take a long call, but I just want to note my own congratulations for the new chair of the Justice Committee, Tom Rutherford. They seem to keep getting better and better and better as the term goes on. With that, I think the leadership shown by the Justice Committee is in good hands, and I commend this bill to the House.
Motion agreed to.
Bills read a second time.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: I declare the House in committee for consideration of the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill.
Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill
Committee of the whole House
Part 1 Amendments to Disputes Tribunal Act 1988

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Members, the House is in committee on the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill.
We come first to the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill, and we begin with the debate on Part 1.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair, for the opportunity to open the committee stage of the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill. I’m pleased to say that there was broad support across the House for this bill at its second reading, and I look forward to hearing the views of the other parties as we debate this bill.

The bill amends five Acts to improve the effectiveness and the efficiency of tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies by reducing barriers to accessing justice and better enabling statutory authorities to investigate and regulate the industry. The amendments will, among other things, give disputes tribunal referees the ability to order a respondent to pay the filing fee to a successful applicant, to simplify the appointment process for disputes tribunal referees and Motor Vehicle Disputes Tribunal adjudicators, and provide a new information-gathering power to the unit responsible for private security investigations and prosecutions. These improvements will support the maintenance and continuous improvement of tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies, and this will help to ensure that the tribunal system is accessible and fit for purpose.

I also wish to draw my Amendment Paper 353 to the attention of the House for consideration during this committee stage. This Amendment Paper is straightforward. It only makes some minor technical changes to ensure the provisions read as intended. I’m happy to take questions on the bill as we go through the committee.

content.speaker: Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan
content.text: Madam Chair.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Yes—just before I call Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan, I was just going to say that I omitted to say, before the Minister made her introduction, that Part 1 of the debate is on clauses 3 to 8A, “Amendments to Disputes Tribunal Act 1988”. The question is that Part 1 stand part.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. I think I want to start by, in some ways, slightly disagreeing with my colleague Steve Abel. I think the regulatory systems bills are some of the most interesting bills in terms of the committee stages, and I always found my engagement with the Minister, in particular, to be really enlightening, and it’s just, in general, a really good way to learn about the different kinds of legislations that we do have in the broader context of our legislative package here in Aotearoa New Zealand. They are quite exciting, in my opinion, but that’s just me.

I want to start by looking at clause 4 for the Disputes Tribunal Act, “Section 8 amended (Selection of candidates for appointment or reappointment as Referees)”. I’ve got two questions for the Minister to begin with, and this also touches on the Minister’s Amendment Paper 353. I’m noting that, in both cases, what we have seen—sorry, this clause 4, subclause (2)—is a shift between using “shall” to “must”. Now, from a legislative drafting perspective, my understanding is that both fulfil the same requirement.

content.speaker: Hon Rachel Brooking
content.text: No: “shall” is out of date.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
content.text: Well, that was my question, the Hon Rachel Brooking. Can I just check with the Minister: are the changes here simply an update from using “shall” to “must” in general? And, if that is the case, are these the only instances in this bill where we’re seeing the change from “shall” to “must”? If not, then why weren’t there—as far as I can see—a complete package of changes from that? Maybe I am old-school, but personally I’m a fan of “shall”. That’s my first question.

My second question to the Minister: one of the things we heard as part of the select committee stage, and I have to refresh my memory a little bit with the departmental report, is around independence when we’re looking at the appointment of referees—noting that the chief executive, in this case, appoints them, and what we’re seeing with this particular section is that it removes the notice period for people to be able to submit names to the appointment or reappointment as referees. But what I’m curious to know is, my understanding of the process is that the chief executive appoints the assessment panel; does the assessment panel then appoint the referee or the assessment panel recommends the appointment of the referee to the chief executive, who then reappoints or appoints the referee? Those are my two questions. Thank you, Minister.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. To speak to the member’s first part, about the “shall”, the “must”, and the little—what’s going on over there, I do actually agree with the member, Rachel Brooking. It is quite important when you use “shall” and when you use “must”, and we are making these minor amendments, really, to just have consistency and clarity when the wording is used, and, of course, that’s why we’re making that small amendment. The member asked why it wasn’t changed originally: these are small little words that often get picked up as officials start going through amendments that came about from select committee and realise, “Oh, actually, a ‘shall’ must be a ‘must.’” That’s why that change is there.

In regard to the suitability of appointed—the referees side of it, as well: what I am told is that the disputes tribunal candidates currently require a nomination by a community member in order to be appointed. The amendment will remove that requirement from the disputes tribunal referee appointment process. The disputes tribunal has a strong appointments process to ensure that the referees are well suited to being appointed, so this change is only simplifying that process. The candidates are still required to name three people who will, indeed, referee as to their character and their capability to be a referee with the assessment panel. That’s all that is changing there; the process itself, after that, is continuing to stay the same.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair, and thanks to the Minister for her engagement. It’s good to have some analysis of that Amendment Paper, which does cover clause 4, so it’s even in the right place in this debate, and I do agree with—

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: That’s always helpful.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH
content.text: That’s right. I do agree with Lawrence Xu-Nan that, actually, for a committee stage, these omnibus regulatory system bills are designed in a way that does make it easier to scrutinise and, also, we get to look at different things.

Sticking with the disputes tribunal amendments in Part 1—and my colleague has spoken to clause 4—I want to look at clauses 5 and 6. I’ve got three questions. The first question is on clause 5. Clause 5 inserts new section 43(5). This is in relation to the filing fee, which is probably one of the major changes in the disputes tribunal; that the respondent may get the applicant’s filing fee paid in whole or part. I wanted to know if this is specifically drafted in a broad way so that it can be up to the discretion of the referee as to whether it’s paid based, basically, on merit, because it might be that the claim is majority unsuccessful but one tiny part of it is successful and, I suppose, in that instance, a filing fee could be ordered. So, any guidance the Minister had—I mean, that’s a possible issue of future statutory interpretation, possibly; Duncan Webb may have some further thoughts on that. Anyway, that was my first question.

The second question I had was following on from that in (6)—so that would be new section 43(6) that is inserted by clause 5. In this, it states that the agreement to pay the filing fee cannot be made—I think—if there’s a settlement agreed. Now, I wanted to just clarify for the Minister that that this isn’t intended to be a prohibition if there’s a settlement made, but, if there was a settlement made, it would be assumed that the settlement would cover the filing fee. That would be my usual understanding.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH
content.text: Yes. Is that how much it is?

content.speaker: Hon Dr Duncan Webb
content.text: It can be—up to.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH
content.text: Up to $450. I think that’s also an important clarification for statutory interpretation, so that it would be allowed to be part of the settlement, not prohibited from that. It would be great, actually, to have some statement or advice from the Minister on there.

My third question—I will move on; others may have further questions on clause 5, but I don’t. On clause 6, I looked back to the original Disputes Tribunal Act, which this deletes section 59 from. That section is about the entitlement of referees to be considered an employee for the purposes of accident compensation. That just seems to be a wholesale deletion of that. I’m not sure if it’s covered somewhere else or what the thinking was behind that, but obviously that would probably be of a concern to referees if they weren’t entitled to ACC—they currently are entitled to ACC as an employee. There may be some context that I’m missing there—maybe it’s inserted somewhere else—but I’d be grateful for some clarification on those three questions.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. I thank the member also for her questions. In regard to the changes in clause 5, we are not inserting a new section 43; we’re just amending section 43. This is in regard to the respondent paying the applicant the cost of any filing fee, wholly or partly successful. The member asked about when a settlement agreement is made and whether or not the referee can then determine whether or not to make a payment. This is actually allowing the referee to be given discretion in order to make such orders. The member was quite right when she indicated there could be a settlement where there is a monetary involvement, but there could also be a settlement where there isn’t. It could be just the handover of a property or something like that. That would then allow, even when there is a settlement, the referee to be able to have that discretion on whether or not to give full or even partial remittance of that filing fee, so just giving them that ability to do that. I hope that answers both the questions on Part 5—please come back if I haven’t.

On clause 6, the deletion in regard to the ACC, we’re repealing that employee provision because the referees around all the other tribunals are contractors and as contractors they pay their own ACC claims. In this particular tribunal, half of them are not contractors. We’re just looking for consistency with all the other tribunal adjudicators where they are all contractors and they all pay their own ACC. At the moment in this one, we’ve have got half paying ACC and half not—half being employees. We just want to ensure that they are all on the same wave length there and they’re all doing exactly the same thing, which is contracting and paying their own ACC levies.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB (Labour—Christchurch Central)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. Thanks to the Minister for Courts for the engagement there. I want to talk about clause 8, and in particular I want to talk about clause 8(2), which is always a tricky one because it says “Revoke rule 36(1).” so you have to go to the rules to find out what it actually does. Rule 36 is about the recruitment process, if you like, for disputes tribunal referees. In fact, 36(1) is the first step. It provides two things: that there should be advertisements in the area that you’re looking for them—interestingly, it doesn’t say “newspaper advertisement”; it just says “advertisement” so it could be anywhere, could be an electronic advertisement—and also to be publicised by such other means as the secretary considers necessary, kind of a general discretion.

Firstly, it would seem odd to remove the clause which says “Go out and publicise that you are looking for dispute tribunal referees.” I accept that there’s always going to be a discretion. There’s no prohibition on doing that. But I would have thought that in what is essentially the Public Service—quasi-judicial officers—that you actually want to go out publicly. Because the other process—and this is what the legal profession has done for centuries—is to look towards people you know. That is to say people like you, who are your mates, and ask them. That’s not always good.

But the other thing is section—or clause, rule, whatever you like—36(1), which actually sets the scene for getting candidates, because it says: “For the purpose of encouraging the nomination, as candidates for appointment as Referees, of men and women from diverse backgrounds and diverse ethnic and age groups, the chief executive shall”—and then it goes on to say advertise. I’m wondering if that’s the reason that was removed, because the Government doesn’t want to emphasise the need for a—and, in fact, disputes tribunal referees, although there are mainly lawyers, they are generally a diverse bunch of people. To be honest, I can’t see why you’d remove that clause. It’s innocuous, it does some useful work, and it gives a theme. If it was the diversity bit that you didn’t like, you could just get rid of that and say, “For the purpose of encouraging the nomination of competent people.” But you still want to have a requirement that it be a public process rather than a closed one—a shoulder-tapping exercise. I’d actually really appreciate the Minister responding as to why rule 36(1) is being revoked.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. In response to the member on clause 8, the clause 8 change in there is a consequential amendment because of the changes that we’re making in clause 4. I’m just advised there is still a publicly advertised advertisement that goes out for this, but it relates to the changes that are made by clause 4. It’s consequential. It removes the requirement for the disputes tribunal candidates to be nominated a community member and to be appointed. All it is, really, is a consequential amendment to the change that we’re making in clause 4 to amend that section 36, and there is still some form of advertisement.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. Just following up from what the Minister for Courts is saying, I think there is another important aspect of the Hon Dr Duncan Webb’s question around the requirement for the diversity component of that.

But the question that I have there is around, like we said before, when we’re looking at the expanded role of referees—or we talked about community magistrates before and a number of other ones. They don’t go through some of the similar processes we see with the appointment of judges. Whether you’re self-representing or have a lawyer present is another matter, but I think one of the things I’m thinking of, particularly as we’re seeing an increase in, for example, Asian populations here in Aotearoa New Zealand who have also started seeing an increasing number of cases going through all stages of our courts. I just wanted to check in terms of, for the candidates or for the appointment of referees—because we do hear from Asian lawyers a number of these sort of nuances within our court system not being understood or accessible to the Asian population, particularly if English is a second language and you are requiring a translator, etc. I just want to check: from an appointment perspective, what are the considerations the Minister has, either in the existing rules or some of the changes we’re seeing here that would take into consideration the nuances of the cultural diversity that we see, not necessarily in the appointment body or the referees themselves, but the broader society in general? That being my first question.

The second question is I want to check with the Minister going back to what the Minister said regarding clause 6, which is consistent between the disputes tribunal referees compared to some of the other tribunal referees who are self-employed and disputes tribunal referees are being employees as opposed to being self-employed. I want to check with the Minister: if they are self-employed, what then would be the financial implication for them when they are paying for ACC as a self-employed person? Because, for example, when we’re looking at some of the questions we asked as a part of the select committee process, we do see that if you are self-employed—for example, if section 59 is repealed—at different earning levels you will be seeing the referees having quite a bit higher levy than you have to pay for ACC.

I want to check with the Minister if this is something that has already been consulted on with existing referees—some of the feedback you’ve heard in terms of now that they are self-employed, there will be additional costs to them in terms of paying for their ACC levy. To give an example, when we’re looking at one of the bands—let’s say if you’re earning $25,000, the existing is $362.50. But then if section 59 is repealed, you need to add in the ACC Work levy, the Working Safer levy, and those additional levies which make it up to $410, which is $471.50 including GST, which is quite a bit higher than $362.50. I just want to check with the Minister on what the feedback is that she has received regarding the increase in ACC cost.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: I was talking a little bit through the member’s questions, so if I have not addressed or do not address all of his questions, I invite him to stand and ask again. Before I start, I’d just like to make a correction to something I said about clause 5, which is the ability for the adjudicator to be able to award the filing fee after a settlement. I made mention, apparently incorrectly, that if there is a settlement, the adjudicator could determine whether or not to pay the filing fee back, and I’ve got that wrong. If there is a settlement, it is the settlement in itself, and a filing fee will not be paid in that instance. That will be up to the adjudicator, just to make sure that there is fairness. This is why the adjudicator is given some leeway there to be able to make the decisions. The referee cannot award a filing fee on top of an agreed settlement. The settlement would cover all matters. If the referee thought that was unfair, they could choose not to endorse it and make the filing fee go to that person instead.

With the referees, again, at clause 6—this is about the ACC. As I mentioned, this is about consistency. It’s to ensure that all tribunal referees—not just tribunal referees in this area; that tribunal referees across the entire tribunal sector are all contractors, and they all pay their own ACC levies. I do have some figures that are there, but it’s creating a fairness so that they are all paying the same amount; you’re not having some pay one amount and others pay another amount. You want all of them across all the tribunals in the court system to be able to be paying that same amount. That’s why we’re looking for that consistency.

To the member’s first question, the policy intent at the time was to ensure that a referee was a person who had standing in the community and that they were nominated by the community. That was, in a way, to try and create the diversity of referees, but the requirement is not being used as intended. There’s not been an independently nominated referee under this system in many, many years. I understand that in practice, there’s a public call for expressions of interest, and this is what I meant by continuing to advertise. As part of that, each candidate has to find a nominee.

This proposal would remove a provision that was introduced to increase diversity among the pool of referees; however, we do note that there is now a greater mix of gender and age groups amongst the referees that we have. Additionally, the Disputes Tribunal has other mechanisms to encourage ethnic diversity, such as the establishment of the Māori referees committee and the establishment of the Pasifika referees committee. I did ask my officials: do we have Asian referees committee? Not yet. Maybe that is something that future Governments can look to.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. Thanks to the Minister. It’s been said before, but we really do appreciate the constructive engagement on some of these issues.

I think the Minister has answered my questions in relation to the earlier questions I had in relation to clauses 5 and 6. The only kind of quick follow-ups that I would want to add are—I understand about the settlement having to cover everything. I think it’s really good to have that direction, because if a settlement didn’t cover a filing fee—for example, it often happens in settlements that perhaps you forget around that filing fee. It could be someone who’s entirely successful—or the application fee or whatever it’s called; yeah, filing fee. I mean, my view would be that the most equitable way would be—obviously, the situation we want to avoid is that we wouldn’t want it to be paid twice. We wouldn’t want a settlement amount to cover the filing fee and then for it to be paid separately again, because that wouldn’t, obviously, be fair. But if a settlement covers the filing fee, then, of course, there shouldn’t be an order. Probably, in an ideal world, the ability to make a filing fee order if the settlement didn’t cover that would be, probably, better.

But I think having clarity for those people in the Disputes Tribunal is important, and that’s why I’m glad that we’ve had these questions. They’ll be on the record if anyone is interested to look at that in the future. They’ll have clarity that, as I understand it, if there is a settlement, that needs to be fulsome, and it needs to include any application for the reimbursement of a filing fee. If that’s wrong, please let me know, but otherwise I think it’s good to have that on the record.

In terms of ending the employment, I do take the point around consistency, but I do wonder, for the group of referees who are currently considered employees, have there been discussions with them around the changes in terms of them doing their own ACC? They wouldn’t be entitled to KiwiSaver. Obviously, employment has a totally different rights profile from contracting. The fact that we’re doing this by statute is significant, and I just wanted to know if there had been any thought and put into that and also if there’s any consequential raise in the amount of remuneration that they would receive. Obviously, it’s not, maybe, a huge amount, probably, for what they’re receiving, for them to pay their own ACC, but that will be a cost that they’re facing that they don’t currently have to face.

I think in relation to that part, which is still Part 1, that’s probably all the questions that I have, so up to the Minister. If anything I’ve said is wrong, it would be good to have clarification. Otherwise, that’s all.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: I think the member has its spot on in regard to the settlement side of it. My apologies for saying the incorrect thing in the first place, but I think that we’ve got to a place where we’ve both been able to make it quite clear for anybody that will be listening.

Again, when we come back to the ACC, we’ve really got to make it so that it’s fair on every tribunal referee. When you have some paying one rate and a few paying another, it’s not fair on the others that are paying less or more than anyone else. As I’ve mentioned before to the Green member, this is really about having consistency across all tribunal referees and adjudicators throughout the country so that they are all paying the same amount dependent on whatever their wages are. Some work part time, some work full time, and those amounts themselves will change depending on what their income is and who they work for.

I will point out as well: some tribunal referees and adjudicators are on multiple different tribunals. Some are paid, I guess, as a contractor, and some are being paid another way. It’s actually going to make it easier for those people that are multiple referees or adjudicators to be able to contract back to the ministry instead of having two different versions of how they go about paying ACC. I come back again to the consistency in ensuring that all adjudicators are paying ACC levies as contractors to the Crown.

content.speaker: Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan
content.text: Madam Chair?

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan—just recognising it’s a smallish part, so we’re just into final points of clarification on this part.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Yep. One final question from me—a short question, and maybe a short response from the Minister. Are the Disputes Tribunal referees the only ones, then, who are currently still employees—everyone else is a contractor now?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: To be fair, I’m actually not aware of whether or not they are. I’m looking at just what’s in front of me, and this is the tribunal that we’re dealing with. I suspect that if we have others like this, we would pull it into a future regulatory standards bill. But this one is talking about tribunals. No one else has come in, so I suspect this may be the only one, but I’m not 100 percent sure.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: The question is that the Minister’s amendments to Part 1 set out on Amendment Paper 353 be agreed to.
Amendments agreed to.
Part 1 as amended agreed to.
Committee of the whole House
Part 2 Amendments to Motor Vehicle Sales Act 2003

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Members, we come now to Part 2, the debate on clauses 9 and 10, “Amendments to Motor Vehicle Sales Act 2003”. The question is that Part 2 stand part. Dan Rosewarne.

content.speaker: DAN ROSEWARNE (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: I know your interest in Holdens will be driving something here.

content.speaker: DAN ROSEWARNE
content.text: Thank you for your contributions so far, Minister. My question is in relation to clause 10, which amends section 82 of the Motor Vehicle Disputes Tribunal, and replacing section 82(3)(a) with subparagraph (a) there. The questions we need to ask here are probably pretty much what the people of New Zealand would want to know. A lot of us buy vehicles, some are second-hand vehicles, we drive them off the lot, and there might be a catastrophic failure—an engine might blow—we might enter into that Motor Vehicle Disputes Tribunal process. I suppose a lot of Kiwis at home would want to know: how would this amendment here improve the motor vehicle dispute process for consumers?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. It’s a good question; I thank the member for it. This is actually going to help speed up the process. At the moment, the Motor Vehicle Disputes Tribunal adjudicators all need to have a current practising certificate. That makes it quite difficult to get people with a current practising certificate to put their hand up to even be adjudicators. This change will mean that they won’t need to have a current practising certificate but they do still need to be legally qualified. You might have, for example, a retired lawyer who doesn’t have an active practising certificate but is still legally qualified. They need to have at least five years’ experience in law—a minimum of five years’ experience—to be considered for this role. This means it’ll be less restrictive and it’s going to help reduce delays in the appointment process. Of course, if we can reduce delays there, then we help reduce delays in the tribunal itself.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. I just want to check with the Minister for Courts one question on clause 10. My understanding of clause 10 is currently the adjudicator has to have a practising certificate for at least five years, and that’s kind of the baseline requirement. But this particular one allows it to be not retrospective, but it allows a barrister or barrister and solicitor to have a past practising certificate that has now lapsed but then they are able to continue to be adjudicators. So you’re looking at maybe a greater pool of people who could be adjudicators maybe, and also now the five years no longer need to be consecutive. I guess my question number one is: does it allow there to be a greater pool of adjudicators as a result of this? Also, has there been any work done? Because it wasn’t, I think, even something we considered as a part of the Justice Committee. Does it affect the quality of the adjudication that you might see if solicitors, for example, their certificate has lapsed and maybe they were a barrister or solicitor 30 years ago for five years and they technically now meet this requirement? Has there been any work done on the quality as well?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. As mentioned earlier, it’s more about trying to get these adjudicators in. They don’t need to have had necessarily just completed five years with the practising certificate—they need to have a minimum of five years’ legal experience. This is where you can get those retired people that come in. They will be appointed based on their abilities. The panel that appoints those individuals will have to look at who those individuals are. It doesn’t really matter whether or not they’ve just retired recently or retired 10 years ago. They have that legal experience behind them. I would have thought that if they retired or left five years ago or 10 years ago, they would have had a lifetime of experience, no doubt. But they still need to fit the criteria for the panel that will appoint them and make sure that they are fit for that. I guess the question that I was asked is: does it increase the pool? It will hugely increase the pool, and it means that we can have more adjudicators in a timely fashion and get people through the system quicker.
Part 2 agreed to.
Committee of the whole House
Part 3 Amendments to Parole Act 2002, and Schedule

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Members, we come now to Part 3, the debate on clauses 11 to 16—“Amendments to Parole Act 2002”—and the Schedule. The question is that Part 3 stand part.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. The Parole Act changes are interesting and I’ve been looking through them to try and understand the purpose—and I’ve got the Parole Act here in front of me as well. I just wanted to ask the Minister for Courts: it appears to me that the main thrust of these changes—and I’m looking at clause 13 and also the new Schedule, which is inserted in clause 14. When I looked at the Parole Act as it currently stands, I think the salaries for members of the Parole Board were set by the Higher Salaries Commission. I’m reliably informed by my colleague that that has been defunct for a while. I wanted to know if that’s correct, and, if so, how have the salaries been determined of the Parole Board? Or is it just something that’s been in a static waiting period until this bill comes into place? That’s on clause 13. That was, I think, in 13(2) the replacement of section 122(1). It seems to refer to the deletion of the Higher Salaries Commission or the reference to that.

I also discussed this with my colleague Dr Duncan Webb, who by the way—and this is referring to the previous section—would fulfil the criteria of someone who could be appointed to the Motor Vehicle Disputes Tribunal board, as would I and many other former lawyers on this house. That shows you how wide the pool could be under that previous part, but I don’t have a question about that—it was just a comment.

In this bill, clause 13(3), which replaces section 122(2), also reflects the fact that a judge could be on the Parole Board and not have it affect their terms and conditions. I understand from my learned colleague that that is quite a usual clause to be put in. I was going to ask a series of questions about, “Why is this? Is this relating to a particular individual?”

content.speaker: Hon Dr Duncan Webb
content.text: Who is it? Who’s the awkward judge?

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH
content.text: Ha, ha! Yeah. If the Minister could confirm if Dr Duncan Webb is right: that it is simply a usual clause to have in this and not related to a single individual.
I suppose the last question I had around the Parole Act at the stage—unless anything major arises—is just in relation to the Schedule, which I think comes into this section?

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Yes, it does.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH
content.text: Yeah. So that’s the Schedule right at the back of the bill, and that appears to me to be a transitional provision. That may assist with my initial question around the Higher Salaries Commission, but just wanting to know basically a sequence of what’s happened—obviously the Higher Salaries Commission not being effective and then us not passing this bill, and then what will happen once this bill is passed in relation to that responsibility for remuneration in clause 13(1), then going back to the actual Parole Board itself.

I would be grateful if the Minister could kind of allay some concerns around the separation in terms of the Remuneration Authority being separate from the Parole Board and then making sure that that is separate. I may have answered my own question with that, but that does appear to be a sufficient separation in the determination of the people who receive the salaries and the people who actually set them.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, and I will clarify for the member and speak to clauses 13, 14, and the Schedule there. Currently, we have four roles on the New Zealand Parole Board where their fees are being determined by the Cabinet Fees Framework. The others, who are members of the judiciary, have their remuneration determined by the Remuneration Authority. The amendment will ensure that the Remuneration Authority considers all of the remuneration for all members, because it’s inappropriate for the Cabinet Fees Framework to be looking at the fees network for what could possibly be judges that come through. It must be independent, so that’s why we’re making that change.

The member is also quite right that the schedule is like a transitional part, because, while we make that change, we need to ensure that those four members of the Parole Board continue to be paid until we get this into force. Clause 14 is amending that schedule to make it transitional to ensure that they continue to be paid while that takes place. The Remuneration Authority is not empowered to make an official remuneration determination until the bill’s commencement date, and that’s why we need to have that transitional period through there. I hope that answers the question.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you for that, Minister. I think, just to follow up, I have never heard of the Cabinet Fees Framework before. One of the questions asked was about the fact that—sorry, this is clause 13(2). What has been replaced—what was previously there—is “Higher Salaries Commission”. Can I just clarify: is the Higher Salaries Commission part of the Cabinet Fees Framework? Does it sit under the Cabinet Fees Framework? I understand the other parts that the Minister for Courts said, in terms of consistency with the Remuneration Authority, but it’s just the current clause and what the Minister said—I don’t know if they are the same thing. That’s all.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: I’d not even heard of that until the member stood up and actually talked about that. All I’m aware of is that they’re currently paid under the Cabinet Fees Framework and this is why we need to change it, to make sure they come under the Remuneration Authority, to ensure that there is that distance, especially between the executive and the judiciary.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Madam Chair, thank you. While the Minister for Courts gets some guidance, I would be quite interested because that’s what it currently says in section 122(1) of the Parole Act. Can I just check: if it’s the Cabinet Fees Framework—we know that the Remuneration Authority is independent, and that’s also good in terms of consistency. Is the Cabinet Fees Framework also, then, an independent thing, or does it get determined “dependently”, I guess? I don’t know how else to phrase that. Is the Cabinet Fees Framework determining their own remuneration, whereas the Remuneration Authority sits outside of all that? I don’t know if that actually makes any sense!

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. No, I didn’t quite get that, sorry. The question that the member Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan is asking me is going a little bit further than what’s actually in the bill, and I’m sure that the member could probably Google that question and get the answer to it. What I’m looking to do is ensure that everybody is paid under the same network, which is the Remuneration Authority, rather than the Cabinet Fees Framework, especially in order that, if there are judges on the Parole Board, they do not come under the executive framework, that they come under an independent one.

Part 4 Amendments to Private Security Personnel and Private Investigators Act 2010

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Members, we come to Part 4, the debate on clauses 17 to 39, “Amendments to Private Security Personnel and Private Investigators Act 2010”. The question is that Part 4 stand part.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB (Labour—Christchurch Central)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. As we move through this Act, I think we’ll probably be through it relatively soon. I want to skip a lot of the technical stuff in the first sections, which appears to be largely wording, and get to new section 73AAA, which is “Complaint against unlicensed persons, etc”.

I can certainly understand why there should be a power to make complaints about people who are behaving as if they are licensed security personnel or private investigators. I guess my question, really, relates to subsection (3) of that new section 73AAA, because, under subsection (2), it says that a constable can file a complaint with the authority or another person with the leave of the authority. I can kind of understand why that would be the case, although, in many ways, I’m not even sure that is appropriate—perhaps a justification of why leave is needed.

Then, in subsection (3), it says the Licensing Authority “may” grant leave—I emphasise that word on purpose—only if the authority is satisfied the complainant has an interest greater than the general public and that it’s not frivolous or vexatious. I can imagine, if you’re at a pub and someone thinks you’ve misbehaved and you get thrown out and it turns out that the person isn’t a licensed security guard, and they should have been, and they acted inappropriately, you should then be able to complain on the basis that they were acting as a security guard when, in fact, they weren’t a security guard. But, I guess, my real point is this—and it may well be in law that the Licensing Authority is obliged to allow you to complain if you’ve got a legitimate complaint. So, rather than saying that the Licensing Authority “may” grant leave, in fact, that shouldn’t be discretionary. The Licencing Authority “must” grant leave where it is satisfied that they have a greater than ordinary interest and it’s a legitimate good-faith complaint.

Private investigators are another thing: if someone’s conducting themselves and presenting themselves as a private investigator, it gives some sort of authenticity to them. People who then deliver up information to them, thinking they’ve got a legitimate and responsible investigation under way, have, essentially, a right to make that complaint rather than a mere discretionary possibility at the hands of the Licensing Authority. I guess, once again, it’s the question about an administrative discretion going a little bit wide.
I guess my next thread, possibly third thread, is: if they don’t get the right to make that complaint—if they are wrongly refused that right—what can they then do? They are my questions.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. If you’d bear with me, Madam Chair, I actually have an answer which might help the member Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan. It’ll be very, very quick. I’m told that the Higher Salaries Commission was replaced by the Remuneration Authority, so that might help us with an understanding there.

In regard to the member Dr Duncan Webb’s questions, currently, the Licensing Authority cannot explicitly accept complaints about security personnel who are or might be in breach of requirements to hold a licence or certificate of approval under the Act. However, in practice, it does accept those complaints, because this is important to ensure that we keep public confidence in the private security industry.

This clause will explicitly confirm the Licensing Authority’s ability to accept those complaints. It will remove any ambiguity and assist the Licencing Authority in carrying out what is its statutory functions.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: With this particular part, I want to check with the Minister in terms of clause 41, section 176 amended. content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. The existence of the Residential Tenancy (Unit Title Disputes) Rules 2011, they seem to be currently not very clear and there is some confusion about whether different documents service provisions in another Act should apply. So this proposal will make it clear that the rules exist and apply to how documents should be served for unit title disputes. So this is going to improve clarity and ease the use of the Act. It also makes absolutely no operational changes.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. I’m just bringing these unit titles up as we speak, but—

content.speaker: Hon Phil Twyford
content.text: Through a loud voice.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH
content.text: Thank you. I just had a question around the Unit Titles Act. The unit titles are a part of our residential property system—and obviously the Unit Titles Act is not one of the oldest Acts that we have. But I just wanted to know, in terms of the future of unit titles, you said that there wasn’t anything that was actually changing the substantive policy intent on this, but was there any advice received on whether this would be something that would be more likely to continue as it is into the future, or is there kind of a view around the nature of how unit titles are looked at. The reason I raise this is in Auckland, for example, we had, for a period of time, a number of different legal ways that ownership was recorded within our kind of wider Torrens system that have now kind of fallen out of favour. So the cross-lease system obviously continues and is still something which is a valid form of legal ownership of land, but it has—this is a generalisation—fallen out of favour with the way that the councils have utilised their powers there. In terms of unit titles, I just wanted to know if that was something that had been thought of in terms of updating that piece of legislation.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: This particular amendment is purely about making sure that there are clear rules that exist—rules that do apply to how documents are served. This is about, now, that service for the unit titles disputes at the moment is not clear. So all this section is doing is making sure that those that are serving documents under this particular section are very clear about how it is that they are meant to do that. That’s all that I have been advised on.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. I just have one final question on this section, and I thank the Minister for that response. Can I just check, in terms of what the Minister says and the clarity provides, because it makes references to the rules made under section 116 of the Residential Tenancies Act, are those existing rules now applicable here or does it in fact empower this section then to go and make additional rules under section 116 of the Residential Tendencies Act?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
