Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill
Committee of the whole House
Part 1 Amendments to Lawyers and Conveyancers Act 2006

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Members, we now come to the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill. We begin with the debate on Part 1. Part 1 is the debates on clauses 3 to 11, Amendments to Lawyers and Conveyancers Act 2006. The question is that Part 1 stand part.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Madam Chair, thank you for the opportunity to open the committee stage of the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill. I’m pleased to say that there was broad support across the House for this bill at second reading, and I look forward to hearing the views of the other parties as we debate the bill. This bill amends the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act, the Prostitution Reform Act, the Real Estate Agents Act, to increase protections for regulated professionals, such as real estate agents, and for consumers of those regulated services. The amendments will, among other things, enable the undertakings or professional commitments of conveyances to be enforced in the High Court in the same way that lawyers’ undertakings are; to remove a disproportionately harsh punishment for real estate agents who failed to complete their continuing professional development or pay their fees on time; and to ensure that the Real Estate Authority has the investigative powers that are required to investigate allegations of unlicensed trading and ensure licensees are meeting their obligations.

These improvements will support the maintenance and continuous improvement of the occupational regulation regimes to ensure that regulated services are performed with reasonable care and skill, and promote and protect the interests of consumers. I also wish to draw to attention my Amendment Paper 636 to the House for consideration during this committee stage. This Amendment Paper makes minor and technical changes to the current drafting in the bill, including an amendment to ensure the policy intent of one of the changes is achieved.

I also note that there are two Amendment Papers to this Amendment Paper in regard to clause 25. These are technical amendments. I am hopeful that the parties across the House got a copy of this beforehand—I did ask my office to get it to you. These are minor amendments that were picked up at the very last minute by the Real Estate Authority. They are just technical amendments—wording changes. They thought that they would take the opportunity to get to this while they could, and I can speak more to that once we get to clause 25. In the meantime, I’m happy to take your questions.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB (Labour—Christchurch Central)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. I know the Minister for Courts was in the House at the second reading, so she knows, essentially, what I’m going to say. I will just ask one question at a time.

My first question is about undertakings by conveyancing practitioners. This is clearly a very good reform, because if you are going to do conveyancing on an even par with lawyers, you need to have enforceable undertakings. The question is whether we’ve now got a second-rate undertaking regime because of subsection (1) of new section 38A, inserted by clause 5, which says, “An affected person may make an application for summary judgment in relation to an undertaking”. It just strikes me that it should simply say, “An affected person may make an application to the High Court in relation to an undertaking given by a conveyancing practitioner”, because summary judgments are a kind of particular form of proceeding where there is no oral evidence. In fact, if you are seeking to enforce a solicitor’s undertaking, you’re actually relying on the inherent jurisdiction of the court to discipline solicitors, who are in fact officers of the court.

Now, I accept that conveyancing practitioners simply don’t neatly fit into that, but I would have thought that by saying “undertakings by conveyancers are enforceable” and “the application to enforce them may be made to the High Court”, that would have been all you’ll need. Now you’ve got to have this unusual procedure, and I guess the challenge is—because summary judgment application is in fact an application which says, “Look, it’s obvious we don’t need to go to full trial; we can do a quick-fire procedure”. If you lose that, it then usually turns into an ordinary proceeding in which you then go and have a full trial. It’s actually unclear, and it’s just unclear to me why summary judgment was thought as appropriate. Here are two questions: why isn’t it just “apply to the High Court”, and what happens if you do this and you lose your summary judgment application?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. I understand that the member was not on this particular Education and Workforce Committee, so I appreciate the question. I hope I can answer it well enough.

The amendment will enable conveyancers’ undertakings to be summarily enforceable in the High Court, similar to how lawyers’ undertakings are currently. I understand that registered conveyancers transact around 280 purchases annually. For each one of these transactions, conveyancers pay up to $500 in additional solicitor costs as a direct result of banks refusing to instruct conveyancers, and these costs are passed on to the consumers. The change in this clause will improve the confidence of banks, lawyers, and consumers to work with conveyancers and bring down the costs for consumers. I also note that this amendment was strongly supported by submitters at the select committee stage. This will help give effect to the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act, which had the aim of increasing competition for conveyancing services and driving conveyancing costs down.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB (Labour—Christchurch Central)
content.text: Yeah, look, I got all that. I basically said that at the beginning when I outlined what an undertaking was, and those are great notes written by officials, but the question is this: why does it say that they must take a summary judgment application and not an ordinary application, and if it has to be a summary application, what happens if they lose that summary judgment application?

content.speaker: Hon PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atatū)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. I’m very keen to hear an answer to the Hon Dr Duncan Webb’s question about why the provisions in this bill, essentially, provide a sort of second-rate or lightweight option for people who want to enforce the undertakings given by a conveyancer. That hasn’t been answered, and as someone who was on the Education and Workforce Committee—

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: I think Dr Webb’s also waiting for the answer to a question, and the Minister is taking advice, so does the member have a further—

content.speaker: Hon PHIL TWYFORD
content.text: Yes—as someone who was on the committee, I would say that this matter was never raised by the officials, by submitters, or by any of the committee members, so I’m glad that Duncan Webb has raised it at this time.
I wanted to ask some questions. Assuming that this matter can be resolved—

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Yeah, we’ll just wait for an answer on this matter. Move on, and then we can come back.

content.speaker: Hon PHIL TWYFORD
content.text: You want to wait for the answer? OK, sure.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: No, I’m happy for you to keep going.

content.speaker: Hon PHIL TWYFORD
content.text: OK. Assuming that that matter can be adequately answered, I’m interested in what thought the Minister for Courts has given to monitoring whether banks will alter their practice following the commencement of this provision, given that we’re trying to improve confidence in conveyancers’ undertakings; whether there’s been any estimate made of the reduction in settlement delays or transaction costs that are likely as a result of this change; and whether or not there will be any operational guidance provided to practitioners or to lenders if this provision enters the law.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: I do not know the answer to the members’ questions, and the officials have advised me that they don’t have an answer to that either, because this is a minor change that relates specifically to new section 38A, which is being inserted here by clause 5. The question that’s being asked is talking about hypothetical situations that have not been considered when just trying to progress through what would be a standard, minor, technical-type change to this.

The members are asking legal questions about what if or why would we not do it somewhere else. The reality is that we have been asked to—the Government is looking to progress changes in this area in this way, and I have detailed the reasoning for that. I’m not in a position to be able to answer extended questions, because they actually don’t relate to what it is that we’re trying to change right here.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB (Labour—Christchurch Central)
content.text: I must say, I find it extraordinary that on a question about why a summary judgment procedure was adopted and not an ordinary procedure, which is the wording of the legislation, why officials can’t answer that beggars belief. If they came here today thinking that this was a formality, well, they’ve got the wrong end of the stick. It might be late in urgency, but we expect the Government to be able to answer questions and justify their position. The fact that it went through a select committee process is neither here nor there; this is the committee stage of the House of Representatives, so I hope I’ll get a better response when I talk about new section 135A, inserted by clause 7. Again, I raised these questions at second reading on purpose. I thought, “If I raise it here, at least officials will get an hour or so’s notice so that they will know it will be raised at committee stage, and they won’t be caught by surprise and be ferreting around.” My question is about section 135A, which allows complaints about lawyers to be summarily dismissed by a Law Society administrator where they are trivial, vexatious, or stale, or on a number of other grounds. My question, fundamentally, is this: if we’re going to have an administrative shutting-down of complaints against lawyers, what is the recourse for that person to have that decision reviewed?  Can they ask either the standards committee to have a look at it or the Legal Complaints Review Officer to have a look at it? Or will they be forced to clog up the high courts by taking it on judicial review?

Now, can I say I support this reform intent—that is to say that complaints that are clearly meritless should be able to be turned away at the first point of contact, where otherwise they would clog up the select committee system, which is a body of six or seven or more people, including lawyers. But they make mistakes. These are not lawyers, necessarily—they may be, but they don’t have to be—but they are, ultimately, part of the internal administrative machinery of the Law Society and they should be subject to some oversight. Look, in terms of the law, I know what the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act says: you can seek a review from the Legal Complaints Review Officer for a standards committee decision, not an internal Law Society administrative decision. So we’ve got a problem.

I hope the Minister isn’t going to say, “Will there be another administrative review?” because that is just giving two problems of the same kind. I do think that there’s a lack here; this section should have said that: “the complainant can seek a review by the standards committee of that decision.” Now, it would still go to the standards committee, and I accept that, but it still acts as an effective filter for 80 or 90 percent of these meritless claims. It’s also the case that some of these claims thought to be meritless, may not be. The administrator may make mistakes, and we need to have an ability for that review process. And, as I said in the second reading, telling someone who is a problematic or querulous complainant or a vexatious complainant that they have no merit, they’re a waste of time, and their vexatious, and we’re not even going to look at your complaint, we’re not even going to send it to the committee of lawyers, is the first way to really upset them. I know from experience that these people will not give up and they will go to the highest level and clog up our higher courts if we don’t give them a safety valve within in the process itself. So I hope we’ve got some better advice on this question.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. One thing I’m going to start off by saying is I do not, in any way, appreciate that member attacking the officials who work really hard to do the work that this Government asks them to do, especially the sheer volume of work that this Government has put through them. I would expect that member to stand up and apologise to the officials for what he has said about them, because if that member wants to say anything, you should be saying it to me and leave the officials out, because that, I think, is a very low blow.

We are looking at these minor changes, and the member is asking for information that goes outside of that and the consequences that goes outside of that, from officials who do not have that information.

content.speaker: Hon Kieran McAnulty
content.text: It’s not his fault you don’t know. For goodness’ sake!

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE
content.text: And it’s not their fault.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: OK. I don’t think we’re going to go into a slanging match between everybody. What Dr Duncan Webb actually said was he was surprised, given the time that had passed, that he’s unable to get the answer that he wanted in that time frame. Now, we’re going to give the Minister an opportunity to say what she was going to say at this point in time. In the absence of an answer, we’re not at the end of this committee stage and we still have some time in the dinner break, but bearing in mind that written questions are an option but can only be asked about policy intent and they can’t go for legal opinion.

So let’s just work this through. I know that Dr Webb was looking for time before and we may be able to get some time here. We may or may not get an answer. I can’t guarantee that the answer that the member’s looking for will come, but this is where we are.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. I’m going to go through parts of clause 6 and clause 7 in an attempt to answer some of that member’s questions. With clause 6, which is amending section 135(1), this is introducing the discretion for the Law Society’s complaint service to refer those complaints to the standards committee in clause 6, and it will enable the triage process, that has been introduced by clause 7 of this bill. The assessment grounds for the triaging would be the same grounds by the standards committee when they are considering complaints. The triaging decisions—the change was supported by submitters, although some suggested that the triaging criteria for the standards committee should come with a right of review. The review and appeal rights are not provided in similar triaging decisions of comparable regulatory bodies such as the Teaching Council, for example. I don’t think review in this case is necessary or appropriate.

Creating a right of review would shift current inefficiencies to an earlier part of the process. If a complainant was to seek a review of the triaging decision, they would need to apply for a judicial review—I know the members spoke about that just before. That is, however, thought to be an appropriate pathway. The Government is confident that the Law Society will have appropriate guidance and policy in place to make well-judged positions.

content.speaker: Hon Phil Twyford
content.text: Madam Chair.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: If there’s a clarification on this, I’ll take it before the dinner break. If it’s a new question—

content.speaker: Hon Phil Twyford
content.text: It’s not a new—

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: —it’s not a new question.

content.speaker: Hon PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atatū)
content.text: Does the Minister think that judicial review is appropriately affordable and accessible for ordinary citizens who might find themselves in a dispute with the Law Society over the handling of a complaint?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Whether it’s affordable or accessible will come down to the individual and their case. What it is, for that member, is a pathway.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: The House is resumed. Members, before the dinner break, the committee was debating Part 1 of the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill. This is the debate on clauses 3 to 11, “Amendments to Lawyers and Conveyancers Act 2006”. The question, again, is that Part 1 stand part.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: In answer to the Hon Dr Duncan Webb’s thoughts earlier, over the dinner break I have had this from my officials: currently the affected person must enforce an undertaking through a separate proceeding in tort, contract, or estoppel, or, alternatively, a deed of undertaking that would need to be relied on, providing the process for enforcing breaches summarily will be simpler and more efficient for the affected person, and use less court and judicial resources. This will extend the range of pathways available to pursue breaches. The change will also improve the confidence of banks to rely on undertakings from conveyancers. If an unaffected person is unsuccessful with their application for summary judgment, the usual court processes apply. If the Hon Dr Duncan Webb is happy with that answer, I implore him to come back down to the Chamber and apologise to the officials that he abused before he left.

content.speaker: Hon PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atatū)
content.text: On clauses 6 and 7, the administrative triaging that we were talking about before the break, I wanted to know from the Minister what consideration she’s given to the trade-off of efficiency against public confidence, in light of the exchange we had earlier in the select committee and now in the Chamber. We support administrative triaging, but I think these are real questions that arise from some of the evidence that we had at the committee.

The Law Society and the Law Association are obviously strongly in favour of this, but they would be because they have a direct benefit, a direct gain, from the efficiency that this will deliver. But not everyone agreed. One submitter argued that complaints should never be dismissed administratively, that there should be some form of independent review, and that concepts such as “frivolous” and “vexatious” required greater definition. Now, ultimately the officials and the committee rejected those recommendations, but I would like to know from the Minister whether or not she has considered the possible lack of public confidence in a process that is, effectively, as was characterised earlier, an administrative employee having the ability to, basically, knock these complaints out with no real accessible right of review other than a judicial review.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Do I have confidence that this is the right way forward? Yes, because the advice that I’ve been given says that. As I mentioned before we went to the dinner break, the Government is confident that the Law Society will have appropriate guidance and policy in place to make well-judged decisions.

I also mentioned the assessment grounds for triaging would be the same grounds used by the Lawyers Standards Committee when considering complaints, and they are also set out in section 138 of the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act, “Decision to take no action on complaint”. I’m just going to go through those grounds very quickly. These grounds are from subsections (1)(a) to (f), paragraph (a) being “the length of time that has elapsed between the date [and] subject matter of complaint … or (b) the subject matter of the complaint [being] trivial; or (c) the complaint [being] frivolous or vexatious or is not made in good faith; or (d) the person alleged to be aggrieved does not desire the action be taken or, as the case may be, continued; or (e) the complainant does not have sufficient personal interest in the subject matter of the complaint; or (f) there is … another adequate remedy or right of appeal”.

Now, with these grounds that have been met, I think it very clearly sets out what those boundaries are before you get to that point of judicial review. So, yes, I do have confidence that I believe that we are on the right pathway here.

content.speaker: Hon PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atatū)
content.text: Thank you, Minister. Further to that, does she expect that the Law Society will be transparent about the handling of complaints under this new mechanism? For example, is there any expectation that they will publish annual statistics showing the number of complaints received, the number triaged, the grounds relied upon, and the complaints referred to the standards committees? Is there any expectation that there will be an ongoing audit to ensure that the triage decisions are being made consistently?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Because this is a regulatory standards bill, which is looking to make just small and minor amendments, we have not gone into every single clause with what is expected of organisations such as the Law Society, but one would hope that we need to get into a position where there is transparency across agencies, whether they be Government agencies or not, in order for the public to have confidence. So one would encourage transparency from all organisations that need to implement the law in some way or another. How they go about doing that, though, is up to them.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. Thank you for that response, Minister, and I do appreciate the Minister for going over some of the questions, for a more detailed response, over dinner. That’s very much appreciated.

Before dinner, Minister, you mentioned something around the changes we’re seeing both in terms of clause 8 but also in terms of clauses 5 and 7 around the guidelines that are going to be developed. Some of the guidelines have been developed alongside this, and this is also something we’ve seen from the submitters as well that is very much welcomed, but then there needs to be further guidelines on that.

I want to check with the Minister whether this is something, again, as we’re seeing with this particular bill, with some of these new additions like undertaking to be enforceable—whether either the Ministry of Justice or the appropriate, I guess, collective agency committee have already started working on some of those guidelines that the Minister referred to.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: My purpose here is to do some small technical amendments. Guidelines is not something that is under my purview, but if you’re going to have any implementation work correctly or work well, you would expect an agency or organisation to be able to get that information out to the users in order for them to be able to work efficiently. But the creation of guidelines is not under my purview.

content.speaker: TANGI UTIKERE (Labour—Palmerston North)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. Can I just ask a question of the Minister that relates to clause 7; this is in relation to new section 135A. The Minister has identified that in terms of the ability to either take no action—it seems to me that there are only two options, either for a referral of the complaint for further consideration or indeed no action. Now, the Minister has identified those particular specific criteria that relate to no action. One of them is in relation, it seems, to time; the period of time that’s elapsed. In a circumstance where there is an active referral that’s being considered, obviously one wants to, potentially, in the interests of natural justice, reach a conclusion at a time that is sufficient and not sort of drawn out so much.

When the Minister identifies the length of time that has elapsed between the date on which the matter of the complaint arose and the date that the actual complaint was made, where in the scheme of things is the quantum of time set in terms of action being taken around what the next step is? So it’s not about the amount of time from actually receiving the complaint, but the period of time from when the complaint is received and when the next step to either refer it or otherwise is taken.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I am advised that the length of time that has elapsed between the date of when the subject matter of the complaint arose and the date of when the complaint was made is such that an investigation of the complaint is no longer practicable or desirable.

content.speaker: TODD STEPHENSON (ACT)
content.text: I move, That debate on this question now close.

content.speaker: TANGI UTIKERE (Labour—Palmerston North)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I thank the Minister for her answer. In terms of being practicable, what sorts of factors would lend themselves to that consideration? It is quite a significant thing as to whether a complaint is heading down that path of referral or not. When she says practicability, practicableness, what sort of things is she envisaging? I know that, in terms of providing some guidance around what that might mean, it would be important.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: As I mentioned before, it is not for me to issue what that guidance is. What is practicable or desirable will come down to those that need to make those decisions, based on the cases that are before them. My role here is to make minor and technical amendments to law in order for them to operate well. The question that I am now being asked is almost a type of operational question which I have no control over.

content.speaker: TOM RUTHERFORD (National—Bay of Plenty)
content.text: I move, That debate on this question now close.

Part 2 Amendments to Prostitution Reform Act 2003

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: Members, we now come to Part 2. This is the debate on clauses 12 and 13, “Amendments to Prostitution Reform Act 2003”. The question is that Part 2 stand part.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I just have a short question for the Minister for Part 2, clause 13, “Section 36 amended”, noting that the current section 36 of this particular Act, “Disqualification from holding certificate”, already has burglary, robbery, extortion/blackmail, and money-laundering within that. Can I just check this is simply because the section numbers have changed around, and this is just to update the section numbers?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: I thank the member for his question. Section 36 of the Prostitution Reform Act 2003 lists quite a wide range of offences, and many of them are out of date. They haven’t been updated since 2003. The amendment updates to the Prostitution Reform Act also correct out-of-date sections that are in the Crimes Act 1961 and also the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975. We’re basically just updating, adding to those, and updating those references to those particular two bills.

content.speaker: TANGI UTIKERE (Labour—Palmerston North)
content.text: Thank you. Thanks to the Minister for that. In light of that response, these regulatory bills don’t come around that often, but when they do, they span quite widely. Is she confident that this process has captured all of the relevant updates in relation to the Prostitution Reform Act? It is a piece of legislation that’s been around for more than 20 years. Is she comfortable that there are no further other options that might need to be addressed?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: At this stage, the answer to that is yes. This change is about ensuring that the Act is not only up to date but it still sticks with its original policy intent as well. Correctly referencing the relevant offence provisions that are in the Crimes Act 1961 and the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975 will ensure that the correct disqualifying factors are applied in that licensing process. At this stage, I do believe that we have caught up, so to speak.
Part 2 agreed to.
Committee of the whole House
Part 3 Amendments to Real Estate Agents Act 2008

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: Members, we now come to Part 3. This is the debate on clauses 14 to 36, “Amendments to Real Estate Agents Act 2008”. The question is that Part 3 stand part.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. Part 3 is, as far as this bill goes, the most substantial part of this bill. It is also the part with the Minister’s amendment, which I’ll come to shortly, because I do have a few questions on the Minister’s amendment, but I’m not quite at clause 25 just yet.

My first two questions are for clause 18. The first one is clause 18(2), replacing section 13(4)(b). This is the new criteria that’s been added in terms of the membership of the authority. I’m guessing it’s just simply moving what is in subclause (1) to a different area, I guess—is that what is being done there?
The second question I have is—

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: Could you repeat the clause again, sorry?

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
content.text: OK. I will restart, very briefly. Clause 18(1), which is deleting “and that member must be a lawyer of not less than 7 years’ legal experience”—is that just simply moving that into a different section, which is now 13(4)(b), being my first question, and are there any implications with that?

The second one is the repeal of section 13(5)—again, I don’t think this is something we looked at specifically, and it’s not in version one of this bill—which is consultation with the Real Estate Institute of New Zealand (REINZ). Can I just check with the Minister: why do REINZ no longer need to be consulted? That’s the part that’s being repealed in clause 18(3). Does REINZ even still exist?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. At the moment, the chairperson of the board needs to be a lawyer with not less than seven years’ experience. What we’re doing is replacing section 13(4) with a new provision that requires at least one of the members of the board to be a lawyer with at least seven years’ experience. Effectively, what we’re saying is it doesn’t have to be the chair that has that, but somebody on the board has to have that.

The reasoning for that is it’s actually really hard to find a lawyer with seven years’ experience who wants to put their hand up to be here. In fact, I would like to do a bit of a shout-out to the current member, because the chair with seven years’ experience at the moment actually wants to resign and hasn’t been able to do so because we can’t replace that person with another lawyer. We’re, effectively, saying someone on the board, please have seven years’ experience—well, you’re going to need to have seven years’ experience, but you don’t need to be the chair. The chair just needs to have a year’s legal experience.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you for that, Minister. I will move on to clause 19. Clause 19 is also the part where the select committee has actually made some changes around the power to require specified documents. I just want to check in this section, when we are looking at that—and I believe I’m looking at clause 19, new section 24A(2). In that—yes, it is (2). Can I just check that still allows for the contravention, for example, which is not listed in (1), around things like privacy, etc.? Just checking that the authority, when requesting “any person to supply the Authority with any specified document”, is also exempted from certain other principles, like the information privacy principles, for example.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. Clause 19 actually makes a few new subsections. The member mentioned 24A(2), but there’s also 24A(3) and 24A(4). What I think I might do is just talk to the changes that we’re making all together. The Real Estate Authority has limited ability at the moment to gather information to support any investigations into breaches of the Act, regulations, or practice rules, and into unlicensed trading. This clause, clause 19, which is inserting the whole of new section 24A, establishes a new power to require documents from licensees and other individuals to facilitate those investigations that they wish to undertake. This change will enable the regulator to better fulfil its functions and better support the consumer protection purpose that is within this Act. The provision is complemented by the introduction of an offence for failure to comply with such a request. We do that in clause 28, with the maximum penalties of $50,000 for a company and $10,000 for an individual. I will just point out, too, that those penalties are consistent with other similar offences in the Real Estate Agents Act. I’ll just throw that in there while I can.

The select committee did make some recommendations, including amending clause 19 to clarify that the Real Estate Authority must have reasonable grounds to believe to initiate the power. It also recommended amending the test for exercising the power to make it consistent with the exercise of other existing powers by the authority under the Act. These changes also make it clear that the reasonable grounds to believe applies to situations involving a licensee’s conduct, not only a person who may be engaging in unlicensed trading.

The select committee, at this clause, also recommended amending the scope of the authority’s ability to require documentation so it could be applied to any person. This ensures that the relevant documentation could be obtained from any parties that may not be involved in illegal activity but who may have relevant information about others. Then, new section 24A(4) has been inserted to clarify that people or organisations can only be required to supply a specified document that is or has been in their possession or in their control. So, for the member, clause 19 and new section 24A and its insertion really is about providing the authority with that ability to be able to get that information in the best way that they can in order to make their judgments.

content.speaker: Hon PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atatū)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chairman. Further on clause 19, I thought it might be worth noting for the committee that the Law Association supported the objective of this section—of strengthening investigations—but it did raise a number of concerns, including the breadth of the power, the threshold for issuing notices, and privacy implications. The Privacy Commissioner came along to the committee and also accepted that there was a sound policy basis for the investigative power to require documents but stressed that it should be accompanied by appropriate limits, particularly in relation to the later use and disclosure of personal information obtained under this new power.

As the Minister pointed out, the committee did strengthen the threshold for reasonable belief, but I don’t think you could say that the committee actually accepted the other proposals that were made by the Privacy Commissioner—for example, around what operational guidance would be provided, the privacy concerns, and reporting and transparency. I want to ask the Minister: why did the Government conclude that the existing safeguards in the bill are sufficient, given that critique by the Privacy Commissioner? The Privacy Commissioner supported the proposal only on the basis that there would be appropriate limits on subsequent use and disclosure of personal information. Where are the safeguards? What limits are there? It’s not clear to me, so I’d be interested to know from her where those safeguards are, if they do exist. Finally, in this contribution: does she expect that the authority will publish operational guidance governing the use of these powers that they’re been given?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. What I have been advised is that this particular provision of this clause will come into effect eight months after the Royal assent of the bill, giving sufficient time for the agency to be able to prepare what I would expect to be guidance to those, because there is a bit of a change here. The delay of that eight months after Royal assent for implementation of this, I believe, would be in order for them to be able to get the House in order and ensure that everybody understands what their obligations will be; perhaps guidelines, as well. As I’ve mentioned earlier, I’m a big fan of transparency and I would explicitly hope that those that have to abide by this will understand exactly what it is that they need to abide by. It’s not a place to put those details into this form of legislation, but one would expect that if people are going to abide by the laws, they need to understand what those parameters are.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. Thank you for that response, Minister. I think my colleague Phil Twyford may have additional questions for clause 19, but I want to ask a question around clause 20, just noting to you, as well, Minister, that I may have a follow-up question on this once we get to the commencement part, which I don’t think I want to discuss at this stage.

The only question I have for this section—this is the part that, from our perspective, we had the greatest issues around, but then we have, like I said, had some of these being teased out during the select committee stage. Looking at it again, one of the things I want to check is about clause 20, “Section 36 amended”, subclause (2), inserting new paragraph (f), in the case of an individual whose licence was cancelled and is applying for a licence within 12 months—they’ve completed that. But, let’s say, should a person complete any required continued education within 12 months but they didn’t apply for a licence or re-licence within that 12-month period, are they again no longer eligible, as well? Is the criteria that you have to apply for it within 12 months, not the continued education part?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: My  understanding is that we have a series of real estate agents that have a qualification, and we have a series of older real estate agents who actually aren’t qualified, but they have a whole lifetime of experience. The requirements when people reapply is that they need to have a qualification, and we’re ensuring that those that don’t have the qualification but have adequate experience don’t miss out on continuing their job.

Now, that 12-month delay that is allowed actually came about as a result of Cyclone Gabrielle. It was a time when people had other things going on, and they couldn’t put in their application. When we think about natural disasters, of which we’re having a few in New Zealand, we need to be mindful that people just actually might not be able to get in and do their application at the time when they need to. There’s two things going on there: one is allowing those without qualifications but with experience to carry on; and the other is, with that 12-month extension, allowing those in predicaments to actually have that bit of extended time to apply.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you for that, Mr Chair. Thank you for that, Minister. That actually does answer my question, because I did wonder where the 12 months came about, and force majeure happens, events happen, and I think that’s reasonable.

I’m actually, if it’s OK, going to move on to—and other members may have questions in between—the Minister’s Amendment Paper 636 but also the two tabled amendments that are on that amendment. The question I have for the Amendment Paper is: when you look at new clause 25, “Section 54 amended”, the “Cancellation of licence”, in terms of the specific phrasing, it states, “is convicted … of a crime … involving dishonesty”, etc., and what we see in new section 54 (i)(i) and in new section 54 (i)(iii) and (iv)— I’ve actually seen that in some of the other legislation as well. Is that just simply updating this part that’s sort of recently been captured in this bill and updating it to be consistent with some of the things I see already in other legislation, being my first question.

My second question is around the Minister’s two tabled amendments. On the first, I thank the Minister for actually communicating with us ahead of time with these ones and with a little bit of explanation for both. I think the amendment itself looks fine, but I was more interested in a process question, which I believe, in the correspondence, it talked about this coming from the Real Estate Authority quite late and they only just picked up on it. I want to check, in terms of the process for such tabled amendments, is it that the authority would contact the Minister and the Minister saying, “These are some amendments.”, then the Minister contacts either the Parliamentary Counsel Office or the officials and going like, “Does this look OK?”, and then it goes into a tabled amendment? I just want to check, do officials need to being involved in any other process? Because I assume that the authority is not the officials.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I’ll start off with just talking about the first Amendment Paper in the way that it relates to clause 21. With the main Amendment Paper—Amendment Paper 636—it adjusts this clause to align with new section 54(i)(ii), which was added by the Amendment Paper, and then the member’s not actually asking me about the two Amendment Papers to the Amendment Paper, but rather the process of it.

The way that it has operated is that my understanding is the Real Estate Authority, last minute, just went through and started having a look at the bill and the Amendment Paper and then realised very quickly, and at the last minute, that a clause had dropped off. I think that was section 54, which we are putting in there now—section 54(k), going by memory. That had accidentally been deleted, and nobody had picked that up. The officials were contacted by the Real Estate Authority, not my ministerial office. The Real Estate Authority went straight to the officials. The officials would in turn have gone to the Parliamentary Counsel Office to check, is that a drafting error, which it was confirmed, and then it was put back in as section 54(k).

Of course, they then found the other one—section 54(i)(v)—as well, which is just a small amendment that they also picked up at the time that they were going through. I do appreciate that it is late notice, but I also appreciate the fact that the Real Estate Authority did find this and it’s not something we will then have to add into another regulatory standards bill in the future or next term. We were just taking the opportunity to fix that, and again, my appreciation to the Real Estate Authority for picking it up.

content.speaker: Dr VANESSA WEENINK (National—Banks Peninsula)
content.text: I move, That debate on this question now close.

content.speaker: Hon BARBARA EDMONDS (Labour—Mana)
content.text: Thak you, Mr Chair. Just wanting to take a question in relation to the Minister for Courts’ Amendments Paper 636, specifically clause 25, which amends the provisions around the cancellation of licence. I’m not quite sure whether the changes in the cancellation of licence actually would fit within the scope of a regulatory systems bill given, actually, it’s bringing in other clauses to cancel a licence. For example, obviously, with regulatory systems bills, they’re usually just technical changes. However, the new clause brings in a whole series of different ways that the cancellation of a licence can be undertaken.

Under section 54 of the Real Estate Agents Act right now, a registrar can cancel the person’s licence if they die, which makes sense obviously; if the person gives written notice to the registrar, which, obviously, if they’ve given up doing real estate; if the person has failed to maintain the prescribed qualification—that’s good, they’ve got to keep their qualifications to maintain their licence; if the person has failed to complete any continuing education—obviously, there’s professional development requirements as part of that; a couple of other sections—section 99 and section 110—in accordance of those; if the licence was granted on the basis of any false or fraudulent representation or declaration made orally or in writing; or if the person has failed to pay any prescribed fees or levies. Other than section 54(g), I can kind of understand where the insertions under the Minister’s Amendment Papers, which is around false or fraudulent representation, kind of still fits within that scheme. Hence why I think, perhaps, this is why it’s been allowed under the regulatory systems amendment bill.

But specifically, my questions for the Minister are in section 54(i)(ii)—“if, during the term of the licence, the person is convicted of an offence under … the Fair Trading Act” and it sets out a whole lot of sections in the Fair Trading Act. For example, section 12A is around unsubstantiated representation; section 14 of the Fair Trading Act is in relation to false representation and misleading conduct in relation to land—that makes absolute sense; section 17 is offering gifts and prizes and not providing them—again, that’s sort of a misleading offence; section 19 is in relation to bait advertising—again, that makes sense, if want to keep your real estate licence, you shouldn’t be doing bait advertising; section 20 of the Fair Trading Act is referral selling; section 21 is demanding or accepting payment without intending to supply a product; section 21C is prohibition on assisting right to payment with respect to unsolicited goods or unsolicited services; section 22 is in relation to misleading representations about certain business elements; and section 24 is around pyramid selling schemes.

I can understand why all those particular sections allow the regulator to cancel the person’s licence, but my question is actually in relation to the sections of the Fair Trading Act which are missing. That’s my question to the Minister, because if you look at that grouping between sections 12A to 24 of the Fair Trading Act, and if you work through the ones that are not included, they also have a similar theme to both the current section 54(g) of the Real Estate Agents Act, as well as the fair trading list. For example, section 23 of the Fair Trading Act, basically, is around harassment and coercion. If you’re a real estate agent, I would hope you’re not harassing and coercing a vendor to potentially buy the house. My question is around why section 12 of the Fair Trading Act is not included. That’s in relation to cancelling their licence if they have misleading conduct in relation to employment. Misleading conduct in relation to employment is quite important. Obviously, for some real estate agents, they are actually employees.

My other question is, why not section 13? Section 13 of the Fair Trading Act is about false or misleading representations in respect to the supply of possible goods. There is some weight to those three particular sections of the Fair Trading Act that have been missed out as a potential reasoning for the cancellation of licence. I just want to ask the Minister whether her or officials had considered those three particular provisions of the Fair Trading Act and as to why they were not included as a reason to cancel a licence.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. The member went quite extensively into clause 54(i)(ii) and laid them all out, but we’re not making any changes there. The Amendment Paper would replace clause 25 to adjust the amendments to section 54. The original wording of clause 25 would not achieve the policy intent to clearly allow the registrar to cancel a person’s licence if they meet the grounds that would prohibit them from holding a licence. The replacement to clause 25 makes more explicit the grounds for cancelling a person’s licence during the term of a licence, which mirrored the disqualifications from holding a licence in the Act now.

The Amendment Papers that we’re making include section 54(k), which I had just spoken to with the other member from the Green Party. The second amendment, to section 54(i)(v), makes a technical amendment to just adjust that section to refer to an agent’s licence. This better aligns the grounds for cancellation of a licence in this section with the current prohibition in section 37(2) for holding an agent’s licence. This amendment will mean that section 54(i)(v) applies to the cancellation of an agent’s licence. The member’s gone into an area that I don’t think actually correlates with what we’re doing here.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: Dr—the Hon Barbara Edmonds.

content.speaker: Hon BARBARA EDMONDS (Labour—Mana)
content.text: That’d be nice, without the PhD—but anyway, thank you, Mr Chair. When the Minister responded that it’s in relation to the original, did you mean when the bill was introduced—the original bill—or the one post - select committee?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: I will say that it relates to probably what was in that original bill. My officials can come and correct me if I am incorrect.

content.speaker: Hon BARBARA EDMONDS (Labour—Mana)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair, and thank you, Minister, for getting your officials to check that, because, if I understand that it is the bill as introduced, this is a new section under the Real Estate Agents Act 2008. That whole section 54(i), inserted by clause 25, is new because the Real Estate Agents Act currently only those to section 54(h). So it is an insertion—obviously an insertion that would have been put in the bill as introduced, but the question still remains: it provides a list of particular offences under the Fair Trading Act. Why have those other three offences, which is also under the Fair Trading Act, been omitted? What is the policy reason for them being omitted, even if it was the original bill, because currently it is a new amendment to the Real Estate Agents Act 2008?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: I thank the member for her question and seeking further clarity. I hope that I can give some of it here, now. Now they’ve not come up to me to say that I was incorrect, and they might do soon, so if they do, I will stand up again. My understanding—you’re quite right. Section 54(i) is a new section requiring the register to cancel the licence “of a licensee company, 10 working days after the licensee’s sole agent licence is cancelled…unless a temporary licence holder or a new [sole] agent licence holder has been appointed for the licensee company.”

So, I think, rather than having the huge list of it, it’s just allowing them that ability to be able to do that. The amendment paper would replace clause 25 to adjust the amendments in section 54, which makes me think that it that’s it is—

content.speaker: Hon Barbara Edmonds
content.text: In addition to it.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE
content.text: Yes.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. Thank you for that, Minister. I’ve got two additional questions, and that’s on clause 27 and clause 28. Again, others may have other clauses in regard to the Minister’s amendment. For clause 27, can I just get clarification from the Minister that the intent over here is that what we’re now seeing in this replacement section 72(b), paragraphs (i) to (iii), will now be relevant for just the licensees conduct in general, not specifically to do with the real estate agency work. Which means that if the licensee, for example, carries on with their day-to-day work, going to the supermarket, etc., and something happens and their conduct falls short of the standards that a reasonable member of the public is entitled to expect, that then would now fall under this particular clause. Would that be a reasonable example—checking with the Minister? That’s my first question.

My second question is on clause 28. Now, this new section 146A inserts not only an offence but also a fine. The fine is quite high. My understanding in terms of that is it may possibly be outdated—do not quote me on this—or that it offers a general understanding that fines should be no more than $1,000, because the thing with the fine is, there’s no way for anyone to respond. It’s not like, you know, upon conviction, you get fined; it’s just you get a fine. So $10,000 and $50,000 is what I would have thought is quite high and above some of the advice I have seen.

Can I just check that with—I have not gone through the entirety of the Real Estate Act, but does this come out from some other parts of the Real Estate Act that matches this particular one, which is why you are able to mirror it for that consistency? Because, otherwise, I would also assume that this is quite new.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. To the member, the change that we’re making in replacement section 72, inserted by clause 27, to expand the definition of “unsatisfactory conduct” is to make sure that real estate agents will be accountable for a broader range of conduct, not just the conduct while carrying out real estate agency work. To give you an example of that, it will include, say, aggressive or abusive behaviour during cold-calling people, or a licensee acting inappropriately towards a client maybe, after a transaction has concluded. At the moment, it’s about the business that they’re doing, but we’re saying, well, actually, you need to behave well, broadly.

The member talked about a fine—well, it’s actually an offence, so it’s not like it’s an infringement fee; it’s an offence. The reason why it’s so much—$50,000—for a company and $10,000 for an individual—is because those penalties and those amounts are consistent with other similar offences, as the member mentioned, within the Real Estate Agents Act.

content.speaker: Hon PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atatū)
content.text: So on clause 27, I remember the Law Association, at the committee, supported this, but they questioned whether or not the drafting provided sufficient certainty. They accepted the arguments about consumer protection, about the need for professional discipline, but they submitted that there was insufficient legal certainty. So, further to the Minister’s response to Lawrence Xu-Nan’s question, I’m interested in whether or not her interpretation of the draft would be that real estate agents could be held accountable for behaviour completely outside their work as a real estate agent—so, not cold-calling potential customers or whatever, but committing a crime when you’re out shopping or watching your kid’s football game, or bringing yourself into disrepute in some way that doesn’t relate at all to your work as a real estate agent. I’m interested in if she could answer that question.

Secondly, how does she expect licensees to know where the boundary lies for unsatisfactory conduct? Because just a plain reading of the provisions doesn’t provide that. Perhaps the Minister could give us some examples of behaviour that would count under this provision as unsatisfactory conduct. Further to that, does she expect that the authority will publish guidance for real estate agents so that they can have some understanding and some clarity?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: I gave some examples just before to the member from the Green Party, so I’ll say that I’ve already delivered that, and I will carry on because I’ve answered your last question first. I’ll now move back to your first question then. My understanding is that the select committee actually raised those concerns as well, because submitters had raised concerns about what actually makes up that unsatisfactory conduct. In response to that, I understand that there are tests of unsatisfactory conduct in the clause that have been clarified. A clearer link has been drawn between unacceptable conduct by a licensee and their profession to emphasise that this test is about upholding consumer confidence in the real estate profession. So as there is a test, I would expect that that test would be made known to the real estate agents in order for them to understand and have knowledge about how to comply.

content.speaker: TOM RUTHERFORD (National—Bay of Plenty)
content.text: I move, That debate on this question now close.

content.speaker: TANGI UTIKERE (Labour—Palmerston North)
content.text: I just have two areas that I’d like to ask the Minister questions about. The first one is a brief one. It’s a response to her to Dr Xu-Nan’s question about having a lawyer as a chair, basically. I accept the Minister has said that history has proven that it’s apparently quite difficult to attract someone into that role. If that is the reason, Minister, was there any thought than to, perhaps, not completely removing that requirement for the chair’s role, but maybe allowing the Minister to make the appointment of the chair with preference given to someone who has that particular qualification in terms of a minimum number of years as a practising lawyer? That’s the first question.

The second one in relation to clauses 20 and 21 in Part 3. This is about the entitlement to a licence and the prohibition on someone from being licensed. In clause 20, which seeks to amend section 36, it identifies the various things that need to be considered for someone who has had a track record of having a licence being cancelled, and it seems to me that in new section 36(1)(f) in clause 20(2), it talks about someone who has had their licence cancelled within the previous 12 months and who has, basically, undertaken a process of professional development. Further down, in new section 36(2)(d) in clause 20(4), it’s around the registrar being satisfied that, actually, the applicant can demonstrate a sufficient level of knowledge and experience of agency work.

In clause 21, it talks about the prohibition on someone who, in the previous five-year period, has had a licence cancelled, and so my question to the Minister is this. Clause 20 is all about those sorts of qualitative considerations around what someone’s record might look like. New section 37(1)(d)(i) in clause 21 is very definitive in that it’s a five-year threshold. Minister, are you satisfied that five years is appropriate, and, if so—or if not, I guess—were there any other considerations as to what that particular time frame would be? How did five years get landed upon?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: I’d note that perhaps the member wasn’t in here when I answered these questions before, and so I’m happy to go through them again.

content.speaker: Tangi Utikere
content.text: This part? I’ve been here for this part.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE
content.text: Yeah. Both the questions that you’ve just asked me, I’ve actually answered, but I’m happy to answer them again for you. With regard to the requirement about the chairperson having seven years’ legal experience, we had mentioned how it’s hard to find a person. We’re not actually removing that from the board, at all. We still want a person with seven years’ experience, if we can find it, to sit on the board—

content.speaker: Tangi Utikere
content.text: Just not as chair?

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE
content.text: —but just not as chair. Effectively, I had spoken about how the current chair with seven years’ experience has been wanting to resign, but we have nobody who is able to replace the dear lady. Her name is Denese Bates, and she does a wonderful job for the real estate agents, but she does want to retire. There is nobody there to replace her, and so we’d like to be able to replace her with someone that has the legal experience, but not so defined as it currently is.

Now, if someone else comes along and they happen to have seven years’ legal experience, we can in the first instance at least get them on to the board, and maybe they could eventually end up in that chair role. It’s just trying to make sure that we have a spin of people that can continue, and the Real Estate Agents Authority can continue in that respect.

In regard to clause 21, the five-year prohibition following grounds for cancelling a licence is really, really extensive, and there is no other organisation or agency that has that sort of penalty. We’re looking to remove that five-year stand-down period as an automatic consequence for not completing compulsory personal development or for failing to pay the annual suspension fee, and, again, this can also come down to people just having a time where they can’t even get in and do their reapplications, etc., for other things like, say, Cyclone Gabrielle, as I had mentioned before.

Again, I will just point out that this will come in eight months after Royal assent in order to ensure that we have it all set up and ready to go in the Act, and so that we are not taking away what could often be a lifetime of work. Real estate agents are often in that job for decades before failing to do something as simple as not doing a particular course or not paying a particular fee at any one time, and, as I’ve mentioned, it’s a punitive and disproportionate consequence when you compare it to so many other professions which don’t have anything anywhere near a five-year suspension.

content.speaker: PAULO GARCIA (National—New Lynn)
content.text: I move, That debate on this question now close.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: Members, we now come to our final debate: clauses 1 and 2. This is the debate on clauses 1 and 2, “Title” and “Commencement”.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I’m signalling that I have just two short questions on this, and they’re all to do with clause 2(1), which is on the commencement date for Part 3.

Of my two short questions, No. 1 is this. Minister, you mentioned that the poor person who has been the chair of the authority now wants to step down. Does that mean that they have to wait eight months before they can step down because this part doesn’t come into effect for eight months? That’s my first question.

My second question is to do with how this interacts with clause 20. We did talk about the fact that if a person’s licence is cancelled, they can reapply within 12 months, and yet the commencement is in eight months’ time. If the commencement is in eight months’ time, does that mean that a person who is within that eight months—because there’s no retrospectivity, as far as I know. So if a person whose licence was cancelled within that eight months, the old rules still apply, and it’s not like in eight months’ time, they have four more months of leeway to go to make that up within 12 months—if that makes sense. Those are my two questions for this.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: My officials and I had the same thought on this, but they’re just going away to double-check and will come back. But there is a delay just in Part 3—which is the real estate agents area—for eight months, and if Denese Bates KC is listening to this, we are of the opinion—

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: Shout-out to Denese.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE
content.text: Shout-out to Denese. She’s going to be there for another eight months unless we do find somebody with that seven years’ experience. But the delay of the commencement is because there is some updating of IT systems, forms—which we were talking about earlier—and training programmes that need to be implemented, and the information on their website also needs to be updated. Unfortunately, the chair side of it is in there too, and so, hopefully, Denese Bates KC will stay on for eight months, and unless we—

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: You might have some answers now.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE
content.text: Clause 18 in Part 3, which amends the membership of the Real Estate Agents Authority, will, however, come into force on the day after Royal assent, as an additional time for the implementation of that particular clause is not required. Denese Bates KC, if you’re listening to this, you can heave a sigh of relief—and I most certainly am—and I hope that that answers the member’s question.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Just checking with the Minister: I had a second part of that question around the reapplication of the licence within that eight months. I understand that the Minister might be seeking some advice, and, Mr Chair, I just wanted to get clarity. That’s my only question. If the Minister is able to get that advice and wants to tie it in to her third reading speech, so to speak, I’m fine with that. I just would like an answer to that—that’s all.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. No, that notification that I had there was saying that it’s only that clause that will be implemented straight away. Everything else will be eight months away, and so—yes—it will take eight months for everything else.

content.speaker: Hon BARBARA EDMONDS (Labour—Mana)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. It is quite an important question, so if I just practically work through it, because this does become important, particularly in the transition period. So, for example, section 54(d), as amended by clause 25, won’t come into effect until March next year. So therefore, “if the person, at any time, ceases to be able to hold a licence on 1 or more of the grounds [that are now] set out under section 37;”—for example, if tomorrow they cannot meet any of those motions, doesn’t matter; it gets to March—this won’t come until effect until March next year, so that notice period of over month is well superseded—therefore, if it means that with the 12-month period, which Dr Xu-Nan referenced, does that mean—April, May, June, July—by July next year, which is 2027, that’s when that cancellation comes into effect, or is it not for another 12 months from March 2027? So it’s just that clarity around when that is.

If the Minister, as you said correctly, that’s when section 54(d) comes into effect, March next year, technically, based on the question by Dr Xu-Nan, it won’t be until March 2028 that that person’s licence can be cancelled.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Mr Chair.

content.speaker: Hon Barbara Edmonds
content.text: Not 23 July.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE
content.text: Yeah. I understand the member’s question, and it probably goes a little bit further than what I’m able to answer. When I looked at the notes that I have, the reason why we have that eight months requirement is to update the IT systems, forms, training programmes, and information on their website. I suspect that information on the website, training forms, information that goes out to the real estate agents, will detail exactly how they will roll that out.

One thing that we have made clear to the real estate authority is to try and ensure that any changes that they make are for the benefit of the real estate agents, hence why we’re removing that five-year suspension as well, because we really just needed to update this.

I think, in the bigger scheme of things, my expectation is the real estate authority would work with an individual depending on what that circumstance is. To give you an example, if that member did something that was really out of order, one would expect them to be suspended and not have to go through the—

content.speaker: Hon Barbara Edmonds
content.text: Not wait until those provisions come in.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE
content.text: —yes, not wait until those provisions—but if it’s something that, perhaps, could be addressed when those provisions come in, there could be the ability, perhaps, for the real estate authority to suspend their decision until that comes in. But it’s very hard to ascertain exactly when or what, because there will be so many variations to what they have to deal with.
Clause 1 agreed to.
Clause 2 agreed to.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: The Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill are set down for third reading immediately.
