Legislative Statement

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: I present the legislative statements on the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: Those legislative statements are—what are the words?

content.speaker: Tom Rutherford
content.text: —published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: —there we go. Those legislative statements are published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
Third Reading

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I move, That the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill be now read a third time.

I’m pleased to take this final call on two practical bills that improve the way parts of our justice and regulatory systems operate. These bills are not about creating unnecessary new layers of regulation, they’re about maintaining the laws we already have, fixing known problems, removing disproportionate penalties, and making sure our regulatory systems work better for the people who use them.

The Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill improves access to justice and supports the effective operation of tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies. It allows successful applicants in the disputes tribunal to recover their filing fee from the respondent where it is appropriate.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: You can get another Minister to read it out for you.

content.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE
content.text: Yes, if you wouldn’t mind.

content.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
content.text: That is a sensible change. People who have had to enforce their legal rights should not be left bearing unnecessary costs when they have been successful.

The bill also strengthens oversight of the private security industry by improving information gathering powers. This will help detect and deter people operating outside the rules. It also makes practical changes to appointments and employment arrangements for tribunal members so these bodies can operate more consistently and efficiently.

The Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill improves the occupational regulation system for both professionals and consumers. It allows conveyancers’ professional undertakings to be enforced in the High Court, as lawyers’ undertakings already are. That will support competition in the conveyancing market and give consumers more confidence in the services they use.

It also removes an overly harsh penalty that disqualified real estate agents from practising for five years for failing to complete continuing professional development or pay fees on time. That kind of penalty is out of proportion to the breach. This bill replaces it with a more sensible and balanced approach. At the same time, the bill strengthens the real estate authority’s ability to investigate unlicensed trading and ensure licensees are meeting their obligations.
I thank officials in the Parliamentary Council Office, for their work on these bills. I commend these bills to the House.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: Just for the Hansard record: that was the Hon Louise Upston. The question is that the motion be agreed to.

content.speaker: GEORGIE DANSEY (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. Well, it was just an hour, maybe two hours ago that I was here speaking on the second reading of these two great bills: the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill.

In the intervening time we’ve had a committee stage and I’ve had dinner—fish and chips; fish and chip Friday—but the point I’m making, is the fact that it’s been such a short time, and here I am speaking now, on the third reading, is the way that this legislation is moving through Parliament at such a rapid pace under urgency.

The need for us to have a process that is robust ensures that the legislation receives the public attention that the public may want to give the legislation—it treats proper scrutiny as an inconvenience—allowing robust debate around this legislation. So it is disappointing to be back here two hours later, in the third reading, to discuss these two important bills, which I would have liked to have more time to consider, as would my colleagues, and I’m sure the public would have appreciated some more time to consider these bills. Nevertheless, I will continue. These bills are a package of four regulatory systems amendment bills administered by the Ministry of Justice. Look, we acknowledge the challenges in our justice system—

content.speaker: Simon Court
content.text: Read it better, Georgie.

content.speaker: GEORGIE DANSEY
content.text: What do you mean “Read it better”? Read what better?

content.speaker: Simon Court
content.text: Your speech.

content.speaker: GEORGIE DANSEY
content.text: I was thinking that, maybe, members on the Government side would take an actual call on this. I challenge—

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: I would actually challenge the member to speak to the piece of legislation, please, because we’ve just had quite an extensive two hours on the committee stage, so there’s plenty to talk about.

content.speaker: GEORGIE DANSEY
content.text: There is plenty. Thank you, Madam Speaker. First of all, I’ll talk about the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill. Within here, there are some technical changes. There are technical changes that will amend the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act 2006, the Prostitution Reform Act 2003, and the Real Estate Agents Act 2008. The aim is to strengthen the ability of occupational regulators to protect consumers, increase efficiency, and remove inconsistent or redundant provisions.

What I wanted to start talking about was the amendments within the Law Society which give the complaints service discretion rather than requirement in referring complaints against lawyers. This has been hashed out a little bit across the board, and the pros and cons of this part of the legislation have been discussed. It is still not completely resolved, and I think there are still questions around who’s making the decision as to whether a complaint progresses through and how that decision was made and then around what the repercussions are if, say, the complainant’s complaint is dismissed but they don’t think their complaint should be dismissed—what process they would go through? Those are still questions we have, and if we had had more time, those could have been addressed.

One of the benefits of this legislation—and I see the intention of it is to increase how quickly complaints can be resolved. As we all know, all facets of society will get complaints about the way things are done, and some of them have basis, and some of them don’t. Not having to go through a full investigation process for every single complaint is surely going to benefit the Law Society. When we’re talking about justice, we have to talk about a fair process and fair access to justice. If we can make things more efficient within the system, which in turn frees up resources and people to concentrate on the important things when it comes to administering justice, then that has got to be a good thing—as long as we are doing so in a way that doesn’t limit access at all and is a robust process.

The next part of the occupational regulation amendment bill that I found quite interesting was around the Real Estate Authority changes. There was some discussion around the changes to the chairperson having to have been a practising lawyer for seven years and that move to that person having to be on the board. I support that change, but, still, I think that having a practising lawyer on the board who has experience of seven years and keeping them there is absolutely vital. I’m really pleased that that’s been put in the mix. As we know, the work that real estate agencies do is very legislation-heavy. They’ve got to get all their ducks in a row; they’ve got to dot their Is and cross their Ts because they are preparing quite serious legal documents, and the importance of that oversight from the board can’t be understated when it comes to the work that they do. The decisions that boards make is vital in that space.

The other aspect of that I want to touch on is just the tidying-up of the ability for the Real Estate Authority to renew a licence for up to 12 months after it expires, rather than requiring a full application, and that flexibility for unforeseen circumstances after what happened with recent flooding that restricted people from accessing the renewal of their licences. That’s good.

I actually had a situation where I was talking to someone in my electorate about their experiences with a real estate agent when they were trying to purchase a house and they were interested in the house and they had an unconditional offer to put on the house, and the agent said, “I’ve already got a conditional offer on this house, but I think it’s going to fall through. If you sign this paperwork for your unconditional offer, and you should get the house.” The person signed the paperwork because they saw the professional in front of them and trusted that they had the correct information at hand. I think it’s fair that citizens, when they are meeting with a real estate agent, think, “I think this person must know their stuff and they must understand this legally binding document I’m signing.”—well, actually, the person probably should have checked with their lawyer, but they didn’t in this case. They then checked with their lawyer after they’d signed the documentation, and the lawyer said, “Well, you’ve actually signed something illegal because there’s already a conditional offer in place, but that’s the legally binding offer on the house. If that one goes through, then the agency would have to reimburse you the cost of the house because they’ve sold the house twice.” Anyway, the conditional offer didn’t go through, so there was no payout required, but the point is that that level of detail required from real estate agencies can have a huge financial burden if they make a mistake. Getting these processes right and making sure the legislation sits well together is a really important part of this.

To finish up, I was going to talk about the other bill, but I don’t seem to have time. I had discussed it a little in my previous speech, which felt like just a minute ago but was two hours ago. The main point is that access to justice needs to be fair for all people. This bill does some technical tidy-up, which moves us in the right direction. There is so much work to do in this space to ensure everyone has good access to justice.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: The member’s time has expired.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Madam Speaker, thank you so much. I am glad to speak on behalf of the Green Party on the third reading of both the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill.

I’m going to start with the first bill that we did our committee stage on, in terms of the tribunals amendment bill, and I’m going to probably start with the most controversial discussion that we had during the committee stage, which is around whether we should use “must” or “shall”. I think this is something the House is very divided on—I’m surprised that we came to a consensus in the end, but I think, unfortunately for me, who prefers “shall”, I lost out on that. Both of these two bills are technical tidy-ups, and, again, the committee stage when we were looking at both bills was an excellent opportunity to engage with the Minister on some of the detail—and, again, the kind of detail that really could affect New Zealanders in quite a significant way. At the same time, these are the sorts of bills that, as we see, have the House’s support and that are housekeeping tidy-up bills, but, like I said, it’s important for us to understand some of the details and some of the nuances.

I already mentioned in terms of the Disputes Tribunal Act—that’s the first one that we are looked at as part of the tribunals amendment bill—that I think the big part of that is around some of the changes around the chief executive appointing a panel to assess people as referees. I am actually really glad to hear from the Minister around the requirements for diversity and inclusion, that reflect, I think, our communities and our society in Aotearoa New Zealand on the whole. It’s good to hear that, for example, there is a Māori referee collective, there is a Pasifika referee collective. The Minister mentioned that there currently isn’t an Asian referees collective, but I’m looking forward to something like that happening with, now, our Asian populations being 17 percent of New Zealand’s population.

But I think the most significant part of this bill is this consistency of basically moving referees as employees and then making them contractors to be more consistent with other forms of referees and adjudicators in our justice system who are also contracted. Now, of course the major impact this will have is on ACC, because obviously now if you’re self-employed there is a higher ACC levy to factor in some additional elements. But again, I the way that the Minister has mentioned it is it does allow for that consistency, particularly when you have someone who is a referee/adjudicator for multiple areas and where they are employees for some and self-employed for others. So I think that is something that’s needed.

The amendments to the Motor Vehicle Sales Act 2003, in terms of adjudicators who have held a practising certificate, this is—although one clause is actually quite significant, because as we discussed through the committee stage, that what you would do is expand the eligibility criteria to more people who could apply to become adjudicators. There are still criteria and requirements, as the Minister communicated to the House, but opening that pool would potentially mean more adjudicators being appointed, which means that more of some of these disputes may be able to take place faster.

For the third part of this particular bill, the Parole Act 2002—I think, for me, what kind of really stood out in this one is the fact that there was an outdated term for the Remuneration Authority that I think none of us had really heard about until we got that clarification, this “Higher Salaries Commission”. I think, again, this just shows that sometimes with these legislations, we do need to have that administrative update for the ability for it to be in line with the most recent terminology that’s being used. So, again, I’m personally always quite excited to learn something new, and the Higher Salaries Commission this time around very much was one of the things.

The fourth part, around the Private Security Personnel and Private Investigators Act was something that we managed to touch on but didn’t get a chance to fully explore. But, you know, it is what it is. So I’m going to move on to Part 5 of the first bill that we looked at, which is under unit titles. I think that what’s particularly important for this part is the clarification from the Minister that existing rules under the Residential Tenancies Act already exist. So this technical update doesn’t necessarily imply that new rules will be created that will fall under whatever remit or secondary legislation or regulatory-making powers that the Residential Tenancies Act itself will have, but it just creates a consistency, particularly around provisions that we see here in the new Unit Titles Act.

Now, moving on to the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill, it’s also one of the things—as I mentioned in my second reading speech—that the last time we had these two associated bills with their back-to-back committee stage, it was two bills that were very similar. So it’s also quite nice that this time round we didn’t accidentally jump between the two, because these two bills are fundamentally quite different. But in terms of the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill, the first part with lawyers and conveyors, that is something that was really interesting in terms of some of the updates around the undertaking. I think that was something that we did explore quite a bit within the committee stage, around whether this is actually going to create new aspects to such undertaking or what that would mean. I think we had a lot of conversations around why, then, the High Court is the best place for it, around some of the undertaking. Because again, we have just seen, in a previous bill, of increasing the High Court judges numbers from 55 to 60. But at the same time, we also now, through this service system, don’t really want to find different ways of accidentally or incidentally clogging up the High Court system. So I think this is something that was covered quite well during the committee stage.

On to Part 2 and Part 3. So Part 2 of the occupational regulation is quite a small part, and, again, just shows one of the things why it is really important for us to do this administrative update for the legislation. This is to do with the Prostitution Reform Act 2003. Specifically, it is simply an update to be in line with the existing phrasing and terminology that is being used, I believe, within the Crimes Act. This is to do with disqualification from holding a certificate.

Finally, for Part 3, real estate agency probably was the most significant aspect of this bill. Again, a shout-out: I did not, unfortunately—and I do apologise for this, Madam Speaker; I cannot remember her name, but I want to, as many other people—

content.speaker: Camilla Belich
content.text: Denese Bates.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
content.text: Denese Bates—shout-out to Denese Bates KC for being a trouper and continuing to be the chair of the Real Estate Authority despite wanting to step down. We’re hoping that this bill allows you the opportunity to step down, and hopefully you will be finding other ways to enjoy your time not being the chair of the Real Estate Authority. So that particular clause, clause 18, of that bill is quite significant.

I think the main thing that was the concern for us, and again we managed to get additional clarifications from the Minister—it’s amazing how quickly 10 minutes can go when you are having fun. But in terms of clause 20, I think the main thing here is the fact that it doesn’t exempt people from having to undertake that sort of outstanding continuing education, but, as the Minister put it, it does allow people more time to reapply, should they get a chance to continue that outstanding education requirement. I think that is significant, particularly in terms of the rationale that the Minister gave.

I think, finally, when we are looking at some of the other things—unsatisfactory conduct, clause 17, is something that we did manage to clarify, and I think the examples the Minister had were sound. We were hoping there would be more examples around that, which would’ve been helpful to better understand the essence of that clause, but overall, we really do support—

content.speaker: JAMIE ARBUCKLE (NZ First)

I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to support the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill in their third readings. As we’ve heard through a number of readings, these are minor or technical changes—so, maintenance of the legislation. The issues have been well canvassed to the committee of the whole House and I commend the bills to the House.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER

content.speaker: SCOTT WILLIS (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise to take my first call on the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill for their third readings. We do support these bills, and I’ve worked my way through them this evening, in detail, to check that I knew what we were talking about because they do deal with a lot of minor detail and very technical detail. I think, Madam Speaker, you’ve just seen how perfectly suited this has been to my colleague Lawrence Xu-Nan.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: Oh yes, we have, and you’re channelling him now, so it should be good.

content.speaker: SCOTT WILLIS
content.text: Until earlier, I was not aware that these bills had been full of controversy, but I have heard since that, you know, the debate—it must have been a high-octane debate, between the words “must” and “shall”. It’s unfortunate that I missed that part of the debate, so I’m going to have to go back and watch. I am going to have to go back and dig into this.

We do support this bill, and it is very good to make small or minor changes to keep our regulatory systems fit for purpose. We’re doing this through urgency, and I think this is notable. It’s notable because we’ve heard some concern during this debate that we might be rushing this bill and that when we’re pushing it through all stages, we might be missing things. Now, personally—

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER

content.speaker: SCOTT WILLIS
content.text: No, that’s right, Madam Speaker—just a few stages. Thank you for that correction—just a few stages. Nevertheless, we are doing it through urgency, and as I have applied myself to these bills earlier to make sure I wasn’t missing anything, personally, I don’t think we are going to miss anything in this bill in supporting it. But what I do think is that we have clearly experienced some risk, through the abuse of urgency by this Government, in other bits of legislation. This is really, really clear: we have had some really poor-quality legislation that has passed through the House under urgency, and we have had to come back and redo it or put in amendments to make changes. It is something we should be mindful of—that when we’re using urgency to such an extent to draft legislation, we should really take care that it’s doing it for an important reason rather than a trivial one.

content.speaker: SCOTT WILLIS

I’d like to make that very clear, if I haven’t already. I am also mindful that we are, on a Friday night, debating this bill. Tomorrow, the All Blacks will be playing in Christchurch—

Those of us who are not speaking on the bills tomorrow afternoon will be able to capture the All Blacks if we can’t get to Christchurch. But I hope that we are able to move through this bill a little bit faster.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER

content.speaker: SCOTT WILLIS
content.text: I’m trying my best, Madam Speaker. I’m trying not to be distracted by the people around me, because they’re offering lots of commentary. My point is that we fully endorse this bill. I’m finding it very distracting, but we are in full support of this bill.

content.text: I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH (Labour)
content.text: Well, Madam Speaker, thank you very much for allowing me the opportunity to take this call. I have a few thoughts that I haven’t yet been able to express on the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and also, if I have time, the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill. You could almost use your entire call reading out the titles of these pieces of legislation, they’re so long.

It was good to be able to speak in the second reading of this earlier today on the tribunals—actually, on both of these bills—and good to be able to participate in the committee stage on the tribunals bill. As you would be aware, I was not able to traverse all of my thoughts in relation to the Private Security Personnel and Private Investigators Act, so I thought I would use this opportunity to set out my thoughts in relation to that particular part of the bill. The other areas I feel I’ve covered more substantively, so we’ll see where we get to.

I did have some questions which I didn’t get to put to the Minister on these private security personnel. One of the things I was interested in was that in this bill, there is a deletion of misconduct or gross negligence as a reason for a complaint to be against a licensee. I thought that was particularly interesting, because it wasn’t clear to me whether this was a weakening or a strengthening of the provisions around misconduct for these private security guards. Obviously, if it was misconduct or gross negligence, you would expect that to be a disciplinary matter, but then, of course—yeah, I was just not really sure of the reason for deleting that and would have been keen to find out from the Minister why that was.

The other thing that I just wanted to flag was that there is a new section that’s been put in after section 104 by this Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill, and that is a specific new right that allows information to be provided on complaints to a chief investigator, so that’s kind of a new right. There isn’t that much—as the Minister said and as has been traversed in this House, many of these changes are administrative. Some of them, I think, go beyond administrative and actually do put in new rights. I think sometimes that’s appropriate—it’s not something that we disagree with—but that is relatively significant, so that is just something I wasn’t able to mention in that bill.

The other aspects of this tribunals bill, first, that I think warrant mentioning are—I do think that there are some more questions that I haven’t been satisfied on in relation to the treatment of judicial officers. This is really interesting, actually, because while we were debating in here today, in the Grand Hall just through those two sets of double doors, many of our greatest judges and lawyers and practitioners in family law were having a conference on the anniversary of the Property (Relationships) Act. Of course, that’s a different area of law, but it does cover, obviously, judicial officers. It was really interesting to reflect on the discussions that we’re having in here today and the kind of complexity of the issues that they were dealing with in there.

One of the things that they are interested in is new Family Court associate judges and their comparative conditions compared to Family Court judges. That is something that is a live issue for them at the moment—making sure that there is that consistency. I think what the Minister said in her reflections today was that she was interested in having consistency around judicial officers as well. I’m a big proponent of employment as a mode of engagement when that truly is the true nature of the relationship. I personally think that there’s a very solid common law test that can be put in place to ascertain whether you’re employed or not. But I do agree and don’t object to people like judicial officers or quasi-judicial—or “quas-eye”; we’ve had a debate about how you pronounce that today—officers having those consistent rights as well.

I wish that we had been able to—and I wasn’t, as I said in my previous contribution, on either select committee at exactly the right time to hear the submissions, but it would be heartening and it would be comforting to know that the people who currently are treated as employees in the Disputes Tribunal were satisfied that these changes were fair in terms of the consistency.

I do see the point of what the Minister is trying to achieve; however, there is an uncomfortable aspect of having a piece of legislation which, effectively, cancels someone’s employment, through the deletion of this clause, and that will be the effect at the end of today. I’m just flagging that as something that may or may not be an issue, but I think it’s important to put the House on notice for that.

The rest of the issues I feel were sufficiently—well, I feel that I covered the issues in the committee stage in respect of tribunals, and so I won’t go over that any further. But I just also recognise, as the rest of the House has done, that it’s important to make these small changes to ensure that our regulatory systems are working effectively, so although they might not be the most interesting bills to us, they have an effect on making the system work better. Thanks to the officials for doing the work on this, and I hope that some of those concerns turn out to be unwarranted.

The other bill that we have been discussing is, of course, the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill. I didn’t participate in that committee stage, but I do think that there are some interesting points here, so I just wanted to, if I have time, mention maybe one point on each of the areas.

The changes to the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act—this is a particularly interesting Act to me. I qualified as a lawyer in 2007, and so this was the regime that was in place when I qualified. I remember discussions around including conveyancers in the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act, and I remember the discussions around the provision of legal advice, because that was particularly relevant to employed solicitors, and I think there was an amendment in that. It’s quite interesting now to see that the provision of regulated services has come up again in this bill, and the provision of regulated services, in this instance, it appears to me—and I wasn’t here for the committee stage, so apologies if this was clarified further—has been taken out of the description of what the people on the Lawyers Standards Committee actually do. That’s particularly interesting, so I just wanted to mention that.

Another thing, kind of reflecting on prostitution law reform, is that I remember when that passed in the House in 2003, and I think it was really unknown as to whether that would pass at all until the numbers were called. I want to acknowledge Labour MP Georgina Beyer, and I think she gave a very amazing speech on that. I remember I was working in a students association at the time, and we had been supporting this change. Essentially, what we have had is a decriminalisation and a regulation of prostitution, which was so controversial. It was quite a few years ago now, over 20 years ago, but to see a minor change made to this in a regulatory systems bill, I suppose, shows how far the debate has come.

It’s not a controversial thing that we have a regulated, legalised system in New Zealand in relation to prostitution. I think this is a good change, too, because we don’t want people legally running brothels who have convictions in burglary, robbery, blackmail, or money laundering, because these are convictions that do reflect on the character of the person, and we want the people who choose to do that work, if they’re legally allowed to, to be of good character. I think that is an interesting reflection.
I don’t know if I’ll have time to cover real estate agents. I think, hopefully, that has been—

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: You’ve got 47 seconds.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH
content.text: I’ve got 47 seconds—what could I say? I think it is a good thing, and most New Zealanders would agree—and, hopefully, this House does too—that the real estate agent profession is regulated and is held to high standards. I do think that the changes in this help to maintain the confidence that New Zealanders should have in what is a profession that maybe we don’t all engage with every day but that is a significant part of one of the most important and significant financial decisions that most people make in their life. The fact that they do so with integrity and they do so in a way which is regulated to a high standard is something that we should support. I commend both these bills to the House.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: With the mental health bill coming next, I commend the bill to the House.

content.speaker: DAN ROSEWARNE (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise on behalf of the Labour Party in support on the third reading of the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill. This is the final stage of Parliament’s consideration of these bills. Over the course of that process, they have been examined by select committees; tested through public submissions; amended, where appropriate; and debated in detail during the committee of the whole House.

Labour supports these bills because they improve the way a number of important regulatory and dispute resolution schemes actually operate. The changes are spread across a range of legislation. They touch on the Disputes Tribunal, the New Zealand Parole Board, private security and investigation services, lawyers and conveyancers, real estate professionals, and several other regulatory regimes. It’s a broad package, but there is a common theme running through it.

The objective is to ensure that the rules, powers, and procedures governing these systems remain workable and relevant as circumstances change over time. One thing that became clear during the process is that many of these amendments have arisen through practical experience. Officials, regulators, tribunal members, and professional bodies have identified areas where legislation is unclear and where powers are incomplete or where administrative requirements no longer match the realities of how these systems operate. What we have before us is largely a response to those issues. It is legislation informed by people who have spent years working within these systems and who have identified areas that could operate better.

The Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill contains several examples of that approach. With changes to the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act, an initial assessment process has been introduced for complaints, and anyone who has worked within the complaints regime knows that there is a difference between receiving a complaint and requiring a full investigation. The bill recognises that distinction and provides a clearer process for determining which matters should proceed and which are better dealt with another way.

Much of that focus is also in the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill. It takes a similar approach, in particular with Part 2, “Amendments to Motor Vehicle Sales Act 2003”, and that was traversed during the committee of the whole House, in particular clause 10, which amends section 82 of the principal Act—replacing section 82(3)(a) with “(a) an adjudicator who has held a practising certificate as a barrister or barrister and solicitor for at least 5 years (which need not be consecutive), whether or not the person currently holds such a certificate;”.

That amendment broadens the scope of who can actually be within that tribunal, and so it provides greater access for those wanting to access those services. The Minister provided a good description on that. It’s very important: if you purchase a used car, for example, you might drive it off the lot and then, a couple of kilometres down the road, you might break down and you might have to enter that disputes tribunal process. It’s quite indicative of this Government, really—you pop the bonnet on this Government and it’s an absolute mess on the inside: you know, the gearbox hasn’t actually been in gear for the last two years, the tank is running on empty, and you know what? It’ll be going to the scrap heap on 7 November. [Interruption] They’re trying very hard—they’ve been parroting a slogan all night. I’ve got a new one here: “Fixing the brakes and blowing the future”—just like a blown engine in a new car that’s going to get traded in on 7 November. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

content.speaker: TIM COSTLEY (National—Ōtaki)
content.text: That’s the first glimpse of life we’ve seen over there. I too, like the honourable member before me, am passionate to see work done for the mental wellbeing of people in Kāpiti and around our country, and that’s why I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB (Labour—Christchurch Central)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I did enjoy Dan Rosewarne’s contribution there. I note that, for the motor vehicle tribunal, that whilst I qualify to be an adjudicator, he would qualify as an assessor—a far more important task. There are, of course, qualified mechanics on that particular tribunal, so perhaps, between the two of us, should we be looking for work in the future, we’ll be able to help that particular tribunal out. Of course, the real estate agent authority has been seen as the last sort of refuge of MPs that have left this House as well, poor things.

But can I just say, I’ve heard Government members say on a number of occasions that this is a technical bill—minor and technical, technical and minor, minor and technical. Whilst regulatory systems bills are intended to do non-contentious work, I think we shouldn’t be too dismissive of them. There was an exchange in the House earlier on in committee stage with the Minister for Courts where I was disappointed with some responses and she was dismissive of me because this was a mere minor and technical bill. I mean, she did come back to the House and gave a much better answer in respect of the undertakings point, so I thank her for that. But I do think that, for the people affected by these provisions—whilst some change “shall” to “must”, that’s truly technical and minor—if you’re a conveyancing practitioner and you are now able to give enforceable undertakings, that’s actually going to transform your practice. In terms of keeping lawyers honest—if it’s possible—and in terms of a competitive sense having conveyancers being able to do business in that conveyancing sphere on pretty much the same footing, as the Minister pointed out, previously, conveyancers would have to go to a lawyer and say, can you give this undertaking because it has to be a solicitor’s undertaking. Now that doesn’t have to happen. It’s an additional cost that they don’t have to bear, and so their business can be conducted on a fair and even footing. That’s good, and it’s actually been a thorn in the side of conveyancing practitioners since 2008 when the conveyancing profession first came into being.

But I’m not actually satisfied that the legislation is in the best form it could be—notwithstanding it being knocked around this House—and the fact that the person who’s affected to go to court has to go via a particular kind of narrow procedure. I forget the exact words Phil Twyford used, but I think he called it a “litigation-lite” or something of that ilk, which is kind of what it is. It’s documents only and then just oral argument in court. The summary judgment procedure isn’t necessarily the right procedure. Having said that, it’s a step in the right direction, and I know the judiciary will pick it up. It’s perfectly possible to simply transform that summary judgment procedure into an ordinary proceeding, which judges may do, but it’s just an additional expense and step, which is kind of the opposite thing to what we want.

In respect of the other main point I raised in respect to the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill, that was around summary dismissal of complaints within the Law Society by the complaints service. Look, I want to be careful what I say because I’ve worked with the complaints service—helping them, not as a respondent—and they do have a lot of good people in there, and a lot of the people who triage those complaints are, in fact, legally qualified. In fact, one of the provisions of this bill—the new section 272A— deals with the fact that lawyers deal with these complaints, and in dealing with complaints, they’re not considered to be providing legal services. The point being you can’t complain about the lawyer who triaged your complaint.

But in terms of this summary dismissal, I do think that a safety valve is needed, because much of the time of complaints services are dealt with in dealing with repeat—or frequent flyers, as they’re sometimes called—complainants who have the same thing to say time and again. They’ll complain against one lawyer and then they’ll complain against another lawyer, then they’ll complain to another complaints institution, and so on and so forth. Now, they are hard to manage, but there are strategies to make their management as simple as possible, and telling them that there’s nothing in their complaint and not giving them an ability to have that reviewed in a kind of natural justice manner is certainly one way to exacerbate the problem.

Having said that, there is a pile of complaints that go to these standards committees, which are—I’m always cautious in using the term “vexatious”, but they’re just ill-founded. Sure, some complaints are made to harass, but some complaints are ill-founded simply because people have unrealistic expectations of the duties that other people, particularly lawyers, owe them. The common one is a complaint against the lawyer for the other side. I would frequently see complaints where the complaint was, if you boiled it down, “The opposition lawyer was mean to me.”

content.speaker: Hon Members
content.text: Ha ha!

content.speaker: Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB
content.text: You may giggle, but it’s a genuine complaint. The fact of the matter is that it is sometimes the job of a lawyer to work as hard as they can against the interests of the other party, and that can come across as them being kind of wantonly mean. Those complaints can probably be dismissed in a pretty summary manner, but my concern nevertheless stands in respect of that clause.

In respect of the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill, there was one thing that I was quite gratified to see and that was the disputes tribunal and the ability to claim back the filing fees. When the Disputes Tribunal Bill went through this House some time ago, but this term, one of my real concerns was the cost, because the cost of filing, I think, was $450,000 for a claim up to $70,000, and that was more than to file in the District Court. I still have a problem with the size of that fee, and the fact that you can’t get a fee waiver, but the fact that you can go to the disputes tribunal, and if you’re successful, in some degree, you can get that fee as part of the decision, whereas, previously, that wasn’t the case. Of course, the fact is that if you’re arguing about $70,000, it’s actually quite likely you’ll also use a lawyer. Those fees won’t be recoverable. It’s important to just note that. If you go to a lawyer and say, “Please write my argument for me because I’m not that articulate”, and that costs you $1,000 or $1,500, that’s going to be part of your costs of bringing your claim. That’s not going to be recoverable as legal costs, but the $450 you paid to file that fee will be recoverable.
Of course, a few tidy-ups—the Parole Act and their remuneration. Interesting—Lawrence Xu-Nan has just arrived, which I’m allowed to say, I think.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: You’re allowed to say he’s in the House.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB
content.text: He’s in the House. Xu-Nan is in the House. Of course, I was surprised to hear that he didn’t know what the Higher Salaries Commission was, but there you go. Even the greatest minds amongst us have their flaws. But he learnt that it was replaced by the Remuneration Authority, and it’s good to see that the Parole Board is being brought up to speed with that remuneration framework, and of course, the motor vehicles tribunal. There is a difficulty, and it may come as a shock, but things like the adjudicators on the motor vehicle tribunal and disputes tribunal referees, they’re actually not paid vast sums of money, so it’s not like people are banging down the door, particularly people who have the necessary skills. They’re not just legal skills; they’re also people skills, conflict resolution skills, and so expanding the pool of people who can be adjudicators in the Motor Vehicle Disputes Tribunal, that also is a good thing.
Yes, there are some chunky kind of so-called technical and minor amendments, but they are, on the whole, going in the right direction. Of course, that’s why we are supporting this bill.

Mental Health Bill
Legislative Statement

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: I present a legislative statement on the Mental Health Bill.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
Second Reading

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: I move, That the Mental Health Bill be now read a second time.

It’s a privilege to be standing here today for the second reading of the Mental Health Bill. I’d like firstly to start by thanking the Health Committee for all their hard work—ably led by the chair, Sam Uffindell—in examining this bill. Can I say, from the start, that I think it’s vitally important for tangata whaiora that this bill comes back with full cross-party support. I’d also like to thank the people who took the time to make a submission and engage with the select committee process—particularly those who shared their personal experience. It is a deeply personal thing to share your own experience, so thank you for your bravery. I do want to acknowledge all those with lived experience.

The committee considered submissions from 358 individuals and groups. Those submitters brought a range of perspectives, including those who have experience of compulsory treatment, those with family with lived experience, clinicians, academics, and mental health organisations. I’d also like to thank the 89 people who spoke directly to the Health Committee to share their views. I’d also like to acknowledge those who bravely came forward to share their stories in the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Historical Abuse in State Care and in the Care of Faith-based Institutions. It is important that we carry their voices, not only tonight but through any work looking into how the State cares for people when they need it the most.

I want to reiterate that this bill will demonstrate meaningful and significant progress by contributing towards at least 10 of the abuse in care recommendations, relating primarily to care safety and monitoring. All of you have helped shape a Mental Health Bill that goes beyond compulsory treatment, as we know it today, and that, instead, firmly places a person at the centre of their care and empowers people to make decisions about their own care.

While most in New Zealand who access specialist mental health and addiction services are not subject to the Mental Health Act, over the course of a year, around 11,000 people receive compulsory care. In an ideal world, we would not need compulsory mental health care; however, we need a system in place for New Zealanders experiencing mental distress at a level that does require intervention to support their recovery. This bill strikes a balance of a future focus on safe and effective mental health care for people who require that State intervention, while having the right safeguards in place to ensure people’s rights are upheld and protected. This bill will be a critical safety net for those experiencing severe mental distress who are unable to make decisions about their own mental health care. I do want to reiterate tonight that it is intended to be used as a last resort only.

The submissions received on this bill represented a variety of views. This is an important piece of legislation, and I expected there to be views across the board on key areas in the bill to assist the Health Committee’s consideration. It has been heartening to see that, of the individuals and groups that commented on the general policy intent of the bill, the majority were supportive. People recognise that we need compulsory care in some form; however, there were divergent views on what people felt this should look like.

I’m also encouraged by the support from submitters for the introduction of compulsory care principles, the supported decision-making provisions, and establishment of new roles and processes to safeguard those under compulsory care. This includes independent support persons and advocates, nominated persons, and collaborative care teams. These are integral to the shifts I want to see under this new legislation.

There were some key changes made through the select committee process. These include introducing a “dignity of risk” principle. This aligns with the legislation’s purpose of promoting decision-making capacity. I believe it’s critical that the legislation recognises a person’s right to take reasonable risks to achieve personal growth, self-esteem, and overall quality of life.

Terminology is really important to how people see themselves and how people are treated. I’m pleased to see the Health Committee has made changes to the term “patient” to instead be “person under compulsory care”. This change responds to submitters who said the term “patient” is stigmatising and can reinforce power imbalances between someone seeking support and professionals. Submitters also said it reinforces a paternalistic approach to care, which we want to move away from.

Offences and penalties are important enforcement tools in the legislation. The royal commission of inquiry raised the need for appropriate and significant penalties for failures to comply with standards of care. I’m very pleased to see that the select committee has made changes to modernise the offences and penalties in this legislation, with a more structured regime as well as more tools for the regulator to use to support greater compliance with the Act.

However, I also recognise that many people who submitted on the bill had concerns about specific areas—in particular, the use of restrictive practices such as seclusion and the use of electroconvulsive therapy, or ECT. People also want strong safeguards for care of those under 18. As I spoke about in the first reading on this bill, these practices have a history of inappropriate use, abuse, and overuse.

I want to be very clear that I remain committed to seeing the reduction and elimination of seclusion. However, it is critical that this is done in a way that minimises the risk of unintended consequences. In particular, I would not want to see an increase in other inappropriate practices such as chemical or physical restraint. The bill strengthens requirements on the use of seclusion to drive the change needed to reduce and eliminate seclusion. The bill prohibits seclusion for children and young people. This is an incremental but significant step towards elimination that I am proud of, but I’m aware that there’s going to be a big shift for mental health workers, and it is important that we manage this change safely for both children and young people as well as staff.

I do want to acknowledge that the Health Committee has made a number of improvements to further strengthen provisions relating to seclusion to ensure there are stronger protections and greater monitoring of progress. The committee received a wide range of views about ECT, from being an effective, life-saving treatment in modern clinical practice through to wanting it banned. The committee has also recommended a range of improvements to make sure there are greater safeguards on the use of ECT, including for people under 18.

From the submissions received, the Health Committee has recommended changes that will improve clarity and ensure greater safeguards for those subject to the Act. The word I want to emphasise here is “balance”; the bill aims to strike a balance between placing limits on people’s rights when there is a need to intervene to provide care and ensuring that this intervention is only done when absolutely necessary and in a way that protects and upholds an individual’s rights.

In closing, I acknowledge that there are diverse views on this piece of legislation, which were heard through the select committee process. Developing this bill has involved careful balancing of all of those views.  I believe the bill represents a meaningful step forward, and I’m pleased to present it to you today. The bill will enable supported decision making, safer practice through stronger protections for people subject to legislation, and care that is provided in the least coercive way—that is therapeutic and responsive to a person’s needs. I hope to see continued cross-party support on this important bill. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: The question is that the motion be agreed to.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: Today, there was a press release that was issued, and anyone who saw TV ONE news would have heard of what has been happening at Wakari Hospital, where the Ombudsman said, “I’m deeply disturbed by what our inspectors found. What they observed at Ward 10A were some of the worst practices we have observed anywhere”. People who are at Wakari Ward 10A or who were there have been kept under the Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act 2003 and the Criminal Procedure Act 2011, but, also, the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992.

The Wakari Hospital developments that have been occurring in Dunedin, very close to my electorate, are a stark example of why we need reform in this area. I welcome the fact that we have a new bill before us. I agree that it would be great to have cross-party support, and I guess it depends on how one measures that. If it’s just on votes, then yes, this is cross-party support. But we really do feel, on this side of the House, that despite the small changes that we were able to make at select committee, it is a bit of a wasted opportunity to make a transformational change to a bill that probably won’t be able to come before the House for another 10 or 15 years.

If I look at what the Ombudsman said had been happening at Wakari Hospital to our intellectually disabled mental health patients, in one instance, a person was tied down on a bariatric or evac-mat to move them across the ward. This was causing physical and mental harm to the person, who suffered carpet burns as a result. Inspectors also found that one person had been secluded in their bedroom for around 18 months with an almost complete lack of meaningful human contact and no access to the outdoors. There were restrictions on dental care and people being denied access to their own money. Staff were observed incentivising good behaviour by rewarding people with access to basic necessities, including dental treatment or the use of a toilet. There was unlawful administration of medication, and serious and significant failures.

I am heartened that, after my calls for an independent inquiry into this—and after not being able to get an urgent debate in the House, unfortunately—the Ministry of Health has accepted the Ombudsman’s recommendation to undertake an independent investigation into the treatment and conditions of people at Ward 10A. That ward is now closing down for that particular purpose, and I would really like to acknowledge the Ombudsman for taking so seriously the work that they’ve done, or that he’s done. I’d like to acknowledge the staff and the PSA union, who’ve worked under incredibly difficult conditions given the structure and the environment that they’ve been working in and the harm that some of them have endured. I’d like to acknowledge Health New Zealand for acting very quickly on the Ombudsman’s recommendation, which was the only thing, really, that they could have done, given the seriousness of that.

But, also, patients and former staff who reached out to me and shared their story, even though they were shattered by their experiences, and some of them who were just too scared to go through official channels. On that note, I’d really like to acknowledge Matthew Littlewood from the Otago Daily Times, who has done an excellent job in bringing this to light.

This is the reason why we need reform in the mental health sphere and the Mental Health Bill—and it’s no small bill: it’s 168 pages, 221 clauses, and two schedules. We’ve had an amendment today, a five-page Government amendment, which tells me that we do have some scope in the committee stage to really forensically look at this. There were submissions that indicated that the process was quite rushed, and there are examples in the bill of typos and questions which would indicate that has happened, and so it would be useful for us to use this time to go through the bill.

The main point I would like to make is that we are supporting it, because the 1992 Act—that’s a long time ago—is absolutely not fit for purpose, but this modern framework does fall short of the transformational reform that was envisaged by the He Ara Oranga report. Where we see the opportunities are around implementation, workforce planning, and accountability that don’t seem to have legislated safeguards. We also would have preferred to see stronger protections for Māori, disabled people, children, young people, and other vulnerable groups. We would have liked a greater emphasis on voluntary participatory care wherever possible, particularly given the evidence we heard at select committee about the way that participatory care contributes to recovery for people journeying through mental health, versus the absolute lack of evidence that compulsory care orders enable recovery—and yet, they seem to be the norm currently.

We definitely would like to see the bill contain a strong commitment to ending seclusion. We are happy with where we landed on electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). It is a vexed issue, and we do see that there could be still some further strengthening, but we do acknowledge that there are some very limited examples where ECT is appropriate.

We are very happy that there have been some small changes—and I would say they’re small, compared to the ones that we would have liked to see—made with the presumption that birthing parents and newborn babies should remain together unless separation is necessary for safety purposes. But, today, we’ve seen this Amendment Paper come into the House, which is really limiting that again, and so we’d like to go through that quite closely to find out whether our change that we had advocated for in select committee actually has any meaning left to it for our birthing parents.

We also are happy that there’s been an acknowledgement of and our recommendation adopted that Labour advocated for, which was children and young people being able to travel with a trusted adult between facilities in what can be a very traumatising journey. That has been adopted without change, so that’s good. The dignity of care provision that the Minister referred to is fantastic but, actually, was a hygiene factor for us. That is something that should have been in the original drafting of the legislation. Nevertheless, it’s good to see it in there.

I do want to acknowledge the Minister, actually, for giving us the opportunity to be reacquainted with the bill just a couple of nights ago and, also, be able to suggest some of our amendments to him in case he would entertain them. I think that’s a very useful final check to go through. Nevertheless, I have got about 40-odd amendments on the Table, and these are not single-word changes or frivolous. These are very thought-through amendments that we believe, on this side of the House, would panel-beat the bill into something that would actually be transformational. We do hope that the House gives them due regard. We would also like to see the giving-effect of Te Tiriti o Waitangi happen in a way that is in the totality of the bill, not just in the particular limited circumstances that have been mentioned, and we will be going through that in the committee stage.

We acknowledge that the bill does limit seclusion to a degree, but I’d like to point out to any media who are watching this that we’re in quite different places around seclusion on this side of the House. When I was being asked to do media reports a couple of weeks ago, I was surprised that media thought that there was a sunset clause on seclusion. That is not the case. There is simply a five-year legislative review. We would have liked that to have been a sunset clause and, at least—at the very least—two-yearly reviews for the House to be able to consider whether we’d move to a place of resourcing where we could do that.

The Minister has mentioned that under-18-year-olds won’t be subject to seclusion, and that’s a good outcome that we support, but there’s a contradiction, then, in the bill, because the Minister has said the reason for not sunsetting seclusion is because it will encourage other forms of restraint unless there’s resourcing. What I’m hearing from that is that, perhaps, our children and young people are in a more vulnerable position as a result, and we would like to interrogate that with the Minister. We did have evidence of places that had been able to eliminate seclusion and we are questioning why that can’t happen if there’s a commitment to resourcing—and yet, the Minister and the Government members have shied away from any kind of legislative commitment to resourcing, which is really the fundamental problem with the bill.

There’s a number of other things that we would like to see, but, in conclusion, we do support the bill, because we cannot remain under the 1992 Act. The story that I told you at the beginning of this is an evolving story. It is huge. It is terrible in the context of abuse in care, and it is terrible because it involves our most vulnerable, marginalised, and invisible people in society. We want to see a bill that has more participation, more human rights at the centre, and stronger implementation, accountability, and safeguards. Thank you.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise on behalf of the Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand to also support the Mental Health Bill in its second reading. Now, I do want to acknowledge both the Minister and also the previous speaker, Ingrid Leary, on this particular bill. I will lay out some of the concerns on this side of the House, though we do support it. I think it’s important to highlight some of the context around this and also some of the positions and also some of the areas we want to engage with the Minister on during the upcoming committee stage.

In terms of this bill, as mentioned previously, this is a bill that replaces an incredibly outdated piece of legislation, the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992. A lot of this came from the 2018 report He Ara Oranga, which was delivered, I believe, to the Minister of Health at the time in December 2018. I think this is a really important starting point that this bill came from. The Minister has already laid out some of the conversations that have been heard during the select committee stage, even though I wasn’t a part of that. I do want to thank all of the members on the Health Committee for taking part in that process, and, particularly, I want to thank all of the submitters who came along, as always, and shared their personal stories and experiences with this bill, particularly when we’re looking at compulsory care.

It’s also important, I think, to contextualise a lot of this with the example that my colleague Ingrid Leary just gave before around the broader context that we saw just over the last year and up until very recently with the royal commission of inquiry into abuse in care and how we’re still seeing some of those really quite severe and horrendous experiences that people are experiencing in compulsory care, which, I think, by any standard as a New Zealander and by any standard internationally, from a rights-based perspective, is unacceptable.

I also want to address the fact that one of the things that did come through the select committee as a part of this process—and, particularly, it was raised by the Ombudsman, was the fact that for such a significant bill and such a significant change, there wasn’t sufficient time given to hear from submitters in an appropriate way. I think that’s really important, bearing in mind that the first reading of this bill was in 2024, and it was referred to the select committee, where it had, I think, by select committee standards, quite a long period that was open for submissions; I believe it was about two months. But, over this period, the report from select committee came back on 17 April 2025—that is over 14 months ago—and we’re now just hearing this bill for the second time now. I think, in hindsight, potentially, with the blessing from the Minister, that select committee could have actually had a longer time to consider this bill and to hear from submitters in a way that is appropriate and that uses different forms to engage with submitters, as we have seen in various other bills that have happened in the House recently.

Now, on to the actual content of the bill, there are eight parts, and we’re looking forward to engaging with the Minister on all of them, but I want to address a few areas that are of significant concern for the Greens. I think the previous speaker has already mentioned the fact that there is still a review period and not a sunset clause for seclusion, even though I think the Minister has laid out that, in certain areas, children and young people, I believe, will no longer be under seclusion, which is an important step. At the same time, seclusion, as we heard from the example before, is something that is deeply traumatic and is actually simply not good for anyone’s wellbeing, mental or physical. Yet it is disappointing to see that there has been no sunset clause on a seclusion commitment in here, whereas I think the Greens would have liked to see a five-year sunset clause, which would have shown that there is some form of commitment around this particular practice.

Now, the other thing that is really important from our perspective is this idea that if we are looking at some of the international standards and if we’re looking at the disability convention and also the rights of tangata whaiora and disabled people and neurodivergent people, we would like to move towards something that is more rights-consistent and that considers the mental and physical wellbeing of these people, where we can start moving towards an area where we can maybe look into replacing compulsory care with a voluntary care order. Again, this is something that the Greens would like to see, as voluntary care orders should be the default, not an option. We are going in a way that best emphasises and also takes into consideration the ability for people to rehabilitate, to recover, and also, like I said before, that considers people’s wellbeing as a starting point before we move into the need for compulsory care. That is something that, for example, the Greens would also like to see, with voluntary care as the default, as opposed to going to more extremes with compulsory care.

I already mentioned before that one of the areas that the Greens has the greatest concern around is, again, the implications that this will have for disabled people and for neurodivergent people and how this would interact and how this would be moving towards a system that will allow them to have more dignity and allow them to maintain their rights and freedom to a greater extent. Like we have said previously, this bill is a significant improvement from the 1992 bill, which is why we do support it.

I also think it’s really heartening to hear from the Minister and also in the engagement from the Minister that we hope that we can move to a stage where we can do better and be able to provide more funding. This is something that I’m hoping that the Minister will be able to consider as well, both in terms of the amendments by my colleague Ingrid Leary but also my colleague Kahurangi Carter, who is our mental health spokesperson, who is also engaging with the Minister as well on this bill. We have also a few amendments on this as well that we would like to engage with the Minister on as part of the committee stage.

There are, obviously, other parts in this bill that I think deserve mention as well. I think this is something that, again, to the best of the select committee’s consideration, there have been amendments to this bill in a way that may have changed some of the aspects further. One of the areas that the Minister has already mentioned and that I think was one of the things that I, in one of the rare opportunities when I subbed in on the Health Committee, did actually hear from the experts, is around the electroconvulsive therapy, or ECT. I think that is something that, from our perspective, we’re still cautious about. We know that is something that the ministry has considered can be an effective treatment for depression, mania, catatonia, and other serious neuropsychiatric conditions. But, again, it’s one of those things where, from our perspective, we would like to see other mechanisms in place and only use this as an absolute last resort.

Again, with those kind of things, particularly from an international convention perspective, what we want to avoid is any sort of therapy or any sort of care, compulsory or otherwise, that would amount to torture. This is something that I think everyone in this House but also something that, for example, OPCAT, which is our obligation under the Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture, will possibly be interested in as well. This is something that our NPMs, the national preventive mechanisms, such as the Ombudsman, Oranga Tamariki, and the Human Rights Commission, would have oversight or some checks and balances on as well. That is just one example that I want to give, on top of everything else I mentioned, that we would like to have more conversations with the Minister on.

Like I said, the Green Party does support this bill. We do have a few amendments that we want to engage the Minister on, but we are looking forward to the upcoming committee stage. With that: yes from the Greens; we support the Mental Health Bill.

content.speaker: CAMERON LUXTON (ACT)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. Look, there’s not much more I can add to what the Minister for Mental Health, Matt Doocey, has contributed. He’s done a great synopsis of the work of the select committee. I can just say that the selection committee did spend a great deal of time talking about this bill, debating the merits and the issues. I think the Opposition members that have raised concerns, as much as those are legitimate concerns, they were dealt with in select committee where there was a robust debate. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: JENNY MARCROFT (NZ First)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise on behalf of New Zealand First in support of the Mental Health Bill. I’d like to acknowledge the Minister, the Hon Matt Doocey, for bringing what he has termed an important bill to the House, and I concur with that sentiment.

It’s important because it will modernise the legal framework for compulsory psychiatric assessment and treatment. I say this as someone who had a family member undergo electric shock treatment—what we called it in the old days—without family consent. And so the changes that this bill will bring about, establishing higher safeguards for electroconvulsive therapy, ECT it’s known as, is a very good thing. I commend it to the House.
[Authorised reo Māori text to be inserted by the Hansard Office.]
[Authorised translation to be inserted by the Hansard Office.]

the Mental Health Bill. I want to acknowledge the Minister, Minister Matt Doocey, and the Health Committee who have gone through this process, and also the He Ara Oranga inquiry that was done in 2018.

I’m very pleased to support this bill. It’s something that’s strongly advocated for in the mental health space, specifically in youth and in rangatahi Māori. The Mental Health Bill—can I also say that this bill includes a Te Tiriti or Treaty clause under the National - Act - New Zealand First Government, which is a big deal for us.

The He Ara Oranga inquiry stated that Māori are 50 percent more likely to experience mental health issues and 30 percent of Māori and other ethnic groups go undiagnosed. Looking at the inquiry and also the report that came out of the Te Hiringa Mahara, the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission, outlining some of the kaupapa that they aligned with this bill.

Te Pāti Māori completely supports this bill. Something that I’ve been passionate about—a story around this is: in 2020, which was my last year of high school, and we were the first ever cohort to go through COVID with exams. I did an inquiry into maramataka Māori and how Māori knowledge can impact and help navigate mental health issues around rangatahi going through COVID. But also that was, I guess, like the beginning of how social media would impact us—that wasn’t even the beginning of artificial intelligence coming into our realm. We developed some resources, Māori and maramataka Māori resources, and books for rangatahi who experienced mental health crises during the COVID 2020 pandemic and how you navigated that through exams. And so, to see, six years later, coming in with legislation that I can support, is pretty cool. So thank you to the Minister and to the select committee.

Outlining some of the recommendations. This is from the—sorry, there’s so many different ingoa I don’t get wrong to get them wrong—Te Hiringa Mahara: access to mental health services to online safety education. I also want to touch on the member’s bill that was brought in by Laura McClure in terms of the deepfake that we supported, and how that closely aligns to having online safety, specifically for young wāhine who experience the online dangers and how that can affect their mental health. So also bringing up that bill—early intervention for kaupapa Māori Services or Pacific Service services; crises response teams; 24/7 access into making sure that there is an online service that can you ring; and also growing the workforce. So those were some of the recommendations in the Te Hiringa Mahara report.

And I just want to say that from the submissions that I’ve heard, from looking into the Mental Health Bill, that a lot of these recommendations were thoroughly thought out in how they could be implemented into this bill, because this bill replaces the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992 to create a modern legislative framework for compulsory mental healthcare. I commend this bill to the House. Tēnā koe e te Pīka.

content.speaker: MIKE DAVIDSON (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I stand on behalf of the Green Party to speak in support of this bill, the Mental Health Bill, at second reading. I’d like to acknowledge the Minister for his mahi in this space and the Health Committee as well, and Kahurangi Carter, the Greens portfolio holder for mental health.

This has been my first interaction with this bill. I’m not on the committee, so trying to get myself up to speed with the bill and the progress of the bill, and, I guess, one of the things that I was first a little bit surprised with is how long it’s been in the House—introduced back in October 2024 and it, obviously, was then reported back in 20 April 2025, and is finally having its second reading now.

When this bill first went to the select committee, we didn’t support it to the sleep committee. It wasn’t perfect at that time, but it was definitely a step in the right direction with repealing the previous Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act, as it was in line with a lot of the statements we were making as well. And through that select committee process, there has been quite a lot of amendments and changes, and most of them have strengthened the bill, but while we do support it, we still don’t think it has gone far enough. We will be trying to see what more improvements we can get to this bill through the committee of the whole House stage, which is obviously coming up very shortly.

I would like to just, I guess, touch on a couple of the points that the Greens still have concerns about. Obviously in the commentary, there’s a joint differing view with Te Pāti Māori, and a lot of the concerns we have, we also shared with the Labour Party as well. We’re very committed, and I know the whole House is committed, in trying, with the importance of improving mental health and how that’s handled. There’s always going to be some differences, and we’ll continue to try and strengthen that and improve the outcomes that we get. It’s really important that when we make the decisions, we do it for all of us.

So, obviously, one of the major concerns we did have, which has been outlined a number of times, but I think it’s really important to continue to outline, is around seclusion Obviously, there’s a review of that in five years, but for the Greens, we would have liked to see that have a sunset clause. Seclusion, as we know, is a harmful and traumatic practice. We do know that there is an issue and you couldn’t go straight to removing that straight away because of workforce issues, but we believe with having a sunset clause in there, and giving that time and ensuring that the staffing levels that were put in place would cater for what was required, we could actually move to it, and having that sunset clause in there would put a definite time limit in there to ensure the resources would be put in place to ensure that happened. I’d just like to note that, obviously, while we as a political party believe that that sunset clause should be in place, that view has been shared by a lot of other people around the motu, and so we really do hope that we can move in that direction.

Another area that we recorded in our differing view was to replace compulsory care with volunteer care orders. We also spoke around neurodivergent children as well, and some proposed changes around clause 6, that voluntary care should be the default, with compulsory care used only when absolutely necessary, and for the shortest duration.

I would like to note that part of the clause was to strengthen—I guess, when you look at what happens with mental health, Māori are disproportionately affected by mental health, and it was really important and good to see that there was a Treaty clause in there which would actually, hopefully, help in that space.

Once again, I would like to reiterate that the Greens support the Mental Health Bill. We still have concerns and we look forward to working on that further as we go through the committee of the whole House stage, which, as I said, is coming up very, very shortly. So on that note, I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: Dr HAMISH CAMPBELL (National—Ilam)
content.text: It’s an honour to rise and speak on the second reading of the Mental Health Bill. I do just want to acknowledge New Zealand’s first Minister for Mental Health, Matt Doocey, and for the work he has done to bring this bill to the House. This bill is replacing the 1992 Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act, which no longer aligns with modern mental healthcare. Therefore, I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour)
