content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s a privilege to rise to take a call on this bill, which has been a long time coming following on from the He Ara Oranga review, and then work by successive Ministers in the Labour Government, and now the National Government. It’s great to see it in the House.

I do have to admit that the select committee hearings feel like quite some time ago now, and it is a shame that such a landmark piece of legislation is being debated under urgency, meaning that we’re not hearing full calls from the other side. This is really important, and I can’t think of much other legislation that has the same human rights impact in the health sector. It was with that lens that I went into the select committee hearings, from which I had my involvement when I was briefly the Minister—well, my engagement with the bill as Minister was brief compared to the other Ministers who have shepherded this bill.

The 1992 Act I would characterise as having the test of who could be placed under compulsory care in the Act, and then the main defence of the person’s human rights under the existing Act is largely through processes of review that are structured throughout the course of the person’s treatment and the time periods at which they must occur. This Act takes a very different approach to upholding the rights of people who are subject to the compulsory treatment clauses of the Act. So, for a start, compulsory treatment should only be used to improve the person’s mental health. So it’s not an opportunity to improve other elements of the person’s health—they still have to consent for that—or their social circumstances. I think that’s important to remember because sometimes some mental health conditions do mean that people’s living circumstances can deteriorate.

The bill requires that the least restrictive option be used. Voluntary care options should be always preferred to compulsory care, and compulsory care should only be used for as short a period as possible. There’s also the reassessments of whether compulsory treatment can be used. Those are positive developments.

In addition, there are some new and innovative concepts that clearly can be done, but it’ll be interesting to see how these practices interact with the law and how, ultimately, people’s care and human rights are affected. This includes the creation of mental health advance directives. That is something viewed favourably in many of the submissions that we received on the committee. But advance directives of all sorts have limitations, and I hope they are not too easily set aside by busy care teams who wonder if the circumstances in which the advance directives were set are no longer in place. There can be good reasons why they’re not followed, and so I hope that we are able to live up to the aspiration in the bill in terms of how we implement those.

I think the appointment of nominated persons to stand up for the rights of the person in compulsory care is as important, as well as the practice of wellbeing meetings. These are practices that may well be being used across the health system already, but they are not mandated. Overall, I think those would be good things.

I think one of the things about the involvement of family and whānau in someone’s care is that, at times, and I guess under the current Act, treatment teams can confuse, and we all as a society can confuse—well, excessive concern about respecting someone’s privacy might lead to the non-inclusion of family members, in some situations. So I think the bill’s presumption is that family member involvement is a good thing and will mean that people have greater access to the supports that they will depend on when they are no longer in compulsory care, and also during the time that they are in compulsory care. So I think that’s positive.

The requirement for independent support people to advocate for the person under the Act and assist them with participating in decision making and exercising their rights is another really, really positive innovation in the Act.

There are some areas where rights have been strengthened as well. People have to be able to understand their rights, and there’s also an entitlement to use aids like mobility and other communication aids, under the Act. I mean, it’s kind of unbelievable that we don’t say that, but, of course, if you’re dependent on a device for your hearing, your communication, your mobility, and not having the ability to get that for yourself, it is important that those things are specified.

I was pleased my colleague Ingrid Leary and I were able to lead a discussion on the committee about the right for a birth parent under compulsory care orders to be able to stay with their baby unless there is a safety risk. I think the presumption that a mother and their baby should not be separated is an important one.

The other area where I paid a lot of attention as the Minister briefly responsible for this bill, and then in committee, was the use of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). In both of those capacities, I held serious questions about whether or not one day we’ll look back on the use of electroconvulsive therapy and regret that we permitted it. It’s not an area of medicine that I have any expertise in, so I was pleased that the select committee gave us the opportunity to gather evidence and to hear from experts on that; we heard from experts at length. We accept the conclusion of expert evidence that it is still a practice that is beneficial for some people and can be done in a humane way. I’m pleased, however, that there are increased protections in this bill around the use of ECT, particularly on people under the age of 18.
So, all in all, there is a lot to be positive about in this bill.

I do want to mention our concern about the continued use of seclusion. Seclusion has been eliminated in some parts of our health system in New Zealand, and good on the teams who have worked really hard in their facilities and hospitals to make that the case. They should be really proud, and we should be really proud as a country if we were able to do away with that.

Resourcing and workforce are always challenges in the health system, and there are always difficult choices about where we place resource and what we prioritise. We have an opportunity in this bill to say that seclusion is something that we would like to make a priority, and to make that staffing to ensure that seclusion is no longer used, a priority.

In my remaining time, I want to tell you why I’m so convinced that that is important. Actually, a Labour Party member who I met through my work in the party in recent years came and talked to me about it two or three years ago. She had had an experience of compulsory care. She described the experience of seclusion and how traumatic it was. I suppose, as a former clinician, I always approach that question from the prism of “But was it justified because otherwise you would hurt yourself?”. But, actually, in talking to her, I realised that it wasn’t justified, because she no longer trusts those people who could provide care for her in the future because of the experience of such a traumatic thing at the hands of people who were meant to be caring for her. For that reason, that is my one reservation about this bill, but there are a lot of other positive developments in it, and I commend it to the House.

content.speaker: Dr CARLOS CHEUNG (National—Mt Roskill)
content.text: This bill is a significant step forward in modernising compulsory mental health care. It puts patients at the centre of decisions about their own care, strengthens protection and safeguards, and improves access to efficient mental health and addiction support. Therefore, I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: GEORGIE DANSEY (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s a hard, hard bill, the Mental Health Bill. It’s a big topic. I’ll start by thanking the Minister and the Health Committee for the work that you all did in this space, and as my colleague the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall has alluded to, the previous Government started the work in this space. This is a really significant improvement on the current Act. As other speakers have spoken to, Labour supports this bill. However, we’d like to see this bill go further and make more transformational reform.

This is a really personal one for me because 11 years ago I lost my brother-in-law who was under compulsory care. The coroner found that the care facility had not cared for him adequately and that resulted in his death. There were multiple downfalls at multiple stages of his care, and multiple times when the ball was dropped. Had there been more effective processes around that facility, then he would, hopefully, still be here today. That kind of loss, obviously, has a lifetime impact on family and whānau members. I’d like to acknowledge everyone else in New Zealand who has lost someone in these circumstances, and really send my aroha to you and the lifelong impacts that this has.

So, really, for me, speaking on this bill—it’s quite deep. I am really pleased to be able to contribute in this small way, and so much thanks to those that have done the real mahi in this space, because this will make a real difference. I appreciated the Minister’s comments around the compulsory psychiatric assessment being the last resort only. I appreciate that, and hope in implementation that that is the case. We need to have a human rights approach to this and that it is the last resort when we require compulsory care, obviously taking into account the health of the person and those around them.

I would like to talk about some of the aspects where we would hope to go further. In regard to He Ara Oranga report, the Government inquiry into mental health and addiction, really, this report falls short of the transformational reform that the report envisioned and the real matter of human rights for people in this space. We would have liked to see a greater emphasis on voluntary participatory care, and supported decision-making, where possible, and where the therapeutic evidence supports this. We also would have liked to see more in the implementation workforce planning and accountability, which still remains a significant concern, in particular, the workforce planning.

From my experience in the system, there were multiple people who didn’t have the training required to do the job to look after the people they were required to care for in quite acute health situations. I would like to see a real emphasis on training for people working in the system, in whatever space they’re in, as healthcare workers. We need to make sure that they are trained and also paid effectively—#EqualPay.
So, thank you. Labour supports this bill. I hope to see more, and I will continue to advocate for more safeguards around compulsory care in the future. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: Dr VANESSA WEENINK (National—Banks Peninsula)
content.text: It is an honour to speak at this historic point in the journey that New Zealand has been on in the care for people who are experiencing mental health crises and mental health ill-health. This takes us forward. The Minister has done excellent work, along with the committee, and I commend the bill to the House.

content.speaker: Dr TRACEY McLELLAN (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I, too, rise to take a call on the Mental Health Bill at this second reading. It’s very appropriate that Labour supports this bill because it is essentially updating—well, it is replacing a very outdated law that we simply can’t continue to operate under: the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992. A lot has changed since 1992. Certainly, the way that society as a whole conceptualises the difference between mental illness, mental health, and mental wellbeing, and a lot of improvement in our understanding—and in our expectations—of what people care could and should expect from their mental health system.

As has been noted, the law was written more than three decades ago. It no longer reflects the modern understanding of human rights, of supported decision-making and how that can be possible, not just in an idealistic way but in a therapeutic way, and something not just to strive towards but something that can be inculcated into something even as complicated and as important as treating mental illness and mental wellbeing.

It also no longer reflects our modern understanding of disability rights and cultural safety, or the importance of involving whānau in care, and all of those other things that, since 1992, we have prided ourselves in this country of improving. So we do think this bill was a substantial improvement.

I’d like to acknowledge the Minister for his work. I’d like to acknowledge the Health Committee for all of the work that they have done. I wasn’t on that committee, but even just listening tonight, you can see the nature of the robust questioning that would have happened, the nature of the genuine and inquisitive inquiries that would have been offered only with the absolute intentionality to do the very best by this bill and the very best by the people who would be most impacted by this bill. I’d also like to acknowledge, no doubt, all of the officials and the people with expertise who submitted, people with lived experience, because only with that breadth of input could we make necessary improvements.

Whilst I say that the bill has made substantial improvements—as we’ve heard, it follows the He Ara Oranga and the royal commission into abuse in care—I do agree also with my colleagues that it does also feel somewhat of a missed opportunity. I understand the tension between fixing something that needs to be fixed because it is outdated and no longer reflects society’s expectations, and the tension between doing something that is much more transformative. That has been the decision that has been made. Would we have made, potentially, a different decision? Yes, probably so, but we do respect where we’ve landed, but it is incumbent upon us to make those notes.

The bill introduces, as I said, a more modern rights-based framework and places a greater emphasis on participation, which we know, therapeutically, is actually a really important factor in the efficacy of any kind of treatment regime, particularly when people are under all sorts of stressors, as is often the case in this domain, but ultimately, always need to be treated with dignity, and voluntary care should always be the goal, so that direction is welcome. We fundamentally believe that compulsion should never be the default simply because there is a lack of time, staffing, or resources.

It’s on that point that I do just want to take a moment because that, for as long as I can remember, has always been a justification, an excuse, a perfectly decent and reasonable explanation—however we want to term it—but for as long as I can remember, a lack of time, staffing, and resources has always held up a different way of doing things in mental health. I’ve worked with many nurses in particular who have worked in mental health, and my goodness, they really do an amazing job. I have worked with nurses who work in all sorts of health sectors. Whilst some people, for instance, might assume that some aspects of nursing are harder than others, I can absolutely tell you that the people that work in mental health have a very unique perspective, and they work incredibly hard under very difficult circumstances, and often face quite personal issues in terms of their own safety in those areas. We shouldn’t be allowed to use a lack of staffing as a means by which to have lower expectations of what the system could look like.

A right written into legislation, ultimately, is only as meaningful when a person can actually exercise it. We do implore, along with our support of this bill, much more focus on increased staffing and even things like increased capital spend, because I’ve seen several facilities that just simply are not designed for what they’re being utilised for, and even just basic layout can pose really, really significant risks to people’s safety, including staff. Without those foundations, there is a risk that the language of this law changes—which it will through the passage of this bill—but people’s experience of the system doesn’t necessarily change if it’s not resourced properly.

We have also touched on tonight, and both of my colleagues on this side of the House have, I think, spoken quite eloquently about the need to have a genuine plan to end seclusion, and Labour supports New Zealand’s commitment to eliminate seclusion. This bill doesn’t go that far. It doesn’t turn that commitment into a credible plan. We acknowledge that annual reporting is important, that the five-year legislative review is better than no review at all, but neither of those things actually amount to a commitment to end seclusion in practice. I acknowledge that that’s a resourcing issue as much as it is an educative and a legislative process, but Labour certainly does believe that the legislation should set a goal of ending seclusion. Even within five years would be a reasonable goal to require a proper systems phase-out plan. That matters because ending seclusion can’t simply be directed from Parliament. It requires, as I’ve said, the investment in workforce capacity first and foremost, therapeutic environments as I’ve mentioned, and appropriate building designs, specialist training, and alternative models of care. All of those things are possible. All of those things are well-advanced in terms of knowledge. There are just some pieces missing to the puzzle, and that is appropriate resource.

With regards to electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), I’d like to echo my colleagues’ reservations and their comments that they made about the process and about making the Health Committee’s ability to be able to make some leeway on what the bill as drafted had in it. I would also like to note that ECT can be a really emotive topic, and it’s one of those things that we’ve heard, quite rightly so, a lot of horror stories over the years. It absolutely is something that has been used abusively over many, many years. It is an area that I’ve had a little bit to do with through my personal background, and I have seen it also be put to incredibly good therapeutic use. When it’s considered as a treatment of last resort, it actually can save lives. I think that this bill does strike a right balance between acknowledging the therapeutic qualities and the necessities that still exist for ECT, but also having much more robust safeguards around when it should be used and on who that should be used too.

Labour will support this bill. We absolutely acknowledge the fact that the 1992 Act is old and not fit for purpose. The bill moves us closer to the goals that I think many of us, regardless of what side of the House we sit on, would agree is an ultimate outcome and an ultimate goal of a much, much better mental health system, and we are therefore happy to commend it to the House.

content.speaker: GREG FLEMING (National—Maungakiekie)
content.text: [Authorised reo Māori text to be inserted by the Hansard Office.]
[Authorised translation to be inserted by the Hansard Office.]
Motion agreed to.
Bill read a second time.

content.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
content.text: The Mental Health Bill is set down for committee stage immediately.
Committee of the whole House
Part 1 Preliminary provisions, and Schedule 1

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: Members, the House is in committee on the Mental Health Bill. Before we begin debating this bill, I will note that Government Amendment Paper 648 on this bill was released at 12.45 p.m. today. I remind members of Speaker Brownlee’s ruling earlier in the sitting that committee stages are always going to proceed slowly when substantive Government amendments are released on the day that the bill is in committee. While I am satisfied that the majority of the amendments in this Amendment Paper are minor and technical, there are some that, on the face of it, appear to be more than minor. The committee stage is always an opportunity to correct matters in a bill, but it is not good practice to release a Government Amendment Paper so close to the beginning of a committee stage, and I will take this into account to enable members to properly scrutinise its contents.
We come first to Part 1. Part 1 is the debate on clauses 3 to 11—“Preliminary provisions”—and Schedule 1. The question is that Part 1 stand part.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Thank you very much, Mr Chair. Can I begin by just acknowledging what you’ve read around the Amendment Paper. I think, in fairness to officials, genuinely, they thought the bill would be up tomorrow afternoon, so putting it up today was going to be a day early. But I think you pointed out, quite rightly, that it could have been in a bit early, so I do accept that.

It is good to be here to debate the Mental Health Bill and Part 1. The bill, as we know, has already been out for extensive public consultation before it was introduced to the House, and is a critical piece of legislation for people experiencing severe mental distress. Part 1 of the bill sets out the foundation for this bill to support a shift towards a rights-based and recovery approach to mental health care; to establish a modern, rights-based framework that promotes decision-making capacity, safeguards rights, supports recovery, and protects the safety and wellbeing of people and their communities.

It’s a key principle in this bill that voluntary and least restrictive practices be used. However, with the exception of extending all rights to voluntary mental health care consumers, the scope of the bill is about the rights of people who are subject to compulsory care, including assessment and treatment. In this part of Part 1, we’re introducing a new decision-making capacity criterion, ensuring compulsory care is only available when a person has seriously impaired mental health, is experiencing serious adverse effects, and lacks decision-making capacity about their mental health care. The compulsory care principles in Part 1 require care to be therapeutic, least restrictive, supportive, and responsive, and to recognise the dignity of risk.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I take on board the direction that you’ve given us around the Amendment Paper today. I understand that when we met with the Minister the other evening, he was of the mind that the bill would be in the House tomorrow. Having said that, this bill has been sitting on a dusty shelf for many months, and so there was plenty of time for that amendment to come before the House.

I thought it may be useful, as I look at Part 1, clause 3, the purpose clause, to just also provide a little bit of an architecture about how we intend to prosecute the bill, because it is a very big and significant bill, as has been said. I want to frame that around the purpose as it’s articulated in clause 3(a), which talks about promoting the decision-making capacity. I will note that it talks about promoting decision making, not safeguarding, so there is a threshold there that the bill purports to put into place. Many of my questions around this very first section are, really, whether that threshold is indeed met or whether those words are appropriate.

You will find, Mr Chair, from our side, that many of our questions will be in Part 1, including the definition section, because that will help to inform the rest of the debate. There will be some questions in Part 2 and probably the fewest questions in Parts 3 to 8, including very little, if anything, in the schedules. But we also would like to debate the amendment that’s before the House, because that is indeed around one of the changes that Labour members had put forward and it does appear to have reduced in scope the protections afforded in there.

When I look at clause 3, there are two things I would like to prosecute, perhaps in a couple of contributions. The first one, really, is around process. It was mentioned in the second reading speeches, but it’s important to bring it up here, just around the time constraints that we’ve had to look at this comprehensive bill. It’s not just us who are saying it. The Ombudsman said at point number 3 of his submission that this is a very short time frame for commenting on such a significant piece of legislation. He also talked about time frames not being appropriate, given key stakeholders included people with lived experience, the mental health workforce, and wider disability community. He mentioned their rights to be involved through the United Nations (UN) Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities’ concluding observations on the second and third periodic reports of New Zealand, and also the UN recommendation to New Zealand that development process for the new legislation actively involves persons with disabilities, particularly persons with psychosocial disabilities. Again, I refer to the word “promote” in the purpose in Part 1 that I am referencing there.

The second issue is that the Ombudsman talked about how this was being compounded by a lack of accessible formats such as Easy Read and/or other accessible and engagement tools. We also found that the advice to the Health Committee, while the officials worked really hard, did feel very rushed and it didn’t cover many of the items raised by submitters. In the end, we drafted a table of 50 areas for discussion and debate, and we had to fight very hard just to have substantive discussions about recommendations, and for many of them we didn’t get to do that. The time frame was extremely tight, and we don’t believe on this side that it did justice to the issues raised by the submitters. Some areas, including forensic mental health, including incarcerated people, got very little, if no, attention, and there’s a whole section of the bill devoted to that that appeared to have been lifted and shifted. It would be good to be able to scrutinise that before it is to come into law.

My questions around process are, really, to ask the Minister: why was the select committee phase of the bill rushed, particularly when it appears to have been languishing—not even on the Order Paper, actually—off the Order Paper and on a shelf for some months, when that could have been valuable time for people to submit? Why were submissions open on 25 October last year for just six weeks, which, if one were cynical, one would say that was just before Christmas. The committee acknowledged the tight turn-around, and Labour asked for an extension. The extension was only until 20 December 2024, so during a very busy time before Christmas. I probably am a bit cheeky asking if that was deliberate, but it does give us pause to wonder why those time frames are chosen.

Just a few more questions on this: why couldn’t submissions have been extended until Parliament resumed in February so people could at least have had the summer period to read the bill and get their heads around it?

While I have the floor, I’ll just also make the point that there seems to have been very little attempt to reach out to disabled communities and neurodivergent communities to solicit their views on the bill in a way that could have afforded them much-needed protections. We have drafted amendments around that, and we heard really compelling evidence from people who were mainly their representatives rather than necessarily their own voice, although there was evidence from some groups as well. But if we think about the context of the young neurodivergent girl who was mistakenly placed under the current Act and given sedation, that is an example of what can go horribly wrong under the Act if we don’t have the right safeguards in place.

I’ve got some more to say about the substance, and I’ll just go into one point around this, still on clause 3, which is that one of the most significant goals of the bill relates to decision-making capacity, including a shift from the current emphasis on risk aimed at eliminating compulsory care. But it involves treatment irrespective of consent, and if someone lacks capacity in a certain area, then proper process must be followed. It seems to be that although there is lip service in clause 3 in talking about promoting the decision-making capacity—and there are other parts of the bill that talk about that—we don’t see in the functioning of the bill that substituted decision-making will be a last resort. It feels like there aren’t ways to do that, and it also feels like there’s a kind of blanket approach to capacity rather than a decision-by-decision basis, which is the modern approach to mental health philosophy.

The questions I have around that are: why does the bill take an approach regarding restoration of capacity, which is a binary approach and doesn’t seem to follow best practice? Wouldn’t the purpose of the bill be better served by ensuring that safeguards are in place to support the full exercise of decision-making capacity? Is there a financial reason why those changes haven’t been made? Ultimately, it might take more investment into the mental health sector—and I do appreciate that; I don’t say that glibly, because it could be a major investment—and yet, if the bill is trying to achieve that, then, perhaps, workforce development and resourcing and legislative safeguards around delivery would be the way require the delivery of that, rather than making it contingent upon the capacity for the Public Service to do that. There will be other questions that really look at the decision-making capacity and the full exercise of that when we come to clause 9 of the bill.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. Look, to start off, I think we’ve all agreed that this is an important bill, right? So we can get up and grandstand, or we can actually get into the issues. I mean, to raise for five minutes the issues of select committee when, obviously, select committees are independent of Ministers is, probably, quite a disappointing first call from the Opposition spokesperson, and I think it says a lot. That Opposition spokesperson should actually—

content.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall
content.text: What! For goodness’ sake.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY
content.text: Well, no, you can’t have it both ways. They are independent of Ministers, and, actually, the select committee was a standard process. You can’t have it both ways—and, actually, as that member will also know, because it happened under her last Government, there was a full public consultation on this policy of this bill by Andrew Little before it came into the House, and there’ll be many members here who probably haven’t debated a bill before that went through such a thorough process before it came to the House. I don’t want to hear, “Oh, well, it could have been transformative.”  I mean, quite frankly, that’s what the problem was under the last Government in mental health, when it was all about transformation, and look where it got them, right? So, actually, everyone has worked hard on this bill—every party—and the public has been fully consulted; and it turns up to the House in very good shape. Not only that, it had an expert advisory panel that fed into it. So, yep, we’re going to debate the points of this bill, but let’s do that.

content.speaker: Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour)
content.text: I want to try and get back a semblance of collegiality in this debate. As the Minister has acknowledged, this is a bill started under our Government and completed under theirs. It is incredibly important, it is historic, and it deals with issues that touch on the human rights of some of the most vulnerable people in New Zealand. I think it behooves us to approach—yeah, as I said— this debate with collegiality. It is late. It’s probably, while we’re talking about mental health, worth reflecting that everyone’s probably quite tired. Why don’t we write some elements of behaviour off as that and try and get off on a different foot?

I think it is fair, for a bill that deals with human rights, for the Opposition to have some concerns about the amendment that we are about to debate. It is an amendment that takes a decision made by the select committee and that affects the rights of mothers to be with their children and changes it substantially. I won’t, in this contribution, pose questions about that, because we’re not up to clause 38A yet, but I think it is an important procedural point to raise that it appears to be a substantial change to an issue that is a very important issue, made under urgency and without the opportunity for the public to consult on this. We will have questions about that, and I understand from my colleague that the nature of this change—we only learned about it when we saw the Amendment Paper. It is not how I would like to participate as a parliamentarian—to be discussing the rights of mothers to be with their babies when I’ve only seen it very recently. That’s not good.

The Minister is entitled to say that other elements of the process have been consultative; they have been. But this particular issue stands out as one that is very problematic and disappointing, because there was such a full process. As I said in my second reading speech, it’s hard to remember all of the submissions. Although my notes are helpful, it’s hard to remember them all, because it was some time ago. I don’t understand why we’re in this position where this change is happening now. It’s been several months since the Health Committee reported back, and the opportunity to have a conversation about what’s on this Amendment Paper when we’re not under urgency for a bill of this importance—it would have been good to take it. It would be good to hear from the Minister what it is that led to the timing of this particularly important amendment only being in front of the Opposition now.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: Before I take the next call—this bill is an important bill. I was listening carefully to the speeches before we stepped into the committee stage here, as well, and so I would ask members on both sides of the House to step through this carefully. I do note the point around process and select committee. Select committees are independent; they make their own choices and so on and so forth, so if we could say that the questions around the internal work of the select committee process have been resolved, then let us step through this carefully. This is important, and I know that people across the country will be looking with the expectation that we do step through this carefully.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I do want to answer the genuine question around the amendment with the birth parent clause. The first point is, I think, that, genuinely, you will find that we have similar intent and we share the intent. The Amendment Paper 648 proposes a change to clause 38A, “Rights of birth parent”. The change ensures the responsible practitioner determines if separation is in the best interests of the person and the baby and ensures that the safety and wellbeing of the baby is the paramount consideration.

This is a really important right that the Health Committee added to the bill, and the changes I’m proposing will not alter the intent. These changes are simply to ensure it is workable in practice and is consistent with guardianship laws. As originally drafted, there was ambiguity as to who made the decisions. Guardianship arrangements can be complex and involve multiple people and views. This change addresses that while maintaining that the baby’s wellbeing is paramount.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I also want to signal to you first, Mr Chair—and my colleague the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall merely alluded to this as something we will be discussing, which is part of Part 2. While the Minister has given the response, somewhat, to this, we want to have the opportunity to examine it further under Part 2.

I will, however, go back to Part 1 and clause 3, at this stage, in particular. I want to focus on the purpose first. Now, a lot of the bills, as we know, have a purpose clause, but quite often, we see the purpose clause used in the legislation—I’m personally most familiar with the Education and Training Act 2020. Sometimes, the operationalisation of the purpose clause doesn’t quite match or meet the expectation of that purpose clause, so you can have a beautifully crafted purpose clause, but it is hard to match it. I think, in this case, it is really important—like the Chair said, this is an incredibly serious issue. So I want to check with the Minister: is the purpose clause an aspiration, or is it binding? I think that is really important so when we go into the subsequent parts discussing the operationalisation of this, we’re able to draw back to: does this meet the standard that we see in the purpose clause? I think that’s one of the most important aspects of this bill.

Now, if we’re looking at the specific elements of this, from subclauses (a) to (d), I know that my colleague Ingrid Leary already mentioned that there are areas that she would like to discuss, but one of the things I would like to discuss, to start with, is around (d), and then I’m kind of going to work my way backwards. The first question I have around (d), which is protecting “the safety and well-being of tāngata whaiora and their communities”, is: how, then, does the Minister define or have an expectation of what is meant by “their communities”? We know that—particularly when we’re looking at not just the tāngata whaiora themselves, their immediate family, the disabled communities, but if we’re looking at the fundamental principle of intersectionality—communities are complex. To give the Minister an example, how, then, would we expect the agency or the community or the hospital, etc., who will be responsible for meeting that purpose would respond to, let’s say, Asian communities, if we have that in there? Would that be done in a way that would be culturally appropriate?
I think that’s my second question to the Minister, and I will leave that there for the time being, Chair, because I want to just ask a few at a time.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I’d like to move to the interpretation section. Just going through part by part, we will have some more questions regarding advanced mental health directives, particularly in the later sections, about how they would be operationalised. But for now, we’re wanting to understand if the definition has the same meaning as it does in the Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers’ Rights. The reason I say that is, for those who are listening at home, an advance directive is basically a statement that you sign saying in advance what kind of treatment you might want in the event that you become unwell. It’s particularly relevant to mental health situations, where an episode of mental illness might leave somebody unable to decide or communicate how they want to be treated. Under the Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers’ Rights, anybody who is legally competent can make one of these. All tāngata whaiora, at some point in their mental health and mental wellbeing journey, would be in a position to make one of these.

What it can do is have a really a profound impact, for example, if you’re in a crisis about what kind of drugs you might not want to be medicated with; whether you are open to electroconvulsive therapy or absolutely do not want it at all; whether you’d prefer to receive services in crisis in your hospital, in a home, in a crisis centre; and so on. We know from the way the legislation is drafted that there is some weighting put on these advance directives to the extent that they are therapeutically useful or to the extent, I guess, that they don’t impede the person from decision-making capacity. It will be good to tease out later which end of the spectrum the Minister sees the legislation being interpreted at.

With the Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers’ Rights, there are five elements to the advance directives for them to apply, which are: was a person competent to make the decision when they made the advance directive; did they make it of their own free will; were they sufficiently informed to make the decision; did they intend the directive to apply to the present circumstances, which could be different from those anticipated; and is the advance directive out of date?

My question to the Minister at this point in the interpretation, clause 4, is: does the Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers’ Rights apply, and if not, why not? If it doesn’t, then how is this bill any different to the 1992 bill? Do the appeal provisions to the Health and Disability Commissioner still stand if someone thinks their directive has not been adequately taken into account under the 2025 Mental Health Bill, or do the bill’s review provisions extinguish or transfer that right of appeal? How do they interact with enduring powers of attorney, for example, through the Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1988, which can apply to many tāngata whaiora? For example, if someone has an enduring power of attorney to make healthcare decisions on their behalf when they are not competent to do so, whose determinations prevail, the attorney’s or the medical practitioner’s? I’m thinking here of, for example, in dementia cases, where, often, a family member will have the ability to make decisions when the person loses capacity, and yet they may also have an advance directive. I’m really wanting to understand that interaction.

I’ll go on, for the purposes of getting through the bill, to a question about the next one, which is an “advocate”, in the interpretation, clause 4. We heard this at select committee and it never got resolved, which is the different roles of the different support people. They seem complex and confusing. Could the Minister please tell us the difference, in his view, or an explanation between the attorney, the independent support person, the support network, and the welfare guardian.

While we’re on that note, why is attorney—it’s got the meaning in section 2 of the Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act—written in the American spelling? Is that a typo or is that being done deliberately? If it’s a typo, perhaps that’s indicative of the rushed process. If it’s been done deliberately, is it because it’s trying to align with that other legislation?

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Just thought I’d answer a couple of questions by the member Lawrence Xu-Nan. He talked about the change from “New Zealanders” to “their communities”. Really, the intent of that change was to capture communities that the person identifies with to make expectations that the care is responsive.

The member also talked about the purpose—is it aspirational or binding? The purpose clauses are a key interpretive aid throughout the legislation’s provision. In interpreting a requirement, decision makers and the courts will interpret clauses with regard to the purpose, especially if there is any interpretive ambiguity.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. Thank you for that, Minister. I think both responses are very helpful, so thank you.

I want to ask one more question on clause 3 before moving on to clause 4. This is, again, a question around a word, because it’s important for us to get understanding as well. I want to focus on clause 3(b), which is “improves equity in mental health outcomes among New Zealand’s population groups”. I want to just also check that when we are looking at outcomes—presumably there will be measures that come with it as well—in this case, the Minister intends outcomes to be genuinely about outcomes and not about output.

Just to give an example to the Minister, when we’re looking at outcomes, are we seeing the fact that the people who are using the care services—and I do have to be careful and I will probably have to refer back to the interpretation for some of the terminologies, because I know that some of the terminologies have changed; the people under compulsory care—are feeling like their wellbeing is looked after, are in the process of either rehabilitation or being within their families and communities. Whereas output, in this case, could be more quantitative and saying, well, we managed to churn X number of people through our system, or we have X number of people here. I want to just check if the Minister wouldn’t mind clarifying how that outcome could potentially be measured.

My next question is also quite a small one. In the interpretation, in clause 4, with “mental health practitioner”—this is page 14, line 14, for both the Chair and the Minister’s reference—I have noted that, previously, when we were looking at some of the other definitions for specific professions, there was an inclusion specifically of the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act (HPCA). I want to check whether, other than the four criteria that are listed in subclauses (a) to (d), is there anyone else within the HPCAA 2003 that could also be captured by this but isn’t included in here?
Those are my two questions. Thank you.

content.speaker: Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour)
content.text: Well, it would be helpful for the officials who may be advising the Minister for Mental Health if my question, which follows on from Dr Xu-Nan’s, is asked now—also clause 4, the mental health practitioner defined as “(a) medical practitioner; (b) nurse practitioner; (c) registered nurse practising in mental health; or (d) any other … class of person appointed under section 149.” The powers of the mental health practitioner comes up in a latter part of the bill, and does include conducting examinations for the purpose of determining if someone should receive compulsory care. My question to the Minister is twofold: (a) is it correct that this paragraph (d) allows non-regulated workforces to take the role of the mental health practitioner and their powers? And second question: does the Minister have an intention of appointing non-regulated professionals—and by non-regulated, I mean under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act—to fulfil the role of a mental health practitioner?

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: Just to follow on as a bit of a supplementary, really. With the “clinical psychologist” definition, the same issue applies where it’s talking about the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act, and we are aware that there is a new associate psychology role. Wanting to understand how tangata whaiora will be assured that the Act doesn’t widen the scope of clinical psychology in particular to people who don’t have the clinical experience to make the decisions.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: Can you just tell me what section?

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY
content.text: Oh, sorry, this is still in the definition section under “clinical psychologist”. And then speaking to the point that both the previous speakers made about the medical—

content.speaker: Hon Matt Doocey
content.text: What clause?

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: What page?

content.speaker: Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan
content.text: Page 11, line 32.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY
content.text: Thank you. It talks about a clinical psychologist being a health practitioner and then it talks about under that Act. But we know that, under this Government, there have been some new roles created that don’t have a clinical element and yet could be considered psychologists for the purposes of other parts of the law. I’m wondering if the Minister for Mental Health would consider, given the concerns raised around the health practitioner definition which have been raised by the previous two speakers, whether he would consider my amendment 1.50.05, which would amend the interpretation of health practitioner in clause 4(1) so that it would say, “for the purposes of the Act, the health practitioner exercising powers or performing functions must have appropriate competence, training, and experience in the assessment, diagnosis, treatment, and care of people experiencing mental distress or mental illness.”? I think, in doing that, we’re looking, again, at using Dr Xu-Nan’s language about the outcome of the level of skill and training and competence of the health practitioner, rather than looking at a kind of regime or more of an input measure of what kind of certification they have. I do have that amendment on the Table and would like to know if the Minister would support that.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. Just gathering up a few questions. There was a question around the new decision-making capacity, enough safeguards, and I think the member Ingrid Leary made the comment, “Is it just lip service?” I’m confident that there are safeguards, and that will explicitly recognise decision making throughout the bill. I would just point to, as an example, the principles of the bill where we have a guide for all decision making in those principles as well.

There was another question around advance directives, and, clearly, within this role, there is a role for advance directives. They are different, much more detailed in the legislative provision of the bill, and more detailed than is present in the Health and Disability Commissioner code. The provisions expand much more on high-level code provisions reflecting the need for legislative clarity in this area, and I think, when you see the principle in the bill around fluctuating capacity, that is why that is required.

There was a question, which I think was from the member Lawrence Xu-Nan, around the different roles. Clearly, the bill, when you read the bill, does introduce several new roles. Each has a defined purpose that is set out in the bill, and I consider this as sufficiently clear, and guidance and communications for people receiving this care will be set out for them.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. It would still be good to hear the Minister for Mental Health’s understanding of what those various roles entail—the attorney, the support network, and so on. That would be very helpful, I think, on the Hansard. If we keep moving through the definition section, I’d like to turn now to the community care order. We did hear evidence from Professor Tony O’Brien, who discussed assertive outreach and was raising queries around community care orders. We’re trying to understand in this section why the wording or the nomenclature has been changed to “community care” rather than “compulsory care order”, which seems to be the better phrase given the effect in the bill, which is, essentially, to keep the treatment compulsory.

The first question is: why is the word “care” included when there’s no proactive duty on the State to actually provide the care? Wouldn’t it have been clearer, for people who have experienced being under the current Act, to perhaps use the same language given that the impact of the changes to the community care orders do not change the compulsory nature of them? Why was the wording changed after the submission period rather than beforehand so that people could submit on it? It is one of the few areas, I think, where people who are subject to these orders could have felt some agency and participation if they had been able to express their responses to that, and yet that seemed to be denied of them. It was changed to “community care order”, and it’s a directive, not an order. We’re trying to understand what the change of the word from “directive” to “order” is trying to achieve. Again, wouldn’t it have been better to stay with the previous—or the current, under the current Mental Health Act—naming so that we don’t overstate the difference in these community care orders, which are pretty similar to under the Act? If they’re not, then I stand to be corrected and it would be great for the Minister to explain the difference in them. We will have a lot more to ask about the community care orders when we come to clause 6.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: I just want to go back to the member, Lawrence Xu-Nan, who asked a question around outcomes, which I think, for mental health, and especially in compulsory care, is a very important topic as well. Within the bill, I think it sets out clearly the importance of strong monitoring, and not only outcomes, but activities and outputs, I think, are important as well. What I’ve focused on, as the Minister for Mental Health, is not only ensuring in this bill, but actually in the wider mental health system, that we do have better public reporting. I’m a big believer that if people feel that there is reporting and there is management and public reporting, then outcomes do improve.

And the last one is ensuring that we get and measure outcomes of people improving under compulsory care as well. That also comes at a population level, and we need to ensure that we are recording and reporting on population groups receiving care as well.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. Thank you for those responses. I am heartened to hear the Minister’s response on my question around outcome. I think that’s quite important. I know that in some of the later sections we’ll get to discuss some of those principles more specifically, but I want to just continue on with the interpretation. I also want to acknowledge the updates the select committee has made on the sensitivity of some of the languages. I think that’s really appreciated.

My question over here is around infringement—let me just double-check—infringement fee and infringement offence. This is page 13 line 38 and page 14 lines 1 and 2. I will double-check on this as well, but my understanding, when it comes to infringement fees, for example, it’s a fine that doesn’t necessarily have to have an offence attached to it. You get given a particular fine and that’s it. There’s really no real recourse for you to challenge that. It’s not upon conviction or anything like that. I could be mistaken, so I think that clarification is needed because I think understanding what that definition for infringement is will be quite relevant to some of the things we see much later on when we get to, possibly, Part 8 of this bill when it comes to regulations, which I won’t touch, but I want to understand that term “infringement”.

My last question over here, I guess, is mainly just when we talked a little bit about some of the definitions around health practitioners, which is page 13, line 20 and line 21. For example, in that case, it does specify the meaning that you have with section 5 of the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act (HPCAA), which I mentioned before. But I’m still just checking with the Minister, around the clarification I was seeking regarding whether there was any mental health practitioners, that were also captured within that, because I’m assuming that we have these definitions between “clinical psychologist”, “health practitioners”, “mental health practitioners”, etc., which will be important in later parts of this bill, but it’s important for us to understand, in the broader context, how they work within the HPCAA.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Thank you very much, Mr Chair. Just responding to the member Ingrid Leary’s question around community care order and why the care when no proactive duty to care. In this bill, the term here refers more to the care plan. So whether the person is in in-patient care or community care, they’re required to have a care plan and that is more holistic here as well. Of course, by definition, the care can only be provided in accordance with the care plan.

Why is it not called “compulsory care order”? I’ve been advised the legal term is already used in intellectual disability compulsory care and the Rehabilitation Act. And as mentioned earlier, the reference of care is more than just treatment, it is a holistic view of that person’s care.

content.speaker: Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. It would, perhaps, help our progress through the bill if we could have an answer to my previous question about whether the definition of “mental health practitioner”, under (d) on page 14, includes non-regulated professionals as defined in the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act. And the second question which was whether the Minister has any intention of appointing non-regulated professions or groups of people to the role of the mental health practitioner.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Yes, thank you very much for the question. The Director of Mental Health can deem someone a mental health practitioner who holds the required skills and competencies. Careful consideration will be given to that, deeming to ensure that there is a qualified clinical care.

content.speaker: Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. Clearly the answer then is “yes”. Could the Minister give some examples of groups of non-regulated workers who might be suitable to have the powers of a mental health practitioner under the Act? I’m aware that non-regulated practitioners are paying an increasing role in our in our health system. So I’m interested to understand his thoughts there.

I guess, I understand the point about skills, that’s clearly the most important thing for exercising those powers, but there are other parts of being a regulated profession under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act, other than just the skills: being on a register, having a community of professional practice that you’re a part of, peer review, sometimes ethical requirements will definitely be one of them. And in the non-regulated professions don’t have that framework applying to. I mean just being on a register means the police can find you, right? So there’s a number of things there. I would like to understand more about the types of groups of workers who might be suitable to exercise the powers of a mental health practitioner but aren’t in the regulated professions.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: Just a supplementary on that to sort of make the point, I guess, if we look at registered nurses practising in mental health: how much experience do they need? If a nurse had just graduated a month prior, would that be enough time? Would they need to have trained and gained qualifications? Same goes with paramedics. We will have more questions on this under clause 149.

I want to go back to compulsory care, but to the assessment and care of a person. Looking at a question that relates to clause 62(2) and the interplay between compulsory care, the definition, and how that plays out. And I hope the Minister’s officials are listening because a little bit complicated, but in the definition section it says—

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: Just feel free to wait while the Minister’s taking advice, if you’d like.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY
content.text: Sure. Yeah, in the definition, compulsory care “means the compulsory assessment and care of a person from the start of the second assessment period until the person is released under section 53, 64, 66 or 76”. So my questions are: what does the start of the second assessment period mean? Is that after they’ve reached the first threshold and prior to the second assessment or is it the day on which they are notified? And if so, what time of that day? Is it on the moment of notification? Is it after notification or is it after the second assessment period until they are released? And if it’s the latter, then what is the period of care called after the initial assessment until the second assessment? This looks directly at the definition of “compulsory care” in the definition section of clause 4 and how it plays out in clause 62(2).

I’ll continue on, noting that I do have that amendment on the table regarding mental health practitioner that the Minister hasn’t indicated whether if he would adopt—that would be helpful to respond to our questions.

In the definition of “court”, it talks about “the court with jurisdiction to hear and determine applications, set out in section 70”. It also talks about the “Court Martial of New Zealand established under section 8 of the Court Martial Act 2007”. My questions around this are related to the stigma and discrimination, and we did hear submissions where people quoted from Te Hiringa Mahara, in 2023, that “the carrying over of Family or District Court arrangements for initial decisions appears at odds with the policy objectives towards a rights-based approach”.

Did the Minister consider using a tribunal decision-making process model instead of court proceedings, particularly to reduce the stigma? We’ve seen that in the Family Court, for example, or a tribunal approach; I know the Minister’s very keen on not necessarily having police be at mental health events unless there’s a requirement for them to be there because of the stigmatisation. Has he considered that? Did he receive any advice on that?

Why do people in the armed forces go through the Court Martial process under this bill rather than a civilian one? If the principles at play are universal and if the risk principles are the same, there wouldn’t seem to be a reason to need to have a Court Martial for the armed forces. Was that a lift and shift from the previous Act, and did he turn his mind to whether it might be better to have universality of the tribunal and the intention to reduce stigma and discrimination, which is the whole purpose of the changes and reforms we’re trying to make in mental health? Doesn’t including the Court Martial element once again entrench the stigma and discrimination?

I do have a second amendment, and my question around that amendment is whether, perhaps, the Court Martial is appropriate only in forensic cases—the equivalent of prison-type, criminal-type cases for Court Martial? If that is the case, I wonder if he would consider my tabled amendment lodged at 1.50.02 p.m., which just says, “in clause 4(1)(b) of the definition of ‘court’, after ‘Armed Forces Discipline Act 1971’, insert ‘for the purposes of this Act’”? That would mean that the Court Martial of New Zealand would only be used within the definition of “court” in relation to persons subject to forensic compulsory care, rather than if they were having a medical mental health event that didn’t involve something that could attract a criminal charge if it wasn’t in an armed service setting.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Thank you very much, Mr Chair. There was a question from the member Ingrid Leary about the reference to the new assistant psychology role, or psychology assistant, in relation to the reference in the bill for “clinical psychologist”. By definition, the psychology assistants aren’t clinical psychologists and, as deemed by the Psychologists Board, don’t have that title.

The question from the member Ayesha Verrall was around the use of the non-clinical workforce, and, as referenced, we have grown the non-clinical workforce. I think it plays a very good role in complementing the clinical workforce, but it wouldn’t be my expectation that the non-clinical workforce would be used for clinical work.

There was also a question from the member Lawrence Xu-Nan around infringement fees, especially around the serving of the notice. Every infringement fee has a requirement to include a statement, and under that requirement, the person who is being served the infringement fee has the right to request a hearing.

content.speaker: Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour)
content.text: Just to follow up on that helpful response from the Minister for Mental Health, the language in the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act is that there are professions that are regulated. Can the Minister confirm that he means that he doesn’t expect “mental health practitioner”, as defined in this bill, would be given to people who are not in a regulated profession?

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Yeah, and I think that’s a fair clarification.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: We’re nearly getting to the end of the definitions section. I have got a couple more amendments. One is around the compulsory care criteria and its interplay with clause 7. We won’t need to revisit this in clause 7, but I’m trying to understand whether the compulsory care criteria are those set out in the definitions section exclusively or whether they’re broader than that. My reading of the bill would suggest that, perhaps, it needs to be only those in the definitions section, so I have proposed an amendment in clause 4(1) to, after “means”, just insert the word “only”, and that would make it really clear that clause 7 doesn’t enable other criteria to be included. I’m hoping to get an answer on that.

Also, in clause 4(1), there is a definition of the “Director-General”, and it says, “who holds the office of Deputy Director of Mental Health”. The problem with the legislation, of course, is that if there is another change to the Ministry of Health, as there has been in the past, or the Director-General title, then the legislation can’t apply. I just wonder if it might be prudent to add, in clause 4(1), replace the definition of “Director-General” with “Director-General means the chief executive of the department responsible for administering this Act, and includes any person to whom that chief executive has delegated a power or function under the Act”. That would future-proof the Act; we wouldn’t have to come back with an omnibus bill for a silly little amendment.

Finally, just talking again around forensic compulsory care, it’s a bit confusing about what that means in relation to clause 113. We don’t need to revisit clause 113, but I’m wondering if it should just be put in the definitions section for clarity so that it would say that clause 113 would be amended by clause 4(1). It would say that clause 113 “applies to a person under forensic compulsory care as defined in clause 4”, and in clause 4, it would simply say “a person under forensic compulsory care means a person described in section 113”. That would be some legislative coherence. As I say, we don’t need to revisit it, but this would make it just a bit easier for people to understand how the interplay of those sections works.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Just in reference to that amendment, which we wouldn’t support, the definition of this bill is standard Parliamentary Council Office practice. The intent is achieved through the Legislation Act 2019.

Just rounding off the question of Court Martial, the Court Martial provision was already in the current Act. Then there was the question around what the start of the second assessment means. I suppose, if we look at the process of compulsory care, the first assessment is undertaken, and when there are reasonable grounds to believe the person meets the compulsory care criteria, that notice is given in writing for the second assessment.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I know that my colleague Ingrid Leary might still have a couple of final questions on clause 4, but I’m going to move on to clauses 5 and 6. I may have follow-up questions for the Minister for Mental Health on clause 5, but I’m going to ask a quick one to begin with, which is: would the Minister anticipate any changes to clause 5 as part of the changes that are intended by the Government around Te Tiriti o Waitangi clauses?  Would that affect this particular one? That will determine some of the questions I might have for the Minister coming up.

I’ll maybe come back later for clause 5, but I do just want to touch on two things for clause 6, and I want to speak to my colleague Kahurangi Carter’s amendments. The first one is around the therapeutic purpose, and this is “Compulsory care principles”, under subclause (1)(a)(ii). The proposal is to maybe insert a new subparagraph (iii), which is that the compulsory care should only be used “with appropriate measures in place to support a person to move from compulsory care to become a voluntary mental health consumer”. Sorry, Mr Chair, this is Amendment Paper 644.

The reason for that is that, as I mentioned in my second reading, one of the things that the Green Party is particularly interested in is the ability for people to fully transition into that voluntary care, and we emphasise that the reduction of compulsion shouldn’t reduce the care and there needs to be some sort of voluntary support. I want to check whether the Minister would be interested in adopting my colleague’s amendment, but, if not, if the Minister wouldn’t mind pointing out another principle that that potentially could be incorporated under.

The next thing I want to mention is Kahurangi Carter’s Amendment Paper 645 and that is to, after clause 6(1)(d), insert new paragraph (6)(1)(e), which is around “Commitment to provide community care”. This does tie in to amendment Paper 644. Again, this is to do with the kind of support that’s expected and the community support commitment that is expected after involuntary hospitalisation becomes voluntary, which, again, shifts us—hopefully—from a high level of compulsory treatment to avoid cases of seemingly indefinite compulsory care. I wanted to check whether the Minister would be interested in those, and I still have further questions on both clauses 5 and 6.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: Thank you. Just on the fact that the Minister won’t clarify, in the bill as it currently, the issue around “person under forensic compulsory care”, I think it is good for us to work out which bit of legislation takes precedence. As I say this, I’m thinking again about the incidence, at Wakari Hospital, of people who would be potentially under both the Mental Health Act currently but also the Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act.

If someone is a special care recipient under section 2 of the Intellectual Disability Act and they also have a mental disorder, which statutory regime will now take precedence, and how does that compare to the current Act? Can the Minister identify any circumstances in which a person could potentially fall under both bits of legislation, given the changes and the fact that we’re not going to clarify that now in the definition section? And, if so, what safeguards exist to ensure that people aren’t inadvertently moved from protections available under the Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act and into the mental health regime? As I say, they sound a bit nitpicky and a little bit conceptual, but they’re very, very real right now, given what’s happened at Wakari Hospital and is mentioned in the Ombudsman’s report. It is worth us understanding the interplay of those two pieces of law.

Going back to the Armed Forces Discipline Act, where I talked previously about “Court Martial”, Part 10 continues to apply under transitional provisions, and yet we don’t have “Court Martial” anywhere else or in any other reference to the Armed Forces Discipline Act, except under Part 10 of that Act. I’m wondering if it’s just an oversight and if we should still remove that from the definition section, or why is it that it doesn’t appear to be anywhere else in this bill?

Then, finally, we’ve covered the medical health professionals—the New Zealand Health Plan; it would be great to understand from the Minister where we are with it. I believe that there has been a draft and there may be a strategy due for finalisation, but it would be good to know when the plan will be published under the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act or if the Minister can let me know if it has been published. I haven’t been able to find it, but it may have been.

content.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall
content.text: Yes, it has been.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY
content.text: The Pae Ora mental health one?

content.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall
content.text: No, the health plan.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY
content.text: The health plan. Sorry, I’m just—oh, no, that was 2025. I’ll leave that, then, because my colleague is telling me that doesn’t apply. So that’s fine. We covered that one off. I think that’s just about all from there. Then if we go to clause 5, which is the Treaty clause—I will sit down and let someone else take a call while I gather my thoughts. Thank you.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Thank you very much, Mr Chair. I just wanted to respond to the member Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan. He’s referencing Amendment Papers 644 and 645 in the name of Kahurangi Carter. Amendment Paper 644, to require measures to support transition from compulsory to voluntary mental health care, looks to add a new compulsory key principle requiring “appropriate measures”, and, for that reason, we would not support that. It would be unclear what “appropriate measures” actually refers to in definitional terms, and it would not be appropriate to include it in the principles of the bill.

Amendment Paper 645 introduces a commitment to provide community care. Look, I understand the intent of the proposal, ensuring those who come out of, potentially, hospital inpatient compulsory care can be joined up with community care. The issue with that proposal is then that you would create, potentially, a new entitlement or preferential access through that route, as well. What I think we all can agree on for community care is that the decisions for referral should be undertaken through established clinical assessment and service eligibility and prioritisation, which currently exists.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. Thank you for the response, Minister. I have to say, it’s very refreshing to get such a detailed response to any Amendment Paper, so I appreciate that. Just picking up from what the Minister is saying—and I’ll get on to the community part—I understand there are currently existing processes, and I acknowledge the Minister’s point around preferential care.

I want to check in terms of clause 6 around “Compulsory care principles”. I’m looking now at subclause (1)(b) regarding the “Least restrictive application”. One of the things that I raised, as well, in my second reading speech is that we want to move in a direction where compulsory care is a last resort. Can I just check if that is in line with the interpretation here under clause (6)(1)(b), which is “be applied in the least restrictive manner”? Would that still imply that compulsory care is being used, but just less restrictively, and that there are different hierarchies of restrictiveness when it comes to compulsory care? But, also, over here in subparagraph (i), the bill mentions that “voluntary care options should be actively offered and preferred”. Can I just check if “preferred”, in this case, would also imply it’s the default starting point for that, and then the level of severity, I guess, depending on diagnosis and the requirement for the person needing compulsory care?

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Thank you for that question from Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan. I think, when you look at the purpose of the Act, especially around the compulsory care principles, it does state around the therapeutic purpose, and I think that is very important in the context of the discussion here.
Not only therapeutic but the least restrictive application as well. What we do find with voluntary care options is that, quite often, they can be the most therapeutic and the least restrictive.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: On the definitions section, this is just a quick note to say that we did have a long discussion about the wording of tāngata whaiora, and some of the Government members didn’t like the definition, but we have it defined in the bill as “people with lived experience of mental distress”. I am interested to understand from the Minister whether speaking of distress rather than mental illness is appropriate or how does he see that, because mental distress tends to be a short duration—less gravity; less, perhaps, diagnosed as a medical illness, and not necessarily a clinical kind of definition—so would it be better to say “mental illness” or would it perhaps be better to have a te reo word that defines what tāngata whaiora is so that we don’t have to try and have this kind of transliteration?

When I go to the Treaty of Waitangi clauses, there were a number of submissions on that, and the biggest impression I had was that there seems to be a commitment to Te Tiriti in an overall sense but that it doesn’t feel like it applies in the delivery of service to tāngata whaiora. I wonder if the Minister would entertain tabled amendment 1.50.06, which says, “in clause 5, after subclause (1), insert ‘that persons exercising powers and functions under this Act must actively support equitable outcomes for Māori and enable Māori participation in decisions affecting the care of Māori receiving services under this Act.’”

If we look again at the promotion of decision-making capacity in clause 3, that would seem to align really well. Alternatively, there is my tabled amendment 3.04.01, which just says that, under the heading, “Every person performing a function or duty or exercising a power under this Act must give effect to the principles of Te Tiriti.” I know that the current wording talks about giving to effect as the bill, but it doesn’t actually require anything of the people delivering services, so that could be another way to do it.

We did have the opportunity to meet the other evening, and I was hoping that the Minister would take on board my tabled amendment on clause 6, which is around disabled and neurodivergent people. We heard that they are implicitly protected in the bill, but I do have tabled amendment 3.04.01, which would explicitly ensure that disability, neurodivergence, and different styles of communication would not be treated as evidence of impaired decision-making capacity. Just another plea to the Minister: I know it didn’t make it over the line the other evening, but this would be of great comfort to our disabled and neurodivergent communities, because, often, with the way that they can present, it is assumed that they are suffering some kind of mental health event when it is actually a form of their expression and communication.

I know the Minister’s going to stand up and say, “Yes, it’s implicit in the bill.”, but disabled and neurodivergent people do not get the protections.
