We know that they are overrepresented in all of the abuse in care scenarios, and so having an explicit mention as per my tabled amendment would be really helpful. The other one, which would be also something that I would have thought the Minister would support because he is a champion of lived experience, is to actually recognise the value of lived experience wherever reasonably practicable. We could do that with my tabled amendment 8.00.01. We could put that into clause 6(1)(c). Then we could actually, after clause 211, have the director-general actually have a plan and a statutory requirement to take into account advice from people with lived experience of compulsory mental health care, some of whom we heard at the committee stage, but also including appropriate Māori, Pacific, disabled, and youth lived experience—again, the most marginalised communities.

Under clause 6, I have tabled amendment 1.50.09 to include the words “including whānau and cultural support”, which would be to specify what kind of support is referenced in the definition section. That would make sure that support was available to the person, including whānau and cultural support, housing, income, education, employment, and so on—all the things that people might need to get onto their journey of recovery. That would then apply the principle of least restrictive care and it would also require some investment into resourcing.
Mr Chair, if I can keep going with these amendments, we’ll get through them really quickly?

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: Well, yes, that’s a good idea to finish them off. We’ll go through them; it would be a nice way to finish your contribution.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY
content.text: Thank you. I’ve got an amendment under clause 8, tabled amendment 15.00.11: which would be, “after the words ‘Seriously impaired mental health’, insert the words ‘without evidence that those matters are contributing to a serious impairment of mental functioning’.” This is another safeguard. We’ve heard that there’s quite a binary position in the bill about people either lacking capacity or not, and yet we heard from expert submitters that those judgments should be made on a decision by decision basis because mental capacity fluctuates. Putting this amendment in clause 8(2) would help to move us into the 21st century when it comes to best practice around how we determine mental impairment and capacity so that it’s no longer binary but more a journey, and appropriate supports can be put in at each gateway.

We also have two amendments on clause 9 which are, again, safeguards for people with intellectual disability, which is that they cannot be presumed to lack capacity to make decisions about their mental health care solely because they have an intellectual disability or a neurological or brain condition. We have seen the Wakari Hospital incident. We have also heard evidence from people where they are the most vulnerable, and just having that safeguarding would be something that would give those communities confidence.

Finally, the “Meaning of capacity to make decisions about mental health”: we could capture all of that in assessing capacity, to say that reasonable steps must be taken to support the person to make or communicate their own decision before determining that the person lacks capacity; so it’s a kind of active or proactive duty of care on officials to take the person as they are before them. Yes, it’s implicit across the bill, but it doesn’t really apply individually on a case by case basis where somebody may be taken at face value rather than for their particular situation or circumstances.

Finally, in clause 12, I suggest amending advance mental health directives so that a copy of the statement that is given must be provided to the person. They must be consistent with that person’s wishes and to the person’s support network and to the independent advocate. This is around giving them reasons why their advance directive might not be followed. We heard a lot about advance directives and people wanting them to be taken more seriously and to be on hand, rather than them just being discarded, and having a duty of care on those choosing not to follow them—probably for good clinical reasons. It would be prudent to have that in writing so that there is a process to safeguard their rights.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Alrighty, hey, let’s get into this; alrighty. We have tabled amendment No. 6 from Ingrid Leary wanting to insert additional requirements around equity and participation for Māori. I would not support that, because there are already overarching principles in the bill, recognising the Treaty of Waitangi—

content.speaker: Hon David Seymour
content.text: It’s “Wai-taa-ngi”.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY
content.text: —Waitangi; apologies—and requiring care to be responsive and meet cultural needs as well. Another tabled amendment—1.50.09—expands the principle to housing, income, education, employment, counselling, and peer support to be available to the person. I would not support that, because, as we do know, care planning already requires a holistic assessment for the person and the support that is required under the bill as well.

There were some quite technical questions/statements, I suppose, around the interface between the Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act 2003 (IDCCR) and the Mental Health Act. No compulsory care order may be made if the person is under IDCCR. If on an ID order, to become under the Mental Health Act, the ID order needs to be suspended.

The next one I have here from Ingrid Leary talks about inserting into the bill compulsory care principles relating to disabled and neurodivergent people. I would not support that, because the compulsory care criteria in the bill already ensures that disability, neurodivergence, and different communication styles are supported.
I have another one here. I’m not sure whether it’s got a number on it, to be honest. Well, the response to it is—the request in the amendment here, I think—sorry, Mr Chair, is that 150.05?

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: I’ve got just a few short questions following on from a previous one. Just the first short question is on clause 6(2). I just want to check, when we’re looking at who determines whether the compulsory care principles have been reasonably practicably met, who would the burden of proof be on? It does mention specifically courts and tribunals. I think that’s an important question: is it up to those who are providing the compulsory care or those who are challenging the provision of that compulsory care? That’s my first question.

My second question—I’m going to move on to clause 8. In clause 8(2), I have noticed that the select committee has made changes, and I do believe the changes are important and significant. However, what I’ve noticed also is that a large number of prohibited grounds for discrimination under section 21 of the Human Rights Act are not in there, so the likes of, for example, sex, ethnicity, physical disability, I believe, etc. Can I just check that, for example, when we’re looking at “a person cannot be assessed to have seriously impaired mental health on the basis of” this list, if it’s inconsistent with section 21 of the Human Rights Act, if someone challenges under the Human Rights Commission, how would that interact with this particular list?

My final question for this contribution is clause 9, and in clause 9, I would like to know, when we are looking at “Meaning of capacity to make decisions about mental health care”, who would be the one assessing this? I also want to check, in terms of the definition, the definition doesn’t give an interpretation for what is considered a “sustained basis”. In this case, we see clause 9(1), line 16 of page 21, explicitly mentions “unless they cannot, on a sustained basis,”. Is there a specific duration? Is there a range of duration?
Those are my three questions at this stage.

I suppose, when you look at compulsory care, it is not limited to a specific diagnosis, because there is a range out there about ensuring we provide timely care and support.

Part 2 Tāngata whaiora rights and support

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: Members, we come now to Part 2. This is the debate on clauses 12 to 40, “Tāngata whaiora rights and support”. The question is that Part 2 stand part.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I don’t have a huge number of suggestions or questions on this part, but I do want to go into the community care orders, because what we currently have is a situation in New Zealand where we use a significant number of these orders, compared with countries that we compare ourselves to. They have a disproportionate effect on Māori in particular, and yet we have before us a bill that purports to strengthen the human rights of tāngata whaiora.

There is international research-based consensus that compulsory community treatment is not effective in achieving its stated aims of reducing hospital readmission and improving mental health outcomes. Given that—and given that it is a significant breach of human rights—we’d expect a substantial amount of evidence of the benefit needed to justify these orders, but that evidence doesn’t seem to exist. In fact, in their submission, the FACTORS team, which included Professor Anthony O’Brien, concluded that, if the bill were to pass in its current form, it would be unlikely to have a significant impact on the current practice or on reducing the use of compulsory community care.

My questions to the Minister are: does he know roughly how many people are currently on compulsory care orders? What evidence does he have that they actually work? Why is he so resistant, and why are his officials so resistant, to making community care orders voluntary? Is it do with a sense of moral panic or the assumptions from medical practitioners, who maybe haven’t seen the evidence, of wanting to do something that looks like they are being accountable and responsible for patients yet doesn’t seem to have the evidence to back up that they actually work? And is he aware of evidence that participation by patients in their own care in the community actually has a better chance of getting people on to the road to recovery? That is my first tranche of questions. I’ll continue so we can move through the bill.

In section 13, there were submissions around the advance mental health directives and the status that they have, where there seems to be—again, I hate to use the words “lip service” because they do have some waiting, so that would be too cynical. What are his reasons for saying that section 13 can be overridden when the advance directive was made by the person when they had capacity? There may be good reasons, but it would be good to understand what they are because I think there is a sense that these community care orders provide a lot more human rights protection than what they actually do in practice. I’ll stop my questions there, and I’ll go into clause 17 later. Thank you.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. Look, I think it’s well traversed with this bill that before it was introduced to the House, there was significant public consultation. On top of that, it had its own expert advisory group. It had a full select committee process. We’re here at 10 minutes to 12, so it would be good to get some questions specific to the clauses, not just general questions that, quite frankly, could have been answered—and probably were—several times with officials in the select committee. We are talking about community care. By definition, if you are not providing that, what sort of level of care are you providing some of the most vulnerable New Zealanders in a time of need? Now, if the member’s advocating that every person needs to then go into inpatient hospital care because there is no community care, then that’s an interesting proposition, because she’s just been going on for the last few days about Wakari and the issues we’ve got in there. The whole principle of this bill is to ensure that we have compassionate care for people at some of the most vulnerable times of their life, and it just, quite frankly, beggars belief that we are now still questioning whether we should have community care in New Zealand.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: Thank you. The Minister has said that we traversed this in select committee. In fact, we didn’t really get much time to look at it. Just for clarity, we’re not suggesting that there wouldn’t be community care. The suggestion is that there would be assertive outreach with statutory resourcing and people being able to participate in their own level of care and that there would be a small number of cases of people who might need to be under compulsory care.

The Minister didn’t answer any of my questions regarding evidence, but the numbers of people under compulsory care at any one time in New Zealand is around 6,000. The researchers who have done this— well-respected university researchers—have shown that around 50 people might need to be held under compulsory care. So the question is not whether to remove community care but whether to remove the presumption of having it be compulsory and, instead, to legislate and resource the care that would be needed for assertive outreach, to make sure that people could participate in their own wellbeing. I did say that very directly in relation to clause 12.

I do have an amendment. I’m not going to read it out, but if the Minister was minded to read it, it is around giving effect to valid advance community care orders. I also have some other amendments, which I may as well go through now, since it is late. Another one is making sure that if somebody’s advance mental health directive is not used, then they would be able to get something in writing around that. I’ve got an amendment to clause 17 around attendance at hui by order, where people should be able to request that somebody else could come along, and there are insertions there in clause 17(4)(a) and (ca).

I have an amendment around clause 23, “Independent supported person”, to make sure that when there are independent supported persons under the bill, they can’t be people working for Health New Zealand, the Ministry of Health, or their agencies. That is just, really, to reflect some of the arrangements that happen because there are so many organisations that have formal relationships through legal relationships that may not necessarily be seen as being independent.

In clause 24, I’ve got an amendment around independent advocates—that we amend clause 24(2)(c) so that they will represent “the views, will, and preferences of persons under compulsory care”. That is to make sure that that person does have a distinct role, compared to a legal advocate, because we didn’t get any clarity from the Minister about what the different roles were in the definition section.

I’ve also got another amendment under clause 24 around what those advocates could do—particularly in relation to electroconvulsive therapy and also seclusion—to strengthen safeguards there, because, as we’ve said, we don’t believe that there are enough safeguards in the bill as it is currently worded. Also, it is making sure, in clause 37, that a responsible practitioner must take all reasonable steps to ensure that a person is able to access independent advice as soon as practicable. That is something that was said to us at select committee would be good, and I don’t believe it was given due regard.

Then we have some other amendments around the rights of children and young persons. A great deal of the evidence that we heard at select committee was around the fact that children and young people are, unfortunately, going into adult institutions. It’s happened under successive Governments. There isn’t any statutory resourcing requirement under this bill, and there is a requirement for children to be put into appropriate care where it’s available, but where it’s not available, there aren’t additional safeguards for them. We heard that there’s nothing to safeguard their educational development, their outdoor living space, the things that would make them feel nurtured and protected. The most we were able to get was the ability for them to be accompanied when they were being transported between facilities. So this amendment in clause 38—[Bell rings]

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)

We need to be moving forward, particularly, with the Minister’s amendments or any other amendments that people have to speak to, but we have had a select committee, and although it was some time ago, we’re not reliving the select committee; we’ve set the scene for this bill pretty well. content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Madam Chair, thank you. Yes, we’re on Part 2—I will just indicate to you, Madam Chair, that I would like to go subpart by subpart, noting the three subparts here.

Starting from Part 2, and particularly later on, we’re getting into the operational bit. So it’s a good chance for me to ask some questions around specific clauses. I’m going to start with clause 12, “Advance mental health directives”, and I want to check with the Minister: clause 12(1) says, “An advance mental health directive may specify the matters …”. Now, we see two columns, the left and the right column. Can I just check: in terms of my interpretation of “may specify”, where the person is performing a function or duty, can they selectively include which part of that column they would use in the exercise of their power—which, to me, is what “may” would imply—or do they have to consider all five aspects of that column but they’re able to add additional things on top of that? So this is page—

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Sorry, which page?

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
content.text: Page 22, clause 12(1)—the very beginning of Subpart 1.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Thank you.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
content.text: Yep, so it’s mainly just on those five criteria that we’re looking at—or content—and the obligations that are associated with that. Does a person performing a function or duty need to include all five, or can they select one or up to five, or do they need to, as a basis, consider all five and then choose to add additional things on top of that? I just want to get a sense of what “may specify” means.

In terms of clause 13, my question is around the process. In clause 13(1), “A person may make or revoke an advance mental health directive” if there’s a mental health practitioner involved. But, then, if you’re looking at the witnessing of the advance mental health directive in a later clause, in clause 14, the mental health practitioner doesn’t need to be present when the directive is revoked or made. Can I just check how that process would work and whether the people who are witnessing the advance mental health directive, either the making of it or the revocation of it, need to have some sense of what the mental health practitioner is informed of.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Thank you very much, Madam Chair. The question was around advance directives and around the five—I think the word to use there is “can”. A mental health directive can set out within those five. On the question about the requirement of tāngata whaiora, which, if I take a step back, is largely a question around whether tāngata whaiora are involved in their care planning, there will be decisions to be put under the compulsory order or discharged from that, and my expectation is they will be part of care planning.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. I’m working around clause 17 of the bill, but I would like to jump now to the Minister’s Amendment Paper, in the interests of getting into probably the most substantive part of this debate, at the start of it, and just make a very short contribution to say that one of the small wins that Labour members were able to make was to get the presumption that mothers and babies would not be separated unless there was good reason to do so. I know that my colleague the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall has a number of questions on this.

My very first question is just: what change, in his words, does the amendment make to the presumption? We did get advice at the time from officials where the wording was provided by them. We knew that this was a real balancing act between the rights of the parent to not have further distress added by their child being taken away, versus the rights to safety of the child. And it is a fine balancing act. I can imagine that the scenario that absolutely everybody wants to avoid is making that wrong judgment and having a child harmed in the process of them being kept together. Nevertheless, when I look at the wording of this Amendment Paper, it does seem to distil down or sort of over-explain the caveats that are already in there. Just a very first explanation of how this differs from the current wording would be helpful.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: This was canvassed last night. The principle here is workability, and it is to keep the intent of what the select committee members intended—but workability with guardianship laws.

content.speaker: Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour)
content.text: If the Minister’s referring to the point in the debate that we had an exchange about last night, actually, the question that was asked at that point was the purpose for the Amendment Paper being presented so late, not the substance of this discussion, which we’re pleased to be having now.

I’d like the Minister to explain: it seems that the guts of this is that whereas we had clause 38A(1), that said a birth parent is entitled to have their baby remain unless they agree or there is felt to be a change necessary in the best interests of the baby, now the clause is rewritten to emphasise that decision makers must favour the interests of the child. I wonder why that change is necessary, because it was already in the version that the select committee voted on—that the safety of the child would be a reason for separating the mother and the infant.

What I guess is uncomfortable, currently, about the Minister’s amendment is that it does seem like what was a statement with an exception that recognised the parent now appears to have no discussion about the right of the parent in the current language. I worry that that will lead to situations where it is just presumed that separating a baby from their mother is always OK. I understand that, in the Minister’s comments last night, he indicated that everyone has the same concern. I think that is correct that we all do. No one wants to see situations where either parent or baby is harmed, but it does appear, in the present wording, that there is very little in there in favour of the rights of a parent who is at risk of losing the opportunity to be with their baby. It’s not an insignificant issue; it’s not a small, rare situation.

Post-partum is a time where there is a higher risk of major depression. Post-natal depression can be a cause for coming under the Act, and there are facilities in New Zealand specialising in the care of people in these situations. So it is important that we get this right, and I’d like to understand why the language seems to have been so substantially reversed so as to now have no statement in the bill outlining why it is important for a mother and their child not to be separated.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: I can assure the committee that the presumption remains that the baby remains with the parent, unless the baby’s safety outweighs this.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: Just a supplementary on that. The language, if we look at that in testing how that applies—

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Just a quick supplementary, please, because I was actually watching this conversation last night and we’re in danger of overdoing it. So be crisp and clear.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY
content.text: Yep. In new clause 38A(1A) on Amendment Paper 648, for example, if we look at paragraph (a), there’s very clear language there that they “must give priority to the safety and well-being of the baby;”. If we look at paragraph (b), it doesn’t say “must consider” or “must give weight” to the preferences as to childcare; it simply says “must make reasonable endeavours to consider—”. That is how watered down the language is, and so there is a clear weighting difference between those two paragraphs. I ask whether the Minister could explain how he believes that that reaches a balance.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: The parent is entitled to remain with their baby unless the practitioner considers separation is in the best interests of the baby.

content.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall
content.text: Madam Chair.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Is it on the same issue—

content.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall
content.text: Yes.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: —because the Minister has been very clear. So is it new?

content.speaker: Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour)
content.text: Well, yes, it is. It seems that the Minister, in order to justify the amendment’s language, has gone back and repeated the language in the Health Committee’s version, and so it seems very odd to me that his justification for what he’s doing was the select committee’s justification. I have not heard a reason why the language needs to change.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Well, we’re now traversing previous ground. We’ve established in the committee that it’s the same intent and presumption, and the change is in line with guardianship laws.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: I’m going to call Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan, but we’re moving on from that particular issue, and I want to focus on the Minister’s Amendment Paper or any changes since the select committee.

content.speaker: Ingrid Leary
content.text: This is the Minister’s Amendment Paper.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Yes, I know that that was. I’m just making it very clear that that’s what we’re focusing on this morning: any amendments, or the Minister’s amendments—new.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Madam Chair, can I just interrupt. I think it is important, because the claim was made that it was the select committee language. It’s not the select committee language; it is the Minister’s language, and it is that the birth parent is entitled to have the baby remain with them.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Madam Chair, thank you. Just for our clarification, because the Minister’s amendment to clause 38 is actually quite far down Part 2, and I still do have questions on earlier clauses in Part 2—would they still be acceptable? I do have—

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
content.text: OK. I do want to seek a couple of clarifications from the Minister on the earlier parts. Just to the Minister’s response to me regarding the advance mental health directive, I think that the clarification I was trying to get at is this. In clause 14, that directive needs to be “witnessed by a person”, but it doesn’t say that a mental health practitioner needs to be present, and so my clarification is: would the witness need to know or to have had interactions with the mental health practitioner ahead of time?

content.speaker: Hon Matt Doocey
content.text: Madam Chair.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
content.text: But I’m—oh, sorry.

content.speaker: Hon Matt Doocey
content.text: Madam Chair, I could answer that directly.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
content.text: Oh, sure—absolutely.

content.text: If the Minister wants to answer it directly—

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
content.text: Yeah, thank you—thank you.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. I do want to speak to specific clauses to ask for specific clarification, and I’m now moving on to Subpart 2. I’m just checking: one of the languages we did see previously was around the term “on a sustained basis,”—

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Which clause in Subpart 2?

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
content.text: Clause 16(2), which begins with “In proceedings or processes to which this section applies,—”. I want to check with that, because we’ve seen the language of “sustained basis” when we are determining if a person under compulsory care—when we’re looking at the maximum degree appropriate to their capacity to participate, would that also require it to be under a sustained basis, or would it just be that while in this minute, the person is able to have the capacity to participate, and they can participate—yeah. So I would like to know what the sustained basis test is, if possible.

My next question for the Minister—and I’m going to keep it to these two because I have only two questions for Subpart 2 of this part—is when we are looking at clause 17, “Hui whaiora (well-being meetings)”, what I can’t see at this stage in this particular clause—clause 17—is how a person who is requesting a hui whaiora is informed. Are they informed of the hui whaiora and the options they have prior to it, because if I’m looking at clause 17(2)(a)(ii), the responsible practitioner must request a hui whaiora if the practitioner is satisfied that “the person under compulsory care— … has requested” it, but a person doesn’t know that there is such a thing as a hui whaiora, how would they request it? I just wanted to check whether, as part of this, a person would be told up front their different options.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: I think that that’s a valid question, and I can confirm that that is the case. The question around decision-making capacity has been well traversed—about the principle of it fluctuating—and that’s why we have the review every three months of the care order and the care plan.

content.speaker: Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour)
content.text: Madam Chair, we may move on from the previous discussion about the amendment and the issues surrounding the separation of mothers and their children. I do want to just put some issues on the record before we move on from that area. Yes, it’s correct that this process isn’t one that can replace a select committee, but we did have a long and fulsome Health Committee hearing and didn’t have the objections that appear to have come from officials raised at that point. For those of us on the Opposition who are considering these very important issues that relate to the human rights of mothers receiving compulsory care, I hope it is understandable to colleagues why it is that we feel we haven’t had a full opportunity to ventilate those issues.

Some of the answers to questions about why the changes are required appear to be somewhat superficial and don’t offer us the reassurance that we might have had if we had either had this discussion at select committee and the opportunity to go into it further with officials, or if we had even had a week of notice and the opportunity to reach out to groups who submitted on these issues, go back to them, and ask their perspective on this change. My colleague, Ingrid Leary, will be caucusing with other members of the Labour caucus about our vote on the amendment. I don’t want to get ahead of whatever decision is made with that, but just to assert that it is very reasonable, for a procedural reason, for the Labour Party to vote against this amendment if that’s the decision colleagues choose to take.

Part 3 Compulsory care, and Schedule 1A

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Members, we come now to Part 3. This is the debate on clauses 41 to 100—“Compulsory care”—and Schedule 1A. The question is that Part 3 stand part.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: Thank you. I have been one of the people bringing the voices of some of those who spoke to us in the Health Committee into the debate, and I intend to do that where it is appropriate, in this section, if that’s alright with the Chair.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: As long as it’s not long.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY
content.text: Given the number of clauses in this rather large bill, we have been running fairly tightly, I would suggest, Madam Chair. If I look at clause 41 now, this is a clause that worries us, because it currently seems to extend powers to non-medical people to be able to make decisions around compulsory care. The questions I have are, really: what has been the basis of this, and has the ministry somehow included in its thinking whether it’s primarily intended to address workforce shortages rather than improve clinical care? I won’t go back into the questions that were raised in the definition phase, but, very clearly, there has been a broadening under some of the definitions of who can make decisions.

My specific questions are: why does clause 41(2) allow any mental health practitioner to be appointed as a responsible practitioner rather than requiring a medical practitioner or a psychiatrist? What clinical decisions are they expected to make under the bill, and are those decisions appropriate to be exercised by someone who is not medically qualified? If they’re not a psychiatrist, who, ultimately, carries responsibility for the diagnosis, the treatment decisions, and the compulsory care reviews? What safeguards are there for the postcode lottery across different districts, where one director may appoint nurses or psychologists in one area, while, in a different area, somebody else might only appoint psychiatrists? If the Government intends psychiatrists ordinarily to perform this role, why is the expectation of that not reflected in the legislation? What evidence demonstrates that extending the role beyond medical practitioners improves patient outcomes?

We do know that we have a shortage of psychiatrists, and that’s, indeed, across the mental health services. The Minister himself alluded to the associate psychologist role and the fact that they do not have clinical competence as currently assessed under the Act. We need to be really clear who is expected to be authorised under this provision and who will be accountable under this provision. Would the Minister look at my amendment 19A, which would tidy this up for him?

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Madam Chair, thank you very much. The substantive part of that line of questioning is around the member’s amendment, which I would not support. The change is unnecessary.

The question was raised about the postcode lottery. Well, I would put the principle of the law that would prevent that postcode lottery, because the Director of Area Mental Health Services needs to be satisfied that the mental health practitioner being appointed has undergone the relevant training and competency. That is important, because only a competent and trained practitioner can properly operate within the scope of practice under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. I want to start with Subpart 1, around compulsory care requirements. I’m going to start with three of the clauses. Starting with clause 41(1), which is that “each person under compulsory care has a responsible practitioner.”, what I can’t find from Part 3 is whether there is a ratio requirement when it comes to how many—

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Dr Xu-Nan, could you just repeat that clause? We just had a distraction here. The Minister is just asking which clause it is.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
content.text: Clause 41(1), page 38.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Thank you.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
content.text: I just want to check if, for each responsible practitioner, there is a ratio for how many persons under compulsory care they should be in charge of.

The second question is on that as well, if the Minister wouldn’t mind clarifying. If you’re looking at regional or rural New Zealand and you have a person under compulsory care, what is the distance or geographical distribution, if that is applicable, of how far a person would need to travel to see—if they do need to see—a responsible practitioner? Or does it allow for, under that clause, the use of audio-visual links, etc.,—people can FaceTime, Zoom, or etc., I just want to kind of understand what it meant by “has a responsible practitioner”. That’s my first question.

My second question is on clause 42(1). This is to do with rōpū whaiora, and it says, “collaborative care team”. I just want to check with the Minister if there is an expectation to what the size of a team is. Presumably, it will be more than one. Has there been any discussions or any base understanding of—are we looking at two to five, etc.? I think that’s also really helpful to know, because, as we see, the intent of the bill is to ensure that people don’t fall through the gaps, so I think that’s an important question.

I am going to jump a little bit—noting that others may have questions before that—but I want to just mention clause 49, which is “Reduction and elimination of seclusion”. I would like to speak to my colleague Kahurangi Carter’s amendment as part of her Amendment Paper 646, noting that there are a few other bits to it on later parts. But I want to speak to her amendment for clause 49. This is something that the Green Party has mentioned. I mentioned in my second reading speech that there doesn’t seem to be a sunset clause when it comes to seclusion. Would the Minister mind considering the amendment, which is to add an extra clause to say that “This section is repealed 5 years after Royal assent”, which would imply that a sunset clause is five years, or would the Minister prefer to give a commitment that we are going to be doing away with seclusion within five years?

Finally, there is the amendment from Kahurangi Carter, inserting new clause 49A, which is just to specify, around the prohibition on the use of seclusion, that a person under compulsory care must not be placed in seclusion. This is, again, something that the submitters have asked for.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair, and thanks to that member for those questions. The first two questions were more around, I suppose, how we operationalise the Act, which I think is a fair question. There’s one around the ratio and the access. This being an operational matter, the guidelines and secondary legislation will guide that practice. And also there was the question around size of the team and, I suppose, multi-disciplinary care planning teams. The size and make-up of a team is expected to reflect the needs of the person.

To the more substantive question around seclusion, I think we’ve heard loud and clear that, as a direction of the country, we need to look towards removing seclusion in our mental health services. The first point I’d raise is it’s not necessarily a question of money. If you look at, potentially, some of the announcements of the last Government around funding into mental health, the data shows seclusion rates actually went up. The conclusion I’ve drawn from being Minister is not only is it about adequate resourcing—I’m not disagreeing with that—there is a particular focus needed on training and the workforce. I would like to share a reflection where I visited an inpatient facility, not far from here, that had actually reached zero seclusion because of a decision made by the clinical leadership team around the culture of the organisation. I think it’s incumbent on us, when we are aware that no comparable countries have achieved the removal of seclusion, that as we move towards potentially being the first country in the world, we ensure that we have the right plan.

I’m comfortable that the regulations in the bill allow for ending seclusion. That’s why I do not believe there needs to be a sunset clause. What I’m also encouraged by is the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission’s recommendation around New Zealand’s first seclusion plan that Health New Zealand has accepted to be published in 2027. My expectation, with that plan, is that it would set out a road map of how we would achieve that and that it would then be incumbent on any Government of the day to ensure that we follow the road map.

The final point I’d make is that the regulations allow for that and actually could be brought well forward from the five-year review and a lot earlier within the regulatory framework that this bill sets up.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. I’m sure we’ll have a number of questions around the Minister’s response to that question on seclusion. I just want to tidy away the last clause that I want to look at before going on to clause 49, which is around care planning. The Minister himself, last night, raised the relationship between the compulsory care order and the person’s care plan under clause 43. It’s important because the compulsory care order authorises compulsory care but the advance directive or the care plan arrangement records a person’s wishes, preferences, and treatments. Understanding what parts of those will be given weight and when is really important.

My questions are: does a compulsory care order compel treatment generally, or does it only authorise the compulsory care that is subject to the treatment safeguards elsewhere in the bill? If a person has an advance mental health directive refusing a particular treatment, how is that reflected under the care plan required under clause 43, and, if they do refuse, what legal effect will that refusal have? Where there is an inconsistency between a care plan and an advance mental health directive, which one of those prevails? And shouldn’t there be a requirement under clause 43 to distinguish between treatment that the person consents to, treatment authorised despite lack of consent under the Act, and treatment that has been expressly refused in an advance mental health directive?

The reason I raise that is because we did hear evidence from people who had been subject to different treatments under the Act—some of them restraint treatments; some of them seclusion. Almost all of them universally talked about the increased trauma and the impact it had on their worsening mental health, and they also talked about not having a voice in the treatment that was applied to them. So, where we have an arrangement where that could be there in writing but there is also the prevailing clauses and powers in the bill, it’s really important to understand what the Minister’s expectation is around how that should prevail and what weight should be given to the wishes of the person receiving the treatment. After this, we intend to go on to seclusion as well.

content.speaker: HŪHANA LYNDON (Green)
content.text: I just wanted to supplement on clause 43 of Part 3 by asking and inviting the Minister to provide an explanation around the role of the whānau of the whaiora who is in care. As we see in the care planning, there’s great detail in terms of the review, the way that notes and the plan need to be updated, the way that the service is being provided to the whaiora, but I haven’t seen, within this part of the legislation, any mention of whānau and what the role of whānau is in the care planning. Further, how is the whānau engaged and kept up to date in terms of care of their whānau member who might be within care at that time? Particularly in the transition component of this clause, where you’re moving from service to service, how is the whānau engaged and how do they maintain connection to the plan of care for their whanaunga or tangata whaiora? I also acknowledge that, maybe, tangata whaiora may not have whānau there in support, so what advocacy or what supports, external to the service, independent or otherwise, may be provided within this care planning process so that whānau or an independent person or agency is there walking alongside the patient in care? Kia ora.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: I thank that member for those questions. I think that the bill, quite rightly, as a part of some of the 10 recommendations, achieves the abuse in care recommendations of new roles, of independent roles, and of advocates as well.

There was a question around involvement of the family, and I think a good example of that is around the new advance mental health directives, where a hui whaiora must be convened if a person under compulsory care does not have an advance mental health directive to assist with decisions about their care. My expectation is that where and as much as it’s appropriate, whānau would be involved; and if there was no whānau, then there would be the use of the new independent role in advocacy roles.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: Turning to seclusion. We did have multiple submissions, including really strong submissions from the Mental Health Commission, page 10, clauses 47 to 50, and also the Ombudsman, pages 18, 19, 20—particularly point 88.

The question that we have is it feels like there is a practicality kind of “we don’t have the resourcing to do this, but we might be able to one day”, and when I heard the Minister talk about a plan being ready in 2027, that sounds like we are inching at a snail’s pace to something that both the Minister has experienced and also we, on the select committee, had heard, has been able to be achieved in this country through planning, culture change, training and so on. So my questions are: if he’s saying that seclusion is an objective of the bill, why is he still declining to set an end date? Doesn’t he accept that if there isn’t an end date, there is less incentive to change the system? The whole point of statutory safeguards is to require systems to get up to speed with things like human rights protections and so on. And, particularly, if there had been a workforce training and resourcing statutory requirement, which is in my amendment, which I think the Minister is probably going to decline, in the workforce capability, then that would be really helpful, because it would set the Minister’s expectation. He’s said it’s his expectation, but there’s nothing in the legislation that reflects that expectation of the Minister. This would strengthen the expectation and make it very clear to the institutions what they need to do and there would be the requirement for there to be adequate funding.

What evidence does he have that five years is the right amount of time to transition away from seclusion? The Minister will be aware of my tabled amendment that says, “at least have two yearly reviews”, so that we can put some kind of pressure on the system to show the direction of travel. What message does retaining an indefinite statutory power to seclusion send to those services who had managed to eliminate it? It’s not just in Wellington; there is one in Auckland as well.

I’m curious to know if it’s the Government’s position that seclusion will always remain necessary somewhere in the system. I know there are different clinical and professional views on this, and I’d like to have on the Hansard what the Minister’s view is on that. I don’t have a position for or against it because I know there’s a lot of discussion and evidence, but it would be helpful to understand what the Minister’s own expectation is of that.

If we’re not ready to move to seclusion, can he tell us what specific workforce, infrastructure or funding milestones remain outstanding? If services are not ready today, isn’t that why the transition period of five years, which does seem generous and does seem proportionate—isn’t that the right time frame to be able to get that in order?

The final couple of points are really that he’s talked about regulation being able to be used in the bill to end seclusion, but, equally, there are force and search powers, in and clause 204, that also relate to those limitations on human rights. That worries us because we all know that any limitation on human rights should be in primary legislation. Wouldn’t it be better to lift and drop both of those elements into the bill? The sunsetting of seclusion as well as the limitations on people through force and search powers—once again, it is feeling like bad law making to be relegating that to regulation. I agree seclusion could be done through that, which is less problematic, but if we’re going to do that, we should have everything in primarily legislation, so we avoid the issues caused by clause 204.

Finally, the Minister has talked about the fact that seclusion won’t apply to under-18-year-olds. That’s something we absolutely welcome. The reason that we’re given also for the non-ending of seclusion is that other restrictive practices that could be harmful, as harmful, or even more harmful to adults will occur as a result. Now, the Minister can’t have it both ways. If that is the logic relating to adults, surely that is the logic relating to young people—many of whom, we have established, are also in these adult secure mental health facilities. Against the backdrop of what we were discussing in the committee last night and with Waikari Hospital and the Otago Daily Times story this morning, I think it’s important, particularly, to hear the Minister’s view about whether there could be an unintended consequence in the way the bill divides up the rights of under-18-year-olds with adults as we discussed seclusion.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: There’s a bit in there, so I’ll step through it. I suppose we are slightly returning to Part 1. If I remind members that one of the principles in this bill is the principle of the least restrictive practice, the second is that this bill brings in quite significant safeguards. I’m confident that we are heading in the right direction as a country. When we came into office, seclusion rates had significantly increased, and the data shows that they have now significantly reduced. So we are on a direction as a country.

As previously said, I’m confident that we’ve got the right regulatory framework to ensure that we continue that direction as we work with the mental health system. I’m acutely aware, as that member is, there is actually a wide-ranging number of views within the existing workforce, and other advocates within the system, that I think we need to bring along in that journey as well.

There is a concern by some of the workforce around the risk of removing seclusion, and I think that does need to be acknowledged; and others, as was well-canvassed during the select committee stage, are concerned about the unintended consequences of seeing a reduction in seclusion but, actually, then seeing an increase in chemical and physical restraint as well.

There was a question about why we are confident we can remove seclusion or prohibit seclusion in under-18s but not apply the same measure in over-18s. Well, the advice around under-18s is that it is a very small number of young people that are secluded. I’ve just got the number here: 32 young people across all inpatient services in 2023-24, compared to 561 adults.

The point I’d make there is that it’s very emblematic of past Governments that think they can put an end date somewhere and it will just happen. I think what we’ve shown around the reduction and the prohibition of seclusion for young people in this bill is that if we take a targeted approach, we can continue to reduce the numbers. That’s why the regulatory framework allows for that and also New Zealand’s first seclusion plan.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. I just have one follow-up question on seclusion for the Minister for Mental Health, and then I’m going to move on to subsequent clauses. This is to do with new clause 49(1A), and it’s to do with reporting annually. Can I just check: as a part of that reporting, would the Minister have an expectation that the average hours and the maximum hours that a person spent in seclusion will also be reported as a part of that report, particularly consecutive hours?

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: That data is already collected. I think it’s a very important point, because it’s not only the unique numbers of people under care but it is the total number of seclusion events, the total number of hours in seclusion, and also the ability to identify where the seclusion is happening within each individual in-patient facility or wider setting as well. We’ve also got the reporting on population groups, because, as we do know, Māori are overrepresented in seclusion rates. That’s why I welcome the public reporting.

Not only that, when you look at the seclusion regime that this is bringing in, there is a lot more requirement now on reporting. Services now have to report every time there is a seclusion, with the reasons why there is as well. That’s why this gives me comfort that, with the framework that this bill sets up, we can continue the direction of travel around reducing and, ultimately, eliminating seclusion.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you for that, Minister. I think that is really heartening to hear, and I think, in that, I also implied that there would be reporting on consecutive hours as well.

I want to move on to clause 50, and this is on ECT, electroconvulsive therapy, and again it’s to do with reporting. I’m looking at clause 50(2): “The responsible practitioner must record the use …”. I wanted to check: with that recording, will they, again, record the frequency of the use on an individual? Again, it’s part of that broader, I guess, accountability mechanism. That’s my question.
I know that others may have additional questions, but to signal to you, Madam Chair, my last question on Subpart 1 is on clause 52(1)(d), and that’s the right to repeal or review.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: You may as well ask it now.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
content.text: Yeah, I’m going to ask that now, and then, depending on the Minister’s response, I’m done with Subpart 1 and I’m happy to move on to Subpart 2.

I want to check with the Minister: paragraph (d) says, “a Judge of the High Court …”. Can I just check whether it is only the High Court that is able to have the right to review this, and is there any sort of advice that the Minister has received on how frequently we would be looking at this anyway? Would it put a strain on the High Court system?

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Just to tie off those last questions around seclusion and electroconvulsive therapy, I think the member Lawrence Xu-Nan does raise an important requirement around reporting and publicly publishing that data. That’s something that I take quite seriously. That would be my expectation.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: I’ll take a call from Ingrid Leary, but I have to say that, on this part, we just need to be focusing on changes—any changes—now.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: Thanks, Madam Chair. I note that, in the definitions section, there doesn’t seem to be a definition of seclusion.

In the Wakari Hospital incident, one of the things that has emerged is that people suffered serious seclusion that wasn’t recorded as seclusion, because of the circumstance of the building. I’m wondering if the Minister could respond to how we’re going to be able to capture those events under the bill, and whether he would entertain a definition of seclusion, to be able to make that something that institutions couldn’t wiggle out of because they don’t have a formal seclusion-type room.

I do think, Madam Chair, we’ve only just started the questioning on electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). ECT is highly controversial, and I think it’s important for the public to know that we looked at this as a select committee really carefully and we’re pretty happy about—

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: I did hear questioning about ECT in last night’s session, so this is specifically around any amendments or adjustments.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY
content.text: Sure. We’re pretty happy about where we’ve landed with safeguards, but we still think there could be additional safeguards. They’re only minor. One of them would be for the consent to be called “fully informed consent” and to take into account future side effects of ECT. The other one was something to ensure the independence of two psychiatrists, because sometimes psychiatrists can work together, or may not—they simply rubberstamp other people’s notes. There are amendments on the Table to that effect. Those are my questions on ECT. I do have more questions on this part, Madam Chair.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. Look, the continual reference to Wakari—patients at Wakari are actually under different legislation, the Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act, so that is clearly out of scope. I have been advised that the seclusion definition is in secondary legislation, and that allows for the adjustment with new practices as well.

I would like to say, in response to the question, that I do welcome the changes at select committee. I think, when you look at Part 1, the principles of the Act are ensuring that we do have safeguards. I welcome now the new safeguards, especially around the second opinions, also around the reporting as well—if you look at seclusion specifically, around having identified seclusion rooms as well. My view is that this bill gives more confidence around the existing practice of seclusion.

Within electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), of course, there was a range of views at the select committee. I respect that. We heard from the Hon Ayesha Verrall in the second reading about her concern and whether we should prohibit the use of ECT, but actually, through the select committee process, the validation and the clinical evidence—but, of course, it is around the safeguards, and I welcome the changes made here today to ensure that we do have those better safeguards.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: Going to clause 70, just a quick question: I know that the Mental Health Bill has been through the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act process, but has he specifically considered section 7 of the Human Rights Act, the requirement of the Attorney-General to bring into the House of Representatives any bill that could be deemed inconsistent or any provision, in relation to community care orders? In other words, what specific advice has he had on that?

I turn now to clause 80. This is around what we heard could be a change in the threshold regarding the determinations that are made. In the previous bill, the practitioners were required to make determinations, and that language is not used in the current bill. There were submissions to suggest that that reduces the level of protection for tāngata whaiora. We know that “reasonable grounds to believe” has been removed from a lot of the provisions, which is really good, but we still don’t have a determination one. We have words like “in their opinion” rather than a determination, which would seem to have a higher clinical threshold. Can he explain if he is happy with that language and why he’s chosen that language rather than determinations?

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: The Minister’s just looking for something, Ingrid Leary, did you have another—Ingrid Leary, the Minister’s just looking up some answers. Did you have further questions?

content.speaker: Ingrid Leary
content.text: I’ll cede to Lawrence Xu-Nan at this point.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. I indicated I’m happy to move on to Subpart 2. I actually only have one question for Subpart 2, on compulsory care assessment. I think Schedule 1A is actually very clear in terms of the process. My only question is around clause 57(1)(a) specifically. This is page 48, line 15. Again, this is when we’re looking at the first assessment. I want to check with the Minister—again, you get the Director of Area Mental Health Services determining the mental health practitioner. Can I just check if that practitioner—I’m just checking, unless I missed it—is able to conduct that first assessment using audiovisual links? For example, I’m, again, thinking about distribution and distance to travel, etc., for rural and regional areas where it might potentially be quite hard to have access to a mental health practitioner to determine that first assessment. I want to the check with the Minister if there’s any consideration of how that could work.

I now want to move on to clause 73. This is in Subpart 3, and this is page 56. The reason I want to speak to this clause—and my question and my next question—is to do with the Minister’s amendment on clause 73 and clause 81. I want to check with the Minister: in clause 73(3)(c), why has the term “proposed” been removed in the Minister’s amendment? Is it just simply to do with the fact—I’m just going to check that there is no explanatory note on this particular bit. Can I just check: is it because the care plan is already in effect, therefore it is not a proposed one, and that’s why that word was removed?

My final question for this contribution is on clause 81, and this is to do with the Minister’s amendment as well. We’re looking at, possibly, the top of page 60, right after line 7, and that’s to do with if the responsible practitioner considers that a person under compulsory care meets the compulsory care criteria. It’s about the record that’s being sent. The Minister’s amendment added this new Director of Area Mental Health Services. I just want to check if there is anyone else who should also be sent a copy, assuming that this is quite a last-minute thing. For example, a person I could think of is—I just mentioned before in terms of the assessment that there is a requirement for the mental health practitioner to conduct an assessment, but I don’t know if the mental health practitioner needs to be also sent a report or if that is encapsulated under clause 81(3)(c) as the primary health care provider. Any clarifications on the Minister’s amendment for clauses 73 and 81 would be appreciated.

content.speaker: Ingrid Leary
content.text: Madam Chair.

content.speaker: Hon Matt Doocey
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair—

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Ingrid Leary—oh, sorry, the honourable Minister.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: There’s a few questions I’ll gather up there around the question of the section 7. The bill was vetted for consistency with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act and considered, in its entirety, to be consistent.

There was a question from Ingrid Leary about the amendment in her name—number 80, if I understand that to be correct—about questioning the reference to “in their opinion”. I’ve been advised that the current reference “in their opinion” makes it clear that the status review decision requires careful assessment to form a reasoned opinion, not just an issued decision.
The questions from Lawrence Xu-Nan, in only, respectfully, a way Lawrence Xu-Nan can, I think some of them by the end of it answered his own questions around clarification. If I don’t—

content.speaker: Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan
content.text: OK. That’s helpful.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY
content.text: Ha, ha! If I don’t answer your questions, then do let me know.
There was one around the practitioner being able to conduct first assessment using audiovisual links (AVL) as well. Clause 215 sets it out when AVL can be used.

There was the question around who would be notified at certain points of the care planning process. Of course, there is the principle of confidentiality. The person under care can nominate people as well, and we expect when this bill is operationalised, we do have comprehensive care planning processes as well.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: I was about to take a call from Ingrid Leary, so I’ll come back.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: Thank you. Moving to clause 85, this is the subsection that talks about the expiry and extension of mental health care orders and, again, involves people making decisions that potentially have an impact on the human rights of those who they’re deciding about. Some of these do seem to be broader in scope than the current Act. Therefore, it’s important to ask questions about them.

The first one is the first extension, which is six months. What additional safeguards, if any, are provided before a person’s compulsory care order is extended to the first six months, and how will the responsible practitioner make the determination about whether they should be under a compulsory care order or whether they’d be better supported through voluntary care? What weight must be given to evidence that the person has regained decision-making capacity or is engaging voluntarily? Does he expect the first extension to be the exception rather than the norm—it would be good to have that on the record—but also, if so, how will that expectation be monitored? There doesn’t seem to be anything in the bill around that, so it would be good to hear what kind of operational monitoring might be occurring.

There’s also, in clause 86, second and subsequent extensions, where, after the first extension, the court can grant an order for up to 12 months, and the Government has increased the maximum duration of subsequent extensions to that level. The committee changed the wording to say for a period of “up to” 12 months, but it does create questions, because it means there’s a discretion. What factors does he expect the court to consider when deciding whether an extension should be, say, three months, six months, or the full 12 months? Wouldn’t it be important, if there is that discretion, which is implicit, to have some safeguarding wording around that?

There are also questions about whether an annual judicial review is sufficient for monitoring those extensions. That means that once a year, there will be some kind of report done, but somebody could potentially just have the order extended over and over again without any kind of transparency or ability in the system to be able to see it as a milestone or a gate to reassess, so what’s in place in the bill to do that? Is there anything in clause 86 that requires the court to grant the shortest extension reasonably necessary, and, if so, can he point to that, please? How will he ensure that there will be consistency across different courts, because at the moment the legislation is silent on that?

I guess we’re really wanting to see some direction from the Minister, given that there isn’t the safeguarding, necessarily, in the bill, of his expectations of how these two clauses, 85 and 86, will, in practice, be delivered.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Thank you. There were the statements made around decision-making capacity and the criteria for being placed under compulsory care. I’m confident they are explicit in the bill. The more substantive question at the end there around the 12 months with the care order—I would just point to the key principle of the legislation, the least restrictive practice, as well as the additional safeguards. What gives me great confidence and also why this meets 10 of the abuse in care recommendations is that there may be a 12-month order, but, of course, because of the requirement for a review every three months, if a person is deemed not to be required to be under the Act, then they won’t remain under the Act.

content.speaker: Hon Member
content.text: Madam Chair—Madam Chair.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Barbara Kuriger)
content.text: Hūhana Lyndon. I said I’d take a call from Hūhana Lyndon.

content.speaker: HŪHANA LYNDON (Green)
content.text: Kia aroha mai [ [sorry], Madam Chair—we skipped ahead, and I wanted to take us back to page 46 for a quick question with the Minister in regards to section 53, in the “Release from compulsory care”. It notes that at any time when a responsible practitioner considers that a patient under compulsory care does not meet the criteria for compulsory care anymore, that the person must be released immediately—ka pai. But then when there’s a disagreement that might occur, the case gets referred on to the Mental Health Review Tribunal. My question is, because we’ve heard data around both youth and overall adult, those who are retained within compulsory care, the monitoring function and the retention of data and reporting of how many contests or challenges around the review of release of release of care—is that recorded? Will it be made public, as a part of the reporting, to show the progress in the way that we are being robust in considering our retention of a person and release of a person from care?

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. I think it’s actually a very important question about the Mental Health Review Tribunal. As I sketched out to the previous member’s question—around the three-monthly review and being discharged from the Act—where there is a disagreement, I suppose, from the person under compulsory care and the responsible practitioner, it does go to the review. So I’m happy to commit to that capturing of the data and publishing it. If that’s not happening already, then that will happen.
