content.text: Members, we come now to our final debate, which is on clauses 1 and 2: “Title” and “Commencement”.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I think it might also be wise to clarify for the committee that while we support the bill overall, we do not support the Minister’s amendment on Amendment Paper 648 to change “Pae Ora (Healthy Futures)” to “Healthy Futures (Pae Ora)”. That was a bill that we did not support and, therefore, I think that in the essence of consistency, we cannot support that part of the amendment.

On the commencement date, the Minister for Mental Health, on his Amendment Paper 648, has changed or, more accurately, has pushed out the commencement date of this bill by a year, and so I think, if it’s OK for the Minister just to give—oh, wait. Let me finish, let me finish. If the Minister wouldn’t mind just elucidating for the committee on why it has been pushed out.

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Look, that’s a very important question, and the quicker we can answer that, the quicker we get on to the third reading. I would point to the current legislation that we’re repealing here. It dates back to 1992. We’re now in 2026. This is a once-in-a-generation, 30-year repeal and replacement of the mental health Act. There are significant changes in the mental health Act that we are bringing into force today. It was always the intention that we would give the health system in New Zealand two years to respond to these changes, and that is why I’m very confident that with this new commencement date, we send a very clear signal.

On saying that, I do want to acknowledge Health New Zealand, from the board right down to our front-line workforce, who, even before this bill will receive Royal assent, have been actively working on the changes that we are proposing. But let’s be very clear: the point of this bill is to ensure that we provide high-quality compulsory mental health care, and I think it’s only right to ensure that we have the appropriate lead times, as was the original intent for this bill when it went through the select committee stage.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. Thank you for that response, Minister. Just two quick questions on top of that, and one may have been partially answered. I wanted to check this in terms of clause 2(2), and this is specifically to do with Schedule 1 and some of the transitional measures, as well. In terms of some of the current concerns that we have about the system, does the Minister think that the transitional measures are sufficient for the commencement date to be pushed out by two years—with that being my first question.
My second question is a very short one, and it’s more of a curiosity. If this bill is being passed in 2026, can it still be called “the Mental Health Act 2024.”?

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: Can I just correct that, and language is important, because we are here today—and have been for four and a half hours—debating the committee of the whole House stage, but the date has not been pushed back. It was always the intention to have a two-year commencement, quite rightly, because Health New Zealand is a big system, and I wanted to ensure that we give the very hard-working front-line mental health and addiction workforce—it’s my support for them to give them this lead time.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: I’m only planning to take one call on this title. I want to echo the Minister’s accolades to our very hard-working mental health staff all over the country for the incredible work that they do under pretty difficult circumstances and, it’s probably fair to say, through successive Government failures to enable them to work in up-to-date and modern facilities, which would make it easier for them to uphold the human rights of our tangata whaiora.

Having said that, I do wonder if we’ve got the name of the bill right. I note that previously, the name of the Act was the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992, and given that we’ve only done a number of fairly incremental changes, in my view—we’ve talked a lot about what we want to do and the direction of travel, but we haven’t really legislated for that—I do wonder if we should make the title really simple and just call it the “Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment) Act”.

The reason I say that is because the Mental Health Bill makes it sound like this is a bill that is going to advance people’s mental health, and I don’t know that it does. Certainly, on this side of the House, what we are looking to do is recognise that mental health is a journey and that mental wellbeing is the destination, and that people cycle in and out. What we have, really, is a bill before us that is very much in the minutiae—as it should be—of when people can be held against their will and have their human rights restricted. So calling it the “Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment) Bill”, in my view, would better encapsulate that.

If it was a mental health bill, I would rather see more provisions in there that were around providing the environment where mental health staff could really lean into the mental wellbeing and recovery of tāngata whaiora, including things like safeguarding for children the environments that children are expected to be kept in, and explicit safeguarding for their development in times of being kept against their will or under the bill; the same for our Māori tāngata whaiora in culturally appropriate care settings, and with culturally appropriate care being delivered. That hasn’t really been legislated for in this bill. There were opportunities to do that through the tabled amendments that we put on the Table, including provisions for people to give effect to Te Tiriti all the way through the various parts of the bill, rather than just having a kind of holistic overview in clause 5.

Alternatively, I think we could call this the “Mental Health (Lost Opportunity) Bill”. That sounds a little cynical, but that is based on the Amendment Paper that the Government brought to the House a couple of days ago, where we did manage to get some real safeguarding for mothers and babies. We know that perinatal mental health is extremely important. We have some of the worst statistics in the world when it comes to maternal suicides, and the involvement of mothers and being able to stay with their babies forms a huge part of their mental wellbeing. When we discussed this at select committee, we were very careful to choose words that would ensure that the safety of the baby was paramount and that the wellbeing and safety of the mothers and babies were paramount. And yet, at the eleventh hour, we had this change to the wording in the amendment. It just loosened all of that quite considerably because it suddenly said, in new clause 38A(1A)(a), “must give priority to the safety and well-being of the baby; and (b) must make reasonable endeavours to consider”. So it wasn’t even a consideration, it was “reasonable endeavours to consider”.
It then also talked about the views of guardians, and we heard a nominal response to our questions about parenting orders and parenting arrangements—

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: I just wonder whether this is a wee way away from the title, and the third reading coming up might be the opportunity.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY
content.text: Sure, Mr Chair, but the point that I’m making is that we really didn’t have a chance to interrogate that. We were minded of this House, if we had had satisfactory answers to our questions on that amendment, to have voted in favour of the Government amendment. We couldn’t satisfy ourselves that we could do that because we didn’t get the opportunity to ask the questions to ensure that mothers would still be able to stay with their babies in the same way as had been intended. That is why I think we could call this the “Mental Health (Lost Opportunity) Bill” because it looks like the amendment that we don’t support is going to erode the one change—the one change—that we were able to make that had any significance, really, in the select committee stage.

Legislative Statement

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: I present a legislative statement on the Mental Health Bill.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House. It can be found on the Parliament website.
Third Reading

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health)
content.text: I move, That the Mental Health Bill be now read a third time.

It is a privilege to stand here as New Zealand’s first mental health Minister, today, at the final stage of this bill. This legislation represents a significant step forward, modernising a system that is more than 30 years old, and bringing it up to date with how we expect mental health care to be to be delivered in this country.

The bill sits within the Government’s broader commitment to improve the effectiveness of mental health and addiction services. It responds to long-standing calls for reform, and contributes to the Government’s response to the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Historical Abuse in State Care and in the Care of Faith-based Institutions, ensuring our system is grounded in human rights, safety, and effective care. It also builds on the work already under way to strengthen our mental health system: improving access, growing the workforce, and strengthening crisis support by helping ensure people receive effective recovery-focused care when they need it.

At its core, this bill shifts us towards a more right space and recovery-focused approach, placing people at the centre of their care and supporting them to make decisions about their own support and recovery wherever possible. It provides a modern legislative framework for when compulsory care is needed as a last resort, while protecting the rights of people under compulsory care and ensuring care is therapeutic, delivered in the least restrictive way, and responsive to individual needs.

I want to acknowledge two areas where the bill introduces particularly important changes. First, on seclusion, the bill takes a much stronger approach to reducing, and, over time, eliminating the use of seclusion. It prohibits its use for children and young people, and strengthens safeguards and oversight to drive its reduction across the system as we work collectively towards eliminating this practice.

Second, on the use of electroconvulsive therapy, or ECT, I want to be clear that while ECT remains an important treatment option for some people, the bill lifts the threshold for its use and puts stronger safeguards in place to ensure it is only used in tightly controlled circumstances in line with best practice.

The bill has been the subject of extensive scrutiny by the Health Committee, which received hundreds of submissions and heard directly from people with lived experience: families, clinicians, advocates, and community organisations. As I’ve said before, I want to acknowledge those who shared their experiences. Your input has directly strengthened this legislation.

Through the committee stage, a number of targeted amendments have been made to ensure the legislation is clear, workable, and provides strong safeguards in practice. These include clarifications to ensure powers and rights are clear for those working under the legislation, such as clarifying when police detention powers begin and end, strengthening requirements for recording and oversight, and refining provisions to ensure they are workable in practice, including those relating to the care of birthing parents and their newborns.

The changes also ensure that the Ministry of Health can require Health New Zealand to provide the information needed to support the ministry’s regulatory monitoring and assurance role. These changes matter and ensure that the intent of the legislation can be delivered effectively on the ground. Ultimately, this will mean people receive care that is more respectful, more responsive, and more focused on supporting their recovery. It ensures people can access care when they need it, while putting stronger protections around how that care is delivered.

While the passing of this bill is a major milestone, I also want to acknowledge the significant amount of work that lies ahead for the sector to implement these changes. This is why the commencement date has been updated to ensure the sector has a full two-year lead-in period following enactment. This reflects feedback from the sector about the need to prepare for these changes and implement them safely.

This is now a bill that is fit for purpose, well scrutinised, and ready to become law. The process has had integrity. People have been heard, concerns have been addressed, and the legislation has been improved as a result. The Mental Health Bill represents a modern, balanced, and more effective approach to compulsory mental health care in New Zealand. Today marks a significant milestone for our mental health system.

To close, I want to acknowledge the many people that have contributed to the development of this legislation, particularly those with lived experience. I want to thank them and their families for helping to improve the system for others in the future. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: The question is that the motion be agreed.

content.speaker: INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri)
content.text: It is ironic today that we are talking about updating mental health laws when the front page of the Otago Daily Times has shone a light on the Ombudsman’s findings of some of the worst abuses of human rights he’s ever encountered at Wakari Hospital, which is detaining people who have mental health issues and intellectual disabilities. I’m not going to go into some of the abuses that they endured, but needless to say, it is just a stark example of why our laws need reforming but also why the legislative safeguards need to be in the reformed laws so that we never ever encounter that kind of abuse again.

We hear that too often in this House. We have the abuse in State care, the abuse in faith-based care, the abuse in Wakari. We have this bill before us, which is certainly an improvement on the current mental health Act, but I know for many tāngata whaiora and people working in the sector, it does not go far enough, and it really does feel like a missed opportunity for us, given that it is unlikely to come back before this House, as the Minister has said, for a decade or perhaps 20 or 30 years. The reason I say that is because we still have the binary definitions of mental health competence in this bill that fly in the face of best practice internationally, which would suggest that better outcomes are reached if people are assessed on their competence on a decision-by-decision basis. Mental competence is a fluctuating experience. It is not a state or a label to be put on to a person. The application of the law as it will currently happen under this bill doesn’t allow us to get up to speed with that international thinking.

The other element is around the participation of tāngata whaiora. A lot of noise has been made in the House about their increased participation, and, indeed, there are some avenues now for them to have more of a voice. But if we were really going to look at the evidence and take an evidence-based approach, I think it’s worth putting on the record that the Health Committee saw no evidence that compulsory care orders work for the 6,000 people in our communities who currently live under them, and yet there is good evidence from other jurisdictions and studies conducted by people in New Zealand to show that those who participate voluntarily in their own mental health journey are far more likely to achieve states of wellbeing and to be in recovery. If we really wanted to make this a mental health bill, we missed the opportunity to think through how we could reduce the number of people on compulsory care orders and how we could skill up the sector and resource the sector to really be able to walk alongside our tāngata whaiora and their families to enable wellbeing.

Instead, what we are often seeing is people cycling in and out of the system—feeling well enough to be out in the community, sometimes well enough to work; an event happens or a crisis point is reached, for whatever reason, in their mental health, and they’re back into the hospital system and back under the Act. We need to be more aspirational than that. We need to be looking at the evidence that tells us how people can achieve recovery longer. I fear that in looking and focusing our efforts on the compulsion elements of this bill, we missed the opportunity to look at recovery through participation.

We also don’t want to overstate the changes that have been made to seclusion, because media seem to be a little confused in saying that this bill will end seclusion. Let me state very clearly in this House: it will not end seclusion. It does signal a direction of travel, and there will be an opportunity for regulations to be made, but certainly the ending of seclusion needs to be led with a legislative commitment. The order of events would seem to make sense to me that when legislation requires something to be done, then resources are freed up and the sector is trained and things happen to enable the legislation, because people do not want to act unlawfully. Without that legislative commitment, I fear that we are simply kicking the can down the road, and with the best will in the world, if we also don’t have legislative safeguards to then monitor how we are doing according to those performance plans of trying to implement an end to seclusion, how are we going to actually measure progress?

The reviews in place for seclusion are five-yearly. What we said in our dissenting opinion on the bill, although we’re supporting the bill, is that we wanted seclusion to be sunsetted within five years. That felt like a reasonable amount of time. We heard a lot of really positive comments from the Minister about all the good moves that are happening currently in the sector to sunset seclusion and to have people trained up and be competent to do that. There are two really good examples in Auckland and Wellington where that has actually happened. Instead of being bold and sunsetting seclusion in five years and then providing the enablers through the legislation, it does feel like we’ve kicked the can down the road. This bill won’t come into effect for a year or two, and so it’s going to be an even longer time. Again, what we don’t have is the requirement to report on it, which could have been made available through some of the 40 or so amendments that we put on the Table.

The other area of strengthening that would have been really valuable would be for vulnerable communities. I’m thinking here about our under-18-year-olds. We heard lots of very powerful submissions about how damaging the current compulsory care orders and the current compulsion under the Act is for our young people, and for them to be accessing adult services. If they are to access adult services while we try to step up resourcing for child-friendly ones, we should at least have legislative safeguards to make sure that those places take into account that they’re young. They need space to be able to move, they need sunlight, they need to feel that they’re in a culturally appropriate setting for their own personal identity, and they need to be able to continue to develop as human beings as they cycle in and out of competence under the Act. We have not put any of those safeguards in, because there is a failure, I think, from the Government to recognise the need for equity in this legislation.

The same applies to the lip service paid to Māori. We have a clause 5 that doesn’t really require application of Te Tiriti principles across different parts of the Act, and certainly no recognition that tāngata whaiora Māori make up the vast numbers of those who are impacted under mental health compulsory orders, particularly in seclusion. If that’s the case, why don’t we give them the assurance that they have been considered and safeguarded? Why didn’t we put those safeguards in?

It’s the same for our neurodivergent and disabled community. Time and time again, it is our disabled community who bear the biggest brunt of abuses to human rights, and yet they are expected to be scooped up in the general provisions of the bill rather than having explicit mention, including the ways that they present in the world, the ways that they communicate, and the assumptions that cannot be made about them when somebody is looking to put them under the powers of the Act.

There was a real opportunity to do that: not only to safeguard their human rights but to send them a message from this House that we do recognise the abuses that have happened, we do recognise their vulnerability, and we do recognise their need for safeguarding. Once again, we have failed that community and I find that quite heart-breaking actually.

The other two areas that are interesting—one is interesting; one is disappointing. The interesting one is that when it comes to children and young people, we welcome the fact that they cannot be kept in seclusion, but we did not hear why they would still be protected from other forms of restraint that could be as bad or worse than seclusion. The reason I raise that is that was the Minister’s response to why we can’t end seclusion for adults: that they could become more vulnerable with other forms of restraint. Now, the logic doesn’t apply both ways and I have a real fear now that our young people, without these extra safeguards, may find themselves in other restraint situations such as with medication or physical restraints that will replace seclusion given that we haven’t safeguarded them.

Finally, there’s the Amendment Paper that was dropped on the Table. We had very little chance to scrutinise it. The Government had months and months to get those changes to us. They were hard-won changes to try and recognise mothers and babies and the need to keep them together unless there are safety issues for the child in particular. We had the wording down pat, it looked safe, the officials had advised us on it, and suddenly there was this Amendment Paper that seemed to undo that presumption and make it much more of a balancing act and involving the opinions of other people—non-clinical opinions and opinions that are not about the safety of the child or the mother. We do support this bill, but we think it could have gone a lot further.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. The Green Party does support this bill, but as the previous speaker has alluded to, there are some serious concerns with this, which will hopefully see further improvements as this bill gets implemented. I do want to acknowledge the engagement from the Minister for Mental Health as part of the committee of the whole House stage; I want to acknowledge the members of the Health Committee; and of course my colleague Kahurangi Carter, who is our mental health spokesperson, in her role in all of this; but also, most importantly, acknowledging the communities, tāngata whaiora, and everyone who submitted and shared their personal stories as we went through the process of this bill. We did have quite a robust discussion during the committee stages on all aspects of this bill. It is quite a substantial bill, with eight parts, and I think, considering a bill of this nature may not come to the House again in a while, it’s important for us to be able to discuss each of these parts in detail.

I think as a part of Part 1, we were looking at the overall purpose and principles. That is incredibly crucial, and I think the fundamental aspect of that—with any purpose clause—is whether they are an aspiration or they are binding. It’s good to hear from the Minister that it is binding; this is something that could be challenged in a court of law if any of our system doesn’t uphold that particular purpose. It’s also heartening, as we go through the rest of the bill, for the Minister to keep drawing back to the principles of this bill. I think that’s an important consistency that we would expect—and we expect no less as this bill gets implemented.

I do want to mention that there are different areas of disappointment for the Greens that we believe could have gone further—reflecting submissions, both the voices from the community but also upon reflection of the most recent royal commission of inquiry around abuse in care and how we can do better as a country overall when it comes to upholding the rights of disabled people here in general and also our global obligation under international conventions around human rights.

Even though we hear from the Minister that the principle of the bill is going with the least restrictive way, we are disappointed that the Government has not, and the Minister has not, accepted my colleague Kahurangi Carter’s amendments around having community and voluntary care as the default and only using compulsory care as a final resort. The fact is that there is currently no specific commitment around the provision of that community care to ensure that there is wraparound support for the wellbeing of tangata whaiora. I think that is an area that we’re hoping we can see improvements as we see in other parts of the health sector in terms of the community health sector, where we’re looking at people wanting to have that home and community care as a starting point and move on to other parts of care only as required.

The other thing that is worth noting in terms of Part 1—which ostensibly could be the most important part because it sets that basis of how we are to understand the rest of this bill and particularly the operationalisation of this bill—that I feel could potentially be a bit of a gap is around clause 8 of this bill regarding the meaning and also under what grounds assessment should not be taken. There are just a little bit of consistency issues when it comes to that and section 21 of the Human Rights Act where certain areas have not been considered. I think when we’re looking at the further part in Part 8, and we’re looking at removal from New Zealand, that during the committee stage we discussed what happens if, for example, for certain cultures and for certain regions unfortunately sex is still an important factor and maybe a considered factor, but that’s not a ground for there to be prohibited grounds for compulsory assessment. I think there are some consistency issues there that will be interesting to see how they would develop.

Moving on to other parts of this bill, noting that the Minister had an Amendment Paper, in most cases we are happy with the minor updates that the Minister has made. But as we heard from the previous speaker, Ingrid Leary, new clause 38A that the Minister has made around the ability for a birthing parent to be entitled to have the baby remain with them is a bit of a concern and does seem like a move away from what the Health Committee has come to in terms of the point they’re making, which is unfortunate.

I think I also want to acknowledge my colleague Kahurangi Carter and her Amendment Paper around the sunset clause for seclusion. Yes, although we’re hearing from the Minister that there is a general moving away, there is no fixed deadline or requirement for there to be no seclusion here. As well as both in terms of seclusion, but also what we’re seeing in clause 50 of this bill around electroconvulsive therapy, I do implore—and it’s good to hear from the Minister as a part of the response—that we can do better in how we report on that and the level of detail that we can report. In the case of seclusion, we must have transparency around the hours that people are spending, particularly the consecutive hours that people are spending in seclusion, which the previous speaker has also alluded to as some of the more egregious findings most recently by the Ombudsman.

In terms of other parts of the bill, I want to tie in a few of the parts, particularly in Part 4, when we’re looking at the forensic compulsive care. I think that’s an interesting interaction with something that we have seen just recently in the House around the debate on the declaration of inconsistency with PPOs and EPOs—with public protection orders and extended protection orders—and what that would mean in the context of the forensic compulsory care.

Particularly, I am still a little bit concerned in terms of the response from the Minister on how some of that biometric data could potentially be used and stored. I think this is an area that has not had thorough consideration. As a member of the Justice Committee, I know that this is something that the Justice Committee actually comes across reasonably frequently. It’s important for us to make sure that, across different agencies and different systems in our public sector, we do have that consistency on biometric data. We’re obviously seeing some of the more concerning areas with biometric data use—most recently within Immigration as well, particularly with The Migration Five—so I think that is an important consideration to make.

Further on in terms of the area we’re looking at with the Mental Health Review Tribunal, it’s also important to note that we did get reassurance from the Minister that the Mental Health Review Tribunal is able to not only actively initiate a review of specific cases or a care plan but also is able to undertake their own research. I think, most importantly, it is heartening to hear that the Minister has made that commitment that the decisions that the Mental Health Review Tribunal make are decisions; they’re not recommendations. We expect there to be a binding nature to that.

Finally, I think it’s also important to discuss that we did also go through some of the offences and regulations. Again, all of these provide the overall package in this particular area of our health system where there hasn’t been the level of accountability we would like to see, and, unfortunately, we have seen people falling through the cracks. Whether it’s regulations or whether it’s offences, it does provide that additional safety net.

I want to finish by saying that, fundamentally, it is important for us to ensure that tāngata whaiora have the safeguards that are based on allowing them to have dignity and to make sure that their wellbeing is front and centre. I do want to thank everyone in our health system for their ongoing mahi in this area.

content.speaker: TODD STEPHENSON (ACT)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Look, I rise on behalf of ACT to add our support to the Mental Health Bill. It’s great that it has got cross-Parliament support to modernise this piece of really important legislation. As we’ve already heard, this is being updated after over 30 years. It is rights based and recovery focused. It is a modernisation. It has almost also been through its own two-year parliamentary process, and I want to thank all of those in the mental health sector who took the time to submit on it, and also the Health Committee and MPs across the House who have engaged on it extensively in the last 24 hours. I will be commending it to the House. Thank you.

content.speaker: JENNY MARCROFT (NZ First)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I rise on behalf of New Zealand First in support of the Mental Health Bill. These reforms in this bill will modernise the compulsory mental healthcare legislation. It is well overdue. The overhaul is absolutely necessary. It will place people at the centre of their care. It’ll be respectful of their rights in terms of their care. I commend it to the House.

content.speaker: ORIINI KAIPARA (Te Pāti Māori—Tāmaki Makaurau)
content.text: E te Pīka, tēnā koe. I want to acknowledge that we are, today, taking an important step, a step that many people, many whānau, and many communities across Aotearoa have waited far too long to see. This bill repeals and replaces the Mental Health Act 1992. It responds to He Ara Oranga, which found the old Act was out of date, overly reliant on coercion, and inconsistent with a modern human rights approach to mental health. For that reason, Te Pāti Māori supports this bill.

Support for this bill doesn’t erase an important question: why did it take so long? This legislation was introduced in 2024, the select committee completed its work in April 2025, yet here we are debating its final stages under urgency, only months before an election. If mental health was truly a priority and if the lives of tāngata whaiora, of rangatahi, of whānau and aiga, and of all New Zealanders were genuinely valued, then why was this bill not completed two years ago instead of today? Mental health worsens when one waits. Every delay matters when people are struggling to access support, when whānau are carrying grief, and when communities are crying out for change.

For Māori, those inequities are even more painful. In the last year alone, 630 lives were lost to suspected suicide in Aotearoa. A week ago, I attended the tangi of Preston Herewini, a young man with young babies and a wife, who is now widowed and bereft of the life that they dreamed of together. I stand here wondering what could have been done for Preston, for his whānau, and for every single whānau carrying immense grief and unanswered questions. E ngau kino nei te mamae me te mauāhara mō rātou, Preston, e ngā huhu a mate. Kia whakawhetūrangihia koutou e Matariki ā kō tonu nei.
[The anguish and resentment afflict me badly for those—Preston—who have passed on. May you soon be immortalised as stars by Matariki.]

Māori continue to experience higher rates of mental distress, suicide, addiction, and unmet needs than non-Māori. These are not failures of our people. They are the consequences of colonisation, of poverty, of disconnection, and of repeated breaches of the Te Tiriti o Waitangi. That’s why Te Tiriti matters. That’s why Te Pāti Māori welcomes the inclusion of a Treaty clause in this bill. In fact, it is the very first bill, this term, that this Government has introduced and has chosen to include one. This is the only one. Before we celebrate, let us acknowledge the contradiction, because this Government removed Treaty provisions from corrections legislation, despite Māori being disproportionately represented in prisons. Yet here, where Māori, also disproportionately represented in poorer mental health outcomes, Te Tiriti is recognised. Where is the consistency?

Te Hiringa Mahara’s latest road map makes clear that urgent action is still needed for Māori, for rangatahi, for rural communities and for those facing barriers to care. Young people continue to experience high levels of psychological distress, while Māori continue to experience significant unmet need. As the member for Tāmaki Makaurau, I see these realities every single day. I see whānau carrying the weight of housing insecurity, poverty, addiction, and disconnection. I see communities doing everything that they can to support one another while struggling to access culturally safe services. That is why equity must mean more than treating everyone the same. It means directing investment where the need is greatest, it means trusting Māori providers, it means funding kaupapa Māori solutions, and, yes, it means investing in Māori proportionate to the burden that Māori carry. That is not preferential treatment. That is fairness. That is honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

Today, we support this bill because it represents progress, but, tomorrow, we will continue to hold the Government to account for its implementation, because legislation alone does not save lives. Whānau do. Communities do. Culture does. And Governments do, only when they match words with action and aroha. Ruia te aroha kia pua mai ai ko te aroha—when kindness is sown, kindness is received.

content.speaker: HŪHANA LYNDON (Green)
content.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. On behalf of the Green Party, I stand to also offer our support towards this legislation, knowing that this is a significant shift and change to the way with which our mental health sector will be delivered into the future when it comes to compulsory assessments and treatment. I pay tribute to the select committee who sat and had rigorous debate, heard submissions from across the community, tāngata whaiora, and officials of the Government who came and presented evidence and entered into a wānanga in terms of what we have today. But also I know that, today, in the committee of the whole House, this side of the House offered a tangible—how would I say it?—amendments that were quite reasonable. These amendments, we thought we could have progressed in a shared understanding of seeking the best for tāngata whaiora, for whānau, and for communities, and particularly also for our kaimahi in the workforce.
I want to note one of those amendments from my colleague Kahurangi Carter, in terms of the solitary confinement, the seclusion, again.

We’ve heard in the House, through and through, our ongoing concerns around the need for a sunset clause. Knowing that we are on track, we have got a work plan, we are working in this space in order to try to find a way whereby we can provide safety of care and also a pathway to tērā pea ka oti tēnei mea ko [potentially end this thing called] solitary confinement. We still remain concerned, because the seclusion was spoken to and has been recommended by the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission and also by the Mental Health Foundation and the Health Action Trust.

We absolutely tautoko the way in which we are putting whaiora in the centre of their care and having the rōpū whaiora and the hauora of the person in care at the centre of how we are trying to navigate them through the system. But, as was raised during the committee of the whole House, again, how do we connect whānau into the care and keep them up to date with what is occurring when we have these collective groups that come together, and navigation for both whānau and whaiora as they move through the system. We look forward to the way whereby we can support those who may have neurodivergence and other intellectual handicaps, whereby we can look at them and provide consistent protections with the disability convention and ensure their pathways are non-coercive, that whānau are involved and centred, and that it is evidence based. That continues to be a theme that we share.

Of course, it’s good that we’ve seen some of the changes in the legislation that embrace and ensure that sexual orientation and gender identity cannot be used as a factor when determining someone’s level of impaired mental health, and the stronger interpretations around the processes and the way that we’re able to, through the committee of the whole House, go step by step in understanding where to from here—what does the hui whaiora do, where does the whānau sit, what is the definition of a mental health practitioner, and how can we keep our babies with patients as much as possible?—taking tāngata whaiora - centred approach.

We do tautoko this legislation, but we do want to see stronger measures around equity of access and the way in which rural and urban populations are can receive the equity of care, as well as tangata whenua. While we do have Te Tiriti o Waitangi provisions within the legislation, there’s always more work to be done. I pay tribute to the way that submitters came into the Health Committee and raised these issues. Knowing that by and large it is tangata whenua who are held in a compulsory nature, how do we take an inclusive approach; how do we support whānau to understand what is happening and also, when they are released, their navigation back into community- or whānau-based care?

These are ongoing conversations, and it’s about resourcing, ultimately. This legislation will only be as successful as how much resource and kaimahi and training is available to support the system to be able to deliver better health outcomes for tāngata whaiora and better health outcomes for our community.

content.speaker: Dr HAMISH CAMPBELL (National—Ilam)
content.text: I rise in support of the Mental Health Bill. We’ve got support right across the House for this bill. It’s modernising our mental health framework. Therefore, I commend it to the House.

content.speaker: Dr TRACEY McLELLAN (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Labour supports this bill. It’s a law, developed more than three decades ago, as has been discussed on several occasions, that no longer reflects society’s more modern understanding of human rights, let alone mental health. This reform is long overdue. The bill establishes, as I said, a much more modern, rights-based framework. It recognises that mental health care in general, where possible, should be delivered with people, not done to them, and these are significant improvements. That is the principal reason as to why Labour will support this bill.

However, at third reading, I just want to take a couple of minutes today to say that we also have to be honest about what this legislation alone can’t do and can’t achieve. The new law can create rights, and it does, and duties and safeguards, which it does, but it can’t by itself provide the staffing, the facilities, the community services, the cultural capability, and all the time required to actually make those rights a reality. That concern has, I think, been raised not only by people on the side of the House but by mental health organisations and clinicians and advocates and people with lived experience, who submitted on this bill during the process. These are not reasons to delay this reform; they are reasons, ultimately, to properly resource it.

I want, also, to take the time to acknowledge everyone that works across the mental health and addiction system, be they psychiatrists, psychologists, nurses, social workers, occupational therapists, counsellors, care support workers, cultural workers, advocates, and all of those community providers and support staff who, quite frankly, don’t get the recognition they deserve and work under really tough circumstances. They often work with people who are at their most vulnerable and experiencing the most frightening moments of their life, and they make considered decisions to make those lives better. A rights-based law must not simply place more responsibility on those very people who are doing that work, on those individual workers, while failing to address some of the conditions in which they actually do that work or are expected to.

To the Government, that means that, whilst we’re happy to support this bill, we acknowledge it is not the end of the road. This is the first step; the next step is that we want to hear and we want to see and we will keep asking questions and keep monitoring as to where a really good implementation plan lands. We welcome the improvements made through the Health Committee, and I’m not going to go into the details. I think they have been well traversed, both through the committee of the whole House and through the contributions to date on the third reading. I do also just want to acknowledge that ending seclusion requires appropriate staffing, and it requires all the requisite therapeutic facilities, specialist training, and those alternative models of care if it’s going to happen. Simply, the intentionality and the purpose within this bill, which will soon be legislation, isn’t going to be enough to achieve that aim unless there’s something a little bit more definitive behind it.

This bill is better than the law it replaces—excellent—but passing it alone is not the end of the reform. As I’ve said, it’s just the beginning of the implementation phase, which we will be keeping a close eye on. Labour does support this bill.

content.speaker: Dr CARLOS CHEUNG (National—Mt Roskill)
content.text: We’ve all learnt from past mistakes in how compulsory mental health care has been handled. This bill modernises the system, strengthens safeguards, and ensures that we don’t repeat those mistakes again. Most importantly, it balances care with dignity and support with human rights. It puts patients at the centre of decisions about their own care. By focusing on patients first, this bill will improve outcomes and enhance wellbeing. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: The time has come for me to leave the Chair for the lunch break. The House will resume at 2 p.m.
Sitting suspended from 12.58 p.m. to 2 p.m.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: The House is resumed on the third reading of the Mental Health Bill. We’re up to a split call, and I think it’s Labour leading—Georgie Dansey.

content.speaker: GEORGIE DANSEY (Labour)
content.text: Thank you. It’s good to take a call on the third reading of the Mental Health Bill. It was really interesting to hear through the committee of the whole House process the questions raised and the answers from the Minister for Mental Health. I wanted to speak to a few of those things today.

The first one I wanted to mention was clause 42 on the decision making for compulsory care. There were questions from my colleagues around ensuring that the decision making for compulsory care was made by medically qualified professionals, and I really wanted to emphasise the importance of having qualified professionals in this space dealing with some—sorry, “dealing” is not a good word; supporting—of our most vulnerable people in New Zealand.

Last night, when I took a call on this bill, I spoke about my brother-in-law Nicky, who passed away 11 years ago while he was in compulsory care. The coroner found that Nicky’s death was avoidable due to a number of mishaps which led to him taking his own life. The reason this is so important to me is to honour Nicky’s life and our whānau who still deal with that loss every single day; my kids, who will never meet their uncle. For him, when he was at the compulsory care facility, he left the facility on unescorted leave, and that was part of what led to him eventually taking his own life. The key thing there, where things fell apart, was that there weren’t medical professionals in place to assess him to see that unescorted leave was not going to be appropriate for him. There was a point where the decisions were made by security guards. I respect security guards a huge amount—they do very, very valuable work across our country—but it’s important that we have medically specialised professionals working with people in order to protect them.

One of the other aspects of this that is important to me is the involvement of whānau and family in decision making, and this bill goes some way in that direction. I think there is more work to do, but it goes some way to ensure that whānau and family are included in the decision making around their loved ones in order to have a holistic approach. Going through the experience that I went through and that our family went through with Nicky, I met person after person after person after person who had their own story of devastating loss for people within the people in mental health system. It’s those stories that empower me to stand and support this bill as a step towards better management in this space. It’s not as far as we would have liked to see. There are many more changes we’d like to see in this space to ensure that we are really respecting all human rights and the independence of individuals, but this a really good step.

The second bit I wanted to talk about very briefly was the amendment to clause 38A in Amendment Paper 648 from the Minister, which substantially reverses the changes made by the Health Committee. This is regarding a parent being able to stay with their baby. I don’t support the amendment and the changes, because I think it’s paramount that, if safe, a child or a baby should always stay with their parent—especially an infant. All the parents in the room understand that connection you have with your children, especially when they’re babies. For a parent dealing with substantial mental health concerns and then, on top of that, potentially having their baby taken away—I think we can do much better than that.
With those two points, I support this bill and commend it to the House.

content.speaker: Dr VANESSA WEENINK (National—Banks Peninsula)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. This Mental Health Bill intends to change substantially the culture and direction within mental health treatment and the compulsory care sector. The implementation of this bill will be the important element of it. Training and further workforce development, which we have led already, will be very vital. I commend the bill to the House.

content.speaker: RACHEL BOYACK (Labour—Nelson)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I rise to take a call on the Mental Health Bill. I just want to traverse some of the reasons Labour is supporting this bill, but I also just note some areas there—and my colleagues have laid a lot of these points out very well already—where we do have some specific concerns around some of the missed opportunities within this bill.

It’s been traversed well today that the current Act from 1992 is very outdated and it no longer reflects modern human-rights standards. This bill is a significant improvement on the current Act, but, as I’ve already said, there are some missed opportunities there. It falls short of some of the transformational reform that could have occurred through this bill. I think there are some letters here around how much further the Government could have gone to really make this a transformational approach.

There continue to be issues around implementation, workforce planning, and accountability. We in particular want to see stronger protections for Māori, for disabled people, for children and young people, and for other vulnerable groups affected by this particular bill but also affected in their daily lives by issues related to mental health. We think that the bill should contain a stronger commitment to ending seclusion. We do note that there have been some strengthened safeguards around the use of electroconvulsive therapy—a complex, and controversial at times, treatment that occurs in mental health—and we believe that, given that, there are some further protections that are warranted.

I wanted to talk briefly about some concerns raised by my colleague Tracey McLellan when she put questions to the Minister for Mental Health in the committee of the whole House stage around the lack of an increase in the number of forensic beds in prisons. This is one of those missed opportunities that I see, as an electorate MP, when dealing with whānau members of people who are in prison who have committed a crime but have a significant mental health need and who are unable to access a forensic bed.

With the growing prison population, what we are seeing is a growing number of people within prisons who are unable to access a forensic bed to receive the treatment that they need. There is one such constituent in my electorate of Nelson, and we’re working very closely with the mother of this particular person, who has unfortunately had repeated time spent in prison. When he is unable to get access to the holistic care and support that he would get from a forensic bed, what it does is it makes his condition worse. He’s, therefore, unable to access opportunities for rehabilitation or care within the prison system. The prison system is doing everything it can for this young man, but without access to proper mental health support, what will happen is, when he returns into the community, he may well return in a state where he’s actually less well than when he first entered. There were some opportunities in this process for that to be recognised.

Labour’s alternative view, which is outlined in the select committee report and through speeches given by my colleagues, was informed by evidence from tāngata whaiora and people with lived experience, their whānau, clinicians, disability advocates, the Ombudsman, and other organisations with safeguarding and oversight responsibilities.

What that clearly showed was the need for stronger safeguards, for better implementation, for greater accountability, and for a more participatory mental health system. We believe that the bill should be strengthened by giving effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi—including explicit recognition of tikanga, hapū and iwi—by strengthening decision-making processes for people to make supported decisions; by moving even further towards voluntary participation wherever possible, where the therapeutic evidence supports this; by improving the treatment of advance mental health directives; by strengthening protections for disabled people, children, and young people, and other vulnerable groups; by requiring legislated implementation planning and workforce training; and by strengthening accountability and public reporting.

In particular, the bill has some changes around seclusion, and we are concerned around the fact that there’s still retention of seclusion in limited circumstances. We support New Zealand’s commitment to eliminate seclusion, but, as my colleague Ingrid Leary pointed out in an earlier contribution today, the Ombudsman continues to make scathing recommendations around the practice of seclusion and how much it harms those people who experience seclusion when they have high mental health needs. We believe that the legislation should include a commitment to ending seclusion within five years, that there needs to be a system-wide phase-out for that, and that this is one of those missed opportunities.

I mentioned the use of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) earlier, in the beginning of my speech. What is good is that the bill provides some additional safeguards for adults, including specialist oversight where statutory authorisation is required. It also provides some additional safeguards for people under 18, so it may only be used in rare and exceptional circumstances where two independent psychiatrists—one with expertise in ECT and one who is a child and adolescent psychiatrist—agree it is necessary to save a life or prevent serious harm, and the young person’s care plan and any advanced mental health directive must also be considered.

It strengthens reporting requirements around the use of ECT and it creates an offence for failing to comply with the statutory ECT safeguards. As I said earlier, ECT is one of those treatments that has controversy, complexity, and concerns around it, and for good reason. Our view on this is that we do accept the evidence that ECT may, in rare and exceptional circumstances, be an appropriate treatment of last resort. We support the strengthened safeguards included in the bill, but we also consider that adults should receive greater protection where they have made an advance mental health directive refusing ECT and that should have greater consideration.

We remain concerned, as well, that the bill contains no legislative requirement for comprehensive implementation planning or workforce training and that, without sustained investment and training and accountability, there is a real risk that the bill—which has a rights-based approach—won’t actually be fully realised in practice. That’s the challenge: it’s all very well for us to put everything that we have into legislation, but we actually need to see that true implementation. I come back to the comments I made earlier around the lack of increase in forensic beds. It’s a very good example of where we’ve got legislative change that is very, very good, and Labour will be supporting it, but we have circumstances where we’re not actually seeing the same uptake in resource that can match that.

Consider a prisoner who may have very serious psychotic conditions where their behaviour leads them into a place of criminality and they are taken through a court process and ultimately end up in prison, which is a place that causes immense stress and harm for them and actually makes their situation worse. I think about a particular young man in my electorate whose family we have supported now for a long time. I think this is a missed opportunity for us to look at what he would need in a system in order to get that care so that, when he returns to the community—because, ultimately, he will return to the community—he returns to the community in a state where he is less unwell. He will never be 100 percent well—that is the nature of his condition—but when he is in a better place, he will not be in a heightened state of constant stress and will be in a better position, and he’ll be better equipped to then face the world when he returns, because he will.

There are stories like this up and down the country. I do want to commend the Minister for the bill making its way through the House this far, and I thank all the officials for the work that they’ve done. It is a very good improvement on what is a very outdated Act, but there are a number of missed opportunities, which I’ve outlined, and Labour believes the Government could have gone further to ensure that the resources are there to properly implement and make the changes that we need so that people that are within the mental health system get the support they need to get well again so that they can continue to be thriving members of our society. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: SAM UFFINDELL (National—Tauranga)
content.text: It was a privilege to chair the committee through the passage of this bill. I want to thank all submitters and members for their unanimous support across the House. The Government is committed to improving mental health outcomes for New Zealanders. I commend this bill to the House.
Motion agreed to.
Bill read a third time.

content.text: I move, That Government order of the day No. 20 for the second reading of the Plain Language Act Repeal Bill be postponed.

Constitution Amendment Bill
Legislative Statement

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice)
content.text: I present a legislative statement on the Constitution Amendment Bill.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
Second Reading

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice)
content.text: I move, That the Constitution Amendment Bill be now read a second time.

This bill makes a small but important change to the Constitution Act to ensure that the post-election process is run smoothly. After the election, there’s a small period of time where there are no members of Parliament, which continues until election results are finalised and the new MPs take up office. During this time, the Constitution Act provides an exception to the rule that Ministers must always be an MP, to ensure the caretaker executive Government can continue to act during the post-election period. This is critical to our constitutional arrangements and the smooth transition of power. Currently, this exception is limited to 28 days.

There are a few circumstances where the conclusion of an election will be delayed—for example, an extreme weather event or a judicial recount. In these cases, the 28-day rule can expire before the new MPs formally take office, meaning Ministers can no longer hold their ministerial office, which can result in a constitutionally untenable position of the Governor-General being left without advisers. This happened in 2023, and while party leaders worked to find a stop-gap solution, I consider a constitutional setting should have clear and fit for purpose rules. Therefore, this bill removes the 28-day rule and replaces it with one that does not give rise to the possibility that ministerial tenure will expire before the post-election period.

The new rule will allow Ministers to continue to hold office until the election writ is returned with the names of the successful electorate MPs and list MPs who have been declared. It means that if there’s a delay to the official vote count, incumbent Ministers remain in office until new MPs are appointed. I want to thank the Justice Committee for all their hard work on this, and I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: The question is that the motion be agreed to.

content.speaker: Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB (Labour—Christchurch Central)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s good to speak on this short but important bill. It is interesting that submitters weren’t absolutely in favour of this, and, certainly, there were some opinions that thought that it was constitutionally problematic for members of the executive, at least in New Zealand, to not be at the same time members of Parliament. This bill, of course, is aimed to address the situation where, as a result of an election and whilst the results are being calculated, a member of the executive has lost their seat. This was in fact the Hon Nanaia Mahuta’s situation.

Whilst the outgoing Labour Government was a caretaker Government in the true sense, the difficulty was that the Minister of Foreign Affairs wasn’t able to hold that office because she was no longer a member of Parliament, having clearly lost her seat, and therefore not being whatever the appropriate term is—there’s a technical term for someone who looks like they’ve won it but haven’t yet been sworn in, but she didn’t hold that position either. So she couldn’t hold her portfolio under the Constitution Act, and I think it might have been Chris Hipkins who held it for about seven weeks, in that situation. That’s a difficult situation because that new, essentially temporary, caretaker Minister doesn’t have any knowledge of the portfolio, doesn’t have the connections within the ministry, and certainly doesn’t have the international connections that were relevant to that particular portfolio.

So this bill does address that, and I do want to address the main criticism, which is “Well, that’s very odd that you’ve got someone who’s a Minister of the Crown who’s been voted out of an electorate or who has clearly not won a place on the party list.” I don’t think that’s a massive problem. Certainly, in other jurisdictions, members of the executive aren’t members of the legislature at all. The fact of the matter is that this is very much a bridging arrangement, so it’s a very short period of time—it’s not until the next Government is formed; it’s actually only until the final announcement is made and decisions are made as to which members are elected to Parliament. So it’s actually a very short period of time.

So for that reason, we’re going to support this bill. It didn’t take long at select committee, but I do want to say that any change to the Constitution Act deserve careful scrutiny and good advice, and the submitters were of the highest quality, and so we absolutely did do that with this bill. Unlike some other very short bills, it didn’t get a cursory treatment; it got thorough treatment and careful consideration. So we will commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. The Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand also supports this bill, and as the previous speaker, the Hon Dr Duncan Webb, has said, I just want to preface this by reaffirming the importance of the Constitution Act, but also in terms of our general constitutional arrangements here in Aotearoa New Zealand. This bill specifically addresses this continuity around the executive, but I think it’s important for us to mention that as part of the submission process, we did get high-quality submitters who submitted on this particular bill—people who are experts in this field.

While the committee that considered this bill, the Justice Committee, are a very busy committee, they only had about 20 individual written submissions. It’s important to highlight some of the processes through that select committee which also helped shape some of the questions that we have for the Minister in the upcoming committee stage, because while we support this bill, it’s really important to have good engagement with the Minister and have certain positions of the Minister on record, which is separate from what we’ve heard in the select committee.

I want to address my first point, which is around our constitutional arrangements in general in terms of the executive but also the legislature. I think members of this House would clearly have experienced and know that, under our current system of MMP, introduced in the 1990s, when we get into a post-election period, we see a period of negotiation between different political parties to form a Government. Ostensibly, the only time under the MMP system that we had negotiations but also a majority was in 2020. The key there, then, is that there is this lull in the period between the election and a new Government being formed, which is where this bill comes in, and I’ll come back to the 28 days in more detail.

Most of the submitters that we heard during the select committee stage did voice their support for this bill. We had 19 submissions from individuals and one from an organisation, but then we did have a few people who opposed this bill, quite a few; we had 15 oppose this bill and four in support of it. But I do want to address some of the concerns people had with regard to their opposition to this bill.

I think it is understandable that there is general concern from the New Zealand public, currently, even with bills that have been introduced and have the support of the whole House, about whether this would be abused by a future Government. I think it’s important to note that the extension of 28 days is mainly to address a current anomaly in our constitutional arrangement, as opposed to any Government finding a way to extend their powers and be able to introduce certain things under a new Government. I think that’s a really important placeholder—more like a custodian role. The main reason for that is that it is absolutely crucial, under our current constitutional arrangements—being part of the British Crown and having a monarchy—that, ultimately, when we go through any bills in this House, we have Royal assent that goes through the Governor-General: the Governor-General must have advisers that do actually advise them on certain things. So without any Ministers, it’s really difficult for the Governor-General to also be able to undertake their role. So in terms of this particular part, we don’t see that being a huge concern.

I think it’s also important, as I did mention before, that we should really touch on the duration that we’re looking at, which is 28 days. We did question during the committee stage as to whether 28 days is the most reasonable length of time when we’re looking at the extension. This is to do with, specifically, aspects of sections 6 and 8 of the Constitution Act, which is clauses 4 and 5 of this particular bill. I think the 28 days is an important provision, potentially, to remove, mainly because of the fact that we have seen instances where, now, particularly under a more thriving MMP environment, sometimes the formation of a Government may take longer than that. So it is important for there to be a level of flexibility. So, again, as some of the advice that we received as part of the committee stage, we did consider this particular part. For example, as demonstrated in the 2023 general election, delays to the return of the writ can mean that new MPs take office more than 28 days after the election.

Other concerns that were raised by the submitters were around the commencement date, and this is bearing in mind that this was something that was considered a little while ago as well by the Justice Committee. At that stage, other bills were going through for things like the parliamentary term, things like the census, and also some of the electoral reforms. So with a whole swathe of electoral reform bills that were going through the Justice Committee—and were in the public consciousness, rightfully—some submitters questioned whether there should be a delay in the commencement of this particular part, just to anticipate other changes with some of the other legislation as well. The select committee was satisfied that the current commencement date, which is the day after Royal assent, is a reasonable one, mainly because this is an election year. I think it is important for us to complete this particular bill so it would be immediately applicable to the 2026 general election regardless of the outcome on 7 November.

One of the things that the Justice Committee did decide to alter is around clause 5—this is section 8 amended—and one of the reasons for that is because the exception to the Parliamentary Under-Secretary must always be an MP to mirror the rule for a Minister. A few of the submitters noted an issue with the drafting, because when we’re looking at this particular rule, they noted that the wording of the bill is not specific about the circumstances under which a Parliamentary Under-Secretary ceases to be an MP, which could result in the rule applying if a Parliamentary Under-Secretary ceases to be an MP for some other reason—they resign part way through a parliamentary term, for example. This is something that the committee did consider seriously and, as people would note in the amended version of the bill, the select committee has made some changes to ensure that there is clarification that Parliamentary Under-Secretaries are a part of this in clause 5 of this bill.

Finally, I think it’s important that—as we kind of go into the progression of this bill through the committee of the whole House stage as well as through the third reading—as I mentioned at the beginning of this speech, I think it’s important to round up looking at the overall context that we’re seeing here in our constitutional arrangement, that, with a thriving MMP system, we may potentially see more and more of this happening; that, actually, in a healthy democratic system, it is OK for a Government—and maybe voters expect—that members and the elected officials take their time to ensure that they form a Government that is democratic and considers the best outcomes for New Zealanders on the whole. We also would like to see this sort of cross-party consensus when it comes to things like automatic voter registration. But in this particular case, the Green Party does support the Constitution Amendment Bill.

content.speaker: TODD STEPHENSON (ACT)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. The Constitution Amendment Bill is supported across the House. It had a vigorous and in-depth select committee process and was well looked through. It’s a very sensible change to make sure our democracy continues to run smoothly and I commend it to the House.

content.speaker: Hon CASEY COSTELLO (Minister of Customs)
content.text: I rise on behalf New Zealand First to speak on the Constitution Amendment Bill. As has been traversed in the House, this is about common-sense practical solutions, which is exactly what New Zealand First stands for. It has been through a robust process. It is critical to deliver a stable Government moving forward after an election, so we commend the bill to the House.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: The next call is a split call.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. It is a pleasure to take a call on the Constitution Amendment Bill. I do have a few points to make on this because it is an important constitutional change. It is really interesting that this is the second bill that we’ve had through the House recently that has looked to make sure that we have sustainable government despite potential emergencies. The first one that we debated earlier in this urgency period was the Emergency Management Bill (No 2) that looked at the continuity of Parliament if there was an emergency situation and the Parliament buildings were not able to be used, and so that’s progressing through the House and passed its second reading. This bill also mentions that one thing that may delay the return of the writ is a weather event or an emergency situation. That is very interesting and probably, slightly, a sign of the times.

As other members have said, we support this bill. I mean, I do support this bill, and I do think there was probably a greater opportunity to think about continuity of Government through an MMP lens, because this bill essentially maintains the existing executive through to the return of the writ, and so, when the next Parliament—I think we’re in the 54th—

content.speaker: Hon Member
content.text: 54th.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH
content.text: It’s the 54th Parliament now, so if this bill passes, then the 55th Parliament would be when this current executive would officially end, and so they would retain their warrants as Ministers, and indeed, the change from the Justice Committee is under-secretaries as well with this particular change, and the current situation, as we know, is 28 days.

We did have a situation last election where we did have a Minister who wasn’t returned to Parliament, and I understand that that created some problems in terms of continuity of Government. I wasn’t part of the Justice Committee when they considered this, regretfully, because it is a really interesting matter, and as colleagues have said, any change to our Constitution Act should be considered in depth. But one of the things that I think would have been quite interesting to look at—and possibly might be a bit of a point against those who oppose the bill—is just to look at where we have elections in New Zealand. It is very, very rare that our three-yearly election will be on the last possible weekend that that election would be due to take place. Generally, it is some time before that. This year we will have a slightly later election, but I don’t believe it’s the last possible election date. If people are concerned about there being no democratic mandate for people to retain their warrant until the writ is returned, I think that’s probably not 100 percent accurate, because we do generally give a mandate to people to be elected for three years or until the next election, and generally, that’s slightly under three years.

I do think in kind of a related point, which I do think is worth considering, is because we are having this election in November, which is a little bit later than we’ve had elections in other years, it does mean that the date for the next election can be pushed out slightly too. I think we’re kind of nearing into slightly dangerous territory with the commencement of Christmas starting quite early in New Zealand. Often we have Christmas parties in November, and people are off for the end of the year, and I don’t think it would be a positive move in our democracy to have elections any closer to Christmas, so just something to keep in mind there.

This is a small change. I think a broader change that would have allowed greater continuity of Government would have been, possibly, the maintenance of warrants until the new executive was sworn in. That possibly may have been less popular with submitters in the sense that I understand there were some concerns around democratic mandate, but that would have probably given the most amount of continuity. But of course, that has to be balanced with the fact that we don’t obviously want a situation—and it is possible under a proportional system to have a situation where a Government, for whatever reason, can’t be formed. We had discussions around that last election. Would there need to be a second election if a Government couldn’t be formed? I don’t think anyone in the House would want that at all, so hopefully there’s a clear result in the change of Government at the election so that doesn’t need to happen. This is important.

I mean, the other thing that happens is Ministers are able to maintain not only their warrant, but their terms and conditions as well so they’re able to be paid as Ministers up to the return of the writ, and then their notice period kicks in. I imagine, if those people had stood for election and not been returned, then they would also have the three months’ notice. In terms of those individuals, that seems perfectly fine.

The other last point I wanted to make—I won’t use all the time for no reason—is the other jurisdictions do have appointed executives. We had that situation in the United States. We had a situation in Canada where we had the current Prime Minister, who was elected in their most recent election, actually became Prime Minister prior to the election taking place, and apparently that was a situation that could have happened in New Zealand up to a certain point where there was a change in our Constitution Act. So that’s another really interesting point, that democracies that we value, that are very close to New Zealand, like Canada, has had a very different situation in relation to the maintenance of executive power. Obviously, other countries like the United States have appointees that are appointed on the basis of skill.

It is important to have this continuity, and I think, reflecting on the way that New Zealand Governments have acted during the caretaker period, that no matter who has been in Government, it’s generally been extremely respectful of the more limited role that caretaker Governments do have during the election period. This will, I think, strengthen that slightly. It’s not a huge massive change, but hopefully, as I said at the beginning of my speech, because we are living in uncertain times, it does give that extra level of certainty while still making sure that the return of the writ is the final day in which the previous administration can maintain that executive power, which, as we know in New Zealand—because we just have a single House—is quite extensive. I won’t take any longer, but Labour does support this bill and look forward to its passage through the House today.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: Just as we get our sequence sorted out, I’m going to take a split call from the Green Party, and just to note the next call will go to the National Party, which is a full 10-minute call.

content.speaker: HŪHANA LYNDON (Green)
content.text: E mihi atu ana ki a tātou i tēnei, tō tātou Rāhoroi noho a te Kāwanatanga. Tēnā tātou.
[Greetings to all of us on this, our Saturday sitting of the Government. Greetings to us all.]

On behalf of the Green Party, I stand to support this piece of legislation. As we’ve heard and look forward to the committee of the whole House, this is a technical change to improve but also to provide continuity of Kāwanatanga in a time of transition at the time of elections.

Now, I want to recognise the submitters that provided feedback, of which there were 20 individual written submissions, as well as 19 of them being from individuals and one from an organisation, and noting that there were concerns, as mentioned previously, around allowing the Kāwanatanga to stay in power longer than necessary.
