We know that these types of contingencies are needed and that the 28-day rule could be prejudicial to providing certainty for those things that we need to do in a caretaker Government, as the transition might occur once the declaration of list MPs as well as electorate MPs is made, continuing on to the time of the writ.

The submitters who did provide comment on this legislation—and knowing that this is an improvement piece of legislation; there is no objection from within the House on it. But they did bring forth broader issues and concerns in the way with which we could make improvements to our constitutional arrangements and the way that Parliament configures itself: for example, reflecting this Act to bring forth Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the Treaty of Waitangi, within legislation more appropriately; examining—which we’re having discussions, of course, around—a four-year parliamentary term; and strengthening enrolment settings for the Electoral Act to facilitate participation.

Noting and thanking those members of the community who did participate, because this is a unique piece of legislation, one that helps us in providing stability in times of change but also the need for us to still have a process whereby community, whānau, and organisational voice can come forward. These are the things that are important in the way that we make decisions and inform lawmaking. That doesn’t happen all the time, as we’ve seen previously in other pieces of legislation, where they come through very quickly.

On balance, this small change will make a big difference. The way with which we might think of the 28-day rule is something that has been there for a long time. It’s important that we reflect the times but also provide the ability for Government to be formed, for decisions to be made, and then for the writ to proceed. On behalf of the Green Party, we tautoko this.

content.speaker: JOSEPH MOONEY (National—Southland)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I rise to speak on the Constitution Amendment Bill, which is to address the risk of a potential gap in the continuity of executive Government following an election. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: PAULO GARCIA (National—New Lynn)
content.text: The Constitution Amendment Bill is an important change to ensure continuity at election time. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: The next call is a split call.

content.speaker: GEORGIE DANSEY (Labour)
content.text: Thank you. It’s good to speak on the Constitution Amendment Bill. It’s really interesting to look at the detail of this and that the Constitution Act, as it is currently, only allows the Minister to continue for 28 days after they cease to be an MP. This bill will ensure that when there are delays in forming the next Government in the future, there is no risk to the continuity of Government. We all support a streamlined approach, and this will, indeed, streamline moving into the next Government more so than we have in our current legislation.

Interestingly, thinking about a caretaker Government and what a caretaker Government might do—as we saw in the previous election, that ministerial portfolio of our foreign affairs Minister was passed on to another Minister. I mean, it sounds like, OK, fine, that’s quite simple, but, actually, when you think about the detail, that’s not really that simple. The kind of administration and effort that goes into swearing in another Minister, even into a caretaking Government, is quite considerable, but also understanding the portfolio. The previous Minister has just had a bunch of time in that portfolio and has a deep knowledge—well, you’d hope would have a very deep knowledge—of that portfolio, and passing it on to someone else for a couple of weeks or however long isn’t that efficient. Also, the connections with stakeholders and the Public Service and ministries is an important aspect of that, and a person having to get their head around a whole portfolio to be in there as a caretaker for a couple of weeks before it goes to the next Government is not streamlined as we would have liked.

I saw, connected to this bill, in the previous Government, Chris Hipkins had to be sworn in again as Prime Minister before the National Government came in. That’s another sort of administrative aspect that isn’t necessary and won’t be necessary under this bill by extending it past the 28 days.

I listened to the other speakers and concerns from submitters—I didn’t sit on the select committee—around giving more power to a departing Government. I think that’s a good thing for us to look at: is this going to give undue power to the Government that is departing? But looking at the legislation and the precedent of a caretaker Government and the respectfulness that parties of all stripes have shown in the past, it feels like that won’t be the case and instead that continuation is going to be the priority. With that, Labour supports this bill.

content.speaker: Dr VANESSA WEENINK (National—Banks Peninsula)
content.text: I commend the bill to the House.

content.speaker: RACHEL BOYACK (Labour—Nelson)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s a pleasure to take a call on the Constitution Amendment Bill. As previous speakers have noted, what this does is ensure there’s continuity of Government following an election and following a potential change of Government.

At the moment, the Constitution Act provides that a Minister can continue as a Minister for 28 days after they cease to be an MP. However, if there are delays after that and a Minister hasn’t been returned as an MP, we have a situation whereby they cannot be sworn in again and continue to be a Minister. This specifically relates to the return of the writ. If the writ is delayed for any reason, if we have some type of crisis, some type of weather event, some type of pandemic—we’ve had these situations in the past, not, thankfully, around election time, but they have occurred and disrupted the ability of State organisations to do their job. There is that risk that if the writ is not returned, we have a situation where a Minister cannot continue to act as a Minister past that 28 days.

It’s worth just noting what happened last time, which was that former Minister Nanaia Mahuta was not returned as an MP, but she was only able to stay as a Minister for 28 days. What happened after that was that the new Government on the other side had not yet been formed, and so while that was actually unrelated to the return of the writ, it did mean that she could no longer operate as a Minister after that 28 days. If that delay hadn’t been caused due to formation of Government but had been delayed due to some type of emergency that caused a delay in the return of the writ, then that would have been a problem in terms of continuity of Government.
It’s interesting to think about what could happen when we have the change of Government in November. We could end up with a few Ministers who may end up being affected by a clause like this.

content.speaker: Glen Bennett
content.text: Really?

content.speaker: RACHEL BOYACK
content.text: There could be a few. I mean, we could end up in a situation where the Minister of Finance may not be able to continue operating as the Minister of Finance after 28 days. We could end up with the person sponsoring the bill today, the Hon Paul Goldsmith, not being able to continue in his duties after 28 days. Mr Bishop, if Mr Bishop loses his seat and he doesn’t get back in on the list—because if people like Carlos Cheung or Vanessa Weenink win their seats, what that does is it means we end up with no list MPs in the National Party. We could have a situation where there are no list MPs in the National Party. Then what happens? We have no Minister of Finance, we have no Mr Bishop, we have no Minister of Justice. Do we even have a Mr Speaker, Mr Speaker?

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: I don’t have a crystal ball, I can’t tell you.

content.speaker: RACHEL BOYACK
content.text: So there’s some very real risk for the National Party here, as we approach this Government. It could also affect the ACT Party, given that we could end up losing a few ACT Party MPs. Yeah, so we might end up in a bit of a strange situation where, you know, we don’t have a Minister of Finance.

content.speaker: Jamie Arbuckle
content.text: A lot more NZ First MPs.

content.speaker: RACHEL BOYACK
content.text: Goodness me—oh, NZ First. I think they might be getting a few more MPs, potentially. That’s sort of how things are looking. So I think they’re going to pinch some off National and ACT, potentially, at this election. So we’ll see, we’ll see. “Minister Arbuckle”, that could be a—Minister Arbuckle could get sworn in for a few days. There we go.

This is an important bill though, because the continuity of Government is important. It’s important that the bills are paid. It’s important that if there is some type of emergency like a pandemic, like a war, that we end up entering into—any of these types of things—that we actually do have a Government that’s able to provide that stability when a change of Government is happening. We look forward to the change of Government on 7 November, and Labour commends this bill to the House.

content.speaker: TOM RUTHERFORD (National—Bay of Plenty)
content.text: I commend the bill to the House.

content.speaker: GLEN BENNETT (Labour)
content.text: Kia ora, Mr Speaker. Thank you for this opportunity. In reflecting and listening to the contributions this afternoon, I looked at the two pieces of legislation that are being discussed. One is the Constitution Act of 1986, and the other is the Electoral Act of 1993. Both the pieces of legislation are Acts that predate MMP, which is 30-years-old this year. Was it 13 October, I think, 1996 was the first MMP election? And so things have changed since then. It is a different time, and in terms of the process of election night and the process of course of counting the votes, and then of course the party vote and trying to figure out and understand what the make up of the new Parliament looks like, it is quite different to what it was in 1986 or what it was in 1993, when it was a far simpler but, I think, a less diverse political system. Therefore, it is good that we bring this piece of legislation to the House this afternoon, to look at what we do and if it is fit for purpose, and we’ll be discussing it in the committee of the whole House stage.

As I was thinking about why we need to do this, one: of course MMP has changed the landscape of what the Parliament looks like, and how long it takes to form a Government or a coalition Government. The second part for me was around looking at models around the world and how different it is. Of course, the Westminster system is very binary, and many of us—well, probably all of us in this House—might remember the morning after the night before of an election. You get that phone call from some random number saying, “Hello, congratulations, you’ve been elected. We’ve just booked a flight for you at 6.30 tomorrow morning. Please be ready to fly to Wellington.” So suddenly you’re on this flight the next day to Wellington and it’s all sort of a, you know, possum in the headlights kind of thing.

Whereas, you look at jurisdictions around the world—an example would be the United States, where they have their elections generally, or depending what cycle it is, but an example is the start of November. So an election is held for a member of Congress at the start of November, but then they don’t actually get sworn in. There’s not actually the transition until the start of January of the next year. So it makes it clearer, and there’s obviously time to make those changes, to put those things in place. We don’t have that here. It is, as I say, one night you win and then 48 hours later, or less, you’re actually down here in Parliament preparing to be sworn in and take up your office. What your area of the office may be.

We look forward to the committee stage and having some good robust discussion, making sure that this is small and simple and it is the right thing to do. But obviously, as members of the Opposition, our job is to scrutinise and to ensure that the public feel confident that we have done due process to make sure that when it comes out the other end, this piece of legislation, when it’s enacted, is effective and will do what it says on the biscuit tin.
Motion agreed to.
Bill read a second time.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: The Constitution Amendment Bill is set down for committee stage immediately. I declare the House in committee for consideration of the Constitution Amendment Bill.
Committee of the whole House
Clause 1 Title

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: Members, the House is in committee on the Constitution Amendment Bill. We start with the debate on clause 1, “Title”. The question is that clause 1 stand part.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. This is probably the—I have a few questions which I’ll ask, kind of in good faith. They’re not trick questions; just to elucidate some answers from the Minister to, I think, probably clarify the intention of the legislation and its constitutional purpose. So just with the title, I understand from Standing Orders that sometimes when you have an overall question around the bill this might be an appropriate place to raise it.

We did have some concerns around this bill, in terms of the fact that after enacting this the executive, rather than ending 28 days after the election, could continue indefinitely until the return of the writ. So I just wondered if the Minister could perhaps assure the public that there are other checks and balances in place that mean that despite this bill, there is a opportunity for there to be regular elections and other constitutional checks that ensure that democracy continues. That is certainly my understanding, but I think, given the tenor of some of the submissions—as I understand, to the select committee—it might be good to have that clarification made by the Minister. So in terms of the fact that there was a singular date of ending, previously, in the Constitution Act, and now that there isn’t a definite date, although there’s a trigger point for that.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. Just also on the title, and I think this is something that we have seen with some of the other titles that are brought in front of the House, where on a bill that has the kind of content which, literally, has constitutional significance, like the Constitution Act, often they could create confusions between what the public perceives as the Constitution Act and now the Constitution Amendment Act. I just want to check with the Minister if any consideration was given on how that could be clearer. Obviously, we’ve seen multiple Acts or bills that go through the House that have the inclusion of a bracket, which makes it a little bit more, I guess, visible to the general public and those who are interested, that it’s referring to a specific thing as opposed to without such additional identifiers as a bracket.

The other thing that I also want to check with the Minister, and I’m assuming this is going to be, hopefully, just a miniature update, noting that we’re no longer in 2025. So whether this will be automatically updated to reflect that it is 2026? So those are my two questions to start with, and I’m noting that my colleague, Camilla Belich and her questions are quite pertinent. I do have questions around that, but I’ll leave it to a later clause.

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice)
content.text: In relation to the first question, which I couldn’t connect with the title but nevertheless I will endeavour to answer it. All this bill does is, rather than 28 days after the election being the trigger point, it is when the writ is returned. Now, that might be 29 days or 30 days, but it doesn’t change the overall checks and balances in our system at all. They remain as strong or as weak as they were before the bill and are not changed by the bill.
In terms of Mr Xu-Nan’s comments, I struggled to make any sense of them. So maybe he might elucidate it again.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: Taking up that invitation, Lawrence Xu-Nan.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Absolutely. I was hoping that—you know what? If we had the Plain Language Act Repeal Bill, then maybe that would have been a little bit clearer. So my question is: is the title sufficiently different enough from “Constitution Act” for it to be made clear? My second question is: will 2025 be updated to 2026?

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice)
content.text: Well, in relation to the second point, I imagine it will. In regard to the first element of it, I think the Constitution Amendment Bill says what it means, which is that we’re amending the Constitution Act.
Clause 1 agreed to.
Committee of the whole House
Clause 2 Commencement

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: We come now to the debate on clause 2, “Commencement”. The question is that clause 2 stand part.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. Noting that the commencement is the day after Royal assent, I want to check: originally, this bill was reported back to the House, I believe, at the end of last year, or even the beginning of this year. It’s been a little while ago, which is why, I think, that Steve said 2025 and not 2026, because we were supposed to pass this last year. Despite the fact that it’s the day after Royal assent, is there sufficient time for elements of this bill to take effect?

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice)
content.text: Yes.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Can I just check from you if the Minister is also taking directions from the Government side in his response?

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: Oh, I think the Minister is experienced enough, probably, to be his own man in the chair.
Clause 2 agreed to.
Committee of the whole House
Clause 3 Principal Act

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: We’re coming now to the debate on clause 3, the “Principal Act”. The question is that clause 3 stand part.
Clause 3 agreed to.
Committee of the whole House
Clause 4 Section 6 amended (Ministers of Crown to be members of Parliament)

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: We come now to clause 4, the debate on “Section 6 amended (Ministers of Crown to be members of Parliament)”. The question is that clause 4 stand part.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. This is probably one of the more substantive clauses of this bill, and enacts, essentially, the purpose of it. I did check back to the Electoral Act and the sections of the Constitution Act that they’re amending, and it appears to me that they look like they’re in order. Hopefully, my colleague Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan has also checked, and he will raise any questions that he has on that at the time. I mean, we are here in urgency discussing a bill—even though it is minor—of constitutional significance, and so it would be appreciated if the Minister could engage with answering what are serious questions and not ask to simply delay it.

There is a change in this bill which means that, rather than 28 days after an election, the executive can continue—as I read it, and please correct me if I’m wrong, Minister—indefinitely until the return of the writ. Some assurances around that, I think, is a legitimate question to ask, which we didn’t hear a response to.

The other questions I have in relation to this bill: if you read the cover note on it, which I know is not part of the bill, it talks about recounts and electorate seats. I did have a bit of a think about how this worked, and my understanding—I’d appreciate, if this is not correct, that this could be clarified—is that the relevance of electoral candidate recounts in relation to the list, which is listed here and there’s a definition of “list candidate” in new section 6(3), inserted by clause 4, the relevance of the recounts is that, if there is a recount in an electorate seat, the list cannot be determined until the recount has been completed. And so, even though the cover note talks about recounts in electorates—it’s obviously the common area to have a recount when you have an electorate vote, whereas the list is obviously over the entire country, and it’s a little bit more difficult to do a full recount of every single booth in the entire country.

The relevance of the electorate seats is that, if there is a recount, then the list can’t be finalised, and the list being finalised is, as I understand, the trigger for the final writ to then be issued and the members of Parliament to be determined. I’d appreciate some confirmation that that is correct, because when you read the cover note and the bill, it isn’t as clear as it could be, but I think, probably, that that is the place to do that.

I do have another question which I might just raise now, which is around whether the Minister thought to consider any advice around caretaker principles at all during that period of time. Obviously, we are talking about a period of time where there has been a general election and prior to a new executive being sworn in. By its nature, that would lend itself to being a caretaker period. That is, I understand, governed by the Cabinet Manual, but, obviously, if there was going to be any legislative change to that or a re-assertion or a codification of that need for the caretaker principles to be in place during that period of time—whether the Minister considered that that might be something to include in this bill so that it was clear the manner in which the executive continued in office, because that is the subject of this bill?

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (National)
content.text: In answer to the last question, no, I didn’t consider changing or legislating differently for the rules in relation to the caretaker period, because the bill doesn’t change it in any way. It does, yes, potentially prolong that period for a number of days if there is a very unusual and unexpected event that delays the announcement of the writ or the declaration of the writ, but, I think, as a country with the potential question marks over the 1984 election and behaviour following that, since that period, there has been no real issues that I can recall from caretaker Governments acting in a way that was at all controversial. I think this country has a good system in place and a good understanding, and so I didn’t give any serious thought to changing that in any way, shape, or form in relation to this legislation.

As regards the first point, why it’s linked to the declaration of the listing fees: yes, that is the final piece of the jigsaw before the writ can be declared, because the outcome of an electorate seat going one way or the other will have implications for the list, because it’s the overall percentage of the votes that are determined by the listing, so the interaction between electorate seats and list MPs is the final piece of the jigsaw.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I’ve got a couple of questions for the Minister on clause 4, as well. I think one of the first questions is something that we were seeing addressed earlier, but if the Minister wouldn’t mind providing further elucidation. The submitters were worried about the kind of decisions that the caretaker Government Ministers would be able to make. It was alluded to in the report that this is something that is currently covered under Cabinet Manual, but if the Minister wouldn’t mind just highlighting what are some of the, I guess, limitations that a caretaker Government is able to make in terms of making such decisions. I think that would be helpful to have on record but, also, for the public and for those who are submitting on this to be reassured by those limitations. That would be my first question.

Following on from what my colleague Camilla Belich mentioned in terms of the list candidates, I think one of the things I want to check with the Minister and, again, I’m not our electoral reform spokesperson, but I’m interested to know what happens in the event of a by-election. We have an example from the 2023 election, particularly with the Port Waikato seat, where a by-election was triggered roughly around the same time as a general election. If someone who was in place at the time who then wasn’t elected and ceased to be an MP, how would they be captured under this particular clause, if at all?

My final question for this contribution is around the changes to clause 4, subclause (1), this replacement section 6(2)(b). Currently the wording is, I believe, “until the expiration of the 28th day after the day on which the person ceases to be a member of Parliament”. Now, I know that a lot of things we’re doing are also precautionary in nature, but I do want to check, except for a few examples, as mentioned, and that, to my knowledge, hasn’t happened recently.

So the question I wanted to ask—which hasn’t been tested recently—is if it’s until “the close of the day after the day on which the Electoral Commission declares,” what then happens in those 24 hours, or potentially longer, from when the Electoral Commission declares until the next day? How does having that extra 24 hours work in this case with regard to our now having declared elected list candidates, but the people are still in their custodial ministerial positions for another 24 hours? According to how it’s written, there might be additional considerations that I’m not aware of, but I wanted to check with the Minister.

Just a point of order, Mr Chairperson. I just wanted to check. I know that a lot of these sections might seem quite small, but it would be good to get engagement from the Minister. But if the Minister is still seeking advice, we will be able to just cover some of that in future parts.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I do have a question that could sit into the next clause, which is what I was considering waiting for, but seeing as the Minister of Justice is getting advice, I’ll ask it here.

We do have an issue in New Zealand where, during the period of time between elections, we don’t actually—as I understand it—have a Speaker. A Speaker, obviously, has control of the Parliament Buildings and they have quite a lot of jurisdiction in relation to that, and so I wanted to ask the Minister whether he had considered including the Speaker—I’m assuming they’re excluded as they’re not a member of the executive—in some of these provisions in order to ensure that continuity.

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice)
content.text: No, I didn’t.
Clause 4 agreed to.
Committee of the whole House
Clause 5 Section 8 amended (Appointment of Parliamentary Under-Secretaries)

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: We come now to clause 5. This is the debate on clause 5, “Section 8 amended (Appointment of Parliamentary Under-Secretaries)”. The question is that clause 5 stand part.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I understand that this is the last bill in urgency, but it would be good to have some constructive engagement. I know that the Minister of Justice has the officials here, and I want to acknowledge the officials, who are here on their weekend. It may be Tuesday here for us, in Parliament, but for the rest of the world, it’s Saturday. I know that they have a lot of knowledge in this area, and so I’m sure that if the Minister wishes to get some advice, he will be able to do that and it will be very good advice.

To the questions I have in relation to clause 5, firstly, this was substantively changed by the Justice Committee, and I wanted to ask the Minister whether he agreed with the changes in relation to Parliamentary Under-Secretaries. I have a genuine question. I haven’t had time to check it prior to now, but I understand that a Parliamentary Under-Secretary isn’t a member of the executive, and I want to just clarify that, because that seems to bring other people into it, which is why I was going to ask about the Speaker in this question, as well.

The other question I had is this. We seem to have a situation here where a list candidate is defined in section 3(1) of the Electoral Act, but this is included in this bill, both in new section 6(3) in clause 4, which we’ve just concluded our debate on, but also in new section 8(40 in clause 5. I just wanted know whether, from a drafting perspective, it is necessary to have those two, essentially, identical provisions, which are only referring back to the exact preceding provision in the reference to a list candidate. But it is, in fact, the same definition.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I just also note, like my colleague Camilla Belich has said, that while this is a bill that we all agree on and it is a reasonably small bill, it does have quite an important role and it holds constitutional significance. We’ve asked quite a few questions on the last clause and we’ve heard very little from the Minister of Justice regarding engagement. But I can see that the officials are, obviously, here and are providing additional information for the Minister, and so if the Minister wouldn’t mind responding to our questions, that would be appreciated.

For clause 5, I wanted to check with the Minister in terms of what the Justice Committee has agreed to update in this new section 8(3)(a) in clause 5, which is around a Parliamentary Under-Secretary continuing to hold office during the period “beginning on the day that they must vacate office as a member of Parliament” under various parts of the Electoral Act. This does, I guess, in some ways tie in to what Camilla Belich mentioned previously regarding the Parliamentary Under-Secretary being in this weird, limbo role between being both in the executive and not in the executive. I wanted to know why that particular provision doesn’t apply, for example, to Ministers of the Crown. For example, do Ministers of the Crown also then have to do that, beginning on the day that they must vacate office as a member of Parliament, under those particular sections. So if the Minister wouldn’t mind, do let us know what the difference is between Ministers of the Crown and Parliamentary Under-Secretaries.

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. In answer to Ms Belich’s question around whether I agree with the amendment which includes Parliamentary Under-Secretaries, yes, I do, and the Government does. It hadn’t been included in the Constitution Act originally, and it’s not an earth-shattering change. Ultimately, it was the Ministers and the executive that were concerned about to ensure that we have Ministers after the 28 days, if there is an issue. But it doesn’t hurt to have Parliamentary Under-Secretaries, as well, and so we’re including them in order to be consistent across the way that the arrangements are in place. So, yes, it wasn’t included; yes, the Justice Committee considered it and recommended it; and, yes, the Government of the day agrees with it.

In terms of the question around whether or not the drafting refers back to the clause before, my advice is that the Parliamentary Counsel Office—which is the part of the Government that drafts these bills—has said that it was necessary for clarity.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I just wanted to check with the Minister of Justice whether the Minister also has the response to what we’ve asked, or, particularly, to what I’ve asked in terms of—let alone that there are still questions outstanding from the previous clause. But in terms of this particular clause—specifically, new section 8(3)(a) in clause 5—I ask whether that particular provision applies only to Parliamentary Under-Secretaries, or should it also be applicable to Ministers of the Crown.

Noting that the Minister is just seeking some additional advice, I do want to check this with the Minister, as well, as a part of this is around the purpose this bill in the sense that it is mainly so that the Governor-General is able to have advisers. From what the Minister said before, which was that it was nice to have Parliamentary Under-Secretaries as part of this, I’m just also checking that Parliamentary Under-Secretaries also, in some ways—maybe via a Minister—also advise the Governor-General.

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice)
content.text: Just returning to the initial question around new section 8(3) in clause 5, about whether what applies to Parliamentary Under-Secretaries also applies to Ministers: yes, it does. That’s in new section 6(2)(b) in clause 4(1), which is the relevant one there. My advice is that they deal with the same issues.
Clause 5 agreed to.
Bill to be reported without amendment.
House resumed.

content.speaker: CHAIRPERSON (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: Mr Speaker, the committee has considered the Constitution Amendment Bill and reports it without amendment. I move, That the report be adopted.
Motion agreed to.
Report adopted.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: The Constitution Amendment Bill is set down for third reading immediately.
Legislative Statement

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice)
content.text: I present a legislative statement on the Constitution Amendment Bill.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono)
content.text: That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
Third Reading

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice)
content.text: I move, That the Constitution Amendment Bill be now read a third time.

I want to acknowledge the support across the House for this legislation after a long period of urgency where Parliament has been very busy for a very extended period of time until late in the evening, with the support of many people across this building. I want to acknowledge the hard efforts of everybody across the House and in the various rooms and back rooms and corridors and all over the place, including security—thank you very much for this extended period, which we’re now coming to the end of.

This bill, as we’ve just heard, is a simple bill that addresses a little issue that has come up in previous elections whereby—after we’ve had an election, and we’re waiting for the final results and what’s called the writ being declared, which has the final results of who are the new MPs in the new Government or the new Parliament—there is a period of time, after 28 days, where MPs are no longer MPs. If you can’t be a Minister or if you’re not an MP, we’ve got a problem, and so this legislation does away with that 28-day rule and has as a trigger point the declaration of the writ. It’s something that everybody across the Parliament agrees with; it changes our settings, and it is just a small detail that we decided is worth getting corrected.

It sits within the context of a parliamentary system that has, throughout its history, managed the transition of power between Governments in our democracy very effectively. This is a small way in which this Government is fixing the basics when it comes to our democratic system so that we can build a future together.

content.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH (Labour)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s a pleasure to take a call on this Constitution Amendment Bill—as the Minister said, the last bill that we’re debating now in this rather long period of urgency, but an important bill. Any amendments to our constitution are important. Of course, in New Zealand, we have the Constitution Act, but we also have an unwritten constitution, so anything that stipulates how our constitutional conventions are to occur is of probably increased importance, because this bill will form a part of our constitution as it stands, as an unwritten constitution.

I think any bill that challenges our democracy does deserve scrutiny. I do know that there are checks and balances in place to ensure that when you have bad faith actors in Government—which hopefully we never will have—these types of provisions aren’t utilised in a way that would seek to defeat the purposes of our democracy. I’m sure that will never happen in New Zealand, but certainly when we are considering these bills, it’s important to scrutinise them and to ensure that those kinds of things wouldn’t happen.

This bill does do an important thing; it does change the 28-day rule for members of the executive—so Ministers and MPs, and in fact the Prime Minister, the leader of our country. Instead of that ending 28 days after an election, it ends with the return of the writ. I think a check and balance on that, which would have been good to hear articulated by the Minister, is that this will only come into effect when there is an election, because the writ will only be able to be returned when there is an election. We would hope that this doesn’t impact—and I’m sure that it won’t—the regularity of our elections, and the good faith, as I mentioned earlier, that we have generally had in New Zealand in relation to the caretaker provisions when there has been an election to ensure the smooth transition of Government, and also the utmost respect that the democratic vote is given to determine the executive.

Of course, that’s not as clear-cut as it is in some jurisdictions, because we have an election and then it’s up to those of us lucky enough to be in a position to earn a seat in this House to try to negotiate the confidence of the House. That confidence of the House can take a period of time, and that does mean that there does need to be different conversations. It is, I suppose, sobering to reflect on—I think my colleague Glen Bennett said it was 30 years from the introduction of MMP. I don’t believe, personally, that that has fully matured as much as it possibly could have in terms of the different repercussions that you do have in an MMP election. I’m sure that we will continue to see that.

Of course, with the last election, we did have a period of time that was protracted—probably more from earning the confidence of the House. The coalition negotiations took a period of time, and we did have a longer caretaker period, which meant that the 28-day rule had to be extended. I understand that that was on the request of the incoming Prime Minister—so, of course, a lot of good faith there and a lot of intention to make sure that this is done properly.

I did want to just echo the comments that we’re obviously in a situation of urgency where we’ve just given speeches on the second reading and obviously had scrutiny in the committee of the whole House stage. I won’t repeat all of those points again, but I did want to just add a little kind of quirky political point. My good friend and former colleague Grant Robertson did write a book, Anything Could Happen, and in that book, he noted a really interesting point around these caretaker provisions, which was that he, prior to coming into Parliament, had been a diplomat, and he had kind of always thought about the position of being Minister of Foreign Affairs. He had, I don’t think, ever been Minister of Foreign Affairs, obviously being the Minister of Finance, which is a very senior and important position within Government.

But, because of this 28-day rule being in place, he was sworn in to be the Minister of Foreign Affairs for a very short period of time, and this was significant for him to note it in his very good book Anything Could Happen. Maybe in future editions, he can reflect on the fact that that situation is unlikely to happen again due to the passage of this Constitution Amendment Bill, which I commend to the House.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN (Green)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Hopefully this is the last time I need to get up during this urgency. I have lost track of how many—I have genuinely lost track. I hope that members of this House also take comfort in knowing that this is the last time that they hear my voice for at least two weeks.

We are kind of on the final stretch of this particular urgency by the Government. I do want to express—because the Minister has sort of opened the scope into just having a broader expression of thanks to everyone who works in Parliament, as well as all of our officials during this period, for providing advice and continuously providing services. That includes, obviously, the Chamber Officers, the Office of the Clerk, those at Copperfield’s, security, officials who have to work very late into the night, and also translators who are, unfortunately, a very small team who may not have the same flexibility as some of the others to be able to do things in shifts. Indeed, even MPs have that flexibility and ability. We do want to thank all of you for this period.

If you’ll indulge me, Mr Speaker, I do want to reiterate the fact that during this urgency period, we have seen 21 bills being discussed in various forms across 34 stages—which some would some is an achievement, and some would say, is it really the best use of Parliament time, but also is this the most democratic? But, you know what, if the Government have KPIs they want to tick off, then KPIs are KPIs.
Just on this bill—as we have mentioned in the second reading—

content.speaker: Grant McCallum
content.text: Commend the bill.

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
content.text: —it is something that is—members on the Government side are saying just to commend the bill, but I think I physically—physically—cannot finish a speech that is shorter than 10 minutes. I will say that the exception that I have given, as people in this House would know, is for the valedictory speech of the Hon Judith Collins. I did shorten my speech, and I made a special mention of that, and that’s just in recognition of her years of service. If anyone who has been around for more than two decades would like to suddenly announce that they are retiring, I will shorten my speech.
In terms of the Constitution Amendment Bill here—

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: Is that an invitation for anyone in the House at the moment?

content.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
content.text: —I do want to say that, with this bill, it is an important change, as we have discussed both in the second reading but also in the committee stage. I think the first thing is to highlight that, as we’re discussing this reasonably short five-clause bill and we go through clause by clause as opposed to part by part, that it is good to hear from the Minister of Justice the reassurance that, despite the fact that this bill was supposed to come back into the House at end of last year, that we are seeing that even though after Royal assent that the nature of this bill does lend itself to be implemented quite quickly. Also, it’s very assuring to hear from the Minister that as well that the title of this bill will be updated to 2026 to reflect the fact that we’re no longer in 2025.

Once we get into the substance of our clause 4 and 5 of the bill, it is worth noting that the previous speaker, Camilla Belich, has already mentioned the constitutional importance of this. We would have liked to see a little bit more engagement from the Minister, in terms of some of the questions and also some of the context that this could come up. Again, even if you look at the departmental report, it’s a very short departmental report, and there is not a lot of information in there. So if a constitutional situation or issue does come up, Hansard then becomes the default of how we are able to have that clarity from the ministerial statement.

There are a few things that I think it’s important for us to address on some of the conversations that we did have here. I think the first one is around the 28 days and the important part around the removal of that—we have discussed the event of force majeure, which, potentially, would affect the way that elections could be conducted. I do want to correct something I said in the second reading, which is around, I guess, Government arrangement, which is more to do with election and the return of the writs. In those cases, the way that the existing legislation in section 6 of the Constitution Act is really triggered around the day after the 28th day, whereas now it could be actually earlier than that because it has now opened this ability to be a little bit more flexible. So the clarification that I was trying to seek from the Minister is around what then happens between when the Electoral Commission declares and the day after, and how would that interact with this new change.

I think, more importantly, one of the things that I asked the Minister, and this is a genuine concern was raised by the submitters, was around what kind of decision-making powers would those caretaker roles and caretaker Ministers would have during this. As we see in the department report, it just simply says, “Look, Cabinet Manual does address this.” But then, when we asked the Minister to potentially elucidate some of that, we didn’t actually get a clarification. I did have a look at the Cabinet Manual on this. This is to do with particularly paragraph 6.31 onwards of the Cabinet Manual, around some of the expectations for the Ministers during this caretaker process. It’s important to note that in the earlier section of the Cabinet Manual it does say that the Ministers have the full power of the Minister—I believe that is around paragraph 6.21, which where it says “the incumbent government is still the lawful executive authority, with all the powers and responsibilities that go with executive office.”

I think one of the things that is worth mentioning—I think this is something that my colleague Camilla Belich alluded to in the committee stage—is while the Ministers do have the executive power, without a Parliament, without a Speaker, that we may not see potentially bills being introduced as a part of that caretaker arrangement. I think that’s an important reminder for people and for those who had concerns on this section, that while they have all of the powers, the ability to make law falls on this House here, as opposed to the Ministers and the executive. So that interaction between the executive and the legislature remain. I think that’s an important reminder.

Some of the other things that we did ask as a part of this is how would that list be finalised, and I think that’s something that, again, this side of the House has asked the Minister around that kind of clarity during the committee stage. It’s unfortunate that I didn’t get a response from the Minister. I’m hoping that presumably that means it’s not applicable, which is fine, or potentially outside the scope. But what would happen if we see—we talked about the fact that other disruptions we see could be a recount or a judicial review, etc., but what happens in the event of a by-election; would that be captured under this scenario as well, or is that something that is completely different?

One of the final considerations that we did discuss as a part of this bill is around clause 5, section 8 amended, around the Parliamentary Under-Secretary, as we alluded to in our second reading, that this is something that the select committee did change to provide more clarity in terms of the role of the Parliamentary Under-Secretary in this sort of arrangement. Actually, I do want to also take this opportunity to acknowledge the Parliamentary Under-Secretary, both current and previous Parliamentary Under-Secretaries—of which Jan Logie, one of our previous Green Party MPs, was one—in terms of the fact that Parliamentary Under-Secretaries do an incredibly important role, but, unlike Ministers, a lot of the work that they do often doesn’t get the same kind of acknowledgment. So I do want to acknowledge that, when we have the opportunity to do so.

Just to finish off, we did get confirmation from the Minister that it is important for the Parliamentary Under-Secretary to be captured as a part of this. So with that, the Green Party does support the Constitution Amendment Bill.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: The question is the motion be agreed to.

content.speaker: LAURA McCLURE (ACT)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. He cut that short by three seconds—Lawrence, I’m a little bit disappointed. I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: Hon CASEY COSTELLO (Minister of Customs)
content.text: I think it’s fitting that we finish this very long Tuesday with a bill that we all have consensus on in the House.

I would like to point out the irony that the gentleman who wanted to acknowledge the hard work of all of the people that worked to make this House run, then protracted this by a further 10 minutes rather than allowing them to go home early. I commend the bill to the House.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: Um—sorry.

content.speaker: Hūhana Lyndon
content.text: Hūhana.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: Mari—sorry.

content.speaker: Hūhana Lyndon
content.text: Hūhana!

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: Hūhana Lyndon. Sorry.

content.speaker: HŪHANA LYNDON (Green)
content.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: That’s my lack of sleep, not yours.

content.speaker: HŪHANA LYNDON
content.text: No, that’s all right. You know, it’s been a long weekend.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: Five minutes.

content.speaker: HŪHANA LYNDON
content.text: Again, giving thanks and praise to our kaimahi that are here with us as we complete this round of urgency. It is good that we’re at this point where we have the Constitution Amendment Bill, where we do have consensus within the House.

The role and function of Kāwanatanga in providing stability for decision making and for officials and Government departments is essential no matter what happens between election time and when the writ is finally passed. So on behalf of the Green Party, we tautoko. Kia ora.

content.speaker: TOM RUTHERFORD (National—Bay of Plenty)
content.text: Mr, Speaker I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: RACHEL BOYACK (Labour—Nelson)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Look, the Labour Party is supporting this bill. It is an important bill in terms of the coalition—sorry, the continuity of Government. The coalition—we could talk about the coalition and the end of the coalition on 7 November; there will, certainly be a new coalition. Our intention is for that to be led by this side of the House following 7 November.

This is an important bill because that continuity of Government is important. We had a unique situation last time where we ended up with Ministers who were unable to retain their ministerial warrants because of the time it took for a Government to be formed. That then has potential implications, in case there may be some type of emergency, there may be some type of scenario where it’s important that you have a Government able to make decisions on behalf of New Zealanders. It is, at the end of the day, the highest jurisdiction in the land in terms of being able to make decisions and ensure that the bills get paid and ensure that the people are governed well. This is a pragmatic bill.

We did have some questions and, unfortunately, we didn’t have all of that engagement with the Minister at the committee of the whole House stage. Some of my colleagues do still have questions that have been somewhat unanswered, and there are probably some elements of this that still need some attention. It’s been raised in the House this afternoon about the role of the Speaker and what happens in that regard in this scenario.

We in the Labour Party think it’s good that this bill has passed in time for the upcoming election. We are very much looking forward to the upcoming election and what we will have from a change of Government, and that, actually, it will be a Labour-led coalition that is forming a Government in that time frame, following the election on 7 November. We very much look forward to that. On that basis, I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: PAULO GARCIA (National—New Lynn)
content.text: I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: Georgie Dansey—five minutes.

content.speaker: GEORGIE DANSEY (Labour)
content.text: Thank you. Oh, you almost gave me 10—I was getting excited. Hey, firstly, I would like to thank all of the staff and the mahi that you have done throughout this week. I’m always blown away at how hard all of the kaimahi in this place work, so thank you all so much. Someone just did this at me, and I love it. How hard you all work for us in Parliament—I hope you have a very nice, well-deserved sleep after this, as I do for all of the members.

I think that this is quite a nice bill to finish on, actually, because of the support from around the House. It’s always nice when we can agree on something. I think this is a very logical bill that makes sense to everyone. Other speakers have spoken to the good faith that departing Governments have waiting for the incoming Government, and that that moves across political stripes. I think that’s something to celebrate here, in a place where often we don’t agree. We have not agreed on many bills that we have debated across urgency, so it is nice to finish on this one and to be able to continue to add some continuity, as much as we can, into Parliament. We debate a lot of regulatory standards bills, I’ve noticed, and that continuity and trying to smooth things out is something where we can usually find common ground, and this is another example of that.

As previous speakers have alluded to, I look forward to the smooth transition of the current Government moving out as Labour moves in on 7 November. It is with that I will finish. Have a wonderful sleep, everybody.

content.speaker: SUZE REDMAYNE (National—Rangitīkei)
content.text: With great pleasure, I commend this bill to the House.

content.speaker: GLEN BENNETT (Labour)
content.text: It is with great pleasure that I would like to contribute to this debate and share some thoughts and reflections as we close. In my second reading contribution, I, obviously, made reference to the 30 years since MMP. Part of the reason this debate has been happening today and it’s been through select committee and through the proper process was around the previous election in 2023. It’s kind of interesting that 30 years on from 1996, we are debating a piece of legislation because of how MMP changed the system. But what is also interesting is that 1996 was the year that the Hon Nanaia Mahuta was first elected to this House. So it is sort of a 30-year process, and here we are today.

My only few comments I want make are that that has changed the landscape of the Parliament and of timing, not only of coalition Government negotiations but also, obviously, of the counting of the vote. I was looking through, and we had the 1996 election, the 1999 election, the 2002 election, 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, 2017, 2020, 2023, until we come to this place. They’ve all had different variations in terms of the make-up, the timing of negotiations of a Government, but also the timing that it’s taken, actually, for the writ be released and for us to know what the outcome is.

My other point I want to make is that, obviously, clause 5 is around the Parliamentary Under-Secretaries. Again, this legislation is changing the legislation that was the Constitution Act 1986, which was that piece of legislation—fun fact; listen up, write this down—when, obviously, Parliamentary Under-Secretaries were first introduced into Parliament and were part of it, so 40 years ago since we’ve had our Parliamentary Under-Secretaries. Obviously, clause 5 was very important to have in this bill to make sure that they were recognised, because they do do heavy lifting—it’s been acknowledged. Often smaller parties, but often the larger parties also have under-secretaries who are often workhorses for the Minister in the main portfolio.

We are here. We are supporting this legislation. I’m glad that that we’ve got to where we’ve got to this week. I don’t think we needed to be here this long, but, hey, we’re here—well, a few of us are here, because most of our colleagues are out campaigning and hoping to win on 7 November. Kia ora koutou.

content.speaker: STUART SMITH (National—Kaikōura)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. It has been a long week—

content.speaker: Hon Members
content.text: A long day.

content.speaker: STUART SMITH
content.text: —since we moved urgency on Tuesday afternoon—well, it is a long day; that is right—so much so that some people are hallucinating on the other side of the of the House. But it is a nice way to end it, on a constitutional bill, small but very vital and important for the running of our country. I commend it to the House.
Motion agreed to.
Bill read a third time.

content.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Greg O'Connor)
content.text: Just before I adjourn the House, thank you, members, for being here. There have been a lot of thankyous—obviously, the staff that have kept this place going while we’ve come and gone. [Applause] There’s another group as well: the families of members that are here, who I know are sitting, waiting, hoping that this moment arrives and you’ll be home tonight to either pick up the kids, take them out for dinner, or perhaps both. Thirdly, another group I think we should acknowledge is that on these seats here and out the back has been a group of public servants, much vilified, but they have been here. I was driving home last night up Molesworth Street, and there was a big group of health officials moving up, and they were walking back this morning when I came back down here. So just a little bit of acknowledgment—there’s a lot of people it takes to keep this going. [Applause] For the rest of you, I hope you can all get home tonight and enjoy whatever might be on, starting at 5 past 7 tonight. The House stands adjourned until 9 a.m. on—sorry, no, it’s not. The House stands adjourned until 2 p.m. on Tuesday.
The House adjourned at 3.48 p.m. (Saturday)
