      Climate Change Response (Tort Liability) Amendment Bill
      Legislative StatementHon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice) (16:14): I present a legislative statement on the Climate Change Response (Tort Liability) Amendment Bill.
      ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Maureen Pugh): That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the parliamentary website.
      First ReadingHon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice) (16:15): I move, That the Climate Change Response (Tort Liability) Amendment Bill be now read a first time. I nominate the Justice Committee to consider the bill. At the appropriate time I intend to move that the bill be reported to the House by 30 July 2026 and that the committee have authority to meet at any time while the House is sitting (except during oral questions), during any evening on a day on which there has been a sitting of the House, on a Friday in a week in which there has been a sitting in the House, and outside the Wellington area, despite Standing Orders 193,195, and 196. 
      This bill clarifies climate change laws to provide businesses and New Zealanders with certainty around their obligations. Ongoing litigation in the High Court, where civil claims have been made, is creating uncertainty in business confidence and investment. It risks the development of a new regime that runs in parallel and it may contradict the framework that Parliament has already enacted to respond to climate change. Ultimately, if there is legal uncertainty, there is less investment over time, and that affects us all by making our country less competitive. Therefore, the Government will amend the Climate Change Response Act 2002 to prevent findings of tort liability for activities that cause or contribute to the emissions of greenhouse gas and, through those emissions, may cause or contribute to climate change harm. 
      A tort is a civil claim brought in private law in situations where the conduct of one person causes harm or invades the interests of another person. Tort law has primarily been developed through the common law, which arises from decisions made by judges in court, rather than by legislation that has developed in Parliament. 
      In the Smith v Fonterra case, the defendant is asking the court to develop a regime to control and reduce the emissions of six of this country’s largest businesses. This would be potentially contrary to the regulatory response set by Parliament under the Climate Change Response Act 2002, which sets out our legal framework for New Zealand’s regulatory response to climate change. This framework includes a 2050 target for emissions reduction and a regime for setting and meeting successive emissions budgets with a view to achieving that target. 
      The Government’s view is that greenhouse gas emissions and climate change harm are best regulated by Parliament and the executive, who take a whole-of-economy approach that carefully considers environmental, economic, and social implications, rather than having that done on a case by case basis through litigation in the courts. A statutory bar prevents courts from issuing a certain type of finding or considering a particular issue. In this case, the bill will prevent a person or entity from being liable in tort law for climate change or harm caused by greenhouse gas emissions. This will apply to all activities contributing to greenhouse gas emissions directly and indirectly, regardless of when or where they occur. 
      However, the bill is targeted and will only affect tort claims relating to climate change damage or harm arising from greenhouse gas emissions. It will not affect traditional environmental torts—for example, where a factory burning fossil fuels causes harm through odour or ash residue. This may still be covered under the tort of nuisance. 
      The bill will also apply to the proceedings of Smith v Fonterra. I acknowledge that care is needed when deciding whether legislation should apply to existing court proceedings. However, these proceedings are still at the procedural stage, and the substantive proceedings have yet to start. 
      Currently, there is no tort liability for climate change damage caused by greenhouse gas emissions, but this is what Mr Smith is asking to be developed. I therefore consider that the application of the bar to existing proceedings that have not been finally determined is necessary. This will ensure that there’s no risk of a parallel regulatory regime being developed in future which applies to some of emitters and is inconsistent with the Government’s regulatory response. As no rights have yet been identified in the existing case, this legislation will not deprive the litigants of the fruit of litigation. 
      The bill clarifies the regulatory framework in which we are operating as a country with regard to climate change. The bill doesn’t change New Zealand’s climate targets or the approach that the Government has taken. Businesses with obligations under the emissions trading scheme will still be required to meet them. We have a good regime in the Climate Change Response Act and the emissions trading scheme, and we’re seeking to make sure this regime is clearly in place without confusion. 
      The bill makes it clear that the response to climate change sits squarely with the elected Parliament and the executive. The bill clarifies the law to ensure that there is certainty around climate change obligations of New Zealand businesses. It also ensures our response to climate change is managed by Parliament and the executive at a national level, rather than on a case by case basis through the courts. On that basis, I commend this bill to the House.

      Legislative StatementHon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice) (20:56): I present a legislative statement on the Crimes Amendment Bill.
      ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Greg O'Connor): That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
      Second ReadingHon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice) (20:57): I move, That the Crimes Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
      One of the core pledges of this Government when we came into office 2½ years ago was to restore law and order. That is the work of generations and is certainly the work of all New Zealanders—to fix the basics and build a future where people feel safe in their communities. That has been an unerring focus of this Government for the last 2½, years, and this bill, the Crimes Amendment Bill, is about putting victims at the heart of our justice system, and it strengthens consequences for crime. It builds on work that we’ve done bringing back real consequences for crime through changes to the Sentencing Act and three strikes, but it also moves its focus to dealing with matters around retail crime.
      I want to thank the Justice Committee for its careful consideration of the bill—very hard-working committee—and extend my hand across the aisle to work and contributions on the other side. The committee received 233 submissions on the bill, and I want to thank all the submitters and the time that they put into it.
      So what does it cover? Coward punch—what it does there is it recognises the horrendous nature of these so-called coward punches, where people come and attack somebody from behind, with no warning, to the head and can turn a life upside down. The bill targets perpetrators of these attacks by adding three coward punch offences to the mandatory sentencing framework of three strikes and maximum penalties for coward punches causing grievous bodily harm increasing to eight and 15 years depending on the intent. The coward punch manslaughter offence defines this category of violent offending and responds to the need for greater denunciation.
      The Act will be another tool for police in their response to violent crime. While I’m sympathetic to calls for even tougher responses around, say, minimum sentences, that can’t be accommodated within the confines of this crimes bill, but it’s something that people can give consideration to over time.
      Now, the committee also notes that the Government’s capping of sentence discounts is already increasing sentences for coward punch offenders and will make it more likely that fewer of such offenders would be eligible for home detention, for example. I’ll continue to monitor the impact of the recent sentencing reforms on penalties imposed for coward punch cases. I also intend to put an Amendment Paper to better address this issue at the committee stage.
      The second area is around citizen’s arrest. There has been a lot of discussion around that matter. We are recognising that we’ve had provisions in place for a long time for things happening at night after 9 p.m., but during the day it’s been a different regime. We were concerned about instances, particularly in the retail crime sector, of people walking off with trolleys full of food, not paying, people seeing that, and undermining public confidence in law and order in our community. We wanted to make it clear that people, security workers for example, can grab hold of somebody and hang on to them, with very clear instructions that they need to immediately call the police and follow the instructions of the police.
      There have been a lot of comments about this, and I just want to make the point, of course, that nobody is compelled to do anything. Everybody will make a judgment based on the circumstances of the time, and whether they think it’s safe to get involved or not. Businesses can decide whether they’ll have protocols around this, or not, but we heard a very strong call, particularly from small, family-owned dairies and retailers who wanted to have another tool available to them to deal with what continues to be a real problem in the retail crime sector.
      Another one is shoplifting. This bill brings in an infringement regime for shoplifting. At the moment, if you steal a small amount of goods from a shop, the only option is to arrest that person and send them off to court. That’s quite a high threshold. Our concern was, well, the outcome of that is that a lot of people tend to, in practice, get away with it and face no real consequences. An infringement regime provides an opportunity for a police officer to bring an instant consequence such as a fine, such as a speeding ticket situation, so that there are immediate consequences. It doesn’t replace our theft offences, but it’s another tool for police to use.
      Finally, our human trafficking offences are strengthened by this bill. As one submitter noted, these reforms are long overdue and warmly welcome. They’ll help close loopholes and better equip law enforcement to hold traffickers accountable, and that’s what we’re prepared to do there. As a result of consultation with agencies, I intend to take a step further with an Amendment Paper which will remove requirements around the Attorney-General’s consent for cross-border trafficking offences.
      Finally, the bill brings in tougher consequences for people who attack first responders, those Kiwis who go racing into danger—our prison officers, constables, ambulance staff, firefighters—and with intent-to-injure offences added to the mandatory sentencing framework for three strikes. All of these, collectively, bring a continuation of this Government’s effort to restore real consequences for crime and to push back against the tide of retail crime that we saw when we came into power 2½ years ago. We’ve made great progress as a country. People do feel safer in this country, but we’re very conscious that there is much, much more to do, and this legislation will continue that effort.

      Land Transport (Revenue) Amendment Bill
      Legislative StatementHon JAMES MEAGER (Associate Minister of Transport) (22:13): on behalf of the Minister of Transport: I present a legislative statement on the Land Transport (Revenue) Amendment Bill.
      ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono): That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
      Second ReadingHon JAMES MEAGER (Associate Minister of Transport) (22:13): on behalf of the Minister of Transport: I move, That the Land Transport (Revenue) Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
      Mr Speaker, colleagues, this bill is yet another step in the evolution of our land transport funding system and it meets our changing circumstances and upholds one of the fundamental principles of how we fund land transport in New Zealand. That principle is that vehicle users should contribute fairly in proportion to the use that they undertake on our roads. Since we centralised our roading system in the 1920s—planning came a bit later—this principle has continued to underpin how we fund and pay for our roading network. However, the system is now under increasing pressure. As our vehicles have become more fuel efficient, and we start to drive more and more electric vehicles, the traditional method of collecting revenue from our petrol excise duties and our fuel taxes has dropped while our transport investment demands have continued to grow. 
      To better support sustainable transport investment, we must ensure that the tools we collect for revenue are sustainable, fair, and fit for purpose. To achieve this, the bill advances the Government’s revenue action plan by proposing amendments that reform the tolling network and modernising the road user charges system. This bill does two key things: it looks at how we toll in a modern day and age, and it reforms our road user system.
      First, to tolling. We’ve actually got a long history of tolling in New Zealand. We’ve been doing it for over 100 years. The Auckland Harbour Bridge was built by tolls. The Lyttleton Tunnel was built by tolls. Tauranga have a few, so there are some people here who are familiar with how they work. What tolling does is it helps us to bring forward investment and build the roads and infrastructure that New Zealand needs sooner. It means the users who benefit most from new roads contribute most to those roads. We currently have toll roads in New Zealand, as I mentioned before, and we now want to progress our roading system plan, so we need to make sure we have the revenue to match those ambitions. It is about fixing the basics of our transport system so we can build a future where New Zealanders can get around our routing network in a quick and efficient manner. 
      The bill does a number of things around tolls. It has gone through the select committee process, and I’ll outline a few of the changes that have come through in a moment. It does allow for the tolling of existing roads where the users benefit from new roads on the same corridor, so that we can take a revenue approach across an entire tolling scheme rather than just on new sections of the road. Road users out there should be aware that the requirement for a feasible, untolled, or free route will remain. Of course, nothing is free in life. Those so-called free roads are still paid for by our road users. However, there will be an untolled alternative to all of our tolled roads. The bill will also enable heavy vehicles to be restricted from using unsuitable alternative routes, but only in specified circumstances. 
      Finally, we’re also updating the rules to toll concessions to make it easier to partner with the private sector to deliver the infrastructure we need. Taken together, these changes will ensure tolling is a more effective tool to help fund new roads, including our roads of national significance, those that deliver the infrastructure that New Zealand needs. 
      The second key thing this bill does is it looks at the road user charge system that we deal with in our modern day State, and it recognises that some changes are needed to be made. We need to modernise the system. We need to keep the system fair. We must ensure it’s ready to go for a shift in the future of all light-petrol vehicles onto the road user charge system. Our current system was designed in the 1970s. It is admittedly a bit clunky. It’s a manual process that relies on us to monitor our own odometers, pre-purchase road-user charges (RUC) in thousand kilometre blocks, and display teeny tiny little paper licences on our windows. 
      I’ve already said many times in this House how annoying those little bits of paper are, particularly when they fall down the dash, and a zealous parking officer comes along and gives you a nice wee donation to make to the local council or to the local NZTA because you haven’t put the right sticker in the right place. This bill does away with those stickers around road user charges. It removes the requirement to display, carry, or produce a RUC licence. In an electronic age, a paper licence should not be a strict requirement where people are paying bills, not to put paper in the front of the windscreens. The bill updates the definition of an electronic distance recorder to address some current restrictions and allow for more flexible, cost-effective approaches to recording distance.
      In a bold modern move, it allows us to have more flexible regular payment systems, so that, instead of that thrill we get when we’re driving along the road and we realise we might be running out of road user charges soon, and we’d better pull over to the side of the road, jump on the NZTA website, and buy another thousand blocks to get us around the countryside a bit more, we’re going to be able to create some new options for some more regular payments to make it a little bit easier to deal with that. Yes, we will no longer get that thrill of driving and seeing the odometer tick over and wonder when that next thousand block will kick in. But maybe—just maybe—it might make it more helpful and easy for us to run our lives as we’re going around the countryside. 
      We are also aiming to change the road user charge retail landscape in general. We’re going to make it easier for other providers to help manage the road user charge system, particularly as we move to a system where all petrol vehicles will be on it at some point. Of course, that makes sense, because as our fuel efficiency increases in our petrol vehicles, we’re going to be using less fuel on the road. That is good, obviously, for our emissions, but it does impact our revenue streams. We’ve got to make sure that those vehicles still have an impact on the road. We’ve still got to make sure they still contribute to the impact on the road that they make, and we’ll be doing that in the future through road user charges rather than fuel tax.
      The Transport and Infrastructure Committee made a number of changes that I’m sure members will go through today. I would like to thank the hard-working and industrious Transport and Infrastructure Committee. I want to thank the 47 written submissions from interested groups and individuals, and the 12 individuals that came to the select committee to provide their views. It did result in a number of changes throughout the process that, hopefully, this House will agree to today. I’ll very, very quickly go through them. 
      The committee has recommended some changes to refining the rules for tolling existing roads on the same corridor as new roads. They’ve tightened when toll revenue can be used for alternative routes. They’ve strengthened the rules for restricting heavy vehicles on alternative routes, and some changes around road-user charges. The updated bill provides that the approval of each alternative payment scheme is a regulatory decision for the RUC collector, rather than requiring Cabinet approval through secondary legislation, which would be a long and lengthy process. The bill now provides the power to set prescribed administration fees for NZTA as well as a separate service fee to cover the agency’s expenses. The bill removes the need for separate approval processes and enables the NZTA to become a provider from the date the Act commences.
      Finally, Mr Speaker, I know you’ve been looking forward to this part of the speech: the end of it. The bill clarifies the power of the RUC collector to monitor and review providers, including any agents or contractors they engage. This change responds to those submitters who had concerns about the importance of oversight for third parties that collect land transport revenue and handle road user information.
      I would like to thank everyone who has contributed towards the development of this bill. This is a practical and important bill that takes us one step closer to a fairer and more sustainable transport revenue system. I look forward to the contributions across the House. I’m sure they will be fulsome and exciting, just as exciting as it is to see the odometer tick over as we travel around the countryside over the next few months. I commend the bill to the House, and I look forward to its passage forthwith.

      Infrastructure Funding and Financing Amendment Bill
      Legislative StatementHon JAMES MEAGER (Associate Minister of Transport) (23:25): on behalf of the Minister for Infrastructure: I present a legislative statement on the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Amendment Bill.
      DEPUTY SPEAKER: That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
      Second ReadingHon JAMES MEAGER (Associate Minister of Transport) (23:25): on behalf of the Minister for Infrastructure: I move, That the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
      I’d like to start this contribution by thanking all of those involved in getting this bill to the second reading. To the members of the Finance and Expenditure Committee for their careful consideration of this bill, to the members of the public who took the time to provide both oral and written submissions: thank you to you all. Your input has helped to strengthen and improve this bill and it is greatly appreciated.
      The rationale for this bill is as follows: we need to increase the effectiveness of the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act. That is a key component of pillar two of the Government’s Going for Housing Growth programme, which is focused on making improvements to infrastructure funding—you might say fixing our infrastructure funding network—and making improvements to the financing tools to help get more housing and the future of New Zealand’s housing built.
      Under the status quo, councils and developers do face significant challenges to fund and finance the enabling infrastructure for housing. This Government and hopefully this House wants to move to a future state where funding and financing tools will enable a responsive supply of infrastructure where it is commercially viable to build new houses. This will shift market expectations of future scarcity, bring down the cost of land for new housing, and improve incentives to develop land sooner instead of holding it for land banking. This is a necessary step to help fix our housing crisis.
      First, some background. The Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act was first established in 2020 as an alternative means to fund and finance infrastructure needed to support urban growth. It was a good idea and it had good intentions. However, the Act has fallen short of delivering additional infrastructure needed to respond to growth. To date, only three levies have been authorised. So this bill has the purpose of removing unnecessary barriers to using the Act to improve its viability for a range of infrastructure projects and to make the levy development and approvals process simpler and more streamlined.
      The bill makes changes to streamline that levy approvals process. Currently, there’s an extensive process required for applicants to have a levy approved, and that can be a barrier when trying to use the Act. This bill will streamline the process and improve certainty for developers by simplifying requirements for levy proposals and recommendation reports, simplifying the mandatory considerations that the Minister of Housing must take into account when assessing the levy and improving certainty for developer-led proposals.
      The bill also broadens the scope of the Act to improve its flexibility and viability for a range of infrastructure projects. This will better reflect the developer-led use of the tool and enable the Act to be used for transport projects delivered by agencies—for example, the New Zealand Transport Agency and KiwiRail—as part of a funding stack for transport infrastructure investment where it benefits property owners.
      The bill also makes changes to enable the Act to be used for water infrastructure investments delivered by new water organisations established through the Local Government (Water Services) Act 2025 and allows for those water organisations to act as the responsible levy authority. In addition, the bill replaces the definition of community infrastructure so it is not required to be owned or controlled by a territorial authority. This broadens the potential use of the Act to therefore include community infrastructure that is owned or controlled by a third party, rather than that vested in a territorial authority. There are a number of other changes that the bill makes that are very, very important, but they are the key ones outlined so far.
      In December last year, the bill was referred to the Finance and Expenditure Committee, so it’s been a while to get to this stage, and we’re hoping that it’ll progress with pace tonight. The bill received submissions from 60 interested groups and individuals and the select committee heard oral evidence from six submitters at hearings in Wellington and some via video conference. The select committee examined the bill and recommended that it be passed with amendments to a number of clauses, which the Government supports in full.
      To strengthen consideration of affordability, the select committee proposed a change so that when the relevant Minister is assessing the affordability of a levy, they will also need to consider the cumulative affordability of the levy when combined with existing levies, rates, and water services charges. That’s sensible change, and I’m glad the select committee offered it forward.
      In respond to feedback from iwi and Māori, an amendment is proposed to require levy proposals to include details of any consultation undertaken, including with affected landowners, iwi, or hapū. This will enable the recommender—that’s the person who assesses levy proposals and writes the recommendation report—and the responsible Minister to consider any consultation that has occurred, including any impacts for Māori raised during consultation as part of overall decision-making on the levy proposal.
      An additional safeguard has also been added to the accelerated recovery mechanism to require a special-purpose vehicle to seek a court judgment for Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act (IFF Act) funding and financing costs before the special-purpose vehicle may apply to the registrar for the sale of undeveloped land. This new step would introduce an independent assessment of the amount of IFF Act funding and financing costs the special-purpose vehicle has determined needs to be repaid, and ensures that there is a judgment issued before sale proceedings may be commenced.
      A number of further technical amendments have also been proposed by the committee to improve the workability of the bill, and, of course, we all agree with them wholeheartedly and look forward to their passage and acceptance in the second reading.
      In conclusion, the changes in the bill and the bill itself will make the Act far more viable and flexible so that councils, developers, and other infrastructure providers can get on with fixing the basics of our housing crisis and building the infrastructure that our growing communities need. I commend it to the House.

      Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) (3 Day Postnatal Stay) Amendment Bill
      Second ReadingHon MATT DOOCEY (Associate Minister of Health) (09:42): on behalf of the Minister of Health: Thank you very much, Mr Speaker. I move, That the Pae Ora (Healthy Future) (3 Day Postnatal Stay) Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
      This bill is about guaranteeing women the choice of a minimum of three days of post-natal in-patient care after childbirth to ensure all mothers and babies get the support they need during this vitally important time. This Government believes that every child deserves the best-possible start in life. That start does not begin weeks or months after birth; it begins immediately, in those first precious days, when mothers are recovering from childbirth and families are learning to care for a newborn together. This bill responds directly to what women and families have told us about their post-natal experiences. They’ve told us that greater certainty and support in the early days following childbirth is needed. We know that quality early post-natal care can shape positive long-term outcomes well beyond the hospital stay.
      It is for these reasons that this Government is proud to back this bill with significant new funding delivered in Budget 2026. We are committed to ensuring that this legislation is matched with the investment needed to deliver it. This new funding of $34.4 million over four years increases maternity system capacity so mothers can confidently choose up to three days of in-patient post-natal stay knowing it will be supported by the beds and the workforce required to do this safely.
      First-time mothers will be the first to benefit. Starting immediately, up to 2,000 new mothers per year will be able to access a three-day post-natal stay within the first two years, utilising existing capacity. As access is expanded to all mothers after three years, we anticipate that up to 18,000 mothers per year will be able to access a 3-day post-natal stay.
      I want to acknowledge the original sponsor of this legislation. How good, Catherine Wedd. This bill began its life as a member’s bill grounded in a genuine concern for the post-natal experiences of women and families. This Government made the decision to adopt the bill because we agreed with the fundamental importance of guaranteeing three days of in-patient post-natal care for all women if they choose to access it.
      I also want to acknowledge and thank the Health Committee, specially chaired by the very hard-working Sam Uffindell, for its consideration of this bill and for the work it has done through the select committee process. I also want to thank the many individuals, the midwives, and other health professionals who took the time to make submissions and share their experiences. There was widespread support for the intent of the bill and for the principle that post-natal care should be a stronger and more consistent part of our maternity system. That feedback reflects just how significant the post-natal period is for families across this country.
      Taking this bill forward with the support of my colleague the Hon Casey Costello also delivers on a clear commitment in the National - New Zealand First coalition agreement to strengthen maternity services and post-natal support for women. Crucially, it’s a practical and compassionate step that puts women and their wellbeing at the centre of our health system.
      I intend to table an Amendment Paper as part of its adoption as a Government bill. The Amendment Paper will include transitional arrangements, requiring Health New Zealand to have a plan setting out how it will progressively build its capability and capacity across New Zealand to deliver this entitlement to all mothers. It also builds in more time to ensure that the system can safely deliver the entitlement to all women.
      This is about increasing maternity services to mothers and babies in a responsible, well-managed, and well-funded way. The Budget allocation of $34.4 million over four years will address the workforce and capacity constraints the system is currently facing. I look forward to consideration of this Amendment Paper when this bill is debated in the committee of the whole House.
      The bill established a clear entitlement that women can access three days of in-patient post-natal care if they choose, rather than leaving that decision uncertain or inconsistently applied. In doing so, it supports better outcomes for mothers and babies and reinforces that post-natal care is a valued and essential part of that maternity journey.
      It does not mandate that women stay in in-patient care for three days. Many women will continue to choose to return home earlier, supported by community-based services and their families, just as they do now. What this bill does is ensure that women who would benefit from staying longer have that option available to them without ambiguity or inconsistency.
      For some families, particularly first-time parents, the early post-natal period can feel overwhelming. There is a great deal to learn in a very short space of time. Having the option of additional support, monitoring, and reassurance within an in-patient setting can make a meaningful difference to confidence and wellbeing. Some women have told us they would have welcomed more time in in-patient care—more time to recover physically, more time to establish breastfeeding, more time to receive advice, and reassurance before returning home. Others have reported leaving hospital within 48 hours, even though they did not feel ready because they were unsure whether staying longer was an option. This uncertainty adds pressure at a time when families already have a great deal to manage. The bill removes the uncertainty and replaces it with clarity and confidence. This bill respects that different families will make different choices about what is right for them, and it ensures the system is better equipped to support those choices.
      This legislation is not the only change. The Government has a broader programme of work to strengthen the maternity system and ensure it can deliver high-quality post-natal care in a sustainable way. Health New Zealand is already taking action to build and support the maternity workforce needed to deliver the strengthened post-natal care set out in this bill. This includes targeted recruitment initiatives, including international recruitment where appropriate, as well as return-to-practice support to help experienced midwives and clinicians re-enter the workforce safely and confidently.
      I also understand that retention matters just as much as recruitment, particularly in districts facing ongoing workforce pressures. Supporting and retaining skilled staff is essential to maintaining safe services, continuity of care, and good outcomes for mothers and babies. That is why I’m focused on backing the maternity workforce and ensuring they’re supported to do their jobs well.
      The community sector will have an important part to play in the implementation of this bill. Primary maternity units run by both the public and community providers, including the private sector, will expand the range of in-patient post-natal care options available to mothers, including care that is closer to home. Mothers may remain in hospital, where hospital level care is required, or transfer to a primary maternity unit once that level of care is no longer needed, depending on their preferences and clinical need. Having a broader range of options, both public and private, reduces pressure on hospital facilities while continuing to deliver safe and appropriate post-natal care to woman and babies.
      Taken together, this work underpins the delivery of this bill and will support its long-term success. It reflects my commitment to ensuring women and their babies receive safe, timely, and appropriate care when they need it. I want to acknowledge the midwives and other health professionals who care for women and babies every day. Their experience and advice has been central to shaping the approach set out in this bill. They understand better than anyone the importance of post-natal support and the need for careful, well planned implementation. I thank them for their professionalism, dedication, and ongoing commitment to high-quality care. In closing, this bill delivers three important outcomes: it provides greater certainty for women and families about post-natal care; it supports choice at a critical moment in family life; and it strengthens our maternity system in a practical and responsible way.       Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill
      Legislative StatementHon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts) (10:54): I present a legislative statement on the Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill.
      ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Maureen Pugh): That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
      First ReadingHon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts) (10:55): I move, That the Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill be now read a first time. I nominate the Justice Committee to consider the bill.
      Too many New Zealanders are spending too long caught in the court system. For victims, delays mean waiting a year or more for a case to be resolved. For witnesses, it means uncertainty and repeated disruption. For defendants, it means cases hanging over their lives. For families, employers, and communities, it means the justice system is not working as quickly as it should. Timely justice matters, because justice delayed is justice denied.
      This Government is focused on practical changes that make the courts work better. This bill is a practical reform that improves access to justice, reduces delays, and makes better use of the resources that we already have. This bill expands the role of community magistrates so that they can deal with more straightforward matters from start to finish. It will reduce unnecessary adjournments, free up District Court judges to focus on more serious and complex cases, and will improve the public’s confidence that the justice system can deliver.
      Community magistrates are not new. The role was introduced in the late 1990s to increase judicial capacity to take pressure off the District Court judges. They were intended to deal with lower-level criminal matters, represent the communities that they serve, and help the courts to operates more efficiently. Community magistrates generally sit part time. They preside over certain lower-level matters in the District Court’s criminal jurisdiction. They are not required to hold a legal qualification, although many of them do. They bring practical experience, judgment, and community knowledge to the court system.
      But at the moment, they are not being used to their full potential. Too often, if a case reaches a point where a decision is needed outside of a community magistrate’s jurisdiction, it has to be adjourned and transferred to a judge. That means another court event, another delay, another day off work, another round of uncertainty for victims and other court users. It also means some cases are never scheduled before a community magistrate in the first place, because everyone knows that they might have to be transferred again later on. That’s not efficient, nor is it fair on court users, and it certainly is not the best use of judicial time and resource.
      This bill changes that. It will enable community magistrates to take guilty pleas for all cases except those tried in the High Court—that means murder, manslaughter—to preside over trials and determine guilt for offences with a maximum penalty of a fine, community-based sentence, or up to three months imprisonment; to order pre-sentencing reports for offences being referred to a District Court judge for sentencing; to make a greater range of bail decisions, where the defendant has pleaded guilty before a community magistrate; and make a greater range of administrative decisions, including transferring proceedings from one District Court to another and hearing unopposed limited driver licence applications.
      These are sensible, practical changes. They do not ask community magistrates to replace judges; they allow community magistrates to do more of the work that they were created to do so that judges can spend more time on cases that genuinely require a judge. It is expected that these changes will free up a net 5.2 District Court judge full-time equivalents. Put simply, this bill is, effectively, five judges for the price of none. This is good value for taxpayers, good for court timeliness, and good for victims who have waited too long for justice. The benefits will be felt across the justice system. When cases move faster victims get answers sooner. Witnesses are not left waiting indefinitely.  Defendants are not held in limbo longer than necessary. Remand pressure can reduce as cases progress more quickly. Judges can focus on the work only they are able to do. 
      Expanding the role of community magistrates is sensible, but it must be done carefully. The public needs confidence that the cases will continue to be dealt with appropriately and consistently. This bill does not change the sentencing jurisdiction of community magistrates. Community magistrates will still not be able to impose imprisonment or home detention. Where a community magistrate considers that either of those sentences may be appropriate, the case must be transferred to a District Court judge, and that is an important safeguard.
      The bill also supports stronger leadership and oversight of community magistrates. Judge Moses has recently been appointed as the first Chief Community Magistrate, recognising the growing importance of community magistrates in the court system in providing judicial oversight for the role. The bill will make it so that there must always be a judge in this role. Budget 2025 also provided funding for three additional community magistrates and extra training to support them in their work.
      This bill is practical, it is targeted, it is common sense, and it makes better use of community magistrates. It frees up more than five full-time judges’ worth of capacity. It helps cases to move faster, it supports victims, it reduces pressure on the District Court, and it does all of that while maintaining appropriate safeguards. I commend this bill to the House.

      Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill
      Legislative StatementHon SCOTT SIMPSON (Minister of Statistics) (11:24): on behalf of the Minister for the Environment: I present a legislative statement on the Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill.
      ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono): That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
      First ReadingHon SCOTT SIMPSON (Minister of Statistics) (11:24): on behalf of the Minister for the Environment: I move, That the Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill be now read a first time. I nominate the Environment Committee to consider the bill.
      New Zealand is undertaking significant transformations regarding how we protect, conserve, and restore our natural environment, how we sustainably use our resources, and how we mitigate and adapt to climate change. However, to understand the impacts that our activities have on the environment and to respond accordingly, we need a comprehensive, reliable, consistent data and information base.
      In 2015, the Environmental Reporting Act was enacted to do exactly that: to establish a trusted, reliable, and independent environmental reporting regime. Since then, we have completed four cycles of environmental reports. The Act has made significant improvements to the previously ad hoc way New Zealand reported on the environment; however, we need to extend its functionality and flexibility so that trustworthy data and information is at the heart of decision making.
      In 2019, the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment released a report raising concerns about gaps and inconsistencies in environmental data. The commissioner noted a reliance on passively harvested data and information collected under other pieces of legislation and a lack of a coordinated environmental monitoring and reporting system. The high frequency of report production placed the Ministry for the Environment and Stats NZ on a never-ending treadmill of report-making. These often recycle old, patchy, and inconsistent data collected using a myriad of disparate monitoring practices. We have a significant opportunity now to address the Parliamentary Commissioner’s concerns, so in this piece of legislation a number of changes are being put forward.
      The Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill before the House represents a commitment by the Government to quality environmental data and information. The bill will refocus reporting content and time frames. It aligns roles and responsibilities, and a more active collection of environmental data and knowledge. The bill ensures improvements to environmental reporting are safeguarded for the future. These include making data available to the public and decision makers when it is ready, rather than when a report is merely published. It also means expanding the reporting and setting up an interim strategic, in-evidence panel.
      The bill will require the Secretary for the Environment to publish a State of the Environment report every six years, independent from political interference. This will achieve a more appropriate balance between reporting timeliness and the rates of change in our environment. The bill stipulates that the first State of the Environment report must be published in 2031.
      The Pressure-State-Impact framework embedded into the Environmental Reporting Act has been expanded to include drivers and outlooks. Drivers describe the long-term social, demographic, economic, and environmental factors that cause pressure on the environment. Outlooks describe how the environment may change in the future based on projections and trends. Their ongoing inclusion will render a more complete picture and bring New Zealand more in line with international best practice.
      The report must continue to describe changes to the state of the environment over time and how it measures against national and international standards. In addition, they can now report on progress towards Government priorities and limits, goals, and policy outcomes set in other legislation. This could include, for example, reporting on limits as proposed in the Natural Environment Bill and any measures set as part of the climate adaptation system, including managing the risk from natural hazards.
      Between the six-yearly State of the Environment reports, a commentary report must be published at least once every 12 months. One of the foundational objectives of the bill is to ensure reporting flexibility. Commentaries report on an issue or topic that sits across one or more of the five environmental domains. The five domains of air, land, fresh water, marine, and atmosphere and climate will remain. All must be reported on at least once in the commentary reports between the State of the Environment reports. However, the amendments recognise that commentary reports may cut across different domains. This change allows for more flexible reporting, which better addresses the urgent needs we face.
      The bill introduces a new requirement for the Secretary for the Environment. In consultation with the Government Statistician, the secretary will produce a priorities report within six months of every State of the Environment report. The report will discuss environmental data, monitoring, and research. It will also list recommended indicators and priority areas for improving data and evidence.
      Several technical advisory groups have provided expert advice on the preparation of synthesis and domain reports over the years. This bill will, however, amend the Environmental Reporting Act to require the Secretary for the Environment, in consultation with the Minister for the Environment, to appoint a strategic evidence panel. The panel will provide independent advice to the Secretary for the Environment on matters related to environmental data monitoring and reporting. The bill also clarifies the roles of the Secretary for the Environment and the Government Statistician. The bill proposes clear roles and also stipulates where consultation between the two organisations is required, such as setting environmental indicators or producing data and evidence priority reports.
      Finally, to bring together all the proposals and drive a cohesive, robust and fit-for-purpose reporting system, the purpose statement has been extended. The current purpose statement simply stipulates that the purpose of the Act is to produce national environmental reports. This has been clarified to align with the underlying policy to inform New Zealanders on the state of the environment and to support evidence-based decisions. This bill responds directly to a review of New Zealand’s national reporting regime. It improves efficiency of our reporting regime, making useful improvements to the frequency of reports, and does so without compromising their timeliness, impact, or independence. Therefore, I commend the Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill to the House.

      Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill
      Legislative StatementHon CHRIS PENK (Minister for Building and Construction) (11:56): Thank you, sir. I present a legislative statement on the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill.
      ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono): That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
      Second ReadingHon CHRIS PENK (Minister for Building and Construction) (11:56): I move, That the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
      The Transport and Infrastructure Committee has considered the bill and recommends that it be passed with amendments. I’m grateful to the people and organisations who made a submission on the bill and of course to the select committee itself, who took the time to hear those submitters and to consider improvements on the bill. Following the Canterbury earthquakes and royal commission of inquiry, the current earthquake-prone buildings regime was introduced.
      I just want to take a moment to acknowledge, as I’m sure all in this House would, the considerable tragedy, the loss of human life, that was entailed by those tragic events. And I don’t wish to bring you into the debate, Mr Speaker, but I will acknowledge that you more than most were familiar with the nature of the tragedy, and of course I commend and salute you for your work following that, of course, to bring that beloved region of yours back to more normal circumstances.
      All that said, of course, I think it’s fairly acknowledged that the introduced legislation at that time—albeit, of course, in good faith and balancing all the relevant considerations—has not worked entirely as intended. It has inadvertently imposed large costs on building owners and communities, including throughout New Zealand, without focusing enough on the buildings that present the greatest risk to people’s lives.
      This cannot continue, and so, even with the recent earthquakes in Venezuela providing a salutary reminder that we do need to prepare further for such events in New Zealand, nevertheless, we have decided that it is important to reform the earthquake-prone building regime to target or refocus on those buildings most likely to cause fatalities in an earthquake. 
      The changes will remove barriers to strengthening high-risk buildings, making retrofits more affordable for their owners and better protecting people in and around them. Focusing effort and investment on the highest-risk buildings will ultimately save more lives than the current one-size-fits-all approach.
      Today I will briefly reiterate the bill’s key elements and summarise the key changes recommended by the select committee. As I say, we have decided to accept those changes.
      First, the bill narrows the systems scope so that it targets only high-risk buildings in medium and high-risk seismic zones. It introduces tiered remediation requirements, amends the definition of priority building, and provides greater flexibility through deadline extensions and lower-cost pathways for alterations and change of use.
      Only two types of buildings will remain designated as earthquake-prone buildings (EPBs): unreinforced masonry buildings and tall heavy material buildings. These are the buildings most likely to cause harm in an earthquake, and these will be only those located in medium- or high-risk seismic zones. Territorial authorities must identify and remove other building types from the EPB register in the three months from 1 July 2027.
      Meanwhile, buildings in Auckland, Northland, and the Chatham Islands will be out of scope. These areas have a scientifically determined lower seismic hazard than other parts of New Zealand. On Royal assent, therefore, earthquake-prone buildings in these areas will have that designation removed.
      At the same time, other provisions of the bill go through coastal Otago, including Dunedin and Oamaru and Stewart Island, will shift from a low to medium seismic zone to reflect the latest scientific understanding of seismic hazard in those places. Current earthquake-prone buildings (EPBs) there will retain their existing remediation deadlines and territorial authorities will have until 1 July 2032 to identify potential EPBs there.
      The bill also narrows the so-called identify at any time pathway for designating buildings as EPBs. Too many low-risk buildings have been designated as earthquake-prone using this pathway. So the bill, as introduced, narrows the pathway to cover only the post-1976, tall, heavy-material buildings that were constructed before 2027. This includes buildings akin to the CTV building in Christchurch. For buildings that remain EPBs, territorial authorities will determine their required remediation measures in accordance with the updated EPB methodology, issue EPB notices, and keep the EPB register up to date.
      The bill narrows the definition of “priority building”. Under the bill, only buildings that could fall on to a busy street or block a strategic transport route will qualify. Buildings that were priority simply because of their usage, such as hospitals or fire stations, will lose that status. Together, these changes provide clearer rules and a stronger focus on the buildings that matter most for public safety.
      The bill also introduces a tiered approach to remediation, replacing the current requirement to strengthen all buildings to 34 percent of the new building standard, commonly known as NBS. There will be two principal forms of remediation measure. Most unreinforced masonry buildings will need to mitigate their risk of facades falling on to people below. Multi-storey concrete buildings and large unreinforced masonry buildings will need targeted work to prevent those buildings collapsing. For unreinforced masonry buildings then that are one or two storeys high and located outside urban centres, no remediation will be required by a set deadline. But, at the same time, I note that owners will need to mitigate the risk of façade collapse if they want the building to be taken off the EPB register. 
      EPB owners will be able to apply to territorial authorities for deadline extensions of up to 15 years, even if the original deadline expired before commencement. This will replace the current “up to 10 year” extension, open only to heritage EPB owners.
      The bill also supports lower-cost compliance pathways for owners carrying out seismic work or changing the use of a building. If the work only involves seismic remediation, no fire or accessibility upgrades will be required. Similarly, if an owner wants to change an EPB’s use, it would only need to meet its remediation requirement, rather than anything higher. Together, these changes provide more practical and cost-effective solutions, more time to comply, and fewer barriers for owners committed to making their buildings safer.
      The Transport and Infrastructure Committee has unanimously recommended amendments to address issues identified by submitters, officials, and the select committee itself. I welcome these improvements and again place on the record my thanks to the committee for their detailed examination of the bill. I note the chair, Mr Andy Foster, and I thank him and his colleagues who did such a careful and coherent job of understanding and in turn explaining the changes that have ultimately been made.
      In response to feedback from submitters, the committee clarified what areas are in “urban centres”, which helps to determine the remediation requirement of an unreinforced masonry EPB. For example, Wellington and Porirua are urban centres, whereas Featherston and Greytown are not. To acknowledge the unique barriers to remediation faced by various buildings, the committee added heritage status to the list of matters that territorial authorities must have regard to when determining whether or not to grant a deadline extension. Some submitters were concerned that the alternation provisions may allow for reduced building code compliance. For example, drilling stabilising rods through walls can increase the risk of fire spreading in one room to the next. The committee introduced a backstop into the bill to ensure that seismic work needs to be done in a way that doesn’t increase the risk of fire spreading or reduce disabled peoples’ access.
      The committee also amended the bill so that warning signs must be displayed on all earthquake-prone buildings, including those that are only recorded on the register or have a seismic work exemption. The committee updated the terms for the required remediation measures to façade risk mitigation and targeted retrofit. This will ensure that approaches to remediation mitigate risk but do not necessarily involve securing a façade or a full retrofit of the building can be used. This bill now also includes high-level descriptions of these measures.
      Some submitters were unsure how buildings with unusually tall storeys or part storeys will be treated—a fair question. The committee clarified that the thresholds for determining how many storeys high an EPB will be will be set out in the EPB methodology. One way that a building can be a priority building with half the remediation time frame is if it may impede a strategic transport route if it were to collapse during an earthquake. Submitters recommended that territorial authorities be allowed to revisit their strategic transport route—again, I think, a very sensible recommendation. The committee therefore amended the bill to empower territorial authorities—councils, in other words—to revise and remove strategic transport routes up to 1 July 2027. No new strategic transport routes may be added, ensuring that no building owners will be worse off.
      Last, in my remaining minute, the committee clarified the meaning of a building within scope. This makes it clearer which buildings are within scope of the system before the reader then looks to the EPB methodology for further technical detail. An unreinforced masonry building must have an exterior masonry wall and satisfy other criteria in the methodology to be within scope. A tall, heavy material building must have one or more significant elements, such as a roof or a floor, built using concrete or other heavy materials and satisfy any other criteria in the EPB methodology. 
      Overall, in summary, the bill creates a more focused and workable earthquake-prone buildings system by targeting the buildings that present the greatest risk, introducing tiered and more cost-effective remediation requirements, and reducing barriers to remediation for building owners. For all those reasons, I commend this bill to the House.
      SPEAKER: The question is that the motion be agreed to.ARENA WILLIAMS (Labour—Manurewa) (12:06): Thank you, Mr Speaker. This is an important bill and an important piece of reform that Labour continues to support, with specific reservations. I’m going to use this speech to set out what those things are. They will be parts that we consider are the most sensitive and are the least well-supported around the House. It is important that we come to consensus on these rules which impact on the long-term viability of buildings and not only those that are being built now but in expensive and costly remediations that are to come in the next five to 10 years. So it is important to flag where we have bipartisan support which is for a sensible set of rules for remediation of the highest-risk buildings, but to indicate that we do have reservations around how some of the exclusions have been applied, particularly around Auckland.
      Maintaining affordability has been our concern here. We want a building system and a built environment which is affordable, where remediations happen from either existing owners or there is an incentive for buildings to be sold to people who can remediate them. Because you do not want a situation like Wellington is experiencing now where some important civic sites and main streets have buildings which have not been remediated because the cost is very high and that continues to pose a risk to neighbours and to people on the street who walk past them. We want a system which incentivises that kind of remediation and where it is affordable in the public interest. So that is why we need some updates to these rules.
      We have vociferously opposed at every opportunity the exclusion of Auckland from the rules for remediation of risky buildings. Colleagues, let me explain what has occurred here. Cabinet has set out to create a set of rules where the highest-risk buildings around the country are the ones that get fixed. That makes sense. We shouldn’t fix buildings which are not posing a risk to peoples’ lives and are not posing a risk to the neighbouring buildings around them. Those rules require expensive fixes and so they should be something which is sensible. There is also a category of buildings under that that require being fixed—they need to be fixed. There shouldn’t be rules which force people to adhere to a certain time line. Building owners in that category should be able to make their own decisions about what kind of risk they will put up with and what kind of risk the building’s users will put up with.
      When I’m talking about these highest-risk buildings, some of those have been excluded from this bill. The way that these rules have been drawn is that if you have a very high-risk building in Auckland which is on the main street, it does not need to be remediated any more. The House must understand that by excluding Auckland, we have drawn lines on a map which mean that those remediations do not need to occur.
      Yes, you could have designed a system where the highest seismic risk regions were the way that we decided what sorts of buildings would be remediated. But that’s actually not what we’ve done. If you drew lines on a map, you might use, say, faults, and areas where say, an eruption around the Alpine Fault was going to cause regional risk and regional land movement. You might have drawn lines around volcanic movements in our shaky isles.
      But that is not the system we have used. We’ve used a system, which is perfectly sensible, whereby you identify the buildings which are at risk of movement in any kind of event like that and how much they are used. So a building that might move the same amount and might have the same kind of risk on the main street in Auckland is a different sort of risk to the one that’s on the West Coast and has two users a year for family weddings. That’s sensible.
      But addition, at the last minute, of an exclusion for Auckland does not fit with the uncontentious and unpolitical way of identifying risk here. It has overlaid a set of judgements that are, simply put, relatively political about whether Auckland should be included or excluded from the rules.
      I think that is the wrong decision. I think we will be back here in this House debating whether that has worked, because it is not a system that the public can have faith in, and it will test confidence and trust in our built environment system and whether central government stands behind the risk that we are asking Aucklanders to take on, not only as a community, but as individual business owners who, say, have buildings next to highly risky buildings and people who maintain other parts of built environment around them that are at risk because of this decision.
      This is not also a minor issue for Auckland. The majority of earthquake-prone buildings are in Auckland, despite many people’s assumptions about the earthquake-prone buildings being in Christchurch; that is a largely an area which has been through a pretty painful process of having to come up to speed with the rules that we required of them. People in Canterbury have done what they have been asked. They have fixed buildings; they have remediated buildings. For some people, have that has been at personal cost, huge personal investment of family savings. For many businesses, it has meant years of having to forward-fund capital investment in their buildings, but they have done that.
      This is an exclusion, now, of another region, in fact, where there are 1,400 earthquake-prone buildings, which was in the queue, and this Government has made a decision to exclude them. That decision will have lasting consequences for generations to come and is, frankly, being made at a time where that is possible for the Government to do it because it’s not in people’s minds.
      The deadline extensions powers in the bill have also been something that the committee worked very closely with, and, ultimately, that is something we do not support. There are shifting goal posts now in the bill, where deadline extensions of up to 15 years don’t come back to this Parliament. They are made away from public scrutiny. What does that mean? It means that building owners don’t have a clear indication of the time that they will need to make remediations in the rest of the country.
      For Wellington apartment owners, who are an important constituency when Governments of both stripes have considered this bill, they now do not have certainty of investment decisions. Little old ladies who live in apartments, and that’s their entire life savings, will be hugely impacted by this bill, and that is a very hard case.
      Labour’s answer to this was not one that National politics supported. It was to use public money to assist those private owners with their private property because we recognise that there is a no-fault element of this and that it would be inequitable to treat this in any different way.
      But there were other choice for the National Government to make, and simply kicking the can down the road is what is being done here in this bill. It’s a very difficult position to be putting those retirees, especially, but also first-home buyers, in, when they are now under water and find themselves without equity to invest in other properties that they would like to live in, especially in the current climate of the Wellington property market.
      The committee had some very useful discussions around the idea of addressing the need for assistance that those apartment owners faced, but, ultimately, Government has not proposed either an insurance product which would help them or a financial scheme which would allow them to sell and then to recover some of the costs for the Government’s coffers. That was what was in place 2022-23 under the Labour Government and that is not what the Government has announced.
      These rules in this bill should have been progressed at the same time as another scheme to properly spread risk between those who can afford it and those who can’t were introduced. Things like body corp rules are critical to getting this regime right. Those have also not been progressed at the same time.
      Ultimately, this is an area where reform is welcome. We need sensible rules for remediation, and the rules aren’t working for a sector which is struggling with the construction and the repair of these buildings right now. We do not have enough capacity in the system to fix all of the earthquake-prone buildings that we need to in New Zealand today. We needed a sensible way for the Government to direct when that work would occur and where.
      But the exclusion of Auckland wholesale should not have been part of the planning of that pipeline. If we’re serious about an infrastructure pipeline which works for people, we also need to consider the built environment and the private buildings which are associated with that—our construction sector needed to be able to plan that out well. There is also an extension in here which means that it might 10 years, it might be 15 years—nobody knows.
      So when we’re accountable to the people in our electorate who are looking at this Parliament and seeing an improvement of the earthquake-prone building rules, we all also have to know that the risk of earthquakes hasn’t gone away, that there are risky buildings out there which this bill doesn’t deal with. Simply sticking a notice on the door doesn’t deal with it, and we all need to wear that for our communities, where there is not just private risk, it is public risk—to our main streets, to the people who use the movie theatres, to the people who use the malls, all of this is something that this Parliament should keep a very close eye on because it does speed up building, but it also spreads the risk in ways we haven’t anticipated.

      Debate resumed.Hon JULIE ANNE GENTER (Green—Rongotai) (12:17): Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Tēnā koutou e te Whare.       Wellington City, which is mainly Wellington Central electorate and Rongotai electorate—both held by Green MPs—was significantly affected by the Kaikōura earthquake and by the changes to the earthquake building standards that were brought in following the Christchurch earthquake.       However, while Christchurch, in the recovery, received a significant amount of central government funding to rebuild horizontal infrastructure and a significant amount of support, Wellington has not really received that level of central government support. And yet, it’s had extreme damage to horizontal infrastructure like the pipes, which only became visible some years after the Kaikōura earthquake. Our town centres have really, really struggled with building owners who simply are not in a position to upgrade the building to make it functional.       So as a Wellington MP, I definitely had to support the changes proposed by the Minister. One thing that was great is sort of trying to make—firstly the prioritisation is not stopping a building from falling down, but protecting loss of life. That is really, really important.
      Secondly, there was kind of no awareness. I think council engineers were quite conservative in terms of putting things on the schedule. They would say a one-storey building that’s, say, a tennis club somewhere in Wellington, which doesn’t have people living in it, doesn’t have people working in it all the time, had to be upgraded, and it was the same test for a multi-storey residential building that had people living in it. Clearly, the risk is different for those infrequently used buildings that are single-storey versus a multi-storey residential building.
      We welcome these changes, but we still have some concerns. The primary concern from my point of view is that everywhere else that I’m aware of—at least, this is what I understood from briefings from officials, and coming from an earthquake-prone part of the world, in California—where there have been increases to building standards, there’s usually some central government or State-level support for helping building owners to fix their buildings to make them safer. So it’s unusual to massively put up the seismic standards and not provide any real support, which is, unfortunately, the situation we’ve been in—and there was a pathway for support.
      I have a constituent, an older lady who lives in a residential apartment in the eastern suburbs of Wellington, who went through this whole process with the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment to try and access the support for remediation to her apartment in the building, to access financial support, and had just gotten through all the bureaucratic hurdles when this Government and the Minister Chris Penk announced that they were not going ahead with that programme. So, suddenly, the money was taken away and it wasn’t available, which was incredibly stressful for a woman, if I recall correctly, in her late 70s or early 80s. During this period while the Government’s been working on this legislation, we still have not seen any financial support for apartment owner-occupiers come through. I know my colleague Arena Williams referred to this in Labour’s concerns around the bill. It is a major concern.
      While there will be fewer buildings that need to be remediated, there are lots of buildings—and there might be 40 residential buildings in Wellington, mostly owner-occupiers; some will be investment properties with renters in them, but mostly owner-occupiers. For those owner-occupiers, where is the financial support to undertake the remediation, especially given that property values in Wellington are not up, so borrowing to pay for that remediation might not be available to those apartment owner-occupiers.
      It would be useful if central government had a fund, even if it’s not grants—but it would be great if it included some grants and some loans, low-interest loans to assist owner-occupiers to fix their buildings so that, you know, they’re not at risk of death. We need them to fix these buildings—like, as a community, we need these buildings to be fixed, and we cannot rely on city council, which has already been, particularly in Wellington’s case, under so much pressure to upgrade its own buildings. It’s made a whole lot of recent projects in Wellington City Council far more expensive because of the complications of the seismic standards, which now are, in some cases, being removed. So they’ve already put a lot of money into this stuff. Ratepayers can’t be the ones bailing out everyone in the city. So I think there is very much a role in calling on Government to do something about this, to offer some sort of financial support.

I think, unfortunately, as we saw with Christchurch, sometimes the most damaging earthquakes are happening in places where we’re not expecting the earthquakes. You know, when you’re looking at those, like, 1940s concrete buildings, unreinforced masonry, there might be some more cost-effective solutions that address the issue without having to do everything that had been recommended prior.       I mean, the reality is we are an earthquake-prone nation; we need to build accordingly. We also have higher costs of building, in some cases, and we have an economy that is struggling slightly.
