      Emergency Management Bill (No 2)
      Legislative StatementHon MARK MITCHELL (Minister for Emergency Management and Recovery) (14:07): Thank you, Mr Speaker. I present a legislative statement on the Emergency Management Bill (No 2).
      SPEAKER: That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
      Second ReadingHon MARK MITCHELL (Minister for Emergency Management and Recovery) (14:07): I move, That the Emergency Management Bill (No 2) be now read a second time.
      Mr Speaker, while you’re in the seat, I just wanted to acknowledge you. As a member of the National Party backbench when we were hit by the awful Christchurch earthquakes, I got to observe your tireless work as emergency management Minister leading the recovery for Christchurch. I just want to think, reflect, and mourn on those that were lost, but also now recognise that Christchurch is a thriving city that is a joy to visit and to see how far they’ve come since that event. I want to acknowledge you, because I got a front-row seat that helped inform me in terms of what I needed to do when I took on the role of emergency management Minister. So thank you for that work.
      I’d like to thank the Governance and Administration Committee for its work to consider this important piece of legislation. I’m pleased to see the select committee was unanimous in its recommendations. This reflects the collaborative cross-party approach that we need to strengthen our emergency management system. In my view, like national security, emergency management should be bipartisan. I want to thank all of the parties that have worked hard and had input into the development of this bill.
      I also want to acknowledge the submitters on the bill. Their input has improved the bill and will also feed into its implementation and other operational improvements. Emergency management is relevant to every person in New Zealand. Submitters’ insights are important to supporting the whole-of-society approach to emergency management we need to adopt as a country.
      The Government’s objectives for reform are to strengthen the role of communities and iwi Māori in emergency management; provide for clear responsibilities and accountabilities at the national, regional, and local levels; enable a higher minimum standard of emergency management; minimise disruption to essential services; and ensure agencies have the tools to do their jobs effectively when an emergency happens.
      The majority of submitters supported this intent. Where submitters sought changes, it’s clear the select committee has given those views careful consideration, and, in many cases, has recommended changes to the bill as a result. These amendments have strengthened the bill, and the Government will be taking them forward. There are some changes I want to highlight, because I see them as particularly helpful in supporting improvements on the ground.
      The bill as reported back extends civil liability protections to official responders when they’re taking precautionary actions immediately before an emergency. These protections will also cover the likes of volunteers and civil contractors when they’re acting under official direction. Concern about civil liability before a state of emergency is declared should not create hesitation to act, because hesitation can result in avoidable damage. At worst, it may cost lives. I welcome the select committee’s recommended changes on this issue, and I thank the submitters who raised it. The committee has also recommended creating a formal link between regional emergency management plans and the long-term planning process under the Local Government Act. Good planning is fundamental to driving action on the ground across the four Rs of risk reduction, readiness, response, and recovery.
      While there was already an expectation that local authorities would implement their emergency management responsibilities through long-term plans, making this link explicit and clarifying how a multi-council planning process should flow into individual councils and their long-term plans was important. Emergency management committees are intended to achieve economies of scale and integrated management of hazards and risks, but they can only be successful if all councils play their part. Linking regional emergency management plans and long-term plans will ensure that committees’ decisions translate into action.
      This change reinforces a key shift the bill is making to put more emphasis on the emergency management role of individual councils. Related changes include creating specific roles for regional emergency management committees and their local authority members, making mayors primarily responsible for declaring states of local emergency and recovery transition periods within their own districts, requiring every territorial authority to have a district controller and district recovery manager with a clear line of accountability to the council’s chief executive, and giving territorial authority chief executives an explicit mandate to coordinate resources provided by other agencies in the lead-up to and during an emergency over that longer-term recovery. In late October last year, severe weather events coincided with the local body elections. Because new mayors had not yet been sworn in, I needed to declare states of local emergency over Southland and Canterbury.
      The committee has recommended a sensible change to address this gap, enabling mayors to be sworn in early on a temporary basis to declare a state of emergency or transition period. This will enable local declarations to continue to be made locally and avoid potential delays in the emergency disruption communications if the emergency is disrupted because of communications between the affected council and the Minister.
      When it comes to improving our resilience to emergencies, this bill is only part of the picture. Councils also hold many tools to address specific hazards under the planning, building, and biosecurity legislation. To name just a few: like under the current Act, emergency management committees are expected to use these tools to support their emergency management responsibilities. I’m pleased to see that the select committee has recommended making the connection between these responsibilities clearer by creating a requirement for emergency management committees and councils to consider whether functions, duties, and powers in other relevant legislation would help meet their emergency management responsibilities.
      New Zealand is one of the most exposed countries to natural hazard risk in the world. I’m sure I don’t need to convince the House about the need for a strong emergency management system. This need is reinforced by every severe weather event, let alone when we consider our most serious risks, like the Alpine Fault. It’s critical we have legislation that sets us up to manage these risks. At its core, New Zealand’s approach to emergency management is based on three key principles: (1) we consider all hazards, natural and man-made; (2) we manage the risk from these hazards by taking action across the four Rs: risk reduction, readiness, response, and recovery; and (3) all parts of society have a role to play in emergency management: central government, local government, communities and businesses, iwi and hapū, and individual households.
      Overall, this bill will better enable our emergency management system to achieve this intent, and deliver the improvements identified through past inquiries and reviews. For that reason, I want to thank, again, the select committee and all of the submitters for the critical role you have played in improving this bill.
      The Emergency Management Bill (No 2) will provide stronger foundations for New Zealand to meet the growing risk we face as a country, and I commend it to the House.CUSHLA TANGAERE-MANUEL (Labour—Ikaroa-Rāwhiti) (14:16): Tēnā koe e te Māngai o te Whare, otirā i te tuatahi i roto i te reo Māori, tēnei te tangi aroha ki te tuahine o Parekura Horomia i hoki atu ki te kōpū o te whenua i te Tūrei kua pahure.

It introduces new ministerial powers, binding national rules, and compliance orders enforceable through courts. While there will certainly be occasions where national leadership is essential, we must remain connected to our local leaders who know their communities so well, they know their rivers so well, they know their whenua so well, they know their roads so well, and they know their bridges so well. A resilient system should trust local expertise as much as central authority.
      We’ve talked about bipartisanship, and I just want to acknowledge all the amazing people both in paid roles and voluntary roles across Aotearoa who do a great job in keeping our communities safe.       Regulatory Systems (Social Security) Amendment Bill (No 2)
      Legislative StatementHon LOUISE UPSTON (Minister for Social Development and Employment) (15:16): I present a legislative statement on the Regulatory Systems (Social Security) Amendment Bill (No 2).
      DEPUTY SPEAKER: That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
      First ReadingHon LOUISE UPSTON (Minister for Social Development and Employment) (15:16): I move, That the Regulatory Systems (Social Security) Amendment Bill (No 2) be now read for a first time. I nominate the Social Services and Community Committee to consider the bill.
      This amendment bill is an omnibus bill that amends legislation administered by the Ministry of Social Development and the New Zealand Defence Force. Specifically, the bill makes a number of minor policy and technical changes to the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001, the Social Security Act 2018, and the Veterans’ Support Act 2014, and repeals the Family Benefits (Home Ownership) Act 1964. This bill is intended to improve the provision of social welfare benefits. The amendments in the bill will update statutory provisions, address regulatory duplication gaps and errors, and bring legislation up to date with public expectations. The bill will reduce the chance of regulatory failure and unintended consequences that harm the wellbeing of New Zealanders. The changes are small and do not warrant stand-alone bills, but together the changes will ensure greater effectiveness and efficiency of the social welfare system.
      The first minor policy change is to extend the sustainable employment trial for supported living payment recipients from 26 weeks to a maximum period of 104 weeks. The supported living payment is a benefit payable to people who are permanently and severely restricted in their capacity to work because of a health condition, injury, disability, or because they are totally blind. The purpose of the sustainable employment trial is to encourage and support supported living payment recipients who want to move into employment or increase their hours of work to establish whether they can sustain that employment and cease receiving the benefit. 
      Feedback from health and disability stakeholders and international evidence indicates that the fear of losing the supported living payment entitlement can be a significant barrier to work and that 26 weeks is not long enough for some recipients to test their ability to work. Furthermore, increasing hours of work incrementally over a longer period better supports people to sustain employment and become independent. Extending the sustainable employment trial to two years will therefore improve incentives for supported living payment recipients to work as much as they can, leading to a better financial position and improved wellbeing outcomes for those who can participate.
      The second policy change is to ensure that residents of the Realm countries of Niue, Cook Islands, and Tokelau cannot use social security agreements to meet the residence requirements for New Zealand superannuation and veterans’ pension. Social security agreements are bilateral treaties between Governments that provide for the reciprocal payment of social security benefits and pensions. These agreements are intended to apply to the residence of the two agreement partner countries. However, the Ministry of Social Development has advised that a court would likely find that some of New Zealand’s social security agreements could apply to people applying for New Zealand superannuation or veterans’ pension while resident in the Realm countries.
      Social security agreements are not intended to apply to residents of the Realm countries. Realm countries do not have the resources to participate in the cost-sharing aspects of social security agreements. Instead, New Zealand superannuation special portability provisions are extended to the residents of the Realm. Therefore, the bill will amend the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001 and the Veterans’ Support Act 2014 to exclude the application of social security agreements to Realm country residents.
      The third minor policy change will enable people who are live organ donors to be eligible for an emergency benefit payment equivalent to the rate of the supported living payment. Currently, a supported living payment recipient who is caring for a person who would otherwise require hospital or residential care is not eligible to receive supported living payments should they be recovering from surgery for a live organ donation. This is because they are not caring for someone while they are recovering from surgery, which is a criterion to receive the supported living payment—caring. Instead, they are transferred on to the emergency benefit while they are in their recovery period and can only receive the rate of the equivalent main benefit that they would be entitled to, which is either the jobseeker support or sole parent support. This anomaly in the supported living payment does not align with the Compensation for Live Organ Donors Act 2016, which is designed to remove financial deterrents to the donation of organs by live donors. Therefore, the bill will establish explicit legal authority to pay emergency benefit to clients at the same rate that they were receiving on the supported living payment on the ground of caring for another person for a period of up to 12 weeks after the donation.
      As I noted earlier, the bill also contains minor technical amendments. These minor amendments are mostly related to the Social Security Act 2018 and the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001. Rather than go through each technical amendment, let me highlight the common themes behind the changes. The majority of the proposed amendments will address errors or omissions found following the rewrite of the Social Security Act 1964 to the Social Security Act 2018. Other changes are aimed to improve the provision of social welfare benefits and strengthen the performance of the social security system. There are also changes which will repeal redundant legislation. For example, the bill will repeal section 190A of the Veterans’ Support Act 2014, which has been replaced by section 127 of the Legislation Act 2019.
      In conclusion, it can be difficult to find time on the parliamentary calendar for repairs and maintenance of existing legislation. This amendment bill is a vehicle for smaller regulatory fixes to be progressed in a timely and cost-effective way in order to improve the provision of social welfare benefits. I commend this bill to the House.

      Second ReadingHon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts) (15:46): I move, That the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
      I am pleased to speak to these bills in the House again today. As I noted in my first reading speech, the regulatory system amendment bills are one of the ways that this Government maintains and repairs existing legislation and ensures that our regulatory systems deliver for New Zealanders. At a high level, these two bills reflect the Government’s commitment to delivering fit for purpose regulation and to improving access to justice. They will have a significant impact on the regulatory regimes that govern tribunals and occupational regulation, enhancing their effectiveness and efficiency while improving consumer protection and the quality of justice legislation.
      The Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill makes practical improvements to tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies. It removes barriers to justice by allowing successful applicants in the disputes tribunal to recover their filing fee from the respondent where it is appropriate. It strengthens the regulation of the private security industry by providing more effective information-gathering powers to investigate breaches. It also streamlines appointments and employment arrangements for tribunal members to ensure these bodies operate efficiently. 
      The Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill strengthens protections for both consumers and regulated professionals while reducing unnecessary compliance costs. One important change allows conveyancers’ professional undertakings to be enforced in the High Court, just as lawyers’ undertakings already are. This promotes competition in the conveyancing market and benefits consumers. 
      The bill also removes a disproportionately harsh penalty that automatically disqualifies real estate agents from practising for five years simply because they failed to complete continuing professional development or pay fees on time. That issue has been recognised by the profession for many years, and this bill delivers a more proportionate response. At the same time, the bill strengthens the Real Estate Authority’s ability to investigate unlicensed trading and ensure licensee’s meet their obligations, improving consumer confidence in the industry.
      Both bills have benefited from the select committee process, and I would like to thank the Justice Committee and the Education and Workforce Committee for their careful consideration, along with everyone who made submissions. Their constructive feedback has resulted in sensible improvements. 
      The Justice Committee has clarified the role of the Complaints, Investigations and Prosecution Unit when dealing with complaints about unlicensed private security operators. The Education and Workforce Committee has recommended that the Real Estate Authority’s new powers be exercised on a reasonable basis and clarified that provisions relating to unsatisfactory conduct apply only where behaviour is connected to a licensee’s professional role and affects public confidence in the profession. These are practical improvements that make already sensible bills even stronger.
      I also thank officials and the Parliamentary Counsel Office for their work in developing these bills. Whether someone is taking a claim to the Disputes Tribunal, buying a home through a conveyancer, or working as a real estate agent, these reforms will make our regulatory systems fairer, more efficient, and easier to navigate. They demonstrate this Government’s commitment to good regulatory stewardship, maintaining the laws we already have, reducing unnecessary compliance, and improving access to justice and ensuring regulations work for the people they are meant to serve.       Third ReadingHon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts) (20:05): Thank you, Madam Speaker. I move, That the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill be now read a third time.
      I’m pleased to take this final call on two practical bills that improve the way parts of our justice and regulatory systems operate. These bills are not about creating unnecessary new layers of regulation, they’re about maintaining the laws we already have, fixing known problems, removing disproportionate penalties, and making sure our regulatory systems work better for the people who use them.
      The Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill improves access to justice and supports the effective operation of tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies. It allows successful applicants in the disputes tribunal to recover their filing fee from the respondent where it is appropriate.
      DEPUTY SPEAKER: You can get another Minister to read it out for you.
      Hon NICOLE McKEE: Yes, if you wouldn’t mind.
      Hon LOUISE UPSTON: That is a sensible change. People who have had to enforce their legal rights should not be left bearing unnecessary costs when they have been successful.
      The bill also strengthens oversight of the private security industry by improving information gathering powers. This will help detect and deter people operating outside the rules. It also makes practical changes to appointments and employment arrangements for tribunal members so these bodies can operate more consistently and efficiently. 
      The Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill improves the occupational regulation system for both professionals and consumers. It allows conveyancers’ professional undertakings to be enforced in the High Court, as lawyers’ undertakings already are. That will support competition in the conveyancing market and give consumers more confidence in the services they use.
      It also removes an overly harsh penalty that disqualified real estate agents from practising for five years for failing to complete continuing professional development or pay fees on time. That kind of penalty is out of proportion to the breach. This bill replaces it with a more sensible and balanced approach. At the same time, the bill strengthens the real estate authority’s ability to investigate unlicensed trading and ensure licensees are meeting their obligations. 
      I thank officials in the Parliamentary Council Office, for their work on these bills. I commend these bills to the House.

      Legislative StatementHon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health) (21:01): I present a legislative statement on the Mental Health Bill.

      Second ReadingHon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health) (21:01): I move, That the Mental Health Bill be now read a second time.
      It’s a privilege to be standing here today for the second reading of the Mental Health Bill. I’d like firstly to start by thanking the Health Committee for all their hard work—ably led by the chair, Sam Uffindell—in examining this bill. Can I say, from the start, that I think it’s vitally important for tangata whaiora that this bill comes back with full cross-party support. I’d also like to thank the people who took the time to make a submission and engage with the select committee process—particularly those who shared their personal experience. It is a deeply personal thing to share your own experience, so thank you for your bravery. I do want to acknowledge all those with lived experience.
      The committee considered submissions from 358 individuals and groups. Those submitters brought a range of perspectives, including those who have experience of compulsory treatment, those with family with lived experience, clinicians, academics, and mental health organisations. I’d also like to thank the 89 people who spoke directly to the Health Committee to share their views. I’d also like to acknowledge those who bravely came forward to share their stories in the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Historical Abuse in State Care and in the Care of Faith-based Institutions. It is important that we carry their voices, not only tonight but through any work looking into how the State cares for people when they need it the most. 
      I want to reiterate that this bill will demonstrate meaningful and significant progress by contributing towards at least 10 of the abuse in care recommendations, relating primarily to care safety and monitoring. All of you have helped shape a Mental Health Bill that goes beyond compulsory treatment, as we know it today, and that, instead, firmly places a person at the centre of their care and empowers people to make decisions about their own care.
      While most in New Zealand who access specialist mental health and addiction services are not subject to the Mental Health Act, over the course of a year, around 11,000 people receive compulsory care. In an ideal world, we would not need compulsory mental health care; however, we need a system in place for New Zealanders experiencing mental distress at a level that does require intervention to support their recovery. This bill strikes a balance of a future focus on safe and effective mental health care for people who require that State intervention, while having the right safeguards in place to ensure people’s rights are upheld and protected. This bill will be a critical safety net for those experiencing severe mental distress who are unable to make decisions about their own mental health care. I do want to reiterate tonight that it is intended to be used as a last resort only.
      The submissions received on this bill represented a variety of views. This is an important piece of legislation, and I expected there to be views across the board on key areas in the bill to assist the Health Committee’s consideration. It has been heartening to see that, of the individuals and groups that commented on the general policy intent of the bill, the majority were supportive. People recognise that we need compulsory care in some form; however, there were divergent views on what people felt this should look like. 
      I’m also encouraged by the support from submitters for the introduction of compulsory care principles, the supported decision-making provisions, and establishment of new roles and processes to safeguard those under compulsory care. This includes independent support persons and advocates, nominated persons, and collaborative care teams. These are integral to the shifts I want to see under this new legislation.
      There were some key changes made through the select committee process. These include introducing a “dignity of risk” principle. This aligns with the legislation’s purpose of promoting decision-making capacity. I believe it’s critical that the legislation recognises a person’s right to take reasonable risks to achieve personal growth, self-esteem, and overall quality of life.
      Terminology is really important to how people see themselves and how people are treated. I’m pleased to see the Health Committee has made changes to the term “patient” to instead be “person under compulsory care”. This change responds to submitters who said the term “patient” is stigmatising and can reinforce power imbalances between someone seeking support and professionals. Submitters also said it reinforces a paternalistic approach to care, which we want to move away from.
      Offences and penalties are important enforcement tools in the legislation. The royal commission of inquiry raised the need for appropriate and significant penalties for failures to comply with standards of care. I’m very pleased to see that the select committee has made changes to modernise the offences and penalties in this legislation, with a more structured regime as well as more tools for the regulator to use to support greater compliance with the Act. 
      However, I also recognise that many people who submitted on the bill had concerns about specific areas—in particular, the use of restrictive practices such as seclusion and the use of electroconvulsive therapy, or ECT. People also want strong safeguards for care of those under 18. As I spoke about in the first reading on this bill, these practices have a history of inappropriate use, abuse, and overuse. 
      I want to be very clear that I remain committed to seeing the reduction and elimination of seclusion. However, it is critical that this is done in a way that minimises the risk of unintended consequences. In particular, I would not want to see an increase in other inappropriate practices such as chemical or physical restraint. The bill strengthens requirements on the use of seclusion to drive the change needed to reduce and eliminate seclusion. The bill prohibits seclusion for children and young people. This is an incremental but significant step towards elimination that I am proud of, but I’m aware that there’s going to be a big shift for mental health workers, and it is important that we manage this change safely for both children and young people as well as staff.
      I do want to acknowledge that the Health Committee has made a number of improvements to further strengthen provisions relating to seclusion to ensure there are stronger protections and greater monitoring of progress. The committee received a wide range of views about ECT, from being an effective, life-saving treatment in modern clinical practice through to wanting it banned. The committee has also recommended a range of improvements to make sure there are greater safeguards on the use of ECT, including for people under 18. 
      From the submissions received, the Health Committee has recommended changes that will improve clarity and ensure greater safeguards for those subject to the Act. The word I want to emphasise here is “balance”; the bill aims to strike a balance between placing limits on people’s rights when there is a need to intervene to provide care and ensuring that this intervention is only done when absolutely necessary and in a way that protects and upholds an individual’s rights. 
      In closing, I acknowledge that there are diverse views on this piece of legislation, which were heard through the select committee process. Developing this bill has involved careful balancing of all of those views.  I believe the bill represents a meaningful step forward, and I’m pleased to present it to you today. The bill will enable supported decision making, safer practice through stronger protections for people subject to legislation, and care that is provided in the least coercive way—that is therapeutic and responsive to a person’s needs. I hope to see continued cross-party support on this important bill. I commend this bill to the House.

They have a disproportionate effect on Māori in particular, and yet we have before us a bill that purports to strengthen the human rights of tāngata whaiora.
      There is international research-based consensus that compulsory community treatment is not effective in achieving its stated aims of reducing hospital readmission and improving mental health outcomes. Given that—and given that it is a significant breach of human rights—we’d expect a substantial amount of evidence of the benefit needed to justify these orders, but that evidence doesn’t seem to exist. In fact, in their submission, the FACTORS team, which included Professor Anthony O’Brien, concluded that, if the bill were to pass in its current form, it would be unlikely to have a significant impact on the current practice or on reducing the use of compulsory community care.
      My questions to the Minister are: does he know roughly how many people are currently on compulsory care orders? What evidence does he have that they actually work? Why is he so resistant, and why are his officials so resistant, to making community care orders voluntary? Is it do with a sense of moral panic or the assumptions from medical practitioners, who maybe haven’t seen the evidence, of wanting to do something that looks like they are being accountable and responsible for patients yet doesn’t seem to have the evidence to back up that they actually work?       ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono): The Mental Health Bill is set down for third reading immediately.
      Legislative StatementHon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health) (12:16): I present a legislative statement on the Mental Health Bill.

      Third ReadingHon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health) (12:16): I move, That the Mental Health Bill be now read a third time.
      It is a privilege to stand here as New Zealand’s first mental health Minister, today, at the final stage of this bill. This legislation represents a significant step forward, modernising a system that is more than 30 years old, and bringing it up to date with how we expect mental health care to be to be delivered in this country.
      The bill sits within the Government’s broader commitment to improve the effectiveness of mental health and addiction services. It responds to long-standing calls for reform, and contributes to the Government’s response to the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Historical Abuse in State Care and in the Care of Faith-based Institutions, ensuring our system is grounded in human rights, safety, and effective care. It also builds on the work already under way to strengthen our mental health system: improving access, growing the workforce, and strengthening crisis support by helping ensure people receive effective recovery-focused care when they need it.
      At its core, this bill shifts us towards a more right space and recovery-focused approach, placing people at the centre of their care and supporting them to make decisions about their own support and recovery wherever possible. It provides a modern legislative framework for when compulsory care is needed as a last resort, while protecting the rights of people under compulsory care and ensuring care is therapeutic, delivered in the least restrictive way, and responsive to individual needs. 
      I want to acknowledge two areas where the bill introduces particularly important changes. First, on seclusion, the bill takes a much stronger approach to reducing, and, over time, eliminating the use of seclusion. It prohibits its use for children and young people, and strengthens safeguards and oversight to drive its reduction across the system as we work collectively towards eliminating this practice.
      Second, on the use of electroconvulsive therapy, or ECT, I want to be clear that while ECT remains an important treatment option for some people, the bill lifts the threshold for its use and puts stronger safeguards in place to ensure it is only used in tightly controlled circumstances in line with best practice. 
      The bill has been the subject of extensive scrutiny by the Health Committee, which received hundreds of submissions and heard directly from people with lived experience: families, clinicians, advocates, and community organisations. As I’ve said before, I want to acknowledge those who shared their experiences. Your input has directly strengthened this legislation. 
      Through the committee stage, a number of targeted amendments have been made to ensure the legislation is clear, workable, and provides strong safeguards in practice. These include clarifications to ensure powers and rights are clear for those working under the legislation, such as clarifying when police detention powers begin and end, strengthening requirements for recording and oversight, and refining provisions to ensure they are workable in practice, including those relating to the care of birthing parents and their newborns.
      The changes also ensure that the Ministry of Health can require Health New Zealand to provide the information needed to support the ministry’s regulatory monitoring and assurance role. These changes matter and ensure that the intent of the legislation can be delivered effectively on the ground. Ultimately, this will mean people receive care that is more respectful, more responsive, and more focused on supporting their recovery. It ensures people can access care when they need it, while putting stronger protections around how that care is delivered.
      While the passing of this bill is a major milestone, I also want to acknowledge the significant amount of work that lies ahead for the sector to implement these changes. This is why the commencement date has been updated to ensure the sector has a full two-year lead-in period following enactment. This reflects feedback from the sector about the need to prepare for these changes and implement them safely.
      This is now a bill that is fit for purpose, well scrutinised, and ready to become law. The process has had integrity. People have been heard, concerns have been addressed, and the legislation has been improved as a result. The Mental Health Bill represents a modern, balanced, and more effective approach to compulsory mental health care in New Zealand. Today marks a significant milestone for our mental health system.
      To close, I want to acknowledge the many people that have contributed to the development of this legislation, particularly those with lived experience. I want to thank them and their families for helping to improve the system for others in the future. I commend this bill to the House.
      ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Greg O'Connor): The question is that the motion be agreed.INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri) (12:22): It is ironic today that we are talking about updating mental health laws when the front page of the Otago Daily Times has shone a light on the Ombudsman’s findings of some of the worst abuses of human rights he’s ever encountered at Wakari Hospital, which is detaining people who have mental health issues and intellectual disabilities.       Constitution Amendment Bill
      Legislative StatementHon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice) (14:16): I present a legislative statement on the Constitution Amendment Bill.
      ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono): That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
      Second ReadingHon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice) (14:17): I move, That the Constitution Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
      This bill makes a small but important change to the Constitution Act to ensure that the post-election process is run smoothly. After the election, there’s a small period of time where there are no members of Parliament, which continues until election results are finalised and the new MPs take up office. During this time, the Constitution Act provides an exception to the rule that Ministers must always be an MP, to ensure the caretaker executive Government can continue to act during the post-election period. This is critical to our constitutional arrangements and the smooth transition of power. Currently, this exception is limited to 28 days. 
      There are a few circumstances where the conclusion of an election will be delayed—for example, an extreme weather event or a judicial recount. In these cases, the 28-day rule can expire before the new MPs formally take office, meaning Ministers can no longer hold their ministerial office, which can result in a constitutionally untenable position of the Governor-General being left without advisers. This happened in 2023, and while party leaders worked to find a stop-gap solution, I consider a constitutional setting should have clear and fit for purpose rules. Therefore, this bill removes the 28-day rule and replaces it with one that does not give rise to the possibility that ministerial tenure will expire before the post-election period. 
      The new rule will allow Ministers to continue to hold office until the election writ is returned with the names of the successful electorate MPs and list MPs who have been declared. It means that if there’s a delay to the official vote count, incumbent Ministers remain in office until new MPs are appointed. I want to thank the Justice Committee for all their hard work on this, and I commend this bill to the House.
